subtopics.name: Logistic regression: Bernoulli likelihood, gradient, Hessian, IRLS
subtopics.learn: Model the log-odds as linear, log(p/(1-p)) = w'x, so p = sigma(w'x), and write the negative log-likelihood L(w) = -sum_i [y_i log p_i + (1 - y_i) log(1 - p_i)]. Using sigma'(z) = sigma(z)(1 - sigma(z)), derive the gradient in three lines to grad L = X'(sigma(Xw) - y) - identical in shape to the OLS gradient, which is the canonical-link property of the exponential family, not a coincidence - and the Hessian H = X'SX with S = diag(p_i(1 - p_i)). Read the two facts that follow: H is positive semi-definite so the objective is convex with no local minima, and the gradient is non-linear in w so there is no closed form, which is why every implementation iterates. Derive the Newton step w <- w + (X'SX)^-1 X'(y - p) and recognise it as iteratively reweighted least squares - a weighted OLS fit on the adjusted response z = Xw + S^-1(y - p) - then implement it and confirm it reaches the same optimum as gradient descent in far fewer iterations. Interpretation follows straight from the link: a unit increase in x_j multiplies the odds by exp(w_j).

resource.label: scikit-learn - Logistic regression (regularised objective, binary and multinomial case)

subtopics.name: scikit-learn's LogisticRegression: C, solvers, separation and convergence
subtopics.learn: Read the API as a set of edits to the objective. It is L2-penalised by default - there is no unpenalised default - and the strength parameter is C = 1/lambda, so smaller C means stronger regularisation and the reflex 'I lowered C to regularise less' is backwards and produces a near intercept-only model. Because the objective is C * sum_i loss_i + 0.5 w'w, the effective regularisation per row shifts with N, so a C tuned on 10k rows is wrong on 200k. Know the solver table: lbfgs (default, L2 or none, handles multinomial), liblinear (L1 or L2 but one-vs-rest only, so its multiclass coefficients are not a softmax), saga (L1, elastic-net, large N, needs scaled data), newton-cholesky (N >> p). Treat a ConvergenceWarning as a bug report and not noise - the usual cause is unscaled features, and raising max_iter until the warning disappears leaves you with coefficients that are wherever the optimiser stopped. Finally, detect quasi-separation: fit the same data unpenalised in statsmodels and watch for a PerfectSeparationError or coefficients of magnitude 1e9 with enormous standard errors, because scikit-learn's default penalty hides that pathology behind a finite, confident-looking number.

resource.label: scikit-learn - LogisticRegression API (penalty, C, solver, class_weight, max_iter)

subtopics.name: Interpreting coefficients without lying: conditional effects, scale, and VIF
subtopics.learn: State the meaning precisely every time: a coefficient is the modelled change in the response (or in log-odds) for a unit change in that feature with all other features in the model held fixed, which means it is conditional on the feature set, changes when a correlated column is added or removed, and is not causal without a design that earns that word (Topic 97). Never rank raw coefficients across differently-scaled features - compare coef_j * std(x_j), or fit on standardised inputs - and never read a coefficient as importance when the feature is collinear with another. Quantify collinearity with the variance inflation factor VIF_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2) from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence.variance_inflation_factor (values above 5 to 10 warrant a conversation), and demonstrate the instability empirically by refitting across bootstrap resamples and drawing a box plot per coefficient: a whisker that crosses zero is a coefficient nobody should build a rule on. When the customer asks 'is this significant', switch to statsmodels for standard errors from sigma^2 (X'X)^-1 (or the inverse Fisher information (X'SX)^-1 for logistic), because scikit-learn deliberately reports none.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Common pitfalls in the interpretation of coefficients of linear models

subtopics.name: Residual diagnostics: seeing an assumption fail
subtopics.learn: Make four plots a habit before any linear model is presented. Residuals versus fitted values: a funnel is heteroscedasticity, so either model the variance (a log or sqrt target transform, or a Gamma/Poisson GLM) or at minimum report heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors with statsmodels' cov_type='HC3', because plain OLS intervals are too narrow and turn noise into a 'significant driver'. Residuals versus each feature: systematic curvature is missing non-linearity and tells you exactly which column needs a spline. A QQ plot: relevant only to small-sample inference, not to prediction. Residual autocorrelation (Durbin-Watson, or an ACF plot when rows are time-ordered): non-zero autocorrelation means your i.i.d. assumption and therefore your shuffled KFold are both invalid, and the CV must become time-based (Topic 108). Add leverage h_ii and Cook's distance to find the handful of rows driving the fit, and know the formal tests by name - het_breuschpagan, het_white, linear_reset - so you can put a p-value next to the picture when a customer's analyst asks.

resource.label: statsmodels - Regression diagnostics and specification tests

subtopics.name: Basis expansion: polynomials, splines, interactions, and when to escalate
subtopics.learn: Keep the model linear in parameters while making it non-linear in the inputs. PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, interaction_only=True) is the cheap way to test whether interactions matter, but understand the combinatorics - 100 features give 4950 pairwise terms - so it must be paired with ridge and with a genuine hold-out. Prefer SplineTransformer (B-splines with n_knots, degree=3 and an explicit extrapolation policy) over high-degree polynomials, because splines are local: a degree-10 polynomial oscillates wildly at the edges of the data (the Runge phenomenon) and extrapolates to absurd values, which is how a house-price model predicts a negative price for the largest lot in the file. Handle categoricals correctly: for unpenalised OLS use OneHotEncoder(drop='first') to avoid the dummy trap of perfect collinearity with the intercept, but keep every level when a ridge penalty is present since the penalty resolves the degeneracy and dropping a level silently changes what the remaining coefficients mean. Know the escalation criterion to Topic 101: when the residual-versus-feature plots show thresholds and non-monotone interactions across many mixed-type columns, a gradient-boosted tree will win - and the linear model stays as the baseline it must beat by more than the CV standard error.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Polynomial regression: extending linear models with basis functions

subtopics.name: Double descent: the caveat to the U-curve you must not overstate
subtopics.learn: The classical bias-variance U-curve is a statement about a fixed estimator family at a fixed sample size, not a law of nature. Belkin et al. show a double-descent risk curve: test error rises to a peak at the interpolation threshold where the number of parameters is about equal to the number of samples, then falls again as the model is over-parameterised further, with minimum-norm interpolation acting as an implicit regulariser. Know the mechanism well enough to state it - past the threshold there are many interpolating solutions and the algorithm picks a low-norm one - and know its relevance here: ridge at small alpha near p = N is exactly where you will see the peak in your own experiments, and it is why 'the model has more parameters than rows, so it must overfit' is a sentence that will be corrected by any deep-learning practitioner in the room. The professional position is that the trade-off is a tool for reading a measured validation curve, never a prediction you make instead of measuring one.

resource.label: arXiv - Reconciling modern machine learning practice and the bias-variance trade-off (Belkin et al.)

subtopics.name: The Kaggle protocol: RMSLE, KFold, and reading the CV-to-leaderboard gap
subtopics.learn: House Prices is scored as RMSLE, which is RMSE on log1p(y), so it measures relative error and penalises under-prediction of expensive houses less harshly than raw RMSE would - fit on log1p(y) through TransformedTargetRegressor and score with root_mean_squared_log_error so the training objective and the metric agree. Use KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=0) inside a Pipeline, report the mean CV score with its standard error across folds, and treat any difference smaller than that standard error as noise no matter what the leaderboard says. Then use the gap diagnostically rather than competitively: the public leaderboard is a single split of roughly 1459 rows, so its own standard error is large, and a small CV-to-leaderboard difference is sampling noise while a large systematic one means leakage, a fold structure that does not match the split, or drift between the two files. That last habit is the entire transfer to customer work - you defend the CV mean plus its uncertainty, and you use any held-out disagreement as evidence about the data rather than as a scoreboard.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Regression metrics (mean squared logarithmic error)

outcomes: You can derive the normal equations both by calculus and by orthogonal projection, closed-book in under five minutes, and state exactly when (X'X)^-1 does not exist and what np.linalg.lstsq returns instead.

You can implement OLS (closed-form and gradient descent), ridge, lasso by cyclic coordinate descent with soft-thresholding, and logistic regression by gradient descent and by IRLS, in NumPy, and show every one agreeing with scikit-learn's coefficients to 1e-6 on a fixed dataset.

You can write the bias-variance decomposition from memory, say what each term is an expectation over, estimate bias and variance by bootstrap on a simulated problem where the truth is known, and commit the stacked bias-variance-total figure.

You can look at a train/validation learning curve and name the correct lever - capacity, penalty, or more rows - and defend the call from the coefficient path and the fold-to-fold error bands rather than from a leaderboard score.

You can explain ridge versus lasso in three registers - constrained-optimisation geometry, the SVD shrinkage factor d^2/(d^2 + lambda), and the Gaussian versus Laplace MAP prior - and say when elastic net is the right answer for correlated predictors.

You can build a leakage-free scikit-learn Pipeline with scaling, encoding and target transformation, tune alpha with nested cross-validation, and quote a score with a standard error you would defend under challenge.

You can derive the logistic gradient X'(sigma(Xw) - y) and Hessian X'SX, prove convexity from the Hessian, explain why there is no closed form, and detect and explain perfect separation instead of shipping the penalty's finite answer as a real coefficient.

You can hand a customer a coefficient table with correct scaling, VIF values, bootstrap coefficient intervals and residual diagnostics, and state in one sentence which coefficients are stable enough to build a business rule on.
failureModes: StandardScaler was fit on the full dataset before cross_val_score, so every validation fold's mean and variance leaked into training; the CV RMSE looked excellent, the customer's fresh extract scored 30 percent worse, and it was investigated as data drift for a week.

Ridge was fitted on unscaled features where lot area is in square feet and a flag is 0/1; the penalty barely touched the large-unit column and crushed the flag, so the coefficient ranking presented as 'the drivers of price' was really a ranking of measurement units.

A lasso selected twelve of nine hundred features and the deck called them 'the twelve drivers of churn'; the features were pairwise correlated above 0.9, a different random seed selected a different twelve, and the customer had already staffed a team against the first list.

Someone set C=0.01 in LogisticRegression believing C was a penalty weight rather than its inverse; the model collapsed to nearly the base rate, and because AUC was still 0.62 nobody noticed until an ops threshold was set on the probabilities.

One-hot encoding kept every level alongside an intercept in an unpenalised OLS; X'X was singular, lstsq quietly returned the minimum-norm solution out of infinitely many, and the coefficients that were compared across two quarterly refits were not even the same estimand.

A perfectly separating feature - a status flag set only after the outcome - drove logistic coefficients to infinity, but scikit-learn's default L2 returned a tidy finite number with a 0.999 AUC, so a leaked column was presented as a model rather than caught as a bug.

Residuals fanned out with fitted value and nobody plotted them; the plain OLS standard errors were far too narrow, three 'statistically significant' drivers were reported to the customer, and none survived when HC3 robust errors were finally used.

Alpha was tuned by GridSearchCV and the best cross-validated score from that same search was quoted as the model's performance; the selection bias was worth several points, and the honest nested-CV number arrived only after the contract had been signed against the optimistic one.
interviewQuestions: Derive the normal equations, then tell me what happens when X'X is singular, what numpy's lstsq returns in that case, and why you would never implement the estimator as inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y even when it is invertible.

Explain ridge versus lasso three ways: the constrained-optimisation picture, what the SVD says each one does to a principal direction, and the prior each corresponds to. Then tell me which you would choose for a customer with 4000 rows, 900 heavily correlated features and a mandate to name the drivers - and what you would say about the stability of that list.

Write down the bias-variance decomposition for squared loss and tell me exactly what the expectation is taken over. Which of the three terms can you estimate from a single customer dataset, which cannot, and how would you get a number for the one that can?

Derive the gradient and the Hessian of the logistic negative log-likelihood. Why is there no closed-form solution, why is the problem convex, and what does the Hessian tell you about what happens when one feature perfectly separates the classes?

Debug: cross-validated R-squared is 0.98 but the holdout file the customer sent back scores 0.42. Walk me through your checks in order, and say which candidate causes would show up in the learning curve, which in a feature-versus-target audit, and which only in the pipeline code.

I show you a learning curve where training error is 0.02, validation error is 0.31, and the gap has not closed by the largest training size. What do you do, and what would have to be different in that plot for 'get more data' to be the wrong recommendation?

A stakeholder points at a coefficient of 1.8 on 'number of support tickets' in a churn model and asks whether reducing tickets will reduce churn. Answer them, and tell me what you would need to change about the study to be allowed to say yes.
100.proofOfWork: A public repo `regularisation-clinic` that turns this material into a diagnostic you can run in front of a customer on their own CSV. One command takes a table, a target column and a task type and emits a single-page report: a learning curve with fold-to-fold bands, a validation curve over log alpha, ridge and lasso coefficient paths on shared axes, a bootstrap coefficient-stability panel (box plot per coefficient plus a lasso selection-frequency bar chart over 200 resamples, so the 'these are the drivers' claim is quantified rather than asserted), a VIF table, and a residual diagnostics grid (residual versus fitted, residual versus each top feature, QQ, Cook's distance) with Breusch-Pagan and RESET p-values printed underneath. The report ends with a machine-written lever recommendation - more capacity, more penalty, or more rows - derived from the measured gap and its standard error, plus the nested-CV score that is the only number allowed on the summary line. The repo also ships `leakage_drill.py`, which fits the identical model twice, once with the scaler and a univariate feature filter fit outside the folds and once inside a Pipeline, and prints the inflation in CV score so the cost of the mistake is a number in your own README; `alpha_translation.md`, a one-page table mapping penalty parameterisations across scikit-learn (Ridge alpha with no 1/N, Lasso alpha with 1/(2N), LogisticRegression C = 1/lambda), glmnet and statsmodels, with a worked example showing the same fitted coefficients reached from all three; and `separation_check.py`, which flags quasi-complete separation in a binary design before anyone quotes an odds ratio. CI runs the pytest suite that asserts the from-scratch OLS, ridge, lasso and logistic implementations match scikit-learn to 1e-6, plus property tests that ridge coefficients shrink monotonically in alpha and that lasso at alpha_max is exactly zero.

101.topic: Supervised learning II: decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting with XGBoost and LightGBM
101.why: Gradient-boosted trees are what actually wins on the data a customer hands you: churn, fraud, demand, pricing and propensity all live in a CSV of forty mixed-type columns with missing values, and a tuned LightGBM beats the neural network they read about in a blog post while fitting in ninety seconds on a laptop. The FDE difference is not calling .fit() - it is standing at their screen, looking at one train/validation curve, and saying 'that is overfit, cut num_leaves before you touch n_estimators' or 'that AUC of 0.99 is a leaked column and here is which one', instead of launching another overnight grid search. And when their data scientist asks why you chose a Poisson objective, what min_child_weight actually thresholds, or whether the SHAP plot about to go in a board deck means what they think it means, you need the derivation on the whiteboard, not the vocabulary.
prerequisites: Topic 100 (Supervised learning I): the bias-variance decomposition, L1/L2 regularisation, and the habit of never reading a number off the training set

Topic 98 (Information theory and loss functions): a loss is a negative log-likelihood, log loss versus squared error, and dL/dz = sigma(z) - y for the logistic case - you will differentiate it again here, twice

Topic 99 (Numerical computing): NumPy argsort, cumsum, boolean masking, broadcasting, and float32-versus-float64 accumulation, because the from-scratch booster is a vectorisation exercise as much as a maths one
Calculus at Topic 94 level: a second-order Taylor expansion around a point, and minimising a one-dimensional quadratic a*w^2 + b*w in closed form - that single step is the entire XGBoost leaf value
pandas at working speed: dtypes, categoricals, groupby, and the ability to say what the grain of a row is before you model it

A pinned environment with scikit-learn, xgboost, lightgbm, matplotlib and optuna installed, plus one real tabular dataset with a genuine train/valid/test split (not iris) to run every diagnostic against

subtopics.name: CART: greedy recursive partitioning and the split search
subtopics.learn: Write the algorithm out before reading any library: at a node holding rows S, for every feature j and every candidate threshold t, form S_L = {x_j <= t} and S_R, score the split by the impurity decrease Delta = I(S) - (|S_L|/|S|) I(S_L) - (|S_R|/|S|) I(S_R), take the argmax over (j, t), recurse until a stopping rule fires. Candidate thresholds are the midpoints between consecutive distinct sorted values, so a continuous feature with a million distinct values offers a million candidates unless you bin it - which is the whole motivation for histogram methods later. Know the cost model: sort each column once at O(n log n) and carry the order downward, and the per-node scan is O(n) per feature; re-sorting at every node is the difference between a two-second fit and an hour, and this is exactly the loop you will write for the deliverable. Internalise that the search is greedy and myopic - it never backtracks, and it cannot find an XOR-style interaction that only pays off two levels down, which is precisely why an ensemble of many shallow trees outperforms one deep tree.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - Chapter 06 Machine Learning, 01. Classical Machine Learning

subtopics.name: Impurity criteria and the piecewise-constant geometry of a tree
subtopics.learn: For regression the impurity is the node variance and the optimal leaf constant is the mean, which falls straight out of setting d/dc sum (y_i - c)^2 = 0; swap to absolute error and the optimal constant is the median, which is where the robustness comes from. For classification, Gini 1 - sum p_k^2 versus entropy -sum p_k log p_k rank splits almost identically - Gini is the second-order approximation of entropy about the uniform point - and Gini is the sklearn default because there is no log to evaluate. Understand the axis-aligned consequence physically: every boundary is a union of axis-parallel boxes, so a 45-degree separating line is approximated by a staircase and consumes many splits, while any monotone transform of a single feature (log, standardisation, rank) changes nothing at all, which is why you never scale features for trees and why a StandardScaler in a tree pipeline is a tell. Know the extrapolation failure cold: outside the training range of a feature the prediction is frozen at the boundary leaf's constant, so a booster trained on 2023 prices can never predict a 2025 price above the highest it ever saw - the single most common surprise on a time-trending target, and the reason you detrend or model deltas.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Decision Trees (user guide: criteria, mathematical formulation, tips)

subtopics.name: Capacity control on a single tree: pre-pruning knobs versus cost-complexity pruning
subtopics.learn: max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, max_leaf_nodes and min_impurity_decrease are all pre-pruning: they halt the recursion early and are therefore greedy about capacity in the same way the split search is greedy about structure, so they can stop just before a split that would have unlocked a strong one below it. Minimal cost-complexity pruning is the principled post-pruning alternative: define R_alpha(T) = R(T) + alpha * |leaves(T)|; for each alpha there is a unique smallest subtree minimising it, and cost_complexity_pruning_path(X, y) hands you the finite ladder of effective alphas with their impurities so you can choose alpha by cross-validation rather than by eye. Fit the whole ladder once, plot test score against alpha, and see the classic hump - that picture is the cleanest demonstration of the bias-variance trade-off you will ever draw for a customer. Then be able to say why boosting almost never uses ccp_alpha: the base learners are deliberately weak (depth 3 to 8), so capacity is governed by the number of trees and the learning rate, not by pruning any one of them.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Minimal cost-complexity pruning (R_alpha(T), effective alphas, pruning path)

subtopics.name: Bagging and the bootstrap: the variance formula and its ceiling
subtopics.learn: Derive the one equation that explains every ensemble: for B identically distributed predictors each with variance sigma^2 and pairwise correlation rho, Var(mean) = rho * sigma^2 + ((1 - rho)/B) * sigma^2. Read both terms out loud - the second vanishes as B grows, so more trees never hurt accuracy and only cost time and memory; the first does not, so rho is a hard floor that no number of trees can break through, and lowering rho is therefore the only remaining lever. Bagging leaves bias roughly unchanged, which is why its base learners should be deep, unpruned, low-bias/high-variance trees - the exact opposite of a boosting base learner, and a distinction people get backwards constantly. Know that a bootstrap sample of size n contains about 1 - (1 - 1/n)^n -> 1 - 1/e = 63.2 percent distinct rows, so roughly 36.8 percent are out-of-bag, which is where the free validation estimate comes from. BaggingRegressor/BaggingClassifier(estimator=..., n_estimators, max_samples, max_features, bootstrap) generalises the whole idea to any base estimator, which is worth knowing when the customer's model is not a tree.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Bagging meta-estimator

subtopics.name: Random forests: decorrelation via max_features, and what OOB is worth
subtopics.learn: The random forest's entire addition over bagging is one line inside the split search - sample max_features columns at each node, not once per tree - and its sole purpose is to lower rho in the variance formula so that one dominant feature cannot make every tree the same tree. Know the current defaults and why they differ by task: max_features=1.0 for RandomForestRegressor and 'sqrt' for RandomForestClassifier; treat max_features as the primary tuning knob and min_samples_leaf as the second, and treat n_estimators as a budget rather than a hyperparameter because the OOB curve flattens monotonically and never turns up. oob_score=True gives a held-out estimate from the ~36.8 percent of rows each tree never saw, but it is valid only for i.i.d. rows: on grouped data (many rows per customer) or time-ordered data it is optimistic by a wide margin and will flatter you into shipping. Extra Trees draw the threshold at random within a feature as well, trading a little more bias for less variance and a substantially faster fit - a good default when n is large and you need a baseline in one minute.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Random forests (max_features, OOB, extremely randomized trees)

subtopics.name: Feature importance: why MDI lies, and what permutation importance costs
subtopics.learn: feature_importances_ on any sklearn tree ensemble is mean decrease in impurity, accumulated on the training set, and it is structurally biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features because such features offer more candidate thresholds and can therefore reduce impurity by chance alone - the canonical demonstration adds a random unique-ID column to the Titanic data and watches it outrank sex. permutation_importance(model, X_val, y_val, n_repeats=10, random_state=0) instead measures the drop in a chosen scoring metric when one column is shuffled, on held-out data, so it answers 'does this model rely on it to generalise' rather than 'did the fitting procedure split on it'. Know permutation importance's own failure mode: correlated features split the credit and both look unimportant because the model recovers the signal from the twin - the fix is to cluster features by Spearman rank correlation and permute whole groups together. Never hand a customer an MDI bar chart captioned 'the drivers of churn'; it is a statement about the fitting procedure, not about their business, and it is the single most common way a model briefing goes wrong.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Permutation Importance vs Random Forest Feature Importance (MDI)

subtopics.name: Forward stagewise additive modelling: deriving the squared-error update by hand
subtopics.learn: Write F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + nu * h_m(x) and the greedy step h_m = argmin_h sum_i L(y_i, F_{m-1}(x_i) + h(x_i)), then make the key move: the steepest-descent direction in function space at row i is the negative gradient g_i = -[dL/dF] evaluated at F_{m-1}(x_i), so you fit a regression tree to the pseudo-residuals r_i = -g_i by squared error and then set each leaf value by a line search over the rows that land in it. Do the squared-error case completely: L = 0.5 (y - F)^2 gives dL/dF = F - y, so r_i = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i) is literally the residual and the line-search leaf value is the mean residual in the leaf, with F_0 = mean(y) as the constant minimiser. Do the same for absolute error and watch the leaf value become the median of the residuals while the fitted tree still uses squared error on the pseudo-residuals - the two are separate choices, and confusing them is a classic implementation bug. Write that whole chain on paper before you write a line of code, then verify your implementation reproduces sklearn's GradientBoostingRegressor to float noise on a small dataset at the same seed, same depth and subsample=1.0.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Gradient-boosted trees (mathematical formulation, loss functions, shrinkage)

subtopics.name: Second-order boosting: gradients, Hessians and the Newton leaf value for log loss
subtopics.learn: Expand the loss to second order around the current prediction: L(y, F + h) ~= L(y, F) + g*h + 0.5*k*h^2 with g_i = dL/dF and k_i = d2L/dF2. For a fixed tree structure, leaf j containing rows I_j emits a single constant w_j, so the objective is separable per leaf and quadratic in w_j and solves in closed form: w_j* = -(sum_{i in I_j} g_i) / (sum_{i in I_j} k_i + lambda). Now do log loss entirely by hand: with p = sigmoid(F), L = -[y log p + (1-y) log(1-p)] gives g = p - y and k = p(1-p), hence w_j = -sum(p - y) / (sum p(1-p) + lambda) - Friedman's leaf value - and F_0 = log(pbar / (1 - pbar)), the base logit, which is why an XGBoost binary model starts from base_score in log-odds space rather than at 0.5. Read off the two consequences you will use in front of a customer: rows the model is already confident about have k -> 0 and stop contributing curvature, so one loud outlier can dominate a leaf's weight; and min_child_weight is a threshold on sum(k) in a child - a minimum amount of remaining uncertainty, not a row count. Squared error has k = 1 identically, so min_child_weight degenerates to a row count there, which is why the same numeric value means completely different things on a regression job and a classification job.

resource.label: XGBoost docs - Introduction to Boosted Trees (second-order expansion, leaf weight, structure score)

subtopics.name: XGBoost's regularised objective: structure score, split gain, gamma and lambda
subtopics.learn: Substitute w_j* back into the quadratic and you get the structure score Obj = -0.5 * sum_j (G_j^2 / (H_j + lambda)) + gamma*T, where G_j and H_j are the summed gradients and Hessians in leaf j - the only principled 'how good is this tree shape' number in the field, and lower is better. The split gain follows in one line: Gain = 0.5 * [ G_L^2/(H_L + lambda) + G_R^2/(H_R + lambda) - (G_L + G_R)^2/(H_L + H_R + lambda) ] - gamma, and a split is accepted only when Gain > 0, so gamma is literally a minimum gain threshold measured in loss units and lambda is ridge shrinkage on leaf weights that also damps splits on small, high-variance leaves. Map maths to flags so you can tune without guessing: lambda = reg_lambda (default 1), alpha = reg_alpha (L1 on leaf weights, default 0), gamma = min_split_loss (default 0), plus max_depth, min_child_weight and max_delta_step as the rest of the capacity budget. Read Section 2 of the paper for this derivation and Sections 3-4 for the systems work - the sparsity-aware split, the weighted quantile sketch, the cache-aware block layout - because 'why is it so fast' is a question you will get and 'it is written in C++' is not an answer.

resource.label: arXiv - XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System (Chen and Guestrin)

subtopics.name: Shrinkage and stochastic subsampling: two independent regularisers
subtopics.learn: The learning rate nu multiplies every leaf value, so nu and n_estimators trade off close to hyperbolically - halving nu roughly doubles the trees needed to reach the same training loss - and a small nu with many trees generalises better because each step commits less to the current residual pattern. Fix the protocol you will use forever: pick a small nu (0.05, or 0.03 when you have the compute), set n_estimators absurdly high, and let early stopping choose the count; never put nu and n_estimators on the same grid, because you are then searching a one-dimensional curve in two dimensions and paying quadratically for it. Row subsampling (XGBoost subsample, LightGBM bagging_fraction with bagging_freq) injects bagging-style noise but applies it per boosting iteration rather than per model; column subsampling in XGBoost is three separate knobs - colsample_bytree, colsample_bylevel, colsample_bynode - and they multiply, so setting all three to 0.5 leaves each split searching 12.5 percent of the columns, which is a much harsher regulariser than anyone intends. Know that subsample < 1 makes the validation curve visibly noisy and the run non-deterministic without a fixed seed, and that column subsampling is the most effective single defence when you have many weakly informative correlated features.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Shrinkage via learning rate (and subsampling)

subtopics.name: Writing the NumPy booster: prefix sums, the split loop, and where it will diverge
subtopics.learn: Plan the implementation before writing it. Presort every column once with np.argsort and carry the ordering down the tree; at each node accumulate G and H with np.cumsum over the sorted rows so every candidate threshold's (G_L, H_L) is one array lookup and an entire feature is scored in a single vectorised expression rather than a Python loop - this is the difference between a toy and something you can actually benchmark. Handle the details that silently produce wrong gains: skip candidate positions where consecutive x values are equal (tied values must fall on the same side), enforce min_child_weight against sum(k) rather than a row count, respect max_depth in the recursion, apply row and column subsampling per tree, and multiply every leaf by the learning rate exactly once. Then expect the divergence from the libraries and be able to explain each source: hist-based XGBoost and LightGBM split on bin edges rather than exact midpoints, their default base_score/init differs, sklearn does a per-leaf line search rather than the Newton form, and float32 accumulation in the libraries against your float64 moves the fourth decimal. Benchmark honestly - RMSE and wall-clock fit time in the same table - and expect to be 50 to 500 times slower, which is the point of the exercise.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - Chapter 06 Machine Learning, 02. Gradient Machine Learning

subtopics.name: Histogram split-finding: tree_method, max_bin, and the approximation you agreed to
subtopics.learn: Exact greedy scans every distinct value at every node; hist buckets each feature into max_bin buckets (256 by default) exactly once, after which split-finding is a scan over 256 bins instead of n rows, turning the per-node cost from O(n) into O(bins) and making the inner loop cache-resident. Know the flags: tree_method in {auto, exact, approx, hist}, with hist the default from XGBoost 2.0 and the only method carrying GPU support via device='cuda'; LightGBM's equivalents are max_bin and min_data_in_bin. Be explicit about what you traded away: thresholds can now only land on bin edges, so a genuinely important cut at the 0.3rd percentile of a heavily skewed feature can be invisible at max_bin=256 - raise max_bin when a feature is skewed and memory allows, lower it deliberately as a regulariser on small noisy data. The histogram subtraction trick - compute the histogram for the smaller child and obtain the sibling by subtracting it from the parent's - is why one child of every split is effectively free, and it is the main structural reason modern GBDT libraries scale to tens of millions of rows on one machine.

resource.label: XGBoost docs - Tree Methods (exact, approx, hist)

subtopics.name: LightGBM: leaf-wise growth, num_leaves, GOSS and EFB
subtopics.learn: XGBoost grows level-wise by default (every node at depth d before any at depth d+1); LightGBM grows leaf-wise, always splitting whichever leaf anywhere in the tree has the highest gain, so at an equal leaf count it reaches a strictly lower training loss - and on small or noisy data it reaches that loss by growing one deep unbalanced branch that memorises a handful of rows. The tuning consequence is concrete: num_leaves is your capacity knob, not max_depth, the guardrail is num_leaves <= 2^max_depth (approaching that bound is just level-wise growth again), and min_data_in_leaf is what actually stops the pathological branch. GOSS is not plain subsampling: it keeps all large-gradient rows, randomly samples a fraction of the small-gradient ones, and multiplies the sampled ones by (1-a)/b to keep the gain estimate unbiased - importance sampling of the gradient. EFB bundles mutually exclusive sparse columns (one-hot blocks that are rarely non-zero together) into a single feature so a ten-thousand-column sparse matrix is scanned as if it had a few hundred. State the rule out loud: leaf-wise plus histogram wins on wide, large-n data; below roughly ten thousand rows, or on a very noisy target, level-wise XGBoost at max_depth 3-6 is the safer default.

resource.label: LightGBM docs - Features (leaf-wise growth, GOSS, EFB, histogram optimisation)

subtopics.name: Reading train/validation curves and naming the knob to turn first
subtopics.learn: This is the diagnostic skill the whole topic exists for. Pull the per-iteration losses out of evals_result_ / evals_result() and plot training and validation together against boosting round, then classify. Both still falling at the final iteration is underfit: raise n_estimators first because it is nearly free, then depth/num_leaves, then lower the regularisation. Training loss near zero while validation turned upward hundreds of rounds ago is overfit, and the order is capacity first: cut max_depth or num_leaves, then raise min_child_weight / min_data_in_leaf, then lower subsample and colsample, then raise reg_lambda, and only then reduce the learning rate - which mostly buys a finer-grained version of the same trade-off rather than a different one. A validation curve that is flat and high from round one is not a tuning problem at all: it is a feature or a target-definition problem, and more compute will not touch it. A validation curve sitting below the training curve means the validation split is easier, is leaking, or a train-only regulariser like DART dropout is active. Work through LightGBM's own 'deal with over-fitting' list so you can cite a source in front of the customer's data scientist instead of asserting a preference.

resource.label: LightGBM docs - Parameters Tuning (faster speed, better accuracy, deal with over-fitting)

subtopics.name: Early stopping mechanics and the eval-set contract
subtopics.learn: Use xgb.train(..., evals=[(dtrain,'train'), (dvalid,'valid')], callbacks=[xgb.callback.EarlyStopping(rounds=50, save_best=True, maximize=False)]) or the equivalent LightGBM lgb.early_stopping(stopping_rounds=50) callback, and know the sharp edge: stopping watches the LAST entry in the evals list, so an evals list that ends with the training set will never stop and you will silently train to the cap. After the fit, best_iteration and best_score are the only numbers to trust, and prediction must use iteration_range=(0, best_iteration + 1) unless the model was saved with save_best - forgetting this ships the overfit tail of the ensemble to production. The discipline that separates honest work from cheating: the early-stopping set is a third split, not your test set, because you have now used it to select n_estimators, so any metric reported on it is optimistically biased and the number you hand the customer must come from data that no fitting decision touched. With subsample < 1 the validation curve is noisy, so rounds=10 will stop on a fluctuation and 50 is a sane floor; and always check whether the run stopped early or simply exhausted n_estimators, because those are opposite diagnoses.

resource.label: XGBoost docs - Callback Functions (EarlyStopping, best_iteration)

subtopics.name: Missing values: the sparsity-aware default direction
subtopics.learn: Trees are one of the few model families that handle NaN natively and correctly, and knowing this stops you from destroying information at the front of the pipeline. XGBoost's sparsity-aware split learns a default direction per node by evaluating the gain twice - all missing rows sent left, then all sent right - and keeping the better one, so missingness itself becomes a usable signal; sklearn's HistGradientBoosting does the same, and LightGBM exposes use_missing and zero_as_missing. The implication for customer pipelines: median-imputing before a booster usually removes information rather than adding it, and a -999 sentinel works but is strictly worse than a learned direction because it also distorts the split candidates. The trap to audit for: when missingness is informative and its mechanism changes between training and production - a source system that starts populating a field in March - the learned direction becomes silently wrong for that feature, so track per-feature missingness rate by time period on both sides of the deployment boundary. Note that plain sklearn DecisionTree and RandomForest only gained NaN support in recent versions, so check the version in the customer's environment rather than assuming.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Histogram-based gradient boosting: missing values support

subtopics.name: Categorical features: native handling versus the target-encoding leak
subtopics.learn: One-hot encoding a 5000-level column is a disaster for trees: each dummy is near-constant, the gain of splitting on it is tiny, and the level's signal is smeared across 5000 weakly informative columns that column subsampling then throws away. Know the three real options and their controls: LightGBM's native categorical_feature (Fisher-style optimal partitioning on categories sorted by their accumulated gradient statistics, with min_data_per_group and cat_smooth to stop it carving out single-row categories), XGBoost's enable_categorical=True with max_cat_to_onehot, and target/mean encoding. If you encode, encode with cross-fitting: sklearn's TargetEncoder uses an internal cross-fitting scheme inside fit_transform precisely so a row's encoding is never computed from that row's own target, and it shrinks rare categories toward the global mean via a smoothing factor. Naive target encoding computed over the whole training set before the split is one of the highest-frequency leaks in real tabular work - the model reads the target back out of the feature, cross-validation looks superb, production does not - and it is worth being able to spot it in someone else's notebook in under a minute. Finally, decide explicitly what an unseen category maps to at inference time, because the default is often a crash.

resource.label: scikit-learn - TargetEncoder (cross-fitting, smoothing)

subtopics.name: Tuning honestly: search order, budget, and the bias of the winning score
subtopics.learn: Fix a search order instead of a grid: learning rate small and fixed, n_estimators by early stopping, then num_leaves/max_depth, then min_child_weight / min_data_in_leaf, then subsample and colsample, then reg_lambda and reg_alpha. Random or Bayesian search dominates full grid search in any space above three dimensions; Optuna's default TPESampler models p(params | good trials) and p(params | bad trials) and samples where their ratio is large, and suggest_float(..., log=True) is mandatory for the learning rate and the regularisation terms because they act multiplicatively. Pair it with a pruner so hopeless trials die at round 50 rather than round 5000, which is usually a 5-10x effective budget increase. Then apply the statistical discipline that most people skip: the CV score of the best of 300 trials is the maximum of 300 noisy numbers and is therefore biased upward by roughly the spread of the fold noise, so quote a nested-CV or untouched-holdout number instead; and choose the split scheme from the data's dependence structure - GroupKFold when many rows share a customer, TimeSeriesSplit when deployment runs forward in time - because a plain KFold on either inflates every figure you are about to present. Topic 103 goes deeper on the evaluation protocol itself.

resource.label: Optuna - TPESampler (Tree-structured Parzen Estimator)

subtopics.name: Choosing the objective: Poisson, Tweedie, quantile and custom losses
subtopics.learn: The objective is a modelling decision, not a default. reg:squarederror fits the conditional mean under Gaussian noise and will cheerfully predict negative counts; count:poisson uses the log link and needs max_delta_step to keep the exponential from exploding, and it is the right call for demand and event counts; reg:tweedie with tweedie_variance_power in (1, 2) covers the zero-inflated positive targets that dominate insurance, usage and revenue data; reg:absoluteerror fits the median; and reg:quantileerror with quantile_alpha (LightGBM: objective='quantile', alpha=) gives you a prediction interval by fitting the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles as separate models - which is usually what a customer actually means by 'how confident is it'. For anything else, supply a custom obj returning (grad, hess) per row, and respect the two rules that make it work: the Hessian must be strictly positive (clip it away from zero or the leaf weights blow up), and you must also supply a custom feval and set disable_default_eval_metric because the built-in metric no longer corresponds to your loss. Always validate a custom objective by reimplementing a built-in one first and matching its loss curve round for round.

resource.label: XGBoost docs - Custom Objective and Evaluation Metric (grad, hess, feval)

subtopics.name: Defending the model: monotonic constraints, TreeSHAP and calibration
subtopics.learn: Three things convert a booster from a black box into something a customer will sign off on. Monotonic constraints (monotone_constraints=(1, 0, -1), or LightGBM's monotone_constraints with monotone_constraints_method) enforce at split time that the model is non-decreasing in price or non-increasing in tenure; they cost a little accuracy and buy a model that cannot produce the embarrassing non-monotone counterexample their domain expert will hunt for in the first ten minutes, and interaction constraints do the same for which features may co-occur on a root-to-leaf path. TreeSHAP computes exact Shapley values for tree ensembles in O(T * L * D^2) rather than exponential time, and its additivity property means every prediction decomposes as base_value plus per-feature contributions that sum exactly to the model output - that exact-sum property is what makes a per-row explanation defensible in a dispute. State the caveat out loud rather than being caught by it: SHAP attributions are conditional on the model, not causal, and the interventional (background-dataset) and tree_path_dependent variants genuinely disagree when features are correlated, so name which one you ran. Finally, a booster stopped at an arbitrary iteration is usually not calibrated - check a reliability curve and fit a sigmoid or isotonic CalibratedClassifierCV on a held-out split before anyone multiplies your output by a dollar amount.

resource.label: Interpretable Machine Learning (Molnar) - SHAP, including TreeSHAP and its caveats

outcomes: You can derive the gradient-boosting update on a whiteboard, closed book, in under ten minutes for both squared error (g = F - y, so pseudo-residuals are literal residuals and the leaf value is their mean) and log loss (g = p - y, k = p(1-p), leaf value -sum(g)/(sum(k) + lambda), F_0 = the base logit).

You can write the XGBoost structure score and split-gain formula from memory, and use it to explain in one sentence what gamma does, what lambda does, and why min_child_weight means a row count under squared error but an uncertainty budget under log loss.

You can ship a NumPy-only gradient-boosted regression tree with vectorised cumsum split-finding, shrinkage, row and column subsampling and early stopping, match sklearn's GradientBoostingRegressor to within float noise at matched settings, and name every remaining source of divergence against XGBoost and LightGBM.

You can look at one train/validation curve and state within thirty seconds whether the model is overfit, underfit, or has a data problem, and name the single knob you would turn first and why - depth/num_leaves, learning rate, n_estimators, subsample or min_child_weight.

You can say when LightGBM's leaf-wise histogram growth beats XGBoost's level-wise growth (wide, large-n, many weak features) and when it overfits instead (small n, noisy target, num_leaves unconstrained by min_data_in_leaf), and defend the choice with the variance and capacity argument rather than a benchmark anecdote.

You can produce a benchmark table on one real tabular dataset with RMSE and wall-clock fit time for a from-scratch booster, sklearn RandomForest, XGBoost and LightGBM at comparable capacity, and explain every gap in it.

You can spot target-encoding leakage, a high-cardinality ID feature riding the MDI chart, and an i.i.d. CV split on grouped or time-ordered data in someone else's notebook, and state what each one does to the reported metric.

You can hand a customer a defensible model briefing: permutation importance on held-out data rather than MDI, a monotonic constraint on the feature their domain expert cares about, a TreeSHAP explanation for one specific row with the variant named, and a reliability curve showing the outputs are probabilities.
failureModes: Mean target encoding was computed over the entire training set before the CV split, so each row's feature encodes its own label; cross-validated AUC came in at 0.97, the model shipped, and production AUC was 0.61 with no code change to blame.

num_leaves was left at LightGBM's default 31 on an 8000-row dataset with min_data_in_leaf untouched; leaf-wise growth drove one branch deep enough to isolate individual rows, training loss went to nearly zero, and the model memorised the training set while every default-looking parameter appeared reasonable in the config.

The evals list passed to xgb.train ended with the training set rather than the validation set, so EarlyStopping watched training loss, never triggered, and the run trained to the 5000-round cap - the log looked clean and nobody noticed until inference latency tripled.

feature_importances_ from a random forest was presented to the customer's leadership as 'the drivers of churn'; the top feature was a near-unique account identifier whose MDI score came from cardinality bias, and a quarter of retention budget was reallocated on the strength of an artefact of the fitting procedure.

A booster was validated with a plain KFold on data holding dozens of rows per customer and months of history; the same customer appeared in train and validation folds, every metric was inflated, and the model that won selection was the one best at recognising customers rather than predicting behaviour.

Predictions were generated with the full ensemble instead of iteration_range=(0, best_iteration + 1) after an early-stopped fit, so the overfit tail of trees was included at inference; scores drifted from the validated numbers by a few points and the discrepancy was investigated for a week as a feature-pipeline mismatch.

A demand model was trained with reg:squarederror on right-skewed daily counts and predicted negative demand for low-volume SKUs, which the downstream ordering system clipped to zero; the clipping hid the misspecification, and the real problem - the wrong noise model, needing count:poisson or a Tweedie objective - went undiagnosed for a full planning cycle.

A booster trained on two years of prices was asked to forecast a period above the historical maximum; because a tree's prediction is the boundary leaf's constant, every forecast flatlined at the highest observed value, and the flat line was read as a stable market rather than an extrapolation failure.
interviewQuestions: Derive the gradient-boosting leaf value for log loss from a second-order expansion. Start from L = -[y log p + (1-y) log(1-p)], get g and the Hessian, write w_j* = -G/(H + lambda), and then tell me what min_child_weight is thresholding and why that value means something completely different on a regression problem.

Write the split-gain formula XGBoost uses and explain from it, not from documentation, what gamma and lambda each do to the resulting tree. What happens to gain when a candidate child contains only rows the model already predicts confidently?

Debug: training RMSE is 0.02 and validation RMSE is 1.4 and rising after round 300, on 6000 rows with 400 features. Give me the order in which you turn knobs and the reason for each, and tell me which of those changes you expect to help least.

When would you pick LightGBM over XGBoost and when would that choice actively hurt you? Explain leaf-wise versus level-wise growth in terms of capacity and variance, and give me the parameter that is your guardrail in each library.

Design: a customer has three years of daily demand per SKU, 40 features, heavy zero-inflation, and wants a number their ordering system can act on plus an interval. What objective, what validation split, what do you do about categorical SKU identifiers, and what do you hand them to show the model is trustworthy?

A colleague shows you a random forest with 0.99 cross-validated AUC and a feature-importance chart. What are the first four things you check, and for each one say what the symptom would look like and what it would do to the reported number?

Explain why bagging needs deep unpruned trees while boosting needs shallow ones. Use the Var(mean) = rho*sigma^2 + ((1-rho)/B)*sigma^2 decomposition in your answer, and say what random forests change to attack which term.
101.proofOfWork: A public repo `boosting-forensics` that turns the from-scratch booster into a diagnostic kit you could hand to a customer's data team. On top of the NumPy GBRT it adds `curve_triage.py`, which takes any fitted XGBoost or LightGBM booster plus its evals_result, plots train and validation loss against boosting round, and emits a one-line verdict with a ranked knob list - 'overfit from round 310: cut num_leaves 63 to 31, then raise min_data_in_leaf, then lower colsample_bytree' - so the diagnosis is reproducible rather than a feeling. It ships `leak_hunt.py`, which runs the four checks that catch most tabular disasters: per-feature permutation importance on held-out data compared against MDI to expose cardinality bias, a target-shuffle null so any feature whose importance clears the permuted-target distribution by an implausible margin is flagged, a group- and time-overlap detector that reports whether the CV split leaks entities or future rows, and a train-versus-serve missingness-rate and category-set diff. `objective_zoo.ipynb` fits the same zero-inflated count target five ways - squared error, Poisson, Tweedie at two variance powers, and a pair of quantile models - and tabulates RMSE, the count of negative predictions, and interval coverage, which is the table that settles the 'why not just use RMSE' argument in one screen. `newton_check.py` is the correctness harness: it asserts that the hand-derived leaf value -G/(H + lambda) matches XGBoost's dumped leaf weights on a single-tree, lambda-fixed fit to five decimal places, and that the structure score computed from the model dump reproduces the reported training loss - the test that proves the derivation and the library agree. The README carries the benchmark table (RMSE and fit time for the NumPy booster, RandomForest, XGBoost and LightGBM at matched capacity) with a written explanation of every gap, plus a one-page `MODEL-BRIEFING.md` template containing the held-out metric, the reliability curve, the monotonic constraints applied and why, and a TreeSHAP explanation of one specific row with the SHAP variant named. CI runs the newton_check assertions and the leak-hunt unit tests against a synthetic dataset with a deliberately planted leak on every push.

102.topic: SVM, k-NN and Naive Bayes: margins, kernels, and when each still wins
102.why: These three are the models a customer already has in production - a spam filter that is multinomial Naive Bayes, a duplicate-ticket matcher that is cosine k-NN, a fraud screen that is an RBF SVM someone tuned in 2019 - and you will be asked to explain, fix or replace them in the room, not to build a transformer. Each fails in a way you can only diagnose from the mathematics: an SVM with 92 percent of rows as support vectors is an overfit you read off the KKT conditions, a k-NN that died at 300 features is the curse of dimensionality you can derive in two lines, and a Naive Bayes returning 0.9999 posteriors is the independence assumption double-counting correlated words. Being able to write the soft-margin objective, its dual, the Cover-Hart bound and the Laplace-smoothed MLE on a whiteboard is what turns 'we should try a neural net' into a defensible recommendation with a latency number attached.
prerequisites: Vectors, inner products, norms, hyperplanes and positive semi-definite matrices, plus the eigenvalue test for PSD (Topic 93, Linear algebra for ML)
Convexity, Lagrange multipliers and constrained optimisation, and what a KKT condition is (Topic 94, Calculus and optimisation)
Bayes theorem, conditional independence, and the multinomial and Gaussian likelihoods (Topic 95, Probability)
Maximum likelihood estimation and why you optimise a log-likelihood rather than a likelihood (Topic 98, Information theory and loss functions)
NumPy vectorisation, broadcasting, float64 underflow and log-space arithmetic (Topic 99, Numerical computing) - the from-scratch implementations live or die on this
Regularisation, the bias-variance trade-off and train/validation/test discipline from Topic 100 (Supervised learning I), plus scikit-learn's fit/predict/Pipeline API

subtopics.name: Three inductive biases, and the shape of data that picks one
subtopics.learn: Say each model's assumption in one sentence before touching any code. SVM: a large-margin linear boundary in a possibly implicit feature space, found by convex optimisation, stored as a handful of support vectors. k-NN: no model at all - the training set is the model, the assumption is local constancy of the label, and every cost is deferred to predict time. Naive Bayes: a generative model p(x|y)p(y) with a factorised likelihood, fitted by one counting pass, O(nd) to train and O(nnz) to score. Build a five-column decision table keyed on n, dimensionality d, sparsity, class balance and p99 latency budget, and fill a cell only when you can name the mathematical reason. Run the classifier-comparison example and be able to identify which boundary belongs to which bias with the labels covered.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Classifier comparison (decision boundaries of the same data under different biases)

subtopics.name: Maximum-margin geometry: functional vs geometric margin and the hard-margin primal
subtopics.learn: For the hyperplane w.x + b = 0, derive that the signed distance of a point is y_i(w.x_i + b)/||w||. Notice the functional margin y_i(w.x_i + b) is scale-dependent - double w and b and it doubles while the geometry is unchanged - so you must fix the scale; the standard normalisation min_i y_i(w.x_i + b) = 1 makes the geometric margin exactly 2/||w||, which converts 'maximise the margin' into min (1/2)||w||^2 subject to y_i(w.x_i + b) >= 1 for all i. Be able to write the objective, the constraint and the margin width from memory in two minutes, and to say why this is a convex QP with linear constraints and therefore has a unique global optimum, unlike anything you will train with SGD. Know where hard margin dies: one mislabelled point inside the other class empties the feasible set, and the solver reports infeasibility rather than a bad fit.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - Chapter 06 Machine Learning, 01. Classical Machine Learning (SVM margins, kernels, Naive Bayes, k-NN)

subtopics.name: Soft margin: slack variables, the hinge loss, and what C actually is
subtopics.learn: Write min (1/2)||w||^2 + C sum_i xi_i subject to y_i(w.x_i + b) >= 1 - xi_i and xi_i >= 0, then eliminate the slacks with xi_i = max(0, 1 - y_i f(x_i)) to get the unconstrained equivalent min (1/2)||w||^2 + C sum_i max(0, 1 - y_i f(x_i)). Read that as hinge loss plus an L2 penalty, so C is inverse regularisation strength: C to infinity recovers the hard margin (narrow margin, few violations, memorisation), C to zero gives a very wide margin that ignores the data. Know the hinge is convex but not differentiable at the margin - its subgradient is -y_i x_i when y_i f(x_i) < 1 and 0 otherwise - and that it is a convex upper bound on the 0-1 loss, which is the justification for minimising it at all. Critically for deployment: scikit-learn's C multiplies a summed, not averaged, loss, so the optimal C shrinks roughly as 1/n and a C tuned on a 5k prototype is the wrong C on 500k rows.

resource.label: scikit-learn - SVM margins with a penalty parameter (effect of C on margin width)

subtopics.name: Lagrangian duality, KKT, and why the solution is sparse in examples
subtopics.learn: Form the Lagrangian with multipliers alpha_i on the margin constraints and mu_i on the slacks, set the stationarity conditions to zero and get the three facts everything else follows from: w = sum_i alpha_i y_i x_i, sum_i alpha_i y_i = 0, and C = alpha_i + mu_i. Substitute back to obtain the dual, max over alpha of sum_i alpha_i - (1/2) sum_i sum_j alpha_i alpha_j y_i y_j (x_i.x_j) subject to 0 <= alpha_i <= C and sum_i alpha_i y_i = 0 - note that the box constraint is exactly where C enters. Read complementary slackness as a taxonomy of every training row: alpha_i = 0 means the point is outside the margin and irrelevant; 0 < alpha_i < C means it sits exactly on the margin and is the only kind of point from which you can recover b; alpha_i = C means it is inside the margin or misclassified. This is why f(x) = sum over support vectors of alpha_i y_i (x_i.x) + b and why predict cost is O(n_SV d). Use n_SV/n as a rough leave-one-out error bound and therefore as a free overfitting diagnostic you can quote to a customer.

resource.label: Chang and Lin - LIBSVM: A Library for Support Vector Machines (dual formulation, KKT conditions, SMO)

subtopics.name: The kernel trick, Mercer's condition, and the cost of the Gram matrix
subtopics.learn: Observe that the dual and the decision function touch the data only through inner products, so replace (x_i.x_j) with K(x_i, x_j) = phi(x_i).phi(x_j) and never construct phi. State Mercer's condition operationally: K is a valid kernel iff the Gram matrix K_ij is symmetric positive semi-definite for every finite sample, which you check on an invented kernel with numpy.linalg.eigvalsh(K).min() >= -1e-8. Memorise the four you will meet - linear x.x'; polynomial (gamma x.x' + r)^d, whose feature map is the finite set of monomials up to degree d; RBF exp(-gamma||x - x'||^2), whose feature map is infinite-dimensional (expand the exponential in a series); and sigmoid tanh(gamma x.x' + r), which is not PSD for most parameter choices. Know the closure properties (sums, positive scalings and products of kernels are kernels) and the hard operational limit: the Gram matrix is dense n by n, so 40k rows in float64 is 12.8 GB - that, not accuracy, is why kernel SVMs stop somewhere around 10^4 to 10^5 rows.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Pairwise metrics, Affinities and Kernels (linear, polynomial, RBF, sigmoid, chi-squared)

subtopics.name: The C-gamma surface, and why unscaled features silently break the kernel
subtopics.learn: Read gamma as an inverse squared length scale. Large gamma means each support vector influences only its immediate neighbourhood, so the boundary becomes islands around training points and the limit is a 1-NN classifier in which every row is a support vector; small gamma makes the kernel nearly constant across the data and the model degenerates into an expensive linear one. Study the validation-accuracy heatmap over the (C, gamma) grid and notice the good region is a diagonal ridge, which is why you search both jointly on a log grid (C in 2^-5 to 2^15, gamma in 2^-15 to 2^3) rather than one at a time. The default gamma='scale' is 1/(d * X.var()), so the RBF exponent is dominated by whichever column has the largest units: a salary column in dollars annihilates every binary flag, and no amount of gamma tuning repairs it. StandardScaler goes inside a Pipeline, fitted on the training fold only.

resource.label: scikit-learn - RBF SVM parameters (the C and gamma validation heatmap)

subtopics.name: Solver complexity: SVC vs LinearSVC vs SGDClassifier
subtopics.learn: SVC and SVR wrap libsvm's SMO, which repeatedly selects a working set of two alphas that maximally violate KKT and solves that two-variable subproblem analytically; empirical cost sits between O(n^2 d) and O(n^3 d) and kernel columns are cached, so raise cache_size from its 200 MB default to 1000 before you conclude the model is too slow. LinearSVC wraps liblinear and runs coordinate descent on the linear problem at roughly O(n * nnz), but it defaults to squared_hinge, penalises the intercept and uses one-vs-rest, so it does not reproduce SVC(kernel='linear') exactly and you should say so rather than debug the difference. SGDClassifier(loss='hinge', alpha=...) takes one subgradient step per sample with alpha equal to 1/(C n), supports partial_fit, and is the only one of the three that survives 10^7 rows. The rule you defend in a room: if n is above roughly 50k, or if d greatly exceeds n, use a linear solver; otherwise try RBF first.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Stochastic Gradient Descent (hinge loss, alpha vs C, complexity, partial_fit)

subtopics.name: Kernel approximation: Nystroem and random Fourier features
subtopics.learn: When the boundary is genuinely non-linear but n is too large for an n by n Gram matrix, approximate the feature map explicitly instead of abandoning the kernel. RBFSampler implements Rahimi-Recht random Fourier features: draw w from N(0, 2 gamma I) and b uniform on [0, 2pi), map x to sqrt(2/D) cos(w.x + b), and the expected inner product of the maps equals the RBF kernel with error decaying like 1/sqrt(D). Nystroem instead samples m landmark rows and builds a rank-m approximation of K, which is usually the better choice when the data has structure. Then feed the D-dimensional dense features to LinearSVC or SGDClassifier and you get near-RBF accuracy at linear cost: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Nystroem(gamma=..., n_components=...), LinearSVC()). Be able to plot accuracy against D and point at the knee.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Kernel Approximation (Nystroem, RBFSampler, AdditiveChi2Sampler)

subtopics.name: Multiclass reductions and what decision_function actually returns
subtopics.learn: An SVM is intrinsically binary. SVC trains K(K-1)/2 one-vs-one classifiers and votes, so ten classes means 45 models but each on a small subset, which is often cheaper overall than one-vs-rest on large classes; LinearSVC and SGDClassifier default to one-vs-rest with K coefficient vectors. Know the shape trap cold: SVC.decision_function returns an (n, K(K-1)/2) array under decision_function_shape='ovo' and an (n, K) array under 'ovr' (the default), so code written against one silently mis-indexes under the other and the bug looks like a labelling error in the data. OvO ties break on summed confidences. By contrast MultinomialNB, GaussianNB and KNeighborsClassifier are natively multiclass - no reduction, no shape surprise - which is a small but real reason they survive in legacy pipelines.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Multiclass and multioutput algorithms (OvO, OvR, natively multiclass estimators)

subtopics.name: k-NN: the estimator, the metric, the weighting, the Voronoi boundary
subtopics.learn: Write the estimator explicitly as a local empirical average: yhat(x) = argmax_c sum over i in N_k(x) of w_i * 1[y_i = c], where N_k(x) is the set of k training points nearest under a metric d. Understand k as the bias-variance dial running backwards: k = 1 gives zero training error and a Voronoi-tessellation boundary of maximum variance, k = n gives the majority class and pure bias, and boundary complexity falls monotonically in between. Choose the metric deliberately - euclidean is meaningless across mixed units without scaling, manhattan degrades more gracefully in high d, cosine is the right choice for TF-IDF text, hamming for categoricals - and know that weights='distance' (weight 1/d) beats 'uniform' when density varies across the space. Two properties to state out loud: k-NN cannot extrapolate beyond the convex hull of the training data, and it reproduces the training class prior exactly, so a shifted prior at serving time is not something the model can absorb.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Nearest Neighbors (metrics, weights, KDTree/BallTree, classification)

subtopics.name: Cover-Hart: 1-NN error is at most twice the Bayes rate
subtopics.learn: State the theorem precisely: as n goes to infinity the asymptotic 1-NN risk R satisfies R* <= R <= R*(2 - M R*/(M-1)) <= 2 R*, where R* is the Bayes error and M the number of classes. Carry the one-line intuition: with enough data the nearest neighbour sits at essentially the same x, so its label is a fresh draw from p(y|x) and you err when either you or it is wrong, giving roughly 2 R*(1 - R*). Name the assumption that has to hold - a metric and densities such that the nearest neighbour actually converges to x, meaning enough data locally - because that is precisely what fails in high dimensions. Use the result twice in customer conversations: to explain why the 'dumb' k-NN baseline is competitive (half the achievable information is already in the nearest row) and to be honest that 'asymptotically' at d = 300 means effectively never.

resource.label: Cover and Hart (1967) - Nearest Neighbor Pattern Classification (the 2 R* bound)

subtopics.name: The curse of dimensionality: deriving why k-NN collapses
subtopics.learn: Do the hypercube calculation on paper: to enclose a fraction k/n of uniformly distributed points in the unit cube of dimension d you need a sub-cube of side l = (k/n)^(1/d); for n = 1000, k = 10, d = 100 that is l = 0.955, so the 'neighbourhood' spans 95 percent of the range of every feature and nothing local survives. Pair it with distance concentration: for i.i.d. coordinates the ratio (d_max - d_min)/d_min tends to 0 as d grows, so all points become nearly equidistant and the argmin over neighbours is decided by noise. Reproduce both numerically - sample 1000 uniform points at d = 2, 10, 100, 1000, plot the histogram of pairwise euclidean distances and watch it collapse into a spike, then hold a two-dimensional signal fixed and pad with noise features while plotting 10-NN accuracy down to chance. Draw the conclusion that decides architecture: what matters is intrinsic dimension, not d, which is why an SVM or NB is untroubled by 30k TF-IDF columns while k-NN needs PCA, NCA or a learned metric first.

resource.label: Cornell CS4780 Lecture 2 - k-nearest neighbors and the Curse of Dimensionality (the l = (k/n)^(1/d) derivation)

subtopics.name: Indexing and the latency budget: brute force, KD-tree, ball tree, ANN
subtopics.learn: Brute force is O(nd) per query but is one BLAS GEMM, so it usually wins below roughly 10^4 rows; a KD-tree gives about O(d log n) per query but degrades to brute force above roughly d = 15 to 20 because of the same curse; a ball tree tolerates higher d and any valid metric. algorithm='auto' chooses for you - verify with a timed benchmark rather than trusting the heuristic. Then face the operational point an FDE is actually asked about: k-NN has zero training time but O(nd) memory that must stay resident and per-query work that grows with the dataset, so it is the model that misses a 20 ms p99 SLA and the model whose 'retraining' is an append. When n is large and approximation is acceptable, IVF, PQ and HNSW indexes trade a stated recall@k for orders of magnitude in latency - always say the recall number out loud, because it is the accuracy you agreed to give away.

resource.label: Johnson, Douze and Jegou - Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs (FAISS: IVF, PQ, recall/latency trade-off)

subtopics.name: The Bayes decision rule, generative vs discriminative, and what 'naive' costs
subtopics.learn: Start from p(y|x) proportional to p(x|y)p(y) and the MAP rule argmax over y of p(y) * product over j of p(x_j|y); the evidence p(x) is constant across classes so you never compute it, which is the mechanical reason NB's outputs are not probabilities. The naive assumption is conditional independence of features given the class: with d binary features it cuts the parameters per class from 2^d - 1 to d, and that collapse is the entire reason NB can be fitted on 200 documents. Be exact about the price: correlated features are counted repeatedly, so the log-posterior is driven towards 0 or 1 while the argmax - the only thing a classifier uses - is frequently still correct. That asymmetry, bad probabilities with good decisions, is the single most useful sentence to have ready about NB, and it connects directly to conditional independence in Topic 95 and log-likelihood in Topic 98.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Naive Bayes (the MAP rule, the factorised likelihood, a from-scratch implementation)

subtopics.name: Multinomial NB: deriving the MLE, Lidstone smoothing and log-space scoring
subtopics.learn: Derive the estimator rather than memorising it: maximising the multinomial log-likelihood subject to sum over j of theta_cj = 1 gives theta_cj = N_cj / sum over j' of N_cj', the share of all token occurrences in class c belonging to word j, with prior N_c / N. Then add smoothing: theta_cj = (N_cj + alpha) / (sum over j' of N_cj' + alpha V), and be able to show this is the posterior mean under a symmetric Dirichlet(alpha) prior, so alpha is not a hack. Know why alpha > 0 is mandatory: a single unseen (word, class) pair zeroes the whole product and no other evidence can recover it. Score entirely in logs - log p(c) + sum_j x_j log theta_cj - and notice this is linear in the count vector, so the whole model is the matrix product X @ log_theta.T + log_prior. That is exactly why a from-scratch NumPy MultinomialNB matches scikit-learn to floating-point precision and scores 20 Newsgroups in milliseconds; reach for scipy.special.logsumexp only when you need normalised posteriors.

resource.label: Manning, Raghavan and Schutze, IIR - Naive Bayes text classification (the multinomial MLE and add-one smoothing)

subtopics.name: Matching the NB variant to the data: Multinomial, Bernoulli, Gaussian, Complement
subtopics.learn: MultinomialNB models counts or TF-IDF weights as a multinomial draw per document. BernoulliNB models binary presence/absence and, unlike Multinomial, explicitly penalises the ABSENCE of every vocabulary word, which is why it beats Multinomial on very short texts and loses on long ones. GaussianNB estimates a per-class mean and variance per feature and adds var_smoothing to the variances so a constant column does not produce a division by zero - and it is only sensible after you have checked the per-class marginals are roughly unimodal. CategoricalNB handles unordered categoricals directly. ComplementNB (Rennie et al.) estimates each class's parameters from the complement of that class and is the documented fix when text classes are imbalanced. Be able to state the single assumption each makes about p(x_j|y) and to construct a small dataset on which each one is the wrong choice.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Naive Bayes (Gaussian, Multinomial, Complement, Bernoulli, Categorical)

subtopics.name: Why Naive Bayes still wins on sparse bag-of-words, and NBSVM
subtopics.learn: Give three reasons, not one. First, in text where d greatly exceeds n the class-conditional word distributions carry most of the signal and the independence violations largely cancel inside an argmax. Second, NB is a single count-and-divide pass, so it fits an entire corpus in the time an RBF SVM spends assembling one block of Gram-matrix rows. Third, the estimator has almost no variance, so it dominates in the small-n regime - the Ng and Jordan observation that a generative model converges to its own (higher) asymptotic error far faster than the discriminative one converges to its lower one, so the curves cross. Know the empirical boundary reported by Wang and Manning: NB tends to win on short snippets, SVM on full-length documents, and their NBSVM - a linear SVM on log-count-ratio features r = log((p + alpha)/(q + alpha)) with interpolated weights - beats both. Implement r in about ten lines and add it as a fourth row in your benchmark table.

resource.label: Wang and Manning (ACL 2012) - Baselines and Bigrams: Simple, Good Sentiment and Topic Classification (NBSVM)

subtopics.name: Calibration: SVM margins are not probabilities and NB posteriors are worse
subtopics.learn: decision_function returns a signed distance to the hyperplane measured in units of 1/||w||; there is no probability in it. SVC(probability=True) runs Platt scaling, a one-dimensional logistic fit sigmoid(A f(x) + B) trained by internal 5-fold cross-validation, which makes fitting several times slower and can make the argmax of predict_proba DISAGREE with predict - know this and never expose both to the same consumer. Read reliability diagrams by shape: an SVM is typically sigmoid-shaped and under-confident in the middle, while NB is pushed hard to 0 and 1 by the double-counted correlated features. Fix with CalibratedClassifierCV(estimator, method='sigmoid' or 'isotonic', cv=5) - sigmoid when calibration data is scarce, isotonic when you have thousands of points and can afford its higher variance - and report Brier score alongside a calibration curve, not accuracy alone, whenever the customer intends to threshold the score.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Comparison of calibration of classifiers (reliability diagrams for SVC and Naive Bayes)

subtopics.name: The honest benchmark: pipelines, leakage, timing and the metric that flatters
subtopics.learn: Every preprocessing step belongs inside a Pipeline so StandardScaler and TfidfVectorizer are fitted on training folds only - a scaler or an IDF vector fitted on the full dataset before splitting is the leak that makes k-NN and SVM look excellent and production look broken, and it is the single most common defect in a customer's existing notebook. Fix random_state, use StratifiedKFold, and tune C, gamma, k and alpha inside a nested cross-validation or on a held-out validation split, otherwise the number you report is selection-inflated. Time the two costs separately because they decide deployment: fit wall time, and predict latency per 1000 rows plus resident memory. Report accuracy alongside balanced accuracy or macro-F1 with the majority-class baseline printed next to them, and record the split, seed and library versions in the README so the numbers reproduce on the customer's box.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Common pitfalls and recommended practices (data leakage, preprocessing inside pipelines, controlling randomness)
