outcomes: You can derive the soft-margin SVM closed-book in under ten minutes in all three forms - constrained primal with slacks, the equivalent unconstrained hinge-plus-L2 objective, and the dual with its 0 <= alpha_i <= C box and sum_i alpha_i y_i = 0 equality - and classify any training point into its KKT case from its alpha.

You can implement a soft-margin kernel SVM, k-NN and multinomial Naive Bayes in NumPy from the equations alone, match scikit-learn's accuracy to within 1 percent on the same split, and show the NB joint log-likelihoods agreeing to 1e-10.

You can predict, before running anything, which way the decision boundary and the support-vector count move when C or gamma is changed, and read a (C, gamma) validation heatmap to point at the overfitting corner, the underfitting corner and the usable ridge.

You can demonstrate the curse of dimensionality numerically - pairwise-distance histograms collapsing to a spike and k-NN accuracy decaying to chance as noise dimensions are appended - and derive l = (k/n)^(1/d) on a whiteboard on request.

You can derive the multinomial NB maximum-likelihood estimator, show that Laplace smoothing is the posterior mean under a Dirichlet prior, and explain in one sentence why alpha = 0 lets a single unseen word veto an otherwise unambiguous document.

You can choose between SVM, k-NN and Naive Bayes from nothing but n, d, sparsity, class balance and a p99 latency budget, name the specific property of the data that decides it, and state the measurement that would change your mind.

You can produce reliability diagrams and Brier scores for an SVM and a Naive Bayes on the same data, explain the shape of each curve from the model's mathematics, and say which output you would let a customer threshold at 0.9.

You can produce a benchmark table of accuracy, macro-F1, fit seconds, predict milliseconds per 1000 rows and resident megabytes on one dense low-dimensional and one sparse high-dimensional dataset, and prove no fold ever saw its own scaler or IDF vector.
failureModes: Features were never scaled before an RBF SVM, so the exponent -gamma||x - x'||^2 is dominated by the one column measured in dollars; every binary flag is invisible to the kernel and two weeks are burned sweeping a gamma grid that cannot repair it.

StandardScaler or TfidfVectorizer was fitted on the full dataset before train_test_split; k-NN and SVM validation scores come in three to five points high, none of it reproduces on the customer's holdout, and the gap is misdiagnosed as distribution drift rather than leakage.

C was tuned on a 5,000-row prototype and carried over to the customer's 500,000-row table; because scikit-learn's C weights a summed rather than averaged hinge loss, the effective regularisation is roughly 100 times weaker and the model memorises while the code diff shows no change at all.

n_SV came back at 92 percent of the training set and nobody looked; gamma was large enough that each support vector covered only itself, so the deployed artefact was an expensive 1-NN with perfect training accuracy, a 40 MB model file and chance-level generalisation.

k-NN was benchmarked on a 5,000-row sample where it beat everything, then deployed against 8 million rows; the index no longer fits the pod's memory limit, p99 latency is 900 ms against a 50 ms SLA, and no hyperparameter fixes it because the cost is structural.

A hand-rolled MultinomialNB shipped without smoothing, or with alpha = 0; one word appearing only in the test set gives a log-probability of negative infinity for one class, and every document containing it is assigned to the other class regardless of the other four hundred words.

A 99-to-1 imbalanced dataset was reported at 98.7 percent accuracy with k = 25; every neighbourhood was majority-class so the model never predicted the positive class even once, and the metric flattered a classifier with exactly zero recall on the only class the customer cares about.

predict_proba from SVC(probability=True) was used for ranking while predict supplied the label; Platt scaling was fitted by internal CV on a small set, the two disagreed on about 1 percent of rows, and the customer's audit surfaced records labelled approved with an approval score of 0.42.
interviewQuestions: Derive the soft-margin SVM dual from the primal. Where exactly do the box constraints 0 <= alpha_i <= C come from, and what does complementary slackness tell you about a point with alpha_i = C versus one with 0 < alpha_i < C?

Explain what C and gamma each do, geometrically and statistically. I hand you a model with 90 percent of rows as support vectors, 100 percent training accuracy and 55 percent test accuracy - which knob do you move, in which direction, and what do you expect n_SV to do?
Why does k-NN break down in high dimensions? Give me both the volume argument and the distance-concentration argument, then explain why a linear SVM on 30,000 TF-IDF features is perfectly fine.

Multinomial Naive Bayes assumes words are conditionally independent given the class, which is plainly false for text. Why does it still classify well, and where precisely does the false assumption show up in the model's output?

Design: a customer has 12 million support tickets, 60,000 TF-IDF features, 8 classes at a 200-to-1 imbalance, needs a label in under 30 ms at p99, and retrains monthly on one 32 GB box. Pick a model, defend it against the other two, and tell me what you would measure to discover you were wrong.
Debug: an RBF SVM cross-validates at 0.97 and scores 0.71 on the customer's holdout from the following month. Give me your ordered hypotheses and the specific check for each, cheapest first.

Someone shows you a ComplementNB text classifier at 94 percent accuracy on a 20-to-1 imbalanced dataset and wants to route tickets on its predict_proba. What do you ask for before you believe the number, and what would you have plotted?
102.proofOfWork: A public companion repo `classifier-triage` that turns the benchmark into a tool you can run on a customer's data during a workshop. A single command profiles an arbitrary feature matrix and prints the numbers that decide the model - n, d, density, class balance, the number of PCA components needed for 95 percent of variance as an intrinsic-dimension proxy, and the pairwise-distance concentration ratio (d_max - d_min)/d_min measured on a sample - then fits all three models plus an NBSVM log-count-ratio baseline inside Pipelines under a fixed wall-clock budget and emits a one-page HTML report containing the (C, gamma) validation heatmap, the support-vector fraction with the n_SV/n leave-one-out bound annotated, reliability diagrams and Brier scores for each model, a k-NN accuracy curve as noise dimensions are appended, and a fit-time / predict-latency / resident-memory table. Alongside it ships `leakage_drill.ipynb`, which reproduces two failures end to end with measured deltas: the pre-split scaler that inflates SVM and k-NN validation accuracy, and the alpha = 0 multinomial NB where one unseen token drives a class log-likelihood to negative infinity and flips the prediction. The repo closes with a one-page decision card written for a customer's engineers - which of the three, keyed on n, d, sparsity, imbalance and latency budget, with the mathematical reason and the disqualifying condition stated for each cell.

103.topic: Model evaluation: cross-validation, data leakage, metric choice, calibration
103.why: Every model you hand a customer arrives attached to a number, and this topic is the difference between a number that survives contact with their production data and one that collapses in week two while you are on the plane home. An FDE is the person in the room who has to say, out loud and without a laptop, why the 0.94 AUC from the pilot became a review queue full of false positives - which means naming the split that did not match how the data was generated, the column that was populated after the outcome, the metric that ignored the prevalence, and the probability that was never calibrated. Get this wrong and you do not merely lose the model: you lose the customer's belief that anything you measure is real.
prerequisites: Logistic and linear regression at Topic 100 level: what a fitted model predicts, what regularisation strength does, and the bias-variance decomposition as a statement about an estimator rather than a slogan
Trees and gradient boosting from Topic 101, including early stopping on a validation set - which is itself a model-selection step that has to live inside the fold
Log loss, Brier score and proper scoring rules from Topic 98 (information theory and loss functions), plus the fact that AUC is invariant to monotone transforms while log loss is not
Statistical inference from Topic 96: estimator, bias, standard error, confidence interval, paired vs unpaired comparison, and what a p-value does and does not say
NumPy at Topic 99 level: fancy indexing, argsort, boolean masks, cumsum, np.testing.assert_allclose, and float32 vs float64 accumulation for a metric summed over a million rows
scikit-learn API fluency: fit/predict/predict_proba/decision_function, clone, Pipeline and ColumnTransformer, and pandas joins well enough to reconstruct how a feature table was built

subtopics.name: What an evaluation number is: empirical risk, the generalisation gap, and the assumption underneath
subtopics.learn: Write the population risk R(f) = E_{(x,y) ~ D}[L(y, f(x))] and the empirical risk R_hat(f) = (1/n) sum_i L(y_i, f(x_i)), and be precise that every score you will ever quote is R_hat on some sample used as a stand-in for R on a distribution you never see. Know that R_hat on the training rows is biased downward by an amount that grows with model capacity (the optimism), so the entire machinery of held-out evaluation exists to buy an unbiased-ish estimate at the cost of data. State the assumption that licenses the whole thing - the held-out rows are drawn from the same distribution as the deployment rows, and independently of the training rows - and get in the habit of asking, before any split, which of the two clauses the customer's data actually violates: identical distribution (fails under drift, seasonality, a new customer segment) or independence (fails for repeated patients, sessions, near-duplicate documents, overlapping time windows).

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - Chapter 06 Machine Learning, 02. Gradient Machine Learning (evaluation, ROC/AUC, cross-validation)

subtopics.name: Hold-out, K-fold, LOO and repeated K-fold: the bias-variance trade of the estimator itself
subtopics.learn: Implement KFold(n_splits=K, shuffle=True, random_state=0) as a partition of indices where every row is tested exactly once and trained on K-1 times, and reason about the estimator, not the model: larger K means each surrogate model trains on n(1 - 1/K) rows so the pessimistic bias shrinks, but the K training sets overlap more so the fold scores are more correlated and the average is not more precise in the way naive intuition suggests. Know the extremes cold - leave-one-out is nearly unbiased for the training-set size but expensive and notoriously high-variance for unstable learners (a single flipped prediction moves a fold score from 1 to 0), while a single 80/20 hold-out on 2,000 rows gives you a metric with a standard error you can compute and will not like. Distinguish KFold from ShuffleSplit (independent random subsets, so a row can appear in several test sets and the 'test size' is decoupled from the number of splits) and know when RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_repeats=5) is the cheap way to stop chasing seed noise. Default position to defend on site: 5-fold repeated 3-10 times for n in the thousands, a single large hold-out only when n is large enough that its standard error is smaller than the effect you care about.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance

subtopics.name: Stratification: preserving the base rate, and the cases where it is not enough
subtopics.learn: StratifiedKFold partitions within each class so every fold carries approximately the population class proportion; do the arithmetic that motivates it - at a 0.2 percent base rate on 5,000 rows there are 10 positives, and plain KFold with K=5 will hand some fold 0 or 1 positive, at which point recall, PR-AUC and any threshold tuned on that fold are noise. Know the mechanics that bite: stratification is on the label only, so it does not balance a feature or a time period; for regression you stratify on a binned target (pd.qcut then pass as y to the splitter); and when you need both grouping and class balance the object is StratifiedGroupKFold, which approximates both and will warn when it cannot. Always print the per-fold positive count and the per-fold prevalence before you trust a single fold score, and treat a fold with fewer than roughly 25 positives as a number you may not quote to a customer.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.model_selection.StratifiedKFold

subtopics.name: Grouped data: the unit of independence, GroupKFold and the repeated-entity leak
subtopics.learn: Before splitting, answer one question in a sentence: what is the unit that is independent - a patient, a customer, a device, a document, a support session, a photo shoot? If a row is not that unit, a random split puts two rows from the same entity on both sides and the model is scored partly on memorised entity identity, which is the single most common way a healthcare or B2B pilot posts an implausible number. Use GroupKFold (deterministic, balances group sizes, guarantees a group appears in exactly one test fold), LeaveOneGroupOut when groups are few and meaningful (one site, one tenant, one country), and GroupShuffleSplit for a grouped hold-out; pass groups= through cross_validate and GridSearchCV, and know it is silently ignored by any splitter that does not accept it. Extend the same logic to near-duplicates that are not tagged with a group at all - re-uploaded documents, retweets, augmented images - and deduplicate on a content hash or a similarity threshold before the split, because a duplicate straddling the split is a group leak wearing a different hat.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.model_selection.GroupKFold

subtopics.name: Time-ordered evaluation: rolling origin, the horizon, and never shuffling
subtopics.learn: For anything with a time index the only honest evaluation is a rolling-origin (walk-forward) backtest: train on data up to time t, predict the horizon h you will actually be asked to predict, roll t forward, and average the errors over origins - which is what forecasters call time series cross-validation and what everybody else discovers after shipping. Match the backtest to the deployment contract precisely: if the model is retrained weekly and scores 14 days ahead, then the evaluation is 'train through Sunday, score the following two weeks', and a random K-fold that trains on December to predict November is not an approximation of that, it is a different question with a better answer. Decide expanding window versus sliding window on evidence (expanding uses all history and is right under a stable process; sliding of length L is right when the process drifts, and the choice of L is itself a hyperparameter you tune out-of-sample), and always report the metric per origin, not just the mean - a mean that hides one catastrophic quarter is how a forecasting pilot gets cancelled in month three.

resource.label: Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed) - Time series cross-validation

subtopics.name: Purging, embargo and the gap parameter when labels overlap in time
subtopics.learn: TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=g, max_train_size=m, test_size=t) yields strictly increasing index ranges, and the gap exists for a reason most people never use: when a label at time i is computed from a window that extends forward (did the account churn within 30 days, did the price move within 5 bars, did the ticket get resolved within a week), then training rows near the boundary have labels that were determined by events inside the test period. Purge those rows - drop every training row whose label window overlaps any test row's window - and then embargo an additional stretch after the test block, because serially correlated features mean rows just after the test period still carry information about it. Be able to state the cost honestly: purging throws away data and makes the estimate more pessimistic, which is exactly the direction of error you want when the alternative is a backtest that shows a Sharpe ratio or an early-churn recall that does not exist. Implement the purge as an interval-overlap test on (label_start, label_end) rather than a fixed row count, because a fixed count is wrong the moment sampling is irregular.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit (n_splits, gap, max_train_size, test_size)

subtopics.name: Pipelines and ColumnTransformer: the mechanism that makes a fold honest
subtopics.learn: The rule is mechanical: anything with a fit method that learns from the data - StandardScaler's mean and std, SimpleImputer's median, SelectKBest's scores, PCA's components, TargetEncoder's per-level means, a vectoriser's vocabulary, a resampler - must be refitted inside every training fold and only applied to the validation fold, and the only reliable way to guarantee that is to put it in a Pipeline and hand the Pipeline to cross_validate, which clones it per split. Build the real thing with ColumnTransformer(remainder='drop') so numeric, categorical and text branches each get their own preprocessing, and know that handle_unknown='ignore' or an explicit unknown category is what stops a level seen only in the validation fold from raising. Understand the size of each violation so you can triage a customer's notebook: scaling on the full dataset before splitting usually inflates the score by a hair, while feature selection or target encoding on the full dataset before splitting can manufacture a completely fictitious model out of pure noise. For resampling, use imblearn's Pipeline rather than scikit-learn's - SMOTE outside the fold means synthetic points interpolated from validation rows are in the training set, and the fold score becomes meaningless.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Pipelines and composite estimators

subtopics.name: A taxonomy of leakage and exactly where each type enters the pipeline
subtopics.learn: Learn leakage as a classification you can run down in a meeting rather than a vague warning: (1) target leakage, a feature that is a proxy for or downstream of the outcome - closed_date, n_collection_calls, account_status, a field the CRM only fills in after the deal is lost; (2) train-test contamination, preprocessing or resampling fitted across the split, or literal duplicate rows on both sides; (3) temporal leakage, any feature whose value at scoring time differs from the value in your training snapshot because the table was overwritten in place; (4) group leakage, the same entity on both sides; (5) availability leakage, a feature that exists in the warehouse but arrives 48 hours after the moment of prediction, so the model is unbuildable in production even though the offline number is real; (6) evaluation leakage, the test set consumed by dozens of iterations until it is a training set with extra steps. The interrogation that catches most of it is one question per column - 'at 09:00 on the day we score, is this value populated, and is it populated with the value it has now?' - backed by a cheap automated screen: fit a single-feature model per column and flag anything with an out-of-fold AUC above roughly 0.9, then explain it or delete it. Kapoor and Narayanan's survey is the artefact to cite when a customer's data scientist thinks this is a pedantic concern: leakage of these types invalidated published results across 17 scientific fields.

resource.label: arXiv - Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science (Kapoor and Narayanan, taxonomy of eight leakage types)

subtopics.name: Model-selection bias: why the winning configuration's CV score is not an estimate
subtopics.learn: If you evaluate 200 hyperparameter configurations on the same folds and report the best one, you have reported a maximum of 200 noisy estimates, and the expected maximum of noisy estimates exceeds the true best value - the selection itself is an optimisation against the validation noise. Cawley and Talbot quantify this and show it is not a small correction on small datasets: the reported score of the selected model can be optimistically biased by more than the difference between the algorithms being compared, which means benchmark tables built this way rank methods by how much they overfit the model-selection criterion. Recognise the same mechanism in disguises you will actually meet: early stopping on the test set, choosing a threshold on the test set, picking the feature set by looking at test performance, and the human loop where an engineer runs 40 experiments and keeps the one with the best hold-out number. The practical rules are three splits with the third genuinely untouched, a written log of every configuration evaluated, and the one-standard-error rule (choose the simplest model within one SE of the best) so you stop selecting on noise.

resource.label: JMLR - On Over-fitting in Model Selection and Subsequent Selection Bias in Performance Evaluation (Cawley and Talbot, 2010)

subtopics.name: Nested cross-validation, and what cross_val_predict does and does not give you
subtopics.learn: Nested CV separates the two questions: the inner loop selects (GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV over the training folds), the outer loop estimates (cross_val_score over the search object), and the number you report is the mean of the outer folds - which is an estimate of the whole procedure including its selection step, not of any one fitted model. Know the cost, K_outer * K_inner * |grid| fits, and the two honest cheap alternatives when that is unaffordable: a single held-out test set touched once, or nested CV over a random subsample with the caveat stated in the write-up. Be able to explain the final-model step without confusion - after estimating performance by nesting, you refit on all the data with the inner-selected hyperparameters, and the outer estimate is the number you quote for that pipeline. Separately, know cross_val_predict's contract: it returns out-of-fold predictions, which are the right input for building a reliability diagram or stacking, but computing a single metric over the concatenated vector is not the same as averaging fold metrics and is invalid for anything not decomposable over rows - and its own documentation says so.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Nested versus non-nested cross-validation

subtopics.name: The confusion matrix family: which metric answers which business question
subtopics.learn: Derive everything from the 2x2 table and be able to write each definition from memory: precision = TP/(TP+FP) answers 'when we flag, how often are we right', recall = TPR = TP/(TP+FN) answers 'of the real cases, how many did we catch', specificity = TN/(TN+FP), FPR = 1 - specificity, F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall (which is why it collapses toward the smaller of the two), F-beta with beta > 1 buys recall at the price of precision, balanced accuracy is the mean of recall and specificity, and MCC is the Pearson correlation of the 2x2 table and the least gameable single number under heavy imbalance. Internalise that all of these are functions of a threshold, so quoting F1 without a threshold is quoting a number about an arbitrary decision, and that accuracy at a 0.2 percent base rate is 99.8 percent for a model that predicts 'no' forever. For multiclass, know precisely what the averaging arguments do - micro equals accuracy in the single-label case, macro gives a five-row class the same weight as a five-million-row class, weighted hides the rare classes again - and always print classification_report plus the confusion matrix rather than one aggregate, because the customer's pain is usually one specific off-diagonal cell.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Metrics and scoring: quantifying the quality of predictions

subtopics.name: ROC-AUC: the rank statistic, its two invariances, and where it flatters
subtopics.learn: Know the identity that makes AUC concrete: it equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored above a randomly chosen negative, which is the Mann-Whitney U statistic divided by n_pos * n_neg, so you can compute it by ranking rather than by integrating a curve (and ties must take average ranks, which is the detail that makes a hand-rolled implementation disagree with scikit-learn in the third decimal). From that follow the two invariances you must be able to state in a meeting: AUC is invariant to any strictly monotone transform of the scores, so a perfectly ranked but wildly overconfident model has a beautiful AUC and unusable probabilities; and both axes are within-class rates, so AUC barely moves when prevalence changes from 50 percent to 0.2 percent even though the precision at every threshold collapses. Use max_fpr for a partial AUC when the customer only ever operates below a 1 percent false-positive rate, and for multiclass know that multi_class='ovr' with average='macro' is a different number from 'ovo' and that you must pass full predict_proba columns in the class order of estimator.classes_. Rule to carry: AUC is a screening and ranking statistic, never evidence that a probability or a threshold is fit to use.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score (average, max_fpr, multi_class)

subtopics.name: Precision-recall curves and average precision under heavy imbalance
subtopics.learn: Average precision is the step-wise sum AP = sum_n (R_n - R_{n-1}) P_n over thresholds, deliberately not a trapezoidal integral, because linear interpolation between PR points is optimistic - which is why auc(recall, precision) and average_precision_score disagree and why the documentation tells you to use the latter. Know the baseline: a random scorer has AP equal to the positive prevalence, so AP = 0.35 is superb at a 0.2 percent base rate and terrible at 40 percent, and AP is therefore not comparable across datasets or across time as prevalence drifts - report the skill ratio AP/prevalence alongside it when you need comparability. Use PR when positives are rare and the cost lives on the positive class, because the PR curve reacts to the FP count directly while ROC dilutes it by the huge TN pool; know the Davis-Goadrich result that dominance in ROC space implies dominance in PR space, so the two never disagree about a uniformly better model - only about how much better. Plot both curves with the operating point marked, and pair them with precision@k when the real constraint is an analyst team that can review 50 alerts a day.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score (step-wise AP, not trapezoidal)

subtopics.name: Choosing the threshold from the cost matrix, not from 0.5
subtopics.learn: Derive the optimal threshold rather than tuning it blindly: acting positive on a calibrated p has expected cost (1-p)*C_fp and acting negative has p*C_fn, so you should flag when p > C_fp/(C_fp + C_fn) - meaning 0.5 is correct only when a false positive and a false negative cost the same, which is essentially never in a customer's business. Build the cost matrix in the room with the customer in their units (an hour of analyst time, a chargeback, a missed renewal), turn it into a scorer, and pick the threshold that minimises expected cost out-of-fold with TunedThresholdClassifierCV(estimator, scoring=make_scorer(cost, greater_is_better=False), cv=5) - and know that scikit-learn's predict() hardcodes 0.5, which is why so many deployed thresholds are an accident. Handle the constrained variant too: when capacity is fixed at k alerts per day the threshold is the k-th highest score, and the metric is precision@k, whose value depends on prevalence and therefore has to be re-checked monthly. Tune the threshold on out-of-fold predictions only - a threshold chosen on the same data that scored the model is a one-parameter model fitted to the test set.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV

subtopics.name: Proper scoring rules: log loss, Brier, and the Murphy decomposition
subtopics.learn: A scoring rule is proper when its expected value is optimised by reporting your true belief; log loss and the Brier score BS = (1/n) sum (p_i - y_i)^2 are proper, while accuracy, F1 and AUC are not - which is precisely how a model can climb on F1 while becoming worse at every decision that multiplies a probability by a cost. Learn the Murphy decomposition BS = reliability - resolution + uncertainty, where uncertainty = pi(1 - pi) is fixed by the base rate, reliability is the calibration term you want near zero, and resolution is the spread of conditional outcome rates you want large; the immediate consequence is that at pi = 0.002 the Brier score is dominated by an irreducible 0.001996 and quoting the raw value tells nobody anything - report the Brier skill score 1 - BS/BS_ref against the constant-prevalence forecaster instead. Know log loss's asymmetry: it is unbounded as p goes to 0 on a positive, so a single confident mistake can dominate a batch, and sklearn clips at eps to keep the number finite, which means an infinite mistake silently becomes a large one. Use log loss or Brier for model selection whenever the downstream decision uses the probability, and AUC only when the downstream decision uses the rank.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.metrics.brier_score_loss

subtopics.name: Reading a reliability diagram
subtopics.learn: Build it with calibration_curve(y_true, y_prob, n_bins=10, strategy='quantile'): bin the predicted probabilities, plot mean predicted probability on x against observed frequency on y, and compare to the diagonal - points below the diagonal mean the model claims more than it delivers (overconfident), above means underconfident. Use strategy='quantile' rather than the default uniform whenever predictions cluster near zero, because equal-width bins at a 1 percent base rate leave eight of ten bins empty and the plot becomes three points and a straight line; always draw the histogram of predictions underneath so the reader can see how much mass each point represents, and put binomial error bars on each bin so nobody reads a bin of 12 rows as a finding. Learn the characteristic shapes and their causes: gradient-boosted trees and deep nets push probabilities toward 0 and 1 (sigmoid-shaped curve, overconfident), while bagged trees and SVMs pull them toward the centre (inverse-sigmoid, underconfident), and any model trained with class weights or on resampled data is shifted wholesale by the changed prior. The decision the plot supports is binary and concrete: can the customer threshold or multiply these numbers as they are, or must you calibrate first.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.calibration.calibration_curve (n_bins, strategy)

subtopics.name: ECE is an estimator, and a gameable one
subtopics.learn: Expected calibration error is ECE = sum_b (n_b/n) |acc_b - conf_b|, a weighted average of per-bin gaps, and everything about the number depends on choices you make: fewer bins average opposing errors against each other and drive ECE toward zero for a model that is badly miscalibrated in both directions, more bins raise the variance and the plug-in estimator's upward bias, and equal-width versus equal-mass binning gives materially different numbers on the same predictions. Know Kumar et al.'s result that the standard binned estimator systematically underestimates true calibration error - so a reported ECE is a lower bound and 'our ECE is 0.01' is not a claim you can verify by looking at it - and that scaling-binning with a debiased estimator gives a value you can actually put a confidence interval on. Because ECE is not a proper scoring rule, always report it beside log loss and Brier and beside the diagram itself; and be precise about which ECE you computed, since confidence-ECE (over the max-probability class only) can be near zero while classwise-ECE over all K classes is large. In your harness, expose n_bins and strategy as explicit arguments and print the ECE across a sweep of bin counts, because a number that changes by 3x between 10 and 50 bins is telling you something the single number hides.

resource.label: arXiv - Verified Uncertainty Calibration (Kumar, Liang, Ma; bias of binned ECE, scaling-binning)

subtopics.name: Recalibrating: Platt, isotonic, temperature, and where the fit data comes from
subtopics.learn: Three tools with three different capacities: Platt scaling fits a two-parameter sigmoid 1/(1 + exp(a*s + b)) by logistic regression on held-out scores and is the right choice on a few hundred calibration rows; isotonic regression fits a non-decreasing step function by pool-adjacent-violators, is far more flexible, and overfits badly below roughly a thousand held-out points (its failure looks like a staircase with a few enormous flat treads); temperature scaling divides logits by a single scalar T fitted by minimising NLL, cannot change the argmax and therefore leaves accuracy and AUC exactly untouched, which is why it is the default for deep classifiers. In scikit-learn this is CalibratedClassifierCV(estimator, method='sigmoid'|'isotonic', cv=5, ensemble=True), and you must know what the arguments mean: cv=5 with ensemble=True fits five clones and averages their calibrated outputs (so the deployed object is an ensemble), ensemble=False calibrates a single model refit on all data, and cv='prefit' calibrates an already-fitted model on a set you must guarantee it never saw. The discipline that makes it defensible: fit the base model on split A, fit the calibrator on split B, measure calibration on split C, and show a before/after table where log loss and Brier improve while AUC is unchanged to four decimals - because AUC not moving is the proof you only remapped the scores monotonically.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.calibration.CalibratedClassifierCV (method, cv, ensemble, prefit)

subtopics.name: How uncertain is the number: fold correlation, bootstrap intervals and paired comparisons
subtopics.learn: Fold scores are not independent draws - the K training sets share most of their rows - so the naive standard error std(fold_scores)/sqrt(K) understates the true variability, and Bates, Hastie and Tibshirani show that intervals built this way under-cover and that cross-validation estimates the average error of the fitting procedure over datasets rather than the error of the specific model you are about to ship. Take two habits from that: quote an interval, not a point, and get it from a percentile bootstrap over test rows (resample rows with replacement, recompute the metric 2,000 times, take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, stratify the resample when positives are rare so you do not draw a replicate with zero positives and an undefined AUC), and never compare two models with an unpaired t-test on fold means. Compare them paired: evaluate both on identical folds, take the per-fold difference, and look at the distribution of differences - or use McNemar's test on the 2x2 table of disagreements on a single large test set, which is the right test for two classifiers on the same rows. The sentence this buys you with a customer is the one that ends arguments: 'model B is 1.2 points better with a 95 percent interval of -0.4 to 2.9, so we cannot yet call it better, and here is the sample size that would settle it'.

resource.label: arXiv - Cross-validation: what does it estimate and how well does it do it? (Bates, Hastie, Tibshirani)

subtopics.name: Building eval-harness in NumPy and proving it against scikit-learn
subtopics.learn: Implement the splitters as generators yielding (train_idx, test_idx) integer arrays and test the invariants rather than chasing byte-identical folds: the test folds partition range(n) exactly once, train and test are disjoint, StratifiedKFold holds each class proportion within 1/n_fold, GroupKFold leaves every group in exactly one test fold, and TimeSeriesSplit has max(train_idx) + gap < min(test_idx). Implement roc_auc via average ranks (scipy.stats.rankdata on the scores, then (sum of positive ranks - n_pos*(n_pos+1)/2) / (n_pos*n_neg)) so ties are handled the way scikit-learn handles them, average_precision as the step sum over the sorted thresholds, Brier as a plain mean squared error, log loss with an explicit eps clip you can see, and ECE with both binning strategies exposed. Then assert agreement with np.testing.assert_allclose(mine, sklearn_version, rtol=1e-10) on adversarial inputs - all-ties scores, a single positive, perfectly separable data, scores containing exact 0 and 1, and n=1 folds - and add property tests that hold regardless of implementation: AUC(-s) = 1 - AUC(s), AUC is unchanged under any monotone transform of s, AP of random scores converges to the prevalence, and Brier equals reliability - resolution + uncertainty from your own decomposition.

resource.label: NumPy - numpy.testing.assert_allclose

outcomes: You can look at any dataset and pick the split in under five minutes - random, stratified, grouped, time-ordered, or grouped-and-time-ordered - by naming the unit of independence and the deployment cadence out loud, and justify it to a customer's data scientist who wanted a random 80/20.

You can find a planted leak in someone else's notebook by running a per-column out-of-fold single-feature AUC screen plus a timestamp audit, name which of the six leakage types it is, point to the exact line where it enters, and quantify the score inflation by re-running with it removed.

You can derive the cost-optimal threshold t* = C_fp/(C_fp + C_fn) from expected cost, build the cost matrix with a customer in their own units, and produce the tuned threshold out-of-fold with its expected weekly cost and alert volume.

You can state, without notes, that AUC is invariant to monotone transforms and near-invariant to prevalence, that average precision's baseline is the prevalence, and that log loss and Brier are proper while F1 and accuracy are not - and pick the reporting metric from the customer's decision rather than from habit.

You can produce a reliability diagram with quantile bins, prediction histogram and binomial error bars, read overconfidence off it, fit a calibrator on a clean split, and show a before/after table where log loss and Brier improve while AUC is unchanged to four decimals.

You can ship an eval-harness whose KFold, StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold and TimeSeriesSplit satisfy the partition, proportion, disjoint-group and time-ordering invariants, and whose ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Brier and ECE match scikit-learn to rtol=1e-10 including the all-ties and single-positive edge cases.

You can put an interval on any reported metric via a stratified percentile bootstrap, compare two models with a paired test on identical folds or McNemar on shared rows, and say how many more labelled rows would be needed to call a 1-point difference real.

You can explain nested cross-validation, say what number it estimates, quantify its cost in fits, and describe the cheaper protocol you would use instead on a customer engagement plus the caveat you would write next to the result.
failureModes: A churn model trained on a warehouse snapshot included `days_since_last_login`, which the ETL recomputes nightly against the current date; churned accounts stopped logging in, so the feature encoded the label, cross-validated AUC was 0.97, and live AUC was 0.61 in the first week.

Medical images were split randomly instead of by patient, so scans of the same 400 patients appeared on both sides; the model learned patient identity, reported 0.95 AUC in the pilot, and dropped to near chance on the customer's next hospital.

SMOTE was applied to the whole dataset before cross-validation, so synthetic minority points interpolated from validation rows sat in every training fold; recall looked transformed, the customer sized a review team from it, and the real recall was roughly half.

Feature selection picked the top 200 of 40,000 columns by correlation with the target on the full dataset, then a clean 10-fold CV ran on the survivors; the model reported 0.88 AUC on data whose labels were randomly permuted, and nobody ran that sanity check for four months.

A demand forecaster was evaluated with shuffled K-fold on a time-indexed table, so every fold trained on the future to predict the past; MAPE looked excellent, and the first real four-week-ahead backtest was three times worse.

Class weights were used for a rare-event model and never undone; the scores were calibrated for a balanced world, the ops team applied the default 0.5 threshold, and a queue built for 20 cases a day received 900 on the first Monday.

The reported metric was 99.4 percent accuracy on a 0.6 percent fraud base rate - a model that predicted 'not fraud' unconditionally scored 99.4 percent, and the deck went to the customer's executive sponsor before anyone plotted a confusion matrix.

ECE was reported at 0.008 with 10 uniform-width bins on predictions that all fell below 0.05; nine bins were empty, the single populated bin averaged an overconfident and an underconfident region together, and the reliability diagram drawn later with quantile bins showed a systematic 3x overstatement of risk.
interviewQuestions: Derive the threshold that minimises expected cost for a calibrated binary classifier given C_fp and C_fn, and tell me what has to be true about the model for that derivation to hold. Then tell me what you do instead when the constraint is not a cost but a team that can review 50 alerts a day.

A customer's model reports 0.94 AUC in cross-validation and 0.62 in production two weeks after launch. Walk me through your diagnostic order - what you check first, second and third - and for each candidate cause tell me the specific artefact that would confirm it.
Explain what cross-validation actually estimates. Given 5-fold scores of [0.81, 0.84, 0.79, 0.86, 0.80], what would you quote to a customer, and why is std/sqrt(5) not the standard error you want?

You are handed a table with a customer_id, an event timestamp, and a label defined as 'churned within 60 days'. Design the evaluation from scratch: the splitter, the purge and embargo, the metric, the threshold procedure, and the three sanity checks you run before you show anyone a number.

Two models have identical ROC-AUC of 0.88. One has log loss 0.31 and the other 0.47. Explain how that is possible, tell me which one you would ship and under what conditions, and describe exactly what you would do to the worse one and what would and would not change afterwards.

Design a leakage screen you could run automatically over any customer feature table before training. What does it compute, what is the threshold for flagging, what are its false positives, and what does it fundamentally not catch?

Someone reports an expected calibration error of 0.01 and concludes the probabilities are trustworthy. What questions do you ask about how that number was computed, and what would you ask to see instead?
103.proofOfWork: A public repo `leak-lab` that turns the eval-harness into a diagnostic you can run on a customer's table on day two of an engagement. It ships `leakage_screen.py`, which takes a dataframe plus a label column, an optional timestamp column and an optional group column, and emits a ranked report: per-column out-of-fold single-feature AUC with a flag above 0.90, exact and near-duplicate row clusters that straddle any proposed split (content hash plus a MinHash pass for text), columns whose null pattern correlates with the label, columns whose values move after the label timestamp when a second historical snapshot is supplied, and a permutation_test_score run on the full pipeline that must produce a chance-level score on shuffled labels or the pipeline is presumed leaky. It ships `split_advisor.py`, which takes the same inputs and prints the recommended splitter with the reason in one sentence, the per-fold positive counts and prevalences, and a red warning when any fold has fewer than 25 positives or when a group or a time boundary is violated by the proposed split. Alongside these, `case_studies/` reproduces four planted leaks end to end - a target-derived column, a group leak on repeated entities, a shuffled split on time-ordered data, and preprocessing fitted before the split - each as a notebook showing the inflated score, the screen catching it, the corrected score, and a two-sentence customer-readable explanation of what was wrong. `calibration_clinic.py` takes any fitted classifier and a held-out set and emits log loss, Brier with its Murphy decomposition, ECE swept across bin counts and both binning strategies, a reliability diagram with quantile bins and binomial error bars, the fitted sigmoid, isotonic and temperature calibrators compared on a third split, and the cost-optimal threshold with a bootstrap interval on the resulting weekly alert volume. CI runs the harness agreement tests against scikit-learn at rtol=1e-10, the splitter invariant tests, and the property tests (AUC(-s) = 1 - AUC(s), monotone invariance, AP of random scores equals prevalence) on every push, and the README opens with a one-page `EVALUATION-CHECKLIST.md` written for a customer's data team: the unit of independence, the split, the leak questions per column, the metric and why, the threshold and its cost basis, and the calibration evidence.

104.topic: Feature engineering, selection, and imbalanced data: SMOTE, class weights, target encoding
104.why: This is the topic where an FDE either earns or loses the customer's data-science team in the first week: they will hand you a table with a 0.2 percent positive rate, a 10k-cardinality merchant column, and a model that already scores 0.98 ROC-AUC, and your job is to say whether that number is real. Almost every catastrophic on-site modelling error lives here - target encoding fit before the split, SMOTE applied outside the fold, a feature computed with future information, a metric chosen because it flatters - and every one of them produces a model that validates beautifully and fails in production, on their data, with your name on it. Being able to derive the shrinkage estimator, name the assumption SMOTE makes, and put a threshold-tuned baseline next to the fancy pipeline is what turns 'the consultant said' into a defensible engineering argument.
prerequisites: Logistic regression fluently: the log-odds parameterisation, log-loss, L1/L2 regularisation and what the intercept encodes (Topic 100, Supervised learning I)
Tree ensembles and their hyperparameters - how a split criterion uses counts, what sample weights do to gradients, early stopping (Topic 101, Supervised learning II with XGBoost and LightGBM)
Cross-validation mechanics, the definition of leakage, and probability calibration as concepts (Topic 103, Model evaluation) - this topic is the applied stress test of that one
Bayes rule, conditional probability, the Beta and Binomial distributions and what a conjugate prior does (Topic 95, Probability)
NumPy vectorisation at the level of fancy indexing, broadcasting and np.random.default_rng - the from-scratch SMOTE must not be a Python loop (Topic 99, Numerical computing)
sklearn's estimator API in practice: Pipeline, ColumnTransformer, cross_validate, and the difference between fit_transform and transform

subtopics.name: What imbalance actually is: base rate, class overlap, and the null model
subtopics.learn: Separate the two things people call 'imbalance': the marginal prior pi = P(y=1), which mathematically only shifts where the optimal decision threshold sits, and class overlap, which is irreducible Bayes error that no resampler removes. Compute the three numbers that actually predict difficulty before touching a model - the absolute positive count n_pos, the ratio n_neg/n_pos, and events-per-variable n_pos/p (below roughly 10 a logistic fit is separation-prone and its coefficients are biased away from zero). Fit DummyClassifier(strategy='prior') and record its average_precision: it equals pi exactly and is the only honest floor for every number you report afterwards. Say the framing out loud on site - with 492 frauds in 284,807 rows the problem is 492 examples, not the 0.17 percent.

resource.label: Google ML Crash Course - Imbalanced datasets

subtopics.name: Metrics that survive a 1 percent base rate: PR-AUC, average precision, recall at fixed precision
subtopics.learn: Derive precision = TPR*pi / (TPR*pi + FPR*(1-pi)) and substitute pi=0.01, TPR=0.90, FPR=0.01: precision is 0.48 while ROC-AUC still looks superb, which is exactly why ROC-AUC is prevalence-invariant and therefore the wrong headline number for a rare target. Use average_precision_score, the step-wise sum over operating points of (R_n - R_{n-1}) * P_n, rather than auc(recall, precision), which trapezoid-interpolates between operating points that do not exist. Report the two numbers a customer can staff against - recall at the precision their review capacity implies, and precision at their required recall - extracted from precision_recall_curve with np.searchsorted rather than read off a plot. Remember PR-AUC is not comparable across datasets with different pi, so always print the baseline pi beside it.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Precision-Recall (incl. average precision definition)

subtopics.name: The decision threshold is the cheapest lever: expected cost and TunedThresholdClassifierCV
subtopics.learn: Treat predict()'s hard-coded 0.5 as an arbitrary default, not a property of the model. For a calibrated score with costs C_fp and C_fn, derive the expected-cost-minimising cut by comparing p*C_fn against (1-p)*C_fp, giving t* = C_fp / (C_fp + C_fn) - a 1:50 cost ratio puts the threshold at about 0.02, which recovers most of what people believe they need SMOTE for. Use TunedThresholdClassifierCV(estimator, scoring=make_scorer(business_metric), cv=5) so the cut is chosen on held-out folds against the customer's actual objective; a threshold picked on the same data used to fit is a second fitted parameter and inflates the score. Make 'untouched model plus tuned threshold' a mandatory arm in every imbalance benchmark you run, because it is free at train time and frequently wins.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Post-hoc tuning the cut-off point of decision function (cost-sensitive learning)

subtopics.name: Cost-sensitive learning: weighted losses, class_weight='balanced', sample_weight
subtopics.learn: Write the weighted log-loss L = -(1/sum_i w_i) * sum_i w_i [y_i log p_i + (1-y_i) log(1-p_i)] and see that class_weight is nothing but w_i = w_{y_i}; sklearn's 'balanced' sets w_k = n_samples / (n_classes * n_k), so at pi=0.01 the positive class gets weight ~50. Know the equivalences and where they stop holding: weighting equals minority duplication for losses that are plain sums over examples, but not for tree split criteria that also use raw counts (min_samples_leaf, min_child_weight), not for early stopping evaluated on an unweighted metric, and XGBoost's scale_pos_weight scales gradients and hessians so it interacts with min_child_weight directly. Understand the consequence you must disclose: weighting moves the decision boundary and therefore decalibrates the output, so a weighted model's p-hat is no longer P(y=1|x) on the deployment population.

resource.label: scikit-learn - compute_class_weight (the 'balanced' formula)

subtopics.name: Prior shift and calibration: what resampling does to the predicted probability
subtopics.learn: Show analytically that for a logistic model, resampling the positives from prevalence pi to pi' changes only the intercept, so the corrected log-odds are logit(p_resampled) - log[(pi'/(1-pi')) / (pi/(1-pi))]; implement that offset and verify the mean predicted probability returns to the true base rate. Measure calibration with brier_score_loss and CalibrationDisplay (strategy='quantile', because uniform bins are empty at the top of a rare-event score) and repair it with CalibratedClassifierCV(method='isotonic' or 'sigmoid') fitted on data that never saw the resampled rows. Be able to state van den Goorbergh et al.'s simulation result in one sentence to a customer: imbalance correction leaves discrimination essentially unchanged and destroys calibration - which is fatal when the output feeds an expected-loss calculation rather than a top-k review queue.

resource.label: arXiv:2202.09101 - The harm of class imbalance corrections for risk prediction models

subtopics.name: SMOTE from first principles and from scratch in NumPy
subtopics.learn: Implement the Chawla 2002 algorithm exactly: for each minority point x_i find its k=5 nearest minority neighbours under Euclidean distance, sample one neighbour x_zi uniformly, and emit x_new = x_i + lam * (x_zi - x_i) with lam ~ Uniform(0,1) - vectorise with NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k+1) (discard the self-match at column 0), an rng = np.random.default_rng(seed), and integer index arrays instead of a Python loop. Name the assumptions you assert by using it: the minority class is locally convex (the segment joining two positives is positive), features are continuous and comparably scaled so Euclidean distance is meaningful (hence SMOTE must sit after the scaler in the pipeline), and interpolation adds zero information - it only reshapes the density the learner sees. Validate yours against imblearn's SMOTE(random_state=0) on identical input for output shape and class counts, and assert every synthetic point lies inside the convex hull of the minority set.

resource.label: arXiv:1106.1813 - SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (Chawla et al., JAIR 2002)

subtopics.name: SMOTE variants and mixed-type tables: Borderline, ADASYN, SMOTENC, hybrids
subtopics.learn: Know precisely what each variant changes: BorderlineSMOTE synthesises only around minority points whose neighbourhood is majority-dominated (the decision boundary), ADASYN allocates more synthetic points where local majority density is higher, which makes it a noise amplifier on mislabelled data, and KMeansSMOTE oversamples within clusters so it stops filling empty space between distant minority islands. For mixed tables use SMOTENC (interpolates continuous columns, takes the neighbourhood mode for categoricals) or SMOTEN with a value-difference metric for all-categorical data - plain SMOTE over one-hot columns emits 0.37 in a binary indicator, a row that cannot exist and that the customer's domain expert will spot immediately. Treat sampling_strategy as a hyperparameter to sweep (it takes a float ratio, 'minority', 'not majority', or a dict); forcing a 1:1 balance is a default, not an answer.

resource.label: imbalanced-learn User Guide - Over-sampling (SMOTE variants, SMOTENC/SMOTEN, sampling_strategy)

subtopics.name: Under-sampling and balanced ensembles: Tomek, ENN, NearMiss, BalancedRandomForest, RUSBoost
subtopics.learn: Distinguish blind random under-sampling (RandomUnderSampler, fast and cheap but discards labelled data the customer paid for) from cleaning methods that remove specific rows: TomekLinks drops mutual-nearest-neighbour pairs of opposite class to thin the boundary, EditedNearestNeighbours drops points their own neighbours misclassify, and NearMiss selects majority points by distance heuristics and routinely selects exactly the wrong ones. Prefer the ensemble forms that achieve balance per-learner without throwing data away globally - BalancedRandomForestClassifier (a balanced bootstrap per tree), RUSBoostClassifier, and EasyEnsembleClassifier (a bag of AdaBoosts each on a different under-sample). Remember these change your model class as well as the class balance, so they must be compared against a plain HistGradientBoostingClassifier with a tuned threshold, not against a strawman.

resource.label: imbalanced-learn User Guide - Ensemble of samplers (BalancedRandomForest, RUSBoost, EasyEnsemble)

subtopics.name: Does balancing actually win? Reading the empirical evidence
subtopics.learn: Read Elor and Averbuch-Elor's benchmark across 73 datasets and internalise the finding: for strong learners such as XGBoost and CatBoost, balancing yields no significant gain once the decision threshold is tuned, whereas it does help weak or heavily regularised learners - which tells you exactly which control arm your benchmark must include. Pair that with the observation that most published SMOTE wins are measured with accuracy or F1 at threshold 0.5 on a single train/test split, a setup that guarantees a resampler looks good. The FDE-usable rule: never claim a balancing method helps without an unbalanced, threshold-tuned control at the same hyperparameter budget, evaluated with repeated stratified CV and reported with a standard deviation.

resource.label: arXiv:2201.08528 - To SMOTE, or not to SMOTE?

subtopics.name: Resampling inside the fold: imblearn Pipeline and the leakage demonstration
subtopics.learn: Learn the ordering law: any transformation that consumes y or changes the row multiset is fit on the training fold only and must never touch validation or test. Use imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline rather than sklearn's - it is the one that calls fit_resample during fit and skips the sampler entirely at predict time, which makes cross_validate, GridSearchCV and Optuna correct by construction. Build the deliberately wrong control on purpose: SMOTE the full X, y and then StratifiedKFold, so near-duplicate interpolants of the same positive land on both sides of the split, and watch PR-AUC jump by tens of points on a model that learned nothing. Be able to explain it to a customer engineer in one line - a synthetic row is a function of its neighbours, so oversampling before the split is train/test contamination even though no literal row was copied.

resource.label: imbalanced-learn - Common pitfalls and recommended practices

subtopics.name: Target encoding: deriving the empirical-Bayes shrinkage estimator
subtopics.learn: Derive the smoothed encoder as a Beta-Binomial posterior mean: with a Beta(alpha, beta) prior matched to the global positive rate, a category c with n_c rows and k_c positives encodes to (k_c + alpha) / (n_c + alpha + beta), which rearranges into the m-estimate (n_c * ybar_c + m * ybar) / (n_c + m) with m = alpha + beta acting as a prior row count. Know exactly what m controls - it is the category size at which the estimate sits halfway between the category mean and the global mean - and be able to argue why a category with one observation must encode to approximately the global mean rather than to 0 or 1. Derive the leakage argument formally: encoding row i using a target mean that includes y_i makes the feature a deterministic function of the label, so a 10k-cardinality ID column becomes a perfect in-sample predictor with zero out-of-sample signal, which is why the encoding must be computed out-of-fold.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - ch.05 Probability, Bayesian methods (conjugate Beta priors, MAP shrinkage)

subtopics.name: Target encoding in practice: sklearn TargetEncoder and cross-fitting
subtopics.learn: Use TargetEncoder(target_type='binary', smooth='auto', cv=5) and understand its deliberate API asymmetry: fit_transform() returns cross-fitted encodings computed on held-out folds, while fit().transform() on the same data returns full-data encodings - calling fit then transform on your training set is the leak, and it is a different code path, not a bug. Set smooth explicitly when you can justify m from the customer's category-size distribution, and know the defined behaviour for unseen categories (they map to the global target mean) and for NaN (its own category). Benchmark it honestly against OneHotEncoder(min_frequency=..., handle_unknown='infrequent_if_exist') and against native categorical splits: for a 10k-cardinality merchant ID, one-hot explodes the design matrix, hashing collides, and target encoding wins only when the cross-fitting is real.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Comparing Target Encoder with other encoders / internal cross-fitting

subtopics.name: The rest of the categorical toolbox: one-hot, ordinal, count, hashing, native splits
subtopics.learn: Match the encoder to the model class: linear models need one-hot (with drop='first' when there is an unregularised intercept) because an ordinal code silently asserts an ordering, while tree ensembles tolerate ordinal codes but need many splits to isolate a single level. Prefer native categorical support where it exists - LightGBM sorts levels by accumulated gradient statistics and finds a subset split in O(k log k), which is why it beats one-hot on high cardinality, with cat_smooth, min_data_per_group and max_cat_threshold as the overfitting knobs; XGBoost's enable_categorical does the partition-based equivalent. Keep count/frequency encoding in mind as the cheap, leak-free fallback that captures 'rare merchant' signal, and the hashing trick (FeatureHasher) when cardinality is unbounded or streaming and you can accept collisions.

resource.label: LightGBM docs - Advanced Topics (categorical feature support and its parameters)

subtopics.name: Numeric feature construction: splines, quantile and power transforms, interactions, monotonic constraints
subtopics.learn: Give a linear model curvature without a polynomial explosion: SplineTransformer(n_knots, degree, extrapolation='periodic') for smooth nonlinearity and cyclical time (hour-of-day, day-of-week), QuantileTransformer(output_distribution='normal') and PowerTransformer(method='yeo-johnson') for heavily skewed monetary amounts (Box-Cox requires strictly positive input, Yeo-Johnson does not). Know that all of these are no-ops for tree ensembles - a monotone transform cannot change split ordering - but decisive for logistic regression, SVM and k-NN, which is the point an FDE must make out loud: half of what a customer calls feature engineering is a model choice in disguise. Add interactions deliberately with PolynomialFeatures(interaction_only=True) or a domain ratio (amount / rolling-mean amount for that card), and encode domain law with monotonic_cst / monotone_constraints when the customer requires that risk cannot decrease as amount rises.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Time-related feature engineering (splines, periodic encoding, interactions)

subtopics.name: Filter selection: mutual information and what its estimator really does
subtopics.learn: Understand what mutual_info_classif computes - I(X;Y) = sum p(x,y) log[p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y))], estimated for continuous X by the Kraskov/Ross k-nearest-neighbour method, which makes it stochastic (set random_state), sensitive to n_neighbors, and dependent on discrete_features being declared correctly or one-hot columns are silently treated as continuous. Know its virtue and its two blind spots: it detects nonlinear and non-monotone dependence that Pearson correlation misses, but it is univariate, so it ranks a redundant copy of a strong feature just as highly, and it scores approximately zero for a feature that only matters in interaction (the XOR case). Apply it as SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=...) inside the pipeline so it is refit per fold, and cross-check its ranking against f_classif and chi2 so you can explain the disagreements instead of trusting one list.

resource.label: scikit-learn - mutual_info_classif (kNN entropy estimator, discrete_features, random_state)

subtopics.name: Permutation importance and the correlated-feature trap
subtopics.learn: Know the algorithm exactly: shuffle one column of the validation set, re-score, average the drop over n_repeats - so it measures how much this fitted model relies on this column on this dataset, not how informative the column is in general. Learn its two dominant failure modes: with correlated features the importance is split or collapses to near zero for both (the model reconstructs the signal from the twin), and permutation destroys the joint distribution so the model is scored on impossible rows. Mitigate by hierarchically clustering the Spearman correlation matrix and permuting whole clusters, or by drop-column importance when you can afford p refits; always compute on held-out data, since permutation importance on the training set of a deep tree ranks everything as important. Contrast with impurity-based MDI (feature_importances_), which is biased towards high-cardinality and continuous features - precisely the merchant-ID column you just target-encoded.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Permutation importance with multicollinear or correlated features

subtopics.name: Embedded and wrapper selection: L1 paths, SelectFromModel, RFECV, stability
subtopics.learn: Use L1-penalised logistic regression or LinearSVC(penalty='l1', dual=False) with SelectFromModel(threshold='median' or 1e-5) and read the regularisation path to see the order in which features enter; know that lasso keeps one arbitrary member of a correlated group and that elastic net is the remedy. Reach for RFECV(estimator, step, cv, scoring, min_features_to_select) when the model exposes coefficients or importances and the feature count itself is an operational constraint, understanding it costs roughly p/step refits per fold. The rule that decides whether your number is real: the selector must live inside the Pipeline so it is refit on every training fold - selecting features once on the full dataset and then cross-validating is the classic selection-bias error that produced a decade of unreproducible gene-expression results. Add a stability check by refitting over bootstrap resamples and keeping only features selected in more than about 60 percent of runs.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Feature selection (SelectFromModel, RFE/RFECV, selection in a pipeline)

subtopics.name: Splitting so the number is real: stratified, grouped and time-based validation
subtopics.learn: Pick the splitter from the data's dependence structure, not from habit: StratifiedKFold when rows are iid and positives are rare (it preserves pi per fold and prevents a fold with zero positives), GroupKFold or StratifiedGroupKFold when rows share an entity such as many transactions per card, and TimeSeriesSplit when deployment means 'predict tomorrow from today'. Enforce point-in-time correctness on every engineered feature - a per-card historical fraud rate computed over the full dataset is a time-travelling feature that evaporates in production, so compute it with an expanding window strictly earlier than each row's timestamp. Report RepeatedStratifiedKFold means with a standard deviation, because at 492 positives a single split's PR-AUC moves several points on reseeding alone, and any 'A beats B' inside that band is not a result.

resource.label: scikit-learn - StratifiedGroupKFold (grouped + stratified cross-validation)

subtopics.name: Shipping it: sklearn-compatible transformers and samplers
subtopics.learn: Write your target encoder and SMOTE against the real contract: __init__ stores hyperparameters only with no validation and no renaming, fit(X, y) validates input, sets learned attributes with trailing underscores (categories_, encodings_) and returns self, transform() calls check_is_fitted so it raises NotFittedError rather than a confusing IndexError, and get_feature_names_out() keeps ColumnTransformer output readable. Inherit BaseEstimator + TransformerMixin for the encoder, but note the sampler is a different interface - fit_resample returns X and y with a different number of rows, which is exactly why it cannot be an sklearn transformer and why imblearn's Pipeline exists. Run check_estimator or parametrize_with_checks in the test suite, verify clone(est) round-trips every parameter, and confirm set_output(transform='pandas') preserves column names, because a transformer that silently drops names is the one that breaks the customer's SHAP plot three weeks after handover.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Developing scikit-learn estimators (API contract, check_estimator, get_feature_names_out)

outcomes: You can take a raw table with a 1 percent positive target and build a single leakage-free imblearn Pipeline - ColumnTransformer with out-of-fold target encoding, scaler, sampler, estimator - that passes cross_validate with no step ever seeing validation rows, and you can point at the line that guarantees each property.

You can derive on a whiteboard the m-estimate target encoding (n_c*ybar_c + m*ybar)/(n_c + m) from a Beta-Binomial posterior, state what m means in rows, and say what a single-row category must encode to and why.

You can implement SMOTE in under 30 lines of vectorised NumPy, reproduce imblearn's class counts on the same seed, and name the three assumptions it makes about the minority class and the feature space.

You can produce a benchmark table over repeated stratified CV comparing plain model, class_weight='balanced', SMOTE, SMOTENC, BalancedRandomForest and threshold tuning on PR-AUC and recall-at-fixed-precision with standard deviations, and state which differences are inside the noise.

You can quantify a leakage bug: run the same pipeline with resampling and target encoding fitted before the split versus inside the fold, and report the exact PR-AUC inflation in points as evidence for the customer.

You can show a calibration curve and Brier score before and after resampling, apply the log-odds prior-shift correction analytically, and demonstrate that the mean predicted probability returns to the observed base rate.

You can rank features by mutual information, permutation importance and L1 path entry, explain why the three rankings disagree on correlated columns, and defend a final feature set with a stability-over-bootstraps number.
You can look at a customer's existing notebook and identify, within ten minutes, every step whose fit consumed information from outside its training fold.
failureModes: The target encoder is fit on the full dataset before the split, so a 10k-cardinality merchant ID becomes an almost perfect in-sample predictor; CV reports 0.95 PR-AUC, production reports roughly the base rate, and the column looks like the model's most important feature in SHAP the whole time.

SMOTE is applied to X, y before StratifiedKFold, putting interpolants of the same positive in both train and validation; the score jumps twenty points, nobody can reproduce it on the holdout month, and the team spends a week blaming distribution shift.

ROC-AUC is chosen as the headline metric because it reads 0.98; at the operating threshold the customer can actually staff, precision is 4 percent, their analysts drown in false positives, and the model is switched off in week three.

A per-card historical fraud rate is computed over the entire dataset rather than an expanding window, so every training row knows about future frauds on that card; the feature dominates importance rankings and contributes nothing after deployment.

class_weight='balanced' is used for a model whose output feeds an expected-loss calculation; discrimination is fine but the probabilities are inflated by the implicit prior shift, so the customer's reserve numbers are systematically too high and no one traces it back to the weighting.

Features are selected once with SelectKBest on the whole dataset and cross-validation is run afterwards on the surviving columns; the selection already saw the validation labels, so every subsequent score is optimistically biased and hyperparameter search happily overfits into the gap.

Multiple transactions per card are split with plain StratifiedKFold rather than StratifiedGroupKFold, so the model memorises cards instead of behaviour and scores far better in CV than on any card it has never seen.

SMOTE is run on one-hot encoded columns, producing synthetic rows with 0.37 in a binary indicator and impossible category combinations; the model learns off-manifold structure, and the customer's domain expert loses confidence in the whole engagement the moment they inspect a generated row.
interviewQuestions: Derive the smoothed target encoding formula from a Beta-Binomial posterior. What does the smoothing parameter mean in units of data, how would you choose it for a column where 80 percent of categories have fewer than five rows, and why must the encoding be computed out-of-fold?

A customer has a 0.2 percent positive rate and their model reports 0.99 ROC-AUC. Write down the relationship between precision, TPR, FPR and prevalence, and use it to explain to their VP why that number tells you almost nothing about whether the model is deployable.

Explain what SMOTE does geometrically and state the assumptions it makes. Given a table with 40 numeric and 12 categorical columns, 3 percent positives, and an XGBoost model, would you use it? Justify with the control arms you would run and the metric you would compare on.

Design the validation scheme for a fraud model where each customer has many transactions, fraud is 0.5 percent, the data spans two years, and the model will score transactions in real time. Name the splitter, the metric, the threshold-selection procedure, and every feature-engineering step that has to move inside the fold.

Debug: a colleague's pipeline scores 0.93 PR-AUC in cross-validation and 0.21 on the holdout month. You have their notebook. What are the four things you check, in order, and what would each look like in the code?

class_weight='balanced' versus SMOTE versus threshold tuning: derive what each one does to the loss, the decision boundary and the predicted probability, and say which you would reach for when the model's output is consumed as a probability rather than a ranking.

Permutation importance says a feature has zero importance, but dropping it and refitting makes the model measurably worse. Explain how both results can be true, and what you would do to get an importance ranking you would show a customer.
104.proofOfWork: A one-page, customer-facing 'imbalance and leakage audit' tool plus the memo it generates, checked in alongside the benchmark repo. The tool is a single function audit(X, y, split_spec, feature_spec) that emits a report for any tabular classification dataset: base rate, absolute positive count, events-per-variable, DummyClassifier PR-AUC floor, the per-column cardinality and category-size histogram (flagging every column where target encoding without smoothing would be dominated by singleton categories), a group-leakage check that reports how many entity IDs appear on both sides of the proposed split, a point-in-time check that flags any engineered feature whose computation window extends past the row timestamp, and a paired benchmark of the four arms (plain, class_weight, sampler, tuned threshold) under RepeatedStratifiedKFold with means and standard deviations. Run it against two datasets - the credit-card-fraud table from the deliverable and one other public imbalanced table with a genuine group structure, such as a churn or readmission dataset - and write the two-page memo it feeds: the recommended arm, the recall achievable at the precision their review capacity implies, the calibration curve before and after any correction, and an explicit 'what we did not do and why' section naming SMOTE if the evidence did not support it. The point of the artifact is that it is the thing you can run in front of a customer's data-science team on day one and have them agree with the numbers before any modelling starts.

105.topic: Hyperparameter optimisation: grid, random, Bayesian search with Optuna
105.why: Tuning is where an FDE most easily manufactures a number that is not real: the search reports 0.91 AUC, the customer's holdout says 0.84, and you have no story for the gap because the cross-validation lived outside the trial or the winner was simply the luckiest of 400 draws. Knowing the actual mechanics - that random search needs only 60 draws to hit the top 5 percent of a space with 95 percent probability, that TPE maximises the density ratio l(x)/g(x) rather than a Gaussian-process EI, that successive halving assumes low-fidelity rank order predicts full-fidelity rank order - is what lets you defend a fixed trial budget on a customer's laptop instead of asking for a GPU cluster. It is also the difference between saying 'we tuned it' and being able to point at a param-importance plot and say 'three of these seven parameters do nothing, drop them and we halve the search'.
prerequisites: Cross-validation mechanics and leakage taxonomy from Topic 103 (Model evaluation): KFold vs StratifiedKFold vs GroupKFold vs TimeSeriesSplit, and why a transform fitted outside the fold is leakage

Gradient boosting from Topic 101 (Supervised learning II): what num_leaves, min_data_in_leaf, learning_rate, feature_fraction and lambda_l2 each do to the fitted trees, plus early stopping with a watchlist
Bias-variance decomposition and regularisation from Topic 100, since every hyperparameter is a knob on one of those two terms
Estimation and interval basics from Topic 96 (Statistical inference): standard error of a mean, why the maximum of k noisy estimates is biased upward, paired comparisons
Probability densities and quantiles from Topic 95: what a log-uniform prior is, what a gamma-quantile split of observed losses means, what a kernel density estimate is
sklearn Pipeline and ColumnTransformer fluency plus a working LightGBM install, since the deliverable tunes one LightGBM model four ways under one budget

subtopics.name: HPO as noisy, expensive, derivative-free black-box optimisation
subtopics.learn: State the problem formally: minimise the expected generalisation risk L(lambda) = E[loss(model trained with lambda)] over a mixed continuous/integer/categorical space, where you can only observe a noisy estimate L_hat(lambda) from cross-validation, each observation costs minutes, and no gradient of L with respect to lambda exists. Every method in this topic is a different answer to 'how do I spend n noisy, expensive evaluations', so name the three axes that decide the answer: dimensionality of the space, cost per evaluation, and the noise floor sigma of L_hat across CV folds. Internalise the consequence that if the fold-to-fold standard error of your metric is larger than the spread between your top ten configurations, no search algorithm can help you - you are ranking noise.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - chapter 06, machine learning

subtopics.name: Why the search itself overfits: the optimistic bias of the argmax
subtopics.learn: Derive the core statistical fact: because E[max_i X_i] >= max_i E[X_i] for noisy estimates X_i, the CV score of the winning trial is an upward-biased estimate of that configuration's true performance, and the bias grows with the number of trials and with the variance of L_hat. This is selection on noise - with 500 trials on a 5000-row dataset you can 'win' 0.02 AUC purely by drawing a configuration that happens to suit your particular fold assignment.
