The two defences are a held-out test set touched exactly once after the search, and nested cross-validation where the inner loop selects lambda and the outer loop estimates the generalisation of the whole tuning procedure; be able to say that nested CV evaluates the procedure, not a specific lambda, and that the two numbers answer different customer questions.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Nested versus non-nested cross-validation

subtopics.name: Grid search: the geometry, and why it dies above three parameters
subtopics.learn: Grid search over d parameters with N values each costs N^d evaluations, so a 6-parameter LightGBM grid at 5 values apiece is 15625 fits - the budget is set by the space, not by you, which is the practical objection. Reproduce Bergstra and Bengio's argument: when only k of the d parameters matter (low effective dimensionality), a grid of n points still probes only N = n^(1/d) distinct values along the important axis, while n random draws probe n distinct values along every axis, so random search dominates for the same budget. Know the two places grid is still correct: a genuinely small discrete space (3 boosting types x 4 max_depth), and a customer-facing sweep where you must show a complete, explainable table rather than the best point. Optuna reproduces it exactly with GridSampler, which makes the four-way comparison in the deliverable apples to apples.

resource.label: Bergstra and Bengio (JMLR 2012) - Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization

subtopics.name: Random search: the 1-(1-p)^n coverage bound and log-uniform priors
subtopics.learn: Derive the budget rule you will quote to customers: if a fraction p of the space is 'good enough', n independent draws miss it with probability (1-p)^n, so P(hit) = 1 - (1-p)^n; n = 60 gives 95 percent coverage of the top 5 percent, and n = 300 gives 95 percent of the top 1 percent, regardless of dimensionality. Then get the priors right, because coverage is over the sampling measure, not the interval: learning_rate on [1e-4, 1e-1] drawn uniformly puts 90 percent of the mass above 1e-2, so use scipy.stats.loguniform (density proportional to 1/x) or Optuna's suggest_float(..., log=True), and use integer log scales for num_leaves. Implement a from-scratch random search with a seeded numpy Generator so the draw sequence is reproducible and can be replayed against a different estimator.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.loguniform

subtopics.name: Keeping cross-validation inside the trial: Pipeline, leakage and the fold boundary
subtopics.learn: The non-negotiable rule: everything fitted from data - imputer, scaler, target encoder, SMOTE resampler, feature selector, PCA - is fitted inside each training fold, which in practice means the objective builds a Pipeline and calls cross_val_score on the pipeline, never on a pre-transformed matrix. Enumerate the leakage channels this closes and the ones it does not: pre-fold target encoding (closed), pre-fold feature selection (closed), the same fold used both for LightGBM early stopping and for scoring (not closed - use an inner split or accept the optimism and say so), the same customer or device in train and validation (needs GroupKFold), and future rows in a past fold (needs TimeSeriesSplit with a gap). Be able to demonstrate the size of the effect: fit a StandardScaler plus SelectKBest on the full training set before CV and show the phantom gain, then move both inside the pipeline and watch it vanish.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Common pitfalls and recommended practices (data leakage)

subtopics.name: What the objective actually returns: metric choice, scorer sign, and aggregation
subtopics.learn: The objective returns one scalar and the search will exploit exactly that scalar, so pick it deliberately: accuracy on a 2 percent positive rate rewards the all-negative model, ROC AUC is threshold-free and insensitive to prevalence while average_precision tracks the minority class, and log_loss is what you want when the customer consumes probabilities rather than labels. Know sklearn's convention that scorers are greater-is-better so error metrics appear as neg_log_loss and neg_root_mean_squared_error, and that make_scorer(..., greater_is_better=False) flips the sign for you. Decide the aggregation across folds and say why: mean is standard, mean minus one standard error is a defensible tie-break that prefers stable configurations, and returning the mean while logging the per-fold spread as a trial user attribute is what later lets you tell the customer whether the winner won by a real margin.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Metrics and scoring (scorer conventions, sign flipping)

subtopics.name: Bayesian optimisation: surrogate model plus acquisition function
subtopics.learn: Understand the loop: fit a probabilistic surrogate to the observed (lambda, loss) pairs, maximise a cheap acquisition function over the surrogate to pick the next lambda, evaluate, refit. With a Gaussian-process surrogate giving posterior mean mu(x) and standard deviation sigma(x), be able to write Expected Improvement in closed form for minimisation - EI(x) = (f_best - mu(x)) * Phi(z) + sigma(x) * phi(z) with z = (f_best - mu(x)) / sigma(x) - and read off the exploration/exploitation split: the first term rewards a low predicted mean, the second rewards uncertainty. Know the alternatives by name (probability of improvement, upper confidence bound mu - kappa*sigma, entropy search) and the practical limits of GPs: cubic cost in the number of trials, awkwardness with categorical and conditional parameters, and sensitivity to the kernel and length-scale, which is precisely why Optuna's default is not a GP. Optuna's GPSampler is available when the space is low-dimensional, continuous and evaluations are genuinely expensive.

resource.label: Distill - Exploring Bayesian Optimization (GP surrogate and acquisition functions)

subtopics.name: TPE: the density ratio l(x)/g(x) that Optuna actually maximises
subtopics.learn: Derive the estimator rather than treating TPE as a black box: sort the observed losses, split them at the gamma-quantile y*, and fit two kernel density estimates over the parameter values - l(x) = p(x | y < y*) from the good trials and g(x) = p(x | y >= y*) from the rest. Expected improvement under this model is proportional to (gamma + (1 - gamma) * g(x)/l(x))^-1, so maximising EI reduces to maximising the ratio l(x)/g(x); TPE therefore samples n_ei_candidates points from l and returns the one with the highest ratio, which is cheap, handles categorical and conditional parameters natively, and scales linearly rather than cubically in trials. Know the knobs and what they mean: n_startup_trials (pure random sampling before the model kicks in, default 10), multivariate=True and group=True to model parameter interactions instead of independent marginals, and constant_liar=True to stop parallel workers proposing the same point. Know its weakness - the univariate default ignores correlations such as the learning_rate/n_estimators coupling.

resource.label: arXiv 2304.11127 - Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator: Understanding Its Algorithm Components

subtopics.name: Writing an Optuna objective: define-by-run, suggest_* and study wiring
subtopics.learn: Write objective(trial) as ordinary Python so the search space is defined by execution, not by a static dict: trial.suggest_float('learning_rate', 1e-3, 3e-1, log=True), trial.suggest_int('num_leaves', 8, 256, log=True), trial.suggest_categorical('boosting_type', ['gbdt', 'dart']), with conditional branches so a parameter only exists when it applies (bagging_freq only when bagging_fraction < 1). Wire the study with optuna.create_study(direction='maximize', sampler=TPESampler(seed=42, multivariate=True), pruner=..., study_name=..., storage='sqlite:///hpo.db', load_if_exists=True) and run study.optimize(objective, n_trials=100, timeout=1800, catch=(ValueError,)) so one exploding configuration does not kill the run. Attach everything you will need later with trial.set_user_attr - per-fold scores, best_iteration from early stopping, fit seconds - and pull the whole record out with study.trials_dataframe(); note that suggest_uniform and suggest_loguniform are deprecated aliases for suggest_float.

resource.label: Optuna API reference - optuna.trial.Trial (suggest_*, report, set_user_attr)

subtopics.name: Pruning: report, should_prune, and the assumption that makes it valid
subtopics.learn: Add trial.report(intermediate_value, step) inside the boosting callback or epoch loop and then 'if trial.should_prune(): raise optuna.TrialPruned()' - the exception is how Optuna records a pruned trial rather than a failed one. Understand MedianPruner precisely: after n_startup_trials completed trials and n_warmup_steps within a trial, it prunes when this trial's best intermediate value at step t is worse than the median of previous trials' intermediate values at the same step, with interval_steps controlling how often the check runs. State the assumption out loud, because it is what breaks: the rank order of partially trained models must predict the rank order of fully trained models, which fails under warmup schedules, cosine restarts, dart boosting, and any configuration that is slow early and best late - a low learning_rate with many trees is exactly the victim. Know SuccessiveHalvingPruner, HyperbandPruner, PercentilePruner and PatientPruner as the alternatives, and that a pruned trial is not a free trial when you are comparing budgets.

resource.label: Optuna API reference - optuna.pruners.MedianPruner

subtopics.name: Successive halving and Hyperband: the budget arithmetic
subtopics.learn: Successive halving takes n configurations at a small resource r (rows, trees, or epochs), evaluates all of them, keeps the top 1/eta, multiplies the resource by eta, and repeats for log_eta(n) rungs, so it spends roughly equal budget per rung while the survivors get exponentially more resource - this is how you evaluate 81 configurations for the cost of a handful of full fits. The bias is explicit: it trades fidelity for breadth and assumes low-fidelity rank order predicts full-fidelity rank order. Hyperband removes the n-versus-r guess by running several brackets with different starting (n, r) trade-offs, from many-cheap to few-expensive, and ASHA makes the rungs asynchronous so workers never idle waiting for a rung to fill. Be able to compute, for eta=3, R=81 and a fixed wall-clock, how many configurations each bracket starts with and how many survive to full fidelity.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Multi-Fidelity Hyperparameter Optimization (successive halving)

subtopics.name: HalvingRandomSearchCV in scikit-learn: the API and its sharp edges
subtopics.learn: You must write 'from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv' before importing the class or the import fails - this is the number one reason the example does not run. Configure it deliberately: factor is eta, resource defaults to 'n_samples' but can be any integer estimator parameter such as 'n_estimators', min_resources takes 'smallest' or 'exhaust', n_candidates takes 'exhaust' to size the first rung to the budget, and aggressive_elimination=True forces extra elimination rounds when the candidates cannot be reduced to one by the last rung. Know the modelling failure the 'n_samples' resource introduces: on small subsamples, heavily regularised, low-capacity configurations look best, so a search that eliminates on 5 percent of rows can discard the high-capacity configuration that wins on the full data. Read cv_results_ columns iter, n_resources and mean_test_score to see the elimination path rather than only the winner.

resource.label: scikit-learn API - HalvingRandomSearchCV

subtopics.name: Designing a LightGBM search space that is worth searching
subtopics.learn: Bound the space from the model's own constraints rather than from a blog post: num_leaves must stay below 2^max_depth to keep the leaf-wise growth from becoming a depth-limited tree, min_data_in_leaf is the strongest anti-overfit knob on small data and should scale with rows per leaf, feature_fraction and bagging_fraction with bagging_freq >= 1 give decorrelation, and lambda_l1/lambda_l2 belong on a log scale spanning several decades including a value near zero. Do not tune n_estimators and learning_rate as independent axes - their product is roughly conserved, so fix n_estimators high, pass early stopping against the fold's validation split, and record best_iteration as a trial user attribute so the refit on full data uses it. Decide up front which parameters are search space and which are fixed policy (objective, metric, deterministic, num_threads, categorical handling), because every unnecessary axis multiplies the volume the sampler must cover.

resource.label: LightGBM docs - Parameters Tuning

subtopics.name: Reading the diagnostics: history, param importances, slice, contour, EDF
subtopics.learn: Learn to make a decision from each plot rather than screenshotting all of them. plot_optimization_history shows best-so-far against trial index: still stepping means keep going, flat for the last third means stop or widen; plot_param_importances runs fANOVA over a surrogate fitted to the trials and decomposes predicted-loss variance into per-parameter contributions, so a parameter under a few percent is a candidate to freeze at its default and remove an axis. plot_slice is the range diagnostic - when the best values pile up at the edge of an interval, the interval is wrong and you widen it; plot_contour exposes two-parameter interactions such as learning_rate against num_leaves; plot_edf compares whole studies by the distribution of achieved objective values, not just their maxima; plot_intermediate_values tells you whether the pruner cut trials that were still climbing. Remember fANOVA importance is importance under your chosen ranges: a parameter looks unimportant if you searched a narrow interval of it.

resource.label: Optuna API reference - visualization module (history, importances, slice, contour, EDF)

subtopics.name: Benchmarking four searches honestly: budget definition, seeds, and paired tests
subtopics.learn: Define the budget in a unit that survives pruning: trial count is not comparable when a TPE run prunes half its trials at 20 percent fidelity, so fix either wall-clock seconds or total full-fidelity-equivalent model fits, and report both. Hold the CV split fixed across all four searches with the same seed so the objective is literally the same function, then vary the sampler seed across at least five repeats and report median and interquartile range of best CV score - a single TPE run beating a single random run is n=1 and means nothing. Compute trials-to-90-percent-of-best from the best-so-far curve as the anytime-performance number that customers actually care about, and when you compare two configurations' CV scores use a corrected resampled t-test rather than a naive paired t-test, because overlapping training sets correlate the folds and inflate the Type I error rate.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Statistical comparison of models using grid search (corrected t-test)

subtopics.name: Multi-objective and constrained search: Pareto fronts and latency budgets
subtopics.learn: When the customer needs accuracy and p99 latency, do not silently collapse them into a weighted sum - use optuna.create_study(directions=['maximize', 'minimize']), read study.best_trials as the Pareto set, and plot_pareto_front to hand the customer the actual trade-off curve so they choose the exchange rate. Know that multi-objective studies use NSGAIISampler or the multi-objective TPE variant, that there is no single best_trial (accessing study.best_trial raises), and that non-dominated sorting plus crowding distance is what maintains front diversity. For a hard limit rather than a trade-off, use a constraints_func returning values that are feasible when <= 0, so infeasible trials still inform the sampler instead of being discarded, or return a large penalty and accept that you have distorted the surrogate.

resource.label: Optuna tutorial - Multi-objective Optimization

subtopics.name: Operationalising a study: storage, parallelism, resume and reproducibility
subtopics.learn: Persist to an RDB with storage='sqlite:///hpo.db' plus study_name and load_if_exists=True so a killed run resumes instead of restarting; know that SQLite is single-writer and fine for one process but that several parallel workers need PostgreSQL/MySQL or the JournalStorage file backend, and that the scale-out pattern is N separate processes running the same study_name, not n_jobs. Understand why study.optimize(n_jobs=-1) is threads and therefore GIL-bound for Python-side work, and why nesting it inside LightGBM's own num_threads oversubscribes the cores and destroys any wall-clock comparison. Be precise about reproducibility: a sampler seed reproduces a sequential single-worker study exactly, but parallel studies are non-deterministic because the sampler conditions on whichever trials finished first - so pin the seed, pin the library versions, log the git SHA and the dataset hash as study user attributes, and treat the trials table, not the notebook, as the record.

resource.label: Optuna tutorial - Easy Parallelization (shared storage, multiple workers)

subtopics.name: When not to tune: diagnosing before spending the budget
subtopics.learn: Establish the honest baseline first - defaults plus a correct CV harness - and compute the fold-to-fold standard error of the metric; if tuning moves the mean by less than one standard error, you have spent a day buying noise and should say so rather than shipping the number. Diagnose which direction to move before searching: a large train-versus-validation gap is a variance problem pointing at min_data_in_leaf, feature_fraction and lambda_l2, while both scores being poor is a bias problem pointing at capacity, more boosting rounds, or better features. Hold the FDE ordering in mind - a fixed label definition, a removed leaked column, or 10x more rows usually beats every hyperparameter you can turn - and be ready to tell a customer that the correct recommendation is to stop tuning and go fix the data.

resource.label: XGBoost docs - Notes on Parameter Tuning (bias-variance control)

outcomes: You can pick between grid, random, successive halving and TPE for a given search space and a fixed trial budget, and defend the choice from the space dimensionality, the cost per evaluation and the fold-to-fold noise rather than from what is fashionable.

You can derive the random-search coverage bound 1-(1-p)^n at a whiteboard, use it to say why 60 trials is the usual floor, and explain why the bound only holds under the sampling distribution you chose (so learning_rate must be log-uniform).

You can write, from memory, an Optuna objective that builds a sklearn Pipeline inside the trial, cross-validates it, reports intermediate values for pruning, records per-fold scores and best_iteration as user attributes, and returns a single scalar - and prove no transform was fitted outside a fold.

You can explain TPE as maximising l(x)/g(x) from a gamma-quantile split of observed losses, name n_startup_trials, multivariate and constant_liar, and say when a GP surrogate would be the better choice instead.

You can read an optimisation-history, param-importance and slice plot and produce one of four decisions - stop, keep going, widen this range, drop this parameter - with the evidence from the plot that supports it.

You can benchmark four search strategies under one identical budget, define that budget in a pruning-proof unit, repeat over five sampler seeds, and report median best CV, trials-to-90-percent-of-best, wall-clock and a single held-out test score per strategy.

You can quantify the optimism of the search: report the winner's CV score, the held-out test score and a nested-CV estimate, and explain to a customer which of the three answers 'how will this model do next month'.
You can convert an accuracy-versus-latency requirement into a two-direction Optuna study, hand back a Pareto front instead of one model, and state which point you recommend and why.
failureModes: The scaler and target encoder are fitted on the full training frame before the Optuna loop starts, so every one of 400 trials scores against leaked statistics; CV reports 0.91 AUC, the customer's holdout returns 0.84, and the search is blamed for overfitting when the harness was wrong before the first trial.

LightGBM early stopping is evaluated on the same fold that produces the trial's score, so the validation set is used twice and every configuration looks a little better than it is - uniformly enough that the ranking survives and nobody notices until the gap appears in production.

The MedianPruner is left at n_warmup_steps=0, so low-learning-rate configurations that are slow for the first 100 trees and best at 900 are killed at trial step 20; the search converges confidently on a high-learning-rate model that is measurably worse at full fidelity.

TPE with 500 trials is compared against random search with 500 trials, but TPE pruned 60 percent of its trials at low fidelity; the comparison is reported as trials-for-trials, TPE looks dramatically better, and the same experiment measured in wall-clock shows no difference.

learning_rate is sampled uniformly on [1e-4, 1e-1] instead of log-uniformly, so 90 percent of draws land above 1e-2, the optimum near 3e-3 is never sampled, and the slice plot showing every good trial pressed against the left edge of the range is never looked at.

HalvingRandomSearchCV eliminates on n_samples with min_resources='smallest', so the first rung ranks configurations on 3 percent of the data where heavily regularised low-capacity models dominate; the high-capacity winner is eliminated in rung one and can never come back.

Two workers run study.optimize against the same SQLite storage with a fixed sampler seed; the run is presented as reproducible, but the sampler conditions on whichever trials committed first, so the rerun for the customer produces a different winner and the whole result loses credibility.

The tuned model beats defaults by 0.004 AUC while the fold-to-fold standard error is 0.02; the improvement is written into a deliverable as a real gain, the customer retrains on next month's data, the ordering flips, and the tuning process is what gets distrusted.
interviewQuestions: Derive the probability that random search finds a configuration in the top p fraction of the space within n trials, and use it to justify a trial budget to a customer. Then tell me what assumption of that derivation your actual search space usually violates.

Explain how TPE picks its next point. Write down what l(x) and g(x) are, how gamma enters, and why maximising expected improvement reduces to maximising the density ratio. When would you use a Gaussian-process surrogate with expected improvement instead, and what does the closed form of EI look like?

Design: a customer gives you a 200k-row tabular dataset, a LightGBM baseline, one 8-core box and four hours. Specify the search space, the CV scheme, the objective, the budget, the pruning strategy, and exactly how you will report the result so it holds up when they retrain next quarter.

Your Optuna study reports 0.93 AUC on the best trial and the held-out test set returns 0.87. Walk me through your diagnosis in order. Which candidate causes are leakage, which are selection on noise, and what experiment separates the two?

Successive halving eliminates on a fraction of the training rows. Explain the bias that introduces, give me a concrete case where the eventual best configuration is eliminated in the first rung, and describe how you would change the resource or the schedule to avoid it.

You have optimisation-history, param-importance and slice plots from a 300-trial study. For each plot, tell me one specific pattern that would make you stop the search, one that would make you widen a range, and one that would make you delete a parameter from the space.

A customer needs AUC above 0.85 and p99 inference latency under 40 milliseconds. How do you set the search up so you are not silently choosing their trade-off for them, and what artifact do you hand back?
105.proofOfWork: A companion `tuning-honesty` module and drill checked into the same repo as hpo-lab, aimed at the part customers actually challenge. It ships (a) `optuna_cv.py`, a small reusable objective factory that takes a Pipeline builder, a CV splitter and a scorer and guarantees the two invariants by construction - every transform is fitted inside the fold, and the held-out test set is inaccessible to the objective (it is not even passed in) - with unit tests that assert a deliberately leaky variant scores higher and that the guarded version does not; (b) a reproduced leakage drill on one dataset showing three numbers side by side for the same winning configuration - best-trial CV, nested-CV estimate of the tuning procedure, and the single held-out test score - with the CV-minus-test gap plotted as a function of trial count so the optimistic bias of the argmax is visible growing from 20 to 500 trials; (c) a pruner-validity check that reruns the top 20 pruned trials at full fidelity and reports the rank correlation between the intermediate value at the pruning step and the final score, which is the evidence that the MedianPruner settings were safe on this problem; and (d) a one-page customer-facing Tuning Report template, filled in for the deliverable's dataset, giving the search space table, the budget in wall-clock and full-fidelity-equivalent fits, the gain over defaults with the fold-to-fold standard error as an error bar, the param-importance ranking with a recommendation to freeze the bottom parameters, and an explicit 'we recommend you stop tuning and do X to the data instead' section when the gain does not clear one standard error.

106.topic: Unsupervised learning: k-means, DBSCAN, hierarchical clustering, PCA, t-SNE, UMAP
106.why: A customer's first 'AI' request is very often unlabelled - segment these 40,000 accounts, find the anomalous machines, tell us what these 200k support tickets are about - and there is no held-out accuracy to hide behind, so the only defence of your answer is the objective you optimised, the metric you optimised it under, and evidence that the result survives resampling. An FDE who cannot say why k=6 rather than k=4, or who cannot say out loud that the gap between two blobs in a UMAP plot carries no information, will have their segmentation quietly overruled by whoever brought the prettier picture. This is also where the most expensive silent errors live: an unscaled column that becomes the entire distance metric, a PCA fitted before the split, and a two-dimensional embedding read as though its axes and distances meant something.
prerequisites: Eigendecomposition and the SVD as things you can compute and interpret - A = U S V^T, orthonormal bases, symmetric positive semi-definite matrices, the spectral theorem (Topic 93, Linear algebra for ML)

NumPy at the level of broadcasting, fancy indexing, argmin over a pairwise distance matrix, and np.linalg.svd / np.linalg.eigh including when eigh is the right call rather than eig (Topic 99, Numerical computing)
Multivariate Gaussians, covariance matrices, maximum likelihood and KL divergence (Topic 95, Probability and Topic 98, Information theory) - the GMM's EM steps and t-SNE's objective both need them

Cross-validation, leakage, and the mechanical rule that anything with a fit method is refit inside the training fold (Topic 103, Model evaluation) - the scaler and the PCA are the two most common leaks in an unsupervised pipeline
Scaling and encoding choices from Topic 104: StandardScaler vs RobustScaler vs QuantileTransformer, and why one-hot columns break Euclidean distance
The distance-based view of feature space from Topic 102 (k-NN) - DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, t-SNE and UMAP are all built on a k-nearest-neighbour graph

subtopics.name: What unsupervised learning is claiming, and what it cannot verify
subtopics.learn: Be precise that clustering does not discover 'the' groups: it returns the partition that optimises a stated objective under a stated metric, and a different objective on the same table returns a different, equally valid partition. Write down the three objectives you will be comparing all day - within-cluster sum of squares for k-means, density-connectivity for DBSCAN, a greedy merge criterion for agglomerative - and note that only the first is a global objective with a scalar value comparable across runs. Internalise Kleinberg's impossibility theorem as the reason there is no universal best clustering (no function satisfies scale-invariance, richness and consistency simultaneously), and take the FDE consequence from it: you never defend a clustering with 'the algorithm found it', you defend it with the objective, the metric, and evidence that the structure survives resampling. Decide and state up front which of the two jobs you are doing - exploratory structure discovery, which must be validated by a domain expert, or compression and feature construction, which is validated by the downstream supervised metric.

resource.label: Google ML - Clustering course overview (what clustering is for, similarity, workflow)

subtopics.name: Distance is a modelling choice: scaling, metrics and distance concentration
subtopics.learn: Every algorithm in this topic is a function of a distance matrix, so the choice of d is a modelling decision you defend, not a default: Euclidean assumes comparably scaled, roughly isotropic continuous features; Manhattan degrades more gracefully in high dimension; cosine ignores magnitude and is what TF-IDF and embedding vectors want; a Gower or matching distance is what a genuinely mixed-type table needs. Run the experiment that proves scaling is mandatory - put annual_revenue in dollars next to n_employees, cluster, and show the partition is a revenue quantile split, then rerun with StandardScaler - and know that RobustScaler (median and IQR) is the right default on the heavy-tailed columns a customer's table always has. Understand distance concentration: for iid features the ratio (d_max - d_min)/d_min tends to zero as dimension grows, so 'nearest neighbour' loses meaning and DBSCAN's eps stops having a good value; the fix is to reduce dimension first, not to tune harder. Note that one-hot columns make Euclidean distance score every 'different category' as sqrt(2) regardless of how different those categories are, which makes plain k-means over one-hot input a bug rather than a choice.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - ch.01 Vectors, 03. Norms and metrics

subtopics.name: k-means: the objective, Lloyd's algorithm, and why it only finds a local minimum
subtopics.learn: Write the objective J = sum over k of sum over i in C_k of ||x_i - mu_k||^2 and derive both update rules as block coordinate descent: with centroids fixed the J-minimising assignment is the nearest centroid, and with assignments fixed dJ/dmu_k = -2 * sum (x_i - mu_k) = 0 gives mu_k as the cluster mean - which is exactly why k-means is tied to squared Euclidean distance, because the arithmetic mean is the minimiser of a sum of squared deviations and of nothing else. Prove that Lloyd's algorithm decreases J monotonically and therefore terminates at a local minimum in finitely many steps, know the per-iteration cost O(n k d), and know that the global problem is NP-hard, which is the entire reason n_init exists and why sklearn returns the restart with the lowest inertia_. Implement it in NumPy using the expansion ||x||^2 - 2 x . c + ||c||^2 to build the (n, k) distance matrix instead of a Python loop, handle the empty-cluster case explicitly by reseeding to the point furthest from its centroid, and stop on a centroid-movement tolerance rather than on exact assignment stability. For n in the millions reach for MiniBatchKMeans, which trades a small inertia penalty for roughly an order of magnitude in wall time.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - ch.06 Machine Learning, 01. Classical machine learning (clustering, k-means, PCA)

subtopics.name: k-means++ seeding, n_init, and what the O(log k) guarantee actually says
subtopics.learn: Implement D^2 seeding exactly: pick the first centre uniformly at random, then repeatedly pick x with probability proportional to D(x)^2, the squared distance from x to the nearest already-chosen centre. Know the theorem and its scope - k-means++ gives E[J] <= 8(ln k + 2) * J_opt in expectation before a single Lloyd iteration, so it is a guarantee about the initialisation, not about the answer you finally report. Know what scikit-learn does around it: init='k-means++' is the default, n_init='auto' runs one restart for k-means++ and ten for init='random', and the fitted model is the restart with the lowest inertia_ - so a customer comparing their k=5 run to yours must match random_state and n_init or the entire comparison is seed noise. Verify your implementation empirically rather than by inspection: over 50 seeds on the same data, D^2 seeding should give a materially lower and lower-variance mean inertia than uniform seeding. When k is large or the data lives in Spark, know that k-means|| oversamples O(k) points per round over O(log n) rounds and then reclusters the sample, which is the parallel variant you will actually meet on a customer cluster.

resource.label: arXiv:1203.6402 - Scalable K-Means++ (k-means|| seeding, D^2 sampling and its guarantee)

subtopics.name: Choosing k: the elbow, the silhouette, the gap statistic, and their disagreements
subtopics.learn: Understand why the elbow is weak but not useless: inertia is non-increasing in k by construction (k=n gives zero), so 'the elbow' is a second-derivative eyeball on a curve that is perfectly smooth whenever clusters overlap - report it, never decide on it alone. Compute the silhouette for point i as s_i = (b_i - a_i)/max(a_i, b_i), with a_i the mean distance to its own cluster and b_i the mean distance to the nearest other cluster; know it lies in [-1, 1], that silhouette_score is the mean over points, and that the per-cluster silhouette plot is far more informative than that mean - one cluster of width 0.05 with a tail of negative-silhouette points hiding behind an average of 0.55 is the usual story. Add the gap statistic (compare log W_k against its expectation under a uniform reference sampled in the PCA-aligned bounding box, and take the smallest k with Gap(k) >= Gap(k+1) - s_{k+1}), Calinski-Harabasz (between-over-within variance ratio, biased towards convex blobs) and Davies-Bouldin (lower is better), and expect them to disagree. The defensible deliverable is a table of k against every index plus a stability score - mean ARI between clusterings of 20 bootstrap resamples - and one sentence on which k the customer can operationalise, because six segments is a marketing plan and forty is not.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Selecting the number of clusters with silhouette analysis on KMeans

subtopics.name: Where k-means is the wrong model, and what to reach for instead
subtopics.learn: The objective encodes assumptions, and you must be able to name them off the plot: squared Euclidean loss induces a Voronoi partition with linear boundaries, which implicitly assumes isotropic clusters of similar variance and similar population. Reproduce the four canonical failures and the diagnostic for each - anisotropically stretched blobs (a linear boundary slices a stretched cluster in half), unequal variances (the wide cluster is consumed by its tight neighbours), unequal cluster sizes (the large cluster is split because splitting it reduces total inertia more than merging the small ones), and non-convex shapes such as two moons or concentric circles (no Voronoi cell can express a ring). Map each failure onto its fix: GaussianMixture with covariance_type='full' for anisotropy and unequal variance, DBSCAN/HDBSCAN or SpectralClustering for non-convex shapes, k-medoids (PAM) when you need an arbitrary metric and the mean is undefined for your data type. State the property that gets abused most in customer work: k-means always returns exactly k non-empty clusters, so it will cheerfully partition uniform noise into k tidy segments and give you a deck to present.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Demonstration of k-means assumptions (anisotropy, unequal variance, unequal sizes)

subtopics.name: Gaussian mixtures: soft assignment, EM, and choosing components by BIC
subtopics.learn: Read the GMM as the probabilistic generalisation of k-means: p(x) = sum_k pi_k N(x | mu_k, Sigma_k), fitted by EM, where the E-step computes responsibilities gamma_ik = pi_k N(x_i | mu_k, Sigma_k) / sum_j pi_j N(x_i | mu_j, Sigma_j) and the M-step sets mu_k, Sigma_k and pi_k to responsibility-weighted moments. Be able to show that k-means is the limiting case as Sigma_k -> sigma^2 I with sigma -> 0, where the responsibilities become hard 0/1 assignments. Know that EM increases the log-likelihood monotonically but converges to a local optimum, and that it can degenerate - a component collapsing onto a single point sends the likelihood to infinity - which is why sklearn exposes reg_covar and why you initialise from k-means. Treat covariance_type ('full', 'tied', 'diag', 'spherical') as the explicit bias-variance knob: 'full' costs k*d(d+1)/2 parameters and overfits wide tables, 'diag' is usually the right compromise. Select the number of components by BIC = -2 log L + p log n over a grid, which is the only genuinely principled 'choose k' procedure in this whole topic, and know BayesianGaussianMixture can prune unused components via a Dirichlet-process prior instead.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Gaussian mixture models (EM, covariance_type, BIC selection)

subtopics.name: Scoring a clustering against known labels: ARI, AMI and correction for chance
subtopics.learn: When the customer does have some labels - a hand-tagged sample, a legacy segmentation - use external indices, and understand precisely what correction for chance buys: the raw Rand index of two random partitions is nowhere near zero and grows with the number of clusters, so you report ARI = (RI - E[RI]) / (max RI - E[RI]), which is 0 for random labelling, 1 for identical partitions, and can go negative. Know when to prefer AMI: mutual information is likewise inflated by many small clusters, adjusted_mutual_info_score corrects for it, and the standard guidance is AMI when clusters are unbalanced and small, ARI when they are large and roughly equal in size. Understand that homogeneity, completeness and V-measure decompose the same idea (each cluster holds one class, each class sits in one cluster, and their harmonic mean) and that V-measure is not adjusted for chance, so it drifts upward with k. Use these to grade your from-scratch implementations against scikit-learn on identical input - the deliverable's ARI >= 0.95 bar - and remember that all of them are invariant to label permutation, which is exactly what makes them the right tool.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Adjustment for chance in clustering performance evaluation

subtopics.name: DBSCAN: core points, density-reachability, and the border points that are not deterministic
subtopics.learn: Learn the definitions exactly, because everything else follows from them: p is a core point when |N_eps(p)| >= min_samples (sklearn counts p itself); q is directly density-reachable from a core point p when q lies in N_eps(p); a cluster is a maximal set closed under density-reachability and joined by density-connectivity; anything not reachable from any core point is noise and gets label -1. Understand what that buys and what it costs - clusters take any shape, k is not a parameter, and outliers get an explicit label - but a border point (non-core, yet inside the eps-ball of core points from two different clusters) goes to whichever cluster reaches it first, so the result depends on row order; this is why implementations legitimately differ on those points and why a border-point assignment must never carry business meaning. Know the cost model: roughly O(n log n) with a spatial index in low dimension, degrading towards O(n^2) as dimension rises and the index stops pruning, and note that a large eps blows up memory because sklearn materialises neighbourhoods - mitigate by passing a precomputed sparse radius-neighbours graph as metric='precomputed'. Note finally that DBSCAN has no predict method by design: scoring a new point requires a re-fit or a nearest-core-point rule that you write and document.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.cluster.DBSCAN (eps, min_samples, core_sample_indices_, noise label -1)

subtopics.name: Setting eps and min_samples from a k-distance plot
subtopics.learn: Fix min_samples first from reasoning rather than search: the standard heuristic is min_samples >= d + 1, often 2*d, and larger for noisy data, and it is directly the answer to 'how many points constitute a cluster rather than noise here'. Then derive eps instead of guessing it: fit NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=min_samples), take each point's distance to its min_samples-th neighbour, sort those distances in descending order and plot them - the knee where the curve turns sharply upward separates points in dense regions from points in sparse ones, and that y-value is your eps; compute the knee reproducibly with a maximum-distance-to-chord calculation rather than eyeballing it. Validate by sweeping eps across a range around the knee and plotting three curves together - number of clusters, noise fraction, and silhouette computed over non-noise points only - because a defensible eps sits on a plateau, and an eps where the cluster count swings from 3 to 40 over a five percent change is telling you the data has no single density scale (which is the argument for HDBSCAN). Be able to say what the -1 label means to the customer in one sentence: these are not anomalies, they are the points our density threshold could not group - and then check that the noise set is not itself a coherent segment you just deleted.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Demo of DBSCAN clustering algorithm (labels, noise, evaluation)

subtopics.name: HDBSCAN: variable density, mutual reachability and the condensed tree
subtopics.learn: When a single eps cannot serve the whole table - dense metropolitan accounts alongside sparse rural ones - HDBSCAN removes eps entirely: define a point's core distance as the distance to its min_samples-th neighbour, define the mutual reachability distance d_mreach(a, b) = max(core_k(a), core_k(b), d(a, b)), which pushes sparse points apart while leaving dense regions untouched, build the minimum spanning tree under that metric, and read a single-linkage hierarchy off it. Understand cluster extraction: condense the tree by enforcing min_cluster_size, then select clusters by excess of mass (cluster_selection_method='eom', the default, which prefers persistent clusters) or 'leaf' (finer, more clusters), with cluster_selection_epsilon as the knob that stops splitting below a distance scale you consider meaningless. Keep the two parameters distinct in your head and in the customer conversation: min_cluster_size is 'the smallest group they would actually act on', min_samples is the conservatism/noise knob - and probabilities_ gives a per-point membership strength, which is a far better artefact than DBSCAN's hard -1. It has shipped in scikit-learn as cluster.HDBSCAN since 1.3, so it costs you no new dependency on a locked-down customer host.

resource.label: hdbscan docs - How HDBSCAN works (mutual reachability, MST, condensed tree, excess of mass)

subtopics.name: Agglomerative clustering: linkage criteria, Lance-Williams, and Ward
subtopics.learn: The algorithm itself is one line - start with n singletons, repeatedly merge the closest pair, stop at one - so every modelling decision lives in the word 'closest'. Know the four criteria and their signatures: single linkage is the minimum pairwise distance (finds elongated and chained shapes, and suffers the chaining effect where a thread of noise points fuses two real clusters), complete linkage is the maximum (compact clusters of similar diameter, sensitive to outliers), average linkage (UPGMA) is the mean, and Ward merges the pair that minimises the increase in total within-cluster variance, which makes it the hierarchical analogue of k-means and therefore valid only with Euclidean distance - scipy's linkage() will reject method='ward' with metric='cityblock'. Know that all of them are computed incrementally by the Lance-Williams recurrence, which is what makes an O(n^2) memory, O(n^2 log n) time implementation possible without recomputing distances after every merge. Know the practical ceiling: the full distance matrix is n^2, so a laptop tops out around 30-50k rows unless you pass a connectivity matrix from kneighbors_graph to AgglomerativeClustering, which both constrains merges to neighbours and makes the run tractable. Be able to say why you would choose it over k-means at all: you get the whole hierarchy, which is what a customer's taxonomy conversation actually needs.

resource.label: SciPy - scipy.cluster.hierarchy.linkage (methods, Ward formula, the linkage matrix Z)

subtopics.name: Reading, cutting and validating a dendrogram
subtopics.learn: Read the linkage matrix Z as (n-1) rows of [idx_a, idx_b, merge_distance, n_points_in_new_cluster], and read the plot as merge height = the dissimilarity at which two groups fused, so a long vertical edge below a merge means those two groups stayed distinct over a wide range of thresholds and is the actual evidence for cutting there. Cut with fcluster(Z, t, criterion='distance') for a dissimilarity threshold or criterion='maxclust' for a fixed cluster count, and treat the cut as a decision you defend with the gap between successive merge heights plus the same silhouette and bootstrap-stability evidence you used to pick k - never with the picture alone. Validate the tree itself with the cophenetic correlation coefficient, the Pearson correlation between the original pairwise distances and the merge heights at which each pair first joins (scipy's cophenet): a value near 0.5 means the dendrogram is a poor summary of the real geometry no matter where you cut it. Watch for inversions, a merge occurring at a lower height than one of its children, which cannot happen for single, complete, average or Ward linkage but does for centroid and median - an inversion is the sign that the plot you were about to put in front of a customer is not a valid hierarchy.

resource.label: SciPy - scipy.cluster.hierarchy.dendrogram (color_threshold, truncate_mode, reading the tree)

subtopics.name: PCA two ways: the covariance eigenproblem, the SVD, and Eckart-Young
subtopics.learn: Derive it once by hand. For column-centred X (n x d), maximise Var(Xw) = w^T S w subject to ||w|| = 1 with S = X^T X / (n - 1); the Lagrangian gives S w = lambda w, so the loadings are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix and lambda_j is the variance explained by component j. Then derive the same thing from the SVD X = U Sigma V^T: the right singular vectors V are exactly those eigenvectors, the scores are X V = U Sigma, and lambda_j = sigma_j^2 / (n - 1) - and know that every real implementation takes this route, because forming X^T X squares the condition number and loses precision on ill-conditioned data. State the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem - truncating to the top r singular triples gives the best rank-r approximation in both the Frobenius and spectral norms - because that is the sentence that makes PCA a compression guarantee rather than an act of faith. Implement it with np.linalg.svd(X_centred, full_matrices=False), reconcile against sklearn's PCA up to a per-component sign flip (the deliverable's 'matching up to sign' clause - resolve it by forcing the largest-magnitude loading in each component to be positive), and confirm for yourself that mean-centring is mandatory while dividing by n-1 rather than n only rescales the eigenvalues.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - ch.02 Matrices, 05. Decompositions (eigendecomposition, SVD, low-rank approximation)

subtopics.name: Reading a scree plot, and the four ways PCA misleads
subtopics.learn: Choose the number of components from explained_variance_ratio_ with a rule you can name and defend: the elbow of the scree plot, a cumulative-variance target (80/90/95 percent), Kaiser's eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule on standardised data (well known to over-retain), or parallel analysis, which compares your eigenvalues to those of a column-permuted copy of the same matrix and is the most honest of the four. Then learn where the method lies. It is scale-dependent, so PCA on unstandardised columns is a report about whichever column has the largest units; it maximises variance rather than discriminative or predictive power, so the component you discard may be the one that separates the classes (contrast with LDA); it is linear, orthogonal and global, so a curved manifold needs many components to describe; and it is a least-squares method, so a handful of outliers can rotate the leading components on their own. Fix the interpretation rules in your head: components_ (the loadings) tell you what a component is made of, the sign of each component is arbitrary, and every component after the first is constrained to be orthogonal to its predecessors, which is a mathematical artefact and not a claim about the customer's domain. Use whiten=True only deliberately - it rescales each component to unit variance, which helps downstream distance-based learners and destroys exactly the relative-importance information the scree plot just gave you.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.decomposition.PCA (n_components, explained_variance_ratio_, whiten, svd_solver)

subtopics.name: PCA when the matrix is large or the structure is nonlinear
subtopics.learn: Know the four escapes and the trigger for each: svd_solver='randomized' (Halko et al.) computes the top r components by projecting onto a random subspace and is what makes PCA on a 100k x 5k table tractable; IncrementalPCA with partial_fit handles data that does not fit in memory and lets you fit from a generator; TruncatedSVD does not centre the data and is therefore the correct choice for sparse TF-IDF or count matrices, where centring would densify them (this is LSA); and KernelPCA(kernel='rbf') performs PCA in a feature space via the centred kernel matrix, costs O(n^2) memory, and needs fit_inverse_transform=True if you want to project back. Be explicit about when PCA is the right preprocessing for the rest of this topic: reducing to 30-50 components before t-SNE or UMAP denoises the data and speeds up the neighbour search, and is standard practice; reducing before DBSCAN changes the very density structure you are about to measure, so do it consciously and report that you did. Last, remember PCA is a fitted transformer with learned state, so inside any supervised pipeline it must live in the Pipeline and be refit on every training fold.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Decomposing signals in components (PCA variants, randomized SVD, KernelPCA)

subtopics.name: t-SNE: the KL objective, perplexity, and the plot you must not over-read
subtopics.learn: Understand the construction end to end: symmetrised conditional Gaussian affinities p_ij in the input space, with a per-point bandwidth sigma_i found by binary search so that the perplexity 2^H(P_i) matches the requested value (an effective neighbour count, typically 5-50); Student-t affinities with one degree of freedom q_ij in the map; and gradient descent on KL(P || Q). Derive why the heavy tail matters - it lets moderately distant points sit far apart in the map at little cost, which is van der Maaten's fix for the crowding problem - and note that the asymmetry of KL(P||Q) makes it expensive to place nearby points far apart and cheap to place distant points nearby, so t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods and discards global geometry by design, not by accident. Learn the parameters that change the answer: perplexity (run 5, 30 and 50 and trust only what is stable across them), learning_rate (sklearn's 'auto' is n / early_exaggeration / 4, and the old default of 200 is what produced the notorious compressed 'ball' on large n), early_exaggeration, n_iter, and init='pca' rather than 'random', now the default and materially better for global structure. Then adopt the three reading rules permanently: cluster sizes carry no information because the per-point bandwidth equalises density, between-cluster distances carry no information, and convincing clusters appear in pure Gaussian noise at low perplexity - a t-SNE plot is a hypothesis generator, never evidence.

resource.label: Distill - How to Use t-SNE Effectively (perplexity, cluster sizes, distances, noise)

subtopics.name: UMAP: the neighbour graph, n_neighbors versus min_dist, and the honest t-SNE comparison
subtopics.learn: Read UMAP operationally rather than categorically: build a k-NN graph, convert distances to fuzzy membership strengths with a per-point local-connectivity normalisation (each point is joined to its nearest neighbour with weight 1, which is the local density-equalisation step), symmetrise by fuzzy union, then lay out a low-dimensional graph by minimising a fuzzy set cross-entropy with negative sampling and SGD - and note that this cross-entropy, unlike t-SNE's KL, penalises both attraction and repulsion errors, which is the technical reason UMAP retains somewhat more global structure. Learn the two parameters that matter and exactly what each controls: n_neighbors trades local against global structure (small values fragment the map into islands, large values smooth toward a manifold-level view), while min_dist controls only how tightly points are packed in the embedding and is therefore a cosmetic parameter that must never be interpreted as cluster tightness. Know the operational advantages that will decide it for you on site - far faster than t-SNE at 10^5-10^6 rows, a real transform() so new points can be embedded into an existing map, and supervised and metric-learning variants - alongside the shared caveat that the 'sizes and distances mean nothing' rules still apply and that results move with random_state and with the approximate neighbour search. Be ready for the strongest criticism too: Chari and Pachter's argument that 2-D embeddings preserve so little of the original distance structure that conclusions drawn from their geometry are unreliable.

resource.label: arXiv:1802.03426 - UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (McInnes, Healy, Melville)

subtopics.name: Measuring what an embedding destroyed: trustworthiness, continuity and stability
subtopics.learn: Stop arguing about which embedding looks better and measure the distortion instead: trustworthiness(X, X_embedded, n_neighbors=k) lies in [0, 1] and penalises points that are k-nearest neighbours in the map but were far apart in the original space (false neighbours - precisely the artefact that creates fake clusters), while its dual, continuity, penalises true neighbours that were torn apart; report both at several values of k, because they trade off against each other. Add the checks that catch the rest: a Shepard diagram correlating original against embedded pairwise distances, which shows explicitly how little global structure survived; three random seeds overlaid so the reader can see which features of the layout are stable; and a run on a column-permuted copy of the data as a null, to see what structure the method invents out of noise. When the customer's real question is 'are these genuinely distinct groups', do not answer it from the picture - cluster in the original or PCA-reduced space, then colour the embedding by that clustering, so the map is used for display while the claim rests on the higher-dimensional analysis. The sentence to carry into the room: the embedding is a lossy visualisation of a neighbour graph, so it can support 'these points are near each other' and can never support 'these two groups are twice as far apart as those'.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.manifold.trustworthiness (definition and n_neighbors)

subtopics.name: Shipping it: pipeline placement, reproducibility, scoring new points, and drift
subtopics.learn: Assemble the real artefact as a Pipeline of ColumnTransformer -> scaler -> PCA -> clusterer, so every fitted step is refit correctly and one code path serves both the analysis and tomorrow's scoring; and settle the architectural question before choosing the algorithm, because KMeans and GaussianMixture expose predict() while DBSCAN, t-SNE and plain agglomerative do not (HDBSCAN needs approximate_predict), so 'score new accounts nightly' silently rules some of them out. Pin reproducibility explicitly with random_state on KMeans, GaussianMixture, TSNE and UMAP, and know that even then BLAS version and thread count can move results in the last decimals, so what you hand over is a serialised fitted model plus a hash of its training input, not a notebook someone reruns. Monitor drift on quantities that actually move: the distribution of distance-to-assigned-centroid (a growing tail means new structure the model cannot express), cluster population shares, and for density methods the noise fraction - and set the retrain trigger on those rather than on a calendar. Finally, make the labels usable: describe each cluster by the z-scored deviation of its centroid from the global mean in a small profile table, which beats any plot in a customer meeting, and keep a stable cluster-ID mapping across retrains, because cluster 3 becoming cluster 5 after a refit breaks every dashboard downstream without raising a single error.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Common pitfalls and recommended practices (data transformation, randomness, random_state)

outcomes: You can implement k-means++ with Lloyd, DBSCAN, agglomerative clustering with single/complete/Ward linkage, and PCA via SVD in vectorised NumPy, and reproduce scikit-learn's partition at ARI >= 0.95 and its components to rtol=1e-10 after fixing the per-component sign convention.

You can derive both k-means update rules by coordinate descent, prove the objective decreases monotonically, and explain from that derivation alone why the method is bound to squared Euclidean distance and the arithmetic mean.

You can choose k on an unlabelled customer table and defend it with a table of inertia, per-cluster silhouette (not just the mean), gap statistic, Calinski-Harabasz and a bootstrap-ARI stability score, and say which k the customer can actually operationalise.

You can produce a k-distance plot, read eps off the knee, sweep it to show the plateau in cluster count, noise fraction and non-noise silhouette, and state precisely what DBSCAN's -1 label does and does not say about those rows.

You can pick between k-means, GMM, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN and Ward agglomerative in under five minutes given a data description, justifying it from cluster shape, density variation, whether new points must be scored, and n.

You can state the three t-SNE and UMAP reading rules from memory and back them with computed evidence: trustworthiness and continuity at several k, a Shepard diagram, a three-seed overlay, and a permuted-data null.
You can read a dendrogram, defend a cut with the gap between successive merge heights, report the cophenetic correlation for the tree, and spot an inversion before the plot reaches a customer.
You can turn anonymous cluster IDs into a z-score profile table a non-technical stakeholder can act on, with a stable-ID mapping across retrains and a named drift trigger beside it.
failureModes: Columns were not standardised before k-means, so annual_revenue in dollars dominated the squared-Euclidean objective; the 'behavioural segmentation' delivered to marketing was a revenue quantile split with extra steps, and nobody noticed until a segment was defined by a currency conversion.

The scaler and PCA were fit on the whole table before the downstream classifier's train/test split, so the clustering-derived features carried information from the test rows and the supervised metric was inflated by several points that evaporated in production.

k was chosen from an elbow that did not exist on a smooth inertia curve; the selected k=4 had a mean silhouette of 0.19 with two clusters containing substantial negative-silhouette membership, and the segmentation did not reproduce on the next quarter's data.

DBSCAN was run over 60 one-hot columns with the default eps=0.5; distance concentration meant the result was either one giant cluster or 90 percent noise, and eps was tuned until the cluster count looked plausible instead of until the k-distance knee justified it.

A t-SNE plot with two clean, well-separated blobs went into a customer deck as evidence of two customer types; the same data showed six blobs at perplexity 5 and one at perplexity 50, and a permuted-data null produced visually similar structure.

Cluster IDs were regenerated on every nightly retrain with no stable-ID mapping, so the dashboard's 'Segment 3' quietly became a different population and every trend line in the customer's QBR deck compared two unrelated groups.

A border point's DBSCAN assignment was used to justify an account's segment; because border points go to whichever cluster reaches them first, re-running with shuffled row order moved several hundred accounts between segments and the customer found it before the team did.

PCA was applied before clustering to 'remove noise', with components chosen at 95 percent cumulative variance on unstandardised data; the discarded low-variance directions were exactly the ones separating the two groups the customer cared about, and no downstream algorithm could recover them.
interviewQuestions: Derive the two k-means update steps from the objective. Why must the distance be squared Euclidean, what does Lloyd's algorithm guarantee about convergence, and what does it explicitly not guarantee?

I hand you a 200k x 80 table of account behaviour, mixed numeric and categorical, and ask for segments I can act on. Walk me through the preprocessing, the distance, the algorithm, how you choose the number of segments, and what artefact you would show me to convince me the segments are real rather than an artefact of the objective.

Explain what DBSCAN's eps and min_samples do and how you would set them without grid-searching for a pretty answer. What is a border point, why is its assignment order-dependent, and how do you score a new point tomorrow against a fitted DBSCAN model?

Derive PCA from both the covariance eigenproblem and the SVD and state what Eckart-Young gives you. Why do real implementations use the SVD rather than forming X^T X, and what exactly does it mean that two implementations' components match 'up to sign'?

A colleague shows a UMAP plot with two large well-separated islands and one small one, and concludes there are three customer types and that the small one is very different from the others. Which parts of that conclusion are supported by the method, which are not, and what would you compute before it goes in front of the customer?

Compare Ward linkage with k-means. Under what conditions do they produce similar partitions, why is Ward restricted to Euclidean distance, and when would you pay the O(n^2) memory cost to get the hierarchy instead?

Debug: your pipeline produced six stable segments in the pilot, and after the customer's next data drop it produces two giant segments plus 30 percent noise. What are the four things you check, in what order, and what would each look like in the data?
106.proofOfWork: A public repo `cluster-audit` that turns this topic into something you can run on a customer's unlabelled table on day two of an engagement, and that produces a memo rather than a notebook. It exposes one entry point, audit(df, numeric_cols, categorical_cols, id_col), which emits five panels: a preprocessing panel reporting per-column scale ratios, cardinality, missingness and a measured distance-concentration statistic ((d_max - d_min)/d_min at several dimensionalities) with an explicit recommendation of metric and scaler; a k-selection panel giving inertia, per-cluster silhouette plots, gap statistic against a PCA-aligned uniform reference, Calinski-Harabasz, Davies-Bouldin and a bootstrap-ARI stability curve over 20 resamples for k in a stated range; an algorithm bake-off running KMeans, GaussianMixture (BIC-selected), Ward agglomerative, DBSCAN (eps from an automated knee on the k-distance curve) and HDBSCAN on identical preprocessing, reported side by side with cluster counts, noise fractions, internal indices and pairwise ARI between the algorithms' partitions so disagreement is visible rather than hidden; an embedding-honesty panel producing t-SNE at perplexity 5/30/50 and UMAP at n_neighbors 5/15/50, each with three seeds overlaid, plus trustworthiness and continuity at k = 5, 15 and 50, a Shepard diagram, and the same panel recomputed on a column-permuted null so the reader can see what the method invents from noise; and a handover panel with the z-score centroid profile table, a stable cluster-ID mapping keyed to the previous run, and the drift monitors (distance-to-centroid tail quantiles, population shares, noise fraction) with proposed retrain thresholds. Run it end to end on two public tables with genuinely different structure - one with well-separated convex clusters and one with variable density or non-convex shape, such as a wholesale-customers table and a geospatial or gesture table - and commit the two generated memos. CI asserts the from-scratch implementations still match scikit-learn (ARI >= 0.95 for the clusterers, components to rtol=1e-10 up to sign for PCA), and the README opens with a one-page CLUSTERING-CHECKLIST.md written for a customer's data team: the metric and why, the scaler and why, the algorithm and why, the k and the three pieces of evidence for it, what the noise label means, and the two sentences on what the embedding plot may and may not be used to claim.

107.topic: Explainability: SHAP, LIME, permutation importance, partial dependence
107.why: An FDE is the person in the room when a customer's risk officer, clinician or ops lead points at one prediction and asks why - and the honest answer requires knowing exactly what quantity your explanation estimates, on what data, against what baseline. Explainability is also your fastest debugging tool on someone else's data: leakage, a broken encoder, a proxy for the label and a feature the model never actually reads all show up first in an importance ranking or a dependence plot, weeks before they show up in a held-out metric. Get the estimand wrong and you do worse than nothing - you hand a customer a confident, wrong causal story with your name on it, and they act on it.
prerequisites: A fitted gradient-boosted tabular model you can retrain in under a minute, plus the XGBoost/LightGBM API surface (Topic 101, Supervised learning II) - almost every explanation here is demonstrated on trees

Honest held-out evaluation: train/validation/test splits, cross-validation, leakage, and the difference between a score and a loss (Topic 103, Model evaluation) - permutation importance is meaningless without a clean held-out set
Linear and logistic regression with regularisation, including the log-odds link and what a coefficient means (Topic 100, Supervised learning I)
Expectation, conditional expectation and marginal vs conditional distributions (Topic 95, Probability) - the entire PDP/ALE/SHAP argument is about which expectation you are taking

NumPy vectorisation, broadcasting, RNG seeding and in-place-copy hazards (Topic 99, Numerical computing) - the from-scratch implementations are 30-line array routines where an aliasing bug silently zeroes results
matplotlib well enough to draw a grid of curves with a rug plot and a colour dimension, since half of this topic is a plot you have to defend

subtopics.name: Which question is the customer actually asking
subtopics.learn: Separate the four questions people conflate under 'explain the model': (a) which features does the model rely on overall - global importance; (b) how does the score move as one feature sweeps - global effect, PDP/ALE; (c) why did this row get this score - local attribution, SHAP/LIME; (d) what would have to change to flip it - counterfactual/recourse. Map each to the method and to the quantity it estimates, and be able to say that all four are properties of the fitted model, not of the world: none is a causal claim unless the model was identified causally (Topic 97). Read Lipton's decomposition of transparency (simulatability, decomposability, algorithmic transparency) versus post-hoc interpretability so you can name in a meeting which one is being requested, and know Rudin's counterargument (arXiv 1811.10154) that for high-stakes decisions the right move is sometimes an interpretable model instead of an explanation of a black box.

resource.label: Lipton - The Mythos of Model Interpretability (arXiv 1606.03490)

subtopics.name: The interpretable baseline: coefficients you can defend
subtopics.learn: Before explaining a GBM, be able to read the model you would otherwise have shipped. For logistic regression, exp(beta_j) is the multiplicative effect on the odds per unit of x_j with the others held fixed; know that standardising changes the units of beta but not the fitted probabilities, that L2 with one-hot dummies spreads one effect across correlated columns, and that a coefficient's sign can flip when a collinear feature enters. Reproduce the sklearn pitfalls example: plot coefficient variability across cross-validation folds, show a huge coefficient on a near-zero-variance feature, and show OLS coefficients swinging fold to fold on correlated inputs while ridge stays put. Carry the lesson into SHAP: an unstable attribution is usually the data's collinearity, not a bug in the method.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Common pitfalls in the interpretation of coefficients of linear models

subtopics.name: Impurity importance (MDI) and why the library default lies
subtopics.learn: MDI for feature j is the sum over all nodes split on j of the sample-weighted impurity decrease, averaged over trees and normalised to sum to 1. Know its two structural biases: it favours high-cardinality and continuous features because they offer more candidate split points (a random UUID or a timestamp ranks near the top), and it is computed on training data, so it rewards exactly what the model overfits. Reproduce the sklearn example where an injected random column outranks a real predictor under MDI and collapses to zero under permutation importance on the held-out fold. Know that XGBoost's importance_type variants disagree with each other - 'weight' counts splits, 'gain' averages loss reduction, 'cover' weights by hessian mass - and that plot_importance defaults to 'weight', the least defensible of the three.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Permutation Importance vs Random Forest Feature Importance (MDI)

subtopics.name: Permutation importance: the estimator, implemented from the definition
subtopics.learn: Implement PFI_j = (1/K) * sum_k L(y, f(X with column j permuted by pi_k)) - L(y, f(X)), evaluated on held-out data with a loss you chose deliberately (log loss for a probabilistic model, MAE for a regressor, ROC AUC only if ranking is the product). In NumPy: save the column, rng.permutation it, score, restore in place - and never permute an already-permuted column, an aliasing bug that silently zeroes every later feature. Report mean and standard deviation over n_repeats: the null is centred near zero, so a feature whose interval straddles zero is indistinguishable from noise and negative values are normal, not a bug. Reconcile digit-for-digit with sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance(model, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=30, random_state=0, scoring='neg_log_loss'), matching both the RNG and the sign convention (sklearn reports baseline minus permuted for a score, so larger is more important).

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Permutation feature importance

subtopics.name: Correlated features: why the ranking moves, and how to fix the question
subtopics.learn: With two near-duplicate columns the model can read either one, so permuting one alone barely hurts the loss and both look unimportant - the importance is split or hidden, never shared. Diagnose it the way the sklearn example does: Spearman rank correlation, convert to a distance, hierarchical cluster with Ward linkage, cut the dendrogram at a threshold, then permute whole clusters jointly and report 'the block {tenure, months_active, days_since_first_seen} is worth 0.08 log loss' instead of three misleading zeros. Understand the second, distinct effect: shuffling one of two dependent columns manufactures impossible rows (age 20 with retired=1), so part of the measured loss increase is extrapolation error rather than reliance, and it inflates rather than deflates the number.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Permutation Importance with Multicollinear or Correlated Features

subtopics.name: When permutation is the wrong estimator: LOCO, drop-column, conditional variants
subtopics.learn: Distinguish reliance of this fitted model (permutation: one fit, cheap, answers 'what does the deployed model read') from importance to the learning problem (drop-column / LOCO: refit without feature j, M+1 fits, answers 'can we stop collecting this field'). Read Hooker and Mentch's argument that permutation evaluates f far off the data manifold and their proposed alternatives - conditional permutation within strata of the correlated features, and permute-then-relearn - and adopt the operating rule: if your recommendation is to remove a field from the customer's pipeline, LOCO is the estimate that supports it; if you are debugging what the shipped model uses, permutation is correct. Whichever you compute, be able to state in one sentence which of the two quantities your number is.

resource.label: Hooker & Mentch - Please Stop Permuting Features (arXiv 1905.03151)

subtopics.name: Partial dependence: the marginal expectation and its Monte-Carlo estimator
subtopics.learn: Derive PD_S(x_S) = E_{X_C}[f(x_S, X_C)] and its estimator (1/n) * sum_i f(x_S, x_C^(i)): the model is evaluated once per observed complement row per grid point, which is why the plot costs |grid| * n forward passes and why it fabricates impossible rows whenever x_S and X_C are dependent. Implement it in NumPy on a percentile grid (5th to 95th, to keep tail noise out), add decile ticks or a rug so the customer can see where there is no data, and state the assumption out loud: PD is a causal effect only if the complement features are not confounders. Reconcile with sklearn.inspection.partial_dependence(est, X, features=[i], kind='average', grid_resolution=50), and know that method='recursion' for trees skips the data pass, is far faster, and answers a different question (training-distribution conditional) than method='brute'.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Partial dependence and individual conditional expectation

subtopics.name: ICE and centred ICE: the heterogeneity the average destroys
subtopics.learn: An ICE curve is f(x_S, x_C^(i)) for one fixed row i as x_S sweeps the grid; the PDP is exactly the pointwise mean of them. Learn to read the shapes: parallel curves mean no interaction with the complement, fanning or crossing curves mean interaction, and a flat PDP with half the curves rising and half falling means two subpopulations cancelling. Use centred ICE (subtract each curve's value at an anchor x_S = x*) so slopes rather than levels are compared. Produce it with PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(est, X, features, kind='both', centered=True, subsample=200), and the moment you see fanning, colour the curves by a candidate feature and find the interaction - that coloured c-ICE panel, not the PDP, is what belongs in the customer deck.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Partial Dependence and Individual Conditional Expectation Plots

subtopics.name: Interactions: two-dimensional PDPs and Friedman's H-statistic
subtopics.learn: H^2_jk = sum_i [PD_jk(x_j^i, x_k^i) - PD_j(x_j^i) - PD_k(x_k^i)]^2 / sum_i PD_jk(x_j^i, x_k^i)^2 is the share of the two-way partial dependence not explained by the two additive parts; the one-versus-all variant H_j does the same against the full prediction. Be able to compute it for one pair and to state its two practical limits: cost is O(n^2) model evaluations per pair so you must subsample rows, and the denominator can be near zero, which produces H values above 1 and unstable rankings on small samples - always recompute on a second subsample before you believe it. Confirm every H flag against a 2-D PDP contour or a SHAP interaction value before telling a customer that two of their fields interact.

resource.label: Friedman & Popescu - Predictive Learning via Rule Ensembles (H-statistic, arXiv 0811.1679)

subtopics.name: ALE plots: the fix when features are correlated
subtopics.learn: Instead of averaging over the marginal of X_C, ALE splits x_j into quantile intervals, computes the local difference f(z_k, x_C) - f(z_{k-1}, x_C) using only rows whose x_j actually falls in that interval, then accumulates and centres - so the model is never evaluated off the data manifold. Learn the three-line contrast you will say out loud: PDP is a marginal expectation, an M-plot is a conditional expectation and therefore mixes in the effects of correlated features, ALE accumulates conditional differences and isolates the effect of x_j. Know the costs: piecewise output, noisy with too many bins, no ICE analogue, and second-order ALE that is hard to read. Operating rule: when |Spearman| between x_j and any other feature exceeds roughly 0.6, show ALE alongside the PDP and explain the gap rather than hoping nobody asks.

resource.label: Apley & Zhu - Visualizing the Effects of Predictor Variables in Black Box Supervised Learning Models (ALE, arXiv 1612.08468)

subtopics.name: Shapley values: the axioms and the exact combinatorial formula
subtopics.learn: Treat one prediction as a cooperative game with value function v(S) = E[f(X) | X_S = x_S] and derive phi_j = sum over S subset of M\{j} of |S|!(M-|S|-1)!/M! * [v(S union {j}) - v(S)] as the unique attribution satisfying efficiency (sum_j phi_j = f(x) - E[f(X)]), symmetry, dummy and linearity. Be able to do this by hand for a three-feature model over all eight coalitions and to verify efficiency numerically. Read Lundberg and Lee's framing of LIME, DeepLIFT and layer-wise relevance propagation as one class of additive feature-attribution methods, and internalise the cost that motivates everything after this subtopic: exact Shapley needs 2^M coalitions, so every practical method is an approximation - coalition sampling, KernelSHAP, or exploiting model structure as TreeSHAP does.

resource.label: Lundberg & Lee - A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions (arXiv 1705.07874)

subtopics.name: KernelSHAP: Shapley values as a weighted least-squares problem
