subtopics.learn: Sample coalitions z in {0,1}^M, map them back to inputs (present = the row's value, absent = drawn from the background set), and fit a weighted linear model minimising sum_z pi(z) [f(h_x(z)) - (phi_0 + sum_j phi_j z_j)]^2 with the Shapley kernel pi(z) = (M-1) / (C(M,|z|) * |z| * (M-|z|)); the fitted coefficients are the Shapley values. Implement it: enumerate all coalitions when M <= 12, otherwise draw by subset size from the kernel's extremes inward, impose the all-zeros and all-ones coalitions as hard constraints so phi_0 = E[f] and sum phi = f(x), add a small ridge term to keep the design matrix invertible, and count model calls as nsamples * |background|. Compare with shap.KernelExplainer(f, shap.sample(X_bg, 100)).shap_values(x, nsamples=2048), watch convergence as nsamples grows, and report the run-to-run variance, because KernelSHAP is a stochastic estimate that will disagree with itself in the third digit.

resource.label: SHAP docs - shap.KernelExplainer API

subtopics.name: TreeSHAP: exact attributions in polynomial time, and its two estimands
subtopics.learn: For tree ensembles, phi can be computed exactly in roughly O(T*L*D^2) by pushing all coalitions through the tree simultaneously and tracking what fraction of each subset flows to each leaf - this is why SHAP is affordable on the customer's XGBoost model and KernelSHAP is not. Know the two flavours and that they give different numbers: path-dependent uses the trees' training cover counts to define the conditional expectation and needs no background data, and can assign non-zero credit to a feature the model never splits on if it correlates with one that it does; interventional (feature_perturbation='interventional') requires a background dataset and computes the marginal/interventional expectation, which is the game the SHAP axioms are usually stated for. Also note model_output='raw' returns log-odds for a classifier, so sum(phi) + base reconciles to the margin, not to the probability.

resource.label: Lundberg et al. - Consistent Individualized Feature Attribution for Tree Ensembles (TreeSHAP, arXiv 1802.03888)

subtopics.name: The background dataset is a modelling decision, not a default
subtopics.learn: Every phi is defined relative to a baseline E[f], so 100 random rows, a shap.kmeans summary, an all-zeros row and a curated 'typical approved applicant' produce different explanations of the same prediction - and change the sentence you say from 'compared with the average applicant' to 'compared with an applicant like you'. Read Chen et al. on true-to-the-model (interventional/marginal: breaks feature dependence, credits only features the model actually uses, correct for debugging) versus true-to-the-data (conditional: spreads credit across correlated features, closer to a scientific claim), and be able to state which you chose and what the other would have shown. Pin the background set with a seed, version it as an artifact alongside the model, and record it in the model card - an explanation regenerated against a different background is not reproducible and cannot be defended six months later.

resource.label: Chen, Janizek, Lundberg & Lee - True to the Model or True to the Data? (arXiv 2006.16234)

subtopics.name: Reading one local explanation and proving it adds up
subtopics.learn: For a single row, render the waterfall from E[f(X)] to f(x) and assert efficiency numerically: np.allclose(expl.values.sum() + expl.base_values, model.predict(x, output_margin=True), atol=1e-6). When that assertion fails, the cause is one of a short list - link-function mismatch (log-odds versus probability), the wrong background set, or an approximate explainer that has not converged - and you must identify which before the number reaches a slide. Then narrate the row properly: the base rate, the three features that pushed up, the two that pushed down, in the correct units, plus the explicit sentence that this is the model's arithmetic and not a causal claim. Remember that force and waterfall plots for a classifier default to log-odds space, so '+0.9' is not 0.9 probability, and contributions are not additive after the sigmoid.

resource.label: SHAP docs - waterfall plot example

subtopics.name: Global summaries built from local values, and what they are not
subtopics.learn: mean(|phi_j|) across a dataset - the beeswarm's row ordering - summarises attribution magnitude, not loss degradation; it never looks at y, so it can rank highly a feature the model leans on that carries no held-out predictive value. Present permutation importance (loss-based, needs labels, answers 'does it help') beside mean|SHAP| (model-based, needs no labels, answers 'does it move the score') and explain any disagreement instead of hiding it. Read Kumar et al. on why the Shapley axioms do not transfer to feature-importance claims: the additive model over coalitions is not the model, credit depends on the assumed feature distribution, and phi_j = 0 does not mean the feature is unused. Use the SHAP dependence plot (phi_j against x_j, coloured by the strongest interacting feature) as the honest global-effect plot and cross-check it against the PDP.

resource.label: Kumar et al. - Problems with Shapley-value-based explanations as feature importance measures (arXiv 2002.11097)

subtopics.name: LIME: the local surrogate and everything you must pin down
subtopics.learn: Implement it: perturb around x (tabular LIME discretises features and samples from training marginals, then measures similarity in the original space), weight each sample by the exponential kernel exp(-D(x,z)^2 / sigma^2), fit a K-sparse ridge or lasso on the interpretable binary representation, and report both the coefficients and the surrogate's local R^2 - the fidelity that most tutorials never print, and without which the explanation is unfalsifiable. Know the four knobs that change the answer: kernel width sigma (default sqrt(n_features) * 0.75, essentially arbitrary), num_samples, the discretiser (quartile by default, so 'age > 43.0' is a bin edge, not a threshold the model uses), and the seed - run the same explanation five times and show the top-3 moving. State what LIME buys you over SHAP: a human-readable rule-like local model, paid for with no efficiency guarantee, since its weights do not sum to the prediction.

resource.label: Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin - Why Should I Trust You? (LIME, arXiv 1602.04938)

subtopics.name: Fragility: explanations can be adversarial, and methods disagree
subtopics.learn: Understand the Slack et al. scaffolding attack: because KernelSHAP and LIME query the model on off-manifold perturbed points, an adversary can wrap a biased model in a detector that recognises synthetic inputs and returns an innocuous surrogate on them - producing a clean explanation for a discriminatory deployment. Take the operational lessons rather than the paranoia: check whether your perturbations are in-distribution (train a quick classifier to separate perturbed rows from real ones), prefer interventional TreeSHAP or background sets drawn from real data, and never accept an explanation produced by an untrusted third party as evidence. Learn the disagreement problem too: on the same row, permutation importance, SHAP and LIME frequently rank differently, and the professional response is to name the estimand each answers and show all three, not to quietly pick the one that supports the story.

resource.label: Slack et al. - Fooling LIME and SHAP: Adversarial Attacks on Post hoc Explanation Methods (arXiv 1911.02508)

subtopics.name: Counterfactual explanations and actionable recourse
subtopics.learn: The question after every SHAP waterfall is 'so what do I change?', and that is a counterfactual, not an attribution. Formulate it as x' = argmin over x' of (f(x') - y')^2 + lambda * d(x, x') with d a MAD-weighted L1 distance, and know the four properties a usable counterfactual needs: validity (it really flips the model), proximity, sparsity (few features changed) and actionability (no immutable attributes, no changes that violate a monotone or logical constraint). Counterfactuals need no model internals and no background dataset, which makes them the easiest explanation to defend in a regulated setting; they are also non-unique, so generate a diverse set and let the customer choose. Say the caveat out loud: a counterfactual is recourse only when the features are causally manipulable - 'raise your credit score by 40 points' is not advice.

resource.label: Wachter, Mittelstadt & Russell - Counterfactual Explanations without Opening the Black Box (arXiv 1711.00399)

subtopics.name: Shipping it: explainer choice, compute budget and the handover artifact
subtopics.learn: Choose the explainer from the model and the SLA rather than habit: TreeExplainer (exact, milliseconds, tree ensembles), LinearExplainer, PermutationExplainer (model-agnostic, roughly 2M+1 forward passes per row at max_evals), the auto-dispatching Explainer(model, masker), GPUTree for large ensembles - and compute the budget as rows * background_size * coalitions model calls before promising per-request explanations behind an API. Design the serving path deliberately: precompute and store phi during batch scoring, cache the background summary and base value as versioned artifacts next to the model, pin explainer + background + model together, and set a latency budget (a 2-second KernelSHAP call inside a 200 ms endpoint is an outage, not a feature). The handover artifact is a model-card section naming the method, the estimand, the background set, the uncertainty of the numbers, and one worked row with the exact sentence you would say to the customer.

resource.label: SHAP docs - API reference (explainers, maskers, plots)

outcomes: You can implement permutation importance, PDP + ICE and KernelSHAP in NumPy straight from their definitions and reconcile each against sklearn.inspection and the shap library to a stated tolerance, explaining every remaining difference (RNG stream, background sample, brute vs recursion, log-odds vs probability).

You can compute Shapley values by hand for a three-feature model over all eight coalitions, verify sum(phi) = f(x) - E[f(X)] numerically, and derive the Shapley kernel as the weighting that makes a weighted least-squares fit return those same values.

You can demonstrate with numbers on one dataset that MDI ranks an injected random column near the top, permutation importance on the test fold does not, and joint permutation of a correlated cluster recovers importance that both single-column permutations reported as zero.

You can look at a c-ICE panel and state whether an interaction exists, identify the interacting feature by colouring the curves, and confirm or refute it with a 2-D PDP or an H-statistic computed on two independent subsamples.

You can choose between path-dependent and interventional TreeSHAP for a given customer question, justify the background dataset in one sentence, and state how the attributions would shift under the other choice.

You can produce a one-page defensible explanation of a single high-stakes prediction: base value, top contributions in correct units, a passing additivity assertion, a fidelity or convergence statistic, a counterfactual for recourse, and an explicit statement of what the explanation does not claim.

You can state the per-row compute cost of each explainer, pick one that fits a latency budget, and design the precompute/caching/versioning path that keeps a stored explanation reproducible months later.

You can show SHAP, LIME and permutation importance disagreeing on the same row and explain the disagreement in terms of the different estimands, instead of selecting the ranking that supports a preferred narrative.
failureModes: Permutation importance is computed on the training set for a deep, barely regularised ensemble; every feature looks important because the model memorised, the customer trusts the ranking, drops the one feature you called weak, and held-out AUC falls.

monthly_spend and annual_spend/12 are both in the frame; each permuted alone costs the model almost nothing, both score near zero, the team removes both to simplify the pipeline, and recall drops six points overnight.

xgboost.plot_importance is pasted into a deck with the default importance_type='weight', so the chart is really a split-count ranking dominated by a high-cardinality near-identifier, and the customer's team spends a sprint investigating a column that carries no signal.

A PDP over a feature correlated at 0.9 with another is presented as 'raising price from 10 to 200 does nothing to churn'; the flat curve came from scoring rows that cannot exist (price 200 with plan='free'), and the ALE plot on the same data shows a steep effect.

TreeSHAP is run with the default path-dependent perturbation and the output is described to a compliance reviewer as each field's contribution to the decision; two correlated fields split credit for a decision the model actually made on only one of them.

A waterfall reading '+1.4 for income' is quoted as a probability change when the explainer returned raw log-odds, so the real effect is about five percentage points, and the correction arrives after the deck is already with the customer's risk committee.

LIME explanations for a disputed case are regenerated a week later with a different seed and num_samples; the top three features change, the customer sees two versions of the same explanation, and nobody had ever printed the local R^2 of 0.18 that would have shown the surrogate never fit in the first place.

The KernelSHAP background was shap.sample(X_train, 100) with no seed and was never saved; six months later, during a dispute, the stored attributions cannot be reproduced and there is no way to show the explanation attached to that decision was ever correct.
interviewQuestions: Derive the Shapley value from its axioms, then show how KernelSHAP recovers it as a weighted linear regression. What is the Shapley kernel, why does it diverge at |z| = 0 and |z| = M, and how does a correct implementation handle those two coalitions?

Your permutation importance ranking on the test set contradicts the customer's domain expert, who insists feature X drives their business. Walk me through the diagnosis: what do you check, in what order, and what does each outcome tell you?
Explain the difference between a PDP, an M-plot and an ALE plot for a feature correlated at 0.8 with another. Which do you show the customer, and what exactly do you say about the other two?

Debug: your from-scratch KernelSHAP values sum to 0.31 for a row where the model's margin minus the base value is 0.44. Give me four candidate causes ranked by likelihood, and the single check that distinguishes each one.

Design: a fraud model scores 40 million transactions a day and compliance wants a per-decision explanation retained for seven years. What do you compute, when do you compute it, what exactly do you store, and what do you tell them the stored numbers do and do not mean?
After seeing your partial dependence plot, a stakeholder asks whether increasing X will increase Y. What is your answer, and under precisely what assumptions would the PDP support a causal statement?
Give me two distinct mechanisms by which a SHAP value of zero does not mean the model ignored that feature, and say how you would detect each one.
107.proofOfWork: An `explanation-audit` pack built on a public high-stakes tabular dataset (UCI Adult or the Home Credit / Lending Club style credit data) that is deliberately shaped like something you would leave behind with a customer's risk team rather than a notebook. It contains: one LightGBM model plus one monotone-constrained variant, so you can show what changes in the explanations when the constraint makes the effect true by construction; a disagreement table for twenty sampled rows listing the top-3 features under permutation importance, mean|SHAP|, interventional TreeSHAP, path-dependent TreeSHAP and LIME, with a written paragraph explaining each disagreement in terms of estimand rather than bug; a PDP/ALE/c-ICE panel for the three most correlated features with the Spearman matrix that motivated showing ALE; a reproduced scaffolding attack from the Fooling LIME and SHAP paper on this dataset, with the innocuous explanation next to the biased model's actual behaviour; and a pytest suite that regenerates every attribution from pinned artifacts (seed, background set hash, model hash, library versions) and fails CI when any stored phi moves by more than 1e-6 or the efficiency assertion breaks. The README states the compute cost per explainer measured on your hardware, the latency budget it would fit, and a one-page model-card section written in the language you would actually use in the room.

108.topic: Time series forecasting: decomposition, ARIMA, Prophet, and honest backtesting
108.why: Forecasting is the request an FDE gets most often and defends worst: demand, headcount, spend, seat growth, capacity. It is also the single easiest place to ship a model that is silently wrong, because a random shuffle-split or an in-sample fit produces a beautiful chart that a customer's finance team will plan against for a quarter before the error surfaces. You need to be the person who can say, at a whiteboard, why the series needed a log and a seasonal difference, what the ACF/PACF and the KPSS test told you about the order, why the winning model beats seasonal-naive by a MASE of 0.71 on a rolling-origin backtest whose cut points you can draw, and which features would have leaked if you had not blocked them.
prerequisites: Probability and estimation at the level of Topic 95 and Topic 96: expectation and conditional expectation, variance of a sum, maximum likelihood, what a null hypothesis and a p-value are (ADF and KPSS have opposite nulls and you must not misread that)
Linear regression and regularisation from Topic 100, including reading an OLS design matrix, because dynamic regression and Fourier-term seasonality are regression with autocorrelated errors
Cross-validation and leakage from Topic 103 - you are about to learn why every one of its assumptions (i.i.d. rows, exchangeable folds) is false here
Gradient boosting from Topic 101 (LightGBM/XGBoost API, categorical features, early stopping) for the global-model subtopic

NumPy vectorisation and numerical stability from Topic 99: STL, the Kalman filter recursion and the ACF are all written as array operations, and log/Box-Cox back-transforms are where float error shows up
pandas fluency: DatetimeIndex, resample, shift, rolling, groupby on a panel of (store, family, date) rows
Working Python env with statsmodels, prophet (or cmdstanpy backend), scikit-learn, LightGBM, matplotlib, and a Kaggle account for the Store Sales data

subtopics.name: What a forecast is: the h-step conditional distribution, and the benchmarks it must beat
subtopics.learn: State the target precisely: you are estimating the distribution of y_{T+h} conditional on the information set I_T = {y_1..y_T, plus any exogenous series known at T}, and a 'forecast' is a summary of it. Know which summary each loss picks: the conditional mean minimises expected squared error, the conditional median minimises expected absolute error, and the tau-quantile minimises pinball loss - so 'the forecast' is not a single number until you name the loss. Implement the four benchmarks by hand before anything else: mean, naive (yhat = y_T), drift (yhat_{T+h|T} = y_T + h*(y_T - y_1)/(T-1)), and seasonal naive (yhat_{T+h|T} = y_{T+h-m(k+1)}). Seasonal naive is not a strawman - on retail daily data it is a strong model, it is the denominator of MASE, and any model you ship must beat it on the same folds or you have shipped complexity for nothing.

resource.label: FPP3 - The statistical forecasting perspective

subtopics.name: Index hygiene: frequency, implicit gaps, zero versus missing, and the plots you draw first
subtopics.learn: Get the index right or every downstream diagnostic lies. Build a complete DatetimeIndex with an explicit freq, reindex the series onto pd.date_range so that days with no rows become explicit NaN, and then make the modelling decision that matters: a closed store is missing (leave NaN or model it), a store that opened and sold nothing is a real zero. Know the difference between resample('W-MON').sum() and asfreq('W-MON') (aggregation versus subsampling), between .shift(1) on position and .shift(1, freq='D') on the calendar, and why a tz-naive index plus a DST boundary silently drops or duplicates an hour on hourly data. Then draw four plots in order: the raw series, a seasonal plot (all years overlaid by day-of-year or day-of-week), a subseries plot (one panel per season with its mean), and the ACF. In the Favorita Store Sales data this immediately shows the Christmas-day gap, the payday spikes on the 15th and month-end, and the April 2016 earthquake - all of which are decisions you will have to defend, not noise.

resource.label: pandas user guide - Time series / date functionality

subtopics.name: Transformations: Box-Cox, log1p, and the back-transform bias nobody adjusts for
subtopics.learn: Apply a variance-stabilising transform when the seasonal amplitude grows with the level: Box-Cox w_t = (y_t^lambda - 1)/lambda for lambda != 0 and log(y_t) for lambda = 0, with lambda chosen by the Guerrero coefficient-of-variation method or profile likelihood (scipy.stats.boxcox returns the MLE lambda). Retail counts contain zeros, so reach for log1p (equivalently a shifted log) and remember that it changes the meaning of the errors. Then internalise the part that gets shipped wrong: back-transforming a point forecast gives a median, not a mean, because E[exp(w)] = exp(mu + sigma^2/2) by Jensen - so exp(what you predicted) is systematically low, and the fpp3 bias adjustment yhat*(1 + sigma_h^2/2) is what restores the mean. Prediction interval endpoints, by contrast, back-transform exactly, because quantiles are equivariant under monotone transforms. If the customer sums your per-store forecasts into a total, the un-adjusted medians do not add up to the total's mean and the sum will read low every month.

resource.label: FPP3 - Transformations and adjustments (Box-Cox, bias adjustment)

subtopics.name: Classical decomposition and exactly where it breaks
subtopics.learn: Write y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t (additive) or y_t = T_t * S_t * R_t (multiplicative, which is additive on logs) and implement classical decomposition: estimate T_t with a centred m-MA, or a 2xm-MA when m is even (because a 12-MA on monthly data is not centred on an observation), detrend, average the detrended values by season index to get S_t, and take the remainder. Then name its three defects out loud, because they are the reason STL exists: the trend is undefined for the first and last m/2 observations - precisely the region your forecast starts from; the seasonal figure is assumed constant across all years, so a store whose weekend pattern changed in 2015 gets a wrong S_t everywhere; and a single outlier (the earthquake week) leaks into the seasonal average for that day-of-week for the entire history. statsmodels seasonal_decompose is this algorithm, which is why it should almost never be the one you ship.

resource.label: FPP3 - Classical decomposition

subtopics.name: STL from scratch: loess, the inner loop, robustness weights, and the two windows
subtopics.learn: Be able to implement STL end to end, because the deliverable asks for it. Inner loop, six steps: detrend (y - T), split into cycle-subseries (all Mondays, all Tuesdays for m=7), smooth each subseries with loess of span s_window, low-pass filter the extended seasonal series with 3xMA plus a loess to strip any low-frequency leakage, subtract that from the smoothed seasonal to get S, deseasonalise, then loess the result with span t_window to get T. Outer loop: form robustness weights rho_t = B(|R_t| / (6 * median|R|)) with B the bisquare, and re-run the inner loop with those weights so outliers stop dragging the fit. Know the knobs in statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.STL: period=m, seasonal= an odd integer (small = seasonality allowed to change fast, 'periodic' = fixed), trend= odd and > period (default roughly ceil(1.5*period/(1 - 1.5/seasonal))), robust=True for the outer loop, and that STL is additive-only and single-seasonality - daily retail with weekly AND yearly cycles needs MSTL or Fourier terms. Validate your implementation by asserting seasonal + trend + resid == observed to float tolerance and by comparing component-wise against statsmodels on the same series.

resource.label: statsmodels API - tsa.seasonal.STL (period, seasonal, trend, robust)

subtopics.name: Stationarity, differencing, and the opposite nulls of ADF and KPSS
subtopics.learn: Define weak stationarity properly - constant mean, finite constant variance, autocovariance gamma_k depending only on lag k, not on t - and know that ARIMA requires it after differencing, while ETS and Prophet do not. Apply first differences nabla y_t = y_t - y_{t-1} for trend and seasonal differences nabla_m y_t = y_t - y_{t-m} for seasonality, and take the seasonal difference FIRST because it often removes the trend too. The trap that gets misread in every review: the ADF null is 'a unit root is present' (rejecting means stationary) while the KPSS null is 'the series is (trend-)stationary' (rejecting means non-stationary) - the tests can disagree or both reject, and 'ADF p = 0.3 therefore it has a unit root' is failing to reject, not evidence. Pick D by seasonal strength F_S = max(0, 1 - Var(R)/Var(S+R)) from the STL components, seasonally difference when F_S > 0.64, then pick d by repeated KPSS. Stop at d <= 2 and D <= 1; over-differencing inflates the innovation variance, widens your intervals, and plants a unit root in the MA polynomial that makes the model non-invertible.

resource.label: FPP3 - Stationarity and differencing (incl. unit root tests)

subtopics.name: ACF and PACF: the estimators, their sampling distribution, and reading orders off the plot
subtopics.learn: Write the estimator down: r_k = sum_{t=k+1}^{T}(y_t - ybar)(y_{t-k} - ybar) / sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t - ybar)^2. Under white noise r_k is approximately N(0, 1/T), which is exactly where the +/- 1.96/sqrt(T) bands come from - so on T = 100 you expect 1 in 20 lags outside the band by chance and 'lag 17 is significant' means nothing on its own. The PACF phi_kk is the correlation between y_t and y_{t-k} with lags 1..k-1 partialled out, computed by the Durbin-Levinson recursion or by OLS of y_t on its first k lags (statsmodels pacf method='ywm' vs 'ols' can differ visibly on short series). Reading rules you must be able to justify, not recite: AR(p) has PACF cutting off after lag p with a decaying ACF; MA(q) has ACF cutting off after lag q with a decaying PACF; a mixed ARMA cuts off in neither, so stop plot-reading and use AICc. A slowly, near-linearly decaying ACF is the signature of needing a difference; spikes at exactly m, 2m, 3m give you the seasonal P and Q.

resource.label: FPP3 - Autocorrelation (r_k, correlogram, white-noise bands)

subtopics.name: AR, MA and ARMA in backshift algebra: causality, invertibility, and the MA(infinity) form
subtopics.learn: Use B with B y_t = y_{t-1} and write the whole family as one line: phi(B)(1-B)^d y_t = c + theta(B) eps_t, with phi(B) = 1 - phi_1 B - ... - phi_p B^p and theta(B) = 1 + theta_1 B + ... + theta_q B^q. Be able to derive that AR(1) with |phi| < 1 has ACF rho_k = phi^k, and that stationarity/causality holds iff all roots of phi(z) = 0 lie outside the unit circle while invertibility holds iff all roots of theta(z) = 0 do. Understand why invertibility matters operationally: only an invertible MA has a convergent AR(infinity) representation, so only then can the model reconstruct the unobserved eps_t from past y - a non-invertible fit (a root on the unit circle, or statsmodels quietly enforcing one) is nearly always the fingerprint of over-differencing, not of a real MA process. Derive the MA(infinity) psi-weights y_{T+h} = sum psi_j eps_{T+h-j}; you need them in the prediction-interval subtopic because Var(e_{T+h}) = sigma^2 * sum_{j=0}^{h-1} psi_j^2.

resource.label: FPP3 - Backshift notation

subtopics.name: SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)m: the multiplicative seasonal polynomial and what each order buys
subtopics.learn: Write the full model: Phi(B^m) phi(B) (1-B)^d (1-B^m)^D y_t = c + Theta(B^m) theta(B) eps_t, and multiply out a (0,1,1)(0,1,1)_7 by hand so you can see it generates terms at lags 1, 7 and 8 - the seasonal and non-seasonal parts interact, which is why 'add a lag-7 term' is not the same model. Be able to say what each order does: d and D remove trend and seasonal level shifts, q and Q say 'shocks persist for a few periods', p and P say 'the level regresses toward its own past'. Know the constant's meaning under differencing: with d = 1 a non-zero c is a linear drift, with d = 2 it implies a quadratic trend and is almost always wrong for a business series. Know the ceiling: SARIMA is intractable for m = 365 (yearly seasonality on daily data) because the seasonal polynomial spans 365 lags - at that point you move to a dynamic regression with Fourier terms plus ARIMA errors, which is exactly the structure Prophet is approximating.

resource.label: FPP3 - Seasonal ARIMA models

subtopics.name: Estimation and order selection: MLE, AICc, and why AIC cannot compare different d
subtopics.learn: Understand that ARIMA coefficients are fitted by maximum likelihood, computed by casting the model in state-space form and running the Kalman filter to get the prediction-error decomposition of the log-likelihood - it is not OLS on lags, and that is why the optimiser can fail to converge and report a boundary solution. Select orders with AICc = -2 log L + 2k + 2k(k+1)/(T-k-1), the small-sample correction that matters when you have 150 monthly points and 8 parameters. The rule that catches people out in review: AIC/AICc are only comparable across models fitted to the SAME differenced data and the same number of observations, so you may use them to choose p, q, P, Q but NEVER to choose d and D - those come from the unit-root tests and seasonal strength. Know the Hyndman-Khandakar stepwise search that auto.arima / pmdarima implements (fit four seeds, step one order at a time, keep the best AICc) and its two known holes: it is greedy so it can stop in a local optimum, and its approximation mode uses conditional sum of squares rather than the exact likelihood, so re-fit the finalist exactly.

resource.label: FPP3 - Estimation and order selection (AICc for ARIMA)

subtopics.name: statsmodels SARIMAX in practice: exog, append/extend, and the dynamic=False trap
subtopics.learn: Drive the actual API: SARIMAX(endog, exog=X, order=(p,d,q), seasonal_order=(P,D,Q,m), trend='c'|'t'|'n', enforce_stationarity=, enforce_invertibility=, simple_differencing=). Learn the four things that bite. (1) exog must be supplied for the forecast horizon too - res.get_forecast(steps=16, exog=X_future) - so any exogenous column you cannot know 16 days ahead (a promo flag decided next week, that day's oil price) is a leak dressed up as a feature, while a holiday calendar is legitimately known. (2) res.get_prediction(start=..., dynamic=False) returns ONE-STEP-AHEAD in-sample predictions that use the true y at every step: they look spectacular and are not forecasts; dynamic=True from a cut point is the honest in-sample analogue. (3) res.append(new_obs, refit=False) and res.extend(new_obs) roll a fitted model forward over backtest folds without re-estimating, turning an O(folds) fitting cost into one fit - use them deliberately and record that you did, because it is slightly optimistic if the orders were chosen on all the data. (4) enforce_invertibility=False will happily hand you a non-invertible MA that forecasts nonsense at long horizons instead of erroring.

resource.label: statsmodels API - tsa.statespace.sarimax.SARIMAX

subtopics.name: Exponential smoothing and ETS: the recursions, damping, and its overlap with ARIMA
subtopics.learn: Derive the recursions rather than memorising them. SES: level l_t = alpha*y_t + (1-alpha)*l_{t-1}, forecast flat at l_T - an exponentially weighted average with weights alpha(1-alpha)^j. Holt adds a slope b_t = beta*(l_t - l_{t-1}) + (1-beta)*b_{t-1}; Holt-Winters adds a seasonal state s_t with additive or multiplicative form. Damped trend replaces the h*b_T extrapolation with (phi + phi^2 + ... + phi^h)*b_T, which converges to l_T + phi*b_T/(1-phi) - and that single knob is usually the difference between a credible 12-month forecast and a straight line through the ceiling. Learn the ETS(Error, Trend, Season) taxonomy: 30 combinations, additive vs multiplicative error give IDENTICAL point forecasts but different prediction intervals, and the model is chosen by AICc over the state-space likelihood. Know the equivalences: ETS(A,N,N) = ARIMA(0,1,1), ETS(A,A,N) = ARIMA(0,2,2), ETS(A,A,A) has a SARIMA equivalent with parameter constraints - and every multiplicative-error ETS has no ARIMA counterpart at all, which is the honest answer to 'why fit both'.

resource.label: FPP3 - A taxonomy of exponential smoothing / ETS state space models

subtopics.name: Prophet end to end: the decomposable GAM, changepoint prior, Fourier seasonality, holidays
subtopics.learn: Prophet is a curve-fitting GAM, not a stochastic process: y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + eps_t, fitted in Stan by L-BFGS MAP (mcmc_samples > 0 switches to full posterior sampling). g(t) is piecewise linear (or logistic with a required cap/floor column) with rate deltas at n_changepoints=25 candidate points placed over the first changepoint_range=0.8 of history, regularised by a Laplace prior delta_j ~ Laplace(0, changepoint_prior_scale) - so that one scalar controls how twitchy your trend is, and raising it from 0.05 to 0.5 is how a 'flat' forecast becomes a hockey stick. s(t) is a Fourier series sum a_n cos(2*pi*n*t/P) + b_n sin(2*pi*n*t/P) truncated at order N (yearly 10, weekly 3), so seasonality is smooth and multi-period seasonalities simply add - which is why Prophet handles daily data with weekly AND yearly cycles where SARIMA cannot. h(t) is holiday indicators with lower_window/upper_window to spread the effect across surrounding days and their own prior scale; add_country_holidays('EC') for the Ecuador calendar in the Favorita data, add_regressor() for oil price or onpromotion (which then needs future values). Know the two things to say out loud to a customer: the uncertainty intervals come from simulating future trend changes at the fitted changepoint rate and are not calibrated coverage, and Prophet leaves autocorrelated residuals by construction because nothing in the model has an error process.

resource.label: Prophet docs - Seasonality, holiday effects, and regressors

subtopics.name: Rolling-origin backtesting: expanding vs sliding, horizon-wise scoring, refit cadence, nesting
subtopics.learn: Build the harness yourself: for a set of origins t_1 < t_2 < ... < t_K, train on data up to t_i and score on t_i+1 .. t_i+h, then aggregate. Expanding window keeps all history (right when the process is stable and data is scarce); sliding window fixes the training length L (right when there is a regime change or the model must forget). Score errors as a matrix e[i][h], and report MEAN BY HORIZON - collapsing to one number hides that your model is excellent at h=1 and worse than seasonal-naive at h=14, which is the horizon the customer actually plans on. Set the fold geometry from the decision, not from convenience: for the Kaggle Store Sales task h=16 days, so every fold is 16 days, spaced by a multiple of 7 so day-of-week alignment is constant across folds. Decide refit cadence explicitly (refit every fold = honest and expensive; fit once then res.extend = cheap and mildly optimistic) and record it in the results table. Nest it: hyperparameters selected on inner folds inside each training block, final numbers reported on outer folds only - selecting orders or changepoint_prior_scale on the same folds you report is how a MASE of 0.8 becomes 1.1 in production.

resource.label: FPP3 - Time series cross-validation (rolling origin)

subtopics.name: Leakage: lags, rolling statistics, fitted transforms, and features that cannot exist yet
subtopics.learn: Enumerate the five leaks and write a test for each. (1) Rolling statistics that include today: df.rolling(7).mean() at row t uses y_t, so every rolling feature must be .shift(1).rolling(w).mean() and the fold needs a gap >= w between train end and test start. (2) Fitted transforms: the Box-Cox lambda, the StandardScaler, the target encoding of store_id, and the MASE denominator must all be estimated on the training slice of the fold, never on the full series. (3) Panel-wide aggregates: 'total national sales that day' or 'that family's share of the store' are computed across the whole frame and encode the future of other series into this one. (4) Exogenous columns without a future value: oil price and onpromotion are given for the test window in this competition, but in a customer deployment they are not - decide per column whether it is known-in-advance (calendar, holidays, planned promos) or must itself be forecast. (5) Structural: sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit gives ordered folds and a gap= parameter but assumes a single sorted series - on a panel of 1782 (store, family) pairs it will slice through a single timestamp unless you split on unique dates. The test that actually catches all of these: for each fold, rebuild the feature matrix from train-only rows and assert it is element-wise equal to the matrix the harness handed the model.

resource.label: scikit-learn API - TimeSeriesSplit (gap, max_train_size, test_size)

subtopics.name: Metrics: MASE and RMSSE, and why MAPE flatters and RMSLE is asymmetric
subtopics.learn: Know what each metric optimises and where it dies. MAE is minimised by the conditional median, RMSE by the conditional mean - so ranking models by RMSE while training on absolute error compares apples to a different fruit. MAPE is undefined at y = 0 (fatal on retail rows where a family sells nothing) and is asymmetric: it caps the penalty for over-forecasting at 100% while under-forecasting is unbounded, so it systematically prefers models that under-predict; sMAPE fixes neither cleanly. Use MASE = mean(|e_j|) / [ (1/(T-m)) * sum_{t=m+1}^{T} |y_t - y_{t-m}| ], where the denominator is the IN-SAMPLE seasonal-naive MAE: it is scale-free, comparable across stores, defined when y = 0, and MASE < 1 literally means 'beat seasonal naive'. RMSSE is the squared-error twin used in M5, and WRMSSE weights each series by its dollar volume so the aggregate reflects the business rather than the long tail. Note the competition's own metric here is RMSLE = sqrt(mean((log1p(yhat) - log1p(y))^2)), which penalises under-forecasting more than over-forecasting, so the RMSLE-optimal prediction is not the conditional mean - train on the log1p target rather than post-hoc logging. Finally, decide aggregation across series consciously: the MEAN MASE over 1782 series is dominated by a handful of near-zero-volume ones, the MEDIAN hides a broken segment - report both plus the count of series where you lose to seasonal naive.

resource.label: Hyndman & Koehler - Another look at measures of forecast accuracy (MASE)

subtopics.name: Distributional accuracy: prediction intervals, coverage, pinball loss and CRPS
subtopics.learn: A point forecast without an interval is not a deliverable. Derive the ARIMA interval from the psi-weights: Var(e_{T+h}) = sigma^2 * sum_{j=0}^{h-1} psi_j^2, giving yhat +/- z_{1-alpha/2} * sqrt(that) - and know the three reasons the real coverage is narrower than nominal: it assumes the parameters are known (no estimation uncertainty), it assumes the model is correct, and it assumes Gaussian innovations. Prefer simulation or bootstrapped residual paths when the residual histogram is skewed. Score distributions with pinball loss L_tau(y, q) = tau*(y - q) if y >= q else (1 - tau)*(q - y), averaged over a grid of quantiles as a discrete approximation to CRPS (sklearn.metrics.mean_pinball_loss). Then always report EMPIRICAL COVERAGE by horizon from the backtest: the fraction of held-out points inside the nominal 80% and 95% bands. An interval that is nominally 95% and empirically 68% at h=14 is a defect you must fix or disclose - it is also, in practice, the number a customer's planner cares about more than your MASE.

resource.label: FPP3 - Evaluating distributional forecast accuracy (quantile/Winkler/CRPS)

subtopics.name: Residual diagnostics: white noise, Ljung-Box degrees of freedom, and what passing does not prove
subtopics.learn: Check the innovation residuals (residuals in the TRANSFORMED space, after any Box-Cox) for four properties: zero mean, no autocorrelation, constant variance, and roughly normal if you want the closed-form intervals. Run the portmanteau test Q* = T(T+2) * sum_{k=1}^{l} r_k^2/(T-k) which is chi-squared with l - K degrees of freedom, where K is the number of estimated ARMA parameters - statsmodels acorr_ljungbox(resid, lags=[l], model_df=K); forgetting model_df inflates the p-value and lets a bad model pass. Use l = 10 for non-seasonal data and l = 2m for seasonal. Read the outcome correctly in both directions: a small p-value means structure is left in the residuals, so your intervals are too narrow and there is signal on the table; a large p-value does NOT mean the model forecasts well, only that the linear autocorrelation is used up - a residual plot fanning out with the level means you needed the log, and a residual ACF spike at exactly lag 7 or 12 tells you which seasonal order you missed.

resource.label: statsmodels API - acorr_ljungbox (lags, model_df, boxpierce)

subtopics.name: Global models: tabularising a panel for LightGBM, recursive vs direct multi-step
subtopics.learn: Know when to abandon one-model-per-series. With 1782 (store, family) series, per-series SARIMA means 1782 fits per fold and no sharing; a single gradient-boosted model over rows keyed (series_id, date) with lag features (y_{t-16}, y_{t-17}, ..., y_{t-365}), shifted rolling means/stds, day-of-week, day-of-month, payday and holiday flags, and store/family as native LightGBM categoricals learns shared seasonality and handles a series with 30 days of history. Choose the multi-step strategy deliberately: RECURSIVE feeds each prediction back as the next lag (needs lag-1, accumulates its own error, and is what produces the flat-line collapse at long horizons), DIRECT trains one model per horizon h with only features available at the origin (16 models here, no error accumulation, higher variance per model). Know the tree-model failure that gets shipped: gradient boosting cannot extrapolate beyond the range of the training target, so a growing series must be modelled on differences or a detrended target, or every forecast is capped at the historical maximum. Elsayed et al. is the reference to cite when a customer asks for a transformer: a well-configured GBRT matches or beats DeepAR and N-BEATS on the standard benchmarks.

resource.label: arXiv:2101.02118 - Do We Really Need Deep Learning Models for Time Series Forecasting?

subtopics.name: Hierarchies and reconciliation: making store, family and national forecasts add up
subtopics.learn: Business forecasts are almost always a hierarchy - item within family within store within region within country - and independently fitted base forecasts do not sum to their parents, which is the first thing a CFO notices. Encode the structure as the summing matrix S so that the coherent vector is ytilde = S*G*yhat, and know the three choices of G: bottom-up (G just selects the leaves - unbiased but noisy when leaves are sparse), top-down (forecast the total, split by historical or forecast proportions - stable but destroys leaf-level signal), and MinT optimal reconciliation G = (S' W^-1 S)^-1 S' W^-1 with W an estimate of the base-forecast error covariance (use the shrinkage estimator; the full sample covariance is singular with 1782 series). The property worth stating to a customer: MinT reconciliation is a projection, so it cannot increase, and in practice reduces, total squared error while guaranteeing coherence for free. The discipline: estimate W from the residuals of THAT FOLD's training data only, or reconciliation becomes a leak that silently improves your backtest.

resource.label: FPP3 - Forecast reconciliation (bottom-up, top-down, MinT)

outcomes: You can take an unseen daily business series, produce in under 30 minutes a defended preprocessing decision - transform (with the Box-Cox lambda and how you chose it), d and D (with the seasonal strength F_S and the KPSS output), and candidate (p,q,P,Q) read off the ACF/PACF - and state which of those choices AICc is and is not allowed to arbitrate.

You can implement STL from scratch (inner loop with cycle-subseries loess and low-pass filter, outer loop with bisquare robustness weights) and show your components matching statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.STL to within float tolerance, plus a reconstruction assertion that seasonal + trend + resid equals the observation.

You can write a rolling-origin backtest harness from scratch supporting both expanding and sliding windows, an embargo gap sized to the widest rolling feature, per-horizon error matrices, and a configurable refit cadence, and draw its cut points on a timeline for a customer.

You can fit seasonal-naive, STL+ETS, SARIMAX and Prophet on identical folds and publish a MASE and RMSSE table broken out by horizon, naming the horizon at which each model stops beating seasonal naive.

You can write a test that fails when any feature sees data past its fold boundary - by rebuilding the fold's feature matrix from train-only rows and asserting element-wise equality - and demonstrate it catching a deliberately unshifted rolling mean.

You can report empirical interval coverage by horizon against the nominal level, explain in two sentences why an ARIMA 95% interval under-covers, and produce a bootstrapped or simulated alternative that covers correctly.

You can run Ljung-Box on innovation residuals with the correct model_df, interpret both a rejection and a non-rejection correctly, and connect a residual-ACF spike at lag m to a specific missing seasonal order.

You can explain to a non-technical stakeholder why the point forecast is a median not a mean after a log transform, what the bias adjustment changes, and why their per-store forecasts previously did not sum to the national total.

You can decide and defend, for a given customer dataset, whether to ship per-series SARIMA/ETS or one global LightGBM, including the recursive-vs-direct multi-step choice and the tree extrapolation problem.
failureModes: The backtest used sklearn KFold or a random train_test_split, so future weeks trained the model that predicts past weeks; MASE came out at 0.4, the deck said 'beats baseline by 60%', and the first live month came in at 1.2.

Rolling features were built as df.groupby('store').sales.rolling(7).mean() without a .shift(1), so every training row contained its own target inside the window; the model looked near-perfect in backtest and collapsed to seasonal-naive quality in production because that feature is unavailable at forecast time.

The Box-Cox lambda and the StandardScaler were fitted on the full series before folding, so every fold's training data carried summary statistics of its own test window; the leak is small, invisible in any plot, and consistently makes the reported error 5-15% too low.

Forecasts were produced on a log scale and exponentiated back without the bias adjustment, so every number shipped was a median; the customer summed 54 store forecasts into a national plan that ran a few percent under actuals every single month and nobody could find the bug.

res.get_prediction(dynamic=False) was used to generate the 'backtest' chart, so every plotted point was a one-step-ahead prediction conditioned on the true previous value; the fit hugged the data beautifully and the model had never once forecast 16 days ahead.

The series was differenced twice 'to be safe' - d=1 plus D=1 on a series that only needed the seasonal difference - which pushed a root of the MA polynomial onto the unit circle; statsmodels enforced invertibility silently, the innovation variance roughly doubled, and the prediction intervals shipped twice as wide as they needed to be.

MAPE was the reported metric on retail data containing zero-sales days; the zero rows were dropped to avoid the division by zero, which quietly removed exactly the hardest observations, and the surviving asymmetry made the systematically under-forecasting model look like the winner.

Prophet was fitted with the default changepoint_prior_scale on a series whose last six weeks were a COVID-style dip; it placed changepoints in that window, extrapolated the dip as the new trend, and produced a confidently declining 12-month forecast with intervals that never covered the recovery.

The Kaggle test window's oil price and onpromotion columns were joined as exogenous regressors and the model was praised for its accuracy; in the customer's deployment neither column exists for future dates, so the whole feature set had to be rebuilt and the accuracy claim retracted.
interviewQuestions: Derive the prediction-interval variance for an ARIMA h-step forecast from the MA(infinity) representation, then tell me three reasons the empirical coverage of that interval will be below nominal on real data and what you would do about each.

I hand you three years of daily sales for 1800 store-product pairs and ask for a 16-day forecast. Walk me from raw CSV to a defended model: what you plot first, how you decide the transform and the differencing orders, what you can and cannot use AICc for, and how you decide between 1800 SARIMAs and one LightGBM.

ADF gives p = 0.28 and KPSS gives p = 0.01 on the same series. What does each test's null hypothesis say, what do you conclude, and what do you do next? Now tell me what it means if ADF gives p = 0.02 and KPSS also gives p = 0.01.

Design an honest backtest for a model whose features include a 28-day rolling mean and a target encoding of store_id, refitting quarterly in production. Specify the window type, the gap, the fold spacing, the refit cadence, how hyperparameters are selected, and one automated test that would fail if any of it leaked.
A colleague's Prophet model reports 8% MAPE in backtest and 22% in production. The code has no obvious shuffle. Where do you look, in what order, and which three checks would you run first?

Explain MASE: write the formula, say why the denominator is in-sample rather than out-of-sample, and explain what MASE = 0.85 means. Then tell me when you would refuse to use it and what you would use instead.

Your per-store forecasts and your national forecast disagree by 3%. Explain to the customer's CFO why that happens, then describe bottom-up, top-down and MinT reconciliation and which one you would ship and why.

You fit SARIMA(1,1,1)(1,1,1)_7 and Ljung-Box on the residuals gives p = 0.003 with a clear ACF spike at lag 30. Interpret it, and tell me what you change about the model versus what you change about the features.
108.proofOfWork: Alongside the `ts-backtest` repo, publish a `forecast-audit` notebook-plus-report that takes someone else's working forecasting notebook - pick a highly-voted public Store Sales kernel - and audits it the way you would audit a customer's incumbent model on day three of an engagement. The report reproduces their headline metric, then re-scores the identical model under your own rolling-origin harness with an embargo gap and per-horizon breakdown, and quantifies the gap between the two numbers attributable to each defect you find: leaked rolling features, transforms fitted before splitting, a metric that rewards under-forecasting, one-step-ahead predictions presented as forecasts, and exogenous columns that would not exist at inference time in a real deployment. Include a coverage table showing nominal versus empirical 80% and 95% interval coverage by horizon for their model and yours, an ablation showing what each defect is individually worth in MASE, and a two-page memo written for a non-technical stakeholder that says what the original model's number really means, what the corrected number is, and what would have to be true operationally - which columns are known in advance, what refit cadence, what monitoring on rolling MASE drift - for the corrected model to hold up in production.

109.topic: Recommenders and anomaly detection: collaborative filtering, matrix factorisation, isolation forests
109.why: These are the two ML asks that arrive unprompted in almost every deployment - 'can you suggest the next best action for each account' and 'can you flag the weird transactions' - and both usually arrive with no labels and a log the customer's own product generated. Being able to derive and implement the factorisation and the isolation forest yourself is what lets you stand in front of their data scientist and say why held-out RMSE improved while recall@10 got worse, why a 0.97 ROC-AUC fraud model will drown their three analysts, and exactly what the system returns on day one for a user it has never seen. These are also the two places where a demo metric most easily flatters a useless model, so the defensible skill here is the evaluation protocol and the stated fallback, not the fit call.
prerequisites: Topic 93 (linear algebra): SVD, low-rank approximation and the Eckart-Young statement, and reading an expression like (Q^T Q + lambda I)^-1 Q^T r without unpacking it
Topic 94 (calculus and optimisation): differentiating a squared loss with an L2 penalty by hand, and what a non-convex but biconvex objective implies about convergence and seeds
Topic 99 (NumPy and numerical computing): fancy indexing, broadcasting, np.add.at, and the reflex never to materialise a dense m x n interaction matrix
Topic 103 (model evaluation): cross-validation discipline, leakage, calibration and metric choice - this topic is a stress test of all three
Topic 104 (feature engineering and imbalanced data): class weights, resampling and why accuracy and ROC-AUC mislead at a 0.17 percent positive rate
Topic 101 (trees and ensembles): binary splits, tree depth and bagging, since an isolation forest is that machinery with a random split criterion and no target

subtopics.name: From an interaction log to a sparse matrix
subtopics.learn: State the density before choosing an algorithm: MovieLens-100K is 943 users x 1682 items with 100,000 ratings, so 6.3 percent dense, while the credit-card fraud set is 284,807 rows x 30 dense float columns - two completely different regimes. Build the matrix with scipy.sparse.coo_matrix((vals, (u_idx, i_idx)), shape=(m, n)).tocsr(), holding integer id maps in both directions (pd.factorize) so a predicted column index turns back into a movie title. Know CSR's three arrays (data, indices, indptr), why R[u].indices gives user u's rated items in time proportional to that user's row, and why the item-side sweep of ALS wants R.tocsc(). Never call .toarray() on a real interaction matrix: 1M users x 100k items in float64 is 800 GB.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.sparse.csr_matrix

subtopics.name: The baselines that must be beaten: global mean, bias model, popularity
subtopics.learn: Implement r_hat_ui = mu + b_u + b_i and fit the biases by alternating shrunk means, b_u = sum over I_u of (r_ui - mu - b_i) / (lambda2 + |I_u|); on MovieLens-100K this alone lands near 0.94 RMSE, and any factorisation that does not beat it is broken, not subtle. On the ranking side the baseline is 'most popular item the user has not seen', which is embarrassingly strong on recall@10 - Dacrema et al reproduced 18 neural recommenders and found most failed to beat tuned kNN and popularity baselines once the baselines were tuned with the same budget. Make the rule non-negotiable: every model is reported next to both baselines, on the same split, with the same tuning budget, or the number is not a result.

resource.label: arXiv 1907.06902 - Are We Really Making Much Progress? A Worrying Analysis of Recent Neural Recommendation Approaches

subtopics.name: Neighbourhood CF: item-item similarity and shrinkage
subtopics.learn: Implement item-item CF as r_hat_ui = sum over j in topN(i) intersect I_u of s_ij * r_uj / sum |s_ij|, with s_ij cosine on mean-centred columns (which is Pearson). Understand the pathology that makes naive similarity useless: two items co-rated by two users can score s = 1.0, so shrink with s_ij' = n_ij / (n_ij + beta) * s_ij for beta around 25-100, exactly what Surprise's pearson_baseline shrinkage does. Choose item-item over user-user when items are far fewer than users and item taste is more stable, when you need an explanation ('because you watched X'), and when new users must be served without retraining - only their history is needed. The cost is an O(|I|^2) similarity matrix, so this is the interpretable fallback you keep, not the model you scale.

resource.label: Surprise docs - Similarity measures (cosine, MSD, Pearson, pearson_baseline shrinkage)

subtopics.name: Latent factors, Eckart-Young, and why truncated SVD is the wrong tool here
subtopics.learn: Start from A = U S V^T and the Eckart-Young theorem: truncating to the top k singular values gives the provably best rank-k approximation in Frobenius and spectral norm. Then be able to say precisely why you cannot just call scipy.sparse.linalg.svds on a ratings matrix: SVD minimises error over every entry, and the stored zeros of a sparse interaction matrix mean 'unobserved', not 'rated zero', so the decomposition is fitted to fabricated data and predicts near zero everywhere. Imputing row or column means instead makes the matrix dense and the factorisation intractable at scale. The fix is to change the objective, not the solver: sum only over the observed pairs K, which destroys the eigen-decomposition route and leaves a non-convex optimisation problem attacked by SGD or ALS. Rehearse that answer in one sentence for the customer data scientist who asks 'why not just SVD?'.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - Chapter 02, Decompositions (SVD, low-rank approximation, pseudo-inverse)

subtopics.name: SGD matrix factorisation from scratch: objective and update rule
subtopics.learn: Derive and implement it: minimise sum over observed (u,i) of (r_ui - mu - b_u - b_i - p_u . q_i)^2 + lambda(||p_u||^2 + ||q_i||^2 + b_u^2 + b_i^2). With e_ui the residual, the updates are p_u += gamma(e_ui q_i - lambda p_u), q_i += gamma(e_ui p_u - lambda q_i), b_u += gamma(e_ui - lambda b_u), b_i += gamma(e_ui - lambda b_i), and you should be able to write those four lines from the gradient without looking. Initialise factors from N(0, 0.1) or scaled by 1/sqrt(k) - never zeros, because a product of zeros has no gradient - shuffle the triple list each epoch with rng.permutation so consecutive updates are not all the same user, and decay gamma_t = gamma_0 / (1 + decay * t). Diagnose from one plot of train and validation RMSE per epoch: validation turning up while train falls is overfit (raise lambda or lower k), both flat and high is too small a learning rate or k, NaN by epoch two is gamma too large, and ||q_i|| growing without bound means the regularisation term never made it into the update.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - 21.3 Matrix Factorization

subtopics.name: ALS: the closed-form ridge step and why it parallelises
subtopics.learn: Fix Q and the objective separates into one ridge regression per user: p_u = (Q_Iu^T Q_Iu + lambda |I_u| I_k)^-1 Q_Iu^T r_u, solved with np.linalg.solve (never np.linalg.inv) at cost O(|I_u| k^2 + k^3), then alternate to the item side. Each half-sweep is convex and the loss is monotone non-increasing, which is why ALS never blows up the way SGD does with a bad learning rate, while the joint problem stays biconvex and non-convex so the optimum still depends on the seed. Weighted-lambda regularisation - scaling lambda by |I_u| - is what stops heavy users being over-regularised relative to users with three ratings. Every user solve is independent, which is exactly why Spark ships ALS and not SGD; be able to state the trade rule out loud: SGD on one box with sparse explicit ratings, ALS when the data is distributed or the feedback is implicit.

resource.label: Apache Spark MLlib - Collaborative Filtering (ALS, implicit feedback, coldStartStrategy)

subtopics.name: Implicit feedback: confidence weighting and the Gram-matrix trick
subtopics.learn: With clicks and plays there are no negatives, only observed and unknown, so the explicit objective does not apply. Hu, Koren and Volinsky binarise preference p_ui = 1 if r_ui > 0 else 0 and set confidence c_ui = 1 + alpha r_ui with alpha around 40, then minimise sum over ALL user-item pairs of c_ui (p_ui - p_u . q_i)^2 plus regularisation - the sum runs over the full matrix so unobserved pairs act as low-confidence negatives. Naively that is O(m n k^2) per sweep; the trick that makes it tractable is Q^T C^u Q = Q^T Q + Q^T (C^u - I) Q, where Q^T Q is computed once per sweep and the second term touches only that user's non-zeros, giving O(k^2 * nnz + (m+n) k^3). Be able to explain to a customer why 200 plays is not 'ten times the rating' of 20 plays but ten times the confidence in the same binary preference.

resource.label: Hu, Koren, Volinsky - Collaborative Filtering for Implicit Feedback Datasets (author PDF)

subtopics.name: Tuning k and lambda honestly
subtopics.learn: Treat k as capacity: k = 1 is barely more than popularity plus biases, k = 200 memorises the training ratings. Sweep k in {8, 16, 32, 64, 128} against lambda in {0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5} on a fixed held-out split and plot validation RMSE against k for each lambda - you should see the classic U, and larger k should need larger lambda. If the best k is the largest one you tried, you have not searched far enough; if the curve is flat, your regularisation is dominating. Fix the seed and epoch budget across the grid, early-stop on validation RMSE with patience, and touch the test split exactly once at the end (Topic 105 automates this with Optuna; do it by hand here so you see the surface). Repeat the winner over three seeds and report the spread, so you never claim a 0.003 RMSE win that is seed noise.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Validation curves: plotting scores to evaluate models

subtopics.name: Pairwise ranking: BPR and matching the loss to the metric
subtopics.learn: BPR-Opt maximises sum over triples (u, i, j) of ln sigmoid(x_ui - x_uj) - lambda ||Theta||^2, where i is an observed item and j is drawn from the user's unobserved set; be able to derive it as MAP estimation under independent user preferences and a Gaussian prior on the parameters. The gradient carries the factor (1 - sigmoid(x_uij)), so badly ordered pairs dominate the update, and with x_ui = p_u . q_i you get p_u += gamma[(1 - sigmoid) (q_i - q_j) - lambda p_u]. Implement uniform negative sampling first, then popularity-proportional sampling, and measure what each does to recall@10. The point to internalise: pointwise squared error asks 'what score would this user give', pairwise asks 'which of these two comes first' - and only the second is the question a top-10 list actually poses, which is the mechanism behind RMSE improving while recall@10 falls.

resource.label: arXiv 1205.2618 - BPR: Bayesian Personalized Ranking from Implicit Feedback

subtopics.name: Splits and leakage: random, leave-one-out, temporal
subtopics.learn: Know the three protocols and what each actually measures. A random hold-out of ratings measures rating prediction and leaks the future into the past; leave-one-out per user (hide each user's last interaction) matches next-item prediction but still leaks other users' futures; a single global temporal cut is the only protocol that answers 'would this have worked in production'. Demonstrate the leak rather than assert it: score the same MF model under a random 80/20 and a temporal 80/20 and report both recall@10 values - the gap is the number you owe the customer. Two more non-negotiables: remove items already in the user's training history from the candidate set before taking the top K, and rank against the full catalogue rather than 100 sampled negatives, because sampled metrics do not preserve the ranking between models. Users with no training history are excluded and counted in a separate cold-start bucket, never silently dropped.

resource.label: scikit-learn - TimeSeriesSplit (forward-chaining splits for time-ordered data)

subtopics.name: Ranking metrics and the RMSE vs recall@10 divergence
subtopics.learn: Implement recall@k = |topk intersect relevant| / min(k, |relevant|), precision@k, MAP@k and NDCG@k = DCG@k / IDCG@k with DCG = sum over positions of (2^rel_i - 1) / log2(i + 1), and check your implementation against sklearn.metrics.ndcg_score on a hand-built fixture before trusting it on 943 users. Then be able to articulate the divergence on demand: RMSE averages squared error over every observed rating and is dominated by the dense mid-scale mass of popular items, while recall@10 depends only on the extreme right tail of each user's score distribution, so a model can genuinely improve its predictions of 3-star ratings that will never enter a top-10 list while reordering the head badly. Always report catalogue coverage and the mean popularity rank of recommended items alongside recall: a model that hands the same 50 blockbusters to everyone can look excellent and be worthless.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.metrics.ndcg_score

subtopics.name: Cold start and the fallback you must state out loud
subtopics.learn: Separate the four cases: new item, new user, new tenant, and the returning user with one interaction. A pure MF model has no factor vector for an unseen id, so the fallback has to be explicit, coded and testable rather than implied. For new items, represent the item as the sum of its feature embeddings (genre, text, price band) plus an id embedding that only starts to matter once interactions accumulate, which is exactly the LightFM hybrid construction; for new users, segment popularity plus an onboarding elicitation of five items; for everyone, a deterministic backfill so the endpoint never returns an empty list. Write the routing rule as code (if n_interactions < 3 then segment_popularity) and put the share of traffic served by each path on the dashboard, because 'what does it do on day one' is asked in every demo and 'it degrades to popularity within the account's segment' is the answer that wins the room.

resource.label: arXiv 1507.08439 - Metadata Embeddings for User and Item Cold-start Recommendations (LightFM)

subtopics.name: Serving: from a dot product to an ANN index
subtopics.learn: Scoring every item for a user is the dense product P[u] @ Q.T, which is fine for MovieLens and impossible at request time for 1M users x 500k items, so the production shape is two stages: candidate generation by approximate maximum inner-product search over Q, then ranking of roughly 500 candidates by an exact model that can use business features (often a gradient-boosted model from Topic 101). Use faiss IndexFlatIP as the exact reference and IVF or HNSW for scale, and know that MIPS is not metric search - either use an inner-product index or transform the vectors so that L2 or cosine ordering matches. Measure the ANN index's recall@10 against brute force as a separate number from model quality, tune nprobe or efSearch against a p99 latency budget, and filter already-seen items at read time rather than baking them into the index.

resource.label: FAISS wiki - Guidelines to choose an index

subtopics.name: Feedback loops, popularity bias and why offline wins evaporate
subtopics.learn: The training log was generated by the previous recommender, so the data is missing-not-at-random: items the old system never surfaced have no positives, and a new model that surfaces them scores worse offline precisely because it is exploring. The consequences to name are popularity self-reinforcement, narrowing catalogue coverage, and systematic offline/online metric disagreement. The mitigations you can actually ship on a customer deployment: log the slot and the serving model for every impression, reserve a small random-exposure slice as an unbiased evaluation set, use inverse-propensity-weighted replay for offline estimates, and hold back an epsilon of traffic for exploration in a contextual bandit. State the decision rule at the start of the engagement: offline metrics gate what is allowed into an A/B test, and only the A/B (Topic 97) decides what ships.

resource.label: arXiv 1003.0146 - A Contextual-Bandit Approach to Personalized News Article Recommendation (LinUCB, unbiased offline replay)

subtopics.name: Anomaly detection: choosing the regime before choosing the algorithm
subtopics.learn: Separate three regimes and say which one you are in before naming a model. Unsupervised outlier detection assumes the training set is already contaminated and has no labels (IsolationForest, LocalOutlierFactor, EllipticEnvelope); semi-supervised novelty detection trains on data believed clean (OneClassSVM, LocalOutlierFactor with novelty=True); supervised detection has labels and should use a weighted classifier from Topic 104. Learn the sklearn contract that unifies them - fit/predict returning +1 for inlier and -1 for outlier, score_samples where higher means more normal, and decision_function = score_samples - offset_. The honest rule for when an isolation forest beats a supervised classifier: no labels, labels that arrive months late, a shifting attack distribution so last quarter's positives do not describe this quarter's, or a day-one model on a new tenant. With thousands of clean labels on a stationary problem the supervised model wins on PR-AUC every time - benchmark suites like ADBench show even partial supervision beating the best unsupervised detector - and volunteering that in the meeting buys more credibility than defending your unsupervised model.

resource.label: arXiv 2206.09426 - ADBench: Anomaly Detection Benchmark (30 algorithms, 57 datasets, effect of supervision)

subtopics.name: Isolation forest mechanics: random cuts, expected path length, the score
subtopics.learn: An isolation tree picks a uniformly random feature and a uniformly random split value between that feature's min and max within the node, recursing until the point is alone or the height limit ceil(log2(psi)) is reached. Anomalies need fewer splits to isolate, so the statistic is the path length h(x) plus an adjustment for the subtree that was never built: c(psi) = 2H(psi - 1) - 2(psi - 1)/psi with H(i) approximately ln(i) + 0.5772156649, the Euler-Mascheroni constant. The score is s(x, psi) = 2^(-E[h(x)] / c(psi)): near 1 means clearly anomalous, near 0.5 means the sample is undifferentiated, below 0.5 means normal. Be able to derive c(psi) from the average unsuccessful search path length in a binary search tree, and to explain why the score is a ratio rather than a raw depth - normalising by c(psi) is what makes scores comparable across subsample sizes and forests. Training is O(t psi log psi) and scoring O(n t log psi), linear in n with tiny constants, which is the practical reason it is the default first detector on wide tabular data.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - IsolationForest example (path lengths, decision boundary, max_samples)

subtopics.name: Reaching parity with sklearn: max_samples, contamination, offset_
subtopics.learn: Write the forest yourself (n_estimators=100, max_samples=256 drawn without replacement per tree, random feature, uniform split inside the node's range) and then reconcile with the library: score_samples returns the NEGATIVE of the 2^(-E/c) score, decision_function = score_samples - offset_, and offset_ is -0.5 under contamination='auto' or the contamination-th percentile of the training scores otherwise. Defend both knobs out loud. max_samples=256 is deliberately small: subsampling reduces swamping (normal points surrounded by anomalies) and masking (a cluster of anomalies hiding each other), so raising it usually makes the detector worse, not better. contamination is a prior on the anomaly rate that moves only the threshold and never the ranking, so set it from the analyst review budget (100 reviews per day out of 200k transactions is 0.05 percent), or keep ranking and thresholding as two separate decisions. Verify parity by Spearman rank correlation against sklearn's score_samples on the same rows (aim above 0.95), not by matching predicted labels.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest (score_samples, decision_function, offset_, max_samples)

subtopics.name: Where isolation forests fail and what to reach for instead
subtopics.learn: Four failure geometries you should be able to name and demonstrate. (a) Cuts are axis-parallel, so a diagonal or interaction-defined anomaly produces rectangular ghost bands in the score field - the Extended Isolation Forest paper visualises this; rotate features with PCA (Topic 106) or use EIF. (b) Local density: a point that is globally normal but abnormal for its own cluster needs LocalOutlierFactor's reachability-density ratio, which an isolation forest cannot express. (c) Clustered anomalies: 300 near-identical transactions from one fraud ring form their own dense region and stop being easy to isolate, so the forest scores them as normal while a clustering or graph method finds them immediately. (d) High dimension with mostly irrelevant features: random feature selection dilutes the signal, path lengths concentrate, and the score histogram collapses into a narrow band around 0.5 - always plot that histogram, and if it has no right tail the detector has found nothing. Also remember the forest is scale-free across features but not immune to a monotone id or timestamp column, which it will happily isolate on.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Comparing anomaly detection algorithms for outlier detection on toy datasets

subtopics.name: Evaluating at 0.172 percent positives: PR-AUC, precision@k and the alert budget
subtopics.learn: With 492 positives in 284,807 rows, 99.83 percent accuracy is achieved by predicting 'not fraud' for everything, so accuracy leaves the report. ROC-AUC also flatters: FPR = FP / (FP + TN) has a 284k denominator, so 5,000 false positives shift it by under 0.02 while destroying an analyst team's week. Use average_precision_score as the PR-AUC, whose no-skill baseline equals the positive rate (0.0017 here), plus precision@k and recall@k at the k the customer can genuinely review, and convert to a lift statement they can act on ('precision@100 = 0.32, which is 186 times base rate'). Threshold selection is a business decision, not a model output: take k from the review budget or the threshold that hits a target recall, and show the confusion matrix at that operating point instead of one scalar. Bootstrap the metric - with 492 positives, precision@100 has a wide interval and a 0.02 gap between two models is usually noise.

resource.label: scikit-learn example - Precision-Recall (average precision, imbalanced settings)

subtopics.name: Non-stationarity: seasonality, drift and the retraining contract
subtopics.learn: Most production anomalies are just Tuesdays. Before scoring any time-indexed signal, remove the structure: STL decomposes a series into trend, seasonal and remainder, and you score the remainder, not the raw value; alternatively forecast the expected value with the models from Topic 108 and treat the standardised residual as the score. Then write the retraining contract with the customer explicitly: refit cadence, training window (a rolling 90 days usually beats all-history once behaviour drifts), a drift monitor on the score distribution itself (PSI or a KS test between the training scores and last week's), and the escalation rule for when the alert rate doubles - is that a fraud wave or model drift? Keep a frozen scored sample from launch so you can tell 'the world changed' from 'my model changed', and version the fitted forest together with the feature-transform code, because a quiet preprocessing change reranks every alert.

resource.label: Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed) - STL decomposition

outcomes: You can derive the biased matrix-factorisation objective and its SGD update rule on paper, implement it in NumPy only, and beat the mu + b_u + b_i baseline on MovieLens-100K held-out RMSE.

You can implement one ALS sweep as a per-user ridge solve with np.linalg.solve, show the training loss is monotone non-increasing across sweeps, and state the conditions under which you would ship ALS rather than SGD.

You can produce one table for MovieLens showing held-out RMSE, recall@10, NDCG@10 and catalogue coverage for popularity, item-item kNN, SGD-MF and BPR-MF under the same temporal split, and explain every row where RMSE and recall@10 disagree.

You can demonstrate the split leak numerically: same model and hyperparameters, random 80/20 versus temporal 80/20, with the recall@10 gap quantified and the candidate set correctly filtered of already-seen items.

You can derive c(psi) = 2H(psi - 1) - 2(psi - 1)/psi and the score 2^(-E[h(x)] / c(psi)), implement an isolation forest from scratch, and reach Spearman rank correlation above 0.95 with sklearn's score_samples on the credit-card data.

You can defend max_samples and contamination in a customer meeting: subsampling as the cure for swamping and masking, contamination as a threshold set from the analyst review budget rather than a model parameter that changes the ranking.
You can report PR-AUC, precision@100 and lift over base rate with bootstrap intervals for two detectors and state, with evidence, whether the difference is real.

You can look at a new dataset and say whether an isolation forest or a supervised model is the right call, naming the geometry (diagonal, local-density, clustered, high-dimensional) that would make you switch, and state the cold-start or fallback path for whichever you choose.
failureModes: A random 80/20 split is taken over a timestamped interaction log, so a user's later sessions sit in train and predict their earlier ones; offline recall@10 reads 0.31, the pilot delivers 0.06, and the model is blamed instead of the protocol.

Truncated SVD is run on the ratings matrix with unobserved entries left as stored zeros; the factors learn to predict near zero, held-out RMSE still looks respectable because the held-out set is zero-heavy too, and the top-K lists are effectively random.

The top-K candidate set is not filtered against the user's training history, so recall@10 is inflated by re-recommending items the user already consumed; the metric halves the day the filter is added, which is the week after the quarterly review.

Model selection is done on RMSE alone: k = 64 beats k = 16 on RMSE by fitting mid-scale ratings on popular items, but recall@10 drops, and the shipped model is worse than the one it replaced while the dashboard says it improved.

The cold-start path is never exercised because every demo user has history; on stage a brand-new tenant's user hits the id lookup, raises a KeyError or returns an empty list, and the meeting is about reliability for the rest of the hour.
