The isolation forest is fitted on raw columns including transaction_id and a monotonically increasing timestamp, so the trees isolate on those; the top 100 anomalies are simply the newest, highest-id rows, and the analyst queue is abandoned within a week.

contamination is left at its default and predict() is wired straight to the alert queue, generating around 1,400 alerts a day for a team that can review 100, of which roughly 96 percent are noise at a 0.172 percent true rate.

The detector is selected on ROC-AUC of 0.95 and described as excellent, while precision@100 is 0.04; the pilot is judged on analyst hours wasted, not on ranking theory, and the project is cancelled with a technically fine model.
interviewQuestions: Derive the regularised matrix-factorisation objective with user and item biases and give me the SGD update for p_u and q_i. Now fix Q and derive the closed-form update for p_u. Which would you run on two billion interactions on the customer's Spark cluster, and why?

Held-out RMSE improved from 0.912 to 0.897 but recall@10 fell from 0.28 to 0.24. Explain the mechanism that produces both at once, tell me which number you take to the customer, and say what you would change about the training objective.

Design a recommender for a marketplace with 4M buyers, 900k listings, no ratings, only clicks and purchases, and 60 percent of listings younger than seven days. Specify model, loss, negative sampling, split, metrics, cold-start path and serving architecture, then tell me where it fails first.
How does an isolation forest score a point? Write the score formula, explain what c(psi) is and where it comes from, and say why the score normalises expected path length rather than using raw depth.

Your isolation forest has PR-AUC 0.31 on labelled historical fraud, but in the pilot the top-100 queue is 95 percent legitimate high-value transactions. List your hypotheses in the order you would test them and say what evidence would settle each.
When would you tell a customer not to use an isolation forest? Give me three concrete data situations and the alternative you would reach for in each.

With 492 positives in 284,807 rows, model A has precision@100 of 0.34 and model B has 0.38. Is B better? Explain how you decide, and what exactly you would put in front of the customer to justify the choice.
109.proofOfWork: A companion repo `metric-divergence-lab` plus a two-page customer-facing note, both reproducible with one make target, that turns the two lessons of this topic into evidence someone else can rerun. The recommender half sweeps k in {8, 16, 32, 64, 128} against lambda over three seeds on MovieLens-100K under both a random and a temporal split, and produces a single figure with held-out RMSE on one axis and recall@10 on the other, annotated with the region where the two disagree, plus a table of popularity, item-item kNN, SGD-MF and BPR-MF that reports RMSE, recall@10, NDCG@10, catalogue coverage and mean popularity rank with bootstrap intervals - including the exact recall@10 delta caused by forgetting to filter already-seen items, and a cold-start section reporting metrics separately for users with 0, 1-2 and 3+ training interactions alongside the routing rule that serves them. The anomaly half generates four synthetic 2-D fixtures (Gaussian blob, diagonal correlated band, two-density clusters, and a 300-point anomaly cluster) plus a 50-dimension version with 45 noise features, scores each with your from-scratch forest, sklearn's IsolationForest, LocalOutlierFactor and EllipticEnvelope, and renders the score fields side by side so the axis-parallel artefacts, the local-density blind spot, the clustered-anomaly miss and the score-histogram collapse in high dimension are all visible rather than asserted; a parity check reports Spearman rho against sklearn on the credit-card data and a sensitivity table shows PR-AUC and precision@100 as max_samples moves from 64 to 8192. The note is written for a customer's data lead: one page on why the model that wins on RMSE is not the model to ship, one page on how the alert threshold follows from their review capacity, each claim pointing at a figure in the repo.

11.topic: Serving models on Kubernetes and GPUs
11.why: A large share of FDE engagements at Anthropic, Palantir and Databricks-style shops end with a customer saying 'we cannot send this data to an API, run it on our GPUs.' The FDE is then the person who has to turn a bare g6e node or an on-prem A100 box into a working, measured OpenAI-compatible endpoint on the customer's Kubernetes, and who has to defend, with numbers, why it costs what it costs and how many users it can hold before p95 latency falls over. Nobody on the customer side knows the driver/CUDA/device-plugin stack, so if you cannot debug 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' or a CUDA OOM at 11pm the whole pilot slips; if you cannot size KV cache you will either buy four H100s for a 7B model or promise 50 users to a card that holds 20.
prerequisites: Kubernetes core from Topic 7: you can write a Deployment, Service and Ingress from memory, read kubectl describe pod Events, and know what an extended resource and a taint are.
Kubernetes production ops from Topic 8: startup vs readiness vs liveness probes, requests vs limits and QoS classes, HPA mechanics, PVC access modes, and kubectl debug / ephemeral containers.
Docker internals from Topic 5: what a runtime hook is, how /dev nodes and host libraries get bind-mounted into a container, what /dev/shm is and why the default 64 MB matters.

Networking from Topic 2: HTTP keep-alive, SSE streaming, proxy read timeouts and idle timeouts on L7 load balancers (ALB 60 s default, nginx 60 s default) since token streams are long-lived responses.
Troubleshooting habits from Topic 3: reading dmesg, exit codes, and top/nvidia-smi side by side; comfortable computing bytes from parameter counts (7B x 2 bytes = 14 GB).

Accounts and budget: a Hugging Face account with Llama gated-model access approved (takes hours, request it on day one), an HF token, and roughly USD 25-40 of GPU-hours on RunPod or a cloud account with a non-zero G/VT On-Demand vCPU quota (new AWS accounts default to 0 and the quota request takes a day or two).

subtopics.name: The GPU stack from silicon to Pod: driver, CUDA, toolkit, device plugin
subtopics.learn: Draw the four layers and who owns each: the kernel module (nvidia.ko) plus libcuda.so live on the node and are the 'driver'; the CUDA toolkit/runtime (libcudart, cuBLAS) lives inside the image; the NVIDIA Container Toolkit is an OCI runtime hook that bind-mounts /dev/nvidia*, libcuda.so and nvidia-smi into the container at create time; the k8s-device-plugin DaemonSet talks to kubelet's device plugin gRPC socket to advertise nvidia.com/gpu as an extended resource and, on allocation, sets NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for the container. Be able to state which layer produced each of these: 'CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version' (image CUDA newer than node driver), 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' (device plugin or scheduling), 'Failed to initialize NVML: Unknown Error' (toolkit/cgroup device access).

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Schedule GPUs (device plugins, node labels, NFD)

subtopics.name: Driver and CUDA compatibility: read nvidia-smi before you pull an image
subtopics.learn: The 'CUDA Version' in the top-right of nvidia-smi is the maximum CUDA runtime the installed driver supports, not what is installed; a driver is backward compatible with older runtimes, and forward compatibility (running a newer runtime on an older driver via the cuda-compat package) exists only for datacenter GPUs. Check the image with python -c 'import torch; print(torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available())' and compare to the node. Know the practical failure: a vLLM wheel built against CUDA 12.8 on a node with a 535 driver fails at import, and the fix is either upgrading the node driver (GPU Operator can do it) or pulling an image built for an older CUDA. Understand why a kernel upgrade on the node can silently break a DKMS-built driver until reboot plus rebuild.

resource.label: NVIDIA docs: CUDA Compatibility

subtopics.name: NVIDIA Container Toolkit on a raw node: nvidia-ctk runtime configure
subtopics.learn: On a bare GPU VM (RunPod secure-cloud or a g5 instance) install nvidia-container-toolkit, run sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=containerd (or --runtime=docker), restart the engine and verify /etc/containerd/config.toml gained the nvidia runtime under plugins.'io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri'.containerd.runtimes. Prove it with docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi. Understand the two env vars the hook reads: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (all, none, 0,1, or GPU-UUID) and NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES (compute,utility is the minimum for CUDA plus nvidia-smi). In Kubernetes, know when you need a RuntimeClass named nvidia (toolkit installed but not set as default runtime) and what the symptom is when you forget it: the pod runs, nvidia.com/gpu is allocated, but the container sees no /dev/nvidia0.

resource.label: NVIDIA Container Toolkit: Installing the NVIDIA Container Toolkit

subtopics.name: GPU Operator: what the Helm chart deploys and when to turn pieces off
subtopics.learn: helm install gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator -n gpu-operator --create-namespace deploys, via a ClusterPolicy CR, a driver DaemonSet, the container-toolkit DaemonSet, the device plugin, DCGM exporter, GPU Feature Discovery (GFD), Node Feature Discovery, MIG manager and a validator pod per node. Learn the two most common overrides: --set driver.enabled=false when the node image already ships drivers (EKS accelerated AMI, GKE, RunPod), and --set toolkit.enabled=false when the toolkit is baked in. Verify with kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator (every nvidia-operator-validator must be Completed) and kubectl get node <n> -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu}'. Know what breaks when the driver DaemonSet is enabled on a node that already has a driver: the container driver fails to load and every GPU pod on that node goes Pending.

resource.label: NVIDIA GPU Operator: Installing the NVIDIA GPU Operator

subtopics.name: Scheduling onto GPUs: extended resources, taints, GFD labels
subtopics.learn: nvidia.com/gpu is requested under resources.limits only (requests, if given, must equal limits), is an integer, cannot be overcommitted, and is not shared between containers in a pod. Taint GPU nodes (nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule) so CPU workloads never land on a USD 4/hour node, and add the matching toleration to the vLLM pod. Pin GPU type with a nodeSelector on the GFD labels nvidia.com/gpu.product (e.g. NVIDIA-A10G, NVIDIA-L40S) or nvidia.com/gpu.memory, and read them with kubectl get nodes -L nvidia.com/gpu.product,nvidia.com/gpu.count. When a pod sits Pending with '0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu', walk the checklist: is the device plugin pod Running on the target node, does Allocatable show the GPU, is another pod already holding it, does the pod tolerate the taint.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Taints and Tolerations

subtopics.name: Managed GPU node groups and scale-from-zero: EKS accelerated AMI, Karpenter
subtopics.learn: Know the cloud GPU menu you will actually be offered: g5 (A10G 24 GB), g6 (L4 24 GB), g6e (L40S 48 GB), p4d (8x A100 40 GB), p5 (8x H100 80 GB); the EKS accelerated AL2023 AMI ships driver and toolkit so you disable them in the operator. Write a Karpenter NodePool whose requirements select karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-name In [l40s] and karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-count In [1], carries the nvidia.com/gpu taint, and has a long consolidateAfter so a 5-minute lull does not delete a node that took 4 minutes to boot. Understand the cold-start chain when scaling from zero: instance launch (2-3 min) plus 10-15 GB image pull plus weight load, so the first user waits 5-8 minutes; mitigate with a warm minimum of one replica and a pre-pull DaemonSet. Check the account's 'Running On-Demand G and VT instances' quota before the customer call; it is often 0.

resource.label: Karpenter docs: NodePools

subtopics.name: vLLM in a container: the vllm serve flags an operator must own
subtopics.learn: Use the official vllm/vllm-openai image and know the flags that change capacity or safety: --model and --served-model-name (what clients put in 'model'), --dtype auto (bf16 on Ampere+), --max-model-len (caps context and therefore per-request KV; do not leave it at the model's 128k default on a 24 GB card), --gpu-memory-utilization (fraction reserved for weights plus KV, default 0.9), --max-num-seqs (hard cap on sequences in one batch, i.e. concurrency), --tensor-parallel-size, --enable-prefix-caching, --kv-cache-dtype fp8, --quantization, --api-key, --port 8000, --download-dir, --trust-remote-code. Know --enforce-eager is for debugging only (disables CUDA graphs, costs throughput). Understand why tensor parallel needs a big /dev/shm and IPC (NCCL uses shared memory) and how that maps to an emptyDir medium Memory in Kubernetes instead of Docker's --ipc=host.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Engine Arguments

subtopics.name: Model weights: getting 16 GB into the cluster without downloading on every restart
subtopics.learn: An 8B bf16 checkpoint is roughly 16 GB in safetensors shards; pulling that from the Hub on every pod start turns a 30-second restart into a 5-10 minute outage and can hit rate limits. Compare the four patterns and pick per customer: a PVC pre-filled by a Job running hf download <repo> --local-dir /models (ReadWriteMany or one pod per PV), a hostPath cache on dedicated GPU nodes, an object-store mount (S3 Mountpoint or GCS FUSE), and baking weights into the image (avoid: 16 GB layers, slow pulls, registry limits). Set HF_HOME or --download-dir to the mount, HF_TOKEN from a Secret for gated Llama models, and HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 in air-gapped sites so vLLM never tries the network. For corporate proxies, know that allowlisting huggingface.co alone is not enough because files are served from cdn-lfs and xethub hostnames.

resource.label: Hugging Face Hub docs: Downloading models (CLI, proxies, allowlist hosts)

subtopics.name: The Deployment manifest: GPU limits, /dev/shm, probes, memory, update strategy
subtopics.learn: Write the vLLM Deployment from scratch and justify every field: resources.limits nvidia.com/gpu: 1 plus a memory request at least the size of the weights (vLLM stages tensors through host RAM while loading; too low and you get OOMKilled during startup, exit 137); an emptyDir with medium: Memory and sizeLimit mounted at /dev/shm; a startupProbe on GET /health with periodSeconds 10 and failureThreshold high enough to cover download plus load (60 = 10 minutes) so the liveness probe never kills a still-loading engine; readinessProbe and livenessProbe on /health with timeoutSeconds 5; terminationGracePeriodSeconds at least as long as your longest generation so in-flight streams finish. Set strategy to Recreate or rollingUpdate with maxSurge 0 when you own exactly one GPU, because the default 25% surge schedules a second pod that can never get a GPU and the rollout hangs forever. Know that zero-downtime rollouts cost an N+1 GPU.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Deployment - Using Kubernetes

subtopics.name: Exposing it: Service, Ingress or Gateway, API key, and streaming timeouts
subtopics.learn: Front the pod with a ClusterIP Service and your Ingress or HTTPRoute from Topics 7 and 8, then exercise the OpenAI-compatible surface: GET /v1/models, POST /v1/chat/completions with stream: true, GET /health, GET /metrics. Streaming responses are long-lived SSE, so raise the proxy read timeout (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: '600') and disable response buffering (proxy-buffering: 'off'); an ALB with the default 60 s idle timeout will cut off any generation longer than a minute with no error in vLLM's logs. Decide where auth lives: --api-key on vLLM is a single shared secret, so put real per-tenant auth on the gateway and keep the vLLM Service unreachable from outside the namespace with a NetworkPolicy. Verify from a laptop with the openai Python client pointed at base_url and from inside the cluster to separate ingress latency from model latency.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Online Serving (OpenAI-compatible server and endpoints)

subtopics.name: Inference-aware routing: why round-robin is the wrong load balancer for LLM replicas
subtopics.learn: A Service spreads requests round-robin and knows nothing about which replica has 40 sequences queued or which one already holds the KV cache for this conversation's prefix. Understand what the Gateway API Inference Extension adds: an InferencePool pointing at the vLLM pods, an endpoint picker (Envoy ext_proc) that reads each replica's queue depth and kv_cache_usage from /metrics and routes to the least-loaded or prefix-affine one, and per-model criticality. Know when it matters (two or more replicas, mixed long and short prompts) and what the cheap substitute is with plain ingress (consistent-hash on a session header for prefix locality, accepting hot spots). Be able to explain to a customer's platform team why their existing LB health check on /health does not protect them from one saturated replica.

resource.label: Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension: Introduction

subtopics.name: Metrics: vLLM /metrics, DCGM exporter, and the six panels that predict an outage
subtopics.learn: Scrape vLLM's Prometheus endpoint (PodMonitor on port 8000, path /metrics) and know the names: vllm:num_requests_running, vllm:num_requests_waiting (queue; the earliest saturation signal), vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc, vllm:num_preemptions_total (any growth means KV cache is too small for the load), vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds, vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds (or time_per_output_token_seconds), vllm:e2e_request_latency_seconds, vllm:prompt_tokens_total and vllm:generation_tokens_total for cost accounting. From the GPU Operator's DCGM exporter use DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED, DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL, DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE, DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP, DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE and DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS. Understand why GPU_UTIL at 100% does not mean saturated (it means a kernel was resident, not that SMs were busy) and why waiting-queue depth plus TTFT p95 is the pair you alert on.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Design - Metrics

subtopics.name: Capacity math: weights plus KV cache decides how many concurrent users fit
subtopics.learn: Do the arithmetic from config.json, not from vibes. Weights = params x bytes per param (Llama-3.1-8B bf16 = 16 GB). KV bytes per token = 2 (K and V) x num_hidden_layers x num_key_value_heads x head_dim x bytes per element; for Llama-3.1-8B that is 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 bytes, i.e. 128 KiB per token thanks to GQA. KV budget = GPU memory x gpu-memory-utilization minus weights minus roughly 1-2 GB of activations and CUDA graphs. On a 24 GB A10G that leaves about 4-5 GB, roughly 35k tokens, so 50 users each holding a 2k-token conversation (100k tokens, 12.8 GB) do not fit at bf16; on a 48 GB L40S they do with headroom. Confirm against the two lines vLLM logs at startup, 'GPU KV cache size: N tokens' and 'Maximum concurrency for X tokens per request: Y', and against kv_cache_usage_perc under load. Levers: lower --max-model-len, --kv-cache-dtype fp8, weight quantization (deferred to Topic 56), or a bigger card. Distinguish 50 named users from 50 in-flight sequences: with think time, 50 users is often 10-20 concurrent requests.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Conserving Memory

subtopics.name: Throughput vs latency knobs: max-num-seqs, max-num-batched-tokens, chunked prefill, preemption
subtopics.learn: Continuous batching means every decode step advances all running sequences by one token; more sequences in the batch raise aggregate tokens per second and raise per-user inter-token latency, while TTFT is governed by prefill work and queue time. Chunked prefill (default in V1) slices long prompts and mixes them with decode steps; --max-num-batched-tokens is the budget per step, where a smaller value protects ITL and a larger one improves TTFT and throughput. When KV blocks run out the scheduler preempts a sequence and recomputes it later, which shows up as num_preemptions_total climbing and e2e latency p99 spiking; the fix is more KV (memory, shorter max-model-len) or a lower --max-num-seqs, never a bigger batch. Write down the SLO you will size against before benchmarking: for a chat UI, TTFT p95 under 1 s and ITL p95 under 50 ms (about 20 tokens per second per user) is a defensible default.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Optimization and Tuning

subtopics.name: Benchmark it properly: vllm bench serve, closed vs open loop, reading the table
subtopics.learn: Run the load generator from a pod inside the cluster so ingress is out of the picture: vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --base-url http://vllm:8000 --model <served-name> --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 256 --num-prompts 500 --max-concurrency N (closed loop, N users hammering) and separately --request-rate R (open loop, Poisson arrivals). Sweep N over 1, 8, 16, 32, 50, 64 and record request throughput, output token throughput, and mean, median and p99 TTFT, TPOT and ITL; the knee where p99 TTFT jumps while throughput flattens is your capacity. Warm up first (CUDA graphs, prefix cache), run each point twice, and use --save-result so the JSON lands in the repo. Also try --dataset-name sharegpt for realistic length distributions and note how much the answer changes versus fixed random lengths.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Benchmark CLI (vllm bench serve)

subtopics.name: Sharing and splitting GPUs: time-slicing vs MIG vs tensor parallel
subtopics.learn: Time-slicing (device plugin ConfigMap with sharing.timeSlicing.resources[].replicas: N) makes one card advertise N nvidia.com/gpu units with no memory isolation: one tenant's CUDA OOM kills the others, so it is for dev clusters, never for a customer's shared production card. MIG on A100 and H100 (nvidia-smi mig -cgi, operator mig.strategy single or mixed, profiles like 1g.10gb through 7g.80gb) gives hard memory and compute partitions and shows up as nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb resources; A10G, L4 and L40S do not support MIG. Tensor parallel (--tensor-parallel-size 2) goes the other way and splits one model across GPUs in the same pod (must divide the attention head count; NVLink versus PCIe changes the result a lot), and multi-node uses pipeline parallel with LeaderWorkerSet. For 50 users on one 8B model the answer is one GPU, one model, no sharing; know how to say that.

resource.label: NVIDIA GPU Operator: Time-Slicing GPUs in Kubernetes

subtopics.name: Autoscaling GPU replicas: HPA cannot see the queue, KEDA plus Prometheus can
subtopics.learn: CPU-based HPA is useless here because a saturated vLLM pod shows low CPU. Scale on vllm:num_requests_waiting or vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc via a KEDA ScaledObject with a prometheus trigger (serverAddress, query such as sum(vllm:num_requests_waiting{app='vllm'}), threshold like '5'), or via HPA plus prometheus-adapter. Set stabilization and cooldown windows in minutes, not seconds, because a scale-up takes 4-8 minutes (node, image, weights) and a flapping scaler will thrash. Keep minReplicaCount at 1 unless the customer accepts multi-minute cold starts, add a PodDisruptionBudget so node upgrades do not take the only replica, and pre-pull the image with a DaemonSet on GPU nodes. Understand that scaling out also multiplies cost linearly with no discount, so present it next to the capacity plan.

resource.label: KEDA docs: Prometheus scaler

subtopics.name: Debugging the GPU node: nvidia-smi, Xid errors, stuck Pending pods, CUDA OOM, NCCL
subtopics.learn: Build the triage sequence you can run in five minutes. Pod Pending: describe it, then check device plugin and validator pods on the target node and node Allocatable. CrashLoopBackOff with torch.OutOfMemoryError or 'No available memory for the cache blocks': lower --gpu-memory-utilization or --max-model-len, or check nvidia-smi for a zombie process from a previous pod still holding memory. 'NCCL error' or hangs with tensor parallel: /dev/shm too small or IPC missing, set NCCL_DEBUG=INFO. Slow or wrong: VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG and confirm the attention backend and dtype in the startup log. Hardware: kubectl exec nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY,ECC and dmesg | grep -i xid on the node; Xid 79 (fallen off the bus) and Xid 48 (double-bit ECC) mean cordon, drain and replace the node, not restart the pod; Xid 31 and 43 usually point at the application. Know what a 'Failed to initialize NVML' after a driver upgrade means for every pod on the node.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Troubleshooting

subtopics.name: Cost and the capacity plan: from USD per GPU-hour to USD per million tokens
subtopics.learn: Turn the benchmark into the two numbers a customer buys on. Take output tokens per second at the highest concurrency that still meets the SLO, then USD per 1M output tokens = hourly GPU price / (tok/s x 3600 / 1e6); an L40S at about USD 1.8-2.0 per hour producing 1,500 tok/s is roughly USD 0.35 per million tokens at full utilization, and 5x that at 20% utilization, which is the honest number for a 50-user internal tool. Put the plan in one table: model and dtype, GPU type, replicas (N+1 if zero-downtime deploys are required), max in-flight sequences, expected named users given think time, SLO targets, KV headroom, monthly cost at expected and at peak utilization, and the same workload priced on a hosted API for comparison. State the quota, lead time and spot-interruption assumptions explicitly, because those, not tok/s, are what usually slips the pilot.

outcomes: You can take a fresh Ubuntu GPU VM with nothing but the driver installed and, in under 20 minutes, have containerd running GPU containers via nvidia-ctk and a single-node cluster reporting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 in Allocatable.

You can write a vLLM Deployment, Service and Ingress from memory with correct GPU limit, memory request, /dev/shm emptyDir, startup/readiness/liveness probes and Recreate strategy, and explain each field to a customer's platform engineer without looking anything up.

You can compute, from a model's config.json and a GPU's memory, the KV cache budget and maximum concurrent 2k-token conversations within 15% of what vLLM prints at startup, and show your working on a whiteboard in under five minutes.
You can run a vllm bench serve concurrency sweep, produce a table of throughput and p50/p99 TTFT and ITL per concurrency level, identify the knee, and state the supported concurrency at a given SLO.

You can triage a GPU pod stuck Pending or CrashLooping to one of: driver/toolkit mismatch, device plugin absent, taint, held GPU, CUDA OOM, shm/NCCL, or hardware Xid, using kubectl describe, nvidia-smi and dmesg, in under ten minutes.
You can configure a Prometheus scrape of vLLM and DCGM metrics and name the two signals you alert on for impending saturation, with the PromQL for each.
You can explain and demonstrate why a streaming completion longer than 60 seconds dies behind a default ALB or nginx ingress, and fix it with the exact annotation or attribute.
You can present a one-page capacity and cost plan for 50 users that a CFO and a platform lead both accept, including USD per million tokens at expected utilization and the hosted-API comparison.
failureModes: The customer's platform team upgrades the node kernel during a patch window; the DKMS driver no longer loads, nvidia-smi says 'NVML: Driver/library version mismatch', the device plugin reports 0 GPUs, and the vLLM pod sits Pending with 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' until someone reboots and rebuilds the module.

A rolling update of the vLLM Deployment with default maxSurge schedules a second pod on a cluster with one GPU; the new pod is Pending forever, the old one keeps serving the previous model, and the release 'succeeded' in ArgoCD because the Deployment never reported failure.

--max-model-len was left at the model's 131k default on a 24 GB card; vLLM reserved almost nothing for KV cache, num_preemptions_total climbed under 12 concurrent users, and p99 latency went from 2 s to 40 s while GPU utilization looked fine on the dashboard.

Long RAG answers were truncated mid-stream at exactly 60 seconds in production but not in staging; the difference was an AWS ALB with the default idle timeout in front of production, and vLLM logged nothing because the client, not the server, was disconnected.

The liveness probe used the same 30-second initial delay as a web service; on a cold node the 16 GB weight load took four minutes, kubelet killed the container at 30 seconds every time, and the pod CrashLooped for an hour before anyone read the events.

Time-slicing was enabled to 'share' one A10G between the dev and staging vLLM instances; a staging load test drove CUDA OOM, which also killed the dev replica mid-demo, and nobody could explain to the customer why two isolated namespaces went down together.

The pilot was sized at 50 users against a benchmark run with 128-token prompts and 128-token outputs; real prompts averaged 3k tokens of pasted documents, TTFT p95 was 9 seconds on day one, and the fix required a bigger GPU that had a two-week quota lead time.
interviewQuestions: A customer hands you an EKS cluster with one g6e.xlarge node and asks for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for Llama-3.1-8B for 50 internal users by Friday. Walk me through everything from node to first token: what has to be installed, every field in the manifest you would write, how you would expose it, and how you would know it is actually ready for 50 people.

Show me how you would compute the maximum number of concurrent 2,000-token conversations a 48 GB L40S can hold for an 8B GQA model at bf16, then tell me what changes if the customer insists on 32k context. Which two flags would you touch first and what does each cost?

A vLLM pod is stuck Pending with 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' on a node where nvidia-smi on the host shows the card. Give me your ordered diagnostic sequence, the commands, and the three most likely root causes with how you would tell them apart.

GPU utilization is 95% on the DCGM dashboard, but users complain the model is slow and p99 TTFT is 8 seconds. Explain why the utilization number is misleading, which vLLM metrics you would look at instead, and what the likely configuration fix is.

Design the autoscaling for this service. Why is CPU-based HPA wrong, what metric would you scale on, what threshold and cooldown, and how do you handle a 6-minute scale-up latency when a marketing team launches an internal announcement that triples traffic at 9 am?

The security team asks you to run three teams' models on one shared A100 with strong isolation, and the platform team suggests time-slicing. Compare time-slicing, MIG and separate nodes on isolation, utilization and operational risk, and tell me what you would recommend and how you would demonstrate the isolation property.

Streaming responses die at exactly one minute in production only. Debug it out loud: where in the path could a 60-second limit live, how do you prove which hop it is without customer downtime, and what is the fix at each candidate layer?
11.proofOfWork: A public repository named vllm-on-k8s containing a Kustomize or Helm deployment of vLLM (Deployment with GPU limit, shm emptyDir, staged probes, Recreate strategy, Secret-fed HF_TOKEN, PVC weight cache with a fill Job, Service, Ingress with streaming timeouts, PodMonitor, KEDA ScaledObject) that a reviewer can apply to any cluster with an NVIDIA GPU Operator; a capacity.py script that reads a Hugging Face config.json plus GPU memory, dtype, max-model-len and gpu-memory-utilization and prints KV bytes per token, KV budget, max in-flight sequences at a given conversation length, and USD per million output tokens from a supplied hourly price, with a test asserting its prediction is within 15% of the 'GPU KV cache size' line captured from a real vLLM startup log checked into the repo; a bench/ directory with the raw --save-result JSON from a vllm bench serve sweep at concurrency 1, 8, 16, 32, 50 and 64 on one GPU type, a script that renders them into a markdown table and a throughput-versus-p99-TTFT plot with the knee marked; and a runbook.md with five incident drills (Pending after kernel upgrade, CUDA OOM, stuck rollout, 60-second stream cutoff, Xid 79) each with the exact commands and the expected output that confirms the diagnosis. The plan deliverable's benchmark table and capacity plan link to this repo as their evidence.

110.topic: Neural network foundations: backpropagation, activations, initialisation, regularisation
110.why: Every deep-learning conversation you will have with a customer eventually collapses into one of four questions - why is the loss NaN, why is validation worse than training, why does it not learn at all, and why did it work on my laptop - and all four are answered by the chain rule, the variance arithmetic of initialisation, and the train/eval semantics of the regularisers. If you have derived and coded the backward pass yourself, a per-layer gradient histogram is a diagnosis rather than a picture, and you can say 'this is a dead-ReLU problem caused by your init scale, not a data problem' in the room instead of promising to look into it. This is also the topic that makes everything downstream honest: batch norm, transformers, LoRA and fine-tuning are all just more computational graph, and you cannot debug a model you can only call.
prerequisites: Matrix calculus at the level of Topic 94 (Calculus and optimisation): Jacobians, the multivariable chain rule, gradient descent, and being able to differentiate a scalar with respect to a matrix
Linear algebra from Topic 93: matrix products and shapes, transposes, inner products, singular values and what a spectral radius says about repeated multiplication
Cross-entropy and maximum likelihood from Topic 98 (Information theory and loss functions) - you must already know that minimising NLL is fitting a categorical likelihood
NumPy vectorisation, broadcasting rules and float32-vs-float64 behaviour from Topic 99 (Numerical computing), including why catastrophic cancellation exists
Regularisation and the bias-variance decomposition as seen for linear models in Topic 100 (Supervised learning I) - L2 on a logistic regression should already be familiar
An honest train/validation/test split discipline and leakage awareness from Topic 103 (Model evaluation), because every ablation number in the deliverable is a held-out number
Python 3.11+ with NumPy and Matplotlib installed, pytest for the gradient-check test, and PyTorch available for cross-checking only (it must not appear in the training path)

subtopics.name: Computational graphs and reverse-mode automatic differentiation
subtopics.learn: Understand that backpropagation is not a special algorithm for neural nets but reverse-mode AD on a DAG: each primitive defines a vector-Jacobian product v -> v^T (df/dx), and the reverse sweep composes them right-to-left. Be able to state the cost argument: for f: R^n -> R, forward mode needs n sweeps (one per input direction) while reverse mode needs one, at the price of storing every intermediate activation - so training memory scales with depth x batch x width, which is why activation checkpointing exists. Know that the reverse sweep visits nodes in reverse topological order, that a node used twice must have its incoming gradients summed (fan-out becomes addition), and that non-differentiable points (ReLU at 0, max, abs) are handled by convention, not by the theory.

resource.label: Baydin et al., "Automatic Differentiation in Machine Learning: a Survey" (arXiv:1502.05767)

subtopics.name: Hand-deriving the backward pass of an L-layer MLP
subtopics.learn: Derive on paper, without notes, for z^l = W^l a^{l-1} + b^l and a^l = phi(z^l): the output error delta^L = grad_{a^L} J (*) phi'(z^L), the recursion delta^l = ((W^{l+1})^T delta^{l+1}) (*) phi'(z^l), and the parameter gradients dJ/dW^l = delta^l (a^{l-1})^T and dJ/db^l = delta^l, where (*) is elementwise. Then redo it in batched row-major layout - A of shape (B, d_in), dZ of shape (B, d_out), dW = A^T dZ, db = dZ.sum(axis=0), dA = dZ W^T - and be explicit about where the 1/B from a mean-reduced loss lives, because putting it in two places is a silent 1/B^2 that looks like a learning-rate problem. Be able to name which activations must be cached during the forward pass for each of these to be computable.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Forward Propagation, Backward Propagation, and Computational Graphs

subtopics.name: Softmax + cross-entropy: the (yhat - y) identity and log-sum-exp
subtopics.learn: Derive the softmax Jacobian dp_i/dz_j = p_i(delta_ij - p_j), i.e. diag(p) - p p^T, then compose it with dL/dp_i = -y_i/p_i and watch everything cancel to the identity dL/dz = yhat - y (per example, divided by B if the loss is mean-reduced). Implement log-softmax with the shift trick log sum_j exp(z_j) = m + log sum_j exp(z_j - m) where m = max_j z_j, and know that computing softmax then log separately overflows for logits around 90 in float32 and underflows to log(0) = -inf for confidently wrong predictions. Know that torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss and torch.nn.functional.log_softmax consume raw logits for exactly this reason, so an extra softmax before the loss is a real and common bug that halves effective gradients rather than crashing.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Concise Implementation of Softmax Regression (Softmax Implementation Revisited / LogSumExp)

subtopics.name: Writing a minimal reverse-mode autograd engine
subtopics.learn: Build a Tensor/Value node holding .data, .grad, a ._backward closure and a set of parents, so that every op (add, mul, matmul, relu, log-softmax) constructs the child node and registers how to push gradient back. Implement backward() as: build the topological order by DFS, seed the output gradient with 1.0, then walk the reversal calling each closure - and always accumulate with += so a tensor consumed by two branches is correct. Get the three details that bite: an explicit zero_grad() between steps (PyTorch accumulates too), a detach()/no-grad path so evaluation does not build graph, and broadcast-aware gradients where a (1, d) bias added to (B, d) must have its gradient summed back over the broadcast axis. Read micrograd once, then write your own from the derivation rather than copying.

resource.label: karpathy/micrograd - a ~150-line scalar reverse-mode autograd engine

subtopics.name: Vectorised NumPy layer implementations and shape discipline
subtopics.learn: Write Linear.forward/backward, ReLU, Dropout and the loss as objects with an explicit cache, and make every backward assert that dW.shape == W.shape and dX.shape == X.shape - a transposed matmul that happens to be conformable is the single most common from-scratch bug and it presents as 'the model trains, badly'. Use A.T @ dZ and dZ @ W.T rather than loops, use np.einsum('bi,bj->ij', A, dZ) when the index bookkeeping gets confusing, and keep the reduction convention (mean over batch) written once in the loss and nowhere else. Run the whole net in float64 for the gradient-check test and float32 for training, and know that np.float32 accumulation over a 60k-row epoch is where your 'reference' numbers start disagreeing at the 1e-4 level.

resource.label: NumPy user guide - Broadcasting

subtopics.name: Finite-difference gradient checking to 1e-7
subtopics.learn: Use the centred difference (J(theta + h e_i) - J(theta - h e_i)) / (2h), which has O(h^2) truncation error versus O(h) for the one-sided form, with h = 1e-5 in float64; score with the relative error |g_analytic - g_numeric| / max(|g_analytic|, |g_numeric|, 1e-8) and treat < 1e-7 as pass, 1e-5 as suspicious, > 1e-3 as a bug. Check a random sample of coordinates per parameter tensor rather than all of them, and check biases separately because they are few and their bugs hide in the average. Control the environment: fix the seed, disable dropout, use a tiny net and a handful of examples, include the regularisation term in J if it is in the gradient, and know that ReLU kinks produce false failures when a pre-activation sits within h of zero - perturb the input away from the kink instead of lowering h until noise swamps the signal.

resource.label: Stanford CS231n notes - Learning and Evaluation (gradient checks, sanity checks, babysitting)

subtopics.name: Cross-checking against torch.autograd.gradcheck
subtopics.learn: Wrap your NumPy layers' forward as a torch function on double-precision tensors with requires_grad=True and run torch.autograd.gradcheck(fn, inputs, eps=1e-6, atol=1e-5), then separately assert np.allclose between your analytic gradients and torch's autograd gradients for an identical net with copied weights. Understand what gradcheck actually does (numerical Jacobian versus the VJP-derived analytic Jacobian, column by column), why it demands float64, and what nondet_tol is for. This is the FDE move: two independent implementations agreeing to 1e-7 is evidence you can put in a README and defend, whereas 'it trains' is not.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Gradcheck mechanics (numerical vs analytical Jacobian)

subtopics.name: Activation functions and their derivatives: saturation and dead units
subtopics.learn: Know each derivative cold and what it does to a product of L of them: sigmoid' = s(1-s) with maximum 0.25 (so >= 4x gradient shrinkage per layer even at the best point, and ~0 in the tails), tanh' = 1 - tanh^2 with maximum 1 and zero-centred output (strictly better than sigmoid for hidden layers), ReLU' = 1[z > 0] which neither shrinks nor saturates on the positive side but is exactly zero on the negative side. Be able to explain dead ReLUs mechanically: one large update drives a unit's pre-activation negative for every input, its gradient becomes identically zero, and it never recovers - caused by too-high learning rate or a large negative bias, and measurable as the fraction of units with zero activation across a validation batch. Know leaky ReLU (slope 0.01) and ELU as the standard mitigations and what each costs.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Multilayer Perceptrons (activation functions)

subtopics.name: Modern activations: GELU and SiLU/Swish
subtopics.learn: Understand GELU(x) = x * Phi(x) as a stochastic-regulariser-flavoured smooth gate (and its tanh approximation, which is what most implementations actually compute), and SiLU(x) = x * sigmoid(x); both are smooth, non-monotonic near the origin and pass a small negative gradient, which is why transformer blocks use them instead of ReLU. Know that their derivatives are not indicator functions, so the clean Kaiming factor-of-2 argument no longer holds exactly - people use the ReLU gain anyway and rely on normalisation layers to absorb the mismatch. In the ablation, treat GELU as the sanity control that shows your framework generalises past the three classical activations.

resource.label: Hendrycks & Gimpel, "Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs)" (arXiv:1606.08415)

subtopics.name: Vanishing and exploding gradients as a product of Jacobians
subtopics.learn: Write the gradient at layer l as a product of (L - l) factors of the form diag(phi'(z)) W^T and reason about it multiplicatively: if the typical singular value of each factor is s, the gradient magnitude scales like s^{L-l}, so s = 0.8 over 20 layers is 0.01x and s = 1.2 is 40x. This is why the fix is variance control (init and normalisation) rather than a bigger learning rate. Instrument it: log the L2 norm of the gradient per layer each epoch and plot on a log axis - a monotone decay towards the input layers is vanishing, a spike then NaN is exploding. Know global-norm gradient clipping (torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_) as the blunt fix, and residual connections as the structural one, because an identity path contributes a Jacobian of I that keeps the product from collapsing.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Numerical Stability and Initialization

subtopics.name: Xavier/Glorot initialisation: derive the variance condition
subtopics.learn: Derive it yourself: assuming inputs and weights are independent with zero mean, Var(z) = n_in * Var(w) * Var(x), so preserving forward variance requires Var(w) = 1/n_in, while preserving backward (gradient) variance requires Var(w) = 1/n_out; Glorot takes the harmonic-style compromise Var(w) = 2/(n_in + n_out), which as a uniform distribution is U[-sqrt(6/(n_in+n_out)), +sqrt(6/(n_in+n_out))]. Be explicit about the assumptions that make this true and where they fail: zero-mean symmetric activation operating in its near-linear regime (fine for tanh, wrong for ReLU), independence between weights and activations (false after the first update), and i.i.d. inputs (false for unnormalised pixel data). This is the derivation an interviewer will ask you to do on a whiteboard.

resource.label: Glorot & Bengio, "Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks" (AISTATS 2010, PMLR)

subtopics.name: Kaiming/He initialisation: where the factor of 2 comes from
subtopics.learn: Redo the variance argument with ReLU in the loop: for z symmetric about zero, E[ReLU(z)^2] = (1/2) Var(z), so half the second moment is destroyed at every layer and the fix is Var(w) = 2/n_in (normal with std sqrt(2/n_in), or the uniform equivalent). Know that mode='fan_in' preserves the forward signal and mode='fan_out' preserves the backward signal, that either is acceptable for a plain MLP but the choice matters in deep conv stacks, and that the leaky-ReLU generalisation is gain = sqrt(2/(1 + a^2)). Be able to state the consequence concretely: with naive 0.01*randn in a 10-layer ReLU net the forward activations decay to ~0 and the loss sits pinned at log(C) forever, which is the single fastest way to convince a customer that init is not a detail.

resource.label: He et al., "Delving Deep into Rectifiers" (arXiv:1502.01852)

subtopics.name: Initialisation in practice: symmetry breaking, biases, framework defaults
subtopics.learn: Know the API surface - torch.nn.init.kaiming_normal_(w, mode='fan_in', nonlinearity='relu'), xavier_uniform_(w, gain=calculate_gain('tanh')), zeros_ for biases - and the rules: never initialise all weights identically (every unit in a layer then computes the same function and receives the same gradient forever), biases at zero is the default and the exceptions are deliberate (LSTM forget-gate bias 1, a final-layer bias set to the log base rate for heavily imbalanced classification). Know that PyTorch's nn.Linear default is kaiming_uniform_(a=sqrt(5)), which is not Kaiming-for-ReLU and is closer to a Xavier-scale init, so 'I used the default' is not the same as 'I used He init'. In deep residual stacks, scaling the residual branch by 1/sqrt(L) or zero-initialising the last layer of each block is the standard stabiliser.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.nn.init

subtopics.name: Batch normalisation: what it actually fixes and its train/eval asymmetry
subtopics.learn: Write the transform: per feature, xhat = (x - mu_B) / sqrt(var_B + eps) then y = gamma * xhat + beta, where mu_B and var_B are computed over the batch, which means the backward pass through them couples every example in the batch - derive the three-term BN gradient at least once so you understand why it is not a pointwise op. Know the train/eval asymmetry cold: training uses batch statistics and updates running_mean/running_var with momentum; evaluation uses the running estimates, so forgetting model.eval() changes predictions and a batch size of 1 or 2 makes the batch statistics noise. Know the empirical result that BN mainly buys robustness to initialisation and larger usable learning rates, that the original 'internal covariate shift' story is contested, and that LayerNorm is the sequence-model replacement precisely because it needs no batch.

resource.label: Ioffe & Szegedy, "Batch Normalization" (arXiv:1502.03167)

subtopics.name: L2 / weight decay: the shrinkage update and where it must not apply
subtopics.learn: Add (lambda/2)||w||^2 to the loss, differentiate, and read off the update w <- (1 - eta*lambda) w - eta * grad L: plain SGD with L2 is literally multiplicative shrinkage each step. Know the MAP interpretation (Gaussian prior on weights, so lambda is a prior precision), and that the penalty applies to weight matrices only - decaying biases and BatchNorm gamma/beta shifts the function for no regularisation benefit. Know the adaptive-optimiser subtlety that trips most people: adding lambda*w to the gradient inside Adam means the penalty gets divided by sqrt(v_hat) like everything else, so large-gradient weights are decayed less; decoupled weight decay (AdamW) applies the shrinkage outside the adaptive scaling and is why torch.optim.AdamW exists. Tune lambda on a log grid (1e-5 to 1e-1) against validation loss, never training loss.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Weight Decay

subtopics.name: Dropout: inverted dropout and the eval-mode bug
subtopics.learn: Implement inverted dropout: at training time sample a Bernoulli(1-p) mask per unit, multiply, and divide by (1-p) so E[activation] is unchanged; at eval time do nothing at all. The backward pass is the same mask and the same scale, and if you scale in forward but not backward the gradient check fails immediately - which is exactly why you write the gradient check first. Know the practical settings (p ~ 0.5 on wide hidden layers, 0.1-0.2 on inputs, usually applied after the activation), why dropout and BatchNorm interact badly (the variance shift between train and eval), and that dropout raises training loss by design, so an ablation must compare validation curves - a dropout run whose training loss is higher is not a worse run.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Dropout

subtopics.name: Early stopping, the generalisation gap, and when more capacity helps
subtopics.learn: Implement early stopping properly: monitor validation loss (not accuracy, which is noisier), keep a patience counter, and restore the best checkpoint rather than returning the last one - 'early stopping' that returns final weights is not early stopping. Know the theoretical hook: for a quadratic objective with small learning rate, stopping after t steps constrains the solution in the same way an L2 penalty does, with the number of steps playing the role of 1/lambda, which is why L2 + early stopping often adds little on top of either. Be able to read the two curves: train falling while validation rises is overfitting, both plateauing high is underfitting or a learning-rate/init problem, and validation improving again after a long worse stretch is the double-descent regime rather than a bug.

resource.label: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning - Chapter 7: Regularization for Deep Learning

subtopics.name: Optimiser and learning rate: SGD + momentum, Adam, bias correction
subtopics.learn: Implement SGD with momentum (v <- mu*v + g; w <- w - eta*v, mu = 0.9) and Adam from the paper: m <- b1*m + (1-b1)*g, v <- b2*v + (1-b2)*g^2, then the bias corrections m_hat = m/(1 - b1^t) and v_hat = v/(1 - b2^t) and the step w <- w - eta * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps). Be able to explain why bias correction exists at all - m and v start at zero, so without it the first ~1/(1-b2) ~ 1000 steps take artificially tiny steps - and why eps sits outside the sqrt in the reference implementation. Learn the LR range test (sweep eta geometrically over a few hundred steps, plot loss, pick just below the minimum) and the standard schedules (step, cosine, linear warmup), and internalise that learning rate is the first knob you touch when the loss is NaN, flat, or oscillating.

resource.label: Kingma & Ba, "Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization" (arXiv:1412.6980)

subtopics.name: Diagnostics: activation, gradient and update-ratio histograms
subtopics.learn: Log three families of per-layer statistics every epoch and be able to name the fix from each: activation histograms (mass piled at the tails means tanh/sigmoid saturation; a spike at exactly zero covering >50 percent of units means dead ReLUs; std shrinking layer by layer means init scale too small), gradient-norm-per-layer on a log axis (monotone decay towards the input = vanishing, spikes = exploding or a bad batch), and the update-to-weight ratio ||eta * grad|| / ||w||, which should sit around 1e-3 - 1e-2 means the learning rate is too high, 1e-5 means the model is barely moving. Produce them with forward/backward hooks and SummaryWriter.add_histogram, or with plain NumPy in your from-scratch net. Then read the loss curve as a fourth signal: a NaN at a specific step is log(0), an exploding gradient, or one corrupt row - bisect the batch to find out which.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.utils.tensorboard (SummaryWriter, add_histogram, add_scalar)

subtopics.name: Training protocol: overfit one batch, fix seeds, run the ablation honestly
subtopics.learn: Adopt the ritual before any real run: get input shapes and the loss at initialisation right (a 10-class net must start near ln(10) = 2.30 - if it starts at 0.3 you have a label leak, if it starts at 15 your init is broken), then overfit a single batch of 32 to near-zero loss with regularisation off, which proves the backward pass and the optimiser before any data question is on the table. Then make the ablation defensible: identical val split and epoch budget for every cell, seeds fixed (np.random.default_rng(seed), torch.manual_seed) and at least three seeds per cell so the README table reports mean +/- std, and report both final validation accuracy and epochs-to-reach-threshold, because a config that wins by 0.2 points but takes 3x the epochs is not the recommendation you give a customer.

resource.label: Karpathy - "A Recipe for Training Neural Networks"

outcomes: You can derive, on a whiteboard and without notes, delta^L = grad_a J (*) phi'(z^L), delta^l = ((W^{l+1})^T delta^{l+1}) (*) phi'(z^l), dJ/dW^l = delta^l (a^{l-1})^T, and restate all of it in batched row-major NumPy shapes including where the 1/B belongs.

You can implement a reverse-mode autograd engine from scratch (topological order, VJP per primitive, gradient accumulation on fan-out, broadcast-aware reductions) and train a multi-layer MLP with it, no framework in the training path.

You can write a centred finite-difference gradient check with a relative-error criterion that passes at ~1e-7 in float64 for weights, biases and the regularisation term, explain why ReLU kinks cause false failures, and have it run as a pytest test in CI.

You can derive Xavier from Var(z) = n_in Var(w) Var(x) and Kaiming's factor of 2 from E[ReLU(z)^2] = Var(z)/2, and predict which of Kaiming, Xavier or 0.01*randn will fail for a given depth and activation before running it.

You can look at per-layer activation histograms, gradient-norm plots and the update-to-weight ratio for a failing run and name one knob - activation, init scale, learning rate, or regulariser - with a stated reason, then show the fixed run.

You can explain the train/eval asymmetry of dropout and batch norm precisely (inverted scaling by 1/(1-p); batch statistics versus running estimates) and demonstrate the exact accuracy delta caused by forgetting model.eval().

You can produce an ablation table over activation x init x regulariser with mean +/- std across three seeds, a fixed val split and a fixed epoch budget, and defend which cell you would ship and why the runner-up lost.

You can implement Adam from the paper including bias correction, explain why the correction matters for the first ~1000 steps, and state why L2-in-the-gradient behaves differently under Adam than decoupled weight decay under AdamW.
failureModes: The 1/B from a mean-reduced loss is applied both in the loss backward and again in the layer backward; gradients are B times too small, the model trains but plateaus early, and three days go into 'the features are too weak' before anyone runs a gradient check.

A softmax is applied inside the model and CrossEntropyLoss is applied on top of it; nothing crashes, the gradients are wrong but still descend, and the model reaches 82 percent instead of 89 percent - a silent modelling error that no test catches without a reference implementation.

The gradient check passes at 1e-7 on a net with dropout accidentally disabled by the fixed seed path, and the dropout backward mask scaling bug ships anyway - the check must be run in the exact configuration being trained, not a convenient one.

A 10-layer ReLU net initialised with 0.01*randn has forward activations that decay to zero by layer 6; the loss sits flat at ln(10) = 2.30 for every epoch and gets diagnosed as 'the dataset is too hard' rather than as a variance-propagation failure fixed by one line of Kaiming init.

Validation is computed without model.eval(), so batch-norm uses batch statistics of the validation minibatches and dropout stays on; the validation number is both noisy and optimistically biased, and the model that wins the ablation is the one that got the luckiest eval batches.

Standardisation statistics (mean and std of Fashion-MNIST pixels) are computed over the whole dataset before the train/val split, leaking validation information into training; the reported gap is smaller than the true one and the customer's held-out result is worse than the deck promised.

Weight decay is added as lambda*w inside the gradient while using Adam, so the effective decay is divided by sqrt(v_hat) per parameter; the regularisation strength varies wildly across layers, the lambda sweep looks flat and non-monotonic, and the conclusion 'L2 does not help here' is recorded as a finding.

Each ablation cell is run once with a different random seed; the 27-cell table has a spread of +/- 1.2 points that is entirely seed noise, and the README recommends a configuration that is not reproducibly better than three of its neighbours.
interviewQuestions: Derive the backward pass for a two-layer MLP with softmax cross-entropy. Show me why dL/dz at the output collapses to yhat - y, and then write the shapes for a batched implementation and tell me where the 1/B goes.

Derive the Xavier initialisation variance condition from scratch, then tell me what changes for ReLU and why the constant becomes 2/n_in. Which assumptions in that derivation are false after the first gradient step, and does it matter?

A colleague's from-scratch net trains but converges to a worse loss than the PyTorch equivalent with identical hyperparameters. Design the debugging sequence - what do you check first, second and third, and what does a gradient check that passes at 1e-7 rule out and not rule out?

Explain exactly what dropout does at training time and at evaluation time, why the 1/(1-p) scaling exists and which side it is applied on, and what happens numerically if someone forgets model.eval() in a network that also has batch norm.
Training loss goes to NaN at step 4,300 having been healthy before. Give me the four most likely causes in order, and the specific instrumentation that distinguishes them.

A customer's 20-layer network learns nothing - the loss is flat at ln(C) from epoch 0. Walk me through diagnosing it from activation and gradient histograms alone, and tell me which of activation choice, init scale, learning rate and normalisation you would change first and why.

Design an ablation over three activations, three initialisers and three regularisers that you would put in front of a customer's ML team. How many runs, what is held fixed, what do you report, and how do you keep someone from reading seed noise as a result?
110.proofOfWork: A companion repo, backprop-forensics, that turns the from-scratch MLP into a debugging clinic: eight deliberately broken variants of the same trainer, each shipping exactly one classic defect - the double 1/B, a transposed dW in the linear backward, softmax applied before cross-entropy, dropout scaled in forward but not backward, dropout left on at eval, 0.01*randn init in a 10-layer stack, learning rate 100x too high, and a mean/std leak computed before the split - together with a make reproduce target that trains each for a fixed budget and emits the same four diagnostic artefacts per run (loss curves, per-layer activation histograms, per-layer gradient norms on a log axis, and the update-to-weight ratio). The README is a one-page diagnostic decision tree mapping each observable signature back to its cause, plus a blind-triage log in which you recorded your diagnosis from the plots alone before revealing which variant was which, with your hit rate stated honestly. Ship it with a scanned or typeset derivation of the batched backward pass and the Xavier/Kaiming variance arguments, a pytest suite where the finite-difference check and a torch.autograd.gradcheck cross-check both run in GitHub Actions, and a 300-word section written for a non-ML customer engineer explaining why initialisation and eval-mode discipline are correctness issues rather than tuning preferences.

111.topic: Training deep networks: optimisers, batch norm, schedules, mixed precision, debugging a bad loss curve
111.why: When a customer's model does not train, the room turns to you with one plot and no hypothesis, and the difference between a senior AI/FDE and a framework user is whether you can look at a loss curve plus a grad-norm log and say 'that is a learning rate above the 2/lambda_max stability bound' or 'that is BatchNorm still in train mode at eval' rather than 'let me try some hyperparameters'. Every knob in this topic - momentum, Adam's second moment, warmup, BatchNorm's running statistics, fp16 loss scaling - is a small piece of arithmetic you can derive on a whiteboard, and deriving it is what lets you defend a fix on the spot instead of promising a week of sweeps. It is also the topic that decides whether the customer's model fits on their GPU and finishes inside their maintenance window, because optimiser state and precision are memory and wall-clock decisions dressed up as mathematics.
prerequisites: Backpropagation derived by hand and an autograd engine written from scratch (Topic 110): you must already be able to say what dJ/dW^l is and which activations must be cached to compute it

Gradient descent, convexity, the Hessian and second-order conditions from Topic 94 (Calculus and optimisation), plus eigenvalues, spectral radius and condition number from Topic 93 (Linear algebra for ML)
Floating point at the bit level from Topic 99 (Numerical computing): mantissa vs exponent, subnormals, catastrophic cancellation, why summation order changes the answer
Cross-entropy as negative log-likelihood from Topic 98, so 'the loss should start at ln(C)' is an identity you can state rather than a rule you remember
Held-out discipline and leakage awareness from Topic 103 (Model evaluation) - every ablation number in the deliverable is a validation number produced under model.eval()

Working PyTorch: nn.Module, DataLoader, a hand-written training loop and .backward() (Topic 112 takes tensors, autograd internals and profiling much further; you only need to be able to run a loop here), plus a CUDA GPU or a Colab/T4-class runtime, since AMP is a no-op on CPU

subtopics.name: The objective and the minibatch gradient estimator
subtopics.learn: Write the training objective as empirical risk J(theta) = (1/N) sum_i loss(f_theta(x_i), y_i) and the minibatch gradient g_B = (1/B) sum_{i in B} grad loss_i, then prove the two facts the rest of the topic rests on: g_B is an unbiased estimator of grad J under uniform sampling (E[g_B] = grad J) and its covariance is Sigma/B, so gradient noise falls as 1/sqrt(B). Know the Robbins-Monro conditions sum eta_t = infinity and sum eta_t^2 < infinity that make a decayed step size converge, and the practical consequence of violating the second one: with a constant eta, SGD does not converge to a point, it bounces inside a noise ball whose size grows with eta and with the gradient noise, which is exactly why the last few percent of accuracy only appears once the schedule anneals. Be able to say why a per-step loss printout that jumped at B=32 is usually noise (plot an EMA and the per-epoch mean before believing anything) and why the same jump at B=1024 is a signal.

resource.label: d2l.ai 12.4 - Stochastic Gradient Descent (dynamics, noise, decaying learning rates)

subtopics.name: Step size versus curvature: deriving the eta < 2/lambda_max bound
subtopics.learn: Derive it on the quadratic f(w) = (1/2) w^T H w: gradient descent gives w_{t+1} = (I - eta H) w_t, so in the eigenbasis each component decays as (1 - eta lambda_i)^t, convergence requires |1 - eta lambda_i| < 1 for every i, hence 0 < eta < 2/lambda_max; the optimum is eta = 2/(lambda_min + lambda_max) with contraction rate (kappa - 1)/(kappa + 1) where kappa = lambda_max/lambda_min. Read the three regimes off that formula: eta slightly too large gives an oscillation that grows geometrically (the sawtooth that ends in inf within tens of steps), a large kappa gives the classic zig-zag across a narrow valley, and this is why momentum (which improves the rate to roughly (sqrt(kappa) - 1)/(sqrt(kappa) + 1)) and preconditioning exist at all. Know the modern caveat before you over-claim in a review: Cohen et al.'s 'edge of stability' result shows real networks drift until eta*lambda_max sits just above 2 and then train non-monotonically, so a mildly ragged curve is not automatically a bug.

resource.label: d2l.ai 12.3 - Gradient Descent (learning rate, local minima, preconditioning, Newton)

subtopics.name: SGD with momentum and Nesterov, implemented and matched to torch.optim.SGD
subtopics.learn: Implement the heavy-ball form PyTorch actually uses - b_t = mu*b_{t-1} + (1 - dampening)*g_t with b_1 = g_1 (not (1-mu)g_1), then w <- w - eta*b_t, and for nesterov=True the step uses g_t + mu*b_t - and understand that this differs from the textbook v <- mu*v - eta*g formulation by where eta sits, which matters the moment you change eta mid-run under a schedule. Derive the steady-state effective step eta/(1 - mu): raising mu from 0.9 to 0.99 multiplies your effective learning rate by ten, so momentum and learning rate must be retuned together and 'I only changed momentum' is never true. Then do the parity test that makes this topic real: same seed, float64, one linear layer, run your optimiser and torch.optim.SGD(momentum, dampening, weight_decay, nesterov) for 100 steps and assert max abs parameter difference < 1e-6, including the fact that torch's weight_decay is coupled (added into the gradient before momentum) rather than decoupled.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.optim.SGD (exact algorithm pseudocode)

subtopics.name: Adagrad to RMSProp to Adam: derive the bias correction, then match to 1e-6
subtopics.learn: Walk the lineage and know what each step fixed: Adagrad accumulates G_t = G_{t-1} + g^2 and steps eta*g/(sqrt(G_t) + eps), whose denominator only grows so the effective rate decays to zero on long runs; RMSProp replaces the sum with an EMA v_t = beta2*v_{t-1} + (1-beta2)g^2; Adam adds the first moment m_t = beta1*m_{t-1} + (1-beta1)g and the corrections m_hat = m_t/(1 - beta1^t), v_hat = v_t/(1 - beta2^t). Derive the correction rather than memorising it: unrolling gives E[v_t] = (1 - beta2^t)E[g^2] for stationary g, so dividing by (1 - beta2^t) removes the zero-initialisation bias that would otherwise make the first ~1/(1-beta2) = 1000 steps take absurdly small steps. Implement it, note that the step size is roughly eta in parameter units when gradients are stationary (Adam is nearly sign-descent, which is why its eta is ~1e-3 while SGD's is ~1e-1), and match torch.optim.Adam to 1e-6 in float64 by following the docs pseudocode exactly - including that eps is added outside the sqrt and that the implementation folds the corrections into the step rather than into m and v.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.optim.Adam (algorithm block, eps placement, amsgrad)

subtopics.name: AdamW: decoupled weight decay and the no-decay parameter group
subtopics.learn: Understand the defect precisely: adding lambda*w to the gradient inside Adam means the penalty is then divided by sqrt(v_hat) like every other gradient component, so parameters with large historical gradients are decayed least - the opposite of what a uniform Gaussian prior means - and the lambda sweep comes out flat and non-monotonic. AdamW applies w <- w - eta*lambda*w outside the adaptive scaling; know that PyTorch multiplies the decay by the current lr, so an LR schedule silently schedules your regularisation too, and that AdamW's default weight_decay is 0.01 while Adam's is 0. Build the parameter groups by hand rather than passing one lambda for everything: weight matrices and conv kernels decay, biases and every LayerNorm/BatchNorm gamma and beta do not (decaying a normalisation scale changes the function without regularising it), and assert in code that the two groups partition model.parameters() exactly - a silent overlap or omission is a favourite source of 'the reproduction does not match the paper'.

resource.label: Loshchilov & Hutter, "Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization" (arXiv:1711.05101)

subtopics.name: Choosing an optimiser in front of a customer: quality, memory, and the honest answer
subtopics.learn: Be able to give the working rule and its evidence: AdamW for transformers and anything with sparse or badly scaled gradients, tuned SGD+momentum for ResNet-style vision where it still matches or beats Adam on held-out accuracy, and never a bare Adam with default weight decay on a model you will hand over. Do the memory arithmetic out loud, because it decides whether the model fits: fp32 weights are 4 bytes/param, gradients another 4, SGD+momentum adds one state tensor (4), Adam/AdamW adds two (8), so a 1B-parameter AdamW run needs ~16 GB of optimiser-related state before a single activation. Know enough about the current alternatives to answer without bluffing - Lion keeps only a momentum buffer and steps on its sign, Muon orthogonalises the momentum matrix via Newton-Schulz for 2D weights while leaving embeddings and the head to AdamW, schedule-free methods remove the decay schedule as a hyperparameter - and then give the honest recommendation: inside a customer's eight-hour budget, tuning the learning rate and the schedule beats swapping optimisers almost every time.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - Chapter 06, "02. gradient machine learning" (SGD, momentum, Adagrad, RMSProp, Adam, AdamW, Lion, Muon, schedule-free)

subtopics.name: Warmup + cosine from scratch, and the schedule bugs nobody sees
subtopics.learn: Write the schedule as a pure function of the global step and implement it under LambdaLR so it is testable: eta_t = eta_max * t/T_warm for t < T_warm, then eta_t = eta_min + 0.5*(eta_max - eta_min)*(1 + cos(pi*(t - T_warm)/(T_total - T_warm))). Plot it for the exact step count of your run before training, then assert it against torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR (or SequentialLR chaining LinearLR and CosineAnnealingLR) to within 1e-9. Know why warmup exists mechanically - Adam's v_hat is estimated from a handful of samples at t small, so the very first steps have an unreliable denominator, and post-LN transformers additionally have large early gradients - and know the four bugs that silently ruin the run: calling scheduler.step() once per epoch when T_max was specified in steps (the schedule finishes in 1/len(loader) of training), calling scheduler.step() before optimizer.step(), resuming without scheduler.state_dict() so the LR restarts at the warmup floor, and stepping the scheduler on an iteration where GradScaler skipped the optimiser step.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR (closed form, chaining caveats)

subtopics.name: The LR range test and one-cycle: getting a defensible learning rate in three minutes
subtopics.learn: Run the range test: save model.state_dict() and optimizer.state_dict(), increase the LR geometrically from ~1e-7 to ~1 over 100-500 minibatches, record the loss each step, restore the saved state, then plot loss against log(LR) and take eta_max about one order of magnitude below the point where the loss turns upward (or at the steepest downward slope). Implement it yourself with LambdaLR so you can run it on a customer's model in one cell and produce a plot rather than an opinion. Know one-cycle as the packaged version - a single warmup to eta_max then annealing well below the initial rate, with momentum cycled inversely - and know its claim (super-convergence on some vision workloads) is workload-specific, so present it as a candidate, not a law. The FDE value here is speed of evidence: 'here is the range test, 3e-4 is the top of the stable band for your model and batch size' ends an argument that a week of grid search would not.

resource.label: Smith, "Cyclical Learning Rates for Training Neural Networks" (arXiv:1506.01186) - the LR range test

subtopics.name: BatchNorm mechanics: the coupled backward pass and running statistics
subtopics.learn: Write the transform per feature - xhat = (x - mu_B)/sqrt(var_B + eps), y = gamma*xhat + beta, with mu and var taken over N for a linear layer and over N,H,W for a conv - and derive the backward at least once until you can write dx = (gamma/sqrt(var_B + eps)) * (dy - mean(dy) - xhat*mean(dy*xhat)); the two subtracted terms are what makes BatchNorm a batch-coupled operation rather than a pointwise one, so one poisoned example perturbs the gradient of every other example in the batch. Know the running statistics exactly: PyTorch's momentum=0.1 is the weight on the new batch value, not the old, so running_mean <- 0.9*running_mean + 0.1*batch_mean; train() uses batch statistics and updates the buffers, eval() uses the buffers and updates nothing, and track_running_stats=False makes eval use batch statistics too. Also know the plumbing details you will be asked about: bias=False on the conv before a BN (beta subsumes it), eps=1e-5 inside the sqrt, and SyncBatchNorm when a DDP job's per-rank batch is too small to estimate a variance.

resource.label: d2l.ai 8.5 - Batch Normalization (from-scratch implementation, training vs prediction mode)

subtopics.name: Why BatchNorm helps, and the couplings it introduces
subtopics.learn: Be able to state the current explanation and not the folklore: Santurkar et al. showed empirically that BN does not reduce 'internal covariate shift' in the sense originally claimed (injecting noise after BN keeps the benefit) and that the real mechanism is a smoother, better-conditioned loss surface, which is what buys the 10-30x larger usable learning rate and the robustness to initialisation scale. Then know the two couplings that produce mysterious results: a BN'd layer is scale-invariant in its preceding weights, so weight decay on those weights does not regularise - it shrinks ||w||, which raises the effective learning rate, meaning 'we removed weight decay' is really 'we changed the LR schedule'; and the train/eval gap grows whenever batch statistics are unrepresentative (batch size 2, a loader that yields class-sorted batches, or an eval distribution that has shifted). Know that gradient accumulation does not give you large-batch BN statistics, and that a batch-size change silently changes the amount of BN regularisation.

resource.label: Santurkar et al., "How Does Batch Normalization Help Optimization?" (arXiv:1805.11604)

subtopics.name: LayerNorm, GroupNorm, RMSNorm, and pre-LN versus post-LN
subtopics.learn: Know the axis each one normalises over and what that buys: LayerNorm normalises across the feature dimension of a single example, so it has no batch coupling, behaves identically in train and eval, and works with batch size 1 and variable-length sequences; GroupNorm splits channels into G groups for small-batch vision; RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction entirely, computing x/sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps)*gamma, which is cheaper and empirically as good, which is why modern LLM stacks use it. Then learn the result that explains half the transformer training folklore: Xiong et al. show post-LN (residual then norm) has expected gradients at initialisation that grow with depth, so it requires warmup and is fragile, while pre-LN (norm inside the residual branch) has well-behaved gradients and trains without warmup - so 'do we need warmup?' is a question about architecture, not taste. Use this as a diagnostic: a NaN at exactly the same step every run in a post-LN model that disappears with warmup is a different failure from a NaN at a random step, which is data or fp16.

resource.label: Xiong et al., "On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture" (arXiv:2002.04745)

subtopics.name: Gradient clipping: global norm, threshold choice, and ordering in the loop
subtopics.learn: Implement global-norm clipping the way torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ does - compute total = sqrt(sum_p ||g_p||^2) over all parameters, and if total > max_norm scale every gradient by max_norm/total so the direction is preserved - and note that the function returns the pre-clip total norm, which is the single most useful scalar to log every step. Choose the threshold from evidence: run 100 steps unclipped, take roughly the 90th percentile of the observed grad-norm distribution, and set max_norm there, rather than copying 1.0 from a blog into a model whose typical norm is 40. Get the ordering right under AMP: backward, then scaler.unscale_(optimizer), then clip, then scaler.step(optimizer) - clipping before unscale_ clips gradients that are still multiplied by a loss scale of order 65536, which makes clipping either a no-op or catastrophically aggressive depending on the scale. Treat a rising clip rate over training as a real instability signal, and remember clipping suppresses the symptom while the cause (LR above the stability bound, a corrupt batch, post-LN depth) is still there.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_

subtopics.name: Mixed-precision numerics: fp16 versus bf16 versus tf32
subtopics.learn: Know the formats by their bits, because every AMP decision follows from them: fp16 is 1-5-10 with a maximum of 65504 and normals down to ~6e-5 (subnormals to ~6e-8), so a gradient of 1e-8 flushes to zero and an activation of 1e5 becomes inf; bf16 is 1-8-7, carrying fp32's exponent range with roughly three decimal digits of precision, so it needs no loss scaling but resolves less; tf32 is a 19-bit-mantissa matmul mode on Ampere and later, enabled per-op through torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 and torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32. Understand the master-weight design: autocast does not convert your model, it runs selected ops (matmul, conv) in low precision while parameters, optimiser state and the update stay fp32, and it keeps reductions, softmax, layer norms and the loss in fp32 because those are where cancellation and overflow live. Be able to answer the customer question 'is this still the same model?' honestly: throughput typically improves 1.5-3x and memory drops substantially, accuracy is usually within noise, and you demonstrate that with a fixed-seed A/B rather than asserting it.

resource.label: Micikevicius et al., "Mixed Precision Training" (arXiv:1710.03740) - loss scaling and fp32 master weights

subtopics.name: autocast + GradScaler in practice, and NaN triage
