subtopics.learn: Write the canonical loop and know why each line is where it is: with torch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.float16) wrapping only the forward and the loss, then scaler.scale(loss).backward(), scaler.unscale_(optimizer), clip_grad_norm_, scaler.step(optimizer), scaler.update(). Understand the dynamic loss scaler as a control loop: it starts around 65536, multiplies the loss so small gradients land inside fp16's normal range, inspects gradients for inf/nan, halves the scale and skips the whole optimiser step when it finds one, and doubles the scale after growth_interval clean steps - so skipped steps early in training are expected, and any per-step bookkeeping (schedulers, EMA, step counters) that assumes the step happened will drift. Know the rules you will otherwise break: do not call .half() on the model, do not wrap backward in autocast, include scaler.state_dict() in every checkpoint, and use a separate scaler per optimiser. Triage NaNs by bisection: rerun the same seed in bf16 - if the NaN survives, it is a modelling or data bug (a log(0), a division by a zero norm, a corrupt label), not a precision bug.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - CUDA Automatic Mixed Precision examples (gradient clipping, accumulation, multiple losses, checkpointing)

subtopics.name: Instrumenting the loop: the five scalars and the sanity ladder
subtopics.learn: Log per step, not per epoch: loss and an EMA of it, the current LR (read from optimizer.param_groups, never recomputed), the pre-clip global gradient norm, the update-to-weight ratio ||eta*update||/||w|| per parameter tensor (healthy is around 1e-3; 1e-2 means the LR is too high, 1e-5 means the model is barely moving), and throughput plus peak memory. Run the ladder in order before any real training: confirm the loss at initialisation equals ln(C) (2.303 for CIFAR-10 - anything else means the head bias, the label mapping or the reduction is wrong), overfit one batch of 32 to below 1e-3 with augmentation, dropout and weight decay disabled, verify every parameter you expect to train appears in optimizer.param_groups and has requires_grad=True, then scale up. Adopt the tuning-playbook vocabulary for the write-up - scientific, nuisance and fixed hyperparameters - and its non-negotiable rule that the learning rate is re-tuned whenever anything else changes, because otherwise your ablation is measuring how well each variant suits the old LR.

resource.label: Google Research - Deep Learning Tuning Playbook

subtopics.name: Loss-curve taxonomy: reading the five broken configs from the plot alone
subtopics.learn: Build the mapping from signature to cause so you can diagnose without touching the code. Flat at ln(C) forever: LR effectively zero, symmetric or zero initialisation, parameters missing from the optimiser, or requires_grad left False after a freeze. Smooth descent that turns into a growing oscillation and then inf inside tens of steps: LR above the 2/lambda_max bound - confirm with the grad norm rising geometrically and the update ratio near 1e-1. Loss decreasing only in visible steps at epoch boundaries: shuffle=False on a class-sorted dataset. Training loss healthy but the validation number collapses only at eval time: BatchNorm running statistics never warmed up, model.eval() missing, or eval running with a batch of 1. A NaN at a random step under fp16 with no GradScaler, which moves under a different seed: underflow to zero followed by a division, or an overflow in the loss. Also learn the non-bugs: validation below training is dropout plus BN accounting or an easier split, and a plateau that coincides exactly with the cosine schedule bottoming out is the schedule, not overfitting.

resource.label: Google ML Crash Course - Interpreting loss curves (oscillating, exploding, step-shaped, and stuck curves)

subtopics.name: Batch size, gradient accumulation and the linear scaling rule
subtopics.learn: Know the rule and its evidence: Goyal et al. scale the learning rate by k when the minibatch is multiplied by k, preceded by a gradual warmup over the first ~5 epochs, and show it holds to about 8k images before quality degrades - so quote it with its validity range rather than as a law. Implement gradient accumulation correctly: divide the loss by accum_steps (or keep mean reduction and scale), call optimizer.step() and zero_grad() every accum_steps microbatches, and be explicit that this is not identical to a real large batch - BatchNorm statistics are still computed per microbatch, dropout masks differ, and under AMP a skipped scaler step throws away the whole accumulated group. Notice the arithmetic everybody forgets: doubling the batch halves the number of optimiser steps per epoch, so holding the epoch budget and the LR fixed quietly halves the number of updates and makes the large-batch run look worse for a reason that has nothing to do with generalisation. Pair this with the memory picture - activations dominate and scale with batch - and know activation checkpointing as the trade you offer when a customer's GPU is too small.

resource.label: Goyal et al., "Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD" (arXiv:1706.02677) - linear scaling rule and gradual warmup

subtopics.name: Determinism, seeds and a checkpoint you can actually resume from
subtopics.learn: Control the randomness you can: torch.manual_seed plus numpy and python random, a DataLoader generator and worker_init_fn so workers do not share a seed, torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) with CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8, and know that torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark=True picks kernels by timing so it is fast and non-reproducible, while atomics in some backward kernels are non-deterministic regardless. Then define the run-to-run spread empirically (train the same config with 3-5 seeds and report mean +/- std) so you can tell a real regression from noise rather than arguing about a single run. Make the checkpoint complete: model state, optimizer state (momentum and Adam moments), scheduler state, GradScaler state, epoch and global_step, RNG states and a hash of the config - a resume that silently drops the optimiser buffers produces a loss spike at exactly the resume step which gets misdiagnosed as data corruption for a day. Test it in CI: train 100 steps, checkpoint, train 100 more; separately resume from the checkpoint and train 100; assert the two final losses agree to 1e-6.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Reproducibility (seeding, deterministic algorithms, DataLoader workers, cuDNN benchmark)

outcomes: You can implement SGD-with-momentum (including dampening and Nesterov) and Adam (including bias correction and PyTorch's eps placement) from scratch and show a pytest assertion that parameters match torch.optim to within 1e-6 over 100 float64 steps across a grid of hyperparameters.

You can derive, on a whiteboard and without notes, that gradient descent on a quadratic requires eta < 2/lambda_max, state the optimal step size and the rate in terms of the condition number, and use it to explain a specific diverging run.

You can write a warmup+cosine schedule as a closed-form function of the global step, assert it against SequentialLR/CosineAnnealingLR to 1e-9, and name the four ways a schedule silently breaks (per-epoch stepping, step ordering, missing scheduler state on resume, AMP-skipped steps).

You can turn on torch.autocast plus GradScaler on an existing training loop, place unscale_ and clip_grad_norm_ correctly, checkpoint the scaler, and produce a measured fp32-vs-fp16-vs-bf16 table of wall-clock, peak memory and final validation accuracy across three seeds with zero NaNs.

You can be handed a loss curve plus per-step logs of LR, grad norm and update-to-weight ratio, and name the cause - LR above the stability bound, bad init, dead units, exploding or vanishing gradients, BatchNorm in the wrong mode at eval, or fp16 overflow - then show the one-line fix and the corrected curve.

You can state BatchNorm's train/eval asymmetry precisely (batch statistics and buffer updates versus frozen running estimates), write its backward pass, and quantify the exact accuracy delta caused by evaluating without model.eval() on your own model.
You can run an LR range test on an unfamiliar model in under five minutes, restore the pre-test state, and justify the chosen eta_max from the plot rather than from a default.

You can produce a resumable checkpoint (model, optimizer, scheduler, scaler, step, RNG state) and prove in CI that a resumed run matches an uninterrupted run to 1e-6, and separately report the seed-to-seed spread of your headline metric so a regression can be distinguished from noise.
failureModes: Weight decay is passed to torch.optim.Adam instead of AdamW, so the penalty is divided by sqrt(v_hat) per parameter; the lambda sweep comes out flat and non-monotonic and the team records 'regularisation does not help on this dataset' as a finding.

scheduler.step() is called once per epoch while T_max was specified in optimiser steps, so a 30-epoch cosine schedule completes inside the first epoch and trains the remaining 29 at eta_min; the curve looks like a healthy early drop followed by a permanent plateau and gets blamed on model capacity.

clip_grad_norm_ is called before scaler.unscale_(), so the norm being clipped is the fp16 loss-scaled norm; clipping becomes a no-op at scale 65536 and catastrophically aggressive after the scaler halves a few times, producing an instability that appears and disappears with the loss scale.

Validation is run without model.eval(), so BatchNorm uses each validation minibatch's own statistics and dropout stays on; the reported accuracy is both noisy and optimistically biased, and the config that wins the ablation is the one that drew the luckiest eval batches.

A model is trained with .half() applied to the weights instead of autocast with fp32 master weights; updates smaller than the fp16 spacing of the parameter are lost entirely on every step, so the loss decreases for a while and then stalls with a perfectly flat curve and a grad norm that is still nonzero.

Batch size is raised from 128 to 1024 for throughput while the learning rate and the epoch budget stay fixed; the run takes one eighth of the optimiser steps, ends two points below baseline, and the large-batch result is written up as a generalisation gap rather than as an under-trained run.

A job is resumed from a checkpoint that saved only model.state_dict(); Adam's moment buffers restart at zero and the bias correction restarts at t=1, so the loss spikes at exactly the resume step and the incident is investigated as corrupted training data.

cudnn.benchmark is on and no seeds are fixed, so two runs of the identical config differ by 0.4 points; a genuinely neutral change is shipped as an improvement and a genuine 0.3-point regression is dismissed as noise, in the same week.
interviewQuestions: Derive the condition on the learning rate for gradient descent to converge on a quadratic with Hessian H. What is the optimal step size, what is the convergence rate in terms of the condition number, and how does momentum change that rate? Then tell me what you would actually look at in a training log to decide whether a run is violating that bound.

Write Adam's update from memory, including the bias corrections, and derive why the corrections are needed. Where does eps sit in PyTorch's implementation, and what changes if you move it inside the square root? Why is Adam's typical learning rate two orders of magnitude smaller than SGD's?

Explain the difference between L2 regularisation added to the gradient and decoupled weight decay under an adaptive optimiser. Which parameters would you exclude from weight decay in a transformer, and why is excluding LayerNorm gains not just a micro-optimisation?

Describe exactly what BatchNorm computes in training mode and in eval mode, including how the running statistics are updated. A model scores 94 percent in training-mode evaluation and 61 percent after calling model.eval(). Give me three candidate causes in order and the experiment that distinguishes them.

Debug: a training run is healthy for 4,000 steps and then goes to NaN, and it does so at a different step each time you rerun it. It uses fp16 autocast with a GradScaler, gradient clipping and a warmup+cosine schedule. Walk me through your triage, in order, and say what each observation would rule out.

Design: a customer has a 20 GB GPU and an 8-hour nightly window, and their current fp32 run takes 14 hours. Walk me through what you change, in what order, and what you measure to prove the model is unchanged - include the optimiser-state and activation memory arithmetic and where mixed precision does and does not help.

You raise the batch size from 256 to 2048 on eight GPUs. What happens to the gradient noise, what do you do to the learning rate and why, what does gradual warmup fix, and what would make you say the linear scaling rule has stopped applying?
111.proofOfWork: A public repo `optimiser-parity` that turns the training-lab work into evidence a customer's ML team can audit. It contains (a) a small from-scratch optimiser library - SGD with momentum, dampening and Nesterov, Adagrad, RMSProp, Adam and AdamW - together with a pytest suite that, for a grid over learning rate, momentum/betas, weight decay and nesterov, runs 100 float64 steps on a fixed-seed two-layer network and asserts max |theta_mine - theta_torch| < 1e-6, plus a closed-form warmup+cosine schedule asserted against SequentialLR to 1e-9; (b) a measured mixed-precision report on one named GPU comparing fp32, fp16+GradScaler and bf16 across three seeds, reporting median step time, peak allocated memory, final validation accuracy with standard deviation, the count of scaler-skipped steps, and the observed loss-scale trajectory, so 'AMP is free' becomes a number rather than a claim; (c) a blind triage log in which someone else ran the five broken configs from the deliverable plus three new ones (weight decay applied to BatchNorm gammas, scheduler stepped per epoch instead of per step, resume without optimiser state) and you recorded your diagnosis from the curves and the four logged scalars alone, with your hit rate stated honestly including the misses; and (d) a one-page 'why is my model not training' decision card written for a customer engineer, mapping each observable signature to its check and its fix, with the update-to-weight ratio and pre-clip grad norm named as the two scalars to log before anything else. The README opens with the derivations - the 2/lambda_max bound, Adam's bias correction and the BatchNorm backward - typeset, because the parity tests are only interesting if you can show where the reference behaviour comes from.

112.topic: PyTorch at depth: tensors, autograd, Dataset and DataLoader, the training loop, profiling
112.why: Every deep-learning claim you make to a customer bottoms out in a PyTorch training loop that you must be able to defend line by line: this loss is over these logits, this gradient is this VJP, this number is a real p95 and not a launch-queue artefact. The bugs that lose deals are silent rather than loud - a broadcast that turns an (N,1) vs (N,) residual into an N-by-N loss, a `model.eval()` you forgot, a `total_loss += loss` that retains the graph until OOM at epoch two, a benchmark taken without `torch.cuda.synchronize()` - and none of them raise an exception; they produce a plausible curve and a wrong model. An FDE who can hand-derive a backward, prove it with `torch.autograd.gradcheck` in float64, and then read a `torch.profiler` table to say 'we are dataloader-bound, give me four workers and pinned memory' is the person the customer's ML team stops arguing with.
prerequisites: Reverse-mode backpropagation on paper: the chain rule over a computational graph, and having already written a NumPy MLP with your own autograd (Topic 110, Neural network foundations)

Matrix calculus: Jacobians, the gradient of x @ W + b with respect to each argument, and why a vector-Jacobian product is cheaper than a Jacobian (Topic 93 linear algebra, Topic 94 calculus and optimisation)
NumPy at depth: ndarray strides, views versus copies, broadcasting rules, float32 versus float64 error budgets and catastrophic cancellation (Topic 99, Numerical computing)

The optimiser and mixed-precision vocabulary from Topic 111 (SGD-momentum, Adam, warmup and cosine schedules, a bad loss curve) - this topic is the implementation and instrumentation view of the same machinery

Python beyond scripting: classes and dunder methods, closures, context managers, iterators/generators, and the multiprocessing fork-versus-spawn distinction, since Dataset workers are separate processes
A working PyTorch 2.x install plus access to one CUDA GPU (a Colab T4 or a rented A10/A100 is enough) - the profiling and mixed-precision subtopics cannot be done CPU-only
pytest and git, because the deliverable's gradient checks and profiler traces belong in CI, not in a notebook

subtopics.name: The tensor memory model: storage, offset, sizes, strides, contiguity
subtopics.learn: Understand a tensor as a four-tuple over a flat buffer - `untyped_storage()`, `storage_offset()`, `size()`, `stride()` - and be able to predict all four after `t[2:, ::2].transpose(0, 1)` before you run it. Know which ops are metadata-only views (`view`, `reshape` when possible, `permute`, `transpose`, `expand`, `squeeze`, basic slicing, `narrow`, `select`) and which must copy (`reshape` on an incompatible layout, `contiguous`, `repeat`, advanced/fancy indexing, `flatten` across non-contiguous dims). Be able to explain the error `view size is not compatible with input tensor's size and stride (at least one dimension spans across two contiguous subspaces)` in stride terms, and why `expand` costs zero memory (it sets a stride of 0) while `repeat` costs the full product. Check with `x.is_contiguous()`, `x.data_ptr()` and `x.is_contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last)` - the last one is what a convolution kernel actually dispatches on.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Tensor Views

subtopics.name: Broadcasting semantics and the silent-bug surface they create
subtopics.learn: State the rule exactly: align shapes from the trailing dimension, each pair must be equal or one of them 1, missing leading dims are treated as 1. Then internalise the two things it costs you: (a) `pred` of shape (N, 1) minus `target` of shape (N,) broadcasts to (N, N), so `mse_loss` happily returns a small smooth number computed over N-squared pairs and the model converges to predicting the mean - no exception, no warning; (b) the backward of a broadcast is a sum over the broadcast axes, so every op you hand-implement must 'unbroadcast' the incoming gradient back to the input shape. Defend against (a) with explicit `keepdim=` discipline, `x.unsqueeze(-1)`, `torch.broadcast_shapes(a.shape, b.shape)` asserted against what you expect, and shape assertions or `einsum`/`einops` strings at every layer boundary. Be able to write the general `unbroadcast(grad, target_shape)` routine: sum away the extra leading dims, then `sum(dim=i, keepdim=True)` wherever `target_shape[i] == 1`.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Broadcasting semantics

subtopics.name: dtype, device and the precision budget you are actually training in
subtopics.learn: Know the four formats by their bit layout and what that implies: fp32 (8 exponent, 23 mantissa, eps about 1.2e-7), tf32 (fp32 range with a 10-bit mantissa, silently used for matmuls on Ampere+ unless you set `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False` or `torch.set_float32_matmul_precision`), fp16 (5 exponent bits, max finite value 65504, so activations and squared terms overflow to `inf`), bf16 (fp32's exponent range with a 7-bit mantissa, eps about 7.8e-3 - no overflow, much coarser rounding). Be able to say why a reduction accumulates in fp32 even when the inputs are fp16, why `torch.allclose` defaults (rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8) are meaningless for a fp16 comparison, and why numerical-gradient checking must be done in float64. Know that `.to()` on a tensor returns a new tensor while `Module.to()` mutates in place, and that a device mismatch raises `Expected all tensors to be on the same device` while a dtype mismatch often just silently upcasts.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Numerical accuracy (TF32, reduced precision reductions, batched computation)

subtopics.name: Aliasing, in-place ops and the autograd version counter
subtopics.learn: Every tensor carries a version counter; autograd records the version of each saved tensor at forward time and compares at backward time, which is what produces `one of the variables needed for gradient computation has been modified by an inplace operation: [torch.cuda.FloatTensor [64, 128]], which is output 0 of ReluBackward0, is at version 2; expected version 1 instead`. Be able to read that message as 'something wrote through an alias of a saved activation' and to find it with `torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True)`, which prints the forward stack of the offending op. Know when `nn.ReLU(inplace=True)` and `x += y` are safe (the input is not needed for any backward) and when they are not (residual branches with two consumers, any op whose backward saves its output). Know the genuinely dangerous case: `.data` and in-place writes through a `detach()`ed alias share storage and bypass the version counter entirely, so gradients come out wrong with no error at all - use `.clone()` when you mean a copy.

resource.label: NumPy docs - Copies and views (the aliasing model PyTorch inherits)

subtopics.name: Reverse-mode autodiff derived: VJPs, not Jacobians
subtopics.learn: Derive it: for a composition f = f_k o ... o f_1 the Jacobian is a product of Jacobians, forward mode evaluates J v (one JVP per input direction, cost proportional to the number of inputs), reverse mode evaluates v-transpose J (one VJP per output direction, cost proportional to the number of outputs). Scalar losses have one output, so reverse mode costs roughly two forward passes for the entire gradient regardless of parameter count - be able to say this in one sentence to a customer asking why training is only ~3x the cost of inference. Understand that `loss.backward()` is `torch.autograd.grad(loss, params, grad_outputs=torch.ones(()))`, that calling `.backward()` on a non-scalar requires you to supply `gradient=v` because there is no canonical seed, and that gradients accumulate with `+=` into `.grad` (hence `zero_grad`). Be able to reach for `torch.func.jacrev`, `jacfwd`, `vmap` and `create_graph=True` when you genuinely need a Jacobian, a Hessian-vector product or a second-order term.

resource.label: PyTorch tutorial - A Gentle Introduction to torch.autograd (vector-Jacobian products)

subtopics.name: The autograd graph at runtime: leaves, grad_fn, retention, no_grad vs inference_mode
subtopics.learn: Walk a real graph in a REPL: `y.grad_fn`, `y.grad_fn.next_functions`, the terminal `AccumulateGrad` nodes, `x.is_leaf`, and `retain_grad()` when you want a non-leaf's gradient. Know that the graph is freed during backward, so a second `.backward()` raises `Trying to backward through the graph a second time`, and that `retain_graph=True` is almost always the wrong fix for what is really a graph you accidentally kept alive across iterations. Distinguish four ways of switching gradients off and when each is right: `torch.no_grad()` (do not record, tensors remain normal), `torch.inference_mode()` (faster, no version counter or view tracking, and its outputs raise `Inference tensors cannot be saved for backward` if they later touch autograd), `.detach()` (cut this tensor out of the graph but keep the storage), `requires_grad_(False)` (freeze a parameter - and remember the optimiser must also exclude it or Adam's decay still moves it). Learn the classic leak by heart: `total_loss += loss` retains every graph in the epoch; write `total_loss += loss.detach()` or `loss.item()`.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.autograd package reference (grad, graph, anomaly detection, hooks)

subtopics.name: Writing a custom torch.autograd.Function and hand-deriving its backward
subtopics.learn: Implement the full contract: `forward` as a `@staticmethod` (or the modern split with `setup_context`), `ctx.save_for_backward(...)` for tensors and plain `ctx.attr` for non-tensors, and a `backward` that returns exactly one gradient per forward input with `None` for non-tensor arguments, gated on `ctx.needs_input_grad[i]`. Derive at least two by hand and implement them: fused softmax-cross-entropy, whose backward collapses to (p - y)/N and is both faster and more stable than composing the pieces, and SiLU/swish y = x*sigmoid(x) with dy/dx = sigmoid(x)*(1 + x*(1 - sigmoid(x))). Know the sharp edges: call it as `MyFn.apply(x, w)` and never `MyFn()(x, w)`; `@once_differentiable` when your backward is not itself differentiable; `ctx.mark_dirty` if you mutate an input; the backward runs under `no_grad` unless you build it from differentiable ops. Use a custom Function when you have a closed-form gradient that beats the composed one, need to save memory by not storing intermediates, or are wrapping a non-PyTorch kernel.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Extending PyTorch (custom autograd.Function, setup_context, forward-mode AD)

subtopics.name: Proving the backward with torch.autograd.gradcheck
subtopics.learn: Understand what gradcheck actually does: it builds the analytic Jacobian from your VJPs and compares it against central finite differences (f(x+eps) - f(x-eps)) / (2*eps), so the comparison is only meaningful when the truncation error (order eps-squared) dominates the rounding error (order machine-eps / eps) - which is why inputs must be `dtype=torch.double` with `requires_grad=True` and why the same check in float32 fails or passes at random. Run `gradcheck(MyFn.apply, (x, w), eps=1e-6, atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-3)` and `gradgradcheck` for second order; use `nondet_tol` only for genuinely nondeterministic kernels and `fast_mode=True` (random projections u-transpose J v) for big inputs. Know its honest failure modes: non-differentiable points (ReLU or abs at exactly 0, ties in `max`) make it fail spuriously - perturb the input away from the kink rather than loosening `atol`, because loosening tolerance until green is how a genuinely wrong backward ships.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Gradcheck mechanics

subtopics.name: Building the ~300-line broadcasting-aware autograd engine
subtopics.learn: Structure it exactly like PyTorch's: a `Tensor` wrapping a NumPy array with `.data`, `.grad`, `._backward` (a closure that pushes gradient into its parents), `._parents`, and a `backward()` that seeds `ones_like`, builds a topological order with a visited set, and walks it in reverse accumulating with `+=`. Implement add, mul, matmul (dA = dC @ B.T, dB = A.T @ dC - derive both and get the transposes right), sum/mean with `keepdim` handling, relu, exp, log, softmax-crossentropy, reshape and transpose. The part that actually distinguishes this from a toy is broadcasting: every binary op's backward runs the gradient through `unbroadcast(grad, parent.shape)` before accumulating, and this is the piece that only breaks on non-square batches - test with shapes like (7, 3) op (3,) and (7, 1) op (1, 3). Verify by running the same 2-layer MLP forward/backward in your engine and in PyTorch from identical initial weights and asserting `np.allclose(mine, torch_grad, atol=1e-6)` per parameter, and make that assertion a pytest, not a print.

resource.label: GitHub - karpathy/micrograd (reference scalar autograd engine to extend to arrays)

subtopics.name: nn.Module internals: parameters vs buffers, state_dict, hooks, train/eval
subtopics.learn: Know that `Module.__setattr__` is overridden so assigning an `nn.Parameter` or a submodule registers it - which is why a plain Python list of layers loses every parameter and you must use `nn.ModuleList`/`nn.ModuleDict`, and why `self.mask = torch.ones(...)` never moves to the GPU unless you call `register_buffer('mask', ...)`. Distinguish `parameters()` (what the optimiser gets), `named_parameters()`, `buffers()` (BatchNorm's `running_mean`/`running_var`, `num_batches_tracked`) and `state_dict()` (parameters plus persistent buffers, which is what you ship); read the `missing_keys` / `unexpected_keys` returned by `load_state_dict(..., strict=False)` instead of ignoring them. Understand exactly what `model.train()` / `model.eval()` toggles - Dropout on/off and BatchNorm using batch statistics versus running statistics - and that it does nothing about gradients. Use `register_forward_hook` to capture intermediate activations for a customer-facing explanation without editing the model's `forward`.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Modules (registration, state_dict, train/eval, hooks)

subtopics.name: The update rules as PyTorch actually implements them: SGD, momentum, Adam, AdamW
subtopics.learn: Write out and be able to reproduce, in a 20-line NumPy loop that matches `torch.optim` step for step: PyTorch's SGD momentum form b_t = mu*b_{t-1} + (1 - dampening)*g_t with p -= lr*b_t (note this differs from the textbook form where lr multiplies inside the buffer, so 'the same' momentum and lr give different trajectories across frameworks); Adam's m_t = b1*m + (1-b1)*g, v_t = b2*v + (1-b2)*g^2, bias corrections m/(1-b1^t) and v/(1-b2^t), update p -= lr * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps) - and note eps sits outside the square root, which is why 1e-8 behaves differently in fp16. Then derive the AdamW distinction that actually matters: L2 regularisation added into g gets divided by sqrt(v_hat), so it is effectively scaled down for high-variance parameters, whereas decoupled decay applies p -= lr*wd*p directly. The operational consequence is a `param_groups` split - weight decay on weight matrices, zero decay on biases, LayerNorm/BatchNorm gains and embeddings.

resource.label: arXiv 1711.05101 - Loshchilov & Hutter, Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (AdamW)

subtopics.name: torch.optim in practice: param_groups, set_to_none, schedulers, resumable state
subtopics.learn: Build the optimiser from explicit groups - `optim.AdamW([{'params': decay, 'weight_decay': 0.1}, {'params': no_decay, 'weight_decay': 0.0}], lr=3e-4)` - and know how to inspect and mutate `opt.param_groups[i]['lr']` at runtime. Know that `zero_grad(set_to_none=True)` is the default from PyTorch 2.0 and that it sets `.grad` to `None`, not zero, so any diagnostic code doing `p.grad.norm()` must handle `None`. Get scheduler discipline right: `LinearLR`/`LambdaLR` warmup chained into `CosineAnnealingLR` via `SequentialLR`, per-iteration versus per-epoch `step()` (OneCycleLR is per-iteration), calling `scheduler.step()` after `optimizer.step()`, and logging `scheduler.get_last_lr()` so a flat loss curve can be attributed to a collapsed LR. Save and load `optimizer.state_dict()` alongside the model - Adam's first and second moments are the reason a resumed run without them shows a loss spike that looks like data corruption.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.optim (param groups, schedulers, foreach/fused implementations)

subtopics.name: Losses and the logits contract
subtopics.learn: Internalise that `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` consumes raw logits and internally applies `log_softmax` + `nll_loss`; feeding it softmax probabilities is a double softmax that flattens the gradient and parks the loss near ln(C) forever, which every junior misreads as a data problem. Same contract for `BCEWithLogitsLoss` versus `BCELoss`: the with-logits version folds the sigmoid into a log-sum-exp-stable expression, so it is the only safe choice, and its `pos_weight` argument is the correct lever for class imbalance. Know the shape and dtype rules cold - input (N, C) with target (N,) of `int64` class indices, or (N, C, d1, d2) with target (N, d1, d2) for segmentation - plus `ignore_index=-100`, `label_smoothing`, and that `reduction='mean'` divides by the sum of class weights, not by N, when `weight=` is supplied. Sanity check every new classifier: an untrained model must report a loss of about ln(C) (2.30 for 10 classes); anything else means the head, the targets or the reduction is wrong before you have trained a single step.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - nn.CrossEntropyLoss (logits contract, shapes, weight, ignore_index)

subtopics.name: The training and evaluation loop, written closed-book
subtopics.learn: Be able to type the canonical loop from memory in under 20 minutes: `model.train()`, then per batch `opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)`, forward under `autocast`, loss, `backward()`, `clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)`, `opt.step()`, `scheduler.step()`; then an eval pass under `model.eval()` and `torch.no_grad()`. Get the two arithmetic details right that quietly corrupt reported metrics: accumulate `loss.item() * x.size(0)` and divide by `len(dataset)` rather than averaging per-batch means (the final short batch otherwise gets equal weight), and compute epoch accuracy from summed correct counts, not from a mean of batch accuracies. Implement gradient accumulation properly - divide the loss by `accum_steps`, step every k micro-batches - and know it does not reproduce a true large batch for BatchNorm, whose statistics are still per-micro-batch. Bake in the two sanity gates before any long run: initial loss must be about ln(C), and the model must be able to drive a single fixed batch to near-zero loss.

resource.label: PyTorch tutorial - Optimizing model parameters (the train/test loop)

subtopics.name: Dataset, IterableDataset, Sampler and collate_fn
subtopics.learn: Write a map-style `Dataset` (`__len__` + `__getitem__`) that opens file handles lazily inside `__getitem__` rather than in `__init__`, because handles and DB connections do not survive process forking. Know when to switch to `IterableDataset` (streams, Kafka, one giant sharded file, unknown length) and its hard rule: you must shard by `torch.utils.data.get_worker_info()` yourself, or every worker yields the identical stream and your epoch silently contains num_workers copies of the data. Understand the split of responsibilities - `Sampler` decides the order of indices (`RandomSampler`, `SequentialSampler`, `WeightedRandomSampler` for imbalance, `DistributedSampler` with `set_epoch`), `BatchSampler` groups them, `collate_fn` turns a list of samples into a batch. Write a custom `collate_fn` for variable-length inputs using `pad_sequence` plus an explicit attention/length mask, and know that `shuffle=True` and a custom `sampler=` are mutually exclusive and `drop_last=True` is what stops a batch of size 1 from blowing up BatchNorm.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.utils.data (Dataset, samplers, collate, worker semantics)

subtopics.name: DataLoader throughput: workers, prefetch, pinned memory, and how workers die
subtopics.learn: Tune the knobs deliberately and measure each: `num_workers` (start at the physical core count, then bisect - too many thrashes the page cache and RAM), `prefetch_factor` (batches queued per worker, default 2), `persistent_workers=True` so you do not pay process startup every epoch, `pin_memory=True` plus `non_blocking=True` on the `.to(device)` so the host-to-device copy can overlap compute - non_blocking is a no-op from pageable memory. Know the worker failure signatures on sight: `DataLoader worker (pid N) is killed by signal: Bus error` is an exhausted `/dev/shm` in a container (raise `--shm-size`), `Too many open files` is the file-descriptor sharing strategy, and a worker's RSS climbing until the OOM killer fires is copy-on-write pages being dirtied by Python refcounting over a large list of objects - store the index as a NumPy array or tensor instead. Remember each worker gets its own copy of the Dataset, so any counter or cache you mutate in `__getitem__` is per-process and per-epoch.

resource.label: PyTorch recipe - Performance Tuning Guide (workers, pinned memory, non_blocking, set_to_none)

subtopics.name: Seeding and determinism: what you can and cannot promise a customer
subtopics.learn: Know the four independent RNGs in play (Python `random`, NumPy, `torch` CPU, `torch.cuda`) and that DataLoader workers get a derived torch seed automatically but *not* a derived NumPy or Python seed - so NumPy-based augmentation in four workers replays the same sequence unless you set it in `worker_init_fn` from `torch.utils.data.get_worker_info().seed`. Pass an explicit `generator=` to the DataLoader so shuffling is reproducible independent of global state. For the GPU: `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` plus `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8` turns nondeterministic kernels into a loud error rather than silent variance, at a real speed cost, and `torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True` speeds up fixed shapes but makes algorithm selection - and therefore results - vary. Be able to tell a customer the honest version: floating-point addition is not associative, so bitwise-identical results across different GPU counts, batch sizes or library versions are not achievable; what you guarantee is a pinned seed, pinned versions and a metric reproducible within a stated tolerance.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Reproducibility (seeding, deterministic algorithms, DataLoader workers)

subtopics.name: Mixed precision: autocast, GradScaler, and where NaNs come from
subtopics.learn: Use `with torch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16)` around the forward and loss only - never the backward, never `optimizer.step()` - and understand the mechanism: autocast keeps master weights in fp32 and casts per-op according to a list (matmul and conv run in reduced precision, softmax, layer norm, and reductions stay fp32). For fp16 you also need `GradScaler`: `scaler.scale(loss).backward()` multiplies the loss so small gradients do not underflow to zero, `scaler.unscale_(opt)` must come before any gradient clipping or norm logging, `scaler.step(opt)` skips the update entirely when it sees inf/NaN, and `scaler.update()` halves the scale on overflow and doubles it every `growth_interval` steps. Know why bf16 usually needs no scaler (fp32 exponent range) but rounds more coarsely, and that a run where the scale collapses toward zero has a real numerical bug rather than a scaler problem. Never call `model.half()` as a substitute - that puts the master weights in fp16 and destroys small updates.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Automatic Mixed Precision package (autocast, GradScaler)

subtopics.name: torch.profiler mechanics: schedule, record_function, key_averages, traces
subtopics.learn: Instrument one real step, not an epoch: `profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA], schedule=schedule(wait=1, warmup=1, active=3, repeat=1), on_trace_ready=tensorboard_trace_handler('./log'), record_shapes=True, profile_memory=True, with_stack=True)` with `prof.step()` at the end of each iteration - the warmup phase matters because the first iterations pay CUDA context creation, allocator growth and cuDNN autotuning. Wrap your own phases in `with record_function('dataload')` / `'forward'` / `'backward'` / `'optimizer'` so the table has your labels next to ATen ops. Read `prof.key_averages(group_by_input_shape=True).table(sort_by='self_cuda_time_total', row_limit=20)` and know precisely what the columns mean: Self CPU excludes children, CPU total includes them, Self CUDA is device kernel time, and Number of Calls is what exposes a thousand tiny kernels. Export with `prof.export_chrome_trace('trace.json')` and open it in Perfetto to see the CPU and CUDA timelines aligned - the gaps are the whole point.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.profiler (profile, schedule, record_function, key_averages)

subtopics.name: Bottleneck triage: dataloader-bound vs kernel-bound vs host-sync-bound
subtopics.learn: Learn the three signatures and the fix for each. Dataloader-bound: the CUDA timeline has a wide idle gap at the start of every iteration while the CPU sits in `enumerate(loader)`; the GPU is under-used and the fix is more workers, prefetch, pinned memory, cheaper decoding, or caching the preprocessed tensors. Kernel-bound: the GPU timeline is near-solid with a handful of long `sgemm`/conv kernels; there is nothing to fix in Python and the levers are batch size, mixed precision, `channels_last`, a better kernel, or `torch.compile`. Host-sync-bound: `cudaStreamSynchronize` or `cudaMemcpyAsync DtoH` appears once per iteration and the CPU blocks - caused by `.item()`, `.cpu()`, `float(loss)`, `print(loss)`, `if torch.isnan(loss)`, or `.tolist()` inside the loop; fix by accumulating metrics in a device tensor and syncing once every N steps. Underpinning all of it: CUDA launches are asynchronous, so `time.time()` around a forward measures launch time only - time with `torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)` or an explicit `torch.cuda.synchronize()`, and read memory with `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()` versus `memory_reserved()` to distinguish a real OOM from allocator fragmentation.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - CUDA semantics (asynchronous execution, streams, pinned memory, events)

outcomes: You can hand-derive the backward for a fused softmax-cross-entropy and for SiLU, implement each as a `torch.autograd.Function` with `save_for_backward` and `needs_input_grad`, and have `torch.autograd.gradcheck` pass in float64 at default tolerances without loosening `atol`.

You can build a ~300-line NumPy-backed autograd engine with broadcasting-aware backward (add, mul, matmul, sum/mean, relu, exp/log, softmax-CE, reshape, transpose) whose gradients match PyTorch to 1e-6 on a 2-layer MLP for non-square, broadcasting shapes, asserted in pytest.
You can predict `size()`, `stride()` and `storage_offset()` after a chain of slice/transpose/expand operations, say in advance whether `view()` will raise, and explain in stride terms why it does.

You can write a complete PyTorch training and evaluation loop closed-book in under 20 minutes - `set_to_none`, autocast, clipping, scheduler ordering, dataset-weighted metric accumulation - and it trains a real model to a sane accuracy on the first run.

You can run `torch.profiler` with a `schedule` over one training step and, from the `key_averages` table plus the Perfetto trace, state whether the step is dataloader-bound, kernel-bound or host-sync-bound, name the specific line responsible, and show a before/after wall-clock improvement.

You can diagnose from the error text alone: an in-place version-counter error, `Trying to backward through the graph a second time`, `Inference tensors cannot be saved for backward`, `Expected all tensors to be on the same device`, and a worker bus error - and give the one-line fix for each.

You can implement a Dataset plus custom `collate_fn` for variable-length inputs, shard an `IterableDataset` correctly across four workers, seed NumPy per worker via `worker_init_fn`, and prove that the loader is not the bottleneck with a measured GPU-idle percentage.

You can state exactly what reproducibility you will guarantee a customer - pinned seeds, pinned versions, deterministic algorithms on, a metric reproducible within a stated tolerance - and explain in two sentences why bitwise identity across hardware is not on the table.
failureModes: The validation loop compares a (N, 1) prediction to a (N,) target, so MSE broadcasts to an N-by-N matrix of pairwise errors; the loss is smooth, small and decreasing, and the model has simply learned to predict the mean of the target.

Somebody passes `softmax(logits)` into `nn.CrossEntropyLoss`; the double softmax squashes the gradient, the loss flattens just under ln(C), accuracy sits barely above chance, and the team spends two weeks blaming label quality instead of one line of code.

`total_loss += loss` inside the epoch retains every iteration's graph, so memory grows linearly and the run dies with a CUDA OOM near the end of epoch one; it gets misdiagnosed as 'the batch size is too large' and the batch is halved, which merely delays the crash.

The eval loop never calls `model.eval()`, so dropout stays active and BatchNorm uses the eval batch's own statistics; validation accuracy is noisy and pessimistic, model selection picks the wrong checkpoint, and the effect reverses if the customer later evaluates with batch size 1.

Latency is benchmarked with `time.time()` around the forward pass without `torch.cuda.synchronize()`, so the number measured is kernel launch time; the deck says 8 ms per inference and production measures 35 ms in front of the customer.

An `IterableDataset` streaming from sharded files is used with `num_workers=4` and no `get_worker_info()` sharding, so every worker emits the same records; each epoch trains on four copies of a quarter of the data, and the only symptom is a train/validation gap nobody can explain.

Augmentation uses `np.random` inside `__getitem__` with `num_workers>0` and no `worker_init_fn`; all workers inherit the same NumPy seed, the same augmentation sequence repeats every epoch, effective augmentation diversity collapses, and the model overfits in a way that looks like a regularisation problem.

A custom `Function`'s backward forgets to sum the incoming gradient back over a broadcast bias dimension; `gradcheck` on a square test input passes by coincidence, tolerances get loosened when it later fails on a real shape, and the bias gradient is wrong by a factor of the batch size on every batch.
interviewQuestions: Derive the backward for y = x @ W + b where x is (B, T, D) and b is (D,). Give dL/dx, dL/dW and dL/db including exactly which axes are summed, then tell me how you would implement it as a `torch.autograd.Function` and prove it with `gradcheck` - including why the test must run in float64.

Explain reverse-mode versus forward-mode autodiff in terms of Jacobian-vector and vector-Jacobian products. Which one does `.backward()` perform, what is the compute and memory cost of a backward pass relative to a forward pass, and when would you reach for `torch.func.jacfwd` instead?

Debug: training loss is decreasing but each step takes 400 ms and `nvidia-smi` shows 20 percent utilisation. Walk me through the profiling run you would set up and how you would distinguish dataloader-bound from launch-bound from host-sync-bound - name the specific evidence you would look for in each case.
Your run produces NaN loss at step 3000 under fp16 autocast. Give me your ordered checklist of causes and the check for each, and explain what the GradScaler is doing at the moment the NaN appears.

Distinguish `torch.no_grad()`, `torch.inference_mode()`, `.detach()` and `requires_grad_(False)`. Give one situation where each is the correct tool and one where using it instead of the right one silently produces a wrong result rather than an error.

Write out the Adam and AdamW update rules. Where exactly does weight decay enter in each, why does that difference matter, and how would you configure `param_groups` for a transformer with biases, LayerNorm gains and embeddings?

Design: a customer hands you 4 TB of JPEGs on an NFS mount and one A100. Design the input pipeline - map-style Dataset or IterableDataset, worker count, collate, caching, sharding, augmentation seeding - and tell me how you would prove to their team that the GPU, not the loader, is the limit.
112.proofOfWork: A public repo `torch-failure-museum`: twelve numbered, self-contained scripts, each a minimal reproduction of one silent PyTorch failure from the list above - the (N,1)-vs-(N,) broadcast loss, the double softmax, the retained-graph OOM, the missing `model.eval()`, the unsynchronised timing, the unsharded `IterableDataset`, the duplicated NumPy seed across workers, the missing unbroadcast in a custom backward, the fp16 underflow with no scaler, the in-place version-counter error, the `.item()` sync in the inner loop, and a `.data` write that corrupts a gradient with no exception at all. Each script prints the misleading-but-plausible output, then a pytest asserts the specific wrong number (loss stuck near ln(C), gradient off by exactly the batch size, measured latency 4x below the synchronised truth), and a `--fixed` flag runs the one-line correction so the same assertion flips. Ship it with a `bench/` harness that times the same ResNet-ish step with CUDA events under six configurations (baseline, +workers, +pin_memory/non_blocking, +bf16 autocast, +channels_last, +torch.compile), a committed `trace.json` plus the `key_averages` table before and after for the one bottleneck you removed, and a one-page PYTORCH-REVIEW-CHECKLIST.md written for a customer's ML team - fifteen questions to ask of any training script before it is trusted, each traceable to one of the twelve reproductions.

113.topic: Computer vision: CNNs, ResNet and EfficientNet, transfer learning, augmentation, detection
113.why: Vision is the most common 'can you just...' an FDE gets - count pallets from a warehouse camera, flag a defective part, read a scanned form - and it is the one where a customer hands you 400 labelled images on Monday and expects a demo on Friday. Being able to hand-compute output shapes, parameter counts and receptive fields is what lets you say in the room why a stride-32 backbone cannot see their 14-pixel objects, and reading a per-class mAP table is what lets you say whether the fix is anchor scales, the NMS/IoU threshold, or thirty more images of the rare class - instead of retraining blind for a week. Transfer learning is the only honest answer to 'we have 400 images', and defending it means knowing exactly which layers you froze, why the BatchNorm statistics still moved anyway, and what your augmentation pipeline is implicitly promising about the deployment distribution.
prerequisites: Backpropagation as the chain rule over a computation graph, plus ReLU, softmax and cross-entropy (Topic 110, Neural network foundations) - you will differentiate a convolution by hand in this topic
The deep-training toolkit from Topic 111: SGD with momentum vs Adam, warmup and decay schedules, batch norm mechanics, mixed precision, and how to read a loss curve that has stopped moving
PyTorch at depth (Topic 112): tensor shapes and broadcasting, autograd and .backward(), writing a custom nn.Module, Dataset/DataLoader/collate_fn, and torch.profiler

NumPy vectorisation, stride tricks and float32 vs float64 error behaviour (Topic 99, Numerical computing) - the from-scratch conv2d is a strides-plus-matmul exercise and a gradient check only means something if you understand the tolerance

Evaluation discipline from Topic 103: stratified and grouped splits, leakage, PR-AUC vs accuracy under class imbalance - detection is imbalance in its most extreme form (thousands of background anchors per object)
A GPU you can hold for a few hours (Colab T4, a rented A10 or better), torch + torchvision installed, and CIFAR-10 downloadable; CPU-only turns the >90% ResNet-18 target into a multi-day job

subtopics.name: Convolution as a layer: cross-correlation, weight sharing, shape and parameter count
subtopics.learn: Know that nn.Conv2d computes cross-correlation, not the flipped convolution of signal processing - the flip is absorbed into the learned weights, so it only matters when you read a maths text or write the backward pass. Be able to write from memory H_out = floor((H_in + 2p - d(k-1) - 1)/s) + 1 (identically for W), the parameter count C_out * (C_in/groups * k_h * k_w) + C_out when bias=True, and the MAC count C_out * (C_in/groups) * k_h * k_w * H_out * W_out (FLOPs approximately twice that). Be able to say what the layer buys over a dense layer: translation equivariance (shift the input, the feature map shifts) plus locality and weight sharing, which is why a 3x3 64->128 layer holds 73,728 weights while a dense map over a 32x32x64 activation would hold billions. Verify every hand computation against x.shape and sum(p.numel() for p in layer.parameters()) before you trust it on a whiteboard.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Convolutions for Images (cross-correlation, feature maps)

subtopics.name: Padding, stride, dilation, groups and the 1x1 convolution
subtopics.learn: Work out what each argument does to shape and cost: padding=(k-1)/2 with odd k and stride 1 preserves H and W (padding='same' is only legal for stride 1 in PyTorch); stride 2 halves the spatial size and quarters the MACs of everything downstream; dilation d makes the effective kernel k_eff = d(k-1)+1 so segmentation nets grow the receptive field without downsampling; groups=C_in makes the layer depthwise, cutting cost by roughly a factor of C_out. Understand the 1x1 convolution as a per-position linear map across channels with zero spatial mixing - it is what makes the ResNet bottleneck (1x1 reduce, 3x3, 1x1 expand) cheap, what projects the shortcut when channel counts change, and what a squeeze-and-excite block uses to produce per-channel gates. Be able to state, for a 256-channel 14x14 activation, the MAC ratio between a 3x3 256->256 and a 1x1 256->256 (9:1) and use it to explain where a network's FLOPs actually sit.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Multiple Input and Multiple Output Channels (incl. 1x1 convolutions)

subtopics.name: Receptive field arithmetic, effective vs theoretical
subtopics.learn: Compute the receptive field with the two-line recursion: jump j_l = j_{l-1} * s_l starting at j_0 = 1, and r_l = r_{l-1} + (k_l - 1) * j_{l-1} starting at r_0 = 1; carry the centre offset if you need to map a feature-map cell back to an input pixel. Run it over ResNet-18 (7x7/2 stem, 3x3/2 maxpool, four stages of two BasicBlocks with stride 2 at the start of stages 2-4) and state the total stride (32) and theoretical RF (hundreds of pixels) at the last stage. Then know the empirical result that matters in practice: the effective receptive field is far smaller than the theoretical one and roughly Gaussian, decaying from the centre, so a unit whose theoretical RF is 400 px may only be meaningfully driven by ~100 px. This is the arithmetic behind the customer conversation 'your objects are 14 pixels wide, the P5 feature map has stride 32, so the object occupies less than half a cell - we need an FPN, a higher-resolution input, or tiling'.

resource.label: Distill - Computing Receptive Fields of Convolutional Neural Networks

subtopics.name: Pooling, global average pooling and the classifier head
subtopics.learn: Implement max pooling and average pooling forward: same output-shape formula as convolution, no learnable parameters, applied per channel. Understand what each gives up - max pooling is a hard argmax that discards everything but the winner and produces sparse gradients, average pooling smooths and keeps all contributions - and why modern nets often replace pooling with a stride-2 convolution so the downsampling is learned. Know that nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1) (global average pooling) is what lets a ResNet accept any input size above the minimum: it collapses C x H x W to C x 1 x 1, so the final nn.Linear(512, num_classes) sees a fixed 512-vector regardless of resolution. Be able to explain why GAP replaced VGG-16's fully connected head - the first 25088->4096 layer alone holds about 103M of the network's ~138M parameters, and the whole head about 124M - and why removing it also made the network far less prone to overfitting a small customer dataset.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Pooling

subtopics.name: im2col: implementing conv2d forward in NumPy as one matmul
subtopics.learn: Turn the convolution into GEMM: pad the input, extract every k x k patch to build X_col of shape (C_in * k * k, N * H_out * W_out), reshape the weights to W_row of shape (C_out, C_in * k * k), and compute Y = W_row @ X_col + b, reshaped back to (N, C_out, H_out, W_out). Build the patch extraction with numpy.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view (then slice with [::s, ::s] for stride) rather than four nested Python loops, and know the trade you just made: im2col replicates each input pixel k*k times, so it costs memory proportional to k^2 in exchange for hitting a BLAS kernel. Cross-check your implementation against torch.nn.functional.unfold (which is exactly im2col) and against F.conv2d on the same random tensors to within 1e-6 in float64. Handle the awkward cases explicitly: batch dimension, stride > 1, asymmetric padding, and groups.

resource.label: NumPy docs - sliding_window_view (strided patch extraction)

subtopics.name: The conv and max-pool backward pass, and a gradient check that cannot lie
subtopics.learn: Derive all three gradients in im2col form: dW_row = dY_row @ X_col.T reshaped to the weight shape, db = dY summed over (N, H_out, W_out), and dX_col = W_row.T @ dY_row followed by col2im, which scatter-adds overlapping patches back (np.add.at, not assignment - overlapping receptive fields must accumulate). Recognise that dX is equivalent to a full convolution of dY with the 180-degree rotated kernel, and that stride s > 1 means dY is first dilated by inserting s-1 zeros between elements. Max-pool backward routes the incoming gradient only to the argmax position of each window (store the indices in the forward pass; define a tie rule and stick to it), and average-pool backward divides by the window size. Then check it properly: wrap your op in a torch.autograd.Function, run torch.autograd.gradcheck on float64 inputs with eps=1e-6, atol=1e-5, and non-trivial stride and padding - a check that passes in float32 with a large eps proves nothing and is how a transposed axis in dW survives to training time.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Gradcheck mechanics (finite differences, tolerances, complex inputs)

subtopics.name: Initialisation: why fan_in and the factor of 2 matter for ReLU nets
subtopics.learn: Derive the variance-propagation argument: for y = Wx with n_in = k*k*C_in independent inputs, Var(y) = n_in * Var(W) * Var(x); requiring Var(y) = Var(x) gives Xavier/Glorot Var(W) = 1/n_in (or 2/(n_in+n_out) for the two-way compromise). ReLU zeroes half the distribution and halves the variance, so He initialisation uses Var(W) = 2/n_in - the difference is a factor of sqrt(2) per layer, which compounds to a 30-layer net whose activations vanish or explode before the first gradient step. In PyTorch this is nn.init.kaiming_normal_(w, mode='fan_out', nonlinearity='relu'); the ResNet paper additionally zero-initialises the final BatchNorm gamma in each residual block so every block starts as the identity. Be able to demonstrate the failure: initialise a 30-layer plain conv net with std=0.01 and print the per-layer activation std on one forward pass, watching it decay geometrically toward zero.

resource.label: arXiv 1502.01852 - Delving Deep into Rectifiers (He initialisation)

subtopics.name: Batch normalisation: the exact computation, train vs eval, and where it breaks
subtopics.learn: Write it out: per channel, over the (N, H, W) axes, mu_B and sigma^2_B, then x_hat = (x - mu_B)/sqrt(sigma^2_B + eps) and y = gamma * x_hat + beta, with eps=1e-5 and 2*C learnable parameters. Know the two modes and the state they hide: in train() mode the layer normalises with batch statistics and updates running_mean/running_var as running = (1 - momentum) * running + momentum * batch (PyTorch momentum defaults to 0.1, the opposite convention from optimiser momentum); in eval() mode it uses only the running estimates. Understand the consequences an FDE hits: the loss for one sample depends on the rest of its batch, so tiny batches give noisy statistics (use GroupNorm or SyncBatchNorm instead), the train/eval gap explains models that score well in the training loop and badly at inference, and BatchNorm makes weight decay on gamma/beta meaningless. Also know that the original 'internal covariate shift' explanation has been challenged - the effect that survives is a smoother loss landscape permitting much larger learning rates.

resource.label: arXiv 1502.03167 - Batch Normalization (Ioffe and Szegedy)

subtopics.name: Residual learning: the degradation problem and what the identity path does to the gradient
subtopics.learn: State the empirical fact the paper opens with: a 56-layer plain CNN has higher TRAINING error than a 20-layer one, so this is an optimisation failure, not overfitting - depth alone does not buy you a strictly larger reachable hypothesis set in practice. The fix is to learn a residual y = F(x, W) + x, so a block that should do nothing only needs F -> 0 rather than fitting an identity through two nonlinear layers. Be able to write the gradient argument from the pre-activation follow-up (He et al. 2016, arXiv 1603.05027): with pure identity shortcuts x_L = x_l + sum F, so dL/dx_l = (dL/dx_L) * (1 + d/dx_l sum F) - the additive 1 means the gradient reaches every earlier layer even when the product of Jacobians is tiny. Know what breaks the guarantee: any shortcut that is not identity (1x1 projection, gating, scaling) reintroduces a multiplicative term, which is why projections are used only where the shape changes.

resource.label: arXiv 1512.03385 - Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (ResNet)

subtopics.name: Building ResNet-18 by hand: the block table, downsample projections and the CIFAR stem
subtopics.learn: Write the architecture from memory: conv7x7/2 to 64 channels, BN, ReLU, maxpool 3x3/2, then stages of [2, 2, 2, 2] BasicBlocks at 64/128/256/512 channels with stride 2 at the first block of stages 2-4, then AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1) and Linear(512, num_classes) - about 11.7M parameters for 1000 classes. A BasicBlock is conv3x3-BN-ReLU-conv3x3-BN, then add the shortcut, then ReLU (the second ReLU goes after the addition, not before); when stride or channel count changes, the shortcut becomes a 1x1 stride-2 conv plus BN. Know why bias=False on every conv followed by BN (the BN beta subsumes it), and why ResNet-50 swaps BasicBlock for Bottleneck (1x1 reduce, 3x3, 1x1 expand by 4) with the stride placed on the 3x3 rather than the first 1x1 in torchvision's ResNet v1.5 variant. For CIFAR-10 at 32x32 you must replace the stem with a 3x3 stride-1 conv and delete the maxpool, or you throw away 8x of resolution before the first block and cap yourself well below 90%.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Residual Networks (ResNet) and ResNeXt

subtopics.name: The training recipe: SGD+momentum, decoupled weight decay, warmup+cosine, AMP and throughput
subtopics.learn: Fix the recipe you will defend: SGD momentum 0.9 with nesterov, base LR 0.1 for batch 128 scaled linearly with batch size, weight decay 5e-4 applied to conv and linear weights ONLY (exclude BN gamma/beta and all biases via two param groups - decaying them costs accuracy and is the single most common silent recipe bug), 5 epochs of linear warmup then cosine decay eta_t = eta_min + 0.5(eta_max - eta_min)(1 + cos(pi * t / T)), label smoothing 0.1, ~100-200 epochs for >90% CIFAR-10. Then make it fast: torch.autocast('cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16 or float16) with GradScaler for fp16, model.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last) which is what actually unlocks tensor cores for convolutions, DataLoader with num_workers = 4-8, pin_memory=True, persistent_workers=True and prefetch, and torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark=True for fixed input shapes. Profile before you optimise: if GPU utilisation sits at 40 percent the bottleneck is your augmentation pipeline, not the model.

resource.label: PyTorch Recipes - Performance Tuning Guide (AMP, channels_last, DataLoader)

subtopics.name: Augmentation as an explicit invariance prior, and the transforms v2 API
subtopics.learn: Treat every augmentation as a claim about the deployment distribution: RandomHorizontalFlip says left-right mirrored inputs are equally likely (false for text, road signs and anything chiral), RandomResizedCrop(scale=(0.08, 1.0)) says the object survives an 8-percent crop (false for small-object detection), ColorJitter and RandomGrayscale say lighting varies (true for a warehouse camera, dangerous for colour-coded defects). Build the pipeline with torchvision.transforms.v2, which accepts and correctly transforms tv_tensors.BoundingBoxes and Mask alongside the image - the reason detection augmentation is not a hand-rolled affair - and compose as v2.Compose([...geometry..., v2.ToImage(), v2.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True), v2.Normalize(mean, std)]) with normalisation LAST. The train transform and the eval transform are different objects: eval is deterministic Resize + CenterCrop + Normalize, and passing the train transform to the validation Dataset is a metric bug, not a regularisation choice. Know test-time augmentation (average logits over flips/crops) as the cheap last 0.5 points, at the cost of N-times inference latency.

resource.label: torchvision docs - Transforming and augmenting images (v2 API)

subtopics.name: Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment and label smoothing
subtopics.learn: Mixup constructs x_tilde = lambda*x_i + (1-lambda)*x_j with lambda ~ Beta(alpha, alpha) (alpha typically 0.2-0.4) and trains on the mixed target, implemented as loss = lambda*CE(pred, y_i) + (1-lambda)*CE(pred, y_j) - it enforces linear behaviour between examples, reduces memorisation of corrupt labels and noticeably improves calibration. CutMix instead pastes a rectangular patch from one image into another and sets lambda to the true area ratio, which preserves local statistics and works better with localisation. RandAugment removes the search: two hyperparameters, N operations sampled uniformly from a fixed list at a single global magnitude M. Label smoothing replaces the one-hot target with 1-eps and eps/(K-1), capping the logit gap the network is asked to produce. Know the practical caveats: these all need longer schedules to pay off, mixup interacts badly with metric-learning heads, and torchvision.transforms.v2 provides CutMix and MixUp as batch-level transforms applied in the collate function, not per-sample.

resource.label: arXiv 1710.09412 - mixup: Beyond Empirical Risk Minimization

subtopics.name: Transfer learning: freeze vs fine-tune, the BatchNorm trap, discriminative learning rates
subtopics.learn: Load pretrained weights via the modern API (weights=ResNet18_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1) and use weights.transforms() so your preprocessing matches training exactly - resize 256, centre crop 224, mean [0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]. Linear probe: replace model.fc with nn.Linear(in_features, n_classes), set requires_grad_(False) on the backbone, and pass ONLY the head parameters to the optimiser. Then internalise the trap: requires_grad=False does not freeze BatchNorm - running_mean and running_var keep updating on every forward pass in train() mode, so a truly frozen backbone needs the BN modules put in eval() after model.train(), or the frozen and fine-tuned arms of your ablation will look suspiciously alike. Full fine-tune uses discriminative learning rates (backbone 1e-4, head 1e-3, roughly 10x apart) because the pretrained features need nudging, not relearning. Choose by data size and domain distance: a few hundred near-ImageNet images means linear probe; thousands of X-rays or satellite tiles means full fine-tune with a longer warmup.

resource.label: PyTorch Tutorials - Transfer Learning for Computer Vision

subtopics.name: EfficientNet: compound scaling, MBConv, and what the FLOP count hides
subtopics.learn: Understand the actual claim: scaling depth d = alpha^phi, width w = beta^phi and resolution r = gamma^phi together beats scaling any one, under the constraint alpha * beta^2 * gamma^2 approximately 2 (because FLOPs grow linearly in depth and quadratically in width and resolution), so total FLOPs scale about 2^phi; B0 is a MnasNet-style searched baseline of MBConv blocks - depthwise separable convolution with an inverted residual, squeeze-and-excite, and swish - and B1 to B7 are the same net at increasing phi. Be able to derive the depthwise separable cost ratio 1/C_out + 1/k^2 (about 1/9 for a 3x3 with many channels) and then say what the paper does not: depthwise convolutions are memory-bandwidth bound, so B4 can have fewer FLOPs than ResNet-152 and still be slower on a T4, and higher resolution inflates activation memory quadratically, which is what caps your batch size on the customer's hardware. This is the answer to 'the benchmark says it is 8x more efficient' - efficient in FLOPs and parameters, not necessarily in latency or memory, and you should benchmark on their device before promising a frame rate.

resource.label: arXiv 1905.11946 - EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for CNNs

subtopics.name: Detection setup: box formats, IoU, anchors and label assignment
subtopics.learn: Get the plumbing exact first, because most detection bugs are here: xyxy vs xywh vs cxcywh, absolute pixels vs normalised, and COCO's 1-indexed category ids with a background class at 0 in torchvision. Compute IoU = area(intersection)/area(union) and be able to code it vectorised over (N, M) box pairs. Anchors are a dense grid of reference boxes at each feature-map location parameterised by scales and aspect ratios; assignment labels each anchor by its best IoU against ground truth (RPN: >= 0.7 positive, < 0.3 negative, in-between ignored; SSD/RetinaNet typically 0.5/0.4), and the regression head predicts offsets t_x = (x - x_a)/w_a, t_y = (y - y_a)/h_a, t_w = log(w/w_a), t_h = log(h/h_a) so the target is scale-invariant and roughly unit-variance. Understand why this is where recall dies: if no anchor reaches the positive IoU threshold with a 14-pixel object, that object contributes no positive sample and the network is never asked to find it - the fix is anchor scales, feature-pyramid level, or input resolution, not the loss weights.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Anchor Boxes (IoU, assignment, offset parameterisation)

subtopics.name: Two-stage vs one-stage, and the foreground/background imbalance
subtopics.learn: Place the families: two-stage (Faster R-CNN, arXiv 1506.01497 - an RPN proposes ~1-2k regions, RoIAlign crops features, a second head classifies and refines) trades latency for accuracy on small and crowded objects; one-stage (SSD, RetinaNet, YOLO) predicts class and box densely in a single pass and is what you deploy at 30 fps. Understand why the one-stage family lagged: roughly 100k anchors per image are evaluated and fewer than a dozen are foreground, so the summed cross-entropy of easy negatives swamps the gradient. Focal loss fixes it in the loss rather than by sampling: FL(p_t) = -alpha_t * (1 - p_t)^gamma * log(p_t) with gamma = 2 and alpha = 0.25, which down-weights an easy negative at p_t = 0.9 by about 100x; it also requires the classification bias initialised to log(pi/(1-pi)) with pi about 0.01 or the first iterations diverge. Contrast with the two-stage answer (sample a fixed 1:3 positive:negative minibatch of RoIs) and know that modern anchor-free heads (FCOS, DETR-style set prediction) replace assignment with centre-sampling or Hungarian matching.

resource.label: arXiv 1708.02002 - Focal Loss for Dense Object Detection (RetinaNet)

subtopics.name: NMS, score thresholds and the operating point you actually ship
subtopics.learn: Non-maximum suppression is greedy: sort boxes by score, take the top one, discard every remaining box with IoU above the threshold against it, repeat. Use torchvision.ops.nms(boxes, scores, iou_threshold) and, crucially, batched_nms(boxes, scores, idxs, iou_threshold) which offsets boxes per class so a car is never suppressed by an overlapping person - class-agnostic NMS on a multi-class problem quietly deletes correct detections. Know the two knobs and that they are not the same: the IoU threshold (0.5-0.7 typical) controls duplicate merging and, when too low, deletes genuinely overlapping objects in crowds; the SCORE threshold controls precision/recall and is the operating point. Evaluation runs at score 0.01-0.05 with maxDets=100 to trace the full PR curve, while a demo or production service runs at 0.3-0.5 - so mAP and your live demo are measuring different things unless you say so. Know soft-NMS (decay scores instead of deleting) for crowded scenes, and that NMS is often the latency floor on CPU deployments.

resource.label: torchvision docs - ops (nms, batched_nms, box_iou, RoIAlign)

subtopics.name: mAP: how COCO computes it, and reading a per-class breakdown
subtopics.learn: Follow the pipeline: for one class, sort detections by score, match each greedily to an unmatched ground-truth box above the IoU threshold (matched = TP, unmatched = FP, unmatched ground truth = FN), accumulate precision and recall, interpolate to 101 recall points, average to get AP; COCO's headline AP averages that over IoU 0.50:0.05:0.95, then over classes, and additionally reports AP50, AP75, AP_small/medium/large (area < 32^2, 32^2-96^2, > 96^2) and AR at maxDets 1/10/100. Learn to diagnose from the table alone: high AP50 with low AP75 means localisation is sloppy, not classification; AP_small near zero with AP_large healthy means resolution, feature-pyramid level or anchor scale; one class near zero with the rest fine means labelling or class imbalance, not architecture; AR far above AP means the detector finds the objects but scores or duplicates them badly, which points at NMS or calibration. Run pycocotools COCOeval on your own predictions and reproduce the summary line by hand for one class so you know exactly what the number means when a customer asks.

resource.label: COCO dataset - Detection Evaluation (AP definition, IoU sweep, area ranges, maxDets)

subtopics.name: Debugging vision training: overfit-one-batch, curve reading, Grad-CAM and leakage checks
subtopics.learn: Run the ladder in order, before touching hyperparameters: (1) overfit a single batch of 8 images to near-zero loss - if it cannot, the bug is in the model, the loss or the label plumbing, never the data volume; (2) check the initial loss equals ln(K) for K balanced classes, which catches a wrong reduction or a double softmax; (3) visualise a batch AFTER the full transform pipeline and denormalise it - this is where you see BGR/RGB swaps, all-black images from a bad resize, and masks misaligned with images; (4) plot train vs val loss and separate overfitting (val rises while train falls) from a broken eval path (val flat and high from epoch one, usually train/eval mode or normalisation); (5) attribute with Grad-CAM - weights alpha_k = global-average-pooled dL^c/dA^k over the last conv feature maps, heatmap = ReLU(sum_k alpha_k * A^k) - and confirm the model is looking at the object rather than a watermark, a timestamp overlay or the background texture that happens to correlate with the label. Finish with the split audit: group by source video, patient, device or session, and hash-dedupe images across train and test.

resource.label: arXiv 1610.02391 - Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks

outcomes: You can hand-compute, on a whiteboard in under two minutes with no library, the output H x W, parameter count and theoretical receptive field at every stage of ResNet-18 for a given input size, and say which stage first stops resolving a 16-pixel object.

You can implement conv2d and max-pool forward and backward in NumPy and have torch.autograd.gradcheck agree with your analytic gradients on float64 with eps=1e-6, including stride 2, padding 1 and a non-square batch.

You can build ResNet-18 from nn.Conv2d/nn.BatchNorm2d/nn.Linear with no torchvision.models, train it past 90% CIFAR-10 test accuracy, and justify every recipe choice (3x3 stride-1 stem, He init, no weight decay on BN and bias, warmup plus cosine, random crop and flip) with the measured cost of removing each.

You can explain the degradation problem with the gradient expression for a residual block, and demonstrate it empirically by training a plain-18 and a ResNet-18 to different TRAINING errors under an identical recipe.

You can state EfficientNet's compound-scaling constraint alpha * beta^2 * gamma^2 approximately 2, derive the depthwise separable cost ratio, and explain why a lower-FLOP model can still miss a latency budget on the customer's specific GPU.

You can produce a transfer-learning ablation table (frozen backbone vs full fine-tune vs augmentation-off) with fixed seeds and repeat runs, and defend which row you would ship for a given dataset size and domain distance.

You can read a COCO per-class AP/AR breakdown including AP50/AP75 and AP_small/medium/large and say from the numbers alone whether anchor scales, the NMS IoU threshold, the score threshold or class imbalance is what to change next.

You can take a model that scored 0.91 offline and 0.40 in a customer pipeline and localise the cause within an hour by checking preprocessing, channel order, resize interpolation, train/eval mode and the split, before touching any weights.
failureModes: The customer's 4,000 images came from 60 video clips; a random split puts adjacent frames in both train and test, validation accuracy reads 0.98, and the model collapses to 0.62 on next month's footage - the split had to be grouped by clip.

The frozen-backbone arm of the ablation calls requires_grad_(False) but leaves the model in train() mode, so BatchNorm running_mean and running_var keep adapting to the new domain; the frozen and fine-tuned rows come out nearly identical and the table's headline conclusion is wrong.

The same transform object is passed to the train and the validation Dataset, so RandomResizedCrop and ColorJitter run at evaluation time; validation accuracy is noisy and several points low, and two days go into tuning a learning rate to fix what is purely a measurement bug.

Training normalises with ImageNet mean/std after ToTensor while the production service feeds uint8 BGR straight from cv2.imread with a different resize interpolation; accuracy drops from 0.91 to 0.40 and is escalated as a data-quality problem for a week.

A defect classifier on 3 percent positives is reported at 97 percent accuracy - exactly the always-negative baseline - and the customer signs off on a model that has never flagged a defect, because PR-AUC and per-class recall were never on the slide.

mAP is computed at score threshold 0.05 with maxDets 100 and reads 0.61, but the shipped service runs at 0.5 and misses half the objects; the evaluation and the deployment are measuring different operating points and nobody says so out loud.

Default anchor scales of 32-512 px are kept on a dataset whose objects are 10-20 px, so no anchor ever reaches the positive IoU threshold, the box head receives almost no positive samples, recall ceilings near 0.3, and three weeks are spent tuning loss weights that cannot fix it.

The NumPy conv2d gradient check passes in float32 with eps=1e-2, hiding a transposed axis in the dW accumulation and a missing np.add.at in col2im; the layer still trains, just to a mediocre plateau that looks convincingly like a data problem.
interviewQuestions: Derive the receptive field at the last conv stage of ResNet-18 for a 224x224 input, showing the jump and RF recursions. The customer's objects are 15 pixels across in a 4K frame - what do you change in the architecture or the input pipeline, and what does each option cost in latency and memory?

Write the gradients of the loss with respect to the weights and the input for a 3x3, stride-1, padding-1 conv layer. Why is dX a full convolution with the 180-degree rotated kernel, what changes when the stride is 2, and how would you verify your implementation so that passing the check actually means something?
