A 56-layer plain CNN has higher training error than a 20-layer one. That is not overfitting - what is it? Write the gradient expression for a residual block that shows what the identity shortcut fixes, and say what breaks that argument when the shortcut is a 1x1 projection.

You are fine-tuning an ImageNet ResNet-50 on 800 customer images. Walk me through linear probe vs full fine-tune, exactly what you do with the BatchNorm layers in each case, what learning rates you use per parameter group, and how you would know within one epoch that it is working.

Debug: detection mAP is 0.61 overall, but AP for one class is 0.08, AP_small is 0.04 while AP_large is 0.72, and AR@100 is 0.79. What do you look at, in what order, and what are your top two hypotheses with the experiment that distinguishes them?

EfficientNet-B4 has fewer FLOPs and parameters than ResNet-152 but runs slower on the customer's T4. Explain compound scaling, explain precisely why the FLOP count misleads here, and describe how you would choose a backbone against a 30 ms per-frame budget on their hardware.

Design: a customer wants conveyor-belt defect detection at 20 fps with 300 labelled images and roughly a 2 percent defect rate. Specify the model, the labelling and split strategy, the augmentation policy and what it assumes, the metric you report, the threshold you ship at, and what you would refuse to promise in the SOW.
113.proofOfWork: A small public tool called conv-arithmetic plus a detection triage report, both in the same repo as the deliverable. The tool is a single module that takes any nn.Module and an input shape and prints a per-layer table of output shape, parameter count, MACs, cumulative stride, theoretical receptive field and the fraction of total FLOPs each layer holds - with every number reproduced independently by your own recursion rather than read from a profiler - and then validates itself two ways: against torch by running the model and comparing shapes and parameter counts layer by layer, and against reality by measuring the EFFECTIVE receptive field empirically (backpropagate a gradient of 1 from a single centre unit of a chosen feature map to the input, plot the magnitude map, and report the radius containing 90 percent of the mass) so the gap between theoretical and effective RF is visible as a figure. Alongside it, run a controlled triage study on a small public detection set: train one baseline, then produce four deliberately broken variants - anchor scales 10x too large, class-agnostic instead of batched NMS, an NMS IoU threshold of 0.3, and a 50:1 class imbalance with plain cross-entropy instead of focal loss - and publish the COCOeval summary table for all five runs side by side, plus a one-page diagnostic key mapping each mAP signature (AP50 vs AP75 gap, AP_small collapse, single-class collapse, AR far above AP) back to its cause. Finish with a two-paragraph handover note written for a customer engineer explaining which single number you would put in an SLA and why the others are not it.

114.topic: Sequence models: RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs, seq2seq and the road to attention
114.why: Sequence models are where an FDE stops being able to blame the data: when a customer's extraction, forecasting or log-anomaly model plateaus on long inputs, the cause is almost always a gradient-path or a masking problem, and unless you can point at the product of Jacobians and name the exact gate that fixes it, the meeting ends at 'we'll try more epochs'. Every architectural argument in the LLM era - why attention exists at all, why the context window is a real constraint, why a KV cache is even possible - is the answer to a failure you can only feel by having built the seq2seq that fails at token 25. And GRUs and LSTMs are still shipping in production for streaming, on-device and low-latency time-series work, so 'just use a Transformer' is a recommendation you have to be able to defend with a latency number or refuse in front of the customer's ML team.
prerequisites: Reverse-mode autodiff, the batched backward pass, finite-difference gradient checking and per-layer gradient-norm diagnostics from Topic 110 (Neural network foundations) - the recurrence here is the same chain rule applied T times
Optimisers, learning-rate schedules, global gradient clipping and reading a bad loss curve from Topic 111 (Training deep networks)
PyTorch at depth from Topic 112: tensor shapes and views, autograd graph lifetime and .detach(), Dataset/DataLoader with a custom collate_fn, and torch.no_grad() at eval
Linear algebra from Topic 93: singular values, spectral radius, and what repeated multiplication by a matrix does to a vector's norm - this is literally the vanishing-gradient argument
Cross-entropy, NLL and perplexity from Topic 98 (Information theory and loss functions), plus log-sum-exp stability from Topic 99 (Numerical computing)
Leakage-aware evaluation from Topic 103, adapted to sequences: splitting by whole sequence or by time, never by shuffled timestep, and holding out a length band you never trained on

subtopics.name: Sequence data, the autoregressive factorisation and Markov truncation
subtopics.learn: Write the joint as p(x_1..x_T) = prod_t p(x_t | x_1..x_{t-1}) and recognise that every sequence model is just a choice of how to summarise the history: an order-n Markov model keeps the last n tokens (parameter count grows like |V|^n), a feedforward net over a fixed window does the same with sharing, and an RNN replaces the window with a learned fixed-size state h_t. State the three properties that break tabular habits - variable length, order carries information, and the i.i.d. assumption behind a shuffled train/test split is false, so you split by whole sequence or by time and hold out a length band. Know the two evaluation quantities cold: mean per-token cross entropy in nats and perplexity exp(mean NLL), and that a uniform model over |V| symbols has perplexity exactly |V|, which is your loss-at-initialisation sanity check before any training question is on the table.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Working with Sequences (autoregressive models, Markov assumption)

subtopics.name: Text to tensors: vocabulary, special tokens, lengths and batch layout
subtopics.learn: Build the exact pipeline the date-normalisation deliverable needs: a character-level vocabulary with reserved ids <pad>=0, <bos>, <eos>, <unk>; encode '3rd of March, 2001' to source ids and '2001-03-03' to target ids wrapped in <bos>/<eos>; pad each batch to its own max length in a collate_fn and carry a lengths tensor alongside, never a global max. Know the two tensor layouts and never mix them - PyTorch RNNs default to (T, B, H) and require batch_first=True for (B, T, H) - because a silently transposed batch does not crash when T happens to equal B, it just trains to garbage. Use nn.Embedding(V, d, padding_idx=0) so the pad row's gradient is zeroed and its vector stays at zero, and know that teacher-forced decoder input is the target shifted right by one, which is the single most common off-by-one in a seq2seq.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Converting Raw Text into Sequence Data (tokenisation, vocabulary, special tokens)

subtopics.name: The vanilla RNN: recurrence, weight sharing, unrolling
subtopics.learn: Implement h_t = tanh(W_xh x_t + W_hh h_{t-1} + b_h) and o_t = W_hq h_t + b_q, and be explicit that W_xh, W_hh and W_hq are shared across all T steps - that sharing is why the model accepts variable length and why every parameter gradient is a SUM over timesteps rather than a single term. Get the shapes automatic: x_t is (B, d), W_xh is (d, H), W_hh is (H, H), h_t is (B, H), and the whole step is one fused matmul of cat([x_t, h_{t-1}], dim=1) against a (d+H, H) weight. Know the h_0 conventions and when each is right - zeros for independent sequences, a learned nn.Parameter when sequences share a prior, and carrying the previous batch's detached h across a contiguous corpus in language modelling - and be able to say in one sentence why 'the entire history is compressed into a fixed-size vector' is simultaneously the RNN's O(T*d^2) efficiency and its hard ceiling.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Recurrent Neural Networks (hidden state recurrence, parameter sharing)

subtopics.name: Deriving backpropagation through time by hand
subtopics.learn: Unroll the graph and derive, for L = (1/T) sum_t l(o_t, y_t), the three results without notes: dL/dW_hq = sum_t (dl_t/do_t) h_t^T; the hidden-state recursion dL/dh_t = W_hq^T (dl_t/do_t) + W_hh^T diag(1 - h_{t+1}^2) dL/dh_{t+1} (the two terms are the local loss at t and everything downstream of t); and dL/dW_hh = sum_t diag(1 - h_t^2) (dL/dh_t) h_{t-1}^T. The two facts you must be able to defend on a whiteboard are that gradients for shared weights ACCUMULATE across timesteps because W_hh is a fan-out node used T times, and that dL/dh_t contains the factor prod_{k=t+1..T} W_hh^T diag(1 - h_k^2), whose length grows with the temporal distance. Write that product down explicitly and keep it: the LSTM, the GRU, gradient clipping and attention are all four responses to this one expression.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Backpropagation Through Time (full computational-graph derivation)

subtopics.name: Where the gradient dies: the Jacobian product and the spectral radius
subtopics.learn: Take norms of that product: ||dh_T/dh_t|| <= (sigma_1(W_hh) * max|phi'|)^(T-t), so with tanh (max|phi'| = 1) the behaviour is decided by the largest singular value of W_hh - sigma_1 = 0.9 over 100 steps gives a factor of 2.7e-5, sigma_1 = 1.1 gives 1.4e4. Reproduce Pascanu et al.'s statement precisely: sigma_1 < 1/max|phi'| is SUFFICIENT for vanishing, sigma_1 > 1/max|phi'| is NECESSARY (not sufficient) for exploding, and be able to explain why vanishing is a representational failure rather than a slow-optimiser failure - the long-range term is buried under short-range terms in the same sum, so no learning rate recovers it. Diagnose it empirically rather than by faith: for a fixed batch, log ||dL/dh_t|| against t on a log axis and read off the decay constant; explosion instead shows as a loss cliff followed by NaN at a specific step.

resource.label: Pascanu, Mikolov & Bengio, "On the difficulty of training Recurrent Neural Networks" (arXiv:1211.5063)

subtopics.name: Truncated BPTT, gradient clipping and the detached hidden state
subtopics.learn: Know the three operational knobs and what each does NOT fix. Truncated BPTT backpropagates only k steps and detaches the carried state (h = h.detach()) at the boundary, bounding memory at O(k * B * H) at the price of never learning dependencies longer than k; forget the detach and you re-backprop through the whole history and get 'Trying to backward through the graph a second time' on step two. Gradient clipping rescales g <- g * min(1, theta/||g||) on the GLOBAL norm over all parameters via torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0), called after backward() and before optimizer.step() (and after scaler.unscale_ under AMP) - global clipping shortens the step without rotating it, per-parameter clipping changes the descent direction. Internalise the asymmetry: clipping cures exploding gradients completely and does exactly nothing for vanishing ones, which is why gates and not clipping are the answer to long-range memory.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ (global-norm clipping)

subtopics.name: The LSTM cell: four gates, the cell state, the constant error carousel
subtopics.learn: Write all six equations from memory: i_t = sigmoid(W_i [x_t, h_{t-1}] + b_i), f_t = sigmoid(W_f [.] + b_f), o_t = sigmoid(W_o [.] + b_o), g_t = tanh(W_g [.] + b_g), then c_t = f_t (*) c_{t-1} + i_t (*) g_t and h_t = o_t (*) tanh(c_t), where (*) is elementwise. The entire point is the ADDITIVE cell-state recursion: dc_t/dc_{t-1} = diag(f_t), so the gradient along the cell path is a product of forget gates in [0,1] rather than a product of W_hh Jacobians - with f_t near 1 the path is near-identity (Hochreiter's 'constant error carousel') and error signal survives hundreds of steps unattenuated. Be able to name each gate's job in customer English (forget = what to erase, input = what to write, candidate = what to write it with, output = how much of memory to expose to the rest of the net), and to note that c_t is unbounded while h_t is squashed by tanh, which is why an exploding LSTM usually shows up first as a huge c.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM): gate equations and memory cell

subtopics.name: The GRU: update and reset gates as a convex interpolation
subtopics.learn: Write r_t = sigmoid(W_r [x_t, h_{t-1}]), z_t = sigmoid(W_z [x_t, h_{t-1}]), h~_t = tanh(W_h [x_t, r_t (*) h_{t-1}]), h_t = z_t (*) h_{t-1} + (1 - z_t) (*) h~_t, and state the convention you are using out loud because the roles of z and (1 - z) are swapped between papers and textbooks. Read the last line as a convex interpolation between carrying and overwriting: z_t = 1 copies h_{t-1} exactly, giving an identity Jacobian and a preserved gradient, z_t = 0 replaces the state entirely - so the update gate is the GRU's whole answer to vanishing gradients, while the reset gate controls how much history is even allowed into the candidate. Count the trade you will have to explain: 3 gate matrices instead of 4 and a single state tensor instead of an (h, c) tuple, so roughly 25 percent fewer parameters and less memory traffic per step, with near-identical accuracy on most tasks - which is exactly the argument for a GRU when the customer's constraint is latency on CPU.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Gated Recurrent Units (GRU): reset and update gates

subtopics.name: Implementing the cells from tensor ops: fusion, forget-gate bias, gate ablations
subtopics.learn: Implement LSTMCell and GRUCell with a SINGLE fused matmul - concatenate [x_t, h_{t-1}] once, multiply by a (d+H, 4H) weight, then torch.chunk(gates, 4, dim=1) and apply sigmoid/sigmoid/sigmoid/tanh - because four small matmuls per timestep is where a from-scratch cell loses several times over to a fused kernel. Get the details that decide whether it trains: initialise the forget-gate bias to 1.0 (Gers/Jozefowicz) so the cell starts in remember mode, assert every gate is (B, H) before the elementwise ops, and note that in the GRU r_t multiplies h_{t-1} BEFORE the candidate matmul, which is why the three GRU gates cannot all share one fused matmul the way the LSTM's four can (cuDNN sidesteps this with the reset-after variant, and that is why weights are not interchangeable between implementations). Then run the Greff et al. ablations on your own cell - remove the forget gate, remove the output gate, couple input and forget - and confirm empirically that the forget gate is the one whose removal destroys the model.

resource.label: Greff et al., "LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey" (gate ablation study, arXiv:1503.04069)

subtopics.name: Gradient-checking a recurrent cell against autograd
subtopics.learn: Write the unit test the deliverable requires: instantiate your cell in float64, wrap the forward as a closure of (x, h, c, weights) with requires_grad=True, and call torch.autograd.gradcheck(fn, inputs, eps=1e-6, atol=1e-5); then add a second, independent test that copies your weight tensors into torch.nn.LSTMCell (respecting its w_ih/w_hh layout and the i,f,g,o chunk order) and asserts torch.allclose on both the outputs and every .grad. Unroll at least 5 timesteps inside the checked function, because a cell can be correct for one step and wrong in how it threads the (h, c) tuple through the loop - the classic bug is returning h_t while feeding c_{t-1} forward, which still trains, just worse. Know why gradcheck insists on float64 (the centred difference has O(eps^2) truncation error and O(machine_eps/eps) roundoff, and in float32 there is no eps where both are small) and what a pass proves: your backward matches your forward, not that your forward is an LSTM - the nn.LSTMCell comparison is what proves the second half.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - Gradcheck mechanics (numerical vs analytical Jacobian)

subtopics.name: Depth and direction: stacked RNNs, bidirectional encoders, and what bidirectionality forbids
subtopics.learn: Stack by feeding h_t^(l) as the input of layer l+1, and know that nn.LSTM(num_layers=2, dropout=0.3) applies dropout BETWEEN layers only and silently ignores the argument when num_layers=1 - people report having 'tried dropout' when they have not. A bidirectional RNN runs a second recurrence right-to-left and concatenates, so the encoder output per position is 2*H wide and encodes both sides of the token; this is legal for an ENCODER (the whole source is available) and illegal for a decoder, a language model or any streaming task, because h_t would depend on future tokens - bidirectional=True in a causal model is a leakage bug whose signature is a spectacular validation perplexity and a model that is useless at inference. For the deliverable, use a bi-LSTM encoder and a unidirectional decoder, and be deliberate about how you build the decoder's h_0 from the two final directions (concatenate then project with a Linear(2H, H) and a tanh, or sum) rather than silently dropping the backward half.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks (and why they cannot be used causally)

subtopics.name: Regularising recurrent nets: variational dropout, weight tying, LayerNorm
subtopics.learn: Understand why naive per-step dropout on the recurrent connection destroys memory: a fresh Bernoulli mask at every timestep injects noise that compounds multiplicatively over T steps, so the state is scrambled rather than regularised. Gal and Ghahramani's variational dropout samples ONE mask per sequence and reuses it at every timestep (justified as an approximate-Bayesian posterior over weights), which is exactly what nn.LSTM's dropout argument does NOT do - it only drops between stacked layers, so getting true recurrent dropout means writing the loop yourself. Know the AWD-LSTM recipe that actually holds up in practice - DropConnect on the hidden-to-hidden matrix, embedding dropout, variational input/output dropout, weight tying between the input embedding and the output projection (halves parameters and usually improves perplexity), plus activation and temporal-activation regularisation - and know that LayerNorm inside the cell is the sequence-safe normaliser because batch statistics over a padded, variable-length time axis are meaningless.

resource.label: Gal & Ghahramani, "A Theoretically Grounded Application of Dropout in Recurrent Neural Networks" (arXiv:1512.05287)

subtopics.name: Packed sequences, masking, and the padded-loss bug
subtopics.learn: Use pack_padded_sequence(x, lengths.cpu(), batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False) -> rnn -> pad_packed_sequence so the cell never steps on pad positions and the returned h_n is each sequence's state at its TRUE final timestep; without packing, h_n is the state after however many pad tokens that batch happened to contain, which makes your encoder summary a function of batch composition rather than of the sentence. On the loss side, either pass ignore_index=pad_id to nn.CrossEntropyLoss or multiply by an explicit mask and divide by mask.sum() - averaging over padded positions makes batches of long sequences look better than batches of short ones and makes the reported validation loss depend on how you sorted the data. Prove you have it right the way an FDE proves anything: run the same trained model over the same validation set at batch size 1 and batch size 64 and show the loss is identical to floating-point noise; if it is not, you have a masking bug, not a variance issue.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence

subtopics.name: seq2seq and the fixed-length context bottleneck
subtopics.learn: Build the Sutskever architecture exactly as published - an encoder RNN reads the source and emits a single context vector c = h_T^enc, the decoder is initialised with c and generates until <eos> - and then state the information problem precisely: c is a fixed d-dimensional vector whether the source is 5 tokens or 50, so per-token capacity falls like 1/T and the encoder is forced to choose what to discard before it knows what the decoder will need. Learn the empirical signature so you can name it in a room rather than investigate for a week: quality is flat and acceptable up to roughly the training length distribution and then falls off a cliff, and the errors are OMISSIONS and repetitions from the middle of long inputs rather than grammatical failures. Know the historical mitigations and why each only postpones the failure - reversing the source sequence (Sutskever reported +4.7 BLEU purely from shortening the average path between corresponding tokens), deeper stacks, and a wider d - because 'make the bottleneck bigger' is the answer a customer will propose and you need the argument for why it does not scale.

resource.label: Sutskever, Vinyals & Le, "Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks" (arXiv:1409.3215)

subtopics.name: Teacher forcing, exposure bias and scheduled sampling
subtopics.learn: During training the decoder is fed the GROUND-TRUTH previous token, which turns generation into T parallel conditional predictions computable in one batched pass; at inference it is fed its own prediction, so the input distribution it sees is one it never trained on - that mismatch is exposure bias, and its signature is a model with excellent training loss that degenerates into a repetition loop or drifts irrecoverably after one early mistake. Implement a teacher_forcing_ratio and know Bengio et al.'s scheduled sampling (sample the model's own token with a probability annealed upward during training) along with the standard objection that the resulting estimator is not consistent for the true conditional distribution. The rule that keeps your numbers honest: training may be teacher-forced, validation and reporting must ALWAYS be free-running - a teacher-forced validation metric on a date-normalisation model can read 99 percent while free-running exact match is 60 percent, and that gap is the whole reason people are surprised in production.

resource.label: Bengio et al., "Scheduled Sampling for Sequence Prediction with Recurrent Neural Networks" (arXiv:1506.03099)

subtopics.name: Bahdanau additive attention: derive the alignment equations
subtopics.learn: Write and be able to derive the four equations at a whiteboard: e_{t,i} = v_a^T tanh(W_a s_{t-1} + U_a h_i) scoring decoder state s_{t-1} against every encoder state h_i; alpha_{t,i} = softmax over i of e_{t,i}; c_t = sum_i alpha_{t,i} h_i; s_t = f(s_{t-1}, y_{t-1}, c_t). Name the three things this removes: the context is recomputed per OUTPUT step so capacity no longer decays as 1/T; the gradient path from the loss at step t back to encoder state h_i is O(1) hops through alpha_{t,i} instead of O(T) hops through the recurrence, which is the vanishing-gradient argument being defeated structurally; and alpha_t is a genuine probability distribution over source positions that you can plot. Get the shapes right - W_a is (d_s, d_a), U_a is (2*d_h, d_a) for a bi-encoder, v_a is (d_a,), alpha is (B, T_src) - and mask pad positions by setting e to -inf BEFORE the softmax, never by zeroing alpha afterwards, because zeroing after leaves the distribution unnormalised.

resource.label: Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio, "Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate" (arXiv:1409.0473)

subtopics.name: Luong multiplicative attention and the 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling
subtopics.learn: Contrast the two families: Bahdanau's additive score is a small MLP with a learned v_a, computed from s_{t-1} and fed back into the RNN input, while Luong's multiplicative scores are dot (s^T h), general (s^T W h) and concat, computed from s_t and fed to the output layer - multiplicative reduces to one batched matmul over the whole source, which is why it is the form that survived into every modern architecture. Then derive the scaling factor yourself: if q and k have i.i.d. zero-mean unit-variance components then Var(q . k) = d_k, so logits grow like sqrt(d_k), the softmax saturates towards one-hot and its Jacobian diag(p) - p p^T goes to zero - hence the 1/sqrt(d_k) in scaled dot-product attention, and hence the observation that additive beats unscaled multiplicative at large d_k. Know Luong's local (windowed) attention and input feeding as the two ideas that did not survive, and be able to write torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention's signature as the modern one-liner your hand-rolled version reproduces.

resource.label: Luong, Pham & Manning, "Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation" (arXiv:1508.04025)

subtopics.name: Attention heat maps as a diagnostic instrument
subtopics.learn: Save the (T_tgt, T_src) alpha matrix for held-out examples and render it with matplotlib imshow, source characters on x and generated characters on y - on the date task a healthy model shows a sharp alignment that is monotonic in blocks with jumps, where the row generating '2001' lights up the year characters in the input and the row generating the month digits lights up 'March'. Learn to read the four failure patterns by sight: a uniform grey map means attention is not being used at all (usually a mask bug, or a decoder whose own state already suffices for a short task), a single hot column repeated on every row means collapse onto one source position, a clean diagonal shifted by one means you scored s_t where you should have scored s_{t-1}, and heat on pad columns means the -inf mask never ran. Treat the heat map as a customer-facing artefact rather than a debugging convenience: it is the cheapest interpretability story in deep learning and it is what makes an alignment claim checkable by a domain expert who cannot read your code.

resource.label: Olah & Carter, "Attention and Augmented Recurrent Neural Networks" (Distill, attention visualisations)

subtopics.name: Decoding and evaluation: beam search, length normalisation, exact match and BLEU
subtopics.learn: Implement greedy decoding, then beam search with width k: keep k hypotheses, expand each by the vocabulary, score by the SUM of log probabilities, prune back to k, and finish a hypothesis when it emits <eos>. Because log p is negative, longer sequences always score worse, so divide by |Y|^alpha with alpha around 0.75 or apply the GNMT length penalty, otherwise beam search systematically returns truncated output and a larger beam makes the model look worse - a genuinely counter-intuitive result you will have to explain. Choose the metric honestly per task: date normalisation is judged by free-running exact-match string accuracy plus per-character accuracy and a confusion breakdown by input format, not by BLEU; for translation use sacreBLEU because corpus BLEU is a modified n-gram precision with a brevity penalty that is not comparable across tokenisations, and know that BLEU-4 is exactly 0 for any sentence with no matching 4-gram, so on short outputs and small eval sets it behaves like a step function rather than a measurement.

resource.label: d2l.ai - Beam Search (greedy vs exhaustive vs beam, length normalisation)

subtopics.name: The road to Transformers: what recurrence costs once you have attention
subtopics.learn: State the two costs recurrence pays that attention removes. First, h_t = f(h_{t-1}) is inherently sequential, so training and inference need O(T) sequential operations no matter how many GPUs you have, while self-attention needs O(1) sequential depth. Second, the maximum path length between two positions is O(T) in an RNN versus O(1) with attention, which is the same product-of-Jacobians argument from the vanishing-gradient subtopic, now solved by construction rather than by gating. Reproduce Vaswani et al.'s complexity table from memory: self-attention is O(T^2 * d) work with O(1) sequential depth and O(1) path length; recurrence is O(T * d^2) work with O(T) depth and O(T) path length - so attention wins on work whenever T < d, which covers most sentences and explains both why the Transformer displaced the RNN and why long-document and streaming settings keep pulling people back to linear-time and recurrent-flavoured alternatives. Be able to give the one-line history to a customer: attention was invented as a patch for the seq2seq bottleneck, and the Transformer is what you get when you delete the RNN and keep only the patch.

resource.label: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need" (arXiv:1706.03762) - see Section 4, Why Self-Attention

outcomes: You can derive backpropagation through time on a whiteboard for a vanilla RNN - dL/dh_t recursion, dL/dW_hh as a sum over t, and the explicit product prod_k W_hh^T diag(1 - h_k^2) - and point at the exact factor that vanishes.

You can write the LSTM's six equations and the GRU's four from memory, and show that dc_t/dc_{t-1} = diag(f_t) for the LSTM and that h_t = z_t h_{t-1} + (1 - z_t) h~_t gives an identity Jacobian at z_t = 1, naming these as the specific fixes for the specific factor above.

You can implement LSTMCell and GRUCell from tensor ops only (fused matmul, chunked gates, forget-gate bias 1.0) and have them pass both torch.autograd.gradcheck in float64 and an allclose comparison against torch.nn.LSTMCell with copied weights, as a pytest test in CI.

You can build a Bahdanau-attention encoder-decoder, write e_{t,i} = v_a^T tanh(W_a s_{t-1} + U_a h_i) with correct shapes and a pre-softmax -inf pad mask, and produce an attention heat map whose alignment a non-ML reader can verify against the input.

You can take a seq2seq whose quality collapses past ~20 tokens, demonstrate empirically that the cause is the fixed-length context vector (quality versus source length, with and without attention, on a held-out length band), and quantify the recovery.

You can name and fix the four silent sequence bugs on sight: unmasked loss over pad positions, h_n taken after padding instead of packing, teacher-forced validation, and bidirectional layers in a causal model.

You can implement beam search with length normalisation, explain why a larger beam without the penalty produces shorter and worse output, and choose between exact match, per-character accuracy and sacreBLEU with a stated reason for the task in front of you.

You can advise a customer on GRU versus LSTM versus Transformer for a given sequence length, latency budget and hardware, backed by the O(T*d^2) versus O(T^2*d) work-and-depth argument and a measured throughput number from your own benchmark.
failureModes: The loss is averaged over every position in the padded tensor instead of over mask.sum(); batches that happen to contain long sequences look better, validation loss changes when you change batch size, and the model that wins the sweep is the one whose batches were most padded.

The encoder uses the RNN's h_n without pack_padded_sequence, so the 'sentence summary' handed to the decoder is the state after k pad tokens; the model still trains, but its quality depends on how the DataLoader happened to bucket lengths and never reproduces on the customer's differently sorted data.

Validation is run teacher-forced because the same forward() is reused for train and eval; the notebook reports 98 percent, the demo in front of the customer free-runs and produces repetition loops, and the gap is diagnosed as a deployment bug rather than exposure bias.

bidirectional=True is left on a decoder or a next-token language model; validation perplexity collapses to near 1 because every position sees its own future, the result is presented as a breakthrough, and the model cannot be run causally at inference at all.

Attention alpha is masked by multiplying by zero AFTER the softmax rather than adding -inf before it, so the distribution no longer sums to one, mass silently drains as batch padding grows, and the heat map looks plausible while the context vector is systematically shrunk.

The from-scratch LSTM returns h_t but keeps feeding c_{t-1} through the loop; the gradient check still passes because forward and backward agree with each other, and the model trains to a mediocre plateau that is blamed on the dataset being too small.

Gradient clipping is applied per-parameter-tensor rather than on the global norm; the descent direction is rotated at every spike, training becomes erratic in a way that looks like a bad learning rate, and the LR sweep comes back flat and uninformative.

Beam search is added with beam=10 and no length normalisation; outputs get systematically shorter, exact match drops below the greedy baseline, and the conclusion recorded is that beam search does not help on this task.
interviewQuestions: Derive backpropagation through time for a vanilla RNN with tanh. Show me the term that vanishes, state the condition on W_hh in terms of its singular values, and then tell me exactly which part of the LSTM and which part of the GRU cancels that term.

Write the LSTM equations. Now compute dc_t/dc_{t-1} and explain why that expression, and not the number of parameters, is why LSTMs learn long-range dependencies. Where does the gradient still vanish in an LSTM?

A customer's seq2seq translation model scores well on their test set but collapses on anything over about twenty tokens. Walk me through your diagnosis, and write the equations for the fix. What would you plot to prove the diagnosis before you change any code?

Explain teacher forcing and exposure bias. Design a validation protocol for a sequence-to-sequence model that cannot be gamed by teacher forcing, and tell me what you would report to the customer alongside the headline number.
Why is dot-product attention divided by sqrt(d_k)? Derive it. Then tell me what happens to the softmax Jacobian if you omit it at d_k = 512, and what the observable training symptom would be.

Design: the customer needs to classify streaming sensor sequences on an edge device with 200 ms of budget and no GPU. Argue for or against a GRU versus a small Transformer, using complexity, memory and the streaming constraint, and say what you would measure before committing.

Debug: a from-scratch LSTM passes a float64 gradcheck at 1e-7 but trains to a worse loss than nn.LSTM with identical hyperparameters and copied initial weights. What does the passing gradcheck rule out, what does it not rule out, and what are the first three things you check?
114.proofOfWork: A companion repo, recurrence-forensics, that turns the theory of this topic into two reproducible experiments a customer's ML team can rerun. The first is a long-range memory benchmark on synthetic tasks with a controllable dependency distance - the adding problem and a copy/recall task at T in {10, 30, 100, 300} - training a vanilla RNN, your from-scratch LSTM, your from-scratch GRU, and an LSTM with the forget gate ablated, each over three seeds, and emitting for every run the loss curve, the per-timestep gradient norm ||dL/dh_t|| plotted against t on a log axis, and the largest singular value of W_hh tracked across training; the README reads that plot back as the prediction from the theory (decay constant approximately sigma_1 per step for the vanilla RNN, near-flat for the LSTM) rather than as a picture. The second is a bottleneck ablation on the date-normalisation task: identical encoder-decoder trained with and without Bahdanau attention, evaluated free-running on a held-out length band longer than anything seen in training, reporting exact-match accuracy as a function of source length with confidence intervals, plus paired attention heat maps for the same three examples under both models. Ship it with a microbenchmark table of tokens per second and peak memory for your fused-matmul cell versus four separate matmuls versus nn.LSTM on CPU and GPU, a pytest suite in GitHub Actions running the gradcheck and the nn.LSTMCell equivalence test, and a one-page note written for a non-ML engineer explaining, with the two plots and no equations, why their long-document model gets worse in the middle and what attention changes.

115.topic: Transformers from scratch: attention maths, positional encoding, build a small GPT
115.why: Every LLM feature you deploy for a customer sits on one architecture, and the difference between an FDE who can only call an API and one the customer trusts is whether you can answer 'why did it do that?' at the level of the attention pattern, the context window and the KV cache rather than at the level of the prompt. When a fine-tune diverges, when a long-context feature degrades past the training length, when a customer asks whether their 40k-token document actually fits, the answer is a property of softmax attention, positional encoding and the causal mask - and you will be asked to give it live, on a call, without looking it up. Writing the ~250 lines yourself is the only reliable way to make the maths load-bearing instead of decorative: after this you can read a model card, a config.json or a training log and know exactly which knob it is describing.
prerequisites: Matrix calculus and the chain rule applied to composed linear maps and softmax (Topic 94, Calculus and optimisation), plus matrix shapes, inner products and low-rank factorisation (Topic 93, Linear algebra for ML)
Cross-entropy as negative log-likelihood, entropy and KL, so 'loss = 4.17 nats' is a number you can interpret (Topic 98, Information theory and loss functions)
Backpropagation, initialisation schemes and why activation/gradient variance must be controlled layer to layer (Topic 110, Neural network foundations)
PyTorch fluency: autograd, .backward(), Dataset/DataLoader, device placement, nn.Module and nn.Parameter registration, torch.profiler (Topic 112, PyTorch at depth)
Optimiser behaviour and LR schedules, mixed precision, and reading a bad loss curve (Topic 111, Training deep networks)
Seq2seq with RNN encoder-decoder plus Bahdanau attention, and the specific bottleneck it removed (Topic 114, Sequence models)
Floating-point behaviour: fp32 vs bf16 range and precision, catastrophic cancellation, why softmax needs a max-subtraction (Topic 99, Numerical computing)
A GPU with >= 8 GB (or a Colab/Modal runtime) plus PyTorch 2.x, because the ablation table needs three full training runs

subtopics.name: The residual stream and the shape contract of a decoder block
subtopics.learn: Before any maths, fix the tensor contract: x is (B, T, d_model) at every point in the network, every sublayer is a function d_model -> d_model added back into x, and the model is `x = x + attn(ln1(x)); x = x + mlp(ln2(x))` repeated n_layer times. Understand the residual stream as a fixed-width communication channel that each block reads from and writes to additively, which is why the residual path carries an identity gradient and why depth does not, by itself, cause vanishing gradients. Write down the parameter count by hand for a config (n_layer, n_head, d_model, vocab, block_size): 4*d_model^2 per attention block (Q, K, V, O), 8*d_model^2 per MLP at 4x expansion, plus vocab*d_model for embeddings - then check it against `sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())` and account for every discrepancy.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - Ch.07 Computational Linguistics, 04. Transformers and language models

subtopics.name: Scaled dot-product attention: derive it on paper, then implement it in five lines
subtopics.learn: Derive Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V from the retrieval story: queries q_i in R^{d_k}, keys k_j in R^{d_k}, a similarity score s_ij = q_i . k_j, a softmax over j turning scores into convex weights a_ij summing to 1, and an output o_i = sum_j a_ij v_j that is a convex combination of value vectors. Be able to state every shape - Q is (B, h, T, d_k), K^T is (B, h, d_k, T), the score matrix is (B, h, T, T), the output is (B, h, T, d_v) - and to say that the T x T score matrix is why memory and FLOPs are O(T^2) in sequence length and why doubling the context window quadruples attention cost. Implement it as a standalone function on random tensors and assert row sums of the weight matrix equal 1 and that permuting the key/value order permutes nothing in the output (attention is permutation-equivariant without positional information - this is the fact that motivates the next-but-one subtopic).

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning 11.3 - Attention Scoring Functions (scaled dot product, masked softmax)

subtopics.name: Why 1/sqrt(d_k): the variance argument and softmax saturation
subtopics.learn: Do the derivation: if q and k have independent components with mean 0 and variance 1, then q . k = sum over d_k terms has mean 0 and variance d_k, so its standard deviation grows as sqrt(d_k); dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores unit variance so the logits entering softmax stay O(1) regardless of head dimension. Then say what goes wrong without it: large-magnitude logits push softmax into a near one-hot regime, and since d(softmax)/dz = diag(a) - a a^T, a saturated a makes the Jacobian nearly zero, so gradients through the attention weights vanish and the head stops learning. Verify empirically - sample q, k for d_k in {8, 64, 512}, plot the histogram of logits and the max softmax weight with and without the scale, and measure the attention entropy -sum a log a in both cases. Know the practical corollary: fp16 overflow in the score matrix and 'attention collapsed to the first token' bugs are usually a missing or wrong scale, not a data problem.

resource.label: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762) - Sec. 3.2.1 and footnote on the scaling factor

subtopics.name: Multi-head attention: head splitting, the reshape/transpose, and einsum
subtopics.learn: Understand multi-head as h independent low-rank attention operations in parallel subspaces: one fused Linear(d_model, 3*d_model) produces Q, K, V, each is viewed as (B, T, h, d_head) with d_head = d_model // h, transposed to (B, h, T, d_head), attended per head, transposed back and reshaped to (B, T, d_model), then passed through W_O. Be able to write the reshape both ways - `x.view(B, T, h, d_head).transpose(1, 2)` and the einsum `torch.einsum('bhqd,bhkd->bhqk', q, k)` - and to say why `.view` after `.transpose` needs `.contiguous()` or `.reshape()`. Know that total FLOPs are roughly independent of h (you split d_model rather than adding capacity), that h must divide d_model, and that the classic head-splitting bug - reshaping to (B, T, d_head, h) or forgetting the transpose - trains to a *plausible* loss curve because the model can partially compensate, which is exactly what makes it so hard to spot. Diagnose it by checking that a single-head model and an h-head model with h=1 produce bitwise-identical outputs.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning 11.5 - Multi-Head Attention

subtopics.name: QK and OV circuits: what the four projection matrices actually parameterise
subtopics.learn: Rewrite a head so the weights appear as two composed matrices rather than four: the attention pattern depends only on W_Q W_K^T (the QK circuit, a bilinear form on the residual stream deciding *where* to look), and the contribution written back depends only on W_O W_V (the OV circuit, deciding *what* is copied). Note that both are rank <= d_head, so each head is a low-rank read-write operation on a d_model-wide stream - this is the cleanest justification for d_head = d_model / h and for why heads are interpretable as somewhat independent. Be able to say what this buys you in front of a customer: 'attention weights show where the model looked, not what it concluded', because a high weight paired with a near-zero OV contribution moves nothing. Use the framing to explain induction heads (a previous-token head feeding a match-and-copy head) as the mechanism behind in-context learning and few-shot prompting.

resource.label: Anthropic - A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits (QK/OV circuits, induction heads)

subtopics.name: The causal mask: the -inf trick, leakage, and off-by-one
subtopics.learn: Build the mask as `torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T)).view(1, 1, T, T)` registered with `register_buffer` (not a Parameter, and it must move with `.to(device)`), and apply it as `scores.masked_fill(mask[:, :, :T, :T] == 0, float('-inf'))` *before* softmax so masked positions get exactly zero weight. Know why -inf and not a large negative constant in fp16 (-1e9 overflows to -inf anyway, but -65504 does not mask reliably), and why a fully-masked row (all -inf) yields NaN out of softmax - the failure mode when you combine a causal mask with a padding mask on a fully-padded row. Understand the leakage tests you must be able to run on demand: change token t and assert logits at positions < t are bitwise unchanged; train, then check that val loss is implausibly low (a no-mask model gets near-zero loss because position t can read token t itself); and confirm the mask is `tril` including the diagonal, since excluding it shifts the whole prediction task by one. Know how `is_causal=True` and `attn_mask` interact in F.scaled_dot_product_attention and that passing both is an error you will hit.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention (attn_mask, is_causal, backends)

subtopics.name: Softmax numerics, log-sum-exp, and attention entropy as a diagnostic
subtopics.learn: Write softmax(z)_i = exp(z_i - max z) / sum_j exp(z_j - max z) and prove the max subtraction is exact, not an approximation; then write log-softmax as z_i - logsumexp(z) and explain why frameworks fuse softmax into cross-entropy (F.cross_entropy takes logits) instead of exposing probabilities that can underflow to 0 and produce -inf in the log. Know the softmax Jacobian diag(a) - a a^T and read from it the two degenerate regimes: uniform a (no signal, gradient small and undiscriminating) and one-hot a (saturated, gradient ~0). Instrument your model to log per-layer, per-head attention entropy H = -sum_j a_ij log a_ij over training - entropy collapsing to ~0 in early steps means the scale or init is wrong; entropy pinned at log(T) for every head means the heads are dead and the model is running on the MLP path alone.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning 4.5 - Softmax Regression Revisited (LogSumExp trick, numerical stability)

subtopics.name: Sinusoidal positional encoding: derive the linear-shift property
subtopics.learn: Start from the fact you proved earlier - self-attention is permutation-equivariant, so without position the model sees a bag of tokens - then define PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d)). Prove the key property on paper: for a fixed offset k, [sin(w(pos+k)), cos(w(pos+k))] is a fixed 2x2 rotation matrix applied to [sin(w pos), cos(w pos)], so relative position by offset k is a *linear* function of the encoding, which is what lets a linear QK circuit express 'attend k tokens back'. Implement it, plot the (T, d) heatmap, and compute the dot product PE(pos) . PE(pos+k) as a function of k to see the monotone-ish decay. Contrast with `nn.Embedding(block_size, d_model)` learned positions: strictly better in-distribution, but undefined beyond block_size - which is exactly the customer question 'what happens if I paste in 200k tokens?'.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning 11.6 - Self-Attention and Positional Encoding

subtopics.name: RoPE and ALiBi: how modern models actually encode position
subtopics.learn: Rotary position embedding applies a position-dependent rotation to q and k *inside each head* (pairs of dimensions rotated by angle m*theta_i, theta_i = base^(-2i/d)) rather than adding a vector to the residual stream, with the consequence that the score q_m . k_n depends only on m - n: relative position falls out of the dot product algebraically. Know the levers you will meet in real configs - `rope_theta` (10000 vs 500000), NTK-aware and linear position-interpolation scaling for context extension, and that RoPE is applied to q and k but not v. Know ALiBi as the cheaper alternative: add a per-head linear bias -m * |i - j| to the scores, no embedding at all, with better length extrapolation. Be able to answer, from architecture rather than folklore, why a model 'gets worse past 8k tokens' - the positions were never trained, so RoPE frequencies land outside the fitted range and attention logits go out of distribution.

resource.label: Su et al., RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding (arXiv:2104.09864)

subtopics.name: LayerNorm, RMSNorm, and pre-LN vs post-LN
subtopics.learn: Write LayerNorm out: mu and sigma^2 computed over the *feature* axis per token (not over the batch - this is the whole reason it works with variable sequence lengths and batch size 1 at inference, unlike BatchNorm), then y = gamma * (x - mu)/sqrt(sigma^2 + eps) + beta with learnable gamma, beta of size d_model. Understand RMSNorm as LayerNorm without mean subtraction and without beta (x / rms(x) * gamma), which is what most modern LLMs use. Then the placement question that decides whether your run survives: post-LN (`x = LN(x + attn(x))`, the original paper) puts the normaliser on the residual path, so gradient magnitude at initialisation grows with depth and you *must* have LR warmup; pre-LN (`x = x + attn(LN(x))`) keeps the residual path clean, gives well-behaved gradients at init, and trains stably without warmup - at a small cost in final quality. Your ablation must show post-LN diverging or needing warmup where pre-LN does not, and you should be able to point at the residual-path argument as the reason.

resource.label: Xiong et al., On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture (arXiv:2002.04745)

subtopics.name: The position-wise feed-forward network and the activation choice
subtopics.learn: The MLP is Linear(d_model, 4*d_model) -> nonlinearity -> Linear(4*d_model, d_model), applied independently and identically to every position - it does no mixing across tokens at all, which is why attention and MLP are complementary: attention moves information between positions, the MLP transforms it in place. Know that the MLP holds roughly two thirds of a standard transformer's parameters (8 d^2 vs 4 d^2), so 'make the model bigger' usually means widening this. Understand GELU (x * Phi(x), a smooth gate by the input's own value) versus ReLU, and SwiGLU as a gated variant (Swish(xW) * (xV))W_2 where the 4x factor is reduced to ~8/3 to keep the parameter count constant - the arrangement in Llama-family models. Implement the block, then verify the 'position-wise' claim empirically by feeding a batch, shuffling the time axis, and asserting the MLP output shuffles identically.

resource.label: Shazeer, GLU Variants Improve Transformer (arXiv:2002.05202)

subtopics.name: Tokenisation: BPE, vocabulary, and why perplexity is not comparable across tokenizers
subtopics.learn: Start with the character-level vocabulary Tiny Shakespeare gives you (65 symbols, trivially reversible) so the GPT is simple, then implement BPE properly at least once: initialise on bytes, count adjacent pair frequencies, merge the most frequent pair, append to the merge list, repeat to the target vocab size; encoding replays the merges in learned order. Know the consequences you will explain to a customer: token count is not word count and varies 2-3x across languages and code, a 128k-token vocabulary buys shorter sequences (cheaper O(T^2) attention) at the cost of a bigger embedding matrix and softmax, and cross-entropy per *token* is only comparable between models sharing a tokenizer - convert to bits-per-byte if you must compare across. Be able to name the classic tokenisation artefacts: leading-space tokens changing behaviour, numbers split inconsistently so arithmetic degrades, and glitch tokens that appear in the vocabulary but never in training.

resource.label: Hugging Face NLP Course - Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization (training and encoding algorithm)

subtopics.name: Embeddings, the unembedding, and weight tying
subtopics.learn: Token embedding is `nn.Embedding(vocab, d_model)` - a lookup that is exactly a one-hot matmul, with a dense gradient only on the rows that appeared in the batch; know `padding_idx` and that the embedding table is often the single largest parameter block in a small model. The unembedding is `Linear(d_model, vocab, bias=False)` producing (B, T, vocab) logits. Weight tying (`lm_head.weight = tok_emb.weight`) shares one matrix for both, cutting parameters by vocab*d_model and usually improving small-model loss; be able to state the reason it is defensible (the same token-identity subspace is used to read in and to read out) and the one thing to check (initialisation scale, since the tied matrix now serves two roles). Initialise embeddings with std 0.02 and scale the residual-projection weights by 1/sqrt(2*n_layer) so the variance of the residual stream does not grow linearly with depth; know that logits at step 0 should be near zero, giving loss ~ ln(vocab).

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.nn.Embedding

subtopics.name: The objective: next-token cross-entropy, the shift, and perplexity
subtopics.learn: The loss is `F.cross_entropy(logits.view(B*T, V), targets.view(B*T))` where targets are the inputs shifted left by one - `x = data[i:i+T]`, `y = data[i+1:i+T+1]` - so every one of the T positions contributes a prediction and the causal mask is what makes that legitimate in a single forward pass. Derive that this is maximum likelihood under an autoregressive factorisation p(x_1..x_T) = prod p(x_t | x_<t), that the loss is in nats per token, and that perplexity = exp(loss). Know the reference numbers cold: a uniform model over vocab V has loss ln(V) (about 4.17 for the 65-character Shakespeare vocabulary), so a loss at step 0 far from ln(V) means broken initialisation, and a loss below the unigram entropy after ten steps means leakage. Use `ignore_index` for padding, and know that averaging over a padded batch without it silently optimises the model to predict pad tokens.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy (logits input, ignore_index, reduction)

subtopics.name: Optimisation: AdamW, warmup + cosine decay, gradient clipping, no-decay groups
subtopics.learn: Write the Adam update from memory - m_t = b1 m_{t-1} + (1-b1) g, v_t = b2 v_{t-1} + (1-b2) g^2, bias-corrected m_hat = m_t/(1-b1^t) and v_hat = v_t/(1-b2^t), step = -lr * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps) - and explain the bias correction as fixing the zero-initialisation of the moments. Understand AdamW's actual contribution: L2 penalty added to the gradient gets divided by sqrt(v_hat) and so is *not* uniform weight decay in Adam, whereas decoupled decay applies -lr * wd * theta directly, which is why you pass `weight_decay` to AdamW and put LayerNorm gains, biases and embeddings in a `weight_decay=0.0` param group. Implement linear warmup over the first few hundred steps then cosine decay to ~10% of peak, clip global grad norm to 1.0 with `clip_grad_norm_` (which returns the pre-clip norm - log it, a spike to 100x is the signature of a bad batch), and set betas (0.9, 0.95) with eps 1e-8 as the LLM default rather than the torch default 0.999.

resource.label: Loshchilov & Hutter, Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (arXiv:1711.05101)

subtopics.name: Debugging a training run: the diagnostics ladder in order
subtopics.learn: Run the ladder before touching hyperparameters: (1) fix all seeds and check loss at init equals ln(vocab) to two decimals; (2) overfit a single batch of 8 sequences to loss ~0 - if it cannot, the bug is in the model or the loss, never in the data or the LR; (3) `torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True)` on a short run to localise the first NaN; (4) assert every parameter has a non-None grad after backward (a missing one means a tensor was created outside the graph or a module was never registered); (5) log global grad norm, per-block activation RMS, attention entropy and the LR each step; (6) only then tune. Learn the signature of each classic bug: loss stuck exactly at ln(V) = dead forward path; loss drops to near zero immediately = mask leakage or targets not shifted; loss is fine but generation is garbage = positional encoding not added, or a train/inference mask mismatch; loss spikes then NaN = LR too high, no warmup with post-LN, or fp16 overflow in the score matrix; train loss falls while val loss rises from step 1 = the val split overlaps the train split.

resource.label: Karpathy - A Recipe for Training Neural Networks

subtopics.name: Designing the ablation table: no-PE, no-causal-mask, post-LN
subtopics.learn: Turn each architectural claim into a controlled experiment rather than a paragraph of prose: hold seed, data, steps, batch size, LR schedule and parameter count fixed, change exactly one flag, and report final val loss plus a 50-token sample. Predict each result *before* running it and record the prediction - no-PE should reach a noticeably worse but non-trivial val loss (character bigram statistics still carry signal) and produce locally-plausible, globally-incoherent text; no-causal-mask should reach an absurdly low val loss and yet generate nonsense autoregressively, because at inference the future it trained on does not exist; post-LN at your LR should either need warmup or diverge. Report mean and spread over three seeds so a 0.01 difference is not presented as a finding, and state the compute cost per run. Read nanoGPT to see the reference implementation of the same block you wrote and to diff your design choices against it deliberately.

resource.label: karpathy/nanoGPT - reference decoder-only GPT (model.py, train.py, config)

subtopics.name: Attention-head heatmaps: producing them and reading them honestly
subtopics.learn: Return the post-softmax (B, h, T, T) weights from your attention module behind a flag (never in the hot path), pick a fixed probe string, and render a lower-triangular heatmap per head per layer with token labels on both axes. Learn to recognise the recurring patterns - a diagonal-adjacent band (previous-token head), a vertical stripe on position 0 (an attention sink, where a head parks probability mass when it has nothing to contribute, and a normal thing to see), a broad uniform triangle (a near-dead head), and the offset-diagonal match-and-copy pattern of an induction head. Learn the honest caveat and be able to say it to a customer: attention weights are not feature attribution, because the OV circuit determines how much any attended token actually changes the output, so a bright cell is evidence of routing, not of reasoning. Save the figures into the README as the deliverable requires, with the probe string and layer/head indices captioned.

resource.label: Brendan Bycroft - LLM Visualization (interactive walkthrough of GPT tensor flow)

subtopics.name: Decoding: greedy, temperature, top-k and nucleus sampling
subtopics.learn: Implement generate() as a loop: crop the context to the last block_size tokens (a hard constraint of learned positional embeddings), forward, take logits at the final position only, divide by temperature, optionally mask to the top-k or to the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds p, softmax, `torch.multinomial`, append, repeat - all under `@torch.no_grad()` and `model.eval()`. Know what each knob does to the distribution: temperature T scales logits so T -> 0 approaches argmax and T > 1 flattens; top-k truncates by rank; nucleus (top-p) truncates by probability mass, which adapts to how peaked the distribution is at that step. Understand the finding that maximum-likelihood decoding produces degenerate repetition loops even in strong models, so 'the model repeats itself' is often a decoding bug and not a training failure - a distinction you will need when a customer reports it. Note that a good val loss with garbled samples points at generation-time bugs: context cropping, forgetting positional offsets, or sampling from all T positions instead of the last.

resource.label: Holtzman et al., The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration (arXiv:1904.09751)

subtopics.name: Making it fast: SDPA/FlashAttention, the KV cache, bf16 autocast, torch.compile
subtopics.learn: Once your hand-written attention is correct, swap in `F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)` and assert `torch.allclose(mine, theirs, atol=1e-4)` before benchmarking - this is the single most valuable test in the repo. Understand why it is faster: FlashAttention tiles the computation and never materialises the T x T score matrix in HBM, turning attention from memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound and cutting activation memory from O(T^2) to O(T). Understand the KV cache for inference: without it, generating n tokens costs O(n^2) forwards because you recompute every prefix; with it, you keep past K and V per layer and each new token is a single query against a growing cache, which is why cache size (2 * n_layer * n_head * d_head * T * bytes) is the real memory constraint on long-context serving and the thing MQA/GQA were invented to shrink. Wrap the forward in `torch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16)` (bf16 needs no GradScaler; fp16 does), set `torch.set_float32_matmul_precision('high')`, apply `torch.compile(model)`, and report tokens/sec and peak memory before and after each change.

resource.label: PyTorch tutorial - Implementing High-Performance Transformers with Scaled Dot Product Attention

outcomes: You can derive scaled dot-product attention on a whiteboard from the query/key/value story, state every tensor shape, and prove the 1/sqrt(d_k) factor from the variance of a d_k-term dot product plus the softmax Jacobian diag(a) - a a^T.

You can write a working multi-head causal self-attention module from memory in under 30 minutes without nn.MultiheadAttention, and show it agrees with F.scaled_dot_product_attention(is_causal=True) to within 1e-4.

You can prove your causal mask is airtight by perturbing token t and asserting that logits at every position before t are bitwise unchanged, and you can explain why a suspiciously low val loss is the expected symptom of failing that test.

You can derive the linear-shift property of sinusoidal positional encoding, implement sinusoidal and learned variants behind one flag, and state precisely what happens - and why - when a model built on learned positions is fed a sequence longer than block_size.

You can train a ~10M-parameter GPT on Tiny Shakespeare to a documented val loss with a reproducible seed, and report the loss at initialisation matching ln(vocab) as evidence the model was correctly initialised.

You can produce an ablation table over no-positional-encoding, no-causal-mask and post-LN variants with three seeds each, and explain each result from the maths rather than from the number - including why the no-mask run has the *best* val loss and the worst samples.

You can look at a broken training run (diverged loss, flat loss, NaN, or good loss with garbled samples) and name the most likely cause among positional encoding, mask leakage, LayerNorm placement and head-dim splitting, then confirm it with a targeted assertion rather than a hyperparameter sweep.

You can explain to a non-ML customer engineer, in five minutes and without notation, why context length is quadratic, what the KV cache costs in gigabytes for their config, and why quality degrades beyond the trained context window.
failureModes: The causal mask is built once for block_size but sliced wrong (or omitted at inference), so training sees the future; val loss drops to 0.2, the ablation table looks spectacular, and the model generates incoherent text - the metric flatters a model that has learned nothing about prediction.

Head splitting reshapes to (B, T, d_head, n_head) instead of (B, T, n_head, d_head), so each 'head' reads an interleaved stride of the feature vector; the model still trains and the loss curve looks normal, just a few percent worse, and the bug survives to production because nothing ever crashes.

The train/val split is made by random sampling of overlapping context windows rather than by cutting the corpus at a byte offset, so validation contexts overlap training contexts and val loss tracks train loss perfectly - the reported number is memorisation, and the customer's held-out data behaves nothing like it.

Positional encodings are computed but never added to the token embeddings (or added after the first LayerNorm and then normalised away); the model becomes a bag-of-tokens predictor, reaches a plausible-looking loss on character data where unigram statistics carry a lot of signal, and only the ablation reveals that the no-PE variant scores the same.

Post-LN is used with no warmup at an LR copied from a pre-LN config; the run diverges at step ~400, and three days are spent on the data pipeline before anyone checks the LayerNorm placement - the residual-path gradient growth with depth is the actual cause.

The mask is stored as a plain tensor attribute rather than a registered buffer, so `.to('cuda')` leaves it on CPU; the code path that hits it raises a device error only for long sequences, or worse, a broadcast silently produces a mask of the wrong shape that masks nothing.

Sampling is done from the logits at all T positions, or the context is never cropped to block_size, so generation is fine for the first block_size tokens and then either crashes on the positional embedding lookup or wraps around and produces nonsense - the training run is blamed for a decoding bug.

Val loss is compared against a published number from a model with a different tokenizer; per-token cross-entropy is not comparable across vocabularies, so the write-up claims a result it has not earned - the fix is bits-per-byte, and nobody notices until a reviewer asks.
interviewQuestions: Derive scaled dot-product attention at the whiteboard and justify the 1/sqrt(d_k) factor. What exactly happens to the forward pass and to the gradients if you drop it, and at what value of d_k does it start to matter?

Walk me through every tensor shape in a decoder block for B=4, T=1024, d_model=768, n_head=12. Where is the O(T^2) term, what is the peak activation memory, and how does FlashAttention change that number without changing the maths?
I have a decoder-only model whose validation loss is 0.08 and whose generated text is gibberish. Give me your ordered hypothesis list and the specific assertion you would write to test each one.

Explain pre-LN versus post-LN in terms of the gradient on the residual path. Why does post-LN need learning-rate warmup, and what would you expect to see in the loss curve and grad-norm log if someone removed warmup from a post-LN model?

A customer says the model 'gets dumber' past 8k tokens even though the API accepts 32k. Explain what is actually happening in terms of positional encoding, and describe two mitigations and the trade-off each one makes.

Design a controlled experiment that proves positional encoding matters, on a 10M-parameter character-level model with a 4-hour compute budget. What do you hold fixed, how many seeds, what do you measure, and what result would falsify the claim?

Explain the KV cache: what is stored, how big is it for a 32-layer, 32-head, d_head=128 model at 8k context in bf16, why generation without it is quadratic, and what MQA or GQA changes about that arithmetic.
115.proofOfWork: A companion repo `attention-forensics` that turns the derivations into executable evidence rather than prose. It ships a pytest suite over your hand-written attention that a reviewer can run in under two minutes: an equivalence test against F.scaled_dot_product_attention(is_causal=True) to 1e-4; a causality test that perturbs token t and asserts bitwise-identical logits at all positions < t; a permutation-equivariance test proving the model without positional encoding is invariant to shuffling the input and that the same test fails once PE is added; a head-splitting test asserting an n_head=1 model is bitwise identical to a single-head implementation; a gradient-flow test asserting every registered parameter receives a non-None, finite gradient after one backward; and a numerical test that a fully-masked softmax row raises rather than silently returning NaN. Alongside it, a `broken/` directory containing six deliberately sabotaged variants of your GPT - missing 1/sqrt(d_k), transposed head reshape, mask excluding the diagonal, PE computed but not added, post-LN with the pre-LN learning rate, and generation without context cropping - each with its loss curve, its sample output and a one-paragraph forensic note naming the observable symptom, the assertion that catches it, and the fix. Finish with a two-page BUILD-VS-BUY memo written for a customer's engineering lead: what a decoder-only transformer costs to train per token at their scale, what the KV cache costs in GB at their target context length, and the three architectural questions (positional scheme, context window, tokenizer) they must answer before anyone writes code.

116.topic: Fine-tuning at depth: full fine-tune vs LoRA, QLoRA and PEFT, DPO, and evaluating the result
116.why: A customer with 8,000 labelled tickets and one 24 GB GPU asks 'can you make the model do this?', and the professional answer is arithmetic, not enthusiasm: 16 bytes per parameter for a mixed-precision full fine-tune versus a 20 MB adapter, a defensible r, lora_alpha and target_modules, and a number for the expected quality gap. Almost every fine-tuning result that gets quietly walked back in month two was never a result at all - the eval set was a paraphrase of the training set, the judge preferred the longer answer, the loss was computed over the prompt tokens, or DPO taught the model a bullet-point format rather than a preference. An FDE who can write the LoRA forward pass on a whiteboard, derive the DPO loss from Bradley-Terry well enough to say what beta buys, and then present a length-controlled win rate with a confidence interval is the person the customer's ML lead stops second-guessing.
prerequisites: Transformer internals from Topic 115: what q_proj/k_proj/v_proj/o_proj and the MLP gate/up/down matrices are and their shapes, because target_modules is a list of exactly those names and the parameter count you quote is computed from those dimensions
PyTorch at depth (Topic 112): nn.Module, named_modules/named_parameters, requires_grad_, state_dicts, autograd graph lifetime, and torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated for measuring peak VRAM

Optimisers and training dynamics from Topic 111: AdamW's two fp32 moment buffers per parameter, warmup plus cosine schedules, gradient clipping, bf16 versus fp16 + GradScaler, and what a broken loss curve looks like

Cross-entropy, KL divergence and maximum likelihood from Topic 98 - the SFT loss is a token-level MLE and the DPO loss is a logistic loss over a KL-regularised reward difference, so neither is memorisable without this

Evaluation discipline from Topic 103 (leakage, grouped splits, metric choice) and interval estimation from Topic 96 (binomial proportions, paired tests) - half of this topic is those two applied to free-form generation
One GPU with at least 16 GB (Colab T4/L4 or a rented A10) plus a Hugging Face account and token; the QLoRA and DPO subtopics cannot be done CPU-only

subtopics.name: The decision: prompt, RAG, LoRA, QLoRA or full fine-tune
subtopics.learn: Fix the decision rule before touching code. Fine-tuning reliably buys format, style, tone, tool-call syntax, latency and prompt-token cost; it does not reliably buy new facts, which is RAG's job, and it cannot fix a task the base model cannot do at all in a 20-shot prompt. Then price the three options for the model in front of you: mixed-precision full fine-tune costs roughly 16 bytes per parameter of static state (2 bf16 weights + 2 bf16 grads + 4+4 AdamW moments + 4 fp32 master copy) before a single activation, LoRA drops grads and optimiser state to the adapter only (megabytes) but still pays full activation memory, and QLoRA additionally shrinks the frozen base to about 4.13 bits per parameter. Carry the empirical prior from 'LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less' (arXiv 2405.09673): on instruction/format adaptation LoRA is close to full fine-tuning, on large domain shift (a new programming language, continued pretraining) it lags, and it forgets the base capabilities noticeably less.

resource.label: Hugging Face blog - Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning using PEFT

subtopics.name: What SFT actually optimises: token cross-entropy under a chat template
subtopics.learn: Write the objective explicitly: L = -(1/|Y|) * sum_t log p_theta(y_t | y_<t, x), teacher-forced, computed only over completion tokens. That last clause is a code detail with a large blast radius: labels must be -100 on every prompt/system token (completion-only loss) or the model spends capacity memorising your system prompt and the train loss looks better while the deployed model starts echoing instructions. Apply tokenizer.apply_chat_template with the base model's own template, verify by decoding a batch that special tokens are not doubled (add_special_tokens plus a template that already emits BOS is the classic duplicate), that add_generation_prompt is used at inference and not in training targets, and that EOS is inside the label span or the model will never stop generating. Know what sequence packing does (concatenate samples to fill max_length for throughput) and that it needs either an attention mask that blocks cross-sample attention or the acceptance that samples bleed into each other.

resource.label: Transformers docs - Chat templates

subtopics.name: Dataset construction and a held-out split that cannot leak
subtopics.learn: Order the operations correctly: normalise, then near-duplicate detect (MinHash/LSH or embedding cosine above ~0.95), then split - deduplicating after splitting is how paraphrases end up on both sides. Split by group, not by row: GroupShuffleSplit or GroupKFold keyed on ticket id, document id or customer, because ten paraphrases of one ticket straddling the split inflate every metric; use a time-ordered split when the data has a timestamp and production will always be predicting the future. Keep three disjoint sets - SFT train, a preference set whose prompts the SFT model has not memorised (DPO pairs drawn from prompts already in SFT train carry almost no signal), and a frozen golden set of 100-300 prompts touched by neither training nor hyperparameter selection. Prefer quality over volume: a curated 1k-example set in the LIMA style routinely beats 50k of scraped noise, and you can read 1k examples yourself.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Cross-validation (incl. grouped and time-series splitters)

subtopics.name: The full fine-tune baseline: TrainingArguments and the knobs that matter
subtopics.learn: Run the full fine-tune first on the small model so you have a ceiling to compare adapters against. Set learning_rate 1e-5 to 2e-5 for full fine-tuning versus 1e-4 to 3e-4 for LoRA - roughly a 10x difference, because the adapter starts at zero and its update is rescaled by alpha/r - with lr_scheduler_type='cosine', warmup_ratio 0.03, max_grad_norm 1.0, weight_decay applied to matrices but not to biases and norms, and bf16=True. Compute the effective batch as per_device_train_batch_size * gradient_accumulation_steps * world_size and quote that number, not the microbatch, when you compare runs. Use num_train_epochs 1-3 (small instruction sets overfit by epoch 2), eval_strategy='steps' with load_best_model_at_end and metric_for_best_model, save_total_limit to survive a small disk, and pin seed and data_seed so a rerun reproduces.

resource.label: Transformers docs - Trainer and TrainingArguments

subtopics.name: The memory ledger: predicting peak VRAM before you launch
subtopics.learn: Be able to produce the ZeRO-style accounting on demand, per parameter: 2 bytes bf16 weight + 2 bytes bf16 gradient + 12 bytes of fp32 optimiser state (4 exp_avg + 4 exp_avg_sq + 4 master weight) = 16 bytes/param for mixed-precision AdamW full fine-tuning; a 0.6B model is therefore about 9.6 GB static before any activation, and a 7B model is about 112 GB, which is the whole reason PEFT exists. For LoRA the frozen base contributes only its 2 bytes/param, and grads plus optimiser state apply to the adapters alone - r*(d_in+d_out) per adapted matrix, typically 0.1-1% of the model. Activations are the term people forget: they scale with batch * seq_len * hidden * layers and are paid in full by LoRA and QLoRA too, since the backward still flows through every frozen layer to reach the adapters. Predict peak VRAM in writing, then verify with torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() and explain any gap - if optimiser state dominates, halving the batch size will not save you.

resource.label: arXiv 1910.02054 - ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (the 2+2+12 bytes/param accounting)

subtopics.name: Activation checkpointing, mixed precision and gradient accumulation
subtopics.learn: Gradient checkpointing stores only block boundaries and recomputes the interior during backward, trading roughly 30% extra compute for a large activation saving; enable it with gradient_checkpointing=True plus gradient_checkpointing_kwargs={'use_reentrant': False}. Learn the trap that follows: when the base model is frozen (LoRA) or quantized, no input to a checkpointed block requires grad, the recomputed graph is empty, and the adapters receive no gradient at all - the fix is model.enable_input_require_grads() (which prepare_model_for_kbit_training does for you), and the symptom is a perfectly flat loss that looks like a data problem. Prefer bf16 (fp32 exponent range, no GradScaler) over fp16 + GradScaler on Ampere and later. With accumulation, know that averaging per-microbatch mean losses over microbatches with unequal token counts silently upweights short samples; normalise by total tokens in the accumulation window when the sequence lengths vary.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.utils.checkpoint (activation checkpointing, use_reentrant)

subtopics.name: LoRA: the maths you must be able to write from memory
subtopics.learn: The claim is that the weight update during adaptation has low intrinsic rank, so parametrise it as delta_W = (alpha/r) * B @ A with A in R^(r x d_in) initialised from a small Gaussian (Kaiming-uniform in the reference implementation) and B in R^(d_out x r) initialised to zero, giving h = W0 @ x + (alpha/r) * B @ (A @ x). Be able to state each consequence: delta_W = 0 at initialisation so the model starts exactly as the base and the first steps cannot damage it; rank(delta_W) <= r; trainable parameters per adapted matrix are r*(d_in + d_out) instead of d_in*d_out; the scalar alpha/r decouples the useful learning rate from r (rsLoRA argues alpha/sqrt(r) is the stable scaling as r grows); and because the update is additive and linear, W0 + (alpha/r)BA can be folded back into the base weight so inference latency is unchanged, which is not true of serial bottleneck adapters. Derive the gradients: with g = dL/dh, dL/dB = (alpha/r) * g @ (A x)^T and dL/dA = (alpha/r) * B^T @ g @ x^T, and note W0 receives no gradient at all.

resource.label: arXiv 2106.09685 - LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

subtopics.name: Implementing LoRA from scratch as a plain nn.Module wrapper
