subtopics.learn: Write class LoRALinear(nn.Module) holding the frozen base nn.Linear plus lora_A = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(r, in_features)), lora_B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(out_features, r)) and scaling = alpha/r, with forward returning base(x) + dropout(x) @ lora_A.T @ lora_B.T * scaling. Inject it by walking named_modules(), splitting the dotted name to fetch the parent with a getattr chain, and setattr-ing the wrapper in place; then freeze everything with p.requires_grad_('lora_' in name) and assert the trainable count with sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad) against your hand-computed r*(d_in+d_out)*n_matrices. Implement merge() that does base.weight.data += scaling * (lora_B @ lora_A) and prove correctness by asserting the max absolute logit difference between merged and unmerged models is below 1e-4 on a fixed batch. Keep dtype discipline: adapters in fp32/bf16 even when the base is 4-bit, and cast x to the adapter dtype inside forward. Compare your wrapper against torch.nn.utils.parametrize, which expresses the same reparametrisation idiomatically.

resource.label: PyTorch tutorial - Parametrizations (reparametrising module weights)

subtopics.name: Choosing r, lora_alpha, target_modules, dropout and the learning rate
subtopics.learn: target_modules must name real submodules - ['q_proj','k_proj','v_proj','o_proj'] is the cheap attention-only default, and adding ['gate_proj','up_proj','down_proj'] is usually what closes most of the remaining gap to full fine-tuning; 'all-linear' is the shortcut, and a typo (Llama/Qwen names on a model that calls it 'query_key_value', or vice versa) either raises or matches nothing useful. Pick r in 8-64 with lora_alpha commonly 2r (scaling 2), lora_dropout 0.0-0.1, learning rate 1e-4 to 3e-4, and know the refinements by name and mechanism: use_rslora=True switches the scaling to alpha/sqrt(r), rank_pattern/alpha_pattern give per-layer ranks, LoRA+ (arXiv 2402.12354) uses a larger LR for B than A, DoRA splits the update into magnitude and direction. Add modules_to_save=['embed_tokens','lm_head'] whenever you add tokens, or the new embeddings stay random. Always call print_trainable_parameters() and read the percentage out loud before starting a long run.

resource.label: PEFT docs - LoRA developer guide (initialisation, rank_pattern, rslora, DoRA, merging)

subtopics.name: PEFT mechanics and shipping the adapter
subtopics.learn: LoraConfig(task_type='CAUSAL_LM', r=..., lora_alpha=..., target_modules=[...]) plus get_peft_model wraps the model; save_pretrained writes adapter_model.safetensors and adapter_config.json, typically a few megabytes, and PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, path) reconstitutes it - so pin the base model repo AND revision hash in the config, because an adapter silently loaded onto a different base revision produces degraded output with no error. For serving choose deliberately: merge_and_unload() returns a plain transformers model that vLLM or TGI can load with zero adapter overhead, versus keeping adapters live so one base can serve many tenants with set_adapter per request. Combine adapters with add_weighted_adapter using TIES or DARE when you have several task adapters. The sharp edge: merging into a 4-bit base is lossy (dequantize, add, requantize), so merge into the fp16/bf16 base, and re-run evaluation after any merge rather than assuming it is a no-op.

resource.label: PEFT docs - Model merging (TIES, DARE, add_weighted_adapter)

subtopics.name: Quantization maths: blockwise absmax, NF4 and double quantization
subtopics.learn: Start from blockwise absmax quantization: split the weight vector into blocks of 64, store c = max|x| per block as the scale, and encode q_i = round(x_i / c * k) so dequantization is x_hat = q_i * c / k - the error is controlled by block size, and one outlier in a block wrecks the resolution of the other 63 values, which is exactly the outlier problem LLM.int8() addressed. NF4 replaces the uniform grid with the 16 quantiles of a standard normal, which is information-theoretically optimal when the weights are approximately zero-mean Gaussian, so each of the 16 codes carries equal probability mass. Double quantization then quantizes the per-block fp32 scales themselves (blocks of 256, 8-bit), cutting the constant overhead from about 0.5 to about 0.127 bits per parameter, giving roughly 4.13 bits/param overall - compute that number for your model and compare it to the measured checkpoint size. Paged optimizers use unified memory so optimiser state can page to host RAM during transient spikes instead of OOM-ing the run.

resource.label: arXiv 2305.14314 - QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs (NF4, double quantization, paged optimizers)

subtopics.name: QLoRA end to end in code
subtopics.learn: BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type='nf4', bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16) at from_pretrained time, then prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model) - which upcasts layer norms and the lm_head to fp32, enables gradient checkpointing and turns on input grads - then get_peft_model with your LoraConfig. Understand the runtime consequence: weights are stored in NF4 but dequantized to compute_dtype block by block for every matmul, so QLoRA is typically 1.3-2x slower per step than bf16 LoRA even though it uses far less VRAM; that trade is the whole point and you should quote both numbers to a customer. Use optim='paged_adamw_8bit' when optimiser spikes are the failure. Expect a small quality cost relative to a 16-bit base with the same adapter, and never merge the adapter into the 4-bit base for serving.

resource.label: PEFT docs - Quantization (bitsandbytes 4-bit, prepare_model_for_kbit_training)

subtopics.name: Reading the run: loss curves, grad norm, and what a broken fine-tune looks like
subtopics.learn: Before any long run, do the wiring test: overfit 8 examples until train loss is near zero - if it cannot, the bug is in masking, dtype or the frozen-parameter setup, not in the data. Then read the real run against known shapes: a smooth decay to a plateau is healthy; train loss collapsing while eval loss turns up after epoch 1 is memorisation, so stop at 1-2 epochs; a step-function drop exactly at each epoch boundary means the model is memorising examples rather than learning the task; a completely flat loss from step 0 means no gradient is reaching the trainable parameters; loss that goes to NaN means LR too high or fp16 overflow. Watch grad_norm as a first-class metric - if clipping is active on nearly every step, the LR is too high. Sweep the learning rate over a decade before spending money on epochs, and log a decoded sample of input_ids and label_ids side by side so you can see the mask boundary with your own eyes.

resource.label: Google Research - Deep Learning Tuning Playbook

subtopics.name: Preference data and the Bradley-Terry model
subtopics.learn: Bradley-Terry states P(y_w preferred over y_l | x) = sigma(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)), so fitting a reward model by maximum likelihood on preference pairs is logistic regression on the reward difference - and the reward is identified only up to an additive constant per prompt, which is precisely the freedom DPO later exploits. Draw the practical consequences: absolute reward values are meaningless and only differences matter; annotator agreement of 65-75% puts a ceiling on achievable pairwise accuracy, so a reward model at 72% may already be at the noise ceiling rather than undertrained; ties must be either dropped or modelled, not coerced into a winner. How pairs are generated decides whether any of this works - pairs sampled on-policy from your own SFT model teach it where its own distribution is wrong, while pairs harvested from a much stronger model are off-policy and mostly teach style.

resource.label: Bradley-Terry model (definition and maximum-likelihood estimation)

subtopics.name: Deriving DPO, and what beta actually does
subtopics.learn: Do this derivation until you can reproduce it in ten minutes on a whiteboard. Start from the KL-regularised objective max_pi E_{y~pi}[r(x,y)] - beta*KL(pi || pi_ref); the closed-form optimum is pi*(y|x) = (1/Z(x)) * pi_ref(y|x) * exp(r(x,y)/beta); invert it to r(x,y) = beta*log(pi*(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)) + beta*log Z(x); substitute into Bradley-Terry and observe that the intractable log Z(x) cancels because it depends only on x, leaving L_DPO = -E log sigma(beta*[log(pi(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x)) - log(pi(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x))]). Read the gradient: the per-pair weight is sigma(-beta*margin), so pairs the implicit reward model currently ranks wrongly dominate the update. Then say what beta controls: beta -> 0 removes the reference anchor and the policy drifts into degenerate text, large beta pins the policy to pi_ref and nothing changes; 0.05-0.5 is the working range, 0.1 the usual default. Note that these log-probabilities are sums over completion tokens - that single fact is where length bias enters.

resource.label: arXiv 2305.18290 - Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model

subtopics.name: DPO with TRL and the reward diagnostics
subtopics.learn: Feed DPOTrainer a dataset of {prompt, chosen, rejected} and a DPOConfig with beta, loss_type, max_prompt_length and max_length (silent truncation of long chosen answers is a real and common bug). Always DPO from your SFT checkpoint and use that same SFT model as the reference; with a PEFT policy you can omit ref_model entirely and TRL computes reference log-probs by disabling the adapter, which halves memory. Use a much lower LR than SFT - 5e-7 to 5e-6 - and 1-2 epochs. Then read the logged metrics correctly: rewards/chosen and rewards/rejected are beta * log-ratios and both normally drift negative, so their absolute values mean nothing; rewards/margins is the quantity that must rise; rewards/accuracies starts near 0.5 and is the fraction of pairs with positive margin. Treat accuracies near 1.0 with a still-modest margin, or logps/chosen falling steeply, as a warning that the model is lowering the likelihood of good answers faster than bad ones. Reach for label_smoothing (cDPO) when annotations are noisy.

resource.label: TRL docs - DPOTrainer (config, reference model, logged reward metrics)

subtopics.name: The alternatives, and when online RLHF still wins
subtopics.learn: Place DPO on the map. Classic RLHF (InstructGPT) trains a reward model, then optimises the policy with PPO under a per-token KL penalty against the SFT model; it is on-policy, so the reward model keeps scoring fresh samples, which is why it can still beat DPO when your preference pairs are stale or off-policy - at the cost of holding policy, reference, reward and value models in memory and tuning a notoriously touchy loop. Know the offline variants by the data they need: KTO (arXiv 2402.01306) takes unpaired binary desirable/undesirable labels, which is exactly the thumbs-up/thumbs-down telemetry a customer already has; ORPO (arXiv 2403.07691) folds an odds-ratio penalty into SFT so there is one stage and no reference model; SimPO (arXiv 2405.14734) uses a length-normalised, reference-free reward; IPO addresses DPO's overfitting when preferences are near-deterministic. State the routing rule to a customer in one line: pairs -> DPO, thumbs -> KTO, one cheap stage -> ORPO, programmatically verifiable rewards (tests pass, JSON parses) -> reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, not preference learning at all.

resource.label: arXiv 2203.02155 - Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT: RM + PPO + KL penalty)

subtopics.name: Length and format artifacts: how a fine-tune fakes a win
subtopics.learn: The DPO implicit reward is a sum of token log-probabilities, so lengthening completions is a cheap way to move the margin, and both human raters and LLM judges have a strong measured preference for longer, more heavily formatted answers - which means 'longer' and 'better' are entangled by default. Defend with three measurements you report every time: mean and median completion token count for base versus tuned, the win rate restricted to length-matched pairs, and a length-controlled win rate in the AlpacaEval 2.0 sense, where the preference is regressed on the length difference and the effect is reported at zero delta. Separately check for format capture - if the tuned model answers every question with a numbered list because the preferred responses did, you have learned a template, not a capability - and re-check degenerate repetition and EOS behaviour after DPO, since a model that stops emitting EOS will score well on verbosity-biased judges and terribly in production.

resource.label: arXiv 2404.04475 - Length-Controlled AlpacaEval: A Simple Way to Debias Automatic Evaluators

subtopics.name: Held-out task metrics without contamination
subtopics.learn: Score the base model and every tuned checkpoint through one harness, with identical prompts, few-shot count, decoding settings (greedy or temperature 0), max_new_tokens and seed - a comparison where the tuned model was sampled at temperature 0.8 and the base at 0 is not a comparison. Pin and record the harness version, because task definitions and prompt formats change scores between releases. Write a task definition over your own frozen golden set rather than leaning on MMLU as a proxy for a customer task, and run an explicit contamination audit: exact plus near-duplicate matching of every eval prompt against the training mixture, with the overlap percentage published in the README next to the score. Report at least one out-of-domain task alongside the target task so capability loss is visible - full fine-tuning degrades unrelated abilities more than LoRA does (arXiv 2405.09673), and a customer will find that regression before you do if you do not measure it.

resource.label: EleutherAI - lm-evaluation-harness (task definitions, reproducible LLM scoring)

subtopics.name: Pairwise win-rate, judges, and whether the delta is real
subtopics.learn: Generate one completion per frozen-set prompt from base and tuned, present each pair to a judge in randomised order, and record win/tie/loss. Control the documented judge pathologies: position bias (run both orders and count only the verdicts that agree with themselves), verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias when the judge and the candidate share a family; calibrate the judge against 50 human-labelled pairs and report its agreement rate before quoting anything it produces. Then treat the win rate as what it is - a binomial proportion: 60 wins out of 100 has a 95% interval of roughly 50-70%, so it is not evidence, and you should compute the interval with scipy.stats.binomtest or a bootstrap and pre-compute the sample size needed for the effect you intend to claim. For paired judgments use the discordant pairs (McNemar) rather than comparing two independent rates. Present win rate, tie rate, interval, mean length delta and the 20 worst regressions verbatim - the regressions are what earn the customer's trust.

resource.label: arXiv 2306.05685 - Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias)

outcomes: You can write h = W0x + (alpha/r)BAx from memory, state that A is Gaussian-initialised and B is zero so delta_W starts at zero, compute the trainable parameter count for a given r and target_modules, and derive dL/dA and dL/dB.

You can produce, before launching, a written per-parameter memory ledger for full fine-tune, LoRA and QLoRA on a named model and GPU, predict peak VRAM within about 20%, and confirm it with torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated().

You can implement LoRALinear as a plain nn.Module with no peft dependency, inject it by walking named_modules, train it to the same eval loss as the peft implementation, merge it, and assert the max absolute logit difference between merged and unmerged is under 1e-4.

You can derive the DPO loss from the KL-regularised objective and Bradley-Terry in under ten minutes on a whiteboard, explain why log Z(x) cancels, and say concretely what changes between beta = 0.01 and beta = 0.5.

You can look at a TRL DPO run's rewards/chosen, rewards/rejected, rewards/margins and rewards/accuracies plus the mean output length and state whether the model learned a preference or a length/format artifact.

You can report a pairwise win-rate with a confidence interval, a tie rate, position-swap-consistent judgments and a length-controlled variant, and correctly refuse to claim an improvement when the interval includes 50%.
You can run a contamination audit that near-duplicate-matches every evaluation prompt against the training mixture and publish the overlap percentage next to the score.

You can hand a customer a one-page recommendation with numbers: method, adapter size in MB, peak VRAM, wall-clock and dollar cost per run, quality delta with an interval, forgetting check, and the serving story (merged weights versus multi-adapter).
failureModes: Eval rows were paraphrases of training rows from the same tickets and the split was random rather than grouped by ticket id; the tuned model scores 18 points above base on the held-out set and is worse than base on genuinely new tickets in week one of the pilot.

Labels were never masked to -100 over the prompt, so the loss rewards reproducing the system prompt; train loss looks excellent, and the deployed model starts answering by restating the instructions before it gets to the customer's question.

target_modules named the wrong projections for the architecture, so few or no modules matched; print_trainable_parameters was never read, the run trained a fraction of what was intended, and the team concluded 'LoRA does not work for this task' and quoted a full fine-tune.

LoRA was launched with the full fine-tune learning rate of 2e-5 instead of 2e-4; the loss barely moves over three epochs and the result is presented as evidence that the base model cannot learn the task.

Gradient checkpointing was enabled on a frozen 4-bit base without prepare_model_for_kbit_training or enable_input_require_grads, so no input required grad, the adapters received no gradient, and a perfectly flat loss curve was debugged for two days as a data-quality problem.

DPO drove rewards/accuracies to 0.95 while mean completion length doubled; the LLM judge, which prefers longer answers, reported a 68% win rate, and the customer's support team complained the assistant now waffles - the entire gain was length.

The adapter was merged into the 4-bit quantized base for serving and evaluation was never rerun; the dequantize-merge-requantize round trip cost several points that showed up only as user complaints about the production model being worse than the demo.

Base was evaluated greedily while the tuned model was sampled at temperature 0.8 with no fixed seed, so run-to-run noise of plus or minus 4 points swamped the claimed 3-point improvement, and the gain vanished when the customer reran the script.
interviewQuestions: Derive DPO starting from the KL-regularised RL objective and the Bradley-Terry model. Where does the partition function go and why is that the key step? What does beta control, and what does the per-pair gradient weight look like?

A customer has one 24 GB GPU, a 7B base model and 12,000 labelled examples. Do the memory arithmetic for full fine-tune, LoRA and QLoRA in bytes per parameter, tell me what you would run, and defend your r, lora_alpha, target_modules and learning rate.

Write the LoRA forward pass and its parameter count. Why is B initialised to zero? Why does the alpha/r scaling exist and what does rsLoRA change about it? What exactly goes wrong if you merge the adapter into a 4-bit base?

Debug: a DPO run reports rewards/accuracies of 0.93, steadily rising rewards/margins, and a 58% win rate against base judged by a strong LLM. The customer says the model got worse. What do you check, in what order, and what would convince you either way?
Debug: a QLoRA run's training loss is flat from step 0 and never moves. Give me five distinct causes and how you would distinguish them in under twenty minutes.

Design the evaluation you would put in front of the customer's VP to justify shipping a fine-tune. Which datasets, which metrics, which statistics, how you control judge bias, and what result would make you recommend against shipping.

When do you tell a customer that fine-tuning is the wrong tool? Name the signals in their request that trigger that call, and say what you would propose instead and how you would prove it was the better choice.
116.proofOfWork: A public repo `finetune-forensics` that is the diagnostic companion to the three-way training repo: six numbered, self-contained scripts, each a minimal reproduction of one silent fine-tuning failure on the same small base model - the unmasked prompt loss that produces a beautiful curve and an instruction-echoing model, the target_modules mismatch that trains 0.02% of what the config claims, gradient checkpointing on a frozen quantized base with no input grads (flat loss, no error), a DPO run driven to a 68% judge win-rate purely by doubling output length, a randomly-split eval set whose paraphrase overlap with training data inflates the score by double digits, and a base-versus-tuned comparison whose 'improvement' is smaller than its own decoding-seed variance. Each script prints the plausible-but-wrong artifact first, then the one diagnostic that catches it. Ship alongside them three reusable tools: `vram_ledger.py`, a ~40-line function that takes parameter count, dtype, optimiser, batch and sequence length and prints predicted peak VRAM per method with the measured value from a real run beside it; `leak_audit.py`, a MinHash near-duplicate check between the training mixture and the frozen golden set that emits the overlap percentage and the offending pairs; and `winrate.py`, which runs position-swapped judging, drops self-inconsistent verdicts, and reports win/tie/loss with a bootstrap confidence interval, a McNemar p-value and the mean length delta. Finish with a two-page customer-facing decision memo template that a non-ML stakeholder can read - method chosen, cost, quality delta with interval, forgetting check, serving plan - filled in with the real numbers from the deliverable's runs.

117.topic: Multimodal learning: CLIP, vision-language models, shared embedding spaces
117.why: Every customer with an image catalogue, a document scanner or a product taxonomy eventually asks for 'search my pictures with words', and the honest answer is a dual encoder whose whole behaviour is decided by one loss, one learned temperature and how many negatives fit in a batch - so if you cannot write the symmetric InfoNCE from memory you cannot say why their demo returns the wrong shoe. This is also the topic where the model looks like it works: retrieval returns plausible images, cosine similarities are all in a comfortable band, and the actual defects (false negatives from duplicate captions, a batch too small to make the loss mean anything, a modality gap that makes every similarity threshold you copied from a text system nonsense) never raise an exception. Every VLM the customer is excited about - LLaVA, BLIP-2, whatever ships next quarter - is a frozen CLIP-style tower plus a projector, so its grounding ceiling is set by material in this topic, and you are the person who has to say that out loud in the room.
prerequisites: Transformers derived and built from scratch (Topic 115): scaled dot-product attention, multi-head projections, positional encoding, and the residual/LayerNorm block - both CLIP towers are transformers

PyTorch at depth (Topic 112): broadcasting and shape discipline, autograd, Dataset/DataLoader with workers, AMP, and reading a torch.profiler table, because the (N,d) x (d,N) logit matrix and the N-by-N label trick are exactly where silent shape bugs live

Cross-entropy as negative log-likelihood, KL divergence and mutual information from Topic 98 (Information theory and loss functions) - InfoNCE is a categorical NLL over a batch, and its log N ceiling is an information-theoretic statement
Optimiser and stability machinery from Topic 111: AdamW, warmup plus cosine, gradient clipping, fp16 loss scaling and bf16 - contrastive training is unusually good at producing NaNs in fp16
Transfer learning and image augmentation from Topic 113 (Computer vision), plus a working ViT or ResNet backbone you can instantiate and freeze

Bi-encoder retrieval vocabulary from Topic 53 (RAG at depth): embedding, ANN index, recall@k, and why a bi-encoder is not a cross-encoder; and honest held-out discipline from Topic 103 (Model evaluation), since every R@K in the deliverable is a held-out number on a stated gallery
One CUDA GPU with at least 16 GB (Colab T4/A10 class is enough for Flickr8k at batch 256), plus disk for Flickr8k and a pretrained open_clip / OpenAI ViT-B/32 checkpoint to compare against

subtopics.name: The dual-encoder contract: what a 'shared embedding space' actually is
subtopics.learn: State the object precisely: two independent encoders f_img: images -> R^{d_i} and f_txt: text -> R^{d_t}, two linear projections W_i and W_t into a common d (512 for ViT-B/32), then L2 normalisation, so the only thing tying the modalities together is a scalar inner product. Understand what that buys and what it forbids - retrieval and zero-shot classification become a single matmul plus argmax, which is why 400M pairs are trainable and why a 1M-image index is one FAISS call, but there is no cross-attention between the modalities, so no per-token grounding, no counting, no 'is the red cube left of the blue one'. Be able to contrast it in one breath with a cross-encoder (scores one pair at a time, far more accurate, O(N) forward passes per query, unusable as an index) and with a captioning/generative model, and state CLIP's actual scale (400M pairs, batch 32768, 32 epochs) so a customer's '5,000 labelled images' is immediately in perspective.

resource.label: Radford et al., "Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision" (CLIP, arXiv:2103.00020)

subtopics.name: InfoNCE from first principles, and the log N ceiling
subtopics.learn: Derive the loss as what it is: a softmax classifier over the batch that must pick the true partner out of N candidates, L_N = -E[log( exp(s_pos/tau) / sum_{j=1}^{N} exp(s_j/tau) )], which is exactly categorical cross-entropy with the diagonal as the label. Then derive the two consequences that decide every practical choice later: at initialisation, with random embeddings, every row of the softmax is uniform so the loss starts at log N (a run that does not start near log N has a bug, not a hyperparameter problem), and the van den Oord/CPC bound I(x;y) >= log N - L_N caps the mutual information you can estimate at log(batch size) - so batch size is not an engineering knob, it is the resolution of the objective. Be able to say why InfoNCE is a lower-bound estimator rather than a divergence you are minimising directly, and why 'the loss went down' is therefore weaker evidence than 'R@1 went up'.

resource.label: van den Oord et al., "Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding" (InfoNCE, arXiv:1807.03748)

subtopics.name: The symmetric loss in fifteen lines, and dL/dlogits by hand
subtopics.learn: Write it closed-book: I = F.normalize(img_proj, dim=-1); T = F.normalize(txt_proj, dim=-1); logits = logit_scale.exp() * I @ T.t(); labels = torch.arange(N, device=...); loss = 0.5*(F.cross_entropy(logits, labels) + F.cross_entropy(logits.t(), labels)). Know why the labels are arange(N) (the k-th image's partner is the k-th caption, so the target class index equals the row index), why the two directions are averaged rather than added (image->text and text->image are different classification problems over the same matrix, and halving keeps the loss comparable to log N), and that F.cross_entropy consumes raw logits so an extra softmax is the same silent bug as in Topic 110. Derive the gradient: for a row with softmax p, dL/ds_ij = (p_ij - 1[i=j]) / N, so gradient mass on a negative is exactly its softmax probability - which is the sentence that explains temperature, batch size and hard negatives all at once. Assert in a test that a random batch gives loss ~= log N and that swapping two rows of T raises it.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss (logit input, class-index targets, reduction)

subtopics.name: L2 normalisation, cosine similarity, and the alignment/uniformity decomposition
subtopics.learn: Know why F.normalize before the dot product is load-bearing and not cosmetic: on the unit sphere s = u.v = cos(theta) is bounded in [-1, 1], so the temperature alone sets the softmax sharpness; drop the normalisation and the model can reduce the loss by inflating embedding norms instead of learning, producing a beautifully decreasing curve and a useless index. Then learn the geometry: Wang and Isola show the contrastive loss asymptotically decomposes into alignment, E ||f(x) - f(y)||^2 over positive pairs, and uniformity, log E exp(-t ||f(x_i) - f(x_j)||^2) over all pairs, and that both are measurable on your own checkpoint in ten lines. Be able to read the two numbers as a diagnosis: alignment good and uniformity bad means representation collapse (everything points the same way, retrieval returns the same hub images for every query); uniformity good and alignment bad means the positives were never learned, usually too high a temperature or too few epochs. Also know ||a - b||^2 = 2 - 2 a.b on the sphere, which is why an L2 index and an inner-product index rank identically once vectors are normalised.

resource.label: Wang and Isola, "Understanding Contrastive Representation Learning through Alignment and Uniformity on the Hypersphere" (arXiv:2005.10242)

subtopics.name: The learned temperature: logit_scale, its gradient, and the clamp
subtopics.learn: Understand the parameterisation CLIP actually uses: a single scalar logit_scale stored in log space and initialised to log(1/0.07) ~= 2.6593, multiplied in as logit_scale.exp(), clamped each step to at most log(100) so tau cannot fall below 0.01. Reason about the limits from dL/ds_ij = p_ij - 1[i=j]: as tau -> 0 the row softmax approaches an argmax, so essentially all gradient mass lands on the single hardest negative - fast early progress, huge gradient variance, and catastrophic sensitivity to a mislabelled or duplicated pair, because one false negative now owns the update; as tau -> infinity the softmax flattens, every negative gets ~1/N of the mass, the loss sits at log N and the encoders drift toward uniformity with no alignment. Know that because tau is learned it will happily run to the clamp on a small or easy batch (the model discovers that sharpening is free when negatives are trivial), which is why an unclamped logit_scale plus fp16 is a reliable NaN. Do the experiment: freeze a trained checkpoint, sweep tau over a fixed batch, and plot both the loss and the fraction of gradient norm attributable to the top-1 negative.

resource.label: Wang and Liu, "Understanding the Behaviour of Contrastive Loss" (temperature, hardness-awareness, the uniformity-tolerance dilemma, arXiv:2012.09740)

subtopics.name: Batch size is the loss: in-batch negatives and how to fake a big batch
subtopics.learn: Internalise that each anchor sees exactly N-1 negatives, all of them sampled uniformly from the data, so as N grows the hardest in-batch negative gets harder and the log N bound rises - CLIP's 32768 is a modelling decision, not an infrastructure one, and a Flickr8k run at batch 64 will plateau for reasons no learning-rate sweep can fix. Know why the naive memory cost is activations for N images (the N-by-N logit matrix itself is tiny: 32768^2 fp16 is 2 GB, but the ViT activations are what OOMs), and learn the three escapes with their real costs: gradient caching (a no_grad pass to collect all embeddings, compute the loss and cache dL/d(embedding), then a second pass in sub-batches that backprops with the cached gradients - mathematically identical, roughly 2x compute), a MoCo-style momentum queue (cheap, but the negatives are stale embeddings from an older encoder), and simply more GPUs. Verify your implementation the only way that counts: assert the cached-gradient parameter update matches a naive full-batch update to 1e-5 on a small model in float64.

resource.label: Gao et al., "Scaling Deep Contrastive Learning Batch Size under Memory Limited Setup" (GradCache, arXiv:2101.06983)

subtopics.name: Distributed contrastive loss: all_gather, local_loss, and the gradient that silently vanishes
subtopics.learn: Read open_clip's ClipLoss line by line, because it encodes the bug you will otherwise ship: torch.distributed.all_gather is not an autograd-aware op, so the gathered tensors from other ranks carry no graph, and if you also overwrite your own rank's slice with the gathered copy, your local embeddings receive zero gradient and the model trains as if world_size were 1 while every log looks healthy. Know the two correct patterns - gather_with_grad (an all_gather with a registered backward that reduces gradients back to the owning rank) and local_loss (each rank computes cross-entropy for its own rows against the full gathered set of columns, with labels offset by rank * local_batch_size) - and be able to say why the second is the memory-cheap default at scale and why the label offset is the classic off-by-one. Confirm empirically: same seed, same data order, run 1 GPU at batch 256 versus 4 GPUs at local batch 64, and assert the losses and gradients match within tolerance.

resource.label: open_clip source - src/open_clip/loss.py (ClipLoss, gather_features, local_loss, gather_with_grad)

subtopics.name: Hard negatives, false negatives, and the duplicate-caption trap
subtopics.learn: Separate the two things people conflate. Hard negatives are genuinely non-matching pairs with high similarity, and the temperature already up-weights them; explicit mining (sampling negatives with probability proportional to exp(beta * s)) accelerates convergence at small batch and is how you get useful behaviour from batch 256 instead of 32768. False negatives are true matches sitting in the denominator, and they are actively harmful because the gradient pushes a correct pair apart: on Flickr8k each image has five captions, so the naive Dataset that yields one row per (image, caption) puts up to five true partners in the same batch, and the loss punishes the model for retrieving them. Fix it deliberately - sample exactly one caption per image per epoch, or build the mask yourself and set the duplicate entries to -inf before the softmax - then run the ablation and report the R@1 delta, because that number is the cheapest credibility you will ever buy in a customer review. Know that the same trap appears in every enterprise catalogue where two SKUs share a description.

resource.label: Robinson et al., "Contrastive Learning with Hard Negative Samples" (arXiv:2010.04592)

subtopics.name: The image tower: ViT patchification, the CLS token, and resolution
subtopics.learn: Be able to write the ViT-B/32 forward from memory: a 224x224x3 image is cut into 7x7 = 49 non-overlapping 32x32 patches, each flattened to 3072 and linearly projected to width 768 (implemented as a stride-32 Conv2d), a learned class token is prepended and learned positional embeddings are added to all 50 tokens, then 12 pre-LN transformer blocks, then LayerNorm on the class token, then the projection to the shared d=512. Know the levers and their cost: patch size dominates compute because token count scales as (H/P)^2 and attention as its square, so ViT-B/16 is roughly 4x the FLOPs of B/32 at the same resolution; changing input resolution requires interpolating the positional embeddings, which is the standard silent accuracy loss when someone feeds 336px into a 224px checkpoint. Know why the ResNet variants of CLIP replace global average pooling with an attention-pooling head, and why a customer's 4000x3000 document photo downsampled to 224 loses exactly the small text they wanted searched.

resource.label: Dosovitskiy et al., "An Image is Worth 16x16 Words" (ViT, arXiv:2010.11929)

subtopics.name: The text tower: tokenisation, the 77-token cap, and which vector you pool
subtopics.learn: Know exactly how a caption becomes one vector in each of the two implementations you will touch. OpenAI CLIP: byte-pair encoding, 49152 vocab, a fixed 77-token context with SOT/EOT sentinels and causal masking, and the sequence representation is taken from the hidden state at the EOT position (argmax of the token ids) before LayerNorm and projection - so anything past 77 tokens is silently truncated, which quietly destroys retrieval on the customer's 300-word product descriptions. DistilBERT (what the deliverable uses): 6 layers, hidden 768, no token_type embeddings, and critically no next-sentence-prediction objective, so its [CLS] vector was never trained as a sentence representation - mean-pooling over the attention mask (sum(h * mask) / sum(mask), not a plain .mean() that averages padding into the answer) is the pooling that works. Be able to state the tokenizer contract: padding='max_length', truncation=True, and that the mask must reach the pooling function, because forgetting it makes batch composition change the embedding of an unchanged sentence.

resource.label: HuggingFace Transformers - CLIP model docs (CLIPTextModel, pooled output at the EOS token, CLIPProcessor)

subtopics.name: Projection heads, and why the best features are the ones you throw away
subtopics.learn: Understand the head as a small map g: R^{d_backbone} -> R^{d_shared} that exists so the two towers can meet, and know CLIP uses a single linear layer with no bias and no nonlinearity while SimCLR-style work uses a 2-layer MLP. Then absorb the finding that changes how you serve the model: the representation before the projection head is consistently better for downstream linear probes than the one after, because the head is trained to discard everything the contrastive task is invariant to (colour, exact pose, style), and that discarded information is often precisely what the customer's classifier needs. The operational rule: use post-projection normalised embeddings for anything cross-modal (retrieval, zero-shot), use pre-projection backbone features for a same-modality linear probe or clustering, and never mix vectors from the two spaces in one index. Verify it yourself on the deliverable: train a logistic regression on both and report the two accuracies.

resource.label: Chen et al., "A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations" (SimCLR - projection head ablation, arXiv:2002.05709)

subtopics.name: The modality gap: two cones, not one sphere
subtopics.learn: Learn the empirical fact and its cause, because it is the single most misread number in a CLIP demo: image and text embeddings do not interleave on the unit sphere, they occupy two narrow, well-separated cones, so the cosine similarity between an image and its own correct caption is typically ~0.2-0.3 while two unrelated images sit at 0.6-0.8. The gap is created at random initialisation by the cone effect of deep nonlinear networks and is then preserved rather than closed by the contrastive objective, since InfoNCE only needs the diagonal to beat the off-diagonal within a row - a constant offset between modalities is free. Know the consequences you must design around: absolute similarity thresholds copied from a text-only system reject every correct match, a single index containing both modalities returns only same-modality neighbours, and shifting embeddings along the gap direction measurably changes both zero-shot accuracy and fairness metrics. Measure it on your own checkpoint and on ViT-B/32: centroid distance ||mean(I) - mean(T)||, overlapping histograms of the diagonal s_ii against the off-diagonal s_ij, and a 2-D PCA scatter coloured by modality - that plot is what you put in front of the customer.

resource.label: Liang et al., "Mind the Gap: Understanding the Modality Gap in Multi-modal Contrastive Representation Learning" (arXiv:2203.02053)

subtopics.name: Zero-shot classification as retrieval, and prompt ensembling
subtopics.learn: Build the classifier explicitly rather than calling a helper: embed one prompt per class, L2-normalise, stack into W of shape (d, C), and classify an image as argmax over normalised_image @ W - a zero-shot classifier is literally a nearest-text lookup with the class names as the gallery. Learn how much of the headline number is prompt engineering: bare class names underperform 'a photo of a {label}.' by several points, CIFAR-10's raw label 'plane' should be 'airplane', and OpenAI's 80-template ensemble (average the normalised embeddings across templates, then re-normalise - average embeddings, not logits) is worth roughly 3-5 points on ImageNet at zero inference cost. Know why 'a photo of a {c}' works at all: it moves the text distribution closer to the caption distribution the model was trained on. Report your zero-shot CIFAR-10 number three ways - raw names, single template, ensemble - so nobody can accuse the comparison against ViT-B/32 of being rigged in either direction.

resource.label: OpenAI CLIP repo - Prompt_Engineering_for_ImageNet.ipynb (the 80 templates and the class-name fixes)

subtopics.name: Retrieval evaluation done honestly: R@K, gallery size, and the five-caption asymmetry
subtopics.learn: Define the two metrics separately and state the convention every time you quote them. Text-to-image R@K: for each test caption, rank the whole image gallery by cosine similarity and count a hit if the one correct image is in the top K. Image-to-text R@K: for each test image, rank all captions and count a hit if ANY of its five captions is in the top K - the standard convention, and roughly a 2x optimistic distortion if you silently apply it to the other direction. Know that R@K is meaningless without the gallery size (R@1 against 1000 Flickr8k test images is not comparable to R@1 against a 5000-image gallery, and a paper's number always specifies which), that you must use a fixed published-style split rather than a fresh random one so the pretrained baseline is measured on the same rows, and that median rank plus mean rank are worth reporting because they expose a long tail that R@10 hides. Implement it as one matmul plus argsort over the whole test set, and add a leakage assertion that no test image id appears in the training pair list.

resource.label: Karpathy and Fei-Fei, "Deep Visual-Semantic Alignments for Generating Image Descriptions" (the retrieval splits and R@K protocol, arXiv:1412.2306)

subtopics.name: Adapting to a customer: zero-shot, linear probe, locked-image tuning, full fine-tune
subtopics.learn: Build the decision table you will actually be asked for, ordered by how much labelled data it needs and how much robustness it costs. Zero-shot: no labels, strong on common concepts, useless on the customer's internal vocabulary. Linear probe on frozen pre-projection features: hundreds of labels, minutes on CPU with sklearn LogisticRegression, cannot fix a backbone that never saw the domain. LiT-style locked-image tuning: freeze the image tower, train only the text tower on the customer's pairs - usually the best value when the images are natural photographs but the language is domain-specific jargon. Full fine-tune: best in-domain, and it demonstrably destroys out-of-distribution robustness, which is why WiSE-FT exists - weight-space ensembling theta = (1-alpha) theta_zeroshot + alpha theta_finetuned recovers most of the shift robustness at no inference cost, with alpha swept on held-out data. Be able to say the sentence that protects the account: 'fine-tuning on your 3,000 pairs will raise this category and quietly lower every category you add next quarter, unless we ensemble the weights and keep the zero-shot eval in CI.'

resource.label: Wortsman et al., "Robust fine-tuning of zero-shot models" (WiSE-FT, arXiv:2109.01903)

subtopics.name: Compositionality: why CLIP behaves like a bag of words
subtopics.learn: Know the concrete failure and its cause. CLIP assigns nearly identical scores to 'the horse is eating the grass' and 'the grass is eating the horse', and shuffling the word order of a caption barely changes retrieval - because the training objective only ever required the true caption to beat random other captions in the batch, and random negatives almost never share the same bag of words, so word order was never a useful feature to learn. Learn the benchmarks that turn this from an anecdote into a number: ARO (attribution, relation and order probes built by perturbing real captions) and Winoground (pairs of images and captions using identical words in different orders, where strong models score near chance). Know the fix and its shape: add hard negative captions constructed by swapping relations and attributes (the NegCLIP recipe) so the loss finally has to look at order. Then apply the judgement: if the customer's queries are 'red running shoe' the bag-of-words limit is harmless, and if their queries are 'invoice with the stamp on the left page' a dual encoder is the wrong architecture and you should say so before the pilot, not after.

resource.label: Yuksekgonul et al., "When and why vision-language models behave like bags-of-words, and what to do about it" (ARO, arXiv:2210.01936)

subtopics.name: Data is the model: web pairs, filtering, dedup and test-set contamination
subtopics.learn: Understand that at fixed architecture and compute, the dataset filtering strategy is the dominant variable - the DataComp result is that a well-filtered 140M subset beats a raw 400M one, and the filters that matter are simple (CLIP-score thresholding against an existing model, English-language detection, image resolution and aspect floors, caption length, near-duplicate removal by perceptual hash or embedding). Know the alignment-noise reality of alt-text: a large fraction of web captions do not describe the image at all, which is exactly the label noise that a low temperature amplifies into the hardest-negative gradient. Take contamination seriously as an evaluation issue rather than an ethics footnote: a web-scale corpus contains many standard benchmark images, so zero-shot numbers must be reported alongside a de-duplication analysis (CLIP's paper does one), and on a customer engagement the equivalent question is whether their 'holdout' images are near-duplicates of training frames from the same shoot. Also know the documented harms in LAION-scale corpora, because 'where did the training data come from' is a procurement question you will be asked under a legal team's eye.

resource.label: Gadre et al., "DataComp: In search of the next generation of multimodal datasets" (arXiv:2304.14108)

subtopics.name: SigLIP: replacing the softmax with a pairwise sigmoid
subtopics.learn: Write the alternative loss and know exactly what it changes: instead of a softmax normalised over the batch, SigLIP treats every one of the N^2 pairs as an independent binary problem, L = -(1/N) sum_i sum_j log sigmoid( z_ij (t' x_i . y_j + b) ) with z_ij = +1 on the diagonal and -1 off it, a learned scale t' and a learned bias b initialised around -10 to counteract the fact that at initialisation there are N positives against N^2 - N negatives. The consequences are the interesting part: with no global normaliser the loss is separable over pairs, so a distributed implementation only needs to pass embedding chunks around the ring instead of materialising and all-gathering the full similarity matrix, memory stops being the batch-size ceiling, and the method works notably better than InfoNCE at small and medium batch - which is precisely the regime of a customer engagement on two GPUs. Be able to say when you would still use softmax InfoNCE (parity with a published baseline, or an existing checkpoint you must match) and implement both behind one flag so the comparison is a single ablation row.

resource.label: Zhai et al., "Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training" (SigLIP, arXiv:2303.15343)

subtopics.name: From dual encoder to VLM: the Q-Former, the LLaVA projector, and where grounding comes from
subtopics.learn: Trace how the same frozen tower becomes a chat model. BLIP-2: freeze a CLIP-style image encoder and freeze an LLM, and train only a Q-Former - a small transformer holding 32 learned query embeddings that cross-attend to the image patch features and emit 32 vectors into the LLM's input space - in two stages (representation learning against the frozen encoder, then generative learning against the frozen LLM). LLaVA: even simpler, a projection (a single linear layer in v1, a 2-layer MLP in v1.5) mapping CLIP ViT-L/14 patch features directly into the LLM token embedding space, trained on instruction data, with the image occupying a few hundred token positions. The FDE-relevant conclusion: a VLM's visual ceiling is its frozen encoder's - if CLIP at 224px cannot read the serial number, no amount of prompting the language model will, and 'the model hallucinated' is usually 'the encoder never had the pixels'. Know that this is why high-resolution tiling and AnyRes-style schemes exist, and be able to test the hypothesis cheaply by scoring the crop directly with CLIP before blaming the LLM.

resource.label: Li et al., "BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models" (arXiv:2301.12597)

subtopics.name: Serving the retrieval demo: normalised vectors, IndexFlatIP, and the failure surface
subtopics.learn: Ship it correctly: L2-normalise once at write time, store float32 C-contiguous arrays, and use faiss.IndexFlatIP so inner product is cosine - IndexFlatL2 on the same normalised vectors ranks identically since ||a-b||^2 = 2 - 2 a.b, but on unnormalised vectors it ranks by norm and you get the same handful of hub images for every query. Know when to move to IVF or HNSW and that the only honest way to tune nlist/nprobe or efSearch is to measure recall against the flat index on your own queries rather than trusting defaults. Then rehearse the demo failure surface, because these are the ones that happen live in front of a customer: typographic attacks - a piece of paper reading 'iPod' taped to an apple flips the zero-shot label, a consequence of the multimodal neurons that fire for a concept in photographs, drawings and rendered text alike; near-duplicate collapse where one product shoot dominates every result; and out-of-vocabulary internal jargon that lands nowhere useful in the text cone. Have a fallback ready for each - a cross-encoder or VLM rerank over the top 50, dedup by embedding similarity, and a curated prompt-template file the customer can edit.

resource.label: FAISS wiki - Getting started (index types, IndexFlatIP vs IndexFlatL2, add/search)

outcomes: You can write the symmetric InfoNCE loss from memory and implement it in about fifteen lines of PyTorch (F.normalize, logit_scale.exp(), a single I @ T.t(), labels = arange(N), 0.5 times the mean of the two cross-entropies), with a pytest that asserts the loss on a random batch equals log N to three decimal places and that permuting the text rows raises it.

You can derive dL/ds_ij = (p_ij - 1[i=j])/N on a whiteboard, state analytically where the gradient mass goes as tau -> 0 and as tau -> infinity, and back it with a measured temperature sweep plotting loss and the share of gradient norm carried by the single hardest negative.

You can train a dual encoder on Flickr8k and report text-to-image and image-to-text R@1/R@5/R@10 next to a pretrained ViT-B/32 baseline, stating the gallery size, the caption-sampling rule and the any-of-five hit convention explicitly, with a leakage assertion that no test image appears in the training pairs.

You can measure the modality gap on your own checkpoint and on OpenAI CLIP (centroid distance, overlapping s_ii versus s_ij histograms, a PCA scatter coloured by modality) and use it to decide whether a bad retrieval result is a gap problem, a false-negative problem or a batch-size problem.

You can build a zero-shot CIFAR-10 classifier as a text-embedding matmul and report the accuracy delta across raw class names, a single 'a photo of a {label}.' template, and an 80-template ensemble averaged in embedding space.

You can raise the effective contrastive batch beyond one GPU's memory with gradient caching or a gradient-aware all_gather, and prove correctness by asserting the resulting parameter update matches the naive full-batch update to 1e-5.

You can implement SigLIP's pairwise sigmoid loss behind the same interface as InfoNCE, train both at batch 256 on identical seeds and data order, and report the R@1 difference with the learned scale and bias trajectories.

You can recommend, for a customer with N labelled pairs and a stated query distribution, one of zero-shot / linear probe / locked-image tuning / full fine-tune plus WiSE-FT, and state the robustness cost of the choice in one sentence they will remember.
failureModes: The Dataset yields one row per (image, caption) on Flickr8k, so up to five true partners for the same image land in one batch and the loss actively pushes correct pairs apart; training converges, the curve looks textbook, and R@1 sits several points below where it should for reasons no learning-rate sweep will find.

F.normalize is omitted on one tower (or applied before the projection instead of after), so the loss can be reduced by growing embedding norms rather than by aligning pairs; the loss falls smoothly, the temperature stops meaning anything, and the retrieval index ranks by magnitude.

logit_scale is left learnable but unclamped, runs past 100 on an easy batch, the softmax saturates and the run NaNs under fp16 at epoch three - which is then debugged for a day as a corrupt-image problem in the dataloader.

Multi-GPU training gathers embeddings with a plain torch.distributed.all_gather and overwrites the local slice, so gradients flow for only one rank's share of the negatives; the 8-GPU run reaches exactly the 1-GPU quality at 8x the cost and the team concludes 'contrastive scaling does not work for us'.

Image-to-text R@K is computed with the any-of-five-captions convention and text-to-image with the one-correct-image convention, then the two are quoted side by side as if symmetric, or the model's R@1 on a 1000-image gallery is compared to a published R@1 on 5000 - the headline number is roughly double what it should be and the customer's own test reproduces none of it.

Zero-shot CIFAR-10 is evaluated with the raw label 'plane' and no prompt template, comes in ten points below the published baseline, and the gap is attributed to the training run rather than to the prompt - so a week is spent tuning a model that was never the problem.

A similarity threshold of 0.5, copied from a sentence-embedding service, is used to decide whether a retrieved image is a match; the modality gap puts true image-caption pairs at 0.25 and unrelated image-image pairs at 0.75, so the system rejects every correct result while confidently deduplicating distinct products.

The whole dual encoder is fine-tuned on the customer's 3,000 in-domain pairs with no weight-space ensembling and no frozen zero-shot regression suite in CI; the pilot category improves, every other category silently degrades, and the failure surfaces two months later as 'the model got worse after your update'.
interviewQuestions: Write the symmetric InfoNCE loss for a batch of N image-text pairs from memory, then derive the gradient with respect to the logits. Why is the loss log N at initialisation, and what exactly does the learned temperature do to that gradient as it goes to zero and as it grows?

A customer's text-to-image demo returns plausible but wrong images. Walk me through your diagnosis in order: what do you measure to distinguish too-few-negatives, false negatives in the batch, hubness or representation collapse, and the modality gap - and what single plot do you put in front of them?

Why is contrastive batch size a property of the objective rather than an infrastructure detail? State the bound it relates to, then give me three ways to get 32k negatives on four GPUs and tell me what each one costs in compute, staleness or correctness.

Explain the modality gap: where does it come from, why does contrastive training not close it, and name one concrete production decision it changes. How would you measure it on a checkpoint you were handed this morning?

SigLIP replaces the batch softmax with a per-pair sigmoid. Write both losses, explain what changes under data parallelism, why the bias term is initialised strongly negative, and when you would still choose softmax InfoNCE.

Design: 40,000 product photos, a one-line merchandiser description each, no labels, one A10, and the customer wants natural-language search live in three weeks. Zero-shot pretrained, locked-image tuning, or train from scratch? Name the eval you would agree with them up front, and say what you would do if R@1 came back at 12 percent.

CLIP scores 'a horse eating grass' and 'grass eating a horse' almost identically. Explain why the training objective permits this, how you would measure it on the customer's own query distribution, and what you would change in training or in the serving architecture to fix it.
117.proofOfWork: A companion repo `contrastive-forensics` that turns the mini-clip training run into a diagnostic instrument a customer's ML team can audit. It ships (a) one shared trainer with the defect switched on or off by flag - duplicate-caption false negatives, missing L2 normalisation, unclamped logit_scale, a plain non-differentiable all_gather, pre- versus post-projection features in the index, and unnormalised vectors in an L2 FAISS index - each producing the same six artefacts per run (loss curve against the log N reference line, learned temperature trajectory, overlapping s_ii versus s_ij histograms, alignment and uniformity values, a modality-gap PCA scatter, and text-to-image and image-to-text R@1/5/10 with the gallery size stamped into the filename); (b) a correctness suite that asserts the loss equals log N at init, that gradient-cached and naive full-batch updates agree to 1e-5, that a 4-rank distributed run matches a single-GPU run at the same global batch, and that no test image id leaks into the training pairs; (c) an ablation table with three seeds and standard deviations covering batch size 64/128/256/512, temperature fixed at 0.07 versus learned, one-caption-per-image versus all five, InfoNCE versus SigLIP, and prompt raw / single-template / 80-template ensemble for zero-shot CIFAR-10 - every row a held-out number rather than a claim; and (d) a two-page handover note written for a non-ML stakeholder that states in plain language what the model can and cannot do, shows the typographic-attack demo failing on purpose, gives the recommended similarity operating point derived from the measured s_ii/s_ij distributions rather than a copied 0.5, and specifies the frozen zero-shot regression suite that must stay green in CI before any fine-tune ships.

118.topic: Graph neural networks: message passing, GCN/GAT, and enterprise graph use cases
118.why: Enterprise data is already a graph - accounts wire money to accounts, users touch products, tickets reference tickets - and the customer who says 'we have a graph problem' is usually asking whether the relational structure carries signal their flat feature table does not. An FDE who has hand-derived the GCN propagation rule and coded the scatter-based message pass can answer that in the room: state the node/edge/graph-level task, measure homophily, show that an MLP on node features plus label propagation is or is not already beating the GNN, and name the depth at which accuracy dies and why. Without that, you ship a two-layer GCN whose 0.99 offline AUC came from supervision edges left in the adjacency, and you find out in production - in front of the customer's fraud team.
prerequisites: PyTorch at depth from Topic 112: custom nn.Module, autograd and vector-Jacobian products, advanced indexing versus views, index_add_/scatter_add_ semantics, and reading a training loop line by line

Backpropagation, initialisation and residual connections from Topic 110, plus optimisers, schedules and bad-loss-curve triage from Topic 111 - a GNN that will not train is usually an ordinary deep-learning bug wearing a graph costume

Linear algebra from Topic 93: symmetric matrices, eigendecomposition, what repeated multiplication by a matrix does to a vector as a function of its spectrum, and why the eigenvalue range of a propagation operator decides whether depth is safe
Scaled dot-product attention from Topic 115 - GAT is attention over an irregular neighbourhood set rather than a fixed-length sequence, and the softmax normalisation domain is the whole difference
Honest evaluation from Topic 103: train/validation/test discipline, leakage, class imbalance, PR-AUC versus ROC-AUC, and reporting mean plus standard deviation across seeds
NumPy/SciPy sparse fluency from Topic 99: COO versus CSR, int64 index arrays, broadcasting, and the memory arithmetic of an N-by-N dense matrix

subtopics.name: Is this actually a graph problem, or a feature join in disguise
subtopics.learn: Before any modelling, be able to argue the relational inductive bias out loud: a GNN imposes permutation-equivariant, locally-shared computation over an irregular neighbourhood, which pays off only when a node's label depends on its neighbours' labels or features in a way you cannot cheaply denormalise. Learn the honest alternative - flatten the graph into aggregate features (neighbour count, sum of neighbour transaction volume, degree, triangle count, PageRank, connected-component id) and train a gradient-boosted tree from Topic 101 - and know that on many enterprise tables this wins, is faster, and is explainable. State the three conditions that actually favour a GNN: the signal is multi-hop, the neighbourhood is variable-sized and unordered, and the graph is large enough that hand-engineered aggregates would be a combinatorial mess. Rehearse saying no to a GNN in one paragraph a customer's architect will accept.

resource.label: Battaglia et al. - Relational inductive biases, deep learning, and graph networks (arXiv:1806.01261)

subtopics.name: Graph representations: adjacency matrix, COO edge_index, CSR, and what each costs
subtopics.learn: Build the same graph four ways and know the costs: dense adjacency A of shape (N, N) in float32 costs 4*N^2 bytes, so 100k nodes is 40 GB and is never the answer; COO edge_index of shape (2, E) int64 is what PyTorch Geometric and your from-scratch layer both consume; CSR (indptr, indices) gives O(1) slicing of a node's neighbours and is what scipy.sparse.csr_matrix and METIS partitioners want; an adjacency list of Python lists is what you will actually be handed. Practise the conversions with scipy.sparse.coo_matrix((data, (row, col)), shape=(N, N)).tocsr() and back. Internalise the traps that silently change your model: an undirected edge must appear twice in edge_index (row->col and col->row) or your message passing is directed; duplicate edges are summed by COO-to-CSR conversion and silently double a neighbour's weight, so coalesce first; and self-loops are absent unless you add them. Compute degrees as A.sum(axis=1) and know that a degree-zero node exists in almost every real customer extract.

resource.label: SciPy docs - Sparse arrays (COO, CSR, construction and conversion)

subtopics.name: Tasks, transductive versus inductive, and the split that leaks
subtopics.learn: Name the three task levels and the loss each implies: node-level (per-node logits, cross-entropy masked to the labelled nodes), edge-level (score a node pair, binary cross-entropy against sampled negatives), graph-level (a readout such as mean/sum/max over node embeddings, then a head). Separate transductive (the whole graph including test-node features and edges is present at training time; only labels are hidden - this is Cora) from inductive (test nodes or whole test graphs are unseen; the model must generalise to new neighbourhoods - this is what a customer deploying on tomorrow's accounts needs), and be able to say which one your customer is actually in. Understand the standard Planetoid split (20 labelled nodes per class, 500 validation, 1000 test) and why Shchur et al. show model rankings flip under different random splits and equal hyperparameter budgets - so report mean and standard deviation over at least 10 random splits and 10 seeds, never a single number. Know the graph-specific leakage forms: edges created after the prediction timestamp, an edge that is itself the label, and near-duplicate subgraphs across folds.

resource.label: Shchur et al. - Pitfalls of Graph Neural Network Evaluation (arXiv:1811.05868)

subtopics.name: Homophily, and the two baselines a GNN must beat
subtopics.learn: Compute edge homophily h = (number of edges joining same-label nodes) / |E| before training anything; Cora is about 0.81, a fraud graph may be near 0.2, and the whole GCN smoothing prior assumes h is high. Then build the two baselines you are obliged to report: (a) an MLP or logistic regression on node features alone, which ignores the graph entirely, and (b) label propagation, which ignores the features entirely and just diffuses known labels. Reproduce the Correct-and-Smooth result: a shallow base predictor plus residual error propagation plus label smoothing matches or beats large GNNs on several OGB node tasks with orders of magnitude fewer parameters. Adopt the rule: if your GCN does not clearly beat max(MLP, label propagation, C-and-S) across seeds, you do not have a GNN problem, you have a feature problem. On heterophilous graphs know the specific failure - averaging over neighbours actively destroys signal - and the design responses (separating the ego embedding from the neighbour aggregate, using 2-hop neighbourhoods, concatenating intermediate layers).

resource.label: Huang et al. - Combining Label Propagation and Simple Models Out-performs Graph Neural Networks (arXiv:2010.13993)

subtopics.name: The message-passing framework: message, aggregate, update, readout
subtopics.learn: Write the general MPNN update and be able to place every architecture in it: m_ij = M_l(h_i, h_j, e_ij); a_i = AGG_{j in N(i)} m_ij; h_i' = U_l(h_i, a_i); and for graph-level tasks y = R({h_i}). The non-negotiable constraint is that AGG must be permutation-invariant over a variable-sized multiset - sum, mean, max, or a learned set function - because a neighbourhood has no order; any AGG that depends on neighbour ordering makes the layer non-equivariant and the model will disagree with itself when the customer's export sorts differently. Know what each aggregator preserves and destroys: sum keeps multiplicity and degree information (and is the one that makes GIN maximally expressive), mean keeps proportions and discards degree, max keeps the presence of a distinctive neighbour and discards counts. Be able to state that L stacked layers give each node a receptive field of exactly its L-hop neighbourhood, which is the single fact that governs everything about depth later in this topic.

resource.label: Gilmer et al. - Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry (arXiv:1704.01212)

subtopics.name: Spectral roots: the graph Laplacian, Chebyshev filters and localisation
subtopics.learn: Define L = D - A and its symmetric normalisation L_sym = I - D^-1/2 A D^-1/2, know that L_sym is positive semi-definite with eigenvalues in [0, 2], that the multiplicity of eigenvalue 0 equals the number of connected components, and that the eigenvector for 0 is proportional to D^1/2 * 1 - the fact that returns as the over-smoothing fixed point. Understand graph Fourier transform as x_hat = U^T x where L = U diag(lambda) U^T, spectral filtering as U g_theta(Lambda) U^T x, and why that is unusable in practice: the eigendecomposition is O(N^3), the filter is not localised, and the basis does not transfer between graphs. Follow Defferrard's fix - approximate g_theta by a truncated Chebyshev expansion in the rescaled Laplacian, giving a filter that is exactly K-hop localised and costs O(K|E|) with no eigendecomposition. You should be able to explain in one sentence why polynomial-in-L equals K-hop localised: L^k has non-zero entry (i, j) only if a walk of length at most k connects i and j.

resource.label: Defferrard et al. - Convolutional Neural Networks on Graphs with Fast Localized Spectral Filtering (arXiv:1606.09375)

subtopics.name: Deriving the GCN layer and justifying D~^-1/2 A~ D~^-1/2
subtopics.learn: Derive Kipf and Welling's layer from Chebyshev order K=1: with lambda_max approximated by 2 the filter becomes theta_0 x + theta_1 (L_sym - I) x = theta_0 x - theta_1 D^-1/2 A D^-1/2 x; tie theta = theta_0 = -theta_1 to get theta (I + D^-1/2 A D^-1/2) x; then apply the renormalisation trick I + D^-1/2 A D^-1/2 -> D~^-1/2 A~ D~^-1/2 with A~ = A + I, giving H^(l+1) = sigma(D~^-1/2 A~ D~^-1/2 H^(l) W^(l)). Be able to write the per-node form h_i' = sigma(sum over j in N(i) union {i} of (1 / sqrt(d~_i * d~_j)) W h_j) and to justify the normalisation against the two alternatives: unnormalised sum makes activation scale grow with degree so a hub's features explode; row-stochastic mean D~^-1 A~ weights every neighbour 1/d~_i, is not symmetric, and ignores how popular the neighbour is; the symmetric form down-weights messages from high-degree neighbours by 1/sqrt(d~_j), keeps the operator symmetric with real eigenvalues, and - the point of the renormalisation trick - keeps the spectrum inside roughly (-1, 1] so repeated application neither explodes nor vanishes. Then state the cost: it is a fixed, non-learned weighting, which is precisely what GAT replaces.

resource.label: Kipf and Welling - Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks (arXiv:1609.02907)

subtopics.name: Implementing message passing: gather-scatter with index_add_ versus a single SpMM
subtopics.learn: Write the layer from a raw edge_index with no PyG layers: row, col = edge_index; msg = (x @ W)[row] of shape (E, d); out = torch.zeros(N, d, dtype=msg.dtype, device=msg.device).index_add_(0, col, norm.unsqueeze(-1) * msg). Compute degrees the same way (deg = torch.zeros(N).index_add_(0, col, torch.ones(E))), then deg_inv_sqrt = deg.pow(-0.5) and - this is the line everyone forgets - deg_inv_sqrt[deg == 0] = 0, because pow(-0.5) on a degree-zero node gives inf and inf*0 gives NaN one step later. Know that index_add_ and scatter_add_ differ in index shape (scatter_add_ needs index broadcast to the src shape, which is the classic silent bug), that both use atomicAdd on CUDA so float summation order is non-deterministic unless you set torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True), and that gradients flow through gather (a sum-scatter on the backward pass) automatically. Then implement the alternative: build a torch.sparse_coo_tensor for D~^-1/2 A~ D~^-1/2 once and use torch.sparse.mm - faster for a fixed operator, but structurally unable to express per-edge attention, which is why GAT must stay in the gather-scatter world. Verify both against torch_geometric.nn.GCNConv with torch.allclose(atol=1e-6) and run torch.autograd.gradcheck in float64 on a five-node toy graph.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.Tensor.index_add_

subtopics.name: GAT: unnormalised scores, neighbourhood softmax, multi-head attention
subtopics.learn: Implement the layer exactly: e_ij = LeakyReLU(a^T [W h_i || W h_j]) with negative slope 0.2, then alpha_ij = softmax over j in N(i) union {i} of e_ij, then h_i' = sigma(sum_j alpha_ij W h_j). The implementation detail that matters is that the softmax is segmented by destination node, not global: compute per-node maxima with a scatter-max for stability, exponentiate the shifted scores, accumulate the denominator with index_add_ on col, then divide - a global softmax over all E edges runs without error and produces a plausible but wrong model. Exploit the decomposition a^T[Wh_i || Wh_j] = a_src^T W h_i + a_dst^T W h_j so you compute two length-N vectors and add them per edge instead of materialising concatenations of size (E, 2d). Know the multi-head convention: concatenate K heads in hidden layers (output dim K*F'), average them in the final prediction layer; the Cora recipe is 8 heads of 8 features with dropout 0.6 applied both to input features and to the attention coefficients themselves. Be able to say why GAT costs more memory than GCN (an (E, K) coefficient tensor plus per-edge intermediates) and when the learned weighting is worth it: heterogeneous neighbour quality, noisy edges, and graphs where degree alone is a bad prior.

resource.label: Velickovic et al. - Graph Attention Networks (arXiv:1710.10903)

subtopics.name: GATv2 and static attention: the assumption GAT quietly breaks
subtopics.learn: Understand the failure precisely: because GAT applies the shared vector a after the concatenation and before the nonlinearity, the score decomposes into a term depending only on i plus a term depending only on j, so argmax_j alpha_ij is the same neighbour ranking for every query node i - GAT computes static attention, not the query-conditioned dynamic attention people assume when they read the paper. GATv2 fixes it by moving the linear layer after the nonlinearity: e(h_i, h_j) = a^T LeakyReLU(W [h_i || h_j]), which is a universal approximator over the pair and restores per-query ranking. Be able to demonstrate the difference on the synthetic bipartite matching problem from the paper, and to state the practical consequence for a customer: if you are about to justify a prediction with 'the model attended most to this counterparty', a plain GATConv may be attending to the same counterparty for every node in the graph. Know that torch_geometric.nn.GATv2Conv is a drop-in replacement with the same head and dropout arguments.

resource.label: Brody et al. - How Attentive are Graph Attention Networks? (arXiv:2105.14491)

subtopics.name: GraphSAGE: neighbour sampling, inductive embeddings, aggregator choice
subtopics.learn: Learn the update h_i' = sigma(W . CONCAT(h_i, AGG({h_j : j in sampled N(i)}))) with optional L2 normalisation of h_i', and note the two structural differences from GCN: the ego embedding is concatenated rather than mixed into the same weighted sum (which is exactly what helps on heterophilous graphs), and the neighbourhood is a fixed-size uniform sample (typically 25 then 10 for two layers) rather than the full set. Understand why this makes the method inductive: the parameters are the aggregator weights, not a per-node embedding table, so a new account that appears tomorrow gets an embedding from its features and neighbours with no retraining - which is the property most enterprise deployments actually need and the reason a transductive matrix-factorisation embedding fails in production. Compare the four aggregators (mean, GCN-style, LSTM over a random permutation - which is not permutation-invariant and is a deliberate compromise - and max-pool with a per-neighbour MLP), and know that sampling makes the forward pass a stochastic estimate, so evaluation should use full neighbourhoods or layer-wise inference to avoid train/serve skew.

resource.label: Hamilton et al. - Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs (arXiv:1706.02216)

subtopics.name: Expressive power: 1-WL, GIN, and what a message-passing GNN provably cannot see
subtopics.learn: Know the theorem: any message-passing GNN with permutation-invariant aggregation is at most as powerful as the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman colour refinement test at distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs, and it attains that bound only when message and readout functions are injective on multisets. That is why GIN uses h_i' = MLP((1 + eps) h_i + sum_{j in N(i)} h_j) - sum rather than mean or max, and an MLP rather than a single linear layer, because mean cannot distinguish multisets with the same proportions and max cannot count. Be able to draw the standard counterexamples on a napkin: two 3-regular graphs (a 6-cycle versus two triangles) that 1-WL and therefore any GCN/GAT sees as identical, and the consequence that a plain GNN cannot count triangles or detect cycles - which matters directly when the customer's fraud pattern is a ring. Know the practical escapes: add structural features as node inputs (triangle count, clustering coefficient, degree, positional encodings), or use subgraph/higher-order methods. This subtopic is what lets you say 'your circular-payment pattern is not learnable by this architecture; here is the feature that makes it learnable' rather than tuning for a week.

resource.label: Xu et al. - How Powerful are Graph Neural Networks? (arXiv:1810.00826)

subtopics.name: Over-smoothing: the Laplacian-smoothing argument and how to measure it
subtopics.learn: Understand the result that a GCN layer is a form of symmetric Laplacian smoothing, so repeated propagation drives node representations within each connected component toward a common fixed point proportional to the dominant eigenvector D~^1/2 * 1 - the features converge, class information is destroyed, and accuracy collapses no matter how well the optimiser is doing. Produce the diagnostic yourself: train GCNs of depth 1 through 10 on Cora with everything else fixed, plot test accuracy against depth (the peak is at 2 or 3 layers and the curve falls off a cliff by 6 or 7), and on the same axes plot a smoothing metric - mean pairwise cosine distance between final-layer node embeddings, or the row-wise variance of H^(L) - and show it collapsing toward zero as accuracy falls. Be able to separate over-smoothing from the confounds that travel with depth: more parameters (control by holding hidden width and total parameter count roughly fixed), vanishing gradients (check per-layer gradient norms as in Topic 110), and plain overfitting (train accuracy stays high under overfitting but falls too under over-smoothing).

resource.label: Li, Han and Wu - Deeper Insights into Graph Convolutional Networks for Semi-Supervised Learning (arXiv:1801.07606)

subtopics.name: Depth remedies, and the SGC ablation that asks whether the nonlinearity earns its keep
subtopics.learn: Know the four families of fix and what each actually does: residual/initial-residual connections and jumping-knowledge concatenation of intermediate layers (keep a path back to the un-smoothed features), PairNorm (rescale so that total pairwise squared distance between node embeddings is preserved across layers, which prevents convergence to a point without forbidding useful smoothing), DropEdge (randomly drop a fraction of edges each epoch, which slows the convergence rate of the smoothing and acts as a data augmentation), and simply not going deep - the correct answer for most 2-hop enterprise tasks. Then run the ablation that keeps you honest: Simplifying Graph Convolutional Networks strips out every nonlinearity to give Y = softmax(S^K X Theta) with S = D~^-1/2 A~ D~^-1/2, a plain logistic regression on K-times-propagated features, and matches GCN on Cora, CiteSeer and Pubmed while training orders of magnitude faster. If SGC ties your GCN on the customer's graph, the propagation is doing the work and the deep model is a liability you now have to operate.

resource.label: Zhao and Akoglu - PairNorm: Tackling Oversmoothing in GNNs (arXiv:1909.12223)
