subtopics.name: Over-squashing: exponential receptive fields compressed into a fixed vector
subtopics.learn: Distinguish the second depth pathology sharply from the first: over-smoothing is representations becoming uniform with depth; over-squashing is that the number of nodes in an L-hop receptive field grows exponentially while the node vector stays a fixed d dimensions, so information from distant nodes is compressed to nothing through graph bottlenecks. Learn the diagnostic signature - the problem radius exceeds 2 or 3, training accuracy itself stays low even with more parameters and no regularisation, and the failure concentrates on node pairs separated by a bottleneck edge - and reproduce it on the NeighborsMatch synthetic task where accuracy falls off a cliff as the required radius grows. Know why adding layers does not fix it and can make it worse, and know the remedies that change topology rather than depth: a fully-adjacent final layer, curvature-based or expander rewiring, virtual/global nodes, and graph transformers with global attention. The customer-facing version: if the signal is 5 hops away in a graph with hubs, a stack of GCN layers is the wrong tool and no hyperparameter search will rescue it.

resource.label: Alon and Yahav - On the Bottleneck of Graph Neural Networks and its Practical Implications (arXiv:2006.05205)

subtopics.name: Scaling past full-batch: neighbour sampling, Cluster-GCN, GraphSAINT
subtopics.learn: Do the memory arithmetic first: full-batch training stores O(L * N * d) node activations plus O(L * E * d) per-edge messages in the gather-scatter formulation, so 2 layers over 5 million edges at d=256 in float32 is already tens of gigabytes and Cora-scale code does not port. Then know the three mini-batching strategies and their distinct biases. Neighbour sampling (NeighborLoader with num_neighbors=[15, 10]) samples a bounded k-hop subgraph per seed node but suffers neighbour explosion with depth and gives a biased/stochastic estimate of the full aggregation. Cluster-GCN partitions the graph with METIS and trains on intra-cluster subgraphs, which is memory-flat and fast but drops every inter-cluster edge during training - a systematic bias if the customer's fraud rings straddle partitions. GraphSAINT samples subgraphs and applies normalisation coefficients so the estimator stays unbiased. In every case, inference must use full neighbourhoods (layer-wise inference) or you ship train/serve skew, and the sampled loader must never sample edges the label depends on.

resource.label: PyTorch Geometric tutorial - Scaling GNNs via Neighbor Sampling

subtopics.name: Heterogeneous and relational graphs: mapping a CRM/transaction schema onto R-GCN
subtopics.learn: Take the customer schema literally - accounts, users, transactions, products, tickets - and make the modelling decisions explicit: which tables become node types, which foreign keys become edge types, and whether an entity with its own attributes (a transaction with amount, timestamp, channel) should be an edge with features or a node of its own connected to payer and payee (usually a node, because an edge cannot easily carry a rich feature vector into every layer). Then implement the relational update h_i' = sigma(sum over relations r of sum over j in N_i^r of (1/c_{i,r}) W_r h_j + W_0 h_i), and know why the naive version explodes: one d-by-d matrix per relation times hundreds of foreign keys is a parameter count that overfits instantly, which is what basis decomposition (share a small set of basis matrices across relations) and block-diagonal decomposition exist to fix. Handle the practical issues an enterprise graph always has: different node types with different feature dimensions (project each type to a shared d first), extreme degree skew (one product node connected to a million users - cap or sample), and bipartite user-product structure. Write down the node/edge/graph-level task statement for the customer graph before any code.

resource.label: Schlichtkrull et al. - Modeling Relational Data with Graph Convolutional Networks (R-GCN) (arXiv:1703.06103)

subtopics.name: Link prediction: the message-passing/supervision edge split and ranking metrics
subtopics.learn: Learn the protocol that most implementations get wrong: the edge set must be partitioned into message-passing edges (used to build the adjacency for the forward pass) and supervision edges (scored by the loss), and a positive supervision edge must be removed from the adjacency, otherwise the model reads the answer off its own input and offline AUC goes to 0.99 while production is random. Implement scoring as a decoder over the two node embeddings (dot product, or an MLP on the concatenation, or DistMult for typed relations) with binary cross-entropy against sampled negatives, and know that the negative sampling ratio and the sampling distribution (uniform over all pairs versus degree-proportional versus hard negatives) change AUC and average precision by tens of points, so it must be reported. Prefer ranking metrics against a fixed candidate set - Hits@K and MRR - to a raw ROC-AUC computed against one negative per positive, because a graph with 10^10 candidate pairs and 10^6 real edges makes any balanced-sample AUC meaningless. Always report the heuristic baselines (common neighbours, Adamic-Adar, preferential attachment); SEAL's contribution is showing a GNN over the enclosing subgraph can learn those heuristics and more, not that it always beats them.

resource.label: Zhang and Chen - Link Prediction Based on Graph Neural Networks (SEAL) (arXiv:1802.09691)

subtopics.name: Fraud and AML on transaction graphs: temporal splits, imbalance, and the tabular baseline that wins
subtopics.learn: Study the Elliptic Bitcoin case as the template for enterprise graph work: about 203k transaction nodes over 49 time steps, roughly 2 percent labelled illicit and 21 percent licit with the rest unknown, so accuracy is a useless metric and you report precision, recall and F1 on the illicit class or PR-AUC. Take the two findings seriously - a random forest on node features is competitive with or better than a GCN, and concatenating GCN embeddings into the random forest helps - because that is the shape of most real engagements and it is a far more defensible thing to present than a GNN that lost. Enforce the temporal discipline: split by time step (train on t <= T, test on t > T), and check that message passing at prediction time never aggregates edges with a later timestamp, because a random split lets tomorrow's transactions explain today's and yields a beautiful number that evaporates. Note the dark-market shutdown in the Elliptic timeline where every model's performance drops - the concrete lesson that a graph model degrades under distribution shift and needs monitoring on a rolling time window, not a one-off holdout.

resource.label: Weber et al. - Anti-Money Laundering in Bitcoin: Graph Convolutional Networks for Financial Forensics (arXiv:1908.02591)

subtopics.name: Explaining a node prediction, and what attention weights do not prove
subtopics.learn: Know what GNNExplainer optimises: a soft mask over edges (and optionally node features) in the L-hop computation subgraph, learned by maximising the mutual information between the prediction on the masked subgraph and the original prediction, with size and entropy regularisers to force a small, near-binary mask - the output is a compact subgraph plus feature subset for one node, which is exactly the artefact a fraud analyst can act on. Be able to state its limits before the customer finds them: the mask is learned per instance and is not unique, the regularisation strength trades faithfulness for readability, and it explains the fitted model rather than the world (the causal caveats from Topic 97 and the estimand discipline from Topic 107 apply unchanged). Separately, refuse the tempting shortcut: attention coefficients from GAT are not an explanation - they are one head of one layer, they are not identifiable, and by the GATv2 result a plain GAT may be ranking neighbours identically for every query node. If you visualise attention for a node's neighbourhood, label it as a diagnostic of the model, not as evidence about the account.

resource.label: Ying et al. - GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks (arXiv:1903.03894)

outcomes: You can derive the GCN propagation rule from the first-order Chebyshev approximation on a whiteboard, write the per-node form h_i' = sigma(sum_j 1/sqrt(d~_i d~_j) W h_j), and justify symmetric normalisation over unnormalised sum and over row-stochastic mean in terms of activation scale, symmetry and the spectrum of the propagation operator.

You can implement GCN and GAT layers from a raw (2, E) edge_index using gather plus index_add_ with a segmented, max-shifted neighbourhood softmax, match torch_geometric.nn.GCNConv and GATConv within atol=1e-6, and pass torch.autograd.gradcheck in float64 on a toy graph.

You can produce a depth-versus-accuracy curve on Cora alongside a measured smoothing statistic, and state from those two plots whether a failing 8-layer model is suffering over-smoothing, over-squashing, vanishing gradients or ordinary overfitting - and name the fix for each.

You can compute edge homophily on a customer graph and report a GNN result only alongside an MLP-on-features baseline, a label-propagation baseline and a Correct-and-Smooth baseline, each as mean plus standard deviation over at least 10 random splits and seeds.

You can take an enterprise schema of accounts, users, transactions and products and write, in under a page, the node and edge types, the task level, the exact label and its timestamp, the time-respecting split, and whether GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT or R-GCN is the right shape with a reason for each rejection.

You can set up a link-prediction experiment with a correct message-passing/supervision edge partition, a stated negative-sampling scheme, Hits@K and MRR against a fixed candidate set, and common-neighbour and Adamic-Adar baselines - and demonstrate the inflated AUC you get when supervision edges are left in the adjacency.

You can size a GNN for a customer's hardware: state the activation and message memory as a function of N, E, d and L, choose between full-batch, NeighborLoader, Cluster-GCN and GraphSAINT, name the bias each sampling scheme introduces, and explain why inference must use full neighbourhoods.

You can explain to a non-ML stakeholder, in two minutes, why a message-passing GNN cannot count triangles, what that means for their circular-payment fraud pattern, and which added structural feature makes the pattern learnable.
failureModes: deg.pow(-0.5) is applied without masking degree-zero nodes, so isolated accounts in the customer extract produce inf, the scatter turns inf*0 into NaN, the loss is NaN by the second epoch, and three hours go into lowering the learning rate before anyone prints the degree histogram.

The customer's undirected relationship table is loaded into edge_index in one direction only; message passing is silently directed, half the neighbourhood never contributes, accuracy sits four to six points below the published number, and it gets debugged as a hyperparameter problem for a week.

GAT's softmax is computed over all E edges instead of segmented by destination node; the code runs, the loss decreases, the attention coefficients sum to one across the entire graph rather than per neighbourhood, and the model quietly degenerates to a degree-weighted average.

Link prediction is evaluated with positive supervision edges still present in the adjacency used for message passing; the model reads the label off its own input, offline ROC-AUC is 0.99, and the deployed recommender performs at chance.

A fraud graph is split uniformly at random rather than by time, so message passing at training time aggregates transactions that had not happened yet; PR-AUC on the holdout is excellent, the live model catches nothing, and the postmortem blames data drift rather than the split.

A two-layer GCN reports 98 percent accuracy on a 2-percent-positive AML graph and is presented as a success; a constant predict-licit baseline scores 98 percent too, and nobody computed precision and recall on the illicit class.

Depth-versus-accuracy falls off after three layers, the team reads it as overfitting and increases dropout and weight decay; training accuracy is also falling because the representations are over-smoothed, so the regularisation makes it strictly worse and the real fix - fewer layers plus a jumping-knowledge or residual path - is never tried.

Cluster-GCN with METIS partitioning trains on intra-cluster edges only while inference uses full neighbourhoods, so the serving-time aggregation is over a distribution the model never saw; the offline validation number was computed on the same truncated graph and did not catch it.

A GAT attention heat map is shown to a customer's analysts as evidence that the model focuses on a particular counterparty; the weights are from one head of one layer, are not identifiable, and by the GATv2 static-attention result the same neighbour may be ranked top for every node in the graph.
interviewQuestions: Derive the GCN layer from the spectral formulation: start at L_sym = I - D^-1/2 A D^-1/2, take the first-order Chebyshev approximation, and get to D~^-1/2 A~ D~^-1/2 H W. Then tell me exactly what the renormalisation trick buys you and what goes wrong with plain mean aggregation instead.

Implement a GCN layer on a whiteboard given only edge_index of shape (2, E) and a feature matrix X, with no library layers. Where does the degree normalisation come from, what happens to a node of degree zero, and how would you change your code to make it a GAT layer?

A customer's GCN gets 79 percent at two layers, 76 at four and 41 at eight. Walk me through how you decide whether this is over-smoothing, over-squashing, vanishing gradients or overfitting. What do you measure, what plot do you produce, and what is the fix in each case?

Design: a bank gives you accounts, users, transactions and products across four tables, and wants to flag accounts likely to be mules within the next 30 days. Define the graph, the task level, the label and its timestamp, the split, the metric, the baselines you must beat, and whether you would reach for GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT or R-GCN - and why you rejected the other three.

Explain why a message-passing GNN is bounded by the 1-WL test. Give me two non-isomorphic graphs it cannot tell apart, and tell me what that implies for detecting a circular-payment ring - including what you would add to the input to make the pattern learnable.

Your team reports 0.99 ROC-AUC on link prediction for a product recommender and it performs at chance in the pilot. List the three most likely causes in order, say how you would test each in under an hour, and describe the evaluation protocol you would have insisted on instead.

The customer's graph has 40 million edges and will not fit in GPU memory full-batch. Compare neighbour sampling, Cluster-GCN and GraphSAINT: what bias does each introduce, how does each interact with the depth you need, and what has to change at inference time so that serving matches training?
118.proofOfWork: A public repo `gnn-baseline-gauntlet` that turns the honesty rules of this topic into a harness anyone can run on a new graph. It takes a graph in one canonical form (edge_index, node features, labels, an optional per-edge timestamp) and produces a single report: measured edge homophily and degree distribution; a leaderboard of MLP-on-features, label propagation, Correct-and-Smooth, SGC, your from-scratch GCN, your from-scratch GAT, GATv2 and GraphSAGE, each reported as mean plus standard deviation over 10 random splits by 10 seeds under an equal hyperparameter budget, with the Shchur-style caveat printed at the top; a depth sweep from 1 to 10 layers plotting test accuracy against a measured over-smoothing statistic on shared axes; and a numerical-equivalence section showing your hand-written layers matching torch_geometric.nn.GCNConv and GATConv to atol=1e-6 plus a passing float64 gradcheck. Add a `leakage_check` module that refuses to run when it detects the three traps - supervision edges present in the message-passing adjacency, edges with timestamps later than the label timestamp, and a random split on a graph that carries timestamps - each failing with a one-line explanation. Ship it with a two-page memo aimed at a customer architect that applies the harness to a synthetic CRM/transaction graph, states the node and edge types, the task level and split, and concludes with an explicit recommendation - including the case where the recommendation is a gradient-boosted tree on graph-derived aggregate features rather than a GNN at all.

12.topic: Restricted-network delivery: offline install bundle, registry mirroring, private CA trust
12.why: The customers who pay for forward-deployed engineers - defence, banks, hospitals, utilities, anyone with a classified or PCI enclave - are precisely the customers whose clusters cannot reach docker.io, whose TLS is intercepted by a corporate CA, and whose registry intake process takes two weeks. Every fast path you rely on at home (helm repo add, pip install, docker pull, a curl | bash installer, Let's Encrypt, a telemetry endpoint) is a hard failure there, and you usually discover which one you forgot while sitting in a windowless room with no way to fetch the missing byte. Getting this right is the difference between a one-day install and a three-week engagement that burns the customer's trust before the product has done anything, and it is one of the few skills that visibly separates an FDE from a strong platform engineer who has only ever deployed to their own cloud account.
prerequisites: Container internals and the registry model: layers, manifests, tags vs digests, docker/ctr/crictl (Topic 5, Docker internals)
Building production images and supply-chain hygiene: multi-stage builds, non-root, SBOM generation, image signing (Topic 6)
Kubernetes core objects plus real debugging reflexes - kubectl describe, events, kubelet logs, Secrets and ServiceAccounts (Topics 7 and 8)
Helm chart anatomy: values, templates, subcharts, hooks, and ArgoCD sync basics (Topic 9, GitOps)
TLS chain of trust end to end: root vs intermediate, SNI, verification failures, and DNS resolution order (Topic 2, Networking)
Hardened bash - set -Eeuo pipefail, traps, retries, idempotency (Topic 0) - because install.sh is the shipped artifact and the customer will read it line by line
A Linux VM you can wreck (multipass, UTM, Lima or a throwaway EC2 instance) plus a local registry (registry:2 or Harbor) and nftables/iptables access to drop egress

subtopics.name: Classify the restriction before you build anything
subtopics.learn: "Restricted network" covers four regimes with different bundles: full egress through an explicit proxy doing TLS interception; allowlist egress where only named FQDNs resolve and everything else is RST or blackholed; mirror-only, where there is no internet but an internal Harbor/Artifactory/Nexus somebody else populates; and a true air gap where bits arrive on removable media or through a one-way transfer with an approval queue. Before writing a line, get written answers to: which registries resolve from which nodes, is TLS intercepted and can we have the CA PEM, who owns the internal registry and what is the intake SLA, what OS/arch/kernel/container runtime the nodes run, whether DNS is restricted to an internal resolver, and the maximum single-file size and cadence of the media transfer. Put those in the site survey (Topic 73) and re-verify on site, because "we have a mirror" routinely means "we have a Nexus nobody has push rights to for two weeks".

resource.label: Zarf - the air-gap delivery problem and package model (README)

subtopics.name: OCI image layout, digests and content addressing
subtopics.learn: Learn what an image is on disk: an `oci-layout` marker file, `index.json` pointing at manifests (`application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json`), each manifest naming a config blob and layer blobs stored once under `blobs/sha256/<hex>`. `skopeo copy docker://ghcr.io/org/app:1.4.2 oci:./bundle/images:app:1.4.2` produces exactly that layout, whereas `docker save` produces the older Docker archive format that loses index-level multi-arch and annotations - use the OCI layout so the bundle is a registry you can inspect with standard tools. Because everything is content-addressed, blobs shared across ten images are stored once, which is why a whole-platform layout is routinely 40 percent of the naive sum of `docker pull` sizes. Internalise the rule that a tag is mutable and a digest is not: the bundle manifest records `image@sha256:...` for every component, the install pushes and pins by digest, and the customer's registry therefore cannot serve something different under the same tag.

resource.label: OCI Image Format Specification - Image Layout

subtopics.name: Multi-arch image indexes and platform selection
subtopics.learn: An image index (`application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json`) lists per-platform manifests with `platform.os`, `platform.architecture` and `variant`; a plain `docker pull` on an Apple Silicon laptop silently selects `linux/arm64` while the customer's nodes are `linux/amd64`. Decide explicitly whether the bundle carries every architecture or exactly one, using `skopeo copy --all` or `--override-os linux --override-arch amd64`, and prove what you captured with `skopeo inspect --raw docker://ref | jq '.manifests[].platform'` or `crane manifest`. Know that buildx attestation manifests appear in the index as `unknown/unknown` entries and that some registries and older Harbor versions choke on them, so strip or carry them deliberately rather than by accident.

resource.label: OCI Image Format Specification - Image Index

subtopics.name: Relocating images with skopeo (and crane as the second opinion)
subtopics.learn: `skopeo copy --all --retry-times 5 docker://src oci:./bundle/images:name:tag` pulls without a docker daemon; `skopeo sync --src yaml --dest dir images.yaml ./bundle` drives a whole list from a file you can diff in review. Learn the flags that matter under pressure: `--authfile` / `--src-authfile` / `--dest-authfile` for per-side credentials, `--src-cert-dir` and `--dest-cert-dir` for a private CA, `--format oci|v2s2`, and `--preserve-digests`, which makes the copy fail loudly rather than silently re-encode a manifest and change its digest - a changed digest breaks every pinned reference and every signature downstream. `--dest-tls-verify=false` belongs in a lab and nowhere else. Keep `crane digest`, `crane manifest` and `crane copy` in your pocket as an independent implementation for verifying that what landed in the customer's registry is byte-identical to what left your build.

resource.label: skopeo-copy(1) man page

subtopics.name: Enumerating every image reference the install will pull
subtopics.learn: Start with `helm template rel ./chart -f prod-values.yaml | yq '.. | .image? // empty' | sort -u`, then treat that output as a hypothesis, not an inventory: it misses initContainers behind a condition, sidecars injected by a mutating webhook (Istio, Vault agent, a logging agent), images named inside CRs that an operator resolves at runtime, Helm hook Jobs, images that only appear when a feature flag is on, and defaults in subcharts you never templated. Also enumerate non-image pulls the app performs at runtime - model weights, tokenizer files, pip or npm packages fetched by an entrypoint, a `busybox` in a debug script, browser binaries. Get ground truth by running the install in a lab cluster whose containerd points at a logging pull-through proxy and diffing the proxy access log against your list; the log is truth, and the delta is exactly the set of images that would have failed at the customer.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs - Images (names, tags, digests, pull policy)

subtopics.name: Vendoring the chart and its dependency tree
subtopics.learn: `helm dependency update` resolves `dependencies:` into `charts/*.tgz` and writes `Chart.lock` with the resolved versions and a digest of the repository index; commit both and ship `charts/` inside the bundle so the install never resolves a repo. Know the difference between `helm dependency build` (install exactly what the lock says - what CI and the bundle build should run) and `helm dependency update` (re-resolve, which is a deliberate change), plus `condition:`, `tags:`, `alias:` for two copies of one subchart, and `import-values` for values that flow upward. Publish the chart itself as an OCI artifact into the customer's registry (`helm push app-1.4.2.tgz oci://reg.customer.internal/charts`) so their GitOps controller (Topic 9) references a repository they own and can restore from, rather than a public URL that will be unreachable the day they need to roll back.

resource.label: Helm docs - helm dependency update

subtopics.name: Rewriting image references so nothing points at the public internet
subtopics.learn: `global.imageRegistry` only works when every subchart reads it; most third-party charts hardcode `image.repository: docker.io/library/redis`, so plan for escalating mechanisms: per-subchart values overrides, a Helm `--post-renderer` that runs kustomize with an `images:` transformer over the rendered output, a full kustomize overlay, or a cluster-wide mutating admission policy that rewrites `.spec.containers[*].image` prefixes for anything the chart cannot reach. Rewrite to digests, not tags (`repository: reg.customer.internal/platform/redis`, `tag: ""`, `digest: sha256:...`), so the pinning survives a mutable tag in their registry. Then make it enforceable: a conftest/OPA or simple `grep -v` gate in CI that fails the build if any rendered manifest references a registry host outside the customer's namespace - that assertion, not your diligence, is what catches the one forgotten sidecar.

resource.label: Helm docs - Subcharts and Global Values

subtopics.name: Pushing into the customer's registry: the distribution API and its politics
subtopics.learn: Know the wire protocol well enough to debug it with curl: `GET /v2/` for the version check and auth challenge, `POST /v2/<name>/blobs/uploads/` then a monolithic or chunked `PATCH`/`PUT` for blobs, `HEAD /v2/<name>/blobs/<digest>` to skip a blob that already exists (and cross-repo mount to avoid re-uploading), `PUT /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` last because a manifest referencing a missing blob is rejected. The token flow is a 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm=...,service=...,scope=repository:x:pull,push`, then a token fetch - so a 401 on push usually means scope, not password. Negotiate the non-technical half before install day: project/namespace to push into, a robot account with push scope, storage quota, whether tag immutability or a mandatory vulnerability-scan gate will reject your push, whether the registry accepts OCI index and artifact media types, and retention rules that might garbage-collect your images after 30 days.

resource.label: OCI Distribution Specification

subtopics.name: containerd registry configuration: certs.d and hosts.toml
subtopics.learn: Modern containerd reads per-registry config from `config_path = "/etc/containerd/certs.d"` set under `[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".registry]` in `/etc/containerd/config.toml`; each host gets `/etc/containerd/certs.d/<host>/hosts.toml` with `server = "https://reg.customer.internal"`, a `[host."https://reg.customer.internal/v2"]` block with `capabilities = ["pull", "resolve"]`, `ca = "/etc/ssl/certs/customer-ca.pem"`, optional `client` mTLS pairs, `skip_verify` (never in production) and `override_path = true` when the mirror serves under a nested path. Critically, once `config_path` is set the legacy `[registry.mirrors]` entries in config.toml are ignored entirely, which is the single most common reason an edit "does nothing". Restart containerd, then verify through the path the kubelet actually uses - `crictl pull` and `ctr -n k8s.io images pull` - because a successful `docker pull` on the same node proves nothing about the CRI runtime's configuration.

resource.label: containerd docs - Registry Configuration (hosts.toml)

subtopics.name: K3s/RKE2 registries.yaml, rewrites, and preloading images onto nodes
subtopics.learn: `/etc/rancher/k3s/registries.yaml` takes `mirrors:` (endpoint lists plus `rewrite:` regex rules such as `"^library/(.*)": "mirror/library/$1"` for registries that require a project prefix) and `configs:` (per-host `auth:` and `tls: { ca_file, cert_file, key_file, insecure_skip_verify }`); k3s renders it into containerd's hosts.toml at startup, so it takes effect only after `systemctl restart k3s`, and only on nodes where the file exists - it must be in your node bootstrap, not applied by hand. Break the bootstrap chicken-and-egg by preloading tarballs: drop images in `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/images/*.tar` or run `ctr -n k8s.io images import`, which is how the in-cluster registry's own image gets onto a node before any registry exists. Decide and document which images are preloaded versus pulled, because a node that joins the cluster three months after your visit will have neither unless the bootstrap does it.

resource.label: K3s docs - Private Registry Configuration (registries.yaml)

subtopics.name: Pull secrets, pull policy and reading pull failures precisely
subtopics.learn: A `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` Secret (`kubectl create secret docker-registry`) is namespaced: a chart that installs into three namespaces needs three copies, and a namespace created later by an operator will fail to pull unless you patch its default ServiceAccount's `imagePullSecrets` or use a cluster-wide mechanism. `imagePullPolicy: Always` on a node holding preloaded images and no reachable registry is a guaranteed outage after any reschedule, and a `:latest` tag implies `Always` by default - use `IfNotPresent` with digest pins. Learn to read the failure at the right layer: `ErrImagePull` with `x509` means trust, with `401` means credentials or scope, with `404`/`manifest unknown` means a wrong repository path or a rewrite rule, `exec format error` after a successful pull means architecture, and `ImagePullBackOff` is just the backoff wrapper - go to `kubectl describe pod` events first, then `journalctl -u kubelet` or `crictl pull` on the node for the underlying error string.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs - Pull an Image from a Private Registry

subtopics.name: System trust stores: where a private CA actually has to land
subtopics.learn: On Debian/Ubuntu the root PEM goes in `/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/customer-ca.crt` followed by `update-ca-certificates`, which regenerates `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` and the symlink farm; on RHEL family it is `/etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/customer-ca.pem` plus `update-ca-trust`, producing `/etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem`. Containers do not inherit the host store: your image needs the `ca-certificates` package plus the PEM baked or mounted, distroless and scratch images need the bundle copied to `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` explicitly, and Alpine needs `apk add ca-certificates` before `update-ca-certificates` does anything. Verify rather than assume with `openssl verify -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt server.pem` and `trust list | grep -i customer`, and check the chain has the intermediate - a bundle missing it works in a browser (which fetches via AIA) and fails in Go and Python, which do not.

resource.label: update-ca-certificates(8) - Debian manual page

subtopics.name: TLS-intercepting proxies: diagnosis, error signatures and proxy plumbing
subtopics.learn: Prove interception before arguing about it: `openssl s_client -connect reg.customer.internal:443 -servername reg.customer.internal -showcerts </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -subject -dates` and read the issuer - a corporate "SSL inspection" CA in the chain means every client must trust it and no amount of vendor pinning will survive. Memorise the error signatures so you can localise in seconds: `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` is Go (containerd, kubectl, helm, most CLIs), `SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` is Python, `unable to get local issuer certificate` is curl/OpenSSL, `SELF_SIGNED_CERT_IN_CHAIN` or `UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY` is Node/npm, `tls: failed to verify certificate` is newer Go. Plumb the proxy deliberately: `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`NO_PROXY` are honoured by Go and curl but daemons need a systemd drop-in (`/etc/systemd/system/containerd.service.d/http-proxy.conf` plus `systemctl daemon-reload`), and `NO_PROXY` matching is host-suffix based with only partial CIDR support - so `.svc`, `.cluster.local`, the node and pod CIDRs, the registry host and `169.254.169.254` must be listed explicitly or in-cluster traffic gets shipped to a proxy that rejects it. Treat `insecure_skip_verify`, `--insecure` and `strict-ssl=false` as findings for the customer's next audit, not fixes.

resource.label: openssl-s_client(1) - OpenSSL 3.0 manual

subtopics.name: Python offline: wheelhouse, hashes and certificate configuration
subtopics.learn: Build the wheelhouse on a machine matching the target: `pip download -r requirements.txt --only-binary=:all: --platform manylinux2014_x86_64 --python-version 3.11 --implementation cp --abi cp311 -d wheels/` (the `--platform` flags require `--only-binary=:all:` because cross-platform source builds are impossible), then install with `pip install --no-index --find-links=wheels/ -r requirements.txt`. Pin with `pip-compile --generate-hashes` and install with `--require-hashes` so the bundle's dependency set is verifiable by the customer's security team rather than trusted. For trust, know that requests/pip use `certifi`'s private bundle and ignore the OS store unless told: set `pip config set global.cert /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` or `PIP_CERT`, and `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` / `SSL_CERT_FILE` for the application at runtime; `--trusted-host` disables verification and is a last resort. Hunt down packages that fetch at first use - tiktoken encodings, HuggingFace weights, nltk corpora, playwright browsers, spaCy models - and bake their caches (`HF_HOME`, `TIKTOKEN_CACHE_DIR`, `XDG_CACHE_HOME`) into the bundle or image.

resource.label: pip docs - HTTPS Certificates

subtopics.name: Node, npm and Go: trust configuration and offline installs
subtopics.learn: npm: `npm config set cafile /etc/ssl/certs/customer-ca.pem` replaces the bundled CA list rather than adding to it, so `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/etc/ssl/certs/customer-ca.pem` is usually the correct knob for both npm and the running Node process; set `registry=` to the customer's Nexus/Artifactory group, and never `strict-ssl=false`. Ship dependencies offline with a pre-populated cache (`npm ci --cache ./npm-cache` on a connected box, then `npm ci --offline --cache ./npm-cache` inside the enclave) or vendored `npm pack` tarballs plus a `.npmrc` pointing at a local file path; `npm ci` requires `package-lock.json` and fails on drift, which is exactly the behaviour a bundle needs. Go-built tooling - helm, kubectl, containerd, argocd, terraform providers - uses `crypto/x509.SystemCertPool`, honouring `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR` on Linux, which is why they all emit the same `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` and why fixing the OS trust store fixes all of them at once.

resource.label: npm docs - config (cafile, strict-ssl, registry, cache)

subtopics.name: git across the gap: bundles, TLS config and the GitOps source of truth
subtopics.learn: Configure trust per host rather than globally where you can: `git config --global http.https://git.customer.internal/.sslCAInfo /etc/ssl/certs/customer-ca.pem`, or `GIT_SSL_CAINFO` in the environment, plus `http.proxy` when the proxy is explicit; `http.sslVerify=false` is a finding, not a fix, and on RHEL the curl backend can behave differently from your laptop's. Move repositories across a true air gap with `git bundle create repo.bundle --all`, verify on the far side with `git bundle verify` and clone straight from the file, then keep day-2 transfers small with incremental bundles (`git bundle create delta.bundle v1.4.2..HEAD`) that apply onto a known base commit. Decide up front what the customer's GitOps controller points at - an internal git server fed by bundles, or a repo they own that you push to during visits - because ArgoCD with an unreachable upstream degrades into a cluster nobody can safely change.

resource.label: git-bundle documentation

subtopics.name: Bundle layout, determinism and transport
subtopics.learn: Lay the tarball out so a stranger can audit it: `manifest.json` (bundle version, build timestamp, git SHA, every image ref with its digest, chart version, tool versions), `images/` as an OCI layout, `charts/`, `wheels/`, `npm/`, `bin/`, `install.sh`, `CHECKSUMS.sha256`. Make the build reproducible - `tar --sort=name --mtime=@${SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH} --owner=0 --group=0 --numeric-owner --format=posix` with a fixed compression level - so two builds of the same commit yield the same sha256 and the customer's security team can independently confirm what you shipped matches your public release. Plan transport as a real constraint: an 8 GB bundle crossing a one-way transfer with a 4 GB per-file limit means `split -b 3G` plus a documented reassembly and checksum step at both ends, because the classic failure is a silently truncated copy that only surfaces halfway through the install.

resource.label: Reproducible Builds - Archive metadata (deterministic tar)

subtopics.name: Signing and verifying with no internet
subtopics.learn: Sign both the bundle and the images so verification never needs a callout: `cosign sign-blob --key cosign.key --output-signature bundle.tar.zst.sig bundle.tar.zst` verified with `cosign verify-blob --key cosign.pub`, and `cosign sign --key cosign.key <image@digest>` for what lands in the customer's registry. Keyless/Fulcio signing does not work in an air gap because it needs an OIDC provider and a Rekor log, so ship a static public key (and document its fingerprint out of band) or carry an offline verification bundle deliberately. Signatures live as separate registry tags of the form `sha256-<digest>.sig`, so a plain `skopeo copy` of `:tag` leaves them behind and the customer's Kyverno or sigstore policy controller then rejects every pod at admission - use `cosign copy` (or copy the `.sig`/`.att` tags explicitly) when relocating. Carry the SBOM (syft) and an offline vulnerability database (`grype db import`, or trivy's offline DB bundle) so their scan gate can run inside the enclave instead of blocking your install.

resource.label: cosign save - moving images and signatures offline

subtopics.name: install.sh as the product: preflight, idempotence, resumability, rollback
subtopics.learn: The script is what the customer's engineer reads over your shoulder and attaches to a change ticket, so write it accordingly: `set -Eeuo pipefail`, a `--dry-run` that prints every push and every helm command without executing, and secrets read from a file or prompt rather than argv. Preflight must fail fast with actionable text: registry reachable and writable (do a one-blob test push, not a ping), kubectl context and version skew, storage class present, CA present in the node trust store, disk space for the image import, node architecture matching the bundle, and no conflicting release or CRD version already installed. The body pushes images by digest, pushes the chart, then `helm upgrade --install --atomic --timeout 15m --wait` so a failed rollout rolls back instead of leaving half a platform, followed by postflight checks (all Deployments available, a real smoke request through the ingress). Make it resumable and idempotent: skip blobs that `HEAD /v2/.../blobs/<digest>` reports present, checkpoint progress to a state file so a 40-minute push interrupted by a dropped VPN continues, and make a re-run against a healthy install a no-op that exits 0.

resource.label: Helm docs - helm install (--atomic, --wait, --timeout)

subtopics.name: The blocked-egress rehearsal, and planning day two before you leave
subtopics.learn: Rehearse on a fresh VM with egress actually dropped rather than assumed: an nftables output chain that permits only the internal registry and resolver (`nft add rule inet filter output ip daddr != { 10.0.0.0/8, 127.0.0.0/8 } counter drop`), DNS pointed at an internal resolver only, then run the install from a clean checkout and record it end to end. Prove the claim with evidence the customer's security team accepts: `tcpdump -n 'not net 10.0.0.0/8'` and the nftables drop counters across the whole run should show zero outbound attempts; every hit is a hidden dependency - a telemetry endpoint, an OCSP/CRL fetch, an operator's default catalog, a `raw.githubusercontent.com` URL in a Helm hook. Then plan day two before you fly home: delta bundles carrying only changed blobs, a rehearsed `helm rollback` path, expiry dates for the CA and registry robot credentials written into the runbook, registry garbage collection so their disk does not fill, and an explicit support/version-skew policy (Topic 78) for how far behind their install may drift between transfers.

outcomes: You can install the full platform on a fresh VM with all egress dropped, from one tarball, and produce packet-capture and nftables counter evidence that zero outbound connections were attempted during the run.
You can relocate every image a chart pulls into an OCI layout and then into a private registry by digest, and prove with skopeo inspect and crane digest that no digest changed in transit.

You can configure containerd certs.d/hosts.toml and k3s registries.yaml for mirroring, path rewriting and a private CA, and demonstrate the kubelet pulling successfully via crictl on a node with no internet.

You can make containerd, helm, kubectl, curl, pip, npm and git all trust a private CA behind a TLS-intercepting proxy, and explain from memory where each toolchain reads its trust material and which environment variable overrides it.
You can enumerate every image an install pulls, cross-check helm template output against a pull-through proxy access log, and name the five classes of reference that templating alone misses.
You can produce byte-identical bundles from two builds of the same commit, sign the tarball and the images, and hand a customer a verification procedure that runs entirely inside their enclave.

You can diagnose an ImagePullBackOff in an enclave down to the exact layer - DNS, TCP, x509, 401 scope, 404 path rewrite, or architecture mismatch - in under ten minutes using describe, crictl, journalctl and openssl s_client.

You can write an install.sh that is dry-runnable, idempotent, resumable after a dropped connection, atomic on failure, and readable enough that the customer's platform engineer approves it in a change review.
failureModes: The bundle is built on an Apple Silicon laptop without --all or --override-arch, so every image is linux/arm64; pods on the customer's amd64 nodes crash with 'exec format error' and there is no path to rebuild from inside the enclave.

helm template missed an image injected by a mutating webhook and one Helm hook Job, so 95 percent of the install succeeds and then a single Job sits in ImagePullBackOff reaching for docker.io at 02:00 the night before go-live.

Images were relocated by copying tags only, leaving the sha256-<digest>.sig signature tags behind in the source registry; the customer's policy controller denies every pod at admission and the install looks like an RBAC problem for three hours.

The private CA was added to the host trust store and every host-level curl works, but the application container is distroless with a stale certifi bundle, so only the app's outbound HTTPS calls fail and the team spends a day chasing a phantom network issue.

registries.yaml was edited by hand on the control-plane node during the visit and never added to the node bootstrap; two months later autoscaling adds a worker that cannot pull anything, and nobody on site knows why that node is special.

imagePullPolicy stayed Always with a :latest tag while images were preloaded from tarballs, so the first node reboot after the bundle was deleted from disk turns a working cluster into a cluster that cannot start a single pod.

NO_PROXY omitted .svc, .cluster.local and the pod CIDR, so in-cluster and kubelet traffic was routed to the corporate proxy which rejected it, producing intermittent DNS and API-server timeouts that were escalated as a Kubernetes bug.

Someone unblocked the install with --insecure-skip-tls-verify and strict-ssl=false 'temporarily'; the settings shipped into the runbook, the customer's audit found them six months later, and the deployment was frozen pending remediation.
interviewQuestions: A customer has no egress, an internal Harbor nobody has push rights to yet, and a corporate CA that intercepts TLS. Design the delivery end to end: what your build pipeline emits, how bits cross the boundary, how images and charts get relocated, what has to change on the nodes, and how you prove to their security team that nothing phoned home.

Explain tags versus digests in a relocation, and why skopeo copy --preserve-digests matters. What specifically breaks if a digest changes during relocation, and what happens to cosign signatures when you copy an image between registries?

Debug live: pods are in ImagePullBackOff after a relocation to the customer's registry. Walk me through your layers of investigation and the exact command at each layer, and tell me which error string distinguishes a trust problem from a credentials-scope problem from a path-rewrite problem.

A chart has fourteen subcharts and only six honour global.imageRegistry. Give me three mechanisms to force every image reference to the customer's registry, ranked by how much you would want to explain them to their platform team, and say how you would prevent a regression in CI.

Everything works on the host - curl, docker pull, helm - but the Python service inside the pod cannot reach the customer's internal API over HTTPS. Walk me through the diagnosis and the fix, and explain why the host tests were misleading.

How do you ship a security patch into an air gap where transfers happen every four weeks and need approval? Describe the delta bundle, the upgrade and rollback procedure, and what support and version-skew policy you would commit to in writing.

The customer's security officer asks you to prove that your install performed no outbound network access. What evidence do you produce, how do you gather it, and what would you do if the capture showed a single unexpected connection two minutes into the run?
12.proofOfWork: A public `airgap-lab` repo that reproduces a hostile customer network on a laptop and lets anyone re-run your proof: a `make enclave` target that builds a two-node k3s VM pair (multipass or Lima) with an nftables output policy dropping everything except an internal CIDR, an internal Harbor and a git server on that CIDR, a self-signed corporate root CA plus a TLS-intercepting forward proxy in front of the only permitted egress path, and DNS restricted to the internal resolver. On top of it, a `make prove` target that installs the airgap-bundle release from the row's deliverable end to end and emits an evidence directory: the nftables drop counters and a tcpdump capture showing zero external attempts, `crictl pull` and `cosign verify` transcripts, a digest-comparison table between the bundle manifest and what Harbor actually stores, and the sha256 of two independent bundle builds from the same commit to demonstrate reproducibility. Include three deliberately broken branches - `broken/arch-mismatch`, `broken/missing-sidecar-image`, `broken/signatures-left-behind` - each with a recorded five-minute diagnosis walkthrough naming the exact command that localised the fault, plus a two-page RESTRICTED-NETWORK-RUNBOOK.md written for the customer's platform team covering CA and robot-credential expiry dates, the delta-bundle upgrade and rollback procedure, and registry garbage collection.

13.topic: Terraform: state, modules, workspaces, drift, CI
13.why: An FDE stands up the customer's environment on week one and hands it to their two-person platform team on week twelve; if the VPC, IAM roles and cluster were built by clicking, nobody can reproduce it in the second region, nobody can audit who changed the security group, and the hand-over is a screenshot deck. Terraform with remote state and plan-on-PR is how you turn 'trust me, it is configured' into a reviewable diff the customer's security team can sign, and how you avoid the two career-ending moments: applying dev code to their production account, and a plan that quietly says 'forces replacement' on the database. Senior FDE loops at Palantir, Anthropic and Databricks ask about state corruption, drift and blast radius because those are the incidents that actually happen at customer sites.

subtopics.name: init, providers, the dependency lock file, and the graph plan builds
subtopics.learn: `terraform init` resolves `required_providers` constraints (`~> 5.0` means >= 5.0, < 6.0), downloads provider binaries into `.terraform/providers/`, and writes `.terraform.lock.hcl` with `h1:` and `zh:` hashes per platform; commit the lock file, and run `terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64` so a lock generated on a Mac does not fail with a checksum error in Linux CI. Set `required_version` in a `terraform {}` block so a colleague on 1.5 cannot apply a config using 1.10 features. Plan builds a DAG from references (`aws_subnet.a.vpc_id` implies an edge) and explicit `depends_on`; render it with `terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > g.svg` and know the default `-parallelism=10` walks that graph concurrently. Understand 'known after apply': any attribute the provider only returns after creation is unknown at plan, and anything computed from it becomes unknown too.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Dependency Lock File

subtopics.name: Reading a plan like a reviewer: symbols, forces replacement, saved plans, exit codes
subtopics.learn: Know the six change markers cold: `+` create, `-` destroy, `~` update in place, `-/+` destroy then create, `+/-` create then destroy (create_before_destroy), `<=` read data source during apply. Every `-/+` line has a `# forces replacement` comment on the attribute responsible; that comment is the single most important line in any review. Use `terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform show -json tfplan | jq '[.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | index("delete"))] | length'` to fail CI on any destroy; a saved plan is a binary bound to the exact config, state serial and provider versions, and it contains sensitive values in plaintext. `-detailed-exitcode` returns 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes, which is what drift jobs key on. `-refresh=false` speeds a plan on a large state; `-target=module.network` is an emergency tool that leaves the rest of the graph unplanned and should never appear in CI; `-replace=aws_instance.bastion` is the modern `taint`.

resource.label: Terraform CLI: plan command

subtopics.name: State internals: what is in terraform.tfstate and why it exists
subtopics.learn: Open a real state file: `version: 4`, `terraform_version`, `serial` (monotonic counter, bumped on every write), `lineage` (UUID assigned at creation; a mismatch means two unrelated states), and `resources[]` each with `mode` (managed or data), `type`, `name`, `module`, `provider`, and `instances[]` carrying `schema_version`, `index_key`, `attributes`, `dependencies` and `sensitive_attributes`. State is the map from Terraform address to real-world ID plus a cache of last-known attributes; without it Terraform cannot tell 'create' from 'update'. Everything a provider returns lands in `attributes` in plaintext, including `random_password.result` and RDS master passwords. Practise `terraform state pull > backup.json` before any surgery and `terraform state push -force` only for a deliberate lineage or serial override. Hand-editing state is a last resort and requires bumping `serial`.

resource.label: Terraform docs: State purpose and structure

subtopics.name: S3 remote backend: locking, encryption, partial config and the bootstrap problem
subtopics.learn: Write `backend "s3" { bucket, key = "network/prod.tfstate", region, encrypt = true, kms_key_id, use_lockfile = true }` (1.10+ native S3 conditional-write locking creating `key.tflock`) or the older `dynamodb_table` with a `LockID` string hash key; `assume_role { role_arn }` inside the backend lets state live in a separate audit account. Backend blocks cannot reference variables, so use partial configuration: `terraform init -backend-config=envs/prod.s3.tfbackend`, and know `-migrate-state` (copy local to remote) versus `-reconfigure` (forget the old backend). The chicken-and-egg: the bucket must exist before the first init, so keep a tiny `bootstrap/` root with local state that creates the bucket with versioning (your only undo for a bad push), Block Public Access, SSE-KMS and a bucket policy denying `aws:SecureTransport = false`, then either import it or accept that one root is local. IAM for the CI role: `s3:ListBucket` on the bucket, `s3:GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject` on the state prefix, `kms:Decrypt/GenerateDataKey` on the key, and for DynamoDB `GetItem/PutItem/DeleteItem` on the lock table. 'Error acquiring the state lock' means a run is active or died; `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` only after confirming no apply is in flight.

resource.label: Terraform docs: S3 backend

subtopics.name: State surgery: state mv/rm/list/show, import blocks, moved and removed blocks
subtopics.learn: `terraform state list`, `terraform state show aws_vpc.main`, `terraform state mv 'module.old.aws_subnet.x[0]' 'module.net.aws_subnet.x["a"]'` (single-quote addresses so the shell leaves brackets alone), and `terraform state rm` to stop managing something without destroying it. Prefer declarative equivalents that go through code review: `moved { from = aws_instance.web  to = module.compute.aws_instance.web }` for zero-downtime refactors across module boundaries, `removed { from = aws_s3_bucket.logs  lifecycle { destroy = false } }` (1.7+), and `import { to = aws_vpc.main  id = "vpc-0abc123" }` (1.5+) combined with `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` to write the HCL for you. Import IDs are provider-specific and documented in the Import section of every resource page: an `aws_security_group_rule` ID is a composite string, an `aws_iam_role_policy_attachment` is `role-name/policy-arn`. The exit criterion for adoption is a plan that says 'No changes' with no `-target` and no `ignore_changes` hiding real differences.

resource.label: Terraform CLI: state subcommands

subtopics.name: Module design: structure, inputs as an API, pinned sources, no provider blocks inside
subtopics.learn: Standard layout: `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`, `versions.tf`, `README.md`, `examples/complete/`. Sources: registry `source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"  version = "~> 5.0"`, Git `source = "git::https://github.com/org/modules.git//vpc?ref=v1.4.0"` pinned to a tag or SHA and never a branch, local `./modules/x` for the same repo. A child module declares `required_providers` but never a `provider` block; the root passes providers with `providers = { aws = aws.us_west_2 }` and the child lists `configuration_aliases` when it needs more than one. Outputs are the module's contract: export IDs, ARNs and CIDRs, not whole resource objects, because whole objects leak schema changes to every consumer. Keep modules cohesive (one network, one cluster), refuse 80-variable 'wrapper' modules, and add `validation {}` blocks and `optional()` attributes with defaults so callers get an error at plan rather than an AWS API error at apply.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Creating Modules

subtopics.name: for_each versus count, dynamic blocks, and the index-shift trap
subtopics.learn: `count` produces list-indexed instances (`aws_subnet.private[0]`), so removing or reordering an element shifts every later index and the plan destroys and recreates them; `for_each` over a `map` or `set(string)` yields stable keys (`aws_subnet.private["eu-west-1a"]`). Build maps with `for_each = { for s in var.subnets : s.name => s }` and reference `each.key` and `each.value`. Keys must be known at plan time: `toset(aws_subnet.x[*].id)` fails with 'keys derived from resource attributes that cannot be determined until apply', so key on static names, not IDs. Convert `count` to `for_each` with one `moved` block per instance (`from = aws_subnet.private[0]  to = aws_subnet.private["a"]`) or the plan will be all destroys. `dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.rules  content { from_port = ingress.value.port ... } }` generates nested blocks; keep `try()`, `lookup()`, `one()` and `coalesce()` in reach for optional structure.

resource.label: Terraform docs: for_each meta-argument

subtopics.name: lifecycle meta-arguments and controlling replacement
subtopics.learn: `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` flips `-/+` to `+/-` so a replacement never leaves a gap, but it propagates to dependents and collides with fixed `name` values, so pair it with `name_prefix`. `prevent_destroy = true` makes any plan that would destroy the resource error out, including a full `terraform destroy`, and does nothing if the resource block itself is deleted from config. `ignore_changes = [tags["LastScanned"], desired_capacity]` is the fix for attributes owned by another controller (cluster autoscaler, a Lambda deploy pipeline, a security scanner adding tags). `replace_triggered_by = [terraform_data.revision]` recreates a resource when something unrelated changes; `terraform_data` is the built-in replacement for `null_resource`. `precondition` and `postcondition` blocks turn assumptions ('the AMI is x86_64', 'the subnet has an IPv4 CIDR') into plan-time errors with a readable message.

resource.label: Terraform docs: lifecycle meta-argument

subtopics.name: Variables, locals, outputs: precedence, type constraints, sensitive and ephemeral
subtopics.learn: Assignment precedence, lowest to highest: `TF_VAR_name` env vars, `terraform.tfvars`, `*.auto.tfvars` in lexical order, then `-var` and `-var-file` in command-line order. Write real types: `object({ cidr = string, azs = optional(list(string), []), nat = optional(bool, true) })` so callers get a type error rather than a silent default, and `validation { condition = can(cidrnetmask(var.cidr))  error_message = "cidr must be IPv4 CIDR" }`. `sensitive = true` redacts plan output and forces `sensitive = true` on any output that carries it, but the value is still in state; `ephemeral = true` (1.10+) is the flag that keeps a value out of state and plan files entirely. `terraform output -raw kubeconfig > ~/.kube/config` and `terraform output -json` are the CI-facing forms. Use `locals` for `merge(var.tags, { ManagedBy = "terraform", Env = var.env })` and provider `default_tags` so every resource is tagged without touching each block.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Input Variables

subtopics.name: Environment strategy: CLI workspaces versus directory-per-environment versus Terragrunt
subtopics.learn: CLI workspaces (`terraform workspace new prod`, `terraform.workspace` in expressions) store state under `env:/prod/<key>` in the same bucket with the same backend credentials and the same provider config; that means one IAM role can touch every environment and a forgotten `workspace select` applies dev values to prod. Directory-per-environment (`envs/dev`, `envs/prod`, each with its own `.s3.tfbackend`, its own `assume_role` target and `allowed_account_ids`) gives real credential and state separation at the cost of duplicated root boilerplate; Terragrunt removes that duplication with `generate` blocks and `run-all`. The FDE default for a customer with separate accounts: one state per (account, region, layer), layers split into network, data and compute so plan time stays under a few minutes and a broken compute plan cannot lock the network state; pass IDs between layers with `terraform_remote_state` or SSM parameters, never by copy-paste.

resource.label: Terraform CLI: Workspaces

subtopics.name: Drift: refresh-only, reconciling click-ops, and the things refresh cannot see
subtopics.learn: Drift is real infrastructure differing from state. `terraform plan -refresh-only` shows exactly what changed outside Terraform without proposing config changes; `terraform apply -refresh-only` accepts reality into state. A normal plan refreshes first and then diffs config against the refreshed state, so a manual security group rule shows up as a `~` update reverting it. Schedule `plan -detailed-exitcode -lock-timeout=2m` nightly; exit 2 means drift, page or open an issue. Triage each diff into one of three actions: revert (someone opened 0.0.0.0/0 on 22), adopt (import the resource they created in the console), or ignore (`ignore_changes` for an attribute owned by an autoscaler or a deploy pipeline). Refresh only inspects addresses already in state, so resources created outside Terraform are invisible to it; that gap needs AWS Config rules or a tag-based sweep (`aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources` filtered on missing `ManagedBy`). A resource deleted manually shows as `+ create`; a resource removed from state but not AWS becomes an orphan billing you forever.

resource.label: Terraform tutorial: Manage resource drift

subtopics.name: Plan on PR, apply on merge: the GitHub Actions pipeline
subtopics.learn: On `pull_request`: `terraform fmt -check -recursive`, `init -input=false -backend-config=...`, `validate`, tflint, trivy config, then `plan -out=tfplan -no-color -input=false -lock-timeout=5m` with `TF_IN_AUTOMATION=1` and `TF_INPUT=0`; post the plan as a PR comment (GitHub truncates at 65,536 characters, so summarise counts and attach the full plan as an artifact) and upload `tfplan` with a short retention because it contains secrets. On `push` to `main`: either apply the exact saved plan from the merged PR or re-plan and `apply -auto-approve`, inside `concurrency: { group: terraform-prod, cancel-in-progress: false }` so applies serialise, and inside a GitHub Environment with required reviewers for prod. Use `hashicorp/setup-terraform` with `terraform_wrapper: false` when you need real exit codes. The plan job executes provider code and data sources, so it must never receive apply credentials and must never run for forks with secrets (`pull_request_target` is the classic mistake). Separate plan and apply roles; the plan role needs read on AWS plus write on the state lock only.

resource.label: Terraform tutorial: Running Terraform in automation

subtopics.name: OIDC federation from GitHub Actions to AWS: no long-lived keys
subtopics.learn: Add `permissions: id-token: write` to the job and call `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` with `role-to-assume` and `aws-region`; the action exchanges GitHub's OIDC token for STS credentials via `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`. In AWS, create the `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` identity provider once, then a role whose trust policy checks `aud` = `sts.amazonaws.com` and `sub` with `StringLike` on `repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main` for the apply role and `repo:org/repo:pull_request` for the plan role; a wildcard `repo:org/*` lets any repo in the org assume your prod role. Set `role-duration-seconds` to the minimum that covers your longest apply. Verify with `aws sts get-caller-identity` as the first step of every job so the account ID is in the log. This is the pattern you will be asked to reproduce at every customer that still has `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` in repository secrets.

resource.label: GitHub Docs: Configuring OpenID Connect in Amazon Web Services

subtopics.name: Static checks and policy: tflint, trivy/checkov, conftest on plan JSON, terraform test
subtopics.learn: `terraform validate` is schema-only and never calls AWS, so it will pass an invalid instance type; tflint with the AWS ruleset (`.tflint.hcl` with `plugin "aws" { enabled = true  version = "..."  source = "github.com/terraform-linters/tflint-ruleset-aws" }`) catches that plus deprecated syntax and unused declarations. `trivy config .` or `checkov -d .` flag misconfiguration classes: unencrypted S3, security groups open to the world on 22 or 3389, IAM wildcards. Policy on the plan is stronger than policy on the source because it sees resolved values: `terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json` then `conftest test plan.json -p policy/` with Rego rules that deny any `resource_changes[_]` where `change.actions` contains `delete` for `aws_db_instance` or where `tags.Owner` is missing. `terraform test` (1.6+) runs `.tftest.hcl` files with `run` blocks, `command = plan` and `assert` conditions so module contracts are tested without creating resources. Order in CI: fmt, validate, tflint, scanner, plan, policy, comment.

resource.label: tflint official repository

subtopics.name: Provider configuration for multi-account, multi-region: aliases, assume_role, allowed_account_ids
subtopics.learn: `provider "aws" { region = "eu-west-1"  assume_role { role_arn = var.deploy_role_arn  session_name = "terraform"  external_id = var.external_id }  default_tags { tags = local.tags }  allowed_account_ids = [var.account_id] }`. `allowed_account_ids` makes the provider refuse to run if `AWS_PROFILE` points at the wrong account, and it is the cheapest guard you will ever add against applying a sandbox config to a customer's production. A second `provider "aws" { alias = "dr"  region = "us-west-2" }` is used with `provider = aws.dr` on a resource or `providers = { aws = aws.dr }` on a module. Never put credentials in HCL; understand the credential chain the provider walks (env vars, shared config profile with SSO, ECS or EC2 instance metadata, IRSA web identity) so you can explain which identity a given plan ran as. `data "aws_caller_identity" "current"` and `data "aws_region" "current"` belong in every root so ARNs are never hard-coded.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Provider Configuration

subtopics.name: Debugging and recovery: TF_LOG, partial applies, errored.tfstate, lock and hash errors
subtopics.learn: `TF_LOG=DEBUG TF_LOG_PATH=./tf.log terraform apply` (levels TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR; `TF_LOG_CORE` and `TF_LOG_PROVIDER` split them) shows the exact AWS API call and response behind an opaque error. A failed apply is normal and partial: every resource that completed is already in state, so the recovery is to read the error, fix, and plan again, never to delete state. If Terraform cannot write state to the backend after applying, it drops `errored.tfstate` in the working directory and tells you; recover with `terraform state push errored.tfstate` before anyone else runs. 'Provider produced inconsistent final plan' is almost always a provider bug or an unknown value that changed between plan and apply; 'Cycle:' errors come from `depends_on` or mutual references and `terraform graph` shows the loop. Set resource `timeouts { create = "30m" }` for EKS and RDS, use `-parallelism=5` when the AWS API throttles, and fix 'checksum mismatch' in the lock file with `providers lock -platform=...` rather than deleting `.terraform.lock.hcl`.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Debugging Terraform

subtopics.name: Building the deliverable: VPC, subnets, NAT and EC2 with the community VPC module, ready for EKS
subtopics.learn: Consume `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` with `cidr`, `azs = slice(data.aws_availability_zones.available.names, 0, 3)`, `private_subnets` and `public_subnets` computed with `cidrsubnet(var.cidr, 4, i)`, `enable_nat_gateway = true`, `single_nat_gateway = true` for dev (one gateway, roughly 32 USD a month plus data) versus `one_nat_gateway_per_az = true` for prod HA, and `enable_dns_hostnames = true`. Tag subnets now so the EKS topic (16) works later: `public_subnet_tags = { "kubernetes.io/role/elb" = 1 }` and `private_subnet_tags = { "kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb" = 1 }`. Add VPC endpoints for S3 (gateway) and ECR (interface) so image pulls do not pay NAT egress. Launch EC2 from `data "aws_ami"` filtered on `al2023-ami-*` with `most_recent = true` and `owners = ["amazon"]`, an instance profile with `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` so there is no SSH key and no port 22, and a security group with no inbound rules. Output `vpc_id`, `private_subnet_ids`, `public_subnet_ids`. Finish every session with `terraform destroy` or a nightly destroy job in the sandbox.

resource.label: terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-vpc official repository

subtopics.name: Secrets in state and what never to put in Terraform
subtopics.learn: State stores every returned attribute in plaintext: `random_password.db.result`, `aws_db_instance.password`, `aws_iam_access_key.secret`, `tls_private_key.private_key_pem`. Mitigate in layers: SSE-KMS on the bucket with a key policy that only the CI roles and a break-glass group can decrypt, bucket policy scoped to those principals, S3 access logging on. Remove the secret from state where the provider allows it: `manage_master_user_password = true` on `aws_db_instance` puts the password in Secrets Manager and leaves only an ARN in state; write-only arguments (1.11+, suffixed `_wo`) and ephemeral resources (1.10+) let you pass a secret at apply without persisting it. Remember `sensitive = true` hides values from CLI output only; `terraform show -json` and the plan artifact reveal them, so lock down CI logs and artifact retention. Do not template kubeconfigs or tokens into local files with `local_file`, and do not manage things that change hourly (feature flags, Lambda code) in the same state as the network.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Sensitive Data in State

outcomes: You can bootstrap an S3 remote backend with versioning, SSE-KMS and locking (use_lockfile or DynamoDB), migrate an existing local state into it with `init -migrate-state`, and name every IAM permission the CI role needs and why.

You can read any plan and, before approving, list which resources will be replaced and which attribute forces it, then rewrite the change so the plan is non-destructive using moved blocks, state mv, ignore_changes, or create_before_destroy as appropriate.

You can adopt an existing click-ops VPC, its subnets and security groups into a module using import blocks and -generate-config-out, and end with `terraform plan` reporting 'No changes' without -target or hidden ignore_changes.

You can write a module with typed object inputs using optional() defaults and validation blocks, no provider block inside, a pinned Git or registry source, and consume it from two environment roots with separate backends, assume_role targets and allowed_account_ids.

You can build a GitHub Actions pipeline that plans on PR under a read-only OIDC role, posts the plan and uploads the artifact, and applies on merge under a separate role inside a concurrency group and a protected environment, with zero AWS access keys anywhere.
You can run a drift review: execute plan -refresh-only, classify every diff as revert, adopt or ignore with a one-line justification, and explain why resources created outside Terraform never appear.

You can recover from a stale lock (force-unlock with a verified lock ID), an errored.tfstate after a backend write failure, and a lock-file checksum mismatch between macOS and Linux CI, each in under ten minutes.

You can argue for an environment isolation strategy (workspaces, directories, Terragrunt) for a customer with three AWS accounts in terms of blast radius, credential separation and plan time, and state what would make you change it.
failureModes: A subnet list built with count gets a new AZ inserted at position 1; the plan replaces two subnets, the apply destroys the ones the customer's RDS subnet group depends on, RDS refuses the change, and state is left half-applied on a Friday evening.

Two engineers apply from laptops against the same S3 backend configured without locking; the second write overwrites the first's state, and the next plan proposes creating 40 resources that already exist, each failing with AlreadyExists.
A workflow uses pull_request_target so plan runs on forks with the apply role; a contributor's PR adds an `external` data source that curls the OIDC token and STS credentials to their server.

The RDS master password and an IAM user's secret key sit in plaintext in state, the state bucket grants s3:GetObject to an engineering-wide role, and the customer's SOC 2 auditor lists it as a finding against your delivery.

A module source pins `ref=main` instead of a tag; a colleague pushes an unrelated change, and the next prod PR's plan shows a NAT gateway replacement nobody asked for, approved by a reviewer who only read the PR description.
Nobody set ignore_changes on the EKS managed node group scaling_config.desired_size; every apply after the cluster autoscaler scales up resets the node count to 2 and evicts customer workloads.

An engineer with AWS_PROFILE pointing at the customer's production account applies the sandbox root because the code is identical and allowed_account_ids was never set; the plan output scrolled past and the prod NAT gateway is gone.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through exactly what happens between `terraform plan` and `terraform apply`: what the lock protects against, what 'known after apply' means, why a plan can succeed and the apply fail, and what state looks like after a failed apply.

A customer has a hand-built VPC with six subnets, twelve security groups and an ALB and wants it under Terraform with zero downtime. Design the adoption: how you import, how you prove the plan is clean, what you do about resources whose config cannot be made to match, and what the first production PR contains.

Your PR plan shows `-/+ aws_db_instance.main (forces replacement)` because someone renamed the identifier. The customer cannot take downtime. Give me your options in order of preference and what each does to state.

Design Terraform CI/CD across dev, staging and prod in three AWS accounts. Where do credentials come from, how do you stop a fork PR from exfiltrating them, how do you stop two applies racing on the same state, and where exactly does a human approve?

A nightly drift job started returning exit code 2 every night on an aws_autoscaling_group and nobody changed anything. What is happening, what are three ways to fix it, and which would you choose for a customer whose platform team will own this in six months?

Workspaces versus directory-per-environment versus Terragrunt: pick one for a customer deployment you will hand over, defend it in terms of blast radius and credentials, and tell me what would make you change your mind.

An engineer ran `terraform state push` with a week-old file and now the plan wants to create everything. What do you do in the first fifteen minutes, and what structural change stops it from happening again?
13.proofOfWork: A public repository, tf-aws-foundation, laid out as modules/network and modules/compute plus envs/dev and envs/prod roots, each root with its own .s3.tfbackend, assume_role target and allowed_account_ids, and a bootstrap/ root that creates the versioned SSE-KMS state bucket and OIDC provider. GitHub Actions plan on PR under a read-only role and apply on merge under a separate role behind a protected environment and a concurrency group; conftest policies that deny untagged resources and any delete on aws_db_instance or aws_s3_bucket; tflint and trivy in the same pipeline. A recorded terminal session (asciinema or pasted output in the README) demonstrates three things end to end: (1) a VPC created by hand with the AWS CLI is adopted with import blocks and -generate-config-out until plan says No changes; (2) a count-based subnet set is migrated to for_each with moved blocks and the plan shows zero destroys; (3) a security group rule added in the console is caught by the nightly plan -detailed-exitcode job and reverted by the next apply. A one-page ADR in the repo explains the choice of directory-per-environment over workspaces and the network/data/compute state layering, in language a customer platform lead could sign off on.

14.topic: AWS networking and compute: VPC, subnets, SG, NACL, ALB across AZs, EC2, Lambda
14.why: FDEs almost never get a greenfield account: you deploy into a customer's VPC, get handed two private subnet IDs and a security-group naming convention, and are asked where your load balancer goes and why your app needs egress. The customer's network and security teams will review every rule before they sign the production change, and when the pilot cannot reach RDS or the model API at 4pm on go-live day, the FDE who can read a route table and a flow log in minutes keeps the account while the one who files a ticket with the customer's platform team loses a week. This topic is the mechanics behind every 'it works in our account but not in theirs' escalation.
prerequisites: Networking from 'Networking: TCP/IP, DNS, TLS, HTTP/2, load balancers, firewalls' (topic 2): CIDR arithmetic by hand, the three-way handshake and what a SYN with no SYN-ACK looks like, ephemeral port ranges, TLS termination, L4 versus L7 balancing, stateful versus stateless filtering

Terraform from 'Terraform: state, modules, workspaces, drift, CI' (topic 12): providers, `for_each`, `cidrsubnet()`, data sources, remote state, and a clean `terraform destroy` habit, since the deliverable is written in it
Linux from topics 1 and 3: systemd units, cloud-init, and reading `ss -tlnp`, `ip route`, `tcpdump -i eth0 port 8080` and `curl -v` on an instance to distinguish a listening app from a blocked path

Enough IAM to attach an instance profile and a Lambda execution role and read a resource-based policy; 'IAM and cloud security: least privilege, roles, IRSA, no long-lived keys' (topic 15) goes deep afterwards

An AWS account with a budget alarm at 20 USD, AWS CLI v2 configured through IAM Identity Center or short-lived credentials (`aws sts get-caller-identity` works), and a DNS zone you control for ACM validation
Docker basics from topic 5 so you can run the sample app on the instance and know why 172.17.0.0/16 matters when you pick a VPC CIDR

subtopics.name: Regions, AZs, and what is zonal versus regional
subtopics.learn: Know that an AZ name (us-east-1a) is randomised per account while the AZ ID (use1-az1) is stable, so two accounts in one customer agreeing on 'zone a' may be talking about different data centres; run `aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --query 'AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId]'` and record the mapping on the diagram. Classify every resource you will create as zonal (subnet, EC2 instance, EBS volume, NAT gateway, ENI, each ALB node) or regional (VPC, route table, security group, NACL, IGW, the ALB as a whole, Lambda function, ACM certificate), because that classification is exactly what tells you which pieces must be duplicated for AZ resilience. A single-AZ event is the failure unit AWS designs for, and anything with one NAT gateway or one subnet has silently opted out of that protection.

resource.label: EC2 User Guide: Regions and Availability Zones

subtopics.name: VPC CIDR planning against a customer's address space
