subtopics.learn: Choose a VPC CIDR between /16 and /28 from RFC 1918 space that does not overlap the customer's on-prem ranges, their other VPCs, or the 172.17.0.0/16 Docker default that bites the moment a container talks to an instance; ask for the corporate IP plan before you pick. Every subnet loses five addresses (network, VPC router at +1, Route 53 Resolver at +2, reserved +3, broadcast), so a /28 has 11 usable IPs and an ALB refuses any subnet smaller than /27 or with fewer than 8 free addresses. Be able to add a secondary CIDR with `aws ec2 associate-vpc-cidr-block` when the first fills up, and know the restrictions (no overlap, at most 5 IPv4 blocks by default). Use `cidrsubnet()` arithmetic to carve a /16 into one block per tier per AZ and write the plan down before touching Terraform.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: VPC CIDR blocks

subtopics.name: Subnets and route tables: public, private and isolated are just routes
subtopics.learn: A subnet is public only because its route table has 0.0.0.0/0 pointing at an igw; private means 0.0.0.0/0 points at a nat; isolated means only the implicit `local` route for the VPC CIDR exists. Every subnet is associated with exactly one route table and falls back to the main route table if you forget the association, which is how a 'private' subnet becomes public when someone edits main. Routes use longest-prefix match, the local route cannot be deleted, and targets can be igw, nat, eni, pcx (peering), tgw, vgw, a gateway-endpoint prefix list (pl-xxx), or a blackhole once the target is deleted. Draw the route table for every subnet on your diagram and be able to reproduce it from `aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-xxx`.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: Route tables

subtopics.name: Internet gateway, public IPs, and one NAT gateway per AZ
subtopics.learn: The IGW performs 1:1 NAT between an ENI's private IP and its public or Elastic IP; the instance never sees its public address, which is why `ip addr` shows only 10.x and why `curl 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/public-ipv4` exists. A public subnet still yields an instance with no public IP unless `map_public_ip_on_launch` is true or you attach an EIP. NAT gateways are zonal: one NAT in AZ-a serving private subnets in AZ-b means an AZ-a outage kills egress for both and you pay cross-AZ data charges on every byte, so the pattern is one NAT per AZ with one private route table per AZ. Know the limits that bite in production: 55,000 simultaneous connections to a single destination IP:port, surfaced as the `ErrorPortAllocation` metric and fixed by attaching secondary EIPs; 5 Gbps baseline scaling to 100 Gbps; and roughly 0.045 USD per hour plus 0.045 USD per GB processed, the line item that shocks customers when a pipeline pulls from S3 through NAT instead of a gateway endpoint. Use an egress-only internet gateway for IPv6 outbound.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: NAT gateways

subtopics.name: Security groups: stateful, ENI-scoped, reference by ID
subtopics.learn: Security groups attach to ENIs, not subnets; they are allow-lists only (no deny), stateful via connection tracking, and default to allow-all egress and deny-all ingress. The single most important habit is referencing other groups instead of CIDRs: the app SG allows tcp/8080 from the ALB's SG ID, the database SG allows tcp/5432 from the app SG ID, so scaling or IP churn never breaks a rule and the diagram reads as a graph of trust. Know the quotas: 60 inbound and 60 outbound rules per group, 5 groups per ENI by default (rules times groups must stay under 1000), and the tracking exception where flows allowed by 0.0.0.0/0 in both directions are untracked and so escape the conntrack table that otherwise shows up as `conntrack_allowance_exceeded` in `ethtool -S eth0`. Read rules with IDs and descriptions via `aws ec2 describe-security-group-rules --filters Name=group-id,Values=sg-xxx`, and in Terraform use `aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule` resources rather than inline blocks so two groups can reference each other without a dependency cycle.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: Security groups

subtopics.name: Network ACLs: stateless, ordered, and the ephemeral-port trap
subtopics.learn: NACLs attach to subnets, are stateless, and evaluate rules from the lowest number upward until one matches, ending in the implicit `*` deny. The default NACL allows everything; a custom NACL denies everything until you add rules, and because there is no connection tracking you must explicitly allow return traffic on ephemeral ports: 1024-65535 for NAT gateways and load balancers, 32768-60999 for modern Linux clients, 49152-65535 for Windows. Know when a NACL is the right tool (blocking a specific abusive CIDR, a compliance requirement for subnet-level deny, a second layer in front of the database tier) and when it is just a source of asymmetric-return bugs. Diagnose a NACL problem from flow logs by the signature ACCEPT inbound then REJECT outbound on the same flow, and remember the 20-rule default quota per NACL.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: Network ACLs

subtopics.name: DNS inside the VPC: the +2 resolver, private hosted zones, hybrid resolution
subtopics.learn: Every VPC gets a Route 53 Resolver at CIDR base +2 (also 169.254.169.253) that answers public names, VPC-internal hostnames such as ip-10-0-1-23.ec2.internal, private hosted zones associated with the VPC, and interface-endpoint private DNS. Both `enableDnsSupport` and `enableDnsHostnames` must be true for endpoint private DNS and public hostnames to work, and `enableDnsHostnames` is false by default on API-created VPCs, which is the first thing to check when a customer's new VPC cannot resolve `sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com` to a private IP. The resolver accepts 1024 packets per second per ENI, so a chatty service without a local DNS cache hits SERVFAIL under load. For hybrid setups understand inbound and outbound Resolver endpoints plus forwarding rules so `corp.example.com` resolves from inside the VPC and the customer's on-prem resolvers can see your private zone.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: DNS attributes for your VPC

subtopics.name: VPC endpoints: gateway versus interface, and why NAT bills drop
subtopics.learn: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, cost nothing, and work by injecting a prefix-list route (pl-xxx to vpce-xxx) into selected route tables so traffic to those services never touches NAT or the IGW; an endpoint policy can restrict which buckets are reachable. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) place an ENI with a private IP into each chosen subnet, are protected by a security group that must allow tcp/443 from your workloads, and with private DNS enabled make the normal service hostname resolve to that ENI so SDKs need no configuration; they cost about 0.01 USD per AZ-hour plus 0.01 USD per GB. Know which endpoints an isolated subnet needs to run a typical FDE workload with no internet at all: ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages for Session Manager, ecr.api, ecr.dkr and the S3 gateway for image pulls, logs for CloudWatch, sts for role assumption, secretsmanager, and bedrock-runtime if the customer insists model calls stay on the AWS backbone.

resource.label: AWS PrivateLink Guide: What is AWS PrivateLink

subtopics.name: Connecting VPCs: peering, Transit Gateway, and reaching the customer's network
subtopics.learn: VPC peering is a one-to-one, non-transitive link: CIDRs must not overlap, you add routes on both sides pointing at pcx-xxx, and within a region you can reference the peer's security group ID in your rules; DNS resolution across the peer is a separate flag on each side. Transit Gateway is a regional hub where each VPC is an attachment with its own TGW route table, so a customer with 40 VPCs and a Direct Connect gateway gives you one attachment and a CIDR allocation rather than 40 peerings. Understand enough about Site-to-Site VPN (two tunnels, BGP or static routes) and Direct Connect to hold a conversation with the customer's network team about how on-prem clients will reach your internal ALB, and know that whichever they choose, the return route from your subnet back to their CIDR still has to exist in your route table.

resource.label: VPC Peering Guide: What is VPC peering

subtopics.name: ALB architecture: nodes per AZ, subnets, addressing, cross-zone
subtopics.learn: An ALB is a regional resource that materialises as one or more nodes (ENIs) in each subnet you enable; you must give it at least two subnets in different AZs, each /27 or larger with 8 free IPs, and the node IPs change as it scales, so clients and firewalls must use the DNS name, never a resolved address. Choose internet-facing (nodes get public IPs, subnets need an IGW route) or internal (private IPs only, the right choice when the customer fronts it with their own edge or VPN). Cross-zone load balancing is on by default for ALB, so a node in AZ-a will send requests to healthy targets in AZ-b; know the connection idle timeout (60 s default, 1-4000 s) and the client keepalive setting, and that the ALB has its own security group which should be the only source allowed to reach the target SG. Set `enable_deletion_protection` in production and understand that the ALB is billed per hour plus LCU-hours across new connections, active connections, processed bytes and rule evaluations.

resource.label: ALB User Guide: What is an Application Load Balancer

subtopics.name: Listeners, rules and TLS termination
subtopics.learn: A listener is protocol plus port; a production ALB has an HTTP:80 listener whose only default action is `redirect` to HTTPS with status 301, and an HTTPS:443 listener carrying an ACM certificate, a security policy (`ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06` unless the customer's compliance team says otherwise) and additional certificates served via SNI. Rules are evaluated by priority (1 to 50000, lowest first, default rule last) and match on host-header, path-pattern, http-header, http-request-method, query-string or source-ip, then take an action: forward (optionally to several target groups with weights for canaries), redirect, fixed-response, or authenticate-oidc and authenticate-cognito to push login to the edge before traffic reaches your app. TLS terminates at the ALB, so the target sees plain HTTP plus `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Port`. ACM public certificates are free but must be issued in the ALB's region and validated by a DNS record in the customer's zone, which is a ticket you open on day one.

resource.label: ALB User Guide: Create an HTTPS listener

subtopics.name: Target groups, health checks and traffic shaping
subtopics.learn: Target groups have a target type (instance, ip, lambda, or alb) that cannot change after creation; instance targets register by ID and receive the client IP in X-Forwarded-For, while ip targets are how you point at ECS tasks, on-prem servers over Direct Connect, or a peered VPC. Health checks default to HTTP GET on `/` every 30 s with a 5 s timeout, 5 healthy and 2 unhealthy threshold, matcher 200; set the path to a real readiness endpoint, keep the interval short enough that a bad deploy is pulled within a minute, and know that when every target in a group is unhealthy the ALB fails open and routes to all of them. Tune `deregistration_delay` (300 s default) down to your longest request so rolling deploys are fast, enable `slow_start` for JVM or model-loading targets, pick `least_outstanding_requests` over round robin when request cost varies, and use `lb_cookie` stickiness (the AWSALB cookie) only when the app truly holds session state, because it defeats even distribution across AZs.

resource.label: ALB User Guide: Health checks for target groups

subtopics.name: Debugging through the ALB: status codes, metrics and access logs
subtopics.learn: Separate `HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count` (the balancer generated it) from `HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count` (your app did), and read the ELB-generated codes literally: 502 means the target closed the connection, sent a malformed response or the Lambda errored; 503 means no registered or no healthy targets; 504 means the target did not answer before the idle timeout or the TCP connect failed; 460 means the client gave up before the ALB idle timeout, common when a customer's proxy timeout is shorter than yours. Enable access logs to S3 and learn the field order well enough to `awk` them: `elb_status_code`, `target_status_code`, `request_processing_time`, `target_processing_time`, `response_processing_time`, where -1 in a processing time means no target was ever selected. Alarm on `UnHealthyHostCount`, `RejectedConnectionCount`, `TargetConnectionErrorCount` and p99 `TargetResponseTime`, and use `X-Amzn-Trace-Id` to join an access-log line to the application log on the instance.

resource.label: ALB User Guide: Troubleshoot your Application Load Balancer

subtopics.name: EC2 as an FDE runs it: instance choice, IMDSv2, user data, no SSH
subtopics.learn: Pick the family by what the workload is bound by (m general, c compute, r memory, g or p GPU, t burstable) and understand the t-family CPU credit model, including that T3 launches in unlimited mode and will quietly bill for sustained CPU. Resolve the AMI at plan time from the SSM public parameter `/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64` rather than hardcoding an ID that differs per region. Enforce IMDSv2 with `HttpTokens=required`, understand the token dance (`PUT /latest/api/token` with `X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds`, then GET with the token header) and the `HttpPutResponseHopLimit` of 1 that breaks the SDK inside a container until you raise it to 2. Bootstrap with user data through cloud-init, debug it in `/var/log/cloud-init-output.log`, attach an instance profile instead of keys, and reach the box with Systems Manager Session Manager (SSM agent, `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`, outbound 443 to ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages) so the security group has no port 22 at all. Know that bandwidth advertised as `Up to 5 Gbps` is a burst figure and that `ethtool -S` exposes `bw_in_allowance_exceeded` and `pps_allowance_exceeded` when you hit the real ceiling.

resource.label: EC2 User Guide: Configure the Instance Metadata Service options

subtopics.name: Auto Scaling groups across AZs behind the ALB
subtopics.learn: An ASG built from a launch template with `vpc_zone_identifier` set to one private subnet per AZ and `target_group_arns` pointing at the ALB target group is the minimum unit of an AZ-resilient compute tier; min_size 2 with the ASG's automatic AZ balancing means one instance per AZ. Set `health_check_type = ELB` so a failed target-group health check replaces the instance instead of leaving a running-but-broken box in service, and set `health_check_grace_period` longer than boot plus warmup or the ASG will kill instances mid-startup in a loop. Use instance refresh with `min_healthy_percentage` to roll a new launch-template version, understand lifecycle hooks for draining, and know the ASG rebalances across AZs by launching in the under-served AZ before terminating in the over-served one. Confirm behaviour by terminating one instance and watching the target group go unhealthy, the ASG launch a replacement, and the access logs show zero ELB-generated 5XX.

resource.label: EC2 Auto Scaling User Guide: Use Elastic Load Balancing to distribute traffic

subtopics.name: Lambda execution model: init, invoke, concurrency and throttles
subtopics.learn: An execution environment goes through Init (runtime plus your module-level code, 10 s limit), Invoke (the handler, up to 900 s), and Shutdown; environments are reused, so anything at module scope (SDK clients, connection pools, model weights) is a cold-start cost paid once and a warm-path win thereafter, and `/tmp` (512 MB up to 10 GB) survives between invocations in the same environment. Memory is the only performance dial: 128 MB to 10,240 MB with CPU scaling linearly and a full vCPU at about 1,769 MB. Account concurrency defaults to 1,000 per region shared across all functions; each function can scale by 1,000 concurrent executions every 10 s; exceeding limits returns 429 `TooManyRequestsException` on synchronous calls and silently retries twice on asynchronous ones, so configure a destination or DLQ. Use reserved concurrency to cap a function that talks to a fragile customer system and provisioned concurrency or SnapStart when cold starts break an SLA; sync payloads cap at 6 MB and async at 256 KB.

resource.label: Lambda Developer Guide: Lambda execution environment

subtopics.name: Lambda inside the VPC and as an ALB target
subtopics.learn: Attaching a function to a VPC creates Hyperplane ENIs per unique subnet-plus-security-group combination, so the execution role needs `ec2:CreateNetworkInterface` and friends (`AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole`), the function never has a public IP, and it reaches the internet only through a NAT gateway in the private subnets you chose; pick subnets in at least two AZs. The function's security group is the source you reference in the RDS or ElastiCache SG. Behind an ALB, register the function in a target group of type lambda, grant `lambda:InvokeFunction` to `elasticloadbalancing.amazonaws.com` in the function's resource policy, return an object with statusCode, headers or multiValueHeaders, body and isBase64Encoded, and stay under the 1 MB response limit; the ALB health check, if enabled, is a real invocation you pay for. For a quick webhook receiver without an ALB, a function URL with `AuthType AWS_IAM` or `NONE` plus CORS is the right tool, and knowing which to choose is a common FDE trade-off with a customer's security team.

resource.label: Lambda Developer Guide: Giving Lambda functions access to resources in a VPC

subtopics.name: Seeing the packets: VPC Flow Logs and Reachability Analyzer
subtopics.learn: Turn on flow logs at the VPC level to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and read the default record (version account-id interface-id srcaddr dstaddr srcport dstport protocol packets bytes start end action log-status), then add the custom fields `tcp-flags`, `flow-direction`, `traffic-path`, `pkt-srcaddr` and `pkt-dstaddr` so you can tell a SYN that was REJECTed by a security group from a flow that was ACCEPTed in and then REJECTed on the way out by a NACL. Know what flow logs do not show: DNS to the VPC resolver, IMDS traffic to 169.254.169.254, DHCP, and anything inside the 60 s or 600 s aggregation window that has not flushed, which is why a fresh reproduction takes a minute to appear. Use Reachability Analyzer to prove a path between two ENIs or an ENI and an IGW; it evaluates route tables, SGs, NACLs and endpoints statically and names the exact component that blocks, which is the artifact to paste into the customer ticket instead of an opinion.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: Logging IP traffic using VPC Flow Logs

subtopics.name: Building the reference VPC and ALB tier in Terraform
subtopics.learn: Compose the whole diagram as code: `data.aws_availability_zones` (state available) feeding a `for_each` over two AZs, `aws_vpc`, `aws_subnet` per tier using `cidrsubnet(var.cidr, 4, index)`, `aws_internet_gateway`, one `aws_eip` and `aws_nat_gateway` per AZ, a public route table plus one private route table per AZ with their `aws_route_table_association`s, `aws_security_group` shells with separate `aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule` and `aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule` resources using `referenced_security_group_id`, `aws_lb` (application, public subnets), `aws_lb_target_group` with a `health_check` block, `aws_lb_listener` for the 80 redirect and the 443 forward with `certificate_arn`, `aws_launch_template` with `metadata_options` setting http_tokens to required and an `iam_instance_profile`, and `aws_autoscaling_group` with `vpc_zone_identifier` and `target_group_arns`. Read the terraform-aws-modules/vpc module source to see how per-AZ NAT is handled, then decide deliberately whether to consume the module or own the resources. Run `terraform plan` until the diff is zero, `terraform destroy` at the end of every session, and keep a cost line in the README.

resource.label: Terraform Registry: AWS provider documentation

outcomes: You can draw a two-AZ VPC (public, private and isolated tiers, per-AZ NAT, IGW, endpoints) from memory and, for every arrow and every SG or NACL rule, state which resource it protects, which direction is stateful, and what breaks if it is removed.

You can stand up an internet-facing ALB in front of an ASG of two EC2 instances in two AZs with Terraform, TLS via ACM, an 80 to 443 redirect and a real readiness health check, and reach a zero-diff `terraform plan` in under an hour from an empty account.

You can take a 'the app is unreachable' report and, within fifteen minutes using only describe-route-tables, describe-security-group-rules, flow logs and Reachability Analyzer, name whether the block is routing, SG, NACL, health check or DNS, with the log line that proves it.

You can read an ALB access log and CloudWatch metrics and distinguish 502, 503, 504 and 460 by cause, tell whether the balancer or the target produced a 5XX, and correlate one request to the instance log via X-Amzn-Trace-Id.

You can explain to a customer's network team, without notes, why they need one NAT gateway per AZ, which VPC endpoints let your workload run with no internet route at all, and roughly what each costs per month.

You can deploy a Lambda function into private subnets, wire it to RDS through a security-group reference, put it behind the same ALB on a path rule, and explain its cold-start, concurrency and 429 behaviour under a burst of 2,000 requests.

You can lock down EC2 the way a security reviewer expects: IMDSv2 required, no port 22, instance profile instead of keys, Session Manager for access, and show the SSM session working from an isolated subnet through interface endpoints.

You can list the quotas that will bite this architecture first (SG rules per ENI, NAT ports per destination, ALB rules per listener, Lambda account concurrency, resolver packets per second) and name the CloudWatch metric or alarm that would tell you.
failureModes: A single NAT gateway in AZ-a serves private subnets in both AZs: AZ-a degrades, every instance in AZ-b loses egress to the model API and package repos, and the 'multi-AZ' pilot goes down with one zone while the customer's dashboard still shows healthy EC2.

The app security group allows tcp/8080 from the ALB subnet CIDRs instead of the ALB's SG ID; a later subnet re-carve or a second ALB in the same subnets silently widens access, and the customer's pen test flags the app port reachable from a jump host.

A custom NACL on the database subnet allows inbound 5432 but the return rule only covers 32768-60999; ALB health checks and NAT-sourced connections using ports below 32768 fail intermittently, half the targets flap unhealthy, and on-call chases a phantom application bug for a day.

The health check path is left at `/` returning 200 from an nginx placeholder while the real app crashed on boot; the target group is green, the ALB happily forwards, and users get 502 from the balancer while every dashboard is healthy.

A Lambda function is attached to the VPC but placed in a subnet whose route table has no NAT route: calls to the Anthropic API hang until the 30 s timeout, the async invocations retry twice with no destination configured, and the customer sees three duplicated webhook side effects hours later.

A data-ingest job reads 20 TB from S3 through the NAT gateway because nobody added the S3 gateway endpoint; the month-end bill has a 900 USD NAT data-processing line, and the customer's FinOps lead asks why your design doc did not mention it.

Someone resolved the ALB DNS name once and put the two IPs into the customer's on-prem firewall allowlist; the ALB scaled and rotated its nodes overnight and the integration went dark, with nothing in your logs because the packets never arrived.
interviewQuestions: Draw a two-AZ VPC for a web tier, an app tier and Postgres that a bank's security team will accept. For every security group and NACL rule you write, tell me exactly what would happen if I deleted it.

A customer says the app behind your ALB returns 502 intermittently, about 3 percent of requests, only during deploys. Walk me through the investigation from ALB metrics to access logs to target-group settings, and name the two configuration values you expect to change.

Explain what happens at each hop when a browser requests https://app.customer.com served by an internet-facing ALB in front of instances in private subnets: DNS, TLS, the ALB node, the target, and the response path. Where does NAT happen and where does it not?

The customer wants zero internet access from the VPC. List the endpoints you need for an EC2 fleet pulling from ECR, logging to CloudWatch, reached over Session Manager and calling Bedrock. What changes if they also need to call an external SaaS API?

Flow logs show ACCEPT on ingress and REJECT on egress for the same 5-tuple. What is the cause, why does a security group never produce that pattern, and how would you confirm without touching production?

When would you put a Lambda function in a VPC and when would you refuse to? Cover cold starts, ENIs, NAT cost, concurrency, and the failure modes of async invocation against a customer system that is not idempotent.

Our Terraform created an ALB in two subnets, but one AZ shows UnHealthyHostCount equal to HealthyHostCount and the other is fine. Give me three plausible root causes in order of likelihood and the single command or console view that rules each one in or out.
14.proofOfWork: A public repository `aws-two-az-breakfix-lab` that extends the plan's Terraform with a `faults/` directory of six deliberately broken variants selected via `terraform apply -var fault=<name>`: missing NAT route in one AZ, NACL ephemeral-port block on the app subnet, app SG allowing from a CIDR rather than the ALB SG, health check on a placeholder path, Lambda in a subnet without egress, and a single-AZ NAT. For each fault the README records the exact evidence that identifies it (the flow-log line with tcp-flags, the Reachability Analyzer blocking component, the ALB access-log fields, or the CloudWatch metric) and the one-line fix, plus a `cost.md` estimating the monthly bill for the reference architecture with and without endpoints. Finish with a ten-minute recorded walkthrough in which you terminate every instance in one AZ while running a load generator against the ALB and show the access logs registering zero ELB-generated 5XX during recovery.

15.topic: AWS data: RDS Postgres, S3, ElastiCache, DynamoDB
15.why: Almost every FDE engagement ends with the customer's data living in one of these four services, on the customer's AWS account, under the customer's compliance rules. The FDE is the person on the call when the CFO asks whether the deleted orders table from Tuesday can come back, when the app team says the cache 'lost data' after a failover, or when the AWS bill for a pilot triples because a lifecycle rule pushed ten million tiny objects into Glacier. Being able to restore a database within a measured RTO, lock down a bucket so the security review passes first time, and say with evidence whether a workload belongs in DynamoDB or Postgres is what lets you be trusted with production in week one instead of month three.
prerequisites: Topic 12 (Terraform): providers, state, plan/apply, lifecycle blocks, import, and why ForceNew attributes destroy resources; every hands-on step here is done through Terraform.

Topic 13 (AWS networking and compute): VPC, private vs public subnets, security groups referencing other security groups, route tables (for gateway endpoints), and the AWS CLI configured with a profile.
Working Postgres: psql, roles, CREATE EXTENSION, pg_stat_statements, what WAL is and why replication lag exists; Topic 29 goes deeper, but the basics are assumed now.

IAM policy reading ability: Effect/Action/Resource/Condition, the difference between an identity policy and a resource policy, and that an explicit Deny wins; Topic 15 formalises this, so at minimum read the IAM policy evaluation logic page first.
Shell and jq fluency from Topic 0 so that aws ... --query and --output json become a scripting substrate rather than something you click through in the console.
An AWS account you can spend roughly 15-25 USD in for a week of db.t4g.medium Multi-AZ time, snapshots and a few GB of S3; set a billing alarm at 30 USD before starting.

subtopics.name: RDS anatomy: instance classes, gp3 vs io2, subnet groups, security groups
subtopics.learn: Know what an RDS instance actually is: an EC2-class VM (db.t4g burstable with CPU credits, db.m memory-balanced, db.r memory-optimised; the g suffix means Graviton) plus an EBS volume you cannot see. For gp3 on PostgreSQL the baseline is 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s under 400 GiB and 12,000 IOPS / 500 MiB/s at 400 GiB and above, so a 100 GiB volume that needs 10,000 IOPS must be resized or moved to io2. Understand storage autoscaling (max_allocated_storage triggers when free space is under 10% for five minutes, then grows by the larger of 10% or 5 GiB with a six-hour cooldown) and the storage-full status that makes the instance unavailable. Place the instance with a DB subnet group spanning at least two AZs of private subnets, a security group that allows 5432 only from the application security group, and publicly_accessible=false; confirm the endpoint resolves to a private IP with dig.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: DB instance storage

subtopics.name: Multi-AZ instance vs Multi-AZ DB cluster vs read replicas, and a forced failover
subtopics.learn: Distinguish the three: a Multi-AZ instance has one synchronous standby that never serves reads and fails over in roughly 60-120 seconds by swapping the CNAME behind the same endpoint hostname; a Multi-AZ DB cluster has one writer plus two semi-synchronous readable standbys, a separate reader endpoint and typically sub-35-second failover; a read replica is asynchronous streaming replication (watch ReplicaLag) that you can promote but that does not fail over automatically. Run aws rds reboot-db-instance --force-failover on your test instance while a psql loop with \watch 1 is running, and time how long connections fail. Then explain why the endpoint's CNAME TTL is only a few seconds and why a JVM with a cached DNS answer (networkaddress.cache.ttl) or a pooled connection with no keepalive keeps failing long after AWS says the failover finished. Know that Multi-AZ replication traffic is not billed but cross-AZ traffic from your app to the DB is.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Multi-AZ deployments

subtopics.name: Backups: automated backups, 5-minute log shipping, snapshots, sharing and copying
subtopics.learn: Understand that automated backups are a daily storage-level snapshot taken in the backup window plus transaction logs uploaded to S3 every five minutes, which is why the RPO of a point-in-time restore is up to five minutes; check the exact number with aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[0].LatestRestorableTime'. Retention is 0-35 days and setting it to 0 deletes all existing automated backups immediately, a change that has been made 'to save money' in real accounts. Manual snapshots persist until deleted and are incremental after the first; backup storage is free up to 100% of the provisioned storage in the region and billed per GB-month beyond that. Know the KMS constraint: a snapshot encrypted with the AWS-managed aws/rds key cannot be shared with another account, so cross-account DR requires a customer-managed key from day one, and cross-region copies re-encrypt with a key in the destination region.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Introduction to backups

subtopics.name: The restore drill: point-in-time restore, repoint, measure RTO and RPO
subtopics.learn: Run the whole drill from the CLI and time every step. Seed the instance with pgbench -i -s 300 (about 4.5 GB), insert a marker row with now(), then drop pgbench_accounts and record the wall-clock time. Restore with aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time --source-db-instance-identifier X --target-db-instance-identifier X-pitr --restore-time <30 s before the drop>, passing --db-subnet-group-name, --vpc-security-group-ids and --db-parameter-group-name explicitly because a restore otherwise lands in the default parameter group and default security group, which is the classic reason the app cannot connect to the 'successful' restore. Time aws rds wait db-instance-available, then time the first SELECT count(*): restored EBS volumes lazy-load blocks from S3, so the first pass is slow and pg_prewarm or a full-table read is part of RTO. Finish by renaming: aws rds modify-db-instance --new-db-instance-identifier on the old instance first, then on the restored one, so the original endpoint hostname is preserved and the app needs no config change. Write down RTO (drop to app healthy) and RPO (marker row present or not) and what dominated each.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Restoring a DB instance to a specified time

subtopics.name: Postgres on RDS: rds_superuser, parameter groups, extensions and logs
subtopics.learn: Know what you lose without real superuser: rds_superuser cannot read pg_hba.conf, cannot install unlisted extensions, and cannot write to the filesystem, so shared_preload_libraries (pg_stat_statements, auto_explain, pg_cron) is set in a custom parameter group rather than postgresql.conf. Understand static versus dynamic parameters: static ones show as pending-reboot in describe-db-parameters and only take effect after aws rds reboot-db-instance, and a modified parameter group attached to an instance is not applied until that reboot. Set log_min_duration_statement, log_connections and log_lock_waits, then ship logs with --cloudwatch-logs-export-configuration '{"EnableLogTypes":["postgresql","upgrade"]}' and read them with aws logs tail. Know rds.force_ssl=1 is the default on PostgreSQL 15+, rds.logical_replication=1 is required for Debezium or DMS and needs a reboot, and that rds.allowed_extensions and rds.restrict_password_commands exist for locked-down customers.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Working with parameters on RDS for PostgreSQL

subtopics.name: Connections: max_connections, RDS Proxy pinning, IAM auth tokens, Secrets Manager
subtopics.learn: Compute the default max_connections from LEAST({DBInstanceClassMemory/9531392},5000): a 1 GiB db.t4g.micro gets about 112, a 4 GiB db.t4g.medium about 450, and 30 Kubernetes pods with a pool of 20 each will exhaust that. Know when RDS Proxy is the answer (Lambda, serverless bursts, many short-lived clients) and what defeats its multiplexing: SET session variables, temp tables, advisory locks, LISTEN and some prepared-statement flows pin the client to a backend connection, visible in the DatabaseConnectionsCurrentlySessionPinned metric. For IAM database authentication, GRANT rds_iam TO app_user, generate a token with aws rds generate-db-auth-token, understand it is valid for 15 minutes and that the service caps roughly 200 new IAM-auth connections per second, so it belongs behind a pool or proxy. Prefer manage_master_user_password (Secrets Manager) over a password in state, and read the secret with aws secretsmanager get-secret-value to see the JSON shape the app must parse.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Amazon RDS Proxy

subtopics.name: RDS observability: Database Insights wait events, Enhanced Monitoring, the alarms that matter
subtopics.learn: Use Performance Insights (now surfaced as CloudWatch Database Insights) to read DB load in average active sessions, split by wait event: IO:DataFileRead means you are disk-bound, Lock:transactionid means row lock contention, LWLock:buffer_content or CPU means a query problem; the top-SQL view maps load back to statements, and seven days of retention is free. Turn on Enhanced Monitoring (monitoring_interval 1-60 s, needs monitoring_role_arn) to get real OS metrics into the RDSOSMetrics log group; CloudWatch CPUUtilization comes from the hypervisor and hides steal and iowait. Alarm on FreeStorageSpace, DatabaseConnections against max_connections, ReplicaLag, DiskQueueDepth, SwapUsage, BurstBalance if anyone still runs gp2, and the two Postgres-specific ones people forget: MaximumUsedTransactionIDs (wraparound) and TransactionLogsDiskUsage plus OldestReplicationSlotLag, which grow when an abandoned logical replication slot pins WAL until the volume fills.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Monitoring DB load with CloudWatch Database Insights

subtopics.name: RDS in Terraform: the aws_db_instance attributes that destroy data or wait for a window
subtopics.learn: Write aws_db_instance with engine="postgres", instance_class, storage_type="gp3", allocated_storage plus max_allocated_storage, storage_encrypted=true with kms_key_id, multi_az=true, db_subnet_group_name, vpc_security_group_ids, parameter_group_name from an aws_db_parameter_group (family "postgres16", static params with apply_method="pending-reboot"), manage_master_user_password=true, backup_retention_period, backup_window, maintenance_window, deletion_protection=true, skip_final_snapshot=false with final_snapshot_identifier, copy_tags_to_snapshot, performance_insights_enabled, monitoring_interval, enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports, iam_database_authentication_enabled and ca_cert_identifier. Learn from the plan which changes are ForceNew (identifier, engine, encryption toggle, kms_key_id) versus modify-in-place, and that with apply_immediately=false (the default) Terraform returns while RDS queues the change for the maintenance window. Use snapshot_identifier or the restore_to_point_in_time block to create from backups, then lifecycle { ignore_changes = [snapshot_identifier, restore_to_point_in_time] } so the next plan does not want to rebuild; pin engine_version only to the major version if auto_minor_version_upgrade is on. Practise terraform import of an instance created by a manual restore and reconciling the config until plan is clean.

resource.label: Terraform AWS provider: aws_db_instance

subtopics.name: S3 data model: consistency, per-prefix request limits, multipart, checksums, conditional writes
subtopics.learn: Internalise that S3 is a flat key space with strong read-after-write consistency for PUT, DELETE and LIST since 2020, so 'eventual consistency' explanations from older material are wrong. Know the scaling unit: about 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD per second per partitioned prefix, that 503 SlowDown means back off exponentially and spread keys across prefixes, and that S3 partitions prefixes over time rather than instantly. Use multipart upload for anything over 100 MB (mandatory over 5 GB single PUT; parts 5 MiB-5 GiB, up to 10,000 parts) and understand that abandoned parts are billed until a lifecycle AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload rule removes them. Do not treat ETag as MD5 (it is not for multipart or SSE-KMS objects); request x-amz-checksum-sha256 or CRC32C/CRC64NVME and verify with head-object --checksum-mode ENABLED. Use conditional writes, If-None-Match: * on PutObject for create-if-absent and If-Match with an ETag for optimistic concurrency, and handle the 412 PreconditionFailed.

resource.label: S3 User Guide: Optimizing S3 performance

subtopics.name: S3 encryption: SSE-S3 vs SSE-KMS, Bucket Keys, KMS key policies, enforce TLS and encryption
subtopics.learn: Know that every new object is SSE-S3 encrypted by default since 2023, so 'is it encrypted' is the wrong question; the customer question is who controls the key and who can be denied. With SSE-KMS and a customer-managed key, every PUT and GET calls KMS (GenerateDataKey and Decrypt), which costs per request and counts against the regional KMS quota (as low as 5,500 requests per second), so a bulk load can throttle; enable S3 Bucket Keys (bucket_key_enabled in Terraform) to cut KMS calls by up to 99%. Understand that a cross-account or cross-role AccessDenied on GetObject is frequently the KMS key policy, not the bucket policy: the principal needs kms:Decrypt in the key policy or via a grant, and for cross-account both the key policy and the caller's IAM policy must allow it. Write the two standard bucket-policy statements, Deny s3:* when aws:SecureTransport is false, and Deny s3:PutObject unless s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption equals aws:kms with your key ARN in s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id, then prove them with aws s3api put-object calls that return 403. Know SSE-C and DSSE-KMS exist and when a regulator asks for them.

resource.label: S3 User Guide: Using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)

subtopics.name: S3 lifecycle, versioning, storage classes and Object Lock: the rules and what they cost
subtopics.learn: Write a lifecycle configuration with Filter (Prefix, Tag, ObjectSizeGreaterThan), Transition, Expiration with ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker, NoncurrentVersionTransition and NoncurrentVersionExpiration with NewerNoncurrentVersions, and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload; in Terraform this is the separate aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration resource. Know the storage-class economics that turn 'archive it' into a bill increase: Standard-IA and One Zone-IA have a 30-day minimum and a 128 KB minimum billable size plus per-GB retrieval fees, Glacier Instant and Flexible have 90-day minimums, Deep Archive 180 days, each transition is a per-1,000-request charge, and Glacier classes add roughly 40 KB of metadata per object, so millions of 10 KB objects cost more in Glacier than in Standard. Intelligent-Tiering charges a per-object monitoring fee but no retrieval fee, which is the right default when access patterns are unknown. Understand versioning (delete creates a delete marker, noncurrent versions are billed) and Object Lock (requires versioning; Governance can be bypassed with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention, Compliance cannot be shortened by anyone including root), and that lifecycle actions run asynchronously about once a day while billing changes on the scheduled date.

resource.label: S3 User Guide: Managing the lifecycle of objects

subtopics.name: S3 access control: Block Public Access, policy evaluation, ACLs off, gateway endpoints
subtopics.learn: Know the four Block Public Access settings, that they are on by default at bucket creation since 2023 and should also be on at the account level, and that BucketOwnerEnforced (ACLs disabled) is now the default so cross-account writers no longer produce objects the bucket owner cannot read. Work through the evaluation order for a same-account request (union of identity and bucket policy, explicit Deny wins) versus cross-account (both sides must allow) and use conditions that customers' security teams expect: aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:SourceVpce, s3:prefix on ListBucket, and aws:SourceArn on service principals. Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 (and one for DynamoDB) so private-subnet workloads do not pay NAT gateway per-GB charges, verify with the route table entry and a traceroute-free check of aws s3 ls working with the NAT detached, then restrict the bucket to that endpoint. Know S3 Access Points for giving each application its own policy on a shared bucket.

resource.label: S3 User Guide: Blocking public access to your S3 storage

subtopics.name: Presigned URLs and direct-to-S3 uploads from a customer's browser or agent
subtopics.learn: Generate SigV4 presigned GET and PUT URLs from the SDK and understand what is actually signed: the method, key, expiry and any headers you include, so a presigned PUT only constrains Content-Type or x-amz-server-side-encryption if you signed them. Know the expiry rules that break in production: up to seven days with long-lived IAM user credentials, but a URL signed with role session credentials (an EKS pod via IRSA, a Lambda) dies when the session does, typically within an hour, regardless of the ExpiresIn you asked for. Configure the bucket CORS rules a browser upload needs (AllowedMethods PUT, ExposeHeaders ETag) and use multipart presigned uploads for large files. Decide when a presigned URL is the right pattern (large files, offloading bandwidth) and when a proxy through your API is better (per-user authorisation, virus scanning, audit).

resource.label: S3 User Guide: Sharing objects with presigned URLs

subtopics.name: ElastiCache topology: Valkey/Redis OSS vs Memcached, cluster mode, replication groups, failover
subtopics.learn: Choose the engine deliberately: Valkey is the priced-down successor to Redis OSS with the same protocol, Memcached is multi-threaded but has no replication or persistence, and ElastiCache Serverless trades per-node control for pay-per-GB-hour and ECPU. Understand cluster mode disabled (one shard, up to five replicas, a primary endpoint that moves on failover and a reader endpoint) versus cluster mode enabled (data sharded across slots, a configuration endpoint, MOVED redirects, multi-key commands only work when keys share a hash tag like {tenant42}:..., and the client library must be cluster-aware). Enable Multi-AZ with automatic failover and know what it promises: the primary DNS flips to a promoted replica within tens of seconds, but replication is asynchronous, so the last writes before the failure are gone; this is why a cache is not a datastore. Turn on in-transit TLS and AUTH or RBAC users, and test a failover with aws elasticache test-failover while a client loop runs, watching for connection resets and how long your client's retry policy takes to follow the new primary.

resource.label: ElastiCache User Guide: Cluster Mode Disabled vs Enabled

subtopics.name: ElastiCache memory, eviction and the metrics that predict an outage
subtopics.learn: Size a node as dataset plus replication buffer plus reserved-memory-percent (default 25%, needed for BGSAVE forks and sync), and set maxmemory-policy on purpose: allkeys-lru for a pure cache, volatile-lru or volatile-ttl when some keys must never be evicted, noeviction when the app must fail loudly rather than lose queue entries. Watch EngineCPUUtilization rather than CPUUtilization because the engine is single-threaded and 90% on one core is saturation while the node reports 25%; alarm on DatabaseMemoryUsagePercentage, Evictions (any sustained non-zero on a cache that assumed a hit rate), CurrConnections and NewConnections (a client without pooling will exhaust maxclients), ReplicationLag and SwapUsage. Learn the workload anti-patterns you will find in customer code: KEYS * in production (use SCAN), big values over 100 KB, hot keys hammering one shard, and TTL-less keys in a 'cache' that never shrinks; and the two caching disciplines from Topic 31 that matter here, TTL jitter and stampede locks with SET NX PX.

resource.label: ElastiCache User Guide: Which metrics should I monitor?

subtopics.name: DynamoDB partitions and capacity: RCU/WCU maths, on-demand vs provisioned, hot partitions
subtopics.learn: Understand the physical model that drives every DynamoDB failure: items (max 400 KB) are hashed by partition key onto partitions that each hold at most 10 GB and serve at most 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU, no matter what the table is provisioned for. Do the arithmetic: one RCU is one strongly consistent 4 KB read per second (eventually consistent reads cost half, transactional reads double), one WCU is one 1 KB write (transactional double), and a 12 KB item read strongly consistently is 3 RCU. Know how on-demand really scales: instantly up to twice the previous peak, throttling beyond that until it adapts, with new tables starting around 4,000 WCU / 12,000 RCU, which is why a 3 a.m. batch job on an idle table throttles; pre-warm with warm throughput or switch to provisioned with auto scaling for predictable loads, remembering scale-in is rate-limited. Recognise a hot partition from ThrottledRequests and ProvisionedThroughputExceededException while ConsumedCapacity is far below provisioned, and fix it with write sharding (key suffix 0-N), a better key, or by moving the hot tenant, not by paying for more capacity.

resource.label: DynamoDB Developer Guide: Read/write capacity mode

subtopics.name: DynamoDB access patterns: Query vs Scan, GSI vs LSI, single-table design, conditions and transactions
subtopics.learn: Start from the access-pattern list, never the entity list: every read must be a GetItem or a Query on a partition key with an optional sort-key condition (=, BETWEEN, begins_with), paginated by LastEvaluatedKey in 1 MB pages; a Scan reads the whole table, consumes RCU for filtered-out items, and is a design failure outside admin jobs or parallel exports with Segment/TotalSegments. Model with generic PK and SK attributes and overloaded GSIs (GSI1PK/GSI1SK) so one table answers many patterns; know that a GSI has its own capacity and is eventually consistent, that a throttled GSI throttles writes to the base table, and that an LSI shares the partition key, must exist at creation and caps an item collection at 10 GB. Use sparse indexes for 'find all pending' patterns. Get idempotency and invariants from ConditionExpression (attribute_not_exists(PK) for create-once, a version attribute for optimistic locking, catch ConditionalCheckFailedException) and from TransactWriteItems (up to 100 items, 4 MB, ClientRequestToken for idempotent retries) rather than from application-side checks.

resource.label: DynamoDB Developer Guide: NoSQL design for DynamoDB

subtopics.name: DynamoDB durability and change: Streams, TTL, point-in-time recovery and what a restore forgets
subtopics.learn: Enable PITR (35-day window) and restore to a new table with aws dynamodb restore-table-to-point-in-time, then check what did not come back: auto scaling policies, IAM policies referencing the old table ARN, CloudWatch alarms, tags, TTL settings, stream settings and PITR itself all have to be reapplied, so the runbook is Terraform plus a rename dance, not one command. Use DynamoDB Streams (NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES, 24-hour retention, ordered per item, consumed by Lambda or Kinesis) for change data capture and outbox patterns. Set TTL on an epoch-seconds attribute and understand deletion is asynchronous and can lag by days, so reads must filter expired items; TTL deletes are free and appear in Streams as REMOVE events with a userIdentity of dynamodb.amazonaws.com. Know on-demand backups and global tables exist and that global tables resolve conflicts with last-writer-wins.

resource.label: DynamoDB Developer Guide: Point-in-time recovery

subtopics.name: Decision framework and cost mechanics: DynamoDB vs Postgres vs ElastiCache for a customer workload
subtopics.learn: Be able to run the decision in a customer meeting. DynamoDB wins when the access patterns are few, known up front and key-based, when the scale or burstiness would require sharding Postgres, when the team wants zero database operations, and when items are small; it loses when the customer needs ad hoc queries, joins, aggregates, reporting, constraints, or has a SQL-literate team that will own the system after you leave, and it punishes late-discovered access patterns with GSI backfills. Compare the cost shapes with real numbers: RDS bills instance-hours and storage whether or not anyone is querying (a Multi-AZ db.r6g.large is roughly 400-500 USD a month before storage and backups), DynamoDB bills per request and per GB-month and can be nearly free at low volume but expensive for scan-heavy analytics, and ElastiCache is a per-node cost that only makes sense when it removes a larger database or latency cost. Write a one-page recommendation for a given workload that states the access patterns, the estimated monthly cost of each option, the operational owner, and the migration cost if the choice is wrong.

resource.label: AWS Decision Guides: Choosing an AWS database service

subtopics.name: Maintenance and upgrades: windows, pending changes, major versions, blue/green, CA rotation
subtopics.learn: Know what happens in the 30-minute weekly maintenance window (OS patches, minor engine upgrades if auto_minor_version_upgrade is on, queued modifications) and how to see pending work with describe-pending-maintenance-actions and the PendingModifiedValues field. For major PostgreSQL upgrades understand the in-place path: a pre-upgrade snapshot, pg_upgrade with minutes to tens of minutes of downtime, read replicas upgraded alongside, extensions needing ALTER EXTENSION ... UPDATE, and statistics not carried over so ANALYZE is mandatory before declaring success. Compare with RDS Blue/Green Deployments, which build a logically replicated green environment you can test and then switch over in under a minute with guardrails; rehearse whichever path you recommend on a restored snapshot first. Track certificate authority rotation: the rds-ca-2019 CA expired in 2024 and instances now use rds-ca-rsa2048-g1 or the ECC/4096 variants, so a client that pins a CA bundle must update it before you change ca_cert_identifier. Subscribe to RDS events via SNS so failovers, storage-full and maintenance land in the customer's Slack.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Maintaining a DB instance

outcomes: You can perform a point-in-time restore of a Multi-AZ RDS Postgres instance from the CLI, repoint the application without a config change by renaming instances, and report a measured RTO and RPO with timestamps for a roughly 5 GB database, in under 45 minutes end to end.

You can force a Multi-AZ failover with reboot-db-instance --force-failover while a client loop runs, state to the second how long connections failed, and explain which client-side settings (DNS caching, pool validation, keepalives) would have extended the outage.

You can write a Terraform module for RDS Postgres with encryption, deletion protection, final snapshot, Secrets Manager password, a custom parameter group and log exports, and predict from terraform plan which attribute changes replace the instance, which apply in place, and which wait for the maintenance window.

You can produce an S3 bucket policy that denies non-TLS and unencrypted writes, a lifecycle configuration that transitions noncurrent versions and aborts incomplete multipart uploads, and a written estimate of the monthly bill change for 10 million 50 KB objects under that policy.

You can take a list of eight access patterns and produce a DynamoDB single-table key schema with GSIs, an RCU/WCU and monthly cost estimate, and a list of which patterns would still require a Scan and what that implies.

You can diagnose a DynamoDB throttling incident or an ElastiCache Evictions spike from CloudWatch metrics alone, name the mechanism (hot partition, on-demand ceiling, memory pressure, missing TTL) and propose the fix ranked by effort.
You can explain to a customer architect in five minutes, using their workload, whether it belongs in DynamoDB, Postgres or a cache, including cost shape and who operates it after you leave.
failureModes: The 'tested' backup has never been restored: the first real PITR comes up in the default parameter group and default security group, the app cannot connect, pg_stat_statements is missing, and a promised 15-minute RTO becomes two hours of a customer watching you read documentation.

skip_final_snapshot = true is left in the Terraform module from dev; months later someone renames the identifier or toggles encryption, the plan shows a replace nobody reads carefully, and the production database is destroyed with no snapshot.

A Debezium or DMS task is decommissioned but its logical replication slot is not dropped; WAL is retained, TransactionLogsDiskUsage climbs for weeks, storage autoscaling masks it until max_allocated_storage is hit, and the instance goes storage-full at 2 a.m.

After a Multi-AZ failover AWS reports 90 seconds of downtime but the application errors for nine minutes because the JVM cached the old DNS answer and the connection pool kept handing out dead sockets; the incident is blamed on RDS.

An SSE-KMS bucket with no Bucket Key takes a bulk backfill of small objects; every PUT calls KMS, the account hits the regional KMS request quota, the loader sees throttling it interprets as S3 flakiness, and the KMS line item is larger than the S3 storage line.

A lifecycle rule moves 40 million 8 KB log fragments to Glacier Flexible Retrieval to save money; transition requests, 40 KB per-object overhead and 90-day minimums make the month more expensive than Standard, and the objects the team then deletes are charged for the full minimum anyway.

A multi-tenant DynamoDB table uses tenant_id as the partition key; one tenant is 60% of traffic, the partition caps at 1,000 WCU regardless of on-demand mode, the SDK's retries hide the throttling as p99 latency, and the customer concludes DynamoDB 'does not scale'.
interviewQuestions: A customer's RDS Postgres orders table was dropped by a bad migration at 14:07 UTC and they noticed at 15:30. Walk me through exactly what you do, in order, what you tell them about RPO before you start, how long it takes on a 500 GB Multi-AZ instance and why, and what the application team must do on their side.

Our Multi-AZ RDS instance failed over last night. AWS's event log shows 75 seconds of failover, but the application had errors for nine minutes. Give me the likely causes, how you would confirm each one, and what you would change so the next failover is invisible.

Design the storage layer for a document-processing pipeline: customers upload files from 1 KB to 2 GB, we extract text and embeddings, users query results, and everything for a customer must be provably deleted 90 days after they leave. Which of RDS, S3, DynamoDB and ElastiCache holds what, where do the keys live, and how do you prove deletion to an auditor?

A customer wants to migrate a 2 TB Postgres orders database to DynamoDB 'for scale'. What are the first five questions you ask, what answers would make you agree, and what answers would make you decline the work?

The S3 bill for a pilot went up four times month over month with no change in stored bytes. Give me your investigation order, the three most likely causes, and the CloudWatch or Cost Explorer evidence that would confirm each.

Compare a Multi-AZ instance, a Multi-AZ DB cluster and a read replica on replication mode, failover time, whether the standby serves reads, and cost. A customer with a read-heavy reporting workload and a 99.95% availability target asks which to buy; what do you recommend and what do you warn them about?

A DynamoDB on-demand table throttles at 3 a.m. during a nightly batch job even though on-demand 'scales automatically'. Explain the mechanism, then give three fixes ranked from least to most effort, and say which one you would ship this week.
15.proofOfWork: A public repository named aws-data-restore-drill that extends the plan's Terraform-plus-RTO deliverable into a repeatable, evidence-backed exercise. It contains a Terraform module that stands up a Multi-AZ RDS Postgres instance on gp3 with a customer-managed KMS key, deletion protection, a Secrets Manager-managed password, a custom parameter group loading pg_stat_statements and auto_explain, log exports to CloudWatch, Enhanced Monitoring and the alarms from the observability subtopic, alongside an S3 bucket module with Bucket Keys, the deny-non-TLS and deny-unencrypted policies, a lifecycle configuration with noncurrent-version expiry and multipart abort, and gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB. A drill.sh seeds the database with pgbench, inserts a timestamped marker row, drops a table, performs a point-in-time restore via the CLI with the correct parameter and security groups, waits for availability, measures first-query lazy-load latency, renames instances so the endpoint is unchanged, verifies the marker row, and appends a line to RTO_LOG.md with every timestamp; the log shows at least three runs with RTO and RPO and a paragraph on what dominated each. A failover.py drives reboot --force-failover and records, per second, connection success from a pooled psycopg client with and without DNS caching disabled, plotted into a PNG. A policy_tests.sh proves each S3 deny statement with aws s3api calls that return 403 and one that succeeds. Finally, a dynamodb/ directory holds a single-table model for a sample multi-tenant workload with eight access patterns, a Terraform aws_dynamodb_table with two GSIs, a small load generator that reproduces a hot-partition throttle on tenant_id and then eliminates it with write sharding, screenshots of the ThrottledRequests metric before and after, and a one-page DECISION.md recommending DynamoDB or Postgres for that workload with a monthly cost estimate for each.

16.topic: IAM and cloud security: least privilege, roles, IRSA, no long-lived keys
16.why: Every FDE deployment into a customer's AWS account ends at the same gate: their security team opens your Terraform, finds the role your workers run as, and asks 'why does this need s3:* and where do the credentials live?' If the answer involves an access key in an environment variable, the pilot stalls for weeks and you are now the vendor who put an AKIA key in a container. The FDE also owns the other side of the boundary: your product assuming a role in the customer's account, CI deploying without stored secrets, and the ExternalId conversation with their CISO. Being able to write the worker policy by hand, wire IRSA correctly the first time, and read an AccessDenied message to its root cause in ten minutes is what separates the engineer who unblocks go-live from the one who files a ticket with the platform team.
prerequisites: Kubernetes from topics 7 and 8: what a ServiceAccount is, how a projected volume mounts a token into a pod, that a mutating admission webhook rewrites the Pod spec at creation time (IRSA is exactly those three things glued to STS), and enough RBAC to keep 'Kubernetes RBAC' and 'AWS IAM' straight when a customer conflates them in a review

AWS networking and compute from topic 13: EC2 instance lifecycle, Lambda, VPC endpoints (aws:SourceVpce), security groups, and the link-local 169.254.0.0/16 range where IMDS and container credential endpoints live
AWS data from topic 14: S3 bucket versus object ARNs, SSE-KMS, Secrets Manager, and DynamoDB table ARNs, since those are the resources every worker policy scopes
Terraform from topic 12: data.aws_iam_policy_document, aws_iam_role, aws_iam_openid_connect_provider, and why a secret in state is a secret in plaintext

Networking from topic 2: TLS, HTTP headers, and enough JWT to base64-decode a token payload and read iss, sub, aud, exp; every keyless mechanism in this topic is an OIDC JWT exchanged for STS credentials

An AWS account you control with a billing alarm, AWS CLI v2, and either a small EKS cluster for two or three hours (about $0.10/hour for the control plane plus one t3.small node) or eksctl to create one on demand; flaws.cloud needs only the CLI

subtopics.name: Policy evaluation order: why an Allow is never the whole story
subtopics.learn: Trace a request through the evaluation logic in the order AWS applies it: implicit deny by default, any explicit Deny anywhere wins, then the request must be allowed by (in a single account) the SCP, the permissions boundary if one is attached, the session policy if one was passed to AssumeRole, and finally either an identity-based policy or a resource-based policy. Know the same-account shortcut (a resource policy that names the principal is sufficient on its own) and the cross-account rule (identity policy in the caller's account AND resource policy in the resource's account must both allow). Know the two nuances that bite: a resource policy that names a role ARN also matches that role's sessions, but one that names a specific assumed-role session ARN does not match the role; and KMS key policies are the one resource policy that is required even for same-account access. Be able to say which document you would open first for a given AccessDenied.

resource.label: IAM User Guide: Policy evaluation logic

subtopics.name: Policy grammar and ARN shapes you must write without a reference
subtopics.learn: Write the JSON from memory: Version 2012-10-17 (without it, policy variables like ${aws:username} are treated as literals), Statement array, Sid, Effect, Action or NotAction, Resource or NotResource, Condition, and Principal only in resource-based and trust policies. Know the ARN format arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource and the per-service quirks: S3 bucket ARNs have no region or account, s3:ListBucket targets the bucket ARN while s3:GetObject targets bucket/*, Secrets Manager secret ARNs end in a six-character random suffix so you match them with -??????, and actions such as ec2:DescribeInstances or s3:ListAllMyBuckets do not support resource-level permissions and require Resource *. Treat iam:PassRole as the privilege-escalation action it is: whoever can pass an admin role to Lambda or ECS is an admin, so scope it by Resource and by the iam:PassedToService condition. Know the limits: 6144 characters for a managed policy, 10240 for inline on a role, 10 managed policies per role by default.

resource.label: IAM User Guide: IAM JSON policy elements reference

subtopics.name: Condition keys and operators: the difference between scoped and theatre
subtopics.learn: Use the global keys that actually constrain blast radius: aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount in service trust policies, aws:PrincipalOrgID in resource policies, aws:PrincipalTag and aws:ResourceTag for ABAC, aws:SecureTransport for TLS-only buckets, aws:SourceVpce to pin access to a VPC endpoint, aws:RequestedRegion in SCPs, aws:CalledVia and aws:ViaAWSService for service-mediated calls, and service keys such as kms:ViaService, s3:prefix, sts:ExternalId and iam:PassedToService. Know the operators (StringEquals, StringLike, ArnLike, Bool, Null, IpAddress, DateGreaterThan) and the two modifiers that change semantics: the ...IfExists suffix, and ForAllValues/ForAnyValues for multi-valued keys such as aws:TagKeys. Memorise the classic trap: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is absent, not false, on requests signed with long-term keys, so a Deny with Bool false never matches and you must write BoolIfExists or use Null. Know that a wrongly typed key in a Condition is not an error; it just silently never matches, which is why validate-policy matters.

resource.label: IAM User Guide: AWS global condition context keys

subtopics.name: Exercise: write the worker policy by hand and validate it
subtopics.learn: Write, from a blank file, the identity policy for a queue worker: sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility and sqs:GetQueueAttributes on one queue ARN; s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::bucket/input/* and s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN with a s3:prefix condition; s3:PutObject on bucket/output/*; secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on one secret ARN with the -?????? suffix; kms:Decrypt on the customer-managed key constrained by kms:ViaService secretsmanager.<region>.amazonaws.com; and logs:CreateLogStream plus logs:PutLogEvents on one log group and its streams. Run `aws accessanalyzer validate-policy --policy-type IDENTITY_POLICY --policy-document file://worker.json` and drive the findings to zero ERROR and zero SECURITY_WARNING, then run parliament locally for the same check offline. Know what validate-policy catches (invalid actions, mismatched action and resource types, overly permissive wildcards, unsupported condition keys) and what it cannot (whether the policy is more than the job needs). Keep this policy: the proof-of-work repo and the interview whiteboard both reuse it.

resource.label: IAM User Guide: Validate policies with IAM Access Analyzer

subtopics.name: Roles, trust policies and STS sessions
subtopics.learn: A role is two documents: a trust policy (who may call sts:AssumeRole, sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity or sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML) and one or more permission policies. AssumeRole returns an ASIA access key, a secret, a session token and an Expiration; DurationSeconds runs from 900 seconds up to the role's MaxSessionDuration (1 hour by default, 12 hours maximum), and any session obtained through role chaining is capped at 1 hour regardless. The RoleSessionName you pass becomes the CloudTrail identity arn:aws:sts::acct:assumed-role/RoleName/SessionName, so make it meaningful (pod name, CI run id, human username); SourceIdentity does the same across chains and cannot be changed downstream. Know the trust-policy footgun: naming a specific role ARN as Principal stores the role's unique AROA id, so deleting and recreating that role silently breaks the trust; name the account root and constrain with the identity policy on the other side, or use aws:PrincipalArn in a Condition. Confirm what you are with `aws sts get-caller-identity` before debugging anything else.

resource.label: IAM User Guide: Roles terms and concepts

subtopics.name: The credential provider chain and how to see which link fired
subtopics.learn: Know the order the SDKs walk: explicit code parameters, environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN), web identity (AWS_ROLE_ARN plus AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE), shared config profiles (role_arn with source_profile or credential_source, sso-session, credential_process), container credentials (AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI on 169.254.170.2 for ECS, or AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI plus AWS_CONTAINER_AUTHORIZATION_TOKEN_FILE for EKS Pod Identity on 169.254.170.23), and finally IMDS; the exact ordering differs slightly per SDK, so check the table for the language you ship. Know that temporary credentials are refreshed by the SDK in the background before expiry, so a long-running process never needs to restart for rotation. Debug with `aws configure list` (shows the source of each value), `aws sts get-caller-identity`, `--debug` to watch providers being tried, and AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true to stop a laptop from hanging on IMDS. Half of all production 'AccessDenied' tickets are a process that picked up a stale env var ahead of the role you intended.

resource.label: AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide: Standardized credential providers

subtopics.name: Why a key in a container is a finding
subtopics.learn: Be able to explain, in the customer's security review, exactly what is wrong with an AKIA key in an image or env var: it never expires, it is bound to an IAM user rather than the workload, it is indistinguishable in CloudTrail from anyone who copied it, it cannot be rotated without a redeploy, and it leaks through `docker inspect`, `docker history` (ENV layers persist), `/proc/<pid>/environ`, crash dumps, CI logs and any registry the image is pushed to. Contrast with ASIA credentials from a role: short-lived, scoped, auto-refreshed, attributed to a session name. Know the compliance hooks the customer will cite: CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark on root keys and 90-day rotation, SOC 2 CC6 logical access, and that AWS itself attaches an AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine policy within minutes of a key appearing in a public repository. Know the detection tooling you will run on their repos and images: trufflehog and gitleaks for AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16} patterns, `aws iam list-access-keys` and `aws iam get-access-key-last-used` for the account side.

resource.label: IAM User Guide: Manage access keys for IAM users

subtopics.name: EC2 instance profiles and IMDSv2 as the SSRF firewall
subtopics.learn: An instance profile is the container for exactly one role attached to an EC2 instance; the SDK fetches ASIA credentials from http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name>. IMDSv1 answers any GET, which is how an SSRF bug in a web app on the instance (the Capital One breach, and flaws.cloud level 5) becomes stolen role credentials. IMDSv2 requires a PUT to /latest/api/token with X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds (max 21600) and then that token in the X-aws-ec2-metadata-token header; PUT requests carrying X-Forwarded-For are rejected, and the response hop limit (default 1) means a packet from a container on a bridge network cannot get the token. Enforce with `aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id i-xxx --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1`, set the account default with `modify-instance-metadata-defaults --http-tokens required`, and prove it with a plain curl returning 401. In Terraform this is metadata_options { http_tokens = "required" } on every aws_instance and launch template.

resource.label: EC2 User Guide: Configure the Instance Metadata Service options

subtopics.name: ECS task roles and Lambda execution roles: two identities per workload
subtopics.learn: Separate the ECS taskRoleArn (what your code is allowed to do) from the executionRoleArn (what the ECS agent needs: ecr:GetAuthorizationToken and pulls, logs:CreateLogStream and PutLogEvents, secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for secrets injected into env); mixing them is the most common over-permissioning in customer task definitions. Task credentials are served at 169.254.170.2 through AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI, and on the EC2 launch type you must block tasks from reaching the instance role with ECS_AWSVPC_BLOCK_IMDS=true in ecs.config or an iptables rule, otherwise every task inherits the node's permissions. Lambda's execution role credentials arrive as temporary AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET/SESSION_TOKEN env vars, and the function needs only its own log group. Whoever registers the task definition or creates the function needs iam:PassRole on that specific role with iam:PassedToService set to ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com or lambda.amazonaws.com, never PassRole on *.

resource.label: Amazon ECS Developer Guide: Task IAM role

subtopics.name: IRSA mechanics end to end, and debugging it when the pod cannot assume
subtopics.learn: Wire it by hand once: read the cluster's issuer with `aws eks describe-cluster --query cluster.identity.oidc.issuer`, create an IAM OIDC identity provider for it (aws_iam_openid_connect_provider with the thumbprint, or `eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider`), write a trust policy with Principal Federated set to that provider ARN, Action sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, and StringEquals on <issuer-host>:sub = system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<sa-name> and <issuer-host>:aud = sts.amazonaws.com, then annotate the ServiceAccount with eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn. The amazon-eks-pod-identity-webhook mutates pods at creation, injecting AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE=/var/run/secrets/eks.amazonaws.com/serviceaccount/token, AWS_STS_REGIONAL_ENDPOINTS=regional and a projected volume with audience sts.amazonaws.com and expirationSeconds 86400; the SDK's web identity provider then exchanges the JWT for ASIA credentials. Debug in order: `kubectl describe pod` shows the env vars (if not, the annotation was added after the pod existed or the SA is wrong; restart the pod); `kubectl exec ... -- cat $AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d` shows the sub and aud you must match exactly in the trust policy; 'Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity' means the trust policy condition does not match (namespace typo, wrong OIDC id, StringLike wildcard that does not cover it). Never write sub as system:serviceaccount:*:* with StringLike; that is every pod in the cluster.

resource.label: Amazon EKS User Guide: IAM roles for service accounts

subtopics.name: EKS Pod Identity versus IRSA: when to pick which
subtopics.learn: Pod Identity replaces the per-cluster OIDC provider with a single service principal: the trust policy allows pods.eks.amazonaws.com to sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession, and the mapping lives in `aws eks create-pod-identity-association --cluster-name X --namespace ns --service-account sa --role-arn ...` rather than a ServiceAccount annotation. The eks-pod-identity-agent add-on (a DaemonSet) serves credentials on 169.254.170.23 and the SDK reaches it through the container credential provider with AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI and AWS_CONTAINER_AUTHORIZATION_TOKEN_FILE, so it needs SDK versions from late 2023 or newer. Sessions carry tags (eks-cluster-name, kubernetes-namespace, kubernetes-service-account, kubernetes-pod-name) you can use in aws:PrincipalTag conditions for ABAC, and one role can serve many clusters without editing trust. Limits to state in a design review: EC2 nodes only (no Fargate at time of writing), Linux first, and cross-account access via role chaining. Pick IRSA when the customer already runs it, has Fargate, or uses older SDKs; pick Pod Identity for new clusters where you want to stop managing OIDC providers per cluster.

resource.label: Amazon EKS User Guide: EKS Pod Identities

subtopics.name: Keyless CI: GitHub Actions to AWS with OIDC
subtopics.learn: Create an IAM OIDC provider for https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com with audience sts.amazonaws.com, give the job `permissions: id-token: write` and `contents: read`, and use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume; the action requests a JWT from GitHub and calls sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. The trust policy must have two conditions: StringEquals on token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud = sts.amazonaws.com AND a StringEquals or tight StringLike on :sub, e.g. repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main or repo:org/repo:environment:production. A trust policy with only the aud condition lets any GitHub repository on the internet assume your deploy role, and sub set to repo:org/* lets any repo in the org; both are real findings. Know that pull_request events from forks produce a different sub, that reusable workflows expose job_workflow_ref for pinning, and that you can customise the sub claim format per repo through the GitHub API when you need environment plus branch. Session duration comes from role-duration-seconds and is bounded by MaxSessionDuration.

resource.label: GitHub Docs: Configuring OpenID Connect in Amazon Web Services

subtopics.name: Humans without keys: Identity Center profiles, MFA conditions, root hygiene
subtopics.learn: Humans use IAM Identity Center permission sets, not IAM users: `aws configure sso` writes an sso-session block into ~/.aws/config, `aws sso login --profile x` caches a short-lived token under ~/.aws/sso/cache, and the CLI mints role credentials per profile for 1 to 12 hours as set on the permission set. For legacy accounts that still have user keys, aws-vault keeps them in the OS keychain and hands processes only session tokens. Where IAM users still exist, the MFA guard is a Deny on everything except the MFA and password actions with BoolIfExists aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent false. Root: hardware MFA, no access keys, and `aws iam get-account-summary` showing AccountAccessKeysPresent 0 is the line you paste into the customer's evidence folder.

resource.label: AWS CLI User Guide: Configuring IAM Identity Center authentication

subtopics.name: Cross-account roles, ExternalId and the confused deputy
subtopics.learn: The standard FDE integration is your product's role in your account assuming a role the customer creates in theirs: their trust policy names your account (or your specific role ARN via aws:PrincipalArn) and requires sts:ExternalId equal to a value you generated and showed them; your identity policy allows sts:AssumeRole on their role ARN.
