24.why: When the system you deployed at a customer breaks at 02:00, the FDE is the person the customer's VP calls, the person who has to run the bridge with the customer's own platform team on it, and the person who has to send the written account the customer's CTO forwards to their board. Nobody on the vendor side has more context than you, so you are the de facto incident commander whether or not anyone gave you the title, and a sloppy incident (three people typing into production, no timeline, a status update that speculated about root cause and was wrong) costs more trust than the outage itself. The postmortem is the artifact that turns an outage into a renewal: a blameless, numbers-first document with dated action items is how a customer decides you are safe to keep in production.

subtopics.name: Severity ladder and the declaration threshold
subtopics.learn: Write a SEV1 to SEV5 ladder for DefenderMate where each level is defined by customer-observable impact and a required response, not by which component broke: SEV1 = customer-facing outage or data loss, IC assigned, status page within 15 minutes, exec update every 30; SEV2 = degraded for a subset, IC assigned, no status page unless it lasts 60 minutes; SEV3 and below are business-hours tickets. Internalise PagerDuty's rule that if you are unsure whether it is a SEV1 or SEV2 you treat it as the higher one, and that declaring an incident is cheap while a late declaration is not. Know the difference between severity (impact) and priority (order of work) and why a SEV1 for one tenant may be a P2 for the platform.

resource.label: PagerDuty Incident Response - Severity Levels

subtopics.name: Roles: Incident Commander, deputy, scribe, comms lead, subject-matter experts
subtopics.learn: Know each role's single job and its anti-pattern: the IC owns decisions and the timeline but never touches a keyboard to debug; the deputy watches the IC (time, fatigue, missed hand-raises) and takes over on a clean hand-off ('you have command', 'I have command'); the scribe records observations, decisions and actions with timestamps; the comms lead owns every message that leaves the room; SMEs run diagnosis and execute tasks the IC assigns. Practise the hand-off protocol and the 'IC role is not seniority' rule: on a customer bridge the customer's principal engineer may be the best SME precisely because they should not be IC. Decide up front how the FDE splits the IC and comms roles when only two people are awake.

resource.label: PagerDuty Incident Response - Different Roles

subtopics.name: Running the bridge: the IC decision loop
subtopics.learn: Run the loop out loud: state current impact and what is known, propose one action, poll for strong objections ('any strong objections?' then a five-second silence, not a discussion), assign it to a named person with a timebox ('Priya, roll back the classifier to the previous revision, report in 5 minutes'), then re-assess when the timebox expires. Enforce one channel and one voice bridge, ban side-threads and 'let me just try something', and never let a task go unassigned or un-timeboxed. Know PagerDuty's explicit rules: the IC may remove anyone who is disruptive, the IC decides rather than seeks consensus, and 'I need someone to' is banned in favour of names. Pin a state summary (impact, current hypothesis, actions in flight, next update time) every 30 minutes.

resource.label: PagerDuty Incident Response - During an Incident

subtopics.name: Scribing the timeline and annotating dashboards
subtopics.learn: Keep a single incident channel where every entry is `HH:MM UTC` plus one of OBSERVED / DECIDED / ACTION / RESULT, and paste raw evidence (the exact error line, the `kubectl rollout history` output, the alert payload) rather than paraphrase. Push the same timestamps into Grafana as annotations (`POST /api/annotations` with `time`, `tags: ["incident","INC-2026-014"]`, `text`) on the DefenderMate SLO dashboard so the postmortem graphs show detection, mitigation and recovery as vertical lines against the burn rate. Configure the dashboard's annotation query to pull by tag so the lines survive dashboard edits. Export the channel history at the end; the timeline is the raw material for the postmortem and it degrades every hour it is not written down.

resource.label: Grafana docs - Annotate visualizations (incl. annotations HTTP API)

subtopics.name: Mitigate first: the five-minute triage decision
subtopics.learn: Adopt the SRE rule that during an incident you stop the bleeding before you find the cause. Within five minutes of declaring, answer three questions: what changed (deploy, config, feature flag, dependency, traffic, certificate expiry, quota), can it be reverted, and can traffic be shed. Know the generic mitigation menu and its order of preference: roll back the last change, disable via flag, scale up, fail over, degrade gracefully (serve cached, drop non-critical path), rate limit, drain. Understand why 'roll forward with a fix' is usually the wrong first move under pressure and when it is the only move (a migration that already ran, a data corruption). Rehearse saying 'we are mitigating; root cause comes after' to a customer exec who wants to know why.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Emergency Response

subtopics.name: Troubleshooting under pressure without fooling yourself
subtopics.learn: Apply the SRE troubleshooting loop deliberately: triage, examine (what the telemetry says, not what you expect), hypothesise, test the cheapest discriminating experiment, repeat. Name the pitfalls you must actively defend against: confirmation bias toward the last thing you touched, correlation with an unrelated deploy, fixing symptoms of a healthy component, and 'it is always DNS' style pattern-matching that skips the evidence. Build the 'is it us or the cloud' reflex: check the provider health dashboard and your dependency status pages before spending 20 minutes on your own code. Keep a written list of hypotheses with the evidence for and against each so a fresh responder can pick up without re-deriving.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Effective Troubleshooting

subtopics.name: Kubernetes mitigation moves for Dokeo and DefenderMate
subtopics.learn: Be able to execute each of these blind and know what it does and does not fix: `kubectl rollout history deploy/dokeo` then `kubectl rollout undo deploy/dokeo --to-revision=N`; `kubectl rollout pause` to freeze a bad progressive rollout; `kubectl scale --replicas=` and temporarily raising HPA `minReplicas`; `kubectl cordon` and `drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data` for a bad node; `kubectl delete pod` on a single CrashLoopBackOff pod (useless if the image is broken, useful if it is a stuck init); `kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` as the first command every time. Know that ArgoCD with `selfHeal: true` will revert your manual `undo` within minutes, so the durable mitigation is `git revert` on the app-of-apps repo or `argocd app set --sync-policy none` first, and that `kubectl rollout undo` changes the pod-template-hash so your dashboards' version labels change too.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs - Deployments: Rolling Back a Deployment

subtopics.name: Data-layer mitigation on Kaupex Postgres
subtopics.learn: Read `pg_stat_activity` for the incident view: `state`, `wait_event_type`, `wait_event`, `xact_start`, `query_start`, and `pg_blocking_pids(pid)` to find the head of a lock queue. Know the difference between `pg_cancel_backend(pid)` (cancels the statement, keeps the session) and `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` (kills the session and rolls back), and that killing an `idle in transaction` session that holds an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock unblocks everything behind it. Know the emergency settings you can `ALTER SYSTEM SET` and `pg_reload_conf()` without a restart: `statement_timeout`, `lock_timeout`, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`. Know what not to do: terminating the walsender to a replica, or a long-running `VACUUM` on a table near wraparound, converts a slow incident into an outage.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - The Cumulative Statistics System (pg_stat_activity)

subtopics.name: Workflow-engine incidents: stuck and poisoned Temporal workflows
subtopics.learn: Diagnose a Kaupex incident where hundreds of workflows are stuck: `temporal workflow list --query 'ExecutionStatus="Running" AND WorkflowType="Onboarding"'`, `temporal workflow describe -w <id>` to see pending activities and their retry state, `temporal task-queue describe` to confirm workers are polling. Know the mitigation ladder: restart workers (safe, execution is durable), `temporal workflow signal` to nudge a waiting workflow, `temporal workflow reset -w <id> --event-id N --reason` to replay from before a bad activity, `temporal workflow cancel` (cooperative) versus `terminate` (immediate, no cleanup), and batch versions of each. Understand the poison-pill pattern where one activity fails forever with an unbounded retry policy and starves the task queue, and why the postmortem action item is a `maximumAttempts` and a non-retryable error type, not a bigger worker pool.

resource.label: Temporal CLI docs - temporal workflow commands (describe, signal, reset, cancel, terminate)

subtopics.name: Alert hygiene: symptoms not causes, grouping, inhibition, silences
subtopics.learn: Audit every DefenderMate alert against the rule that a page must be urgent, actionable, and about a user-visible symptom (SLO burn rate, error ratio, latency), with cause-based alerts (pod restarts, CPU) demoted to tickets or dashboards. In Alertmanager, configure `route.group_by` so one incident is one notification rather than 40, `group_wait` and `group_interval` to batch, `repeat_interval` long enough not to re-page during the incident, and `inhibit_rules` so a cluster-down alert suppresses every downstream service alert. Know `amtool silence add alertname=... --duration=2h --comment='INC-014'` and that silences during an incident are logged in the timeline, and put a `runbook_url` annotation on every paging rule so the responder lands on the mitigation steps, not a search box.

subtopics.name: On-call design and escalation policies
subtopics.learn: Set up a real schedule and escalation chain in Grafana IRM (or PagerDuty free tier): primary, secondary after a 5-minute unacknowledged timeout, then the engineering lead, with an override mechanism for hand-offs and a weekly rotation. Know the SRE numbers: no more than two incidents per 12-hour shift so responders can actually do postmortems, and page volume is a reliability metric, not a badge. Decide what the FDE embedded in a customer's rotation looks like: who pages you, through which system, with what SLA in the SOW, and what you do when the customer's own on-call does not acknowledge. Write the hand-off note format: open incidents, known-flaky alerts, changes scheduled in the next 24 hours.

resource.label: Grafana Cloud docs - Alerting and IRM (schedules, escalation chains)

subtopics.name: Customer and executive communication during the incident
subtopics.learn: Write and rehearse the three message types: the initial status post within 15 minutes of a SEV1 ('We are investigating elevated errors affecting X; next update by HH:MM'), the periodic update every 30 minutes even when the content is 'no change, still investigating', and the resolution post with impact window and a promise of a postmortem date. Use the impact / what we know / what we are doing / next update structure and never state a cause you have not confirmed; 'a database issue' becomes the headline the customer repeats to their board and you will spend the postmortem walking it back. Separate the war-room channel from the stakeholder channel and let only the comms lead post in the latter. As the FDE, decide in advance which incidents the customer hears about from you proactively versus from their own monitoring, and write that into the engagement runbook.

resource.label: Atlassian Incident Management Handbook - Incident communication

subtopics.name: Writing the blameless postmortem
subtopics.learn: Use the Google template sections and know why each exists: summary with impact in numbers (requests failed, tenants affected, minutes of SLO budget burned, revenue if known), trigger versus root cause versus contributing factors, detection (how long from first bad request to first human knowing, and whether a human or an alert found it), the timeline with UTC timestamps, lessons learned split into what went well / what went wrong / where we got lucky, and action items each with owner, type (prevent, detect, mitigate, process), priority and ticket link. Enforce blamelessness mechanically: no names in the causal chain (roles instead), no counterfactuals ('should have'), and every human action described in terms of what made it reasonable at the time. Write it within 48 hours, circulate for comment before the review meeting, and publish it where the customer can read it.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

subtopics.name: Facilitating the debrief when the customer's team pulled the trigger
subtopics.learn: Run the postmortem meeting as a facilitated debrief rather than a status review: open with the purpose (learning, not accountability), walk the timeline asking 'what did you see at that moment' and 'what made that the obvious next step' instead of 'why did you do that', and pull out the tacit knowledge (who knew the runbook was stale, who had seen this error before) that never appears in tickets. Know how to handle the hardest case for an FDE: the customer's engineer ran the migration that caused the outage, their manager is in the room, and your postmortem has to be honest about the trigger without making the vendor look like it is assigning blame. Practise redirecting 'who' questions to 'what conditions' and recording disagreements about causation rather than forcing consensus.

resource.label: Etsy Debriefing Facilitation Guide (GitHub)

subtopics.name: Action items that actually close
subtopics.learn: Turn each lesson into an action item that passes the test in the SRE Workbook chapter: specific, has one owner, has a due date, is tracked as a ticket with a priority that competes honestly with feature work, and is classified so the mix is visible (if every item is 'add an alert' and none is 'prevent', say so). Distinguish the immediate fix from the systemic fix and record both. Set up the review loop: a monthly check of open postmortem action items with the customer, and a rule that a repeat incident with an unclosed action item is escalated as a process failure, not another SEV. Include near-misses in the process; the cheapest postmortem is the one for an incident that did not quite happen.

resource.label: Google SRE Workbook - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

subtopics.name: Incident metrics and the monthly reliability report
subtopics.learn: Compute and report time-to-detect, time-to-acknowledge, time-to-mitigate and time-to-resolve per incident from the timeline, incident count by severity per month, and SLO budget consumed per incident, and know why an averaged MTTR across heterogeneous incidents is a vanity number that hides one four-hour outage behind fifty two-minute blips. Map your SEV definitions onto the customer's contractual SLA (monthly availability percentage, exclusions for scheduled maintenance and customer-caused issues, the service-credit process) so the reliability report answers the question their finance team will ask. Build the one-page monthly format: budget remaining, incidents with links to postmortems, open action items with ages, and one recommendation.

resource.label: Atlassian Incident Management Handbook - Common incident management metrics

subtopics.name: Wheel of Misfortune and disaster role-playing
subtopics.learn: Design and run a tabletop from the SRE book's format: a game master holds a real past incident (or one of your topic 22 chaos scenarios) as a script, reveals information only when the responder asks the right question or runs the right command, injects a twist at the ten-minute mark (a second alert, a customer exec joining the bridge), and stops at 30 minutes for a debrief. Score the responder on declaration time, mitigation-first behaviour, communication cadence and timeline quality, not on finding the root cause. Rotate roles so you play IC, scribe and game master at least once each. Keep the scenario bank versioned in the Dokeo repo and add one scenario after every real incident.

Describe a Temporal or queue-based system in which one bad message or workflow starves everything else. How do you detect it during the incident with the CLI, what is the immediate mitigation, and what retry-policy or error-classification change goes into the postmortem so it does not recur?
24.proofOfWork: A public `incident-kit` directory in the Dokeo repository that a hiring manager can read in ten minutes and a friend can use to run a drill in thirty. It contains: (1) a one-page incident playbook with the SEV ladder, role cards, the IC decision-loop script, the status-update templates and the Kubernetes / Postgres / Temporal mitigation menu with exact commands; (2) three Wheel of Misfortune scenario scripts derived from the topic 22 chaos experiments, each with the game master's hidden timeline, the information-release triggers and the scoring rubric; (3) a recorded 30-minute drill (screen and audio) in which you are IC and a friend is game master, with the exported incident channel timeline and the Grafana dashboard screenshot showing detection, mitigation and recovery annotations; (4) the resulting postmortem written to the Google template, redlined by a second reader for blame language and counterfactuals, with every action item linked to an issue in the repo and a `postmortem-review.md` recording what the reviewer challenged; and (5) the Alertmanager or Grafana alerting config diff that came out of the postmortem, showing the symptom-based rule, the `runbook_url` annotation, and the inhibition rule, plus a `promtool test rules` or equivalent unit test proving the new alert would have fired on the recorded incident data.

25.why: Every enterprise deal an FDE touches has a security questionnaire line that reads 'state your RTO and RPO' and a CTO who asks 'what happens if the region goes down' in the second architecture review, and the answer determines whether the pilot is allowed near production data. The FDE also inherits the customer's existing Postgres, their single-AZ Kubernetes cluster and their untested nightly dump, and is the person on the bridge when a migration drops a table or an AZ degrades. An FDE who has personally restored a database to a timestamp and measured the clock can make commitments and price them; one who has only read about it will either overpromise or stall the deal.
prerequisites: Topic 13 (AWS networking and compute): what an Availability Zone and a Region are, subnets per AZ, cross-zone load balancing, and why an ALB in one AZ is not redundant.
Topic 14 (AWS data): you have already run an RDS point-in-time restore and a forced Multi-AZ failover; this topic does the self-managed Postgres equivalent and then zooms out to the whole system.

Topic 8 (Kubernetes production ops): Deployments, StatefulSets, PersistentVolumes, node drains and readiness probes, so PodDisruptionBudgets and topology spread constraints have something to attach to.
Topic 20 (SRE fundamentals): SLIs, SLOs and error budgets; RTO and RPO are the same discipline applied to the recovery half of an outage.
Working Postgres: psql, what WAL and checkpoints are, that replicas replay WAL, and how to run pg_dump; Topic 29 goes deeper but the vocabulary is assumed now.

A target to drill on: the Kaupex Postgres on the Hetzner VPS (or a clone of it in Docker) plus an S3-compatible bucket you control (Hetzner Object Storage, Backblaze B2 or AWS S3) for the WAL archive; budget a few USD and about 20 GB.

subtopics.name: Availability arithmetic: nines, serial and parallel composition
subtopics.learn: Convert nines into budget you can feel: 99.9% is roughly 43 minutes of downtime per month, 99.95% about 22, 99.99% about 4.4. Hard dependencies in series multiply, so an app at 99.95% on a database at 99.95% behind DNS at 99.99% caps at about 99.89% before you write a line of code; redundant components in parallel give 1-(1-a)^n only when their failures are independent, and a shared deploy pipeline, shared AZ or shared control plane makes them correlated. Availability equals MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR), which is why a measured RTO is a direct lever on the SLO. Practice: take the Kaupex stack (VPS, Postgres, object storage, LLM provider, DNS) and compute its honest ceiling, marking each dependency hard or soft.

resource.label: AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar - Availability

subtopics.name: RTO and RPO as negotiated business numbers, per tier
subtopics.learn: RTO is the elapsed time from declaring a disaster to the service serving users again, and it includes detection and decision time, not just the restore; RPO is the maximum window of committed data you may lose, expressed in time. Both are set from business impact (revenue per hour, regulatory retention, contractual penalties), never from what the current infrastructure happens to offer, and cost rises steeply as either approaches zero. Build a tier table for a customer workload: Tier 0 for auth and payments (RTO 15 min, RPO near zero), Tier 1 for core product (RTO 1 h, RPO 5 min), Tier 2 for analytics and logs (RTO 24 h, RPO 24 h). Always record objective next to measured; the gap column is the DR plan.

resource.label: Reliability Pillar - REL13-BP01 Define recovery objectives for downtime and data loss

subtopics.name: Failure domains, correlated failure and blast radius
subtopics.learn: Enumerate the failure domains of a stack explicitly: host, AZ, Region, cloud account, control plane, deploy pipeline, DNS zone, identity provider, TLS certificate, a single KMS key, a single Terraform state file. Redundancy only protects against domains you have actually separated; two replicas in one AZ behind one single-AZ load balancer is one failure domain wearing three costumes. Learn the correlated failures that defeat N+1: the same bad deploy rolled to all AZs, one certificate expiring everywhere, one account-level quota, one shared secret rotated. Understand cell-based architecture and shuffle sharding as ways to cap the fraction of customers any single failure can reach, and draw the dependency graph for Kaupex with each edge labelled hard or soft.

resource.label: Reliability Pillar - Use fault isolation to protect your workload

subtopics.name: Static stability: surviving an AZ loss without the control plane
subtopics.learn: During an AZ impairment the control plane (RunInstances, Auto Scaling launches, volume creation, IAM changes, Kubernetes node provisioning) is the first thing to degrade or throttle, so a design that needs new capacity to recover is not resilient. Statically stable design pre-provisions N+1 across AZs so that losing one AZ requires no launches: three AZs each running at 50% utilisation tolerate one AZ loss with headroom. Prefer data-plane dependencies (Route 53 answers, already-issued credentials, pre-pulled images, warm caches) over control-plane calls in the recovery path, and avoid fallback code paths that only execute during a disaster because they are by definition untested. Map this onto Kubernetes: cluster-autoscaler launching nodes is a control-plane dependency; the fix is spare capacity, not a faster autoscaler.

resource.label: Amazon Builders' Library - Static stability using Availability Zones

subtopics.name: The four DR strategies and why the data tier decides
subtopics.learn: Know the ladder cold: backup and restore (RTO hours, RPO hours, cheapest), pilot light (data replicated live, compute off, RTO tens of minutes), warm standby (scaled-down full stack, RTO minutes), multi-site active/active (RTO and RPO near zero but requires write partitioning or conflict resolution). Compute is trivially recreatable from IaC and images; data is the constraint, and whatever your replication or archive lag is becomes your real RPO regardless of the slide. Choose per tier rather than per company: most customers should run pilot light for the primary database and backup and restore for everything else. List what the DR region must already contain before the disaster: images, secrets, KMS key grants, IAM roles, service quotas, DNS records, IdP configuration.

resource.label: AWS whitepaper - Disaster recovery options in the cloud

subtopics.name: Postgres backup methods: pg_dump, pg_basebackup, WAL archiving
subtopics.learn: pg_dump is logical: it takes a consistent snapshot inside a REPEATABLE READ transaction, writes portable SQL or a custom archive (-Fc, or -Fd with -j N for parallel dump and pg_restore -j for parallel restore), survives major-version upgrades, but cannot recover to a point in time and gets slow past a few hundred GB. pg_basebackup is physical: it copies the whole cluster over the replication protocol (--checkpoint=fast to avoid waiting for the next checkpoint, -X stream to include the WAL generated during the copy, --manifest-checksums=SHA256), is bound to the same major version and architecture, and is the base for PITR. Continuous archiving sets archive_mode=on and archive_command (or archive_library in PG15+) to ship every 16 MB WAL segment off-box, with archive_timeout bounding RPO on idle systems. Match method to failure: logical corruption needs PITR, migration needs pg_dump, RPO in minutes needs WAL archiving.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Chapter 25 Backup and Restore

subtopics.name: Point-in-time recovery by hand: recovery.signal, restore_command, recovery targets and timelines
subtopics.learn: Restore the base backup into an empty PGDATA, create recovery.signal, set restore_command='cp /archive/%f %p' (or the pgbackrest archive-get equivalent) and choose a target: recovery_target_time='2026-09-05 14:06:30+00', recovery_target_lsn, recovery_target_xid, or recovery_target_name pointing at a pg_create_restore_point() you made before a risky migration. Understand recovery_target_inclusive and recovery_target_action=pause (default) versus promote or shutdown, and that after pause you inspect the data and call pg_wal_replay_resume() to promote. Learn timelines: promotion writes a new .history file and starts a new timeline, so a second attempt after a wrong target needs recovery_target_timeline='latest' or the specific ID to replay the right branch. Watch the log for 'consistent recovery state reached' before trusting anything. Run this on a Kaupex clone and write down the wall-clock time of every phase.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - 25.3 Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery

subtopics.name: Verifying backups: manifests, checksums and restore-as-test
subtopics.learn: pg_verifybackup validates a base backup against its backup_manifest (file list, sizes, per-file checksums) and confirms the WAL range needed to reach consistency is present (-w to point at the WAL directory, -n to skip WAL parsing, -i to ignore paths). Enable data checksums (initdb --data-checksums, or pg_checksums --enable on a stopped cluster) so torn or bit-rotted pages fail at read time on the primary rather than at restore time in a disaster. Treat a backup as verified only when it has been restored and queried: schedule an automated restore to a scratch instance, run SELECT count(*) on the largest table and the application's smoke query, and alert if the newest recoverable point is older than the RPO. Monitor pg_stat_archiver (failed_count, last_failed_wal, last_archived_time) because a silently failing archive_command is the most common way a PITR chain gets a gap.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - pg_verifybackup

subtopics.name: pgBackRest in production: stanza, S3 repo, retention and restore --type=time
subtopics.learn: Configure pgbackrest.conf with [global] repo1-type=s3, repo1-s3-bucket, repo1-s3-endpoint, repo1-s3-region, repo1-path, repo1-retention-full=2, repo1-retention-diff, repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc with repo1-cipher-pass, process-max, start-fast=y, and a [kaupex] stanza with pg1-path; point Postgres at it with archive_command='pgbackrest --stanza=kaupex archive-push %p'. Run stanza-create, check (proves archiving works end to end), backup --type=full|diff|incr, info, and expire; understand why every incremental depends on a restorable full and how block incremental (repo-block) shrinks diffs. Restore with restore --type=time --target='...' --target-action=promote, and use --delta to reuse unchanged files in place for a faster RTO. Barman and WAL-G implement the same concepts; the vocabulary transfers.

resource.label: pgBackRest User Guide

subtopics.name: Streaming replication, synchronous_commit and what RPO zero costs
subtopics.learn: Build a hot standby: standby.signal, primary_conninfo, a physical replication slot on the primary with max_slot_wal_keep_size set so a dead standby cannot fill the primary's disk, hot_standby=on for reads. Learn the synchronous_commit ladder: off, local, remote_write, on (flushed on the standby), remote_apply (visible on the standby), and synchronous_standby_names='ANY 1 (s1, s2)' versus FIRST; with a single synchronous standby, losing it blocks every commit, which is the availability price of RPO zero. Read pg_stat_replication (sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn, replay_lag) and derive RPO directly from replay lag; check pg_replication_slots.wal_status for 'lost'. Promote with pg_ctl promote or SELECT pg_promote(), then fence or pg_rewind the old primary so it can never accept writes again; this is why Patroni with a DCS exists.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - 26.2 Log-Shipping Standby Servers (streaming, slots, synchronous replication)

subtopics.name: Managed cross-region replication: RDS replicas, Aurora Global, S3 CRR
subtopics.learn: An RDS cross-region read replica is asynchronous streaming; its ReplicaLag metric is your RPO, promote-read-replica breaks replication and takes minutes, and the promoted instance needs Multi-AZ and automated backups turned on afterwards or you have just created a single point of failure with no backup. Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer with typical sub-second lag: managed switchover is planned and lossless, unplanned failover detaches and promotes with RPO equal to lag. S3 Cross-Region Replication copies only new objects unless you run Batch Replication, does not replicate delete markers unless DeleteMarkerReplication is enabled, needs KMS key configuration for encrypted objects, and Replication Time Control adds a 15-minute SLA. DynamoDB global tables are last-writer-wins. In every case the RPO is a lag metric, so alarm on it.

resource.label: Amazon RDS User Guide - Creating a read replica in a different AWS Region

subtopics.name: Immutable, cross-account backups against ransomware and fat fingers
subtopics.learn: The failure most DR plans forget: any credential that can delete production can usually delete the backups too. Copy backups to a separate backup account with AWS Backup cross-account copy, and lock the destination vault with Vault Lock in compliance mode, which after its cooling-off period cannot be shortened even by the account root; use S3 Object Lock compliance mode for object-store backups. Check the key path: a snapshot encrypted with a customer-managed key is unreadable if that key is scheduled for deletion or the DR account lacks kms:Decrypt and kms:CreateGrant, so use multi-Region keys or re-encrypt on copy and test decrypting from the DR account. For self-hosted Postgres, put the pgBackRest repo bucket in a different account with an IAM policy that allows PutObject and GetObject but not DeleteObject, turn on versioning, and expire old versions with lifecycle rules rather than credentials. This is the 3-2-1 rule made concrete: three copies, two media, one outside the blast radius of the production account.

resource.label: AWS Backup Developer Guide - AWS Backup Vault Lock

subtopics.name: Kubernetes across AZs: topology spread, PodDisruptionBudgets and zonal volumes
subtopics.learn: Spread replicas with topologySpreadConstraints using topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, maxSkew: 1, whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule (ScheduleAnyway when you would rather run unbalanced than not at all), and add a hostname-level podAntiAffinity so two replicas do not share a node. Write PodDisruptionBudgets with percentages: a PDB of minAvailable: 1 on a one-replica Deployment blocks every kubectl drain and every managed node-group upgrade indefinitely, and PDBs never protect against involuntary disruption such as node loss. EBS PersistentVolumes are zonal: set volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer in the StorageClass so the volume is created where the pod lands, and understand that after an AZ loss a StatefulSet pod whose volume lives in the dead zone stays Pending until that zone returns, so database redundancy must come from Postgres replication, not from storage. Use one node group per AZ so the autoscaler can rebalance.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs - Pod Topology Spread Constraints

subtopics.name: Traffic failover: Route 53 health checks, failover records and the manual switch
subtopics.learn: Route 53 health checks come as endpoint, calculated and CloudWatch-alarm types; with the standard 30-second interval (10 seconds for fast) and FailureThreshold 3, detection alone is around 90 seconds before the record TTL and client caches add more. Failover routing uses PRIMARY and SECONDARY records, and alias records need EvaluateTargetHealth set to true or the health of the target is ignored. Point the health check at a deep endpoint that exercises the database, but keep it separate from the load balancer's shallow liveness path so a slow query under load does not fail the whole region. Fully automatic DNS failover of a database-backed application is dangerous because a transient primary blip can leave writes on both sides; Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls give a highly available manual switch with readiness checks and safety rules. Explain to the customer that 'DNS failover' is minutes, not seconds, because of resolver and JVM caching.

resource.label: Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide - Configuring DNS failover

subtopics.name: Testing DR: game days, FIS AZ scenarios and a drill log that measures RTO
subtopics.learn: A DR test passes only when the application served real requests from recovered infrastructure and every phase has a timestamp; 'the snapshot exists' is not a test. Climb the ladder: tabletop walkthrough, single-component restore drill, AZ impairment using the AWS FIS 'AZ Availability: Power Interruption' scenario (stops instances in the AZ, pauses Auto Scaling, fails over Multi-AZ RDS, blackholes subnet traffic), then a full Region failover. Define the drill log columns before you start: T-declare, T-decision, T-restore-start, T-db-consistent, T-app-healthy, T-traffic-cut, T-verified, and record every surprise (missing secret, expired token, quota, wrong parameter group) as a ticket. Re-run until measured RTO is at or below objective, then schedule quarterly, because every deploy that adds a dependency silently rots the plan.

resource.label: AWS Fault Injection Service User Guide - What is AWS FIS

subtopics.name: Data integrity: soft deletes, logical corruption and defence in depth
subtopics.learn: Most real data loss is logical (a bad migration, a buggy batch job, an admin with the wrong WHERE clause) and replicates perfectly to every standby, which is why replication is availability and not backup. Layer the defences: soft deletion with a delayed purge and an application-level undelete, PITR for the recent window, cold backups for the long horizon, and continuous validation that compares counts and checksums across layers. Take from the SRE book the reframing that users want their data back, not backups, so the metric to own is time-to-restore-user-data, and that failures combine cause, scope and rate into many cases a single backup schedule cannot cover. Ask of every plan: what happens when the corruption started nine days ago and the PITR window is seven?

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Chapter 26 Data Integrity: What You Read Is What You Wrote

subtopics.name: Writing and presenting the DR plan and runbook
subtopics.learn: Structure the document: scope and tiers; RTO/RPO objective versus measured for every data store; failure scenarios covered and, explicitly, those not covered; declaration criteria and who may declare; roles; a runbook with literal commands and expected output including prechecks (is pg_stat_archiver current, does the DR account decrypt a test snapshot); the DR-region prerequisites checklist (images, secrets, KMS grants, quotas, DNS, IdP); the communications template; the failback procedure, which is harder than failover because you must reverse replication and reconcile writes made during the outage; and the test history. Keep it in git beside the IaC, and make any change that adds a dependency also update the plan. Present it to a customer as a menu of tiers with cost against RTO and RPO, anchored to their own revenue-per-hour figure, not as a single recommendation.

resource.label: Reliability Pillar - Plan for Disaster Recovery (DR)

outcomes: You can take a customer's architecture diagram and within ten minutes list its failure domains, its hard dependencies with their availability ceilings, and state the highest availability it can honestly promise, with the multiplication shown.

You can perform a point-in-time restore of a self-hosted Postgres from a pgBackRest S3 repository to a named timestamp with --target-action=pause, verify a marker row, promote, and report RTO and RPO with wall-clock timestamps, in under 30 minutes for a roughly 10 GB database.

You can produce a tier table for a workload with objective and measured RTO and RPO for each data store, plus a monthly cost for backup-and-restore, pilot light and warm standby, and defend the recommended tier with the customer's own downtime cost.

You can configure a streaming standby with synchronous_commit=remote_apply, kill the primary mid-write-loop, promote, and show zero lost commits, then repeat with asynchronous replication and quantify both the lost commits and the commit-latency you saved.

You can write topologySpreadConstraints and PodDisruptionBudget manifests for a stateful service, cordon and drain every node in one zone, and show which pods kept serving, which went Pending, and why the Pending ones are tied to zonal volumes.

You can design a backup scheme that survives full compromise of the production account's credentials and prove it with a denied DeleteObject against the repo bucket and a rejected attempt to shorten a locked vault's retention.
You can run a timed DR drill, hand the customer a log with every phase timestamped, and present the gap between objective and measured along with the three changes that close it.
failureModes: The team says 'we have HA' because there is a Multi-AZ standby and two read replicas, then a migration runs DROP TABLE orders and every replica applies it within a second; with no WAL archive, the only recovery point is last night's pg_dump and the RPO is 20 hours.

archive_command has been failing for five weeks since the object-storage credentials rotated, pg_stat_archiver.failed_count is in the thousands and nobody alerted on it, pg_wal fills the disk and crashes the primary, and the 'backups' turn out to be unrestorable because the WAL chain has a gap.

The DR runbook restores an encrypted snapshot into the recovery account, which has no grant on the production KMS key; the restore fails with a KMS access error, the key admin is on holiday, and a 30-minute RTO becomes a day of support tickets.

A PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 1 sits on a single-replica StatefulSet; the managed node-group upgrade stalls for hours, the on-call force-deletes the pod to unblock it, and the only instance of the service goes down during the change window.

Automatic DNS failover flips traffic to the DR region during a 40-second primary blip; both regions accept writes for six minutes before anyone notices, and failback needs a manual reconciliation of orders that the customer's finance team has to sign off on.

A 'multi-AZ' Kubernetes cluster runs Postgres as a StatefulSet with an EBS volume in one zone; when that zone is impaired the pod stays Pending forever because the volume cannot move, and the customer discovers their database was single-AZ all along.

The DR plan is a Confluence page last edited eighteen months ago; it references a deprecated CLI flag, a Terraform workspace that no longer exists and an engineer who left, so the real RTO is the time it takes to rediscover the system under pressure.
interviewQuestions: A customer wants 99.99% availability for an application that hard-depends on their SSO provider at 99.9% and on our LLM API at 99.9%. What do you tell them, what would you change in the design to get closer, and what number do you actually write into the SOW?

Design DR for a self-hosted Postgres plus a Kubernetes API tier with a 30-minute RTO and a 5-minute RPO across two regions, on a budget that rules out a hot standby. What replicates continuously, what stays cold, what must already exist in the DR region, and how do you prove the numbers to the customer?

Your restore drill came in at three hours against a one-hour objective. Walk me through how you break down where the time went, which phases are fixable with configuration versus architecture, and what you would ship this week.

A primary's pg_wal directory has grown to 400 GB and the disk is at 98%. Give me the candidate causes, how you confirm each in under a minute with pg_stat_archiver and pg_replication_slots, and the sequence of actions that recovers the disk without losing the ability to restore.

Should failover of a database-backed service between regions be automatic? Argue both positions, then tell me what you would actually build for a payments customer and how the switch would be implemented and protected.

A security questionnaire asks whether a compromised production admin credential could destroy your backups. Design the answer you want to give, name the controls behind each clause, and describe the test that proves it.

Compare a Multi-AZ standby, a cross-region read replica, continuous WAL archiving and a nightly snapshot: which failures does each recover from, what are their RTO and RPO, and in what scenario is the nightly snapshot the only thing that saves you?
25.proofOfWork: A public repository named kaupex-dr that turns the plan's DR document into reproducible evidence. It holds a pgbackrest.conf targeting an S3-compatible bucket in a separate account whose IAM policy allows PutObject and GetObject but denies DeleteObject, with versioning and a lifecycle rule, and a policy_test.sh showing the denied delete. A drill.sh seeds a Kaupex clone with pgbench, inserts a timestamped marker row, runs a destructive migration, then restores to a scratch cluster with pgbackrest restore --type=time --target-action=pause, checks the marker, promotes, and appends every phase timestamp to DRILL_LOG.md, which contains at least three runs with RTO and RPO and a sentence on what dominated each. A standby/ directory has a docker-compose with a primary and a synchronous standby plus kill_primary.py, which runs a write loop, kills the primary, promotes, and reports lost commits under remote_apply and under asynchronous replication. A k8s/ directory has a StatefulSet with topologySpreadConstraints and a percentage PDB, and zone_loss.sh cordons and drains one zone on a kind or EKS cluster and records how many pods kept serving versus went Pending. DR_PLAN.md contains the tier table with objective versus measured, declaration criteria, the literal runbook, the DR-region prerequisites checklist, failback steps and an explicit list of untested scenarios; a ten-minute recorded walkthrough presents it to an imagined customer CTO as a cost-versus-RTO menu.

26.topic: Supporting a deployment you cannot log into: preflight checks, support bundles, remote diagnosis
26.why: The engagements that pay an FDE the most are the ones where the software runs inside a bank, a hospital or a defence contractor: on-prem, BYOC or fully air-gapped, where you have no SSH, no kubectl, no screen share, and a change-control board between you and the next piece of evidence. In those accounts your entire diagnostic capability is whatever you shipped in the installer months earlier - the preflight that refused to install on an undersized node, the collector that grabbed the right log, the redactor that made it legal for that log to leave the building. An FDE who can read a support bundle cold and name the root cause turns a two-week escalation into a same-day answer; one who cannot is reduced to asking the customer's admin to paste screenshots, which is how pilots die.
prerequisites: Topic 7 and Topic 8 (Kubernetes core and production ops): you can read Deployment/StatefulSet status, Events, Pod conditions, PVC binding and RBAC, because a support bundle is mostly those objects serialised to disk.
Topic 9 (GitOps: Helm charts and ArgoCD): you ship DefenderMate as a chart, so you can add hooks, templated values and extra manifests to it.
Topic 22 (Observability): structured JSON logs carrying trace_id, tenant_id and a build SHA - collectors are only as good as the logs they pick up.
Topic 24 (Incident response and postmortems): severity, IC role, timeline discipline. This topic is the version of that where you cannot see the system.
Topic 32 (Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems): what counts as PII in DefenderMate's alert payloads and LLM prompts, since that decides what may be collected at all.

A cluster you can break and the tooling installed: kind or k3s, the DefenderMate chart, and the Troubleshoot kubectl plugins (krew install preflight support-bundle) plus sbctl, tar, jq and ripgrep locally.

subtopics.name: The access ladder: what 'cannot log into' actually means
subtopics.learn: Classify every engagement by exactly what you can obtain, worst case, at 02:00: (a) break-glass SSH or kubectl, (b) a supervised, time-boxed screen share, (c) the customer runs commands you dictate and pastes output, (d) a support bundle only, (e) an air-gapped site where the bundle leaves on removable media after a human inspects it, (f) a facility where nothing leaves and only the analyzer verdicts may be read aloud. Know the deal shapes that force each: self-hosted enterprise, BYOC in the customer's VPC, air gap with a mirrored registry and an offline licence, FedRAMP/ITAR/hospital networks. Write the access level into the SOW and the runbook rather than assuming a call will be possible, and internalise the rule that governs everything else in this topic: the diagnostic capability you did not ship in the installer is capability you do not have.

resource.label: Replicated - Air gap installation with Embedded Cluster

subtopics.name: Environment requirements as a testable contract, not a wiki page
subtopics.learn: Before writing a check, enumerate what DefenderMate needs from a cluster you will never see and write each line so it can become an assertion: Kubernetes version range, distribution and CNI caveats, CPU/memory per node and in total, a StorageClass with the required accessModes and allowVolumeExpansion, an IngressClass and a certificate source, outbound destinations with host/port/protocol, an image registry or the air-gap bundle, a Postgres major version plus required extensions, cgroup v2, and working NTP. The discipline: if you cannot express a requirement as a check with a pass/fail message and a fix, it is not a requirement, it is a hope. Version the document with the chart (docs/requirements.md), get the customer's platform team to sign it during the site survey (Topic 73), and keep a two-column table mapping every requirement line to the analyzer that enforces it - an empty cell on either side is a bug.

resource.label: Replicated - Installation requirements (worked example of a requirements contract)

subtopics.name: Preflight anatomy: spec, outcomes, strict, and the exit-code contract
subtopics.learn: A preflight is `apiVersion: troubleshoot.sh/v1beta2, kind: Preflight` with `spec.collectors` and `spec.analyzers`; each analyzer emits `outcomes` of `pass`/`warn`/`fail`, each with `when`, `title`, `message` and `uri`. Run it with `kubectl preflight ./preflight.yaml`, or straight from a URL or an OCI/Helm-templated file, and script it with `--interactive=false` plus `--format=json`. Branch on the exit codes exactly: 0 all passed, 1 catch-all error usually unrelated to a specific check, 2 invalid input or an invalid spec, 3 at least one FAIL, 4 no FAIL but at least one WARN. `strict: true` marks an analyzer that must not fail; `exclude: true` (templatable from Helm values) skips checks for components the customer did not enable. Treat exit 2 as your bug, exit 3 as a blocked install, exit 4 as a warning the customer may override in writing.

resource.label: Troubleshoot - Preflight exit codes

subtopics.name: Cluster analyzers that catch the install failures you actually see
subtopics.learn: Write the eight checks that prevent most first-week escalations: `clusterVersion` with a minimum and a recommended range, `distribution` (accept EKS/GKE/OpenShift/k3s, reject Docker Desktop or minikube for production), `nodeResources` with `filters` on allocatable CPU/memory plus `count()`/`sum()` expressions so 'three nodes with 8 GB each' is enforceable, `storageClass` for the exact class name and provisioner, `ingressClass` and `ingress` for the routing path, `crd` to detect a conflicting cert-manager or Prometheus Operator CRD already owned by another team, `imagePullSecrets` for registry credentials, and `clusterPodStatuses`/`deploymentStatus` for the upgrade case where the previous release is already unhealthy. Each failure message must name the fix in the customer admin's vocabulary and carry a `uri` to your docs, because nobody is going to be on a call to explain it.

resource.label: Replicated - Define preflight checks

subtopics.name: Version skew and API deprecation: the upgrade that breaks in six months
subtopics.learn: Preflights are not only about install day. Pin `kubeVersion` in Chart.yaml so Helm itself refuses an unsupported cluster, run `helm template --validate` or `helm install --dry-run=server` so the API server validates against the real schema, and check the deprecation guide for the removals that will bite the versions your customers actually run (batch/v1beta1 CronJob, policy/v1beta1 PodDisruptionBudget, autoscaling/v2beta2 HPA, the PSP removal in 1.25). Know the Kubernetes version-skew policy so you can say which control-plane/kubelet combinations you support, and add an analyzer that warns when the cluster is within one minor of a version your chart has not been tested on. The failure this prevents: a customer upgrades their cluster on their schedule, your chart silently stops rendering, and the first symptom is a failed ArgoCD sync at midnight in a timezone you do not work in.

resource.label: Kubernetes - Deprecated API migration guide

subtopics.name: Host preflights for VM, bare-metal and embedded installs
subtopics.learn: When you ship an appliance or an embedded cluster rather than a chart, the failures move below Kubernetes, so run host collectors/analyzers on every node before anything is installed: `cpu` and `memory` for sizing, `blockDevices` and `diskUsage` for the specific mount points (/var/lib/containerd, /var/lib/etcd, the PV path) with both percent and absolute thresholds, `filesystemPerformance` to benchmark sequential write latency because etcd on a slow SAN is the classic 'your product is slow' ticket, `time` for NTP sync and drift, `tcpPortStatus`/`udpPortStatus` for the ports the cluster needs open between nodes, `ipv4Interfaces` and `subnetAvailable` so your pod/service CIDRs do not collide with the customer's corporate range, `kernelModules` and `hostOS` for the distro and kernel features, and `hostServices` for a firewalld or SELinux state that will block you later. Ship these as a single YAML the customer runs per node before the installer, and read the collected results back in the same bundle format.

resource.label: Troubleshoot - All host collectors and analyzers

subtopics.name: Egress, proxies, TLS interception and registry reachability
subtopics.learn: Enterprise networks break outbound calls in four distinctive ways, and each needs its own check. Reachability: an `http` collector from inside the cluster to every destination DefenderMate calls (the LLM provider, your licence endpoint, the customer's SIEM webhook) with the status code analyzed, plus `registryImages` to prove every image in the chart is pullable before install. Proxying: HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY must be templated into every Deployment and the NO_PROXY list must include the in-cluster service CIDR, or your own service-to-service calls get routed to the corporate proxy. Interception: a middlebox re-signs TLS, so `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host -showcerts` shows a corporate issuer, and you must collect the CA bundle and mount it via SSL_CERT_FILE / NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS / REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE. Expiry and DNS: check certificate notAfter and split-horizon DNS resolution from a pod, not from the admin's laptop.

resource.label: OpenSSL - openssl-s_client (inspecting the served chain and issuer)

subtopics.name: Wiring the preflight into the install and upgrade path so it cannot be skipped
subtopics.learn: A preflight nobody runs is documentation. Bind it to the lifecycle: ship the spec as a ConfigMap in the chart and run it from a `helm.sh/hook: pre-install,pre-upgrade` Job with `hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded` and a `hook-weight` that puts it first, so a non-zero exit aborts the release; the ArgoCD equivalent is a `PreSync` hook resource. Give the hook Job its own least-privilege ServiceAccount with read-only RBAC on the resources the collectors touch, and set `activeDeadlineSeconds` plus `backoffLimit: 0` so a hung check does not wedge the release. Provide a documented escape hatch (`--set preflight.enabled=false`) so an emergency upgrade is possible, log loudly when it is used, and record in the runbook that a skipped preflight is a support-contract exception, not a default.

resource.label: Helm - Chart hooks (pre-install, pre-upgrade, weights, delete policies)

subtopics.name: Support bundle anatomy: spec, defaults, multiple specs and in-cluster discovery
subtopics.learn: `kind: SupportBundle` has the same collectors/analyzers/redactors shape as a preflight and runs entirely client-side: `kubectl support-bundle ./spec.yaml` produces support-bundle-<timestamp>.tar.gz whose top level holds `analysis.json`, `cluster-info/`, `cluster-resources/` and one directory per named collector. In-cluster bundles always add `clusterInfo` and `clusterResources` even when `collectors:` is empty (opt out with `exclude: true`). Since v0.42 you can pass several specs at once - a URL, a local file and a Secret - and since v0.47 `--load-cluster-specs` discovers any Secret or ConfigMap labelled `troubleshoot.sh/kind: support-bundle` whose data key is `support-bundle-spec` or `redactor-spec` (`-l/--selector` overrides the label). Ship your spec inside the chart so the customer's command is always the same one line, and version the spec with the release so you know which collectors a given bundle could possibly contain.

resource.label: Troubleshoot - Discover cluster specs (--load-cluster-specs)

subtopics.name: Choosing collectors from the questions you must be able to answer
subtopics.learn: Do not collect everything; write the question first and pick the one collector that answers it. `clusterResources` for object state, `logs` for behaviour, `configmap`/`secret` (keys and existence, values redacted) for wiring, `copy` for a file inside a container and `copy-from-host` for node-level artefacts, `data` to stamp your own metadata into the tarball, `dns` and `etcd` for control-plane symptoms, `http` for outbound reachability from where the app actually runs, `exec` to run a read-only diagnostic in a pod that already exists, `postgresql`/`redis` for the data tier, `registryImages` for pull failures, and `helm` for the release values that were actually applied. Treat `runPod` and `runDaemonSet` as privileged: they schedule new workloads in the customer's cluster, need justification in the collection manifest, and must reference an image already present in an air-gapped registry - a spec pinned to `alpine:3` produces an empty result exactly where you needed data.

resource.label: Troubleshoot - All collectors

subtopics.name: Log collection that is still diagnostic three time zones away
subtopics.learn: The `logs` collector takes a label `selector`, a `namespace`, optional `containerNames`, and `limits: {maxAge: 720h, maxLines: 10000}`; it keeps the most recent lines, so a 10k cap on a chatty pod silently discards the panic that started the incident forty minutes earlier - size the limits against your actual log rate and cap noisy sidecars separately. Always collect previous-container logs for CrashLoopBackOff, because the interesting process is already dead. The collector cannot recover what the node already rotated, so the real fix is upstream: JSON logs with RFC 3339 UTC timestamps, level, `trace_id`, `tenant_id`, `build_sha` and a stable event name (Topic 22), so a bundle can be sorted into one timeline with jq. Add a `data` collector that stamps chart version, image digests, licence ID and collection time into the tarball, so you never have to ask 'which version is this?' as your first question.

resource.label: Troubleshoot - Pod logs collector (selectors and limits)

subtopics.name: Self-diagnostics you must build into the product itself
subtopics.learn: A bundle can only collect what the application exposes, so design for the interrogation you will never get to do live: a `/version` endpoint returning git SHA, chart version, image digest, licence ID and enabled feature flags; `/healthz` for liveness and a `/readyz` that reports each dependency (Postgres, Redis, the LLM provider, the SIEM webhook) with its last error and last success timestamp; an effective-config dump with secret values masked so you can diff what the customer is running against the golden values; and a stable error catalogue - `DM-1042 llm_provider_unreachable` - returned in API errors as RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance` and a documentation URL. One pasted problem+json object from a customer's browser console should be enough to route the ticket, and every error code should map to a `textAnalyze` analyzer and a runbook entry.

resource.label: RFC 9457 - Problem Details for HTTP APIs

subtopics.name: Redaction: what it does, how to verify it, and what it can never protect
subtopics.learn: `kind: Redactor` applies `fileSelector` (`file`/`files` globs) plus `removals` containing `values` (literal strings), `regex` (either a bare `redactor` pattern or a `selector` that anchors to the following line, with the named group `(?P<mask>...)` replaced by `***HIDDEN***`) and `yamlPath` (e.g. `abc.xyz.*`). Built-in redactors catch common credentials, but the gaps are what get you: base64 Secret data, JWTs and bearer tokens inside log lines, heap dumps and env dumps collected with `copy`, connection strings in Helm values, and - the big one for DefenderMate - customer PII inside alert payloads and LLM prompts (hostnames, usernames, email addresses, IPs, ticket text). Never put the sensitive value in the redactor spec itself, since specs live in plaintext ConfigMaps. Verify empirically: plant canary secrets in a test install, generate a bundle, `rg` the extracted tarball for every canary, and run that check in CI so a new collector cannot ship without a matching redactor.

resource.label: Troubleshoot - Redactors (fileSelector, values, regex, yamlPath)

subtopics.name: The customer-approvable collection manifest
subtopics.learn: Turn the spec into a document a security team can approve once instead of debating per incident: for every collector, one row giving what is collected, why it is needed, whether it can contain PII under the NIST SP 800-122 categories (direct identifiers, linkable data, IP addresses, free text), which redactor covers it, where the bundle is stored, who may read it, how long it is retained and how deletion is proven. State the legal frame plainly - the bundle is a data transfer, so it belongs in the DPA and the subprocessor list - and offer the tiered fallback that closes most objections: full bundle, redacted bundle, or analyzers run locally with only `analysis.json` leaving the boundary. Add chain-of-custody mechanics: a ticket ID, a `sha256sum` recorded on both sides, and a named recipient. This manifest is what converts 'we do not send logs to vendors' into a signed exception.

resource.label: NIST SP 800-122 - Guide to Protecting the Confidentiality of PII

subtopics.name: Getting the bundle out of the environment, and handling it once it arrives
subtopics.learn: Bundles from a busy cluster reach several gigabytes, which collides with a 25 MB mail limit and a review desk that inspects every file leaving an air gap. Practise the mechanics: trim with log limits and `exclude`, then `split -b 512M`, record `sha256sum` for every part, encrypt to your team's public keys with `age -R recipients.txt` (or gpg) so the file is safe on a USB stick and on the customer's upload portal, and document the exact reassembly command. On receipt, treat the tarball as untrusted input from a compromised host: extract into a disposable directory with `tar --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions -C sandbox/`, never into a shared analysis box; scan for unredacted credentials before it is attached to a ticket, and if you find one, the credential is burned and must be rotated by the customer that day. Set a retention job that deletes bundles on the schedule the manifest promised.

resource.label: age - simple, modern file encryption (recipients, -R)

subtopics.name: Analyzer outcomes: writing a verdict a customer admin can act on
subtopics.learn: Each analyzer's `outcomes` array is evaluated in order and stops at the first entry whose `when` is truthy, so it reads like a switch statement: the tightest failure first, then warnings, then a final `pass` with no `when` as the default arm. `title` is one truncated line in the UI, `message` carries the detail (it supports templating of collected values so you can print the actual number), and `uri` is the Read More link that must point at a runbook section, not your marketing site. Write messages in the second person with the fix: 'Node ip-10-0-3-11 has 4 GiB allocatable; DefenderMate requires 8 GiB. Resize the node group or set classifier.replicas=1 for the pilot.' Use `checkName` to give the check a stable, greppable identity, `strict` for the ones that must block, and keep the failure/warning thresholds identical between the preflight and the support bundle so a check cannot pass at install and disagree at diagnosis.

resource.label: Troubleshoot - Analyzer outcomes (pass/warn/fail, when, title, message, uri)

subtopics.name: textAnalyze: turning every past escalation into an automatic diagnosis
subtopics.learn: The `textAnalyze` analyzer runs a `regex` or `regexGroups` over a file the collectors produced - a log, a `copy`-ed config, the output of an `exec` - and emits outcomes from the match, with `regexGroups` binding named captures so you can compare a captured number in `when` (for example a pool size or a version). This is where support knowledge gets codified: every escalation you resolve becomes one signature ('pq: too many connections', 'x509: certificate signed by unknown authority', 'context deadline exceeded' against the LLM host, an OOMKilled reason in the events file), with a message naming the cause and the fix. Keep the regexes anchored and cheap, add `ignoreIfNoFiles` semantics deliberately so a missing file does not read as healthy, and build the habit that the closing task on every escalation ticket is the pull request adding its analyzer. The target state: `analysis.json` names the root cause before a human opens the tarball.

resource.label: Troubleshoot - Regular expression (textAnalyze) analyzer

subtopics.name: Reading a bundle cold: triage order and sbctl
subtopics.learn: Fix a repeatable order so you do not wander: read `analysis.json` first, then the version/metadata stamp, then `cluster-resources/events` and pod statuses for the last hour, then the failing workload's current and previous logs, then its config and Secret key list, then the data tier and egress collectors, and only then the whole-cluster material. Build a timeline in one file with `jq -r` across the JSON logs plus event timestamps, normalising to UTC, and mark the first anomaly rather than the loudest one. Use `sbctl serve` / `sbctl shell` to mount the bundle behind a local API server so `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl describe` and `kubectl get events -A` work offline against the frozen cluster state - it turns unfamiliar file archaeology into the tooling you already have muscle memory for. Finish every diagnosis by naming the collector, redactor or preflight that should have made it a one-minute answer.

resource.label: sbctl - serve a support bundle as a local Kubernetes API server

subtopics.name: Remote diagnosis discipline and the question budget
subtopics.learn: With one bundle every 48 hours because of change control, hypothesis quality is the whole job. Work the Google SRE loop explicitly - triage and stabilise before you explain, examine the evidence you have, form hypotheses that predict something absent from the bundle, and only then spend a round trip - and write each hypothesis down with the exact file or command that would falsify it, so you never spend a request confirming what you already believe. When you do ask, send a copy-pasteable block: the single command, the expected runtime, the expected output, what to do if it errors, and what you will conclude from each outcome, written for a busy admin who is not on your team. Bundle several independent questions into one request. Recognise the three moments to stop asking and escalate to a supervised session or a break-glass account: suspected data corruption, an active security incident, and a hypothesis that needs interactive state.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Effective Troubleshooting

subtopics.name: Closing the loop: coverage metrics and phone-home telemetry when it is allowed
subtopics.learn: Run the support surface as a product with two numbers: the share of escalations diagnosed from the first bundle with no follow-up round trip, and the share of preflight-preventable incidents (an install-time condition that a check could have caught but did not). Every escalation closes with one of three artefacts - a new collector, a new analyzer, or a new preflight - and each is a diff against the chart, so coverage compounds. Where the customer permits outbound calls, a lightweight instance-telemetry channel reporting version, uptime, resource pressure and a coarse health status turns unknown-unknowns into a dashboard and lets you open the ticket before they do; where they do not, the equivalent is a scheduled local bundle whose `analysis.json` the customer's own monitoring alerts on. Publish the collection manifest, the coverage numbers and the diagnosis-time trend in the QBR - it is the cheapest trust you will ever buy in an on-prem account.

resource.label: Replicated - Instance details (what vendor-side instance telemetry reports)

outcomes: You can write a Preflight spec for DefenderMate that blocks installation on an undersized node, a missing or wrong StorageClass, an unreachable image registry and an unsupported Kubernetes version, and demonstrate exit code 3 on failure, 4 on warning and 0 on a healthy cluster.
You can ship that preflight as a Helm pre-install/pre-upgrade hook with least-privilege RBAC and prove that a failing check aborts `helm upgrade` rather than leaving a half-applied release.

You can write a SupportBundle spec with collectors, redactors and analyzers, distribute it in-cluster so the customer's command is `kubectl support-bundle --load-cluster-specs`, and produce a bundle from a broken install in under five minutes.
You can prove redaction empirically: plant canary credentials and PII in a test install, generate a bundle, and show a CI job that fails the build if any canary survives into the tarball.

You can diagnose at least three seeded faults (OOMKilled classifier, expired or MITM-intercepted TLS to the LLM provider, exhausted Postgres connections) from bundles alone with no cluster access, and for each one name the collector, redactor or preflight that should have caught it earlier.
You can serve a support bundle with sbctl and answer questions with ordinary `kubectl get/describe/events` against the frozen cluster state, offline.

You can produce a one-page collection manifest - per collector: what, why, PII class, redactor, storage, retention, recipients - that a customer security reviewer can sign, plus the reduced-scope fallback where only analysis.json leaves the boundary.

You can convert a resolved escalation into a merged textAnalyze analyzer whose message names the cause and the fix, and show `analysis.json` diagnosing a fresh bundle of the same fault without human reading.
failureModes: The support-bundle spec uses `runPod` with `alpine:3`; in the customer's air-gapped cluster the image cannot be pulled, the collector writes an error file instead of data, and the one directory you needed is empty after a two-day change-control round trip.

The `logs` collector caps at `maxLines: 10000` and the classifier logs 400 lines a second, so the bundle contains the last four minutes and the panic that started the outage forty minutes earlier is gone forever, because the node rotated it too.

Redactors cover connection strings but not alert payloads, so the bundle carries customer hostnames, usernames and email addresses from LLM prompts into your ticketing system, and a support ticket becomes a notifiable data incident under the DPA.

The node-sizing check was written as a `warn` rather than a `fail` because someone wanted the pilot to install cleanly; the customer runs on 4 GiB nodes, the classifier starts OOMKilling under real alert volume three weeks later, and the preflight output has already scrolled out of anyone's terminal.

Preflights run only on install, never on upgrade; the customer moves their cluster to a newer Kubernetes minor on their own schedule, a removed API version stops the chart rendering, and the first signal is a failed ArgoCD sync at 01:00 in a region with no on-call.

The customer's admin runs the bundle with a ServiceAccount that cannot read Secrets or nodes; several collectors fail partially, the analyzers see no evidence of a problem, and `analysis.json` reports all-clear on a cluster that is actively broken.

Node clocks drift because NTP is blocked outbound and one component logs in local time with no offset; the reconstructed timeline puts the webhook after the database error, the wrong service is blamed, and two days of engineering go into a component that was healthy.

The 6 GB bundle bounces off the mail gateway, so the admin uploads it to a public file-sharing link with no expiry; it contains an unredacted Postgres URI, and the remediation is a customer-side credential rotation plus a security review of your entire support process.
interviewQuestions: Design the preflight and support-bundle pair for shipping our product into a bank's air-gapped OpenShift cluster. What do you check before install, what do you collect after a failure, what do you deliberately refuse to collect, and how do you get the bundle out of the building?

A customer emails 'the classifier is down' and attaches a 4 GB support bundle. Walk me through your first fifteen minutes: what you open, in what order, and what you would say in the first customer reply.

Explain the preflight exit-code contract and how you would wire it into a Helm-based install so a FAIL blocks the release but a WARN does not. What is your policy for upgrades, and what is the escape hatch when the customer must upgrade during an outage?

How do you convince a CISO that a support bundle is safe to send? Describe the redaction mechanisms, how you verify them, what redaction fundamentally cannot protect against, and what you offer when the answer is still no.

Debug this: `analysis.json` says every check passed, but the customer's dashboard is empty and their users are complaining. Give me the three most likely reasons the bundle is lying to you and how you would distinguish them.
You cannot reproduce the issue, and change control means one more bundle in 48 hours. How do you spend that single request? Write me the message you send the customer's admin.

How do you decide what belongs in a support bundle in the first place, and how does that set change over the life of an account? What would you measure to know your support surface is actually improving?
26.proofOfWork: A public repo `blind-bundle-drill` that turns this topic into a repeatable exercise rather than a document. It contains a `make cluster` target standing up kind or k3s with the DefenderMate chart, a `make fault-N` fault injector seeding eight realistic breakages (undersized node, missing StorageClass, wrong image registry credentials, expired and MITM-intercepted TLS to the LLM provider, exhausted Postgres connections, a NetworkPolicy blocking the webhook path, clock skew, and a Secret key renamed between chart versions), and the shipped `preflight.yaml`, `support-bundle.yaml` and `redactors.yaml` under `charts/defendermate/templates/` with the in-cluster ConfigMap labelled `troubleshoot.sh/kind: support-bundle`. A partner (or a script) picks a fault, runs the bundle and hands you only the tarball; you diagnose with sbctl and no cluster access, timing each attempt, and record every run in `DRILL-LOG.md` with the fault, your diagnosis, elapsed time, and the collector/analyzer/preflight you added afterwards so the next run is faster - the log should show first-bundle diagnosis time falling across the eight faults. CI runs `kubectl preflight --interactive=false` against a deliberately undersized kind cluster and asserts exit code 3, generates a bundle from a healthy install and greps the extracted tarball for planted canary credentials and PII, failing the build on any hit. The repo ships two customer-facing artefacts: `COLLECTION-MANIFEST.md`, the one-page per-collector table (what, why, PII class, redactor, storage, retention, recipients) written for a security reviewer to sign, and `docs/requirements.md` with the two-column table mapping every stated environment requirement to the analyzer that enforces it, so an empty cell in either column is visibly a bug.

27.topic: Production Python architecture: domain models, repositories, DI, packaging
27.why: An FDE writes code that the customer's own engineers will own six weeks after the engagement ends, so the real deliverable is not the feature but a codebase a stranger can extend in a day without calling you. The same service is deployed against different databases, secret stores and model providers per customer (Postgres here, Snowflake there; Anthropic direct here, Bedrock behind a gateway there), which is only cheap if persistence, config and LLM calls sit behind ports that the composition root wires up. Take-home graders at Palantir, Anthropic and Databricks read your module layout, your pyproject.toml and your tests before they run anything; a flat script with SQLAlchemy models as the domain model is the most common reason a strong candidate gets a 'no'.
prerequisites: Python 3.11+ fluency: type hints and generics, dataclasses, context managers, decorators, generators, `__eq__`/`__hash__` semantics, how `import` executes module code
SQL and Postgres basics (a table, a transaction, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) from 'AWS data: RDS Postgres, S3, ElastiCache, DynamoDB' (topic 14); the deep planner work in topic 29 is not required yet
pytest basics: writing a test file, fixtures, `-k`, `-x`, `--lf`; the property-testing and contract material in topic 35 builds on what you do here
Docker multi-stage images and non-root containers from 'Production images and supply chain' (topic 6), because the packaging subtopics end in a Dockerfile
Git branch hygiene from topic 4 so the restructure of the Kaupex Task Compiler lands as a reviewable series of small commits rather than one 3,000-line diff
Read access to the current Kaupex Task Compiler code and a written list of its three worst pain points (where a change today touches the most files)

subtopics.name: Layers and the dependency rule, enforced by the build
subtopics.learn: Draw the four layers you will use for every service: domain (pure Python, no I/O), service layer (use cases that orchestrate domain objects through ports), adapters (SQLAlchemy, HTTP clients, LLM SDKs, filesystem), entrypoints (FastAPI routes, Temporal activities, CLI). The rule is that imports only point inward: domain imports nothing from the other three, service imports domain and port interfaces only, adapters implement ports, entrypoints wire everything. Encode the rule as an import-linter contract in pyproject.toml (`[tool.importlinter]` with `root_package = "kaupex"` and a `type = "layers"` contract listing `kaupex.entrypoints`, `kaupex.adapters`, `kaupex.service_layer`, `kaupex.domain` top to bottom) and run `lint-imports` in CI so a `from sqlalchemy import ...` inside `domain/` fails the build instead of a code review.

resource.label: Import Linter documentation (layers and forbidden contracts)

subtopics.name: Entities and value objects with dataclasses
subtopics.learn: Model value objects as `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)` so equality is by value, instances are hashable and usable as dict keys and set members, and accidental mutation raises `FrozenInstanceError`. Model entities with identity: keep `eq=False` or override `__eq__` to compare on the id field and set `__hash__` accordingly, because the default dataclass `__eq__` on all fields makes two snapshots of the same task unequal. Use `field(default_factory=list)` for mutable defaults, `kw_only=True` to make constructors readable in the service layer, and `__post_init__` to assert invariants (a `TaskSpec` with an empty step list is never constructible). Know the cost model: `slots=True` cuts per-instance memory roughly in half and blocks `__dict__` monkeypatching in tests, which is what you want in the domain.

resource.label: Python docs - dataclasses

subtopics.name: Typed identifiers, domain exceptions and invariants
subtopics.learn: Give every identifier its own type with `typing.NewType("TaskId", str)` so mypy rejects passing a `TenantId` where a `TaskId` belongs; the cost is zero at runtime.
