subtopics.learn: Every route must declare what it can actually return: `response_model=`, `status_code=201`, and `responses={404: {"model": Problem}, 409: {"model": Problem}, 422: {"model": Problem}}` with `content` keyed by `application/problem+json`, otherwise Schemathesis `status_code_conformance` and `content_type_conformance` fail on the first real error. Set stable operation ids with `generate_unique_id_function=lambda r: f"{r.tags[0]}_{r.name}"` (or `operation_id=`) because generated clients and OpenAPI links key on them. Make request models `ConfigDict(extra="forbid")` so the schema emits `additionalProperties: false` and `negative_data_rejection` has teeth; push `Field(min_length, max_length, pattern, ge, le)` constraints into the schema so generated data hits real boundaries; document response headers under `responses[200]["headers"]`; hide `/healthz` and `/readyz` with `include_in_schema=False`; use `openapi_extra` for anything FastAPI cannot express, such as `links`.

resource.label: FastAPI docs - Additional Responses in OpenAPI

subtopics.name: Committed schema snapshot and breaking-change detection with oasdiff
subtopics.learn: Commit `openapi.json` and add a test `assert app.openapi() == json.loads(Path("openapi.json").read_text())` with a `make openapi` target to regenerate, so any schema change appears as a reviewable diff in the PR rather than a surprise to the customer's client generator. In CI fetch the base with `git show origin/main:openapi.json > base.json` and run `oasdiff breaking base.json openapi.json --fail-on ERR`; know the classes it flags: removed path or method, new required request property, removed or renamed response property, type narrowing, enum value removed from a request or added to a response, `required` added to a response schema, and know which of those are ERR versus WARN and why an added optional response field is not breaking. Use `oasdiff changelog` output as the PR comment and the customer-facing release note. Define the policy: a breaking diff requires a `/v2` path or a major version bump plus a deprecation window, and the CI job enforces it rather than a reviewer's memory.

resource.label: oasdiff - OpenAPI diff and breaking-change detection (GitHub)

subtopics.name: Schemathesis CLI: phases, checks, and reading a failure
subtopics.learn: Run `schemathesis run http://127.0.0.1:8000/openapi.json --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --max-examples 100 --seed 42 --max-failures 10 --wait-for-schema 30 --report junit` (or a file schema plus `--url`) and understand the four phases: examples (schema `example`/`examples` values), coverage (boundary values, `maxLength+1`, missing required fields, wrong types), fuzzing (Hypothesis-generated data) and stateful (OpenAPI links). Know each default check and what a failure means for Kaupex: `not_a_server_error` (unhandled exception), `status_code_conformance` (undocumented 403), `content_type_conformance`, `response_headers_conformance`, `response_schema_conformance` (nullable field not marked), `negative_data_rejection` (invalid body accepted), `positive_data_acceptance` (valid body rejected), `missing_required_header`, `unsupported_method`, `use_after_free`, `ensure_resource_availability`, `ignored_auth` (endpoint answers without a token). Tune with `--exclude-checks`, `--include-path-regex '^/v1/tasks'`, `--max-response-time 1.5`, `--phases`, and `schemathesis.toml` sections such as `[checks.negative_data_rejection] expected-statuses = ["400", "422"]`; reproduce a failure from the printed curl command and `--report-vcr-path`.

resource.label: Schemathesis docs - Checks reference

subtopics.name: Schemathesis inside pytest: from_asgi, parametrize, OpenAPI links, stateful
subtopics.learn: Load the schema straight from the app with `schema = schemathesis.openapi.from_asgi("/openapi.json", app)`, or from a fixture via `schemathesis.pytest.from_fixture("api_schema")` so the app under test carries the same `dependency_overrides` (test DB, fixed clock) as the rest of the suite; write `@schema.parametrize() def test_api(case): case.call_and_validate(headers=auth)` and scope with `schema.include(operation_id=...)` / `schema.exclude(path_regex=...)`. Add explicit `links` under `responses.201` via `openapi_extra` (`"operationId": "tasks_get_task", "parameters": {"task_id": "$response.body#/id"}`) so `APIWorkflow = schema.as_state_machine(); TestAPI = APIWorkflow.TestCase` chains create, get, transition and delete and `use_after_free` catches a GET 200 after DELETE. Retrofit conformance onto existing handwritten API tests with `schema["/v1/tasks/{task_id}"]["GET"].validate_response(response)`. Mark all of this `@pytest.mark.contract` and run it as its own CI job because it is minutes, not seconds.

resource.label: Schemathesis docs - Testing Python Apps (from_asgi, from_fixture)

subtopics.name: Coverage that measures the truth: branch, greenlet concurrency, exclusions, fail_under
subtopics.learn: Configure `[tool.coverage.run]` with `source = ["kaupex"]`, `branch = true`, `parallel = true`, `relative_files = true` and `concurrency = ["thread", "greenlet"]`: SQLAlchemy's asyncio bridge runs DB calls inside greenlets and without the greenlet tracer the lines inside repositories report as never executed. In `[tool.coverage.report]` set `fail_under = 85`, `show_missing = true`, `skip_covered = true`, and `exclude_also` for `if TYPE_CHECKING:`, `raise NotImplementedError`, `@abstractmethod` and the `__main__` guard; `omit` generated migrations. Drive it through pytest-cov (`--cov=kaupex --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing:skip-covered --cov-report=xml --cov-fail-under=85`) and use `--cov-context=test` to see which test covers which line when deciding what to delete. Know the difference between line and branch percentages, why an `except` clause with no test is a branch miss, and why the number is a floor for finding untested modules (`coverage report --sort=miss`) rather than a quality score.

resource.label: coverage.py docs - Configuration reference

subtopics.name: Subprocess and worker coverage: parallel data files and combine
subtopics.learn: Code that runs in a child process is invisible to coverage by default: a Temporal worker started with `subprocess.Popen`, a CLI invoked in an integration test, or a `multiprocessing` pool. Enable measurement either with `patch = ["subprocess"]` in `[tool.coverage.run]` (coverage 7.10+) or the older `COVERAGE_PROCESS_START=pyproject.toml` environment variable plus the `.pth` hook, set `sigterm = true` so a worker killed by SIGTERM still flushes its `.coverage.<host>.<pid>.<random>` data file, and add `multiprocessing` to `concurrency` when pools are involved. After the run, `coverage combine` merges the data files, then `coverage report` and `coverage xml -o coverage.xml`; pytest-cov does the combine automatically for xdist workers but not for your own subprocesses. When unit and integration run in separate CI jobs, upload the `.coverage.*` files as artifacts and combine in a final job, which only works with `relative_files = true` because the checkout paths differ.

resource.label: coverage.py docs - Measuring sub-processes

subtopics.name: CI wiring: unit, integration and contract jobs that block merge
subtopics.learn: Split the workflow into a `unit` job (`pytest -m "not integration and not contract" -n auto`), an `integration` job with `services: postgres: image: postgres:16` plus `options: --health-cmd pg_isready --health-interval 10s --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 5` and `ports: ["5432:5432"]`, and a `contract` job that starts `uvicorn kaupex.main:app --port 8000 &` then runs `schemathesis run http://127.0.0.1:8000/openapi.json --wait-for-schema 30 --report junit --max-examples 50 --seed ${{ github.run_id }}` and uploads `schemathesis-report/` with actions/upload-artifact (or uses `schemathesis/action@v3`). Add the `oasdiff breaking` step, `--junitxml` for the test summary, `actions/cache` on `.hypothesis`, `timeout-minutes` on every job and `concurrency: group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true`. Then make it a gate: branch protection with all three jobs as required status checks, so 'a failing contract breaks the build' is enforced by the repository, not by the reviewer noticing a red check.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Creating PostgreSQL service containers

subtopics.name: Publishing coverage: Codecov upload, patch gates, and the badge
subtopics.learn: Upload `coverage.xml` with `codecov/codecov-action@v5` (`files: coverage.xml`, `fail_ci_if_error: true`, `token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}`), then write a `codecov.yml` where `coverage.status.project.default.target: auto` with `threshold: 1%` stops regressions and `coverage.status.patch.default.target: 80%` is the gate that actually matters on a PR: new code must be tested even when the repo total is low. Embed the badge markdown from the Codecov settings page in the README so the number is public and updates itself. Know the SaaS-free alternative for a customer's air-gapped repo: `coverage json` and `jq .totals.percent_covered` produce a shields endpoint JSON (`{"schemaVersion": 1, "label": "coverage", "message": "87%", "color": "green"}`) committed to a gh-pages branch or gist and rendered via `img.shields.io/endpoint?url=...`, and publish `htmlcov/` as a build artifact so a reviewer can open the missed lines.

resource.label: Codecov docs - Status badges

subtopics.name: Flaky tests: ordering, clocks, timeouts and quarantine policy
subtopics.learn: Install pytest-randomly so every run shuffles test order and reseeds `random`, Faker and NumPy; when a failure appears, reproduce with the printed `--randomly-seed=N` and disable with `-p no:randomly` only to bisect, never in CI. Add pytest-timeout (`timeout = 120` in ini, `--timeout-method=thread` when signals are unavailable) so a hung Temporal client fails the job in two minutes instead of six hours. Control time with time-machine (`time_machine.travel(...)`) rather than `sleep()`, and replace sleeps in async tests with a poll-until-deadline helper. Know the five root causes to check in order: shared mutable state across tests, clock, network, ordering, event loop or connection reused across loops. Define a quarantine policy: a `@pytest.mark.flaky` marker excluded from the required job, a ticket with owner and expiry, and `pytest-repeat --count=50` to prove a fix; never put pytest-rerunfailures on the required check because it converts a real race into green.

resource.label: pytest-randomly - official repository (README)

subtopics.name: Mutation testing and assertion quality: why coverage lies
subtopics.learn: Configure `[tool.mutmut] paths_to_mutate = ["src/kaupex/domain/"]` and `tests_dir = ["tests/unit/"]`, run `mutmut run`, then `mutmut results` and `mutmut show <id>` (or `mutmut browse`) to read surviving mutants: a flipped `<` to `<=` or a removed `raise` that no test noticed. Every survivor is a line that is covered but not asserted, which is how a 92% covered module still ships a wrong transition guard. Fix survivors by strengthening assertions, not adding tests: `pytest.raises(InvalidTransition, match=r"queued -> done")` instead of bare `pytest.raises(Exception)`, exact `response.json() == {...}` instead of `"id" in response.json()`, `pytest.approx` with explicit tolerance, and `assert result` never on its own. Run mutation testing on the domain package only and on a schedule or on demand, not as a required gate, because a full run is minutes to hours.

resource.label: mutmut docs - mutation testing for Python

outcomes: You can run `pytest -m unit` on the Kaupex Task Compiler in under five seconds and the full suite (unit, integration against a testcontainers Postgres, API, contract) in CI, with `--strict-markers --strict-config`, `filterwarnings = error` and `xfail_strict = true` enforced and every marker registered.

You can write a Hypothesis `RuleBasedStateMachine` for the Task lifecycle that, when a deliberately planted bug allows cancel after complete, prints a minimal three-step counterexample which you turn into a pinned regression test with `@reproduce_failure` or `@example`.

You can make a full `schemathesis run` against the Kaupex `/openapi.json` pass with all default checks enabled and at least one OpenAPI link exercised in the stateful phase, and explain from the failure output which handler or schema field was wrong for any check you had to fix along the way.

You can demonstrate that adding a required property to a request model or deleting a response field fails the `oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR` job and the committed `openapi.json` snapshot test, while adding an optional response field passes both.

You can show branch coverage for the async repository layer moving from near zero to accurate by adding `concurrency = ["thread", "greenlet"]`, and explain why the pre-fix number was wrong rather than low.

You can configure a Postgres-backed test suite to run under `pytest -n auto` with one database per xdist worker derived from `PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER`, with zero cross-worker failures across ten consecutive runs.

You can set up branch protection so a PR cannot merge while any of unit, integration, contract or oasdiff jobs is red, and a Codecov patch status below 80% is visible on the PR with the badge in the README reflecting main.
You can run `mutmut` on `kaupex/domain`, pick three surviving mutants and kill each by tightening an assertion rather than adding a test, explaining what the original assertion failed to check.
failureModes: A route returns 409 from the `Conflict` handler but only 200 and 422 are declared in `responses=`; the customer's generated TypeScript client treats 409 as an unknown error and retries the task creation in a loop, producing duplicate tasks until Schemathesis `status_code_conformance` is finally added to CI three months later.

Repository tests run against a mocked SQLAlchemy Session that returns whatever the test says; the real query has a missing `tenant_id` predicate, tests are green, and the first cross-tenant data exposure is found by the customer's security team during UAT.

Coverage is 91% and celebrated, but `concurrency` was never set so every line inside the greenlet-bridged async repository counts as executed only when the sync fallback path runs; after a refactor the badge stays green while the actual async code path has no test.

The API suite shares a module-scoped async engine with function-scoped tests under pytest-asyncio's default function loop; the second test fails with 'Future attached to a different loop', the team adds `pytest-rerunfailures`, and a genuine connection-pool leak hides behind retries for months.

`openapi.json` is regenerated on every deploy but never committed or diffed; a pydantic model rename changes `status` to `state` in the response, no test fails because the app and its own schema still agree, and the customer's integration breaks on Monday morning.

Hypothesis runs with the default 200 ms `deadline` on shared CI runners; property tests fail intermittently under load, someone adds `suppress_health_check` and `@settings(max_examples=5)` to make CI green, and the tests stop finding anything.

Integration tests `TRUNCATE` tables between runs but xdist workers share one database; tests pass locally with `-p no:xdist` and fail randomly in CI, so the team drops parallelism and the suite grows to a 40-minute serial run that nobody waits for before merging.
interviewQuestions: A customer's integration team says our API 'changed under them' although every deploy passed CI. Walk me through what a contract-testing setup that would have caught it looks like, what specifically runs in CI, what counts as a breaking change, and how you would roll the change out instead.

Design the test strategy for a FastAPI service backed by Postgres with row-level security and Temporal workers. What runs at each layer, what is real versus faked, how do you isolate tests that must commit, and how do you keep the whole thing under ten minutes in CI with parallel workers?

You have 90% line coverage and a production bug in a state-transition guard that every test exercised. Explain why coverage did not catch it, what mutation testing would have shown, and how you would decide which assertions to strengthen.

Schemathesis reports `response_schema_conformance` failures on GET /v1/tasks/{id} for about 2% of generated cases and `ignored_auth` on one endpoint. Debug both: what are the likely causes in a pydantic/FastAPI app, how do you reproduce one case, and which fix belongs in the schema versus the handler?

Write a property-based test for the Kaupex task compiler that would find an ordering bug the parametrised unit tests cannot. What property do you state, what strategy generates the inputs, how do you keep it deterministic in CI, and what do you do when Hypothesis reports Flaky?
Our integration suite against Postgres is flaky under `pytest -n auto` but green serially. Give me your diagnosis procedure and the three most likely root causes in order, and the fix for each.

A customer's security questionnaire asks for our test coverage and how we prevent regressions in the API they consume. What do you send them, how is it produced, and what claim would you refuse to make from a coverage number alone?
39.proofOfWork: A pull request against the Kaupex Task Compiler repository that intentionally introduces one breaking API change (renaming `status` to `state` in the task response) and one behavioural regression (allowing `cancel` from `completed`), with the CI run attached showing exactly which gates caught which defect: the committed `openapi.json` snapshot test and `oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR` fail on the rename, the Hypothesis `RuleBasedStateMachine` prints the minimal counterexample for the illegal transition, and the Schemathesis stateful phase reports `use_after_free` or a schema conformance failure with the reproducing curl command. The PR description contains a short table mapping each defect to the job that caught it, the time to first red check, and a one-paragraph note on why branch coverage stayed above the `fail_under` threshold for both defects, demonstrating in one artefact why contracts and properties are gates and coverage is only a floor.

40.topic: Warehouse layer: dbt, DuckDB, dimensional modelling
40.why: FDEs are routinely the person a customer asks for 'just a weekly report' out of the product database, and the naive answer - a cron job running SELECTs against the OLTP primary - is what pages their DBA at 03:00 and produces numbers that disagree with the invoice. A tested, documented dbt + DuckDB mart is the smallest thing that gives you a stable grain, history that survives source overwrites, a reconciliation you can show the customer, and a project that ports to their Snowflake/BigQuery/Databricks by swapping the adapter when they outgrow one box. Dimensional-modelling vocabulary (grain, SCD2, conformed dimensions, additivity) is also the shared language with the customer's data team, and Palantir/Databricks-style loops test it directly.
prerequisites: SQL beyond SELECT: CTEs, window functions, multi-aggregate GROUP BY, joins with time-range predicates (Topic 29, PostgreSQL at depth)

DefenderMate's Postgres schema (tenants, users, conversations, messages, llm_calls, tool_calls, audit_log) and its RLS policies, because the extraction role must read across tenants (Topic 30, Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems)
Python 3.11+ virtualenv hygiene and pinned requirements - dbt-core and dbt-duckdb are pip packages and version drift between them bites
YAML and Jinja2 basics: dbt projects are mostly YAML config and Jinja-templated SQL
Tests-as-assertions mindset from Topic 35 (Testing and contracts) - dbt tests are assertions over data, not code
Git branches plus a CI runner (GitHub Actions) for scheduling the nightly run and doing state-based builds

subtopics.name: When a warehouse layer is the right call, and when DuckDB is the right warehouse
subtopics.learn: Know the three reasons to stop reporting from the OLTP primary: row-store scan cost (Postgres reads whole 8 KB heap pages to aggregate three columns; a columnar engine reads only those columns and skips row groups via min/max zone maps), lock and IO contention with the production write path, and the need for history the application overwrites or deletes. Place DuckDB on the spectrum: in-process, single-node, vectorised, zero infrastructure, comfortable from gigabytes to low terabytes on one box; versus a Postgres read replica (no new tech but still row-store) versus Snowflake/BigQuery/Databricks (multi-user concurrency, governance, per-query cost). State the customer-facing rule you will use: start with DuckDB + Parquet + dbt when there is one consumer and the data fits on a disk, because the dbt project moves to a cloud warehouse later by changing profiles.yml, not by rewriting SQL.

resource.label: DuckDB - Why DuckDB

subtopics.name: Kimball four-step design and declaring the grain
subtopics.learn: Apply the four steps to DefenderMate before writing a line of SQL: (1) pick the business process ('an LLM call was made', 'a conversation ran'), (2) declare the grain as a sentence - 'one row per llm_call', 'one row per tenant per day' - (3) identify dimensions as everything true at the moment of the event (tenant, user, model, date, tool), (4) identify facts as numeric measurements at that grain (input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens, latency_ms, cost_usd). Recognise a mixed-grain fact table (conversation-level fields repeated on call-level rows) as the root cause of double counting in every downstream sum. Make the grain sentence the model's description: in YAML and enforce it with a unique test on the natural key or dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns, so a duplicated extract fails the build instead of inflating the email.

resource.label: Kimball Group - Four-Step Dimensional Design Process

subtopics.name: Fact table types and additivity: transaction, periodic snapshot, accumulating snapshot
subtopics.learn: Distinguish the three fact shapes and pick one per question: transaction facts (fct_llm_calls, one row per call, fully additive tokens and cost), periodic snapshots (fct_tenant_daily, one row per tenant per day whether or not anything happened - built by cross-joining a date spine to dim_tenant and zero-filling), and accumulating snapshots (one row per conversation with started_at, first_tool_call_at, resolved_at columns that get updated as milestones land). Classify every measure: additive (tokens, cost_usd), semi-additive (active_users - sums across tenants, not across days), non-additive (p95 latency, success ratio - never sum; store numerator and denominator, or recompute from the transaction grain). Understand why the weekly email must read the daily snapshot rather than re-aggregating transactions each time: stable, replayable numbers and explicit zero rows for silent tenants.

resource.label: Kimball Group - Periodic Snapshot Fact Tables

subtopics.name: Dimension design: surrogate keys, date dimension, conformed, role-playing, junk, degenerate, unknown member
subtopics.learn: Build dim_tenant, dim_user, dim_model, dim_date with a surrogate key (dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key over natural key plus dbt_valid_from for versioned rows), keep the natural key alongside it, and seed an 'unknown' member (-1 / 'unknown') so a fact row never loses its join when a lookup fails. Date dimension: generate with dbt_utils.date_spine, key it as a YYYYMMDD integer, include iso_week, week_start_date, is_weekend and any fiscal columns the email needs; role-play it as started_date and resolved_date by joining twice with aliases. Know when to fold low-cardinality flags (finish_reason x is_tool_call x is_cached) into a junk dimension and when to leave conversation_id on the fact as a degenerate dimension. Denormalise hierarchies (tenant -> plan -> region) into the dimension row rather than snowflaking; dimensions are small, so redundancy is cheaper than the extra join.

resource.label: Microsoft Learn - Modeling dimension tables (surrogate keys, SCD, special dimensions, date dimension)

subtopics.name: Slowly changing dimensions: Type 1 vs Type 2 with dbt snapshots
subtopics.learn: Decide per attribute whether a change is Type 1 (overwrite: user email, display name) or Type 2 (new version: tenant plan tier, model list price). Implement Type 2 with dbt snapshots: strategy: timestamp with updated_at when the source timestamp is trustworthy, strategy: check with check_cols when it is not; understand dbt_valid_from / dbt_valid_to (NULL means current), hard_deletes: invalidate | new_record (1.9+) and dbt_valid_to_current so you can avoid the NULL-handling branch in joins. Snapshots are append-only and cannot be regenerated from source - back the snapshot table up before any --full-refresh, and never snapshot an already-transformed or ephemeral model. Join facts to the version in effect at event time: f.created_at >= d.dbt_valid_from AND f.created_at < coalesce(d.dbt_valid_to, '9999-12-31'), and test that every fact row matches exactly one version.

resource.label: dbt docs - Add snapshots to your DAG

subtopics.name: Extracting from Postgres into DuckDB without hurting production
subtopics.learn: INSTALL postgres; LOAD postgres; ATTACH 'dbname=defendermate host=... user=reporting' AS pg (TYPE postgres, READ_ONLY); then CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE raw.llm_calls AS SELECT * FROM pg.public.llm_calls WHERE updated_at > (SELECT max(updated_at) FROM raw.llm_calls) - INTERVAL 1 HOUR. Use postgres_query('pg', '...') to push a filter to the server when the extension would otherwise pull the whole table; know that pg_use_ctid_scan and pg_pages_per_task parallelise the scan and what that does to the source's IO. Store credentials with CREATE SECRET (TYPE postgres, ...), not inline DSNs. Extraction hygiene an FDE is judged on: dedicated read-only role with statement_timeout, read from a replica when one exists, watermark on updated_at plus a lookback window for late-committing transactions, add an _extracted_at column, and reconcile nightly counts per day against the source. RLS from Topic 30 means the reporting role needs BYPASSRLS or a policy granting every tenant, otherwise the extract silently returns a subset.

resource.label: DuckDB docs - PostgreSQL extension (ATTACH, postgres_query, COPY, secrets)

subtopics.name: Parquet as the storage layer: COPY TO, hive partitioning, row groups, schema drift
subtopics.learn: Land raw extracts and published marts as Parquet: COPY (SELECT ...) TO 'lake/llm_calls' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (event_date), COMPRESSION zstd, ROW_GROUP_SIZE 122880, OVERWRITE_OR_IGNORE). Read back with read_parquet('lake/llm_calls/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true, union_by_name = true) and know partition pruning only happens when the WHERE clause is on the partition column. Sizing rules from the DuckDB performance guide: row groups of 100K-1M rows, files of 100 MB-10 GB, at least as many row groups as threads; per-tenant-per-hour partitions producing hundreds of thousands of tiny files is the classic mistake. Use parquet_metadata() and parquet_schema() to detect type drift between days (an INT64 column that became VARCHAR after an app deploy). Know dbt-duckdb's materialized='external' writes a model straight to Parquet using location and external_root from the profile.

resource.label: DuckDB docs - Reading and Writing Parquet Files

subtopics.name: dbt + dbt-duckdb project wiring: profiles.yml, dbt_project.yml, ref/source, compiled SQL
subtopics.learn: profiles.yml: type: duckdb, path: warehouse.duckdb, extensions: [parquet, httpfs, postgres], settings: {memory_limit: '8GB', threads: 4}, attach: for a second DuckDB file or Postgres; understand that threads at the profile top level is dbt's model-level parallelism, distinct from DuckDB's own threads setting. dbt_project.yml: model-paths, a models: block with per-folder +materialized and +schema, vars:, on-run-start / on-run-end, require-dbt-version. ref() and source() are what build the DAG - a hardcoded table name is an invisible dependency that will run out of order. Read target/compiled/ and target/run/ to see the exact SQL DuckDB executed; use dbt compile --select model when debugging Jinja; dbt debug verifies the profile and connection; dbt deps installs packages.yml.

resource.label: dbt docs - DuckDB setup (dbt-duckdb profile)

subtopics.name: Layering: staging, intermediate, marts, and choosing a materialization per layer
subtopics.learn: Staging (stg_pg__llm_calls): one model per source table, view materialization, rename/cast/no joins, the only layer allowed to call source(). Intermediate (int_calls_with_costs): ephemeral or view, where joins and business rules live. Marts (fct_llm_calls, fct_tenant_daily, dim_tenant): table or incremental, the only layer consumers may query, landing in a marts schema via +schema. Decide materialization by asking: how often is it read versus how expensive is it to rebuild, does anyone query it directly, and how many rows. Understand that ephemeral models are injected as CTEs so compiled SQL balloons and error line numbers become useless - use views in dev and tables in prod by branching on target.name. Know why one model per source table matters: when the customer renames a column you fix one file.

resource.label: dbt docs - How we structure our dbt projects

subtopics.name: Incremental models: unique_key, strategies, lookback windows, late-arriving rows
subtopics.learn: {{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='llm_call_id', incremental_strategy='delete+insert', on_schema_change='append_new_columns') }} with {% if is_incremental() %} WHERE updated_at > (SELECT max(updated_at) FROM {{ this }}) - INTERVAL 1 HOUR {% endif %}. Know what each strategy does on a duplicate key (append duplicates, delete+insert replaces the key set, merge upserts) and which ones dbt-duckdb supports. The lookback window is what saves you from long-running source transactions that commit with older timestamps; on_schema_change defaults to ignore, which silently drops new source columns. dbt run --full-refresh rebuilds from scratch - guard expensive models with full_refresh: false. For fct_tenant_daily, key on (tenant_sk, date_day) and recompute the trailing N days each night rather than only yesterday so late events are absorbed. Late-arriving dimensions: coalesce a failed surrogate-key lookup to the unknown member and re-resolve within the lookback window.

resource.label: dbt docs - Configure incremental models

subtopics.name: Jinja, macros and dbt_utils: surrogate keys, date spine, safe division, DRY logic
subtopics.learn: {{ }} renders a value, {% %} controls flow. Write a cents_to_usd(col) macro and a limit_in_dev() macro keyed on target.name. Use dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['tenant_id', 'dbt_valid_from']) for versioned dimension keys, dbt_utils.date_spine(datepart='day', start_date=..., end_date=...) to build dim_date and the snapshot spine, dbt_utils.safe_divide(successes, attempts) for tool-success ratios that must not divide by zero, and dbt_utils.star(from=ref(...), except=[...]) to avoid hand-listing columns. Pin packages.yml versions and understand dispatch picks the adapter-specific implementation. Jinja runs at compile time: {{ run_started_at }} is fixed for the whole invocation while current_timestamp is evaluated per statement, which matters when you stamp _loaded_at on multiple models.

resource.label: GitHub - dbt-labs/dbt-utils (macros and generic tests)

subtopics.name: Data tests: generic, singular, thresholds and stored failures
subtopics.learn: Generic tests in YAML: unique and not_null on every key, accepted_values on finish_reason (end_turn, max_tokens, tool_use, stop_sequence), relationships so every fact tenant_sk exists in dim_tenant. dbt_utils tests that catch real regressions: unique_combination_of_columns (the grain), accepted_range (cost_usd >= 0, latency_ms between 0 and 600000), not_null_proportion, equal_rowcount between stg and raw, recency (mart refreshed within 26 hours). Singular tests in tests/*.sql for cross-model reconciliation: sum of fct_tenant_daily tokens per day must equal sum of fct_llm_calls tokens for that day. Configure severity: warn, warn_if: '>0', error_if: '>100' so a handful of bad rows does not block the email while a flood does; store_failures: true writes failing rows to <schema>_dbt_test__audit so you can show the customer the exact offending rows. Remember dbt build skips children of a failing test.

resource.label: dbt docs - Add data tests to your DAG

subtopics.name: Unit tests and model contracts: pinning logic and schema
subtopics.learn: Unit tests (dbt 1.8+) mock inputs and assert outputs: unit_tests: - name: prices_apply_cache_discount, model: int_calls_with_costs, given: [{input: ref('stg_pg__llm_calls'), rows: [...]}, {input: ref('dim_model'), rows: [...]}], expect: {rows: [...]}. Aim them at the pricing formula, UTC-vs-tenant-local day bucketing, and the SCD2 join-window predicate; use overrides to pin is_incremental() and vars. Model contracts: config: contract: enforced: true plus columns: - name: tenant_sk, data_type: bigint, constraints: [{type: not_null}] make the build fail when the SELECT's output schema drifts, which is what protects the email template from a renamed or retyped column. Contracts require every column listed with a data_type and are checked at build time before the table is swapped in.

resource.label: dbt docs - Unit tests

subtopics.name: Source freshness and exposures: knowing the data is late, and who consumes it
subtopics.learn: Declare sources: with loaded_at_field: _extracted_at and freshness: warn_after: {count: 6, period: hour}, error_after: {count: 26, period: hour}; dbt source freshness writes target/sources.json and --select source_status:fresher+ builds only models whose sources actually moved. Add an exposures: entry (type: application, name: defendermate_weekly_email, owner:, url:, depends_on: [ref('fct_tenant_daily'), ref('dim_tenant')]) so the lineage graph ends at the customer email and dbt build --select +exposure:defendermate_weekly_email builds exactly that path. Treat the freshness thresholds as the mart's SLA contract with the customer and alert on them, not on 'the cron ran'.

resource.label: dbt docs - Add sources to your DAG (incl. source freshness)

subtopics.name: Documentation and lineage: descriptions, doc blocks, catalog and manifest
subtopics.learn: Every mart column gets a description:; define conformed definitions once as {% docs tenant_sk %}...{% enddocs %} blocks and reference them with '{{ doc("tenant_sk") }}' so the same column is not described three different ways. dbt docs generate writes catalog.json and manifest.json; dbt docs serve renders the searchable site and lineage DAG. Put the grain sentence, the freshness SLA and the owner in the model description rather than a wiki so they cannot drift from the code. Know manifest.json is machine-readable: it drives state:modified selection and you can turn it into a customer-facing data dictionary with a 30-line script.

resource.label: dbt docs - About documentation

subtopics.name: dbt build and node selection: tags, graph operators, state and result selectors
subtopics.learn: dbt build runs seeds, snapshots, models and tests in DAG order and skips descendants of failures. Selection syntax: --select tag:nightly, path:models/marts, stg_pg__llm_calls+ (downstream), +fct_tenant_daily (upstream), @fct_tenant_daily (children plus their parents), --exclude. State-based CI: keep the last production manifest.json and run dbt build --select state:modified+ --state prod-artifacts/ so a PR builds only what changed; after a partial failure rerun only the broken path with --select result:error+ --state target-prev/; --defer resolves unbuilt refs to production. Know --fail-fast to stop on first error and --empty for a schema-only dry run.

resource.label: dbt docs - Node selection syntax overview

subtopics.name: DuckDB analytical SQL for the mart: windows, QUALIFY, ASOF JOIN, PIVOT, list aggregates
subtopics.learn: Write the weekly-email queries idiomatically: lag(tokens, 7) OVER (PARTITION BY tenant_sk ORDER BY date_day) for week-over-week, sum(cost_usd) OVER (PARTITION BY tenant_sk ORDER BY date_day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) for rolling 7-day, quantile_cont(latency_ms, 0.95) for p95, QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY tenant_id ORDER BY dbt_valid_from DESC) = 1 for current-version dedup without a subquery, ASOF JOIN dim_model_price p ON c.model = p.model AND c.created_at >= p.effective_from to attach the price in effect at call time, PIVOT fct_tenant_daily ON model_name USING sum(cost_usd), and list() / string_agg for the 'top 5 tools' line. Use GROUP BY ALL, SELECT * EXCLUDE (...), date_trunc('week', ...) and timezone(tz, ts) for tenant-local weeks. Confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that filters push into the Parquet scan.

resource.label: DuckDB docs - Window Functions (incl. QUALIFY and frame clauses)

subtopics.name: DuckDB operability: memory limits, spilling, threads, single-writer concurrency, EXPLAIN ANALYZE
subtopics.learn: SET memory_limit = '6GB'; SET threads = 4; SET temp_directory = '/data/tmp'; SET max_temp_directory_size = '50GB'; SET preserve_insertion_order = false for large loads. Understand that hash joins, aggregates and sorts spill to temp_directory once memory_limit is hit, and that a missing or full temp directory is an OOM in disguise. Concurrency: one process may open a .duckdb file read-write; other processes may only attach with access_mode = 'READ_ONLY' and only if no writer holds it - so the nightly dbt job and the email renderer must not both open the same file read-write. Pattern: dbt writes warehouse.duckdb, then publish marts to Parquet or copy the file and atomically rename for readers. Threads within a process use MVCC and the second writer to the same row fails with a conflict error. Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE: estimated vs actual cardinality per operator, timings, and the accidental cross join that turns 4 minutes into 90.

resource.label: DuckDB docs - Tuning Workloads (performance guide)

subtopics.name: Nightly orchestration and the weekly-email consumer: scheduling, run_results.json, alerting, idempotency
subtopics.learn: A nightly run is: extract (DuckDB postgres ATTACH -> raw Parquet) -> dbt source freshness -> dbt build --select tag:nightly -> publish -> notify. Schedule with GitHub Actions on: schedule: cron: (know it runs on the default branch and can be delayed or dropped at high load) or a Temporal schedule from Topic 34 when you need retries and visibility; make every step idempotent so a 03:00 rerun is safe. Parse target/run_results.json: results[].status (success, error, fail, skipped, warn), failures, execution_time, adapter_response.rows_affected; post a summary to Slack and persist it to an ops.dbt_runs table via on-run-end. The weekly-email renderer (Python + Jinja2) opens the published DuckDB file with read_only=True or reads the Parquet marts, queries fct_tenant_daily for the trailing seven complete tenant-local days, and refuses to send when the recency test or freshness check failed - a late email beats a wrong one. Define the SLA explicitly: mart complete by 06:00 tenant-local, with freshness thresholds aligned to it.

resource.label: dbt docs - Run results JSON artifact

outcomes: You can write the grain of each fact table as a single sentence, encode it as a unique_combination_of_columns test, and demonstrate the build failing when a duplicated extract is loaded.

You can run dbt build on a fresh clone with only a Postgres DSN and end with fct_llm_calls, fct_tenant_daily, dim_tenant (SCD2), dim_model and dim_date materialised in DuckDB, every test passing, and dbt docs generate producing a lineage graph that terminates at the defendermate_weekly_email exposure.
You can change a tenant's plan tier in Postgres, run dbt snapshot, and show two versions in dim_tenant with correct dbt_valid_from/dbt_valid_to while historic calls remain attributed to the old tier.
You can insert an llm_call with a created_at three days in the past, rerun the incremental models without --full-refresh, and show the corrected fct_tenant_daily row for that day.

You can prove reconciliation to a customer: a singular test comparing per-day token sums between raw and fct_tenant_daily passes, and when it fails you can name the exact rows from the dbt_test__audit schema.
You can read EXPLAIN ANALYZE output on a query over hive-partitioned Parquet, state whether partition pruning and filter pushdown happened, and fix the layout or predicate so they do.
You can open run_results.json after a failed nightly run, identify the failed node and its skipped descendants, rerun only result:error+ with --state, and state whether the email is safe to send.

You can size DuckDB for a customer's box (memory_limit, threads, temp_directory), show a larger-than-memory aggregation completing by spilling, and explain the single-writer constraint to their ops team in two sentences.
failureModes: The reporting role extracted from a Postgres database with RLS enabled but had no BYPASSRLS and no policy; the extract silently returned rows for one tenant, not_null tests passed on the tiny table, and every other customer received a weekly email reporting zero usage.

An incremental fact filtered on created_at > max(created_at) with no lookback; a batch committed by a long-running transaction with older timestamps never landed, and weekly totals came in 4 percent below the invoice, which the customer noticed first.

Someone ran dbt snapshot --full-refresh on dim_tenant after adding a column, wiping version history; every historic fact then joined to the current plan tier and three months of reports silently changed.

Parquet partitioned by tenant_id and hour produced 400k files of a few kilobytes; DuckDB spent longer opening files than scanning them and the nightly run grew from 4 minutes to 90 before anyone looked.

The email renderer opened warehouse.duckdb with the default read-write mode while dbt was writing; the lock conflict surfaced on Monday morning as 'email service down' and was debugged as a networking problem for two hours.

on_schema_change was left at the default ignore, so a new cache_read_tokens column added upstream never reached fct_llm_calls; cost_usd omitted cache discounts for six weeks until the customer disputed the bill.

A refactor changed latency from milliseconds to seconds; the accepted_range test with max_value 600000 still passed and there was no contract pinning the unit, so p95 latency in the email read 0.8 for a month and nobody trusted the report afterward.
interviewQuestions: A customer wants a weekly usage-and-cost email per tenant from a Postgres OLTP database holding 200 million llm_call rows. Design the warehouse layer: which fact tables at which grain, which dimensions are SCD2, how you extract without hurting the primary, and what runs fine on a 16 GB box versus when you would move them to Snowflake or Databricks.

Explain the difference between a transaction fact and a periodic snapshot fact and why the weekly email should be built from the snapshot. What exactly goes wrong if you sum a p95 latency column across days, and how do you store it so the email is still right?

Your incremental model filters on updated_at > max(updated_at). Give me three concrete ways rows get lost or duplicated, and say which of unique_key, incremental strategy and a lookback window addresses each.

A tenant moved from 'pro' to 'enterprise' on March 3rd. Write the SQL that joins March calls to the plan in effect at call time using a dbt snapshot table, and tell me what breaks if dbt_valid_to is NULL for current rows and you forgot the coalesce.

dbt build failed at 03:14 on a relationships test between fct_llm_calls and dim_model. What do you look at in run_results.json and the stored-failures table, what are the two most likely root causes, and how do you decide whether the 07:00 customer email can still go out?

Why does DuckDB allow only one writer process, and how do you architect a nightly writer plus a daytime read service around that constraint? Separately, what is the difference between threads in profiles.yml and DuckDB's own threads setting?

A query over two years of hive-partitioned Parquet takes 40 seconds filtered on tenant_id but 400 milliseconds filtered on event_date. Explain why, and describe two different ways you would change the layout or the query so both are fast.
40.proofOfWork: A reproducible customer-handover package for the DefenderMate warehouse, checked into the repo alongside the dbt project: a single make nightly target that, from a fresh clone plus a Postgres DSN, extracts to Parquet via the DuckDB postgres extension, runs dbt source freshness and dbt build --select tag:nightly, publishes the marts, and appends the parsed run_results.json to an ops.dbt_runs table; a recorded drift drill in which you change a tenant's plan tier and insert a back-dated llm_call in Postgres, rerun the pipeline, and show dim_tenant with two versions, the corrected fct_tenant_daily row, the singular reconciliation test passing, and dbt docs lineage terminating at the weekly-email exposure; and a one-page ops runbook stating the mart SLA, the DuckDB memory_limit/threads/temp_directory settings for the customer's box, the single-writer constraint and how the email service avoids it, and the exact rerun command (dbt build --select result:error+ --state ...) after a partial failure. Finish with a rendered weekly email for one sample tenant generated from the mart, showing week-over-week token, cost and p95 deltas.

41.topic: React and Next.js for FDE demos and internal tools
41.why: The customer never sees your FastAPI service, your Temporal workflows or your eval harness; they see a screen, and in week two of every engagement someone asks 'can you put a UI on that so the ops team can use it'. An FDE who can stand up a typed, authenticated, streaming Next.js front end over their own API in an afternoon turns a backend demo into a pilot the customer can click through, and can also read and fix the customer's existing Next.js code (most enterprise platform teams already run it). Take-homes at Palantir, Anthropic and Databricks routinely include a small UI, and the difference between a screen that streams tokens through the customer's Nginx and one that freezes for eight seconds is exactly the kind of production detail this topic drills.
prerequisites: TypeScript at the level of topic 28 (TypeScript and Node for FDEs): generics, discriminated unions, `satisfies`, async iteration, ESM vs CJS, `tsc --noEmit` in CI
A running DefenderMate backend from topics 26, 27 and 32: a token or OIDC login endpoint, at least one JSON list/detail endpoint, and an SSE endpoint relaying Claude's event stream
HTTP mechanics from topics 2 and 32: cookies and SameSite, CORS preflight, chunked transfer encoding, the SSE frame format, and where reverse proxies buffer
Auth from topic 27: verifying an RS256 JWT against a JWKS URL, refresh-token rotation, tenant claims, CSRF and why httpOnly cookies beat localStorage
Docker multi-stage builds and non-root images from topic 6, plus an Nginx or ALB in the path from topics 13 and 16 so streaming can be tested realistically
Node 20.9+ and pnpm or npm installed; working HTML/CSS basics (semantic elements, native form controls, flex and grid)

subtopics.name: React rendering model: state ownership, derived values, keys
subtopics.learn: Walk through render -> commit -> browser paint and be able to say, for any screen in an internal tool (run list, run detail, streaming answer pane), which component owns each piece of state and which values are derived and must not live in `useState`. Practise 'lifting state up' and 'colocating state' on the DefenderMate run list: filter text lives in the list component, the selected run ID lives in the parent, the streaming buffer lives next to the reader. Know why `key` must be a stable identity (run ID, never array index) for lists that reorder or stream in, and what breaks when it is not: preserved input state on the wrong row, lost focus, remounted children.

resource.label: react.dev - Thinking in React

subtopics.name: Effects only for external systems: subscriptions, aborts, StrictMode double-invoke
subtopics.learn: Adopt the rule that `useEffect` exists to synchronise with something outside React (an EventSource, a WebSocket, a timer, the DOM) and never to compute derived data or respond to a prop change. Write the canonical fetch-in-effect correctly once: create an `AbortController`, pass `signal`, return a cleanup that aborts, and watch `StrictMode` mount-unmount-mount in dev prove your cleanup works. Understand the race where two rapid selections resolve out of order and how the abort or an `ignore` flag in cleanup fixes it. Know when `useSyncExternalStore` replaces an effect-plus-state pair for external stores.

resource.label: react.dev - You Might Not Need an Effect

subtopics.name: Server and Client Components: what the boundary actually is
subtopics.learn: Internalise that `'use client'` marks a module boundary, not a place where code 'runs only in the browser': everything imported from a client module is bundled to the browser and still server-rendered to HTML once. Server Components can be async, read `cookies()`/`headers()`, hold secrets, and never re-render; props crossing the boundary must be serialisable (plain objects, arrays, Date, Map, Set, Promises, Server Functions; no class instances, no event handlers). Master the composition pattern: a client `<Tabs>` receives server-rendered `children`, so interactivity does not force data fetching into the browser. Add `import 'server-only'` to every module that touches tokens or the FastAPI base URL so a client import fails at build time rather than leaking at runtime, and check the Network tab to see what the RSC payload actually contains.

resource.label: Next.js docs - Server and Client Components

subtopics.name: App Router file conventions: layouts, pages, dynamic segments, async params
subtopics.learn: Know exactly what each file does: `layout.tsx` (persists across navigations, does not re-render, cannot read `searchParams`), `page.tsx`, `loading.tsx` (an automatic Suspense boundary), `error.tsx`, `not-found.tsx`, `route.ts`, and route groups `(admin)` for grouping without a URL segment. Since Next 15 `params` and `searchParams` are Promises: `const { id } = await params` in `app/runs/[id]/page.tsx`, with the generated `PageProps<'/runs/[id]'>` type from `next typegen` giving you typed segments. Build the shell for DefenderMate: `app/(app)/layout.tsx` with nav and auth check, `app/(app)/runs/page.tsx`, `app/(app)/runs/[id]/page.tsx`, `app/login/page.tsx`, and use `<Link>` prefetching plus `useRouter().refresh()` deliberately, not by accident.

resource.label: Next.js docs - Layouts and Pages

subtopics.name: Fetching from FastAPI inside Server Components: auth forwarding, parallelism, typed responses
subtopics.learn: Fetch DefenderMate from the server with the session cookie translated into `Authorization: Bearer` inside a `server-only` API client, and know that Next's `fetch` default is 'auto no cache' (request-time unless you opt in with `cache: 'force-cache'` or `next: { revalidate, tags }`). Avoid waterfalls: start independent requests before awaiting (`const runsP = getRuns(); const statsP = getStats(); const [runs, stats] = await Promise.all([runsP, statsP])`), and use the preload pattern for data a child needs. Throw on `!res.ok` with the status and a redacted body so `error.tsx` catches it. Generate response types from the FastAPI OpenAPI document (`openapi-typescript`) so a schema change in topic 35's contract tests also fails `tsc` here; never hand-write the run model twice.

resource.label: Next.js docs - Fetching Data

subtopics.name: Streaming the page: Suspense boundaries, loading.tsx, and use()
subtopics.learn: Understand that the App Router streams one HTTP response: the shell renders immediately and each `<Suspense fallback>` island is filled in as its promise resolves, in the same response body, so headers (including redirects and cookies) cannot be changed after the first flush. Place boundaries where latency actually differs: the run header is fast, the Claude-generated summary is slow, so wrap only the summary. Pass a promise from a Server Component to a Client Component and unwrap it with `use(promise)` when the client needs to own the pending state. Size fallbacks to the final content to avoid layout shift, and test with a throttled FastAPI endpoint (`await asyncio.sleep(3)`) to see the streaming order in the Network waterfall.

resource.label: react.dev - <Suspense>

subtopics.name: Cache Components: use cache, cacheLife, cacheTag, updateTag
subtopics.learn: Learn the Next 16 model: with `cacheComponents: true` in `next.config.ts`, nothing is cached unless you say so and any request-time data (`cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`, uncached `fetch`) must sit under a Suspense boundary or the build fails with an 'uncached data accessed outside Suspense' error. Mark a function or component with `'use cache'`, set its lifetime with `cacheLife('minutes' | 'hours' | 'days' | 'max')` or a custom profile, label it with `cacheTag('runs')`, and after a mutation call `updateTag('runs')` (read-your-own-writes in the same request) or `revalidateTag('runs', 'max')` for stale-while-revalidate. Use `connection()` when you need to force request-time rendering without reading a dynamic API. Know which of the DefenderMate screens should be cached at all: reference data yes, a tenant's run list no.

resource.label: Next.js docs - Caching and Revalidating (Cache Components)

subtopics.name: Route Handlers as the backend-for-frontend, including streaming pass-through
subtopics.learn: Write `app/api/runs/[id]/stream/route.ts` exporting `GET(request: NextRequest, ctx: RouteContext<'/api/runs/[id]/stream'>)` that reads the session cookie, calls FastAPI with `Authorization: Bearer`, and returns `new Response(upstream.body, { headers })` with `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform` and `X-Accel-Buffering: no`. Set `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`, `runtime = 'nodejs'` and `maxDuration` appropriately. Pass `request.signal` to the upstream `fetch` and verify with FastAPI logs that closing the tab stops the Claude generation within a second; if your Next version does not propagate the abort, wrap the upstream in a `ReadableStream` whose `cancel()` aborts an `AbortController`. Know why the BFF exists at all: the browser never holds the API token, CORS disappears, and the customer's SSO cookie stays first-party.

resource.label: Next.js docs - Backend for Frontend guide

subtopics.name: Consuming the token stream in a Client Component without melting the UI
subtopics.learn: Read the Route Handler stream with `fetch` plus `res.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader()` and parse SSE frames yourself: split on blank lines, carry partial lines across chunks in a buffer, dispatch on `event:` (DefenderMate relays Claude's `content_block_delta`, `message_stop`, error events from topic 32) and parse `data:` as JSON. Tie an `AbortController` to both component unmount and a Stop button. Do not `setState` per token: append to a ref and flush at most once per animation frame or via `startTransition`, or the 40 re-renders per second stall typing in the input. Know why `EventSource` is a poor fit here (GET only, no custom headers, but cookie auth does work) and when its automatic reconnect with `Last-Event-ID` is still worth it.

resource.label: MDN - Using readable streams

subtopics.name: Forms with Server Functions, Zod 4 validation, useActionState and useOptimistic
subtopics.learn: Write `'use server'` functions that receive `FormData`, parse it with Zod 4 (`schema.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData))`, `z.flattenError` for field errors) and return a `{ errors, values }` state object; wire it with `useActionState(action, initialState)` to get `[state, formAction, isPending]` and render field errors next to inputs. Prove progressive enhancement by disabling JavaScript: the form still submits and the errors still render because the action is a plain POST. Use `useFormStatus()` in a child submit button, `useOptimistic` to add the new run to the list instantly and roll back on failure, and `redirect()` after success (never inside try/catch: it throws). Call `updateTag`/`revalidateTag` in the action so the list is fresh on the next render.

resource.label: Next.js docs - Forms guide

subtopics.name: Server Functions are public POST endpoints: authorisation, arguments, CSRF, size limits
subtopics.learn: Treat every Server Function as an unauthenticated HTTP endpoint identified by an action ID visible in the Network tab: authorise inside the function (`const session = await verifySession()`), validate every argument (the client can send anything), and never trust that 'only admins see the button'. Know that closure-captured values are encrypted with a build-time key and that multi-replica deployments need `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` set consistently or actions fail after a rolling deploy. Configure `serverActions.allowedOrigins` when a reverse proxy makes `Origin` differ from `Host` (Next's built-in CSRF check compares them), and `serverActions.bodySizeLimit` (default 1 MB) before a file-upload form silently 413s in the customer's environment.

resource.label: Next.js docs - serverActions config (allowedOrigins, bodySizeLimit)

subtopics.name: Auth: session cookie, Data Access Layer, JWKS verification against FastAPI
subtopics.learn: Implement login as a Server Function that posts credentials (or completes the OIDC code exchange from topic 27) to FastAPI, then `(await cookies()).set('session', token, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/', expires })`; cookies can only be set in Server Functions and Route Handlers, not in Server Components. Build a `server-only` Data Access Layer with `verifySession()` wrapped in React `cache()` so it runs once per request, verifying the JWT with `jose` (`jwtVerify` against `createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(issuer + '/.well-known/jwks.json'))`, checking `iss`, `aud`, `exp` and the tenant claim) and returning a DTO with only the fields the UI needs. Every data function calls the DAL; layouts are not a security boundary because they do not re-render on navigation. Handle refresh-token rotation and logout (`cookies().delete`) and confirm a tampered cookie yields a redirect to `/login`, never a stack trace.

resource.label: Next.js docs - Authentication guide

subtopics.name: proxy.ts (formerly middleware): matchers, optimistic redirects, request headers
subtopics.learn: Write `proxy.ts` at the project root exporting `default function proxy(request: NextRequest)` with `export const config = { matcher: ['/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)'] }` so it skips static assets. In Next 16 it runs on the Node.js runtime by default but still executes on every matched request before the cache, so keep it cheap: check cookie presence for an optimistic redirect to `/login`, stamp `x-request-id` and tenant headers onto the request with `NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } })`, and rewrite for A/B or maintenance pages. Do not verify JWTs or call databases here; the DAL is the real check. Know the middleware-to-proxy migration so you can read customer codebases on either name.

resource.label: Next.js docs - proxy.ts file convention

subtopics.name: Error boundaries, digests, not-found, and redaction in production
subtopics.learn: `error.tsx` must be a Client Component receiving `{ error: Error & { digest?: string }, reset: () => void }`; in production Next redacts server error messages and ships only a `digest`, which you must log server-side to correlate. `global-error.tsx` replaces the root layout and must render `<html>` and `<body>` itself. Call `notFound()` for a missing run so the segment's `not-found.tsx` renders with a 404. Errors thrown after streaming has started become inline error boundaries, not HTTP 500s, so monitor them via `instrumentation.ts` `onRequestError(err, request, context)` rather than status codes. Put a 'copy digest' button in your error UI so a customer screenshot is enough to find the log line.

resource.label: Next.js docs - Error Handling

subtopics.name: OpenTelemetry from Next.js into your FastAPI traces
subtopics.learn: Add `instrumentation.ts` with `export function register()` that calls `registerOTel({ serviceName: 'defendermate-ui' })` from `@vercel/otel` (or a manual `NodeSDK` guarded by `process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME === 'nodejs'`), export to the same collector as topic 21, and read Next's built-in spans: `BaseServer.handleRequest`, `AppRender.getBodyResult`, `AppRouteRouteHandlers.runHandler`, `AppRender.fetch`. Confirm `traceparent` is propagated on the server-side `fetch` to FastAPI so one trace spans page render, BFF hop and Claude call; set `NEXT_OTEL_VERBOSE=1` when you need per-component spans. Implement `onRequestError` to record the digest, route, and `renderSource` on the active span so a digest-to-trace lookup is one query.

resource.label: Next.js docs - OpenTelemetry guide

subtopics.name: Internal-tool UI kit: Tailwind v4, shadcn/ui, TanStack Table, accessibility
subtopics.learn: Do not design a component library on a customer's clock: `npx shadcn@latest init` then `add button input table dialog form` copies accessible components (over Radix or Base UI primitives) into `components/ui` that you own and can edit. Tailwind v4 is CSS-first (`@import "tailwindcss"` and `@theme {}` tokens, no `tailwind.config.js` by default); use the `cn()` helper for conditional classes. Build the runs table with TanStack Table `useReactTable({ data, columns, getCoreRowModel, manualPagination: true, pageCount })` driven by `searchParams` (`?page=2&sort=created_at.desc`) so every view is a shareable URL and pagination happens in FastAPI, not the browser. Keep native `<label htmlFor>`, focus rings and `aria-live="polite"` on the streaming pane; load heavy widgets (charts, code editors) with `next/dynamic` and check `@next/bundle-analyzer` before the demo.

resource.label: shadcn/ui docs

subtopics.name: TanStack Query where it earns its place: polling, mutations, hydration
subtopics.learn: Use TanStack Query v5 only for client-owned data: polling a running agent with `useQuery({ queryKey: ['run', id], queryFn, refetchInterval: (q) => q.state.data?.status === 'running' ? 1000 : false })`, `useMutation` with `onSuccess: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['runs'] })`, and `staleTime` tuned so navigation does not refetch. Prefetch on the server with `queryClient.prefetchQuery` and hand it to the client via `<HydrationBoundary state={dehydrate(queryClient)}>` so there is no double fetch after hydration. Create the `QueryClient` per request on the server (an `isServer` check in a `getQueryClient()` helper) and once per browser on the client via `useState(() => new QueryClient())`; a module-level client on the server leaks one user's cache to the next request.

resource.label: TanStack Query docs - Advanced Server Rendering (App Router)

subtopics.name: Hydration mismatches: dates, locales, window checks, extensions
subtopics.learn:
Know the causes cold: `new Date().toLocaleString()` rendered on a UTC server and a local-time client, `Math.random()` or `crypto.randomUUID()` in render, `typeof window !== 'undefined'` branches that change output, invalid HTML nesting (`
` inside `

`), and browser extensions that mutate the DOM before hydration. Fixes: render timestamps with a fixed timezone or format them in a Client Component after mount, use `useId()` for IDs, `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot)` for client-only values like `matchMedia`, and `suppressHydrationWarning` only on the single text node that legitimately differs. Understand that a mismatch makes React 19 throw away the server HTML and re-render on the client, so the page 'works' but pays full client-render cost and floods the console the customer's security team is watching.

resource.label: react.dev - hydrateRoot (hydration errors)

subtopics.name: Shipping to a customer VPC: runtime env, standalone Docker, Nginx, skew
subtopics.learn: Understand that `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` is inlined at `next build`, so one image cannot carry different API URLs per environment; read environment-specific values on the server only (in the DAL or a Route Handler) and pass what the browser needs as props. Build with `output: 'standalone'`: a multi-stage Dockerfile that copies `.next/standalone`, `.next/static` and `public`, runs `node server.js` as a non-root user with `HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0` and `PORT`, and installs `sharp` for image optimisation. In front of Nginx, send `X-Accel-Buffering: no` (via `headers()` in `next.config.ts` or on the streaming response) and know that `next start`'s built-in `compress` can buffer SSE, so set `compress: false` and compress at the proxy. Set `deploymentId` so clients holding old HTML during a rolling deploy do not hit `ChunkLoadError`, and configure a shared `cacheHandler` (Redis, topic 31) when you run more than one replica with cached segments.

resource.label: Next.js docs - Self-Hosting guide

subtopics.name: Testing the UI: Playwright e2e with storageState, Vitest for client components, build as a gate
subtopics.learn: Write Playwright tests that log in once in a setup project and reuse `storageState`, then assert the real behaviours: the runs table renders rows from a seeded FastAPI, the stream pane accumulates text (`await expect(page.getByTestId('answer')).toContainText('...', { timeout: 30_000 })`), Stop cancels the request, and the form shows field errors with `javaScriptEnabled: false`. Use Vitest plus Testing Library for pure Client Components only; Next documents that async Server Components are not supported by Vitest, so cover them end to end. Make `tsc --noEmit`, `next typegen` and `next build` the CI gate and read the build route table (static vs dynamic markers) as a review artifact; run the Playwright suite against the built container, not `next dev`.

resource.label: Next.js docs - Testing with Playwright

outcomes: You can scaffold a Next 16 App Router app and, in under two hours, ship a typed list/detail UI over an existing FastAPI service with server-side fetching, a `loading.tsx` skeleton and an `error.tsx` boundary, with `next build` passing type-check and showing each route's static/dynamic marker.

You can draw the server/client boundary for a given screen on a whiteboard, naming which components are Server Components, which are `'use client'`, exactly what crosses the boundary as props, and where the secret-bearing fetch runs, and justify each choice in one sentence.

You can stream Claude output from DefenderMate through a Route Handler to a Client Component with a working Stop button, show in FastAPI logs that the upstream generation stops within one second of abort, and demonstrate it working behind a default-config Nginx after adding the documented headers.

You can implement login as a Server Function that sets an httpOnly, secure, SameSite=Lax session cookie, gate every data fetch through a `server-only` Data Access Layer that verifies the JWT with `jose` against FastAPI's JWKS, and show that a missing cookie redirects and a tampered cookie yields a clean redirect, never a stack trace or a digest.

You can validate a form with Zod 4 on the server via `useActionState`, render field-level errors with JavaScript disabled, and show `useOptimistic` updating the list before the server responds and rolling back on failure.

You can explain the Cache Components model and demonstrate `'use cache'` plus `cacheTag` plus `updateTag` fixing a stale dashboard after a mutation, and reproduce the build error you get when request-time data is read outside a Suspense boundary.

You can build one standalone Docker image that runs unchanged in staging and prod with no `NEXT_PUBLIC_` environment leakage, runs as non-root, and passes a Playwright smoke test executed against the container in CI.
You can take an `error.digest` from a customer screenshot, find the matching `onRequestError` log line, and follow the propagated `traceparent` into the FastAPI span in the trace backend.
failureModes: The customer's Nginx (and `next start`'s own gzip layer) buffered the SSE stream so the whole answer appeared after eight seconds; the demo looked broken until `X-Accel-Buffering: no` was sent and `compress: false` moved compression to the proxy.

`NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` was baked into the image at build time pointing at staging; the production demo silently showed staging data, and the 'fix' of rebuilding per environment destroyed the one-image-everywhere reproducibility the customer's platform team required.

An admin 'delete tenant' Server Function had no authorisation inside the function because 'only admins see the button'; anyone who copied the action ID from the Network tab could POST it, and it was found in the customer's pentest.

A dashboard showed yesterday's numbers because the fetch sat inside `'use cache'` with `cacheLife('days')` and the mutation only called `revalidatePath`, which never touched the tag; the customer concluded the ingestion pipeline was down.

`new Date().toLocaleString()` rendered in server UTC and client local time caused a hydration mismatch on every page; React discarded the SSR tree and re-rendered client-side, adding a visible flash and a wall of console errors that the customer's security reviewer logged as a finding.

A rolling deploy without `deploymentId` left open tabs requesting chunk hashes that no longer existed, so every user in the customer's morning stand-up hit `ChunkLoadError` at once and the FDE was paged from the meeting.

A module-level `new QueryClient()` imported by a Server Component was shared across requests on one pod, so user A briefly saw user B's cached run list; it passed every test because the e2e suite ran a single user.
interviewQuestions: Draw the request lifecycle for an authenticated dashboard page in the App Router: browser, proxy.ts, layout, page, Data Access Layer, FastAPI, RSC payload. Where does the JWT live at each hop, and where exactly do you enforce that a user only sees their own tenant's runs, and why not in the layout?

A customer says streaming works on the engineer's laptop but in their Kubernetes cluster the answer appears all at once after eight seconds. Walk me through localising the buffering hop across the Client Component, the Route Handler, `next start`, the ingress and the FastAPI pod, and the specific change at each.

For a run-monitoring screen, when do you fetch in a Server Component versus a Route Handler versus TanStack Query in a Client Component versus a Server Function? Defend the split and explain how you avoid a double fetch after hydration.

Explain what `'use client'` actually does to a module graph. A colleague added it to the root layout to fix a `useState` error and the bundle tripled. What happened, and how do you restructure with the composition pattern?

Design forms for an internal tool at a customer whose corporate proxy sometimes strips JavaScript and enforces a strict CSP: progressive enhancement, validation, error display, optimistic updates, and the CSRF story for Server Functions behind a reverse proxy where `Origin` and `Host` differ.

We ship one Docker image to five customer environments with different API URLs and SSO issuers. How do you configure a Next.js app at runtime without rebuilding, what breaks if you rely on `NEXT_PUBLIC_`, and how do you keep Server Functions working across replicas and deploys?

After a deploy, 5 percent of users see 'Application error: a server-side exception has occurred' with a digest. Walk me from that digest to root cause, and tell me what you would add so the next incident is self-explanatory from a single customer screenshot.
41.proofOfWork: A recorded ten-minute 'customer demo' plus a public repo that a platform team could clone and run. The repo contains the Next 16 app over DefenderMate built as a standalone, non-root Docker image behind an Nginx container with default settings; a one-page architecture diagram in the README marking the server/client boundary, the session-cookie auth flow through the Data Access Layer, and the streaming path from Claude to the browser; a `docs/streaming-drill.md` with before/after HAR captures showing the buffered stream and the fix (headers and `compress: false`); a `docs/runtime-config.md` proving the same image digest runs against two different FastAPI base URLs and issuers without rebuilding; a Playwright suite (login via `storageState`, table pagination via URL, stream with Stop asserting the FastAPI log line for the aborted generation, form validation with `javaScriptEnabled: false`) running in GitHub Actions against the built container; and a `docs/digest-to-trace.md` walkthrough with screenshots going from an `error.digest` in the UI to the `onRequestError` log entry to the trace in the collector that includes the FastAPI span, so a customer support engineer could repeat the lookup unaided.

42.topic: PySpark (optional: Databricks- or Palantir-style roles only)
42.why: At Databricks and Palantir the FDE works inside the customer's lakehouse: their logs, transactions and eval sets already sit in Delta tables or Foundry datasets at hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes, and the fastest path to a demo on real data is a PySpark transform that runs where their pipelines run, under their cluster's memory limits and their security team's eyes. The differentiator in those loops is not API trivia but being able to look at a stage that has run for forty minutes and say 'one tenant is 40 percent of the rows, that task is the skew, here is the salt' instead of 'Spark is slow', which requires the driver/executor model and the physical plan to be in your head. This topic is optional: if your target list is API-company FDE roles only, topic 36 (DuckDB and dbt) covers the analytics you need and this six hours is better spent on topic 43.
prerequisites: SQL at the level of topic 29 (PostgreSQL): GROUP BY semantics, window functions with frames, join types, null behaviour in aggregates and joins; you will rewrite an existing SQL aggregation and validate the PySpark output against it row for row

Topic 36 (dbt, DuckDB, dimensional modelling): what Parquet is, why data is partitioned by date, and how to export DefenderMate's `llm_calls`, `messages` and `tenants` tables from Postgres to partitioned Parquet with DuckDB `COPY ... TO ... (FORMAT PARQUET, PARTITION_BY (dt))`
Python packaging from topic 25 (`pyproject.toml`, wheels, virtualenvs), because getting your code onto every executor is a packaging problem, not a Spark problem

A laptop with Java 17 installed and `JAVA_HOME` set (`java -version` prints 17 or 21), 8 GB or more of free RAM, and Docker from topic 5 in case you want an isolated `spark` image; `pip install pyspark` does not install a JVM
Enough JVM vocabulary to read an executor log: heap, off-heap, garbage collection pause, `OutOfMemoryError`, what exit code 137 means in a container (topic 5, topic 8)
S3 semantics from topic 14: object listing cost, eventual visibility of partial writes, and the absence of atomic directory rename, which drives the output-commit section of this topic

subtopics.name: When Spark is the right tool, and the driver, executor and cluster-manager model
subtopics.learn: Spark is a driver process (your Python script plus a JVM it controls through Py4J) that turns DataFrame code into a DAG, and a set of executor JVMs that each run `spark.executor.cores` tasks at a time, one task per partition, with a cluster manager (standalone, YARN, Kubernetes, or the one Databricks and Foundry hide from you) handing out the containers. In `local[*]` the driver and a single executor share one JVM with one thread per core, which is why a job that works on your laptop fails the first time data must cross a network or exceed one container's memory. Deploy mode `client` runs the driver where you typed `spark-submit` (a notebook kernel, a laptop, a CI runner that gets killed at the 60 minute mark); `cluster` runs it on the cluster, and standalone mode does not support cluster mode for Python applications at all. Before any of this, apply the test from topic 36: if the customer's dataset fits in RAM plus local SSD on one large box (tens to a few hundred gigabytes), DuckDB or Polars will finish before a Spark cluster has started; Spark is justified when data is larger than one node or when the customer already lives in Databricks, EMR or Foundry and your job must run where theirs do.

resource.label: Spark docs: Cluster Mode Overview

subtopics.name: Local install, SparkSession.builder and the spark-submit flags that matter
subtopics.learn: `pip install pyspark` ships the Spark jars but not a JVM; Spark 4.x needs Java 17 or 21 (3.5 accepts 8, 11 or 17), and a missing `JAVA_HOME` surfaces as a Py4J gateway error rather than a clear message. Build one session: `SparkSession.builder.master("local[4]").appName("usage").config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "8").config("spark.driver.memory", "4g").getOrCreate()`, knowing `spark.driver.memory` cannot change after the JVM is up, so in a notebook it is silently ignored unless the kernel was started with it. Learn the submit line you will type on a customer's edge node: `spark-submit --master yarn --deploy-mode cluster --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=400 --py-files src.zip --packages io.delta:delta-spark_2.13:4.0.0 --archives venv.tar.gz#env job.py --input s3://... --output s3://... --run-date 2026-09-01`. `--packages` resolves Maven coordinates on the driver and ships the jars (the Delta coordinate must match the Spark and Scala versions exactly), `--py-files` adds `.py`, `.zip` and `.egg` to every executor's `sys.path`, `--files` distributes side files, and `PYSPARK_PYTHON` / `spark.pyspark.python` pins the executor interpreter so you never see `Python in worker has different version than that in driver`. The Web UI is on port 4040 (4041 if taken) for the life of the driver only.

resource.label: Spark docs: Submitting Applications (spark-submit)

subtopics.name: Lazy evaluation: transformations, actions, jobs, stages, tasks and the shuffle boundary
subtopics.learn: Transformations (`select`, `filter`, `withColumn`, `groupBy().agg`, `join`) only extend a logical plan; nothing executes until an action (`count`, `collect`, `show`, `take`, `first`, `write`, `foreach`) submits a job, so a bug in a `filter` raises at the `show()` ten lines later, and a DataFrame consumed by two actions is recomputed twice unless persisted. Each job is cut into stages at wide dependencies, meaning anything that regroups rows by key (`groupBy`, `join`, `distinct`, `repartition`, `orderBy`, a window with `partitionBy`); the rows between stages are written to local disk as shuffle files and fetched over the network by the next stage; a stage is a set of tasks with exactly one task per partition, and a task is the unit that runs on one executor core. Narrow transformations (`select`, `filter`, `union`, `coalesce`) stay inside a stage and are pipelined row by row.
