Inspect partition counts with `df.rdd.getNumPartitions()`: input partitions come from splitting files at `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (128 MB), post-shuffle partitions from `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (200). The drill: read a job, write down how many jobs and stages it will produce and where each shuffle is, then run it and check the Jobs tab; if the prediction is wrong you do not yet understand the cost of the code.

resource.label: Spark docs: RDD Programming Guide (transformations, actions, shuffle operations)

subtopics.name: Reading CSV, JSON and Parquet: explicit schemas, malformed-record policy, partition discovery
subtopics.learn: `spark.read.option("header", True).option("inferSchema", True).csv(path)` performs a full extra pass over the data to guess types and will guess differently tomorrow when one row changes; on any real export pass a schema (a `StructType` or the DDL string `"tenant_id STRING, ts TIMESTAMP, input_tokens BIGINT"`) and choose `mode`: `PERMISSIVE` (default; bad rows become nulls plus a `_corrupt_record` column you must explicitly select to keep, named by `spark.sql.columnNameOfCorruptRecord`), `DROPMALFORMED`, or `FAILFAST` for anything feeding billing. Know that `enforceSchema` defaults to true, so header names are ignored and columns are matched by position, and learn `multiLine`, `escape`, `nullValue`, `timestampFormat` and `dateFormat` (patterns follow Spark's datetime pattern reference, not Java's `SimpleDateFormat`). JSON is line-delimited unless `multiLine=true`; nested fields are addressed as `F.col("usage.output_tokens")`, arrays flattened with `F.explode`, and JSON strings parsed with `F.from_json(col, schema)`. Parquet carries its own schema, is columnar (only selected columns are read), pushes predicates down to row-group statistics, and turns `key=value` directories into partition columns; set `basePath` when reading a subset of partitions so the partition columns survive, and only set `mergeSchema=true` when files genuinely differ because it costs one footer read per file.

resource.label: Spark docs: CSV Files data source options

subtopics.name: Types, nulls and ANSI mode: the silent-null era versus Spark 4
subtopics.learn: With `spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false` (the Spark 3.x default) an invalid cast, an integer overflow, an out-of-range array index and division by zero all return null, so `CAST(tokens AS INT)` on a bad row quietly shrinks a billing total without any error; Spark 4.0 flips the default to true and those become `CAST_INVALID_INPUT`, `ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW` and `DIVIDE_BY_ZERO` exceptions, which is the first thing that breaks when a customer upgrades their runtime. Reach for `try_cast`, `F.try_divide`, `F.try_add` and `F.try_to_timestamp` where null-on-failure is the intended behaviour, and know the type ladder: `IntegerType` is 32-bit and overflows at 2.1 billion tokens per tenant per period, `DecimalType(18, 6)` for money, `TimestampType` is an instant rendered in the session zone while `TimestampNTZType` (3.4+) is wall-clock time, and `spark.sql.session.timeZone` decides how `F.date_trunc("day", ts)` buckets rows, so set it to `UTC` in code or daily totals differ between your laptop and the cluster. Nulls are skipped by `sum`, `avg` and `count(col)` but counted by `count("*")`, never equal in joins (every null key drops out, or with `eqNullSafe` hashes to one partition), and `F.when(...)` without `.otherwise(...)` yields null.

resource.label: Spark SQL reference: ANSI Compliance

subtopics.name: Rewriting the SQL aggregation in the DataFrame API: groupBy, agg, pivot, exact versus approximate distincts
subtopics.learn: Take DefenderMate's usage query (per tenant per day: calls, input and output tokens, cost, distinct users, p95 latency) and write it twice: as `spark.sql()` over `df.createOrReplaceTempView("llm_calls")`, and as `df.groupBy("tenant_id", F.date_trunc("day", "ts").alias("day")).agg(F.count("*").alias("calls"), F.sum("input_tokens").alias("input_tokens"), F.sum(F.col("output_tokens") * F.col("price_per_token")).alias("cost"), F.countDistinct("user_id").alias("users"), F.percentile_approx("latency_ms", 0.95, 10000).alias("p95_ms"))`, then prove with `explain()` that both compile to the same physical plan, because they do. Know the traps: `F.countDistinct` over several columns forces an `Expand` operator that multiplies the row count, so use `F.approx_count_distinct(col, rsd=0.01)` (HyperLogLog++) for dashboards and exact counts only where money depends on them; `F.collect_list` and `F.first` have no defined order without a window; `pivot("model", values=[...])` with explicit values avoids an extra distinct job; `rollup` and `cube` emit grouping-set rows with nulls you must label using `F.grouping_id`. Conditions use `&`, `|` and `~` with parentheses, never Python `and`/`or`; `F.expr("...")` is fine when a SQL fragment is clearer. Alias every aggregate so the output schema is stable for tests and downstream readers.

resource.label: PySpark API reference: pyspark.sql.functions

subtopics.name: Window functions: dedup-to-latest, lag-based sessionisation, frame semantics, the single-partition trap
subtopics.learn: `w = Window.partitionBy("tenant_id", "conversation_id").orderBy(F.col("ts").desc())` then `F.row_number().over(w)` and `.filter("rn = 1")` is the canonical dedup-to-latest; `F.lag("ts", 1).over(w)` compared against a gap threshold, followed by a cumulative `F.sum("is_new_session").over(w.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow))`, gives session ids with no UDF. Learn the frame rules that differ from intuition: with `orderBy` and no explicit frame the default is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, so tied rows share a running total; `rangeBetween` requires a single numeric or date ordering column while `rowsBetween` counts rows; without `orderBy` the frame is the whole partition, which is exactly what `F.max("ts").over(Window.partitionBy("tenant_id"))` wants. A window with no `partitionBy` logs `WARN WindowExec: No Partition Defined for Window operation!` and moves every row to a single task, the number one cause of a stage that never finishes on a customer cluster. Every window costs a shuffle plus a sort, but consecutive windows over identical partition and order keys share one Exchange, so define `w` once and reuse it. Run the same dedup and sessionisation as Postgres window queries (topic 29) on the same export and diff the results.

resource.label: PySpark API reference: pyspark.sql.Window

subtopics.name: Joins: broadcast versus sort-merge, shuffle partitions, AQE, and salting a skewed key
subtopics.learn: For an equi-join Spark chooses BroadcastHashJoin when one side's estimated size is under `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (10 MB; `-1` disables) and otherwise SortMergeJoin, which shuffles both sides on the key into `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (200) partitions and sorts each; a non-equi join falls to BroadcastNestedLoopJoin or a Cartesian product that will not finish. Force a small dimension with `F.broadcast(tenants)` or `df.hint("broadcast")` (`MERGE` and `SHUFFLE_HASH` hints also exist), remembering the broadcast side is collected to the driver first, so a 2 GB 'small' table kills the driver, and `spark.sql.broadcastTimeout` (300 s) fires when the build side is slow. Adaptive Query Execution (`spark.sql.adaptive.enabled`, on by default since 3.2) uses real shuffle statistics to coalesce the 200 partitions towards `spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes` (64 MB), to swap a planned SMJ for a broadcast when a side turns out small, and to split skewed join partitions when `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled` sees one larger than `skewedPartitionFactor` (5) times the median and above `skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` (256 MB). AQE does nothing for skew in a `groupBy`: for a tenant holding 40 percent of rows, salt with `F.concat(F.col("tenant_id"), F.lit("_"), (F.rand() * 16).cast("int"))`, aggregate, strip the salt, aggregate again. Join with `on=["tenant_id"]` (string form) so the key appears once and downstream selects avoid `AMBIGUOUS_REFERENCE`, and filter nulls out of join keys because every null hashes to the same partition.

resource.label: Spark SQL guide: Performance Tuning (joins, AQE, broadcast hints)

subtopics.name: Reading the physical plan: Exchange, partial/final HashAggregate, FileScan pushdown, codegen breaks
subtopics.learn: Run `df.explain(mode="formatted")` and read bottom-up. `FileScan parquet [tenant_id#3, tokens#7] Batched: true, PartitionFilters: [(dt#9 = 2026-09-01)], PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(tenant_id)], ReadSchema: struct<...>` tells you column pruning worked, which partitions were skipped, and which predicates reached the Parquet reader; a UDF or a cast wrapped around the column in a filter removes it from `PushedFilters`. `HashAggregate(keys=[tenant_id#3], functions=[partial_sum(tokens#7)])` followed by `Exchange hashpartitioning(tenant_id#3, 200)` and a second `HashAggregate(... functions=[sum(tokens#7)])` is the map-side partial aggregation that makes `groupBy` cheap; `ObjectHashAggregate` shows up for `collect_list`, and `SortAggregate` is the slow fallback. Every `Exchange` is a shuffle and a stage boundary: `hashpartitioning` from groupBy or join, `rangepartitioning` from `orderBy`, `SinglePartition` from a window without `partitionBy` or a `coalesce(1)`, `BroadcastExchange` from a broadcast join. A `*(2)` prefix means WholeStageCodegen stage 2 fused those operators into one generated Java loop; `BatchEvalPython` or `ArrowEvalPython` in the tree marks exactly where a Python UDF broke that fusion. `AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false` means the printed plan is the pre-execution guess; the SQL tab in the UI renders the final plan with real row counts per operator.

resource.label: PySpark API reference: DataFrame.explain (modes simple, extended, codegen, cost, formatted)

subtopics.name: Spark UI and history server: diagnosing skew, spill, small tasks and GC from stage metrics
subtopics.learn: Open `http://localhost:4040` while the job runs, or set `spark.eventLog.enabled=true` and `spark.eventLog.dir` and read it afterwards through the history server on port 18080, which is what you will actually have on a customer cluster. Jobs tab: one job per action; click through to stages. Stages tab: 'Summary Metrics for N Completed Tasks' gives min, 25th percentile, median, 75th and max for Duration, GC Time, Input Size, Shuffle Read, Shuffle Write and Spill (Memory and Disk). Read them like vitals: a max duration many times the median with one giant Shuffle Read is key skew; any non-zero Spill means execution memory ran out and sorts or aggregations went to `spark.local.dir`, so add partitions or memory; thousands of tasks lasting tens of milliseconds means partitions too small (raise `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` or coalesce); GC Time above roughly 10 percent of duration means the heap is thrashing. The Executors tab shows per-executor task time and failures but not Python worker memory, which is why container kills look mysterious (next subtopic). The SQL/DataFrame tab renders the final adaptive plan with rows output and spill per operator. For monitoring, `spark.ui.prometheus.enabled=true` exposes executor metrics at `/metrics/executors/prometheus`, and the REST API at `/api/v1/applications/<id>/stages` lets a CI step fail a build whose stages spilled.

resource.label: Spark docs: Web UI (Jobs, Stages, Storage, Executors, SQL tabs)

subtopics.name: Executor and driver memory: unified memory, overhead, Python worker memory, exit 137 versus Java OOM
subtopics.learn: An executor container is `spark.executor.memory` (JVM heap) plus `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` (max(384 MB, `spark.executor.memoryOverheadFactor` 0.10, or 0.40 for non-JVM jobs on Kubernetes) covering JVM native memory, shuffle buffers and, unless `spark.executor.pyspark.memory` is set, every Python UDF worker) plus `spark.memory.offHeap.size` when enabled. Inside the heap 300 MB is reserved and `spark.memory.fraction` (0.6) of the rest is unified memory shared between execution (shuffles, sorts, joins, aggregations) and storage (cached blocks), with `spark.memory.storageFraction` (0.5) as the soft floor storage can be evicted down to; the remaining 40 percent is user memory for your own objects and metadata. Learn the three deaths by their signatures: `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` in executor stderr is the heap; `Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits` or a Kubernetes pod exiting 137 with no Java stack trace is the container total, which in PySpark almost always means Python workers, so raise overhead to 20 to 30 percent or bound them with `spark.executor.pyspark.memory`; a driver death traces to `collect()`, `toPandas()`, a broadcast build side or `collect_list` landing on the driver, guarded by `spark.driver.maxResultSize` (1 GB, error text 'Total size of serialized results ... is bigger than spark.driver.maxResultSize'). Start from 4 to 5 cores per executor, partitions of 100 to 200 MB, heap sized for the largest partition times cores, and only then tune.

resource.label: Spark docs: Tuning Spark (memory management, data structures, GC)

subtopics.name: Python UDFs, pandas UDFs and Arrow: what gets serialised and what Catalyst can no longer see
subtopics.learn: A plain `@F.udf(returnType=...)` runs row by row in a forked `pyspark.daemon` worker on each executor with rows pickled across a socket in batches, and Catalyst treats it as a black box: no predicate pushdown through it, no whole-stage codegen, no null short-circuit, and its cost appears as `BatchEvalPython` in the plan. A `pandas_udf` with type hints (`def f(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series`) moves Arrow record batches of `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch` (10,000) rows instead and is routinely 10 to 100 times faster; `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled=true` also makes `toPandas()` and `createDataFrame(pdf)` use Arrow. `mapInPandas(func, schema)` hands you an iterator of pandas frames per partition (model scoring), and `groupBy().applyInPandas(func, schema)` hands you one frame per group, which means one skewed tenant's entire group must fit in a single Python worker's memory. Spark 3.5 adds Arrow-optimised regular UDFs (`@udf(useArrow=True)`) and Python UDTFs. The rule before writing any UDF: check `pyspark.sql.functions` and the higher-order array functions (`F.transform`, `F.filter`, `F.aggregate`, `F.exists`) first, because most UDFs in customer code are `to_timestamp`, `regexp_extract`, `from_json` or `split` written by hand. Python exceptions inside a UDF surface as `PythonException` with the Python traceback in the driver output (`spark.sql.execution.pyspark.udf.simplifiedTraceback.enabled`); `print` inside a UDF goes to executor stderr, not to your notebook.

resource.label: PySpark tutorial: Apache Arrow in PySpark (pandas UDFs, mapInPandas, applyInPandas)

subtopics.name: Writing output: partitionBy, file sizing, overwrite semantics, and atomic commits on S3
subtopics.learn: `df.repartition("tenant_id", "dt").write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("tenant_id", "dt").option("compression", "zstd").parquet(out)` yields one file per output directory because the rows for each partition value are colocated in one task; without the `repartition`, every task writes a file into every directory it touches, and 200 tasks times 500 tenants times 30 days is three million small files that make listing slower than reading. `coalesce(n)` merges partitions without a shuffle but also lowers the parallelism of the entire upstream stage, `repartition(n)` shuffles round-robin, `option("maxRecordsPerFile", n)` caps file size; aim for files of 128 MB to 1 GB. Save modes are `append`, `overwrite`, `ignore` and `errorifexists` (default), and `overwrite` with `partitionBy` deletes the whole output path first under the default `spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode=static`; set `dynamic` so re-running one `dt` replaces only that partition, which is what makes the job idempotent per run date. On S3 there is no atomic rename, so the Hadoop `FileOutputCommitter` v1 renames every file twice and is slow, v2 (`mapreduce.fileoutputcommitter.algorithm.version=2`) leaves partial output visible on failure, and the correct answer is the S3A committers (`spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.committer.name=magic` with `spark.sql.sources.commitProtocolClass=org.apache.spark.internal.io.cloud.PathOutputCommitProtocol` and `spark.sql.parquet.output.committer.class=org.apache.spark.internal.io.cloud.BindingParquetOutputCommitter`) or a table format such as Delta. Readers gate on the `_SUCCESS` marker or a table commit, never on the presence of files.

resource.label: Spark docs: Integration with Cloud Infrastructures (S3 committers, consistency, rename)

subtopics.name: Delta Lake: transaction log, MERGE for late data, time travel, OPTIMIZE and VACUUM, schema enforcement
subtopics.learn: Delta is Parquet plus a `_delta_log/` of JSON commits (with a Parquet checkpoint every 10) giving ACID table-level commits under optimistic concurrency, so a failed job leaves no partial files visible and two writers to the same partition get a `ConcurrentAppendException` instead of corrupt data. Enable it with `pip install delta-spark` and `configure_spark_with_delta_pip(builder)`, which sets `spark.sql.extensions=io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension` and `spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog=org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog`. Late-arriving DefenderMate events are absorbed with `DeltaTable.forPath(spark, out).alias("t").merge(updates.alias("s"), "t.tenant_id = s.tenant_id AND t.day = s.day").whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute()`; dedupe the source first or MERGE fails with 'multiple source rows matched', and put partition predicates in the ON clause so it prunes files. `spark.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", 12).load(out)` and `DESCRIBE HISTORY` let you show a customer exactly what the billing table said last Tuesday. `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (tenant_id)` compacts the small files that MERGE and streaming create; `VACUUM ... RETAIN 168 HOURS` deletes unreferenced files and also destroys time travel past that horizon, which is why `spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled` refuses shorter windows by default. Schema enforcement rejects a write whose columns differ with an `AnalysisException`; evolve deliberately with `.option("mergeSchema", "true")`, and use `.option("replaceWhere", "day = '2026-09-01'")` for a partition-scoped overwrite. Databricks layers Photon, liquid clustering and deletion vectors on top; the log format is the same one you run locally.

resource.label: Delta Lake docs: Table deletes, updates, and merges (MERGE INTO)

subtopics.name: cache, persist and checkpoint: when materialisation helps and when it removes pushdown
subtopics.learn: `df.cache()` is `persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)` for DataFrames (RDDs default to `MEMORY_ONLY`), is lazy until the next action, and only pays off when the same DataFrame feeds two or more actions, such as a `count()` for a data-quality gate followed by a `write`, or an iterative algorithm; a frame cached and used once just costs memory plus the conversion to columnar blocks. Cache after your filters, not before: reads from a cached relation come from `InMemoryTableScan`, so predicates no longer reach the Parquet scan and partition pruning is gone for every downstream query. Watch the Storage tab for 'Fraction Cached' below 100 percent, meaning blocks were evicted because execution memory reclaimed the space and recomputation is happening anyway; call `unpersist()` when finished or `spark.catalog.clearCache()`. `checkpoint()` (after `sc.setCheckpointDir`) writes the data to reliable storage and truncates lineage, which is the fix when a plan is so deep that Catalyst analysis itself takes minutes or a `StackOverflowError` appears on the driver, typically in loops that keep re-assigning `df = df.join(...)`; `localCheckpoint()` does the same to executor disk without durability. Never `cache()` to make a one-shot job faster; fix the plan.

resource.label: PySpark API reference: DataFrame.persist and StorageLevel

subtopics.name: Testing and packaging a job that runs identically on a laptop and on the customer's cluster
subtopics.learn: Structure the job as pure functions, `def daily_usage(llm_calls: DataFrame, tenants: DataFrame) -> DataFrame`, with a thin `main()` that parses `--input`, `--output` and `--run-date` and builds the session, so tests call the functions on `spark.createDataFrame([...], schema)` using a session fixture built with `master("local[2]")`, `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=2` and `spark.ui.enabled=false` (session-scoped, since JVM startup costs seconds). Assert with `pyspark.testing.assertDataFrameEqual(actual, expected, checkRowOrder=False)` and `assertSchemaEqual`, and include one test that runs the reference Postgres SQL against exported fixtures and compares row for row; that is the test that catches time zone and null-handling drift. Packaging is where laptop-green jobs die on clusters: any module imported inside a UDF or transform must exist on every executor, so ship it with `--py-files src.zip` (pure Python) or build the environment with `venv-pack -o venv.tar.gz` and submit `--archives venv.tar.gz#env --conf spark.pyspark.python=./env/bin/python` (or `conda-pack`, or a Docker image on Kubernetes); `ModuleNotFoundError` thrown from inside `BatchEvalPython` is this bug every single time. Pin `pyspark` to the cluster's exact minor version in `pyproject.toml`, set `spark.sql.session.timeZone=UTC` in code rather than trusting the cluster, and log from the driver's Python logger only, because executor stderr is not yours to read on a customer's platform.

resource.label: PySpark tutorial: Python Package Management (py-files, archives, venv-pack, conda-pack)

subtopics.name: Where PySpark lives in Databricks and Foundry, and what Spark Connect changes
subtopics.learn: On Databricks `spark` is pre-created in every notebook, production work runs as Jobs on job clusters (ephemeral, cheaper) rather than all-purpose clusters, tables live in Unity Catalog as `catalog.schema.table` and are Delta by default, Photon swaps the execution engine underneath without code changes, and Databricks Connect runs your local IDE's PySpark against a remote cluster because it is built on Spark Connect. In Palantir Foundry the unit is a dataset (a versioned, branchable Parquet or Delta directory) and the code is a transform: `@transform_df(Output("/Org/usage/daily"), calls=Input("/Org/raw/llm_calls"))` returning a DataFrame, built by Foundry's scheduler with lineage recorded, while `@incremental()` transforms read only `.dataframe("added")` rows since the previous build, which is how a Palantir FDE ships a daily pipeline in an afternoon. Spark Connect (3.4+, `SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://host:15002")`, the `pyspark-client` package in 4.0) replaces the in-process Py4J driver with a thin gRPC client: the DataFrame API is unchanged, but `sparkContext`, RDDs and `df.rdd.getNumPartitions()` are gone, and a client crash no longer kills the driver. Know these three well enough that a customer conversation about 'our pipelines' goes straight to their transform code.

resource.label: Palantir Foundry docs: Python transforms overview

outcomes: You can rewrite DefenderMate's per-tenant, per-day usage aggregation (calls, tokens, cost, distinct users, p95 latency) as a PySpark job, run it with `spark-submit --master local[4]` over Parquet exports, and show with `assertDataFrameEqual` that it matches the Postgres query row for row, including on days with nulls and time zone edges.

You can draw the driver, executor and cluster-manager diagram from memory, place the Python process, the JVM, Py4J and the Python UDF workers on it, and state which process dies and with what error for `collect()`, an oversized broadcast, an `applyInPandas` group, and a large shuffle.

You can read `explain(mode="formatted")` for an unfamiliar job and identify every Exchange and its cause, the join strategy chosen, whether filters reached the Parquet scan, and where a Python UDF broke codegen, and predict the number of stages before running it.

You can open the Spark UI on a slow stage and within five minutes distinguish key skew, spill, too many small tasks and GC pressure from the stage summary metrics, naming the code or config change for each.

You can choose between broadcast and sort-merge joins from table sizes, set `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` and AQE deliberately, salt a skewed `groupBy` key, and demonstrate the stage time before and after on a synthetically skewed tenant.

You can write partitioned Parquet or Delta output that is idempotent per run date (dynamic partition overwrite or MERGE), produces files between 128 MB and 1 GB rather than thousands of small ones, and commits atomically on S3 with a committer you can name.

You can package the job so it runs unchanged on a laptop and on a customer's YARN or Kubernetes cluster (pure-function transforms, pytest with a local session, `--archives` venv, pinned pyspark), and explain each `spark-submit` flag you used.

You can tell a customer in one minute whether Spark is the right tool for their 50 GB or 5 TB, and if they are on Databricks or Foundry, describe where your transform would live and how it would be scheduled.
failureModes: `inferSchema=true` on a nightly CSV export doubles the read and infers `tenant_id` as long on Monday and string on Tuesday when one UUID appears; the downstream join silently drops every row and the dashboard shows zero usage before anyone notices the schema flip.

`df.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("dt").parquet(path)` under the default `partitionOverwriteMode=static` deletes two years of history in the customer's bucket during a one-day backfill, and the only copy was the output of the job that deleted it.

A Python UDF parses timestamps over two billion rows: thirty times slower than `F.to_timestamp`, predicate pushdown gone, and the `pyspark.daemon` workers push each Kubernetes pod over its limit, so executors die with exit code 137 and no `OutOfMemoryError` anywhere in the logs.

One tenant holds 40 percent of rows; `groupBy("tenant_id")` sends all of them to one task that runs three hours while the other 199 finish in seconds, AQE skew handling does not apply because it is an aggregation rather than a join, and the nightly SLA is missed until someone salts the key.

`toPandas()` on a 'small' filtered result that is actually 6 GB kills the driver with `spark.driver.maxResultSize` after two hours of upstream compute; the fix was to write the result to a table and read one partition, and to put a `count()` guard in front of any driver-side collection.

The job passes locally and fails on the cluster with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'defendermate_utils'` inside `BatchEvalPython`, because the package was installed on the edge node only and never shipped with `--py-files` or an `--archives` environment.

`spark.sql.session.timeZone` is the laptop's local zone in development and UTC on the cluster, so `date_trunc("day", ts)` buckets shift by several hours between environments; the PySpark daily totals disagree with the Postgres billing query and the discrepancy is blamed on Spark for a week.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through exactly what happens, process by process, when this line runs: `df.groupBy("tenant_id").agg(F.sum("tokens")).write.parquet(path)`. How many jobs and stages, where is the shuffle, what does the driver do versus the executors, and what changes if `df` came from a Python UDF?

A customer's nightly PySpark job went from 20 minutes to 3 hours after they onboarded one large new client. The code did not change. Take me through your diagnosis in the Spark UI and the fixes you would try, in order, with the trade-off of each.

Design a pipeline that ingests LLM call logs (JSON, about 2 TB per day, events arriving up to 48 hours late) into a per-tenant daily usage table that finance bills from. Cover idempotent reruns, late data, partitioning and file sizing, and how you validate against the source of truth.
When would you use a pandas UDF versus a plain Python UDF versus a built-in expression? For each, what exactly is serialised, where does it run, and what does Catalyst lose the ability to do?

Executor containers are being killed with exit code 137 but there is no `OutOfMemoryError` in any JVM log. Explain the memory regions involved in a PySpark executor and what you would change, and how you would confirm the fix from the UI or metrics.

Explain sort-merge join versus broadcast hash join: how Spark chooses, what goes wrong when you force a broadcast, how AQE changes the decision at runtime, and why AQE still will not save a skewed groupBy.

A customer with 50 GB of data wants everything on Spark because 'that is what Databricks is for'. Are they right? How would you decide, what would you propose instead if not, and how would you say it to their head of data without losing the room?
42.proofOfWork: A public repository `defendermate-spark-usage` containing: (1) an exporter that dumps `llm_calls`, `messages` and `tenants` from DefenderMate's Postgres to Parquet partitioned by `dt`; (2) `jobs/usage_daily.py` written as pure-function transforms with an argparse `main()` taking `--input`, `--output` and `--run-date`, writing with dynamic partition overwrite so any day can be rerun; (3) `sql/usage_daily.sql`, the reference query run in Postgres, and a pytest that asserts the PySpark output equals it with `assertDataFrameEqual`; (4) `NOTES.md` holding the annotated `explain(mode="formatted")` output with every Exchange and the join strategy labelled, a before-and-after table of stage summary metrics (median versus max task duration, shuffle read, spill) from salting a synthetically skewed tenant given 40 percent of rows, and a memory table listing the four OOM scenarios you actually triggered (`collect()`, oversized broadcast, `applyInPandas` on the skewed tenant, shuffle spill) with the exact error text and which process died; (5) a Delta variant of the writer that absorbs a replayed batch of late events via MERGE, with the `DESCRIBE HISTORY` output showing the commit and a `versionAsOf` read proving the previous state is recoverable. This is the artefact you open when a Databricks or Palantir interviewer says 'show me Spark you have written'.

43.topic: Designing Data-Intensive Applications and Kleppmann's lectures
43.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
43.why: Every FDE engagement eventually reaches the meeting where the customer's architect asks 'is this strongly consistent', 'what happens when the replica is behind', or 'can we just add a distributed lock', and the FDE either answers in terms of user-visible anomalies and concrete costs or loses the room. DDIA plus Kleppmann's Cambridge lectures are the shared vocabulary that Palantir, Databricks and Anthropic loops assume you already have: replication lag, quorums, isolation levels, linearizability, total order broadcast, Raft, CDC. The Gossip Glomers force you to feel the failures (lost messages, partitions, stale reads on a sequentially consistent store) in code, so that when a customer's Kafka consumer double-counts or a Postgres failover loses writes you recognise the mechanism inside a minute instead of a week.
prerequisites: PostgreSQL at depth (Topic 29): MVCC (xmin/xmax), WAL, EXPLAIN, row locks, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE - replication and isolation levels here build directly on that mental model
Kafka and event-driven design (Topic 33): partitions, keys, consumer groups, offsets, log compaction - Kafka is the worked example of a partitioned replicated log throughout
Networking (Topic 2): TCP retransmission and timeouts, why a timeout is not a failure signal, what a network partition physically looks like (asymmetric loss, one-way links)
High availability and DR (Topic 24): failover, promotion, RPO/RTO vocabulary, and the idea that an async replica is a lossy backup, not a hot standby

Enough Go to write a 300-line program with goroutines, sync.Mutex, context.WithTimeout, time.Ticker and encoding/json - the supported Gossip Glomers path is the Go Maelstrom library (if you insist on Python you must write the stdin/stdout JSON loop and RPC correlation yourself)
Temporal sagas (Topic 34): compensation-based workflows, because the 2PC subtopic compares against them

subtopics.name: Storage engines and encoding in 35 minutes (DDIA ch 3-4 skim)
subtopics.learn: Cover just enough of chapters 3-4 to answer the two questions customers actually ask: 'why is our write-heavy store slow to read' and 'will old consumers break when we add a field'. LSM-tree path: memtable, flush to immutable SSTables, leveled versus tiered compaction, bloom filters to skip files, and the write/read/space amplification triangle; versus B-tree: in-place page writes plus a WAL for crash recovery and more predictable read latency. Encoding: Avro/Protobuf/Thrift field tags, the compatibility rules (never reuse a field number, only add optional fields with defaults, never change a field's type), and why a jsonb column in Postgres breaks in exactly the same ways without any tooling to warn you.

resource.label: RocksDB wiki - RocksDB Overview (LSM architecture, compaction, bloom filters)

subtopics.name: System models, the two generals problem and failure detectors (Kleppmann lectures 1-2)
subtopics.learn: State the assumptions every later argument rests on: network model (reliable / fair-loss / arbitrary), node model (crash-stop / crash-recovery / Byzantine), timing model (synchronous / partially synchronous / asynchronous). Explain why the two generals problem means 'did the customer's payment go through' cannot be answered with certainty over a lossy link, and why every real system resolves it with idempotency keys, retries and a reconciliation job rather than a cleverer protocol. Know that a perfect failure detector is impossible in an asynchronous system, that timeouts give you an eventually-perfect one at best, and that FLP says deterministic consensus cannot be guaranteed to terminate under fully asynchronous assumptions - which is exactly why Raft uses randomised election timeouts and assumes partial synchrony.

resource.label: Kleppmann - Distributed Systems lecture notes (Cambridge, PDF)

subtopics.name: Clocks: wall time, monotonic time, Lamport and vector clocks, TrueTime
subtopics.learn: Distinguish CLOCK_REALTIME (NTP-slewed or stepped, can jump backwards, leap seconds) from CLOCK_MONOTONIC (only for measuring durations; time.monotonic() in Python, Go's time.Now() carries both readings). Know realistic NTP skew (tens of milliseconds on well-run hosts, seconds on neglected VMs) and conclude that timestamps from two machines never establish order. Lamport clocks: t = max(local, received) + 1 gives a total order consistent with causality but cannot detect concurrency; vector clocks / version vectors detect concurrent writes (neither dominates), which is how Dynamo-style stores decide to keep siblings rather than overwrite. Spanner TrueTime exposes an [earliest, latest] interval and commit-waits until latest has passed, so external consistency is bought with latency proportional to clock uncertainty. Be able to explain, with a two-node timeline, why last-writer-wins on wall clocks silently discards acknowledged writes.

resource.label: Lamport - Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System (PDF)

subtopics.name: Single-leader replication mechanics in PostgreSQL
subtopics.learn: Trace one write: WAL record, fsync on the primary, walsender streams to the standby's walreceiver, standby writes then replays. Know the settings and what each waits for: wal_level = replica | logical; max_wal_senders; synchronous_commit = off | local | remote_write | on | remote_apply; synchronous_standby_names with FIRST n (...) and ANY n (...) quorum syntax; physical replication slots (they stop WAL recycling and will fill the disk if the consumer dies - cap with max_slot_wal_keep_size); hot_standby_feedback trading primary-side bloat for fewer 'canceling statement due to conflict with recovery' errors. Failover: pg_ctl promote or SELECT pg_promote(), the timeline switch, and why the old primary must be fenced before the new one accepts writes (split brain); know what Patroni does with a DCS lease to automate exactly that. Distinguish statement-based, WAL-shipping and logical (row-level) replication and which one survives a major-version upgrade.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Log-Shipping Standby Servers (streaming replication, synchronous replication)

subtopics.name: Replication lag anomalies and how to actually deliver read-your-writes
subtopics.learn: Name the three guarantees weaker than linearizability that customers actually want and the anomaly each prevents: read-your-writes (user saves profile, refreshes, sees the old one), monotonic reads (page goes back in time between two refreshes hitting different replicas), consistent prefix reads (the answer appears before the question). Implementations you can defend: route a user's reads to the primary for N seconds after their last write; or capture pg_current_wal_lsn() after commit, store it in the session, and on the replica wait until pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= that LSN before serving; or pay for synchronous_commit = remote_apply on the write path. Measure lag from pg_stat_replication (write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag) and alert on byte lag (pg_wal_lsn_diff) as well as time, because time-based lag reads zero on an idle replica that is actually disconnected.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - System Administration Functions (pg_current_wal_lsn, pg_last_wal_replay_lsn, pg_promote)

subtopics.name: Multi-leader and leaderless replication: quorums, conflicts, anti-entropy
subtopics.learn: Do the quorum arithmetic (w + r > n) and then list why it is still not linearizable: sloppy quorums and hinted handoff, concurrent writes to different replicas, partial write failures with no rollback, and read repair racing with a second read. Know read repair versus anti-entropy (Merkle-tree comparison), last-writer-wins and why Cassandra's cell-level LWW with client-supplied timestamps loses writes under skew, and version vectors with sibling resolution as the alternative. Map Cassandra consistency levels (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, EACH_QUORUM, ALL) onto multi-datacenter latency and availability, and know that DynamoDB ConsistentRead=true costs double the read capacity units. Multi-leader use cases (multi-region active-active, offline clients, collaborative editing), conflict avoidance by giving each record a home region, and convergent merge functions or CRDTs when you cannot avoid conflicts.

resource.label: Amazon - Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (SOSP 2007, PDF)

subtopics.name: Partitioning: key choice, hot spots, secondary indexes, rebalancing, routing
subtopics.learn: Compare key-range partitioning (range scans work, sequential keys create a hot tail) with hash partitioning (even spread, range scans become scatter-gather). Know the fixed-slot schemes in tools your customers run: Redis Cluster's 16384 hash slots via CRC16, Kafka's murmur2(key) mod partition count - and why increasing a topic's partition count silently changes the key-to-partition mapping and breaks per-key ordering for in-flight consumers. Hot partitions: the celebrity-key problem, DynamoDB's per-partition ceiling (about 3000 RCU / 1000 WCU) and adaptive capacity, and the fix of salting a hot key with a small suffix and fanning reads back out. Secondary indexes: local/document-partitioned (scatter-gather reads, Cassandra, Elasticsearch) versus global/term-partitioned (asynchronous updates, DynamoDB GSIs). Rebalancing: many fixed partitions per node, dynamic splitting (HBase, DynamoDB), never hash mod N. Routing: coordination service (ZooKeeper in Kafka's older design), gossip (Cassandra), or smart clients following MOVED redirects (Redis).

resource.label: AWS DynamoDB Developer Guide - Partitions and Data Distribution

subtopics.name: Transactions: isolation levels, their anomalies, and Postgres specifics
subtopics.learn: Define each anomaly with a two-session example you can type into psql: dirty read/write, read skew (non-repeatable read), lost update, write skew, phantom. Map them to levels as PostgreSQL actually implements them: READ COMMITTED takes a snapshot per statement (the default); REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation with first-updater-wins (ERROR 40001 on a concurrent update); SERIALIZABLE is SSI, tracking rw-dependencies with SIReadLocks and aborting with 'could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies' (also SQLSTATE 40001), so the application needs a retry loop. Know the four fixes for lost updates (atomic UPDATE ... SET x = x + 1, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, compare-and-set WHERE version = $1, or SSI) and the write-skew canon (on-call doctors, double-booked rooms) including the materialise-conflicts trick with a row per bookable slot when you cannot afford SERIALIZABLE. Run Hermitage's scripts against Postgres and one store your customer uses and record where the isolation names lie.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Transaction Isolation (Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable/SSI)

subtopics.name: Linearizability, CAP, and what 'strong consistency' means in a design review
subtopics.learn: Define linearizability precisely: every operation appears to take effect atomically at some instant between its invocation and its response, and once any read returns the new value every later read returns it - a single-copy illusion in real time. Separate it from serializability (ordering of multi-object transactions, no real-time constraint) and strict serializability (both). Know the defaults of the systems you will meet: etcd reads are linearizable by default, ZooKeeper writes are but reads are not unless preceded by sync(), single-node Postgres is for single-object operations, Cassandra QUORUM is not, DynamoDB is only with ConsistentRead. Know where it is genuinely required (leader election, uniqueness constraints, locks, cross-channel timing such as 'file uploaded then message queued') and what it costs (a quorum or leader round trip, unavailability during partition). Retire CAP as a design tool - it is a theorem about one narrow model - and reason instead with 'linearizable or not' plus 'available under partition or not' plus the latency you pay even with no partition. Understand how Jepsen's checker (Knossos/Elle) tests a history for linearizability so you can read a Jepsen report and explain it to a customer.

resource.label: Jepsen - Consistency Models: Linearizable

subtopics.name: Ordering, total order broadcast, atomic commit and two-phase commit
subtopics.learn: Separate causal order from total order and show why Lamport timestamps alone cannot enforce a uniqueness constraint (you would have to hear from every node first). Define total order broadcast - reliable delivery plus identical order at every node - and know its equivalence to consensus and its real-world instances: ZooKeeper's ZAB and a single Kafka partition. Atomic commit across participants: 2PC prepare/commit, the coordinator's log write as the point of no return, in-doubt participants holding row locks forever after a coordinator crash (2PC is blocking), and why 2PC is not fault-tolerant consensus (one coordinator, no election). In PostgreSQL: PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid', COMMIT PREPARED, ROLLBACK PREPARED, max_prepared_transactions defaults to 0, and pg_prepared_xacts to find orphaned in-doubt transactions that are blocking VACUUM. Know XA in the Java world and why most current systems replace 2PC with idempotent, log-based sagas (Topic 34).

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - PREPARE TRANSACTION

subtopics.name: Consensus: Raft mechanics, the Paxos family, safety versus liveness
subtopics.learn: Work through Raft at the level of the paper's Figure 2: terms as epochs; randomised election timeouts (150-300 ms in the paper); RequestVote's up-to-date check (compare last log term, then last log index); AppendEntries with prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm as the consistency check and how followers truncate conflicting suffixes; commitIndex advancing only when a majority stores an entry from the leader's current term (the Figure 8 subtlety); the Log Matching and Leader Completeness properties; why a leader never overwrites or deletes its own entries; membership change via joint consensus or single-server changes; snapshots and InstallSnapshot for log compaction. Know Paxos vocabulary (proposers, acceptors, ballots) and that Multi-Paxos with a stable leader is what Raft makes explicit. Quorum arithmetic for the customer: 2f+1 nodes tolerate f failures, so 3 tolerates 1, 5 tolerates 2, and 4 tolerates the same 1 as 3 while costing more; every cross-region write pays at least one WAN round trip to a majority.

resource.label: Ongaro and Ousterhout - In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft paper, PDF)

subtopics.name: Coordination services in practice: leases, fencing tokens, ephemeral nodes
subtopics.learn: Know what ZooKeeper and etcd actually give you: linearizable writes, session or lease-scoped ephemeral keys (etcd Lease with TTL and KeepAlive; ZooKeeper session timeout and ephemeral znodes), watches, and a monotonic counter usable as a fencing token (ZooKeeper sequential znodes, etcd's revision / ModRevision). Understand the lease-expiry hole: a process paused by GC, VM live migration or SIGSTOP still believes it holds the lock after the lease expired; the correct fix is a fencing token that the protected resource checks and rejects if lower than the last one it saw - the lock alone is never sufficient. Know etcd's documented guarantees (linearizable reads by default, serializable reads when you opt in via --consistency=s, revision semantics) and why Redlock is contested. When a customer asks for a 'distributed lock', your first questions are 'what resource does it protect' and 'can that resource check a token'.

resource.label: etcd docs - API guarantees (linearizability, serializability, revisions)

subtopics.name: Derived data: dual writes, outbox, log-based CDC (DDIA ch 11-12)
subtopics.learn: Diagnose the dual-write problem (write to Postgres, then publish to Kafka: either step can fail, and two writers can interleave differently in each system) and know the two fixes: a transactional outbox table drained by CDC, or log-based CDC straight from the database. For Postgres logical decoding know wal_level = logical, CREATE PUBLICATION, the logical replication slot, the pgoutput plugin, and that Debezium emits before/after images tagged with LSN and transaction id; know that an abandoned slot retains WAL until the disk fills. Distinguish CDC from event sourcing, use log compaction to hold keyed state, and describe rebuilding a search index, cache or warehouse table by replaying the log from offset zero. Make consumers idempotent on (source LSN or event id) and evolve schemas through the log, not around it.

resource.label: Debezium docs - PostgreSQL connector (logical decoding, slots, publications, event envelope)

subtopics.name: Stream processing semantics: event time, watermarks, exactly-once (DDIA ch 11)
subtopics.learn: Separate event time from processing time and explain why a late-arriving mobile event changes an already-emitted hourly count. Know the window types (tumbling, hopping, sliding, session), watermarks as the operator's promise that no earlier events will arrive, and what to do with late data (drop, side output, retract). Cover the three join shapes (stream-stream, stream-table, table-table) and why stream-table joins are time-dependent. Fault tolerance via periodic checkpointing plus replay from the log, and the honest definition of exactly-once: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional sinks - Kafka's enable.idempotence, transactional.id and isolation.level = read_committed cover Kafka-to-Kafka, but an external sink still needs its own idempotency key.

resource.label: Apache Flink docs - Concepts: Timely Stream Processing (event time, watermarks, lateness)

subtopics.name: Maelstrom harness and Glomers 1-2: echo and unique IDs under partition
subtopics.learn: Install Maelstrom (a JDK, Graphviz and gnuplot) and run the echo workload. Learn the protocol cold: newline-delimited JSON on stdin/stdout, every message is {src, dest, body}, body carries type, msg_id and in_reply_to; the first message is init with node_id and node_ids; replies use type = request type + '_ok'; errors carry a numeric code (0 timeout, 11 temporarily-unavailable, 13 crash, 14 abort, 20 key-does-not-exist, 22 precondition-failed) and are either definite or indefinite; logs go to stderr because stdout is the wire. In the Go library: maelstrom.NewNode(), n.Handle(type, fn), n.Reply(msg, body), n.Send(dest, body), n.RPC(dest, body, callback), n.SyncRPC(ctx, dest, body), n.Run(), n.ID(), n.NodeIDs(). Challenge 1 is echo. Challenge 2 runs with --node-count 3 --rate 1000 --availability total --nemesis partition: generate IDs with no coordination (node id plus a local counter, or a timestamp-node-sequence layout) and be able to say why any scheme that talks to another node would fail the total-availability check. Read results.edn and store/latest until 'Everything looks good' means something to you.

resource.label: Maelstrom docs - Protocol (message format, init, RPC, error codes)

subtopics.name: Glomers 3a-3c: broadcast, gossip, and fault tolerance under partitions
subtopics.learn: 3a (single node): handle broadcast, read and topology; store a set of ints behind a sync.Mutex; return read_ok with messages. 3b (multi-node): forward each newly-seen value to your neighbours from the topology message (or a topology you choose), deduplicate so you only forward on first sight, and avoid echoing back to the sender. 3c runs with --node-count 5 --time-limit 20 --rate 10 --nemesis partition: inter-node messages will be dropped, so keep a per-neighbour pending set and retry unacknowledged sends from a background goroutine (ticker plus n.RPC callback or n.SyncRPC with a context timeout) until acked; never block the request handler on the network, never spawn an unbounded goroutine per retry, and run go test -race or go build -race to catch the shared-map race you almost certainly have. Success criteria from the challenge text: values propagate to all nodes by the end of the test, and each node returns only its own local values.

resource.label: Fly.io Gossip Glomers - Challenge 3c: Fault Tolerant Broadcast

subtopics.name: Glomers 3d-3e: efficient broadcast and reading Maelstrom's stats
subtopics.learn: Run with --node-count 25 --time-limit 20 --rate 100 --latency 100 and hit the stated limits: 3d requires messages-per-operation below 30, median latency below 400 ms and maximum below 600 ms; 3e requires below 20, below 1 s and below 2 s. Read results.edn properly: :net :servers :msgs-per-op counts only inter-server traffic, and :workload :stable-latencies gives quantiles {0, 0.5, 0.95, 0.99, 1} measured from broadcast acknowledgement to the value being present on every node. Do the arithmetic before coding: with 100 ms per hop a grid topology is several hops deep, so switch to a spanning tree or hub-and-spoke (one or two hops), and batch pending values per neighbour on a ticker (every 100-500 ms) so one message carries many values. Re-run with --nemesis partition after every optimisation, because the challenge text is explicit that you must not trade safety for the numbers.

resource.label: Fly.io Gossip Glomers - Challenge 3d: Efficient Broadcast, Part I

subtopics.name: Glomers 4: grow-only counter on a sequentially consistent KV
subtopics.learn: Use maelstrom.NewSeqKV(n): seq-kv offers Read, Write and CompareAndSwap with sequential consistency, meaning operations are totally ordered and each client's order is respected, but a read may return a value that is old in real time. Two designs: (a) a single shared counter updated by a CAS loop - kv.ReadInt, then kv.CompareAndSwap(ctx, key, from, to, createIfNotExists) and retry on PreconditionFailed (code 22), handling KeyDoesNotExist (code 20) on first write; (b) a G-counter CRDT where each node only increments its own key (its node id) and read sums every node's key, which has no contention and survives partitions cleanly. Handle stale reads honestly: because reads are only sequentially consistent, perform a write (to a throwaway key with a unique value) before reading so your subsequent reads are ordered after it, or merge the store's value with your local knowledge. Run with --node-count 3 --rate 100 --time-limit 20 --nemesis partition; the final read must equal the sum of all acknowledged adds. Be able to explain why this design passes while an LWW register keyed on wall time would not.

resource.label: Maelstrom docs - Services (lin-kv, seq-kv, lww-kv semantics and operations)

subtopics.name: The client-architect explanation: a 20-minute whiteboard script without notes
subtopics.learn: Assemble and rehearse the explanation the depth target demands. Replication: leader/follower, sync vs async, what lag means, and which of read-your-writes / monotonic reads / consistent prefix their product actually needs. Partitioning: key choice, hot spots, rebalancing, and the cost of secondary indexes. Consistency: linearizable versus eventual versus the in-between guarantees, each expressed as a user-visible anomaly rather than a term of art. Consensus: why 3 or 5 nodes, what a lease is, what happens during a partition, what a fencing token protects. Transactions across services: outbox or saga, never 2PC by default. Use the 'stop calling databases CP or AP' framing to head off the CAP conversation, carry a one-page decision table (use case, required guarantee, cost in latency and availability), record yourself, time each section, and cut every sentence you cannot back with an anomaly example.

resource.label: Martin Kleppmann - Please stop calling databases CP or AP

outcomes: You can draw PostgreSQL single-leader replication on a whiteboard and, for each synchronous_commit setting (off, local, remote_write, on, remote_apply), state exactly which failure loses acknowledged writes and how a client would observe it.

You can take a user story such as 'saved my profile, refreshed, saw the old one', name the missing guarantee (read-your-writes), and describe two implementations, one of them the LSN-tracking approach using pg_current_wal_lsn() and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn().

You can take five concurrent-transaction scenarios, predict which anomaly occurs under READ COMMITTED and under REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL, and prove it in two psql sessions, then show the SERIALIZABLE retry loop or explicit lock that removes it.

You can explain Raft leader election and log replication from memory, including why a candidate with a longer log but an older last-entry term loses the vote, and answer 'why five nodes and not four' with quorum arithmetic.

You can complete Gossip Glomers 1 through 4 with Maelstrom reporting 'Everything looks good', including 3d and 3e within the stated messages-per-operation and latency limits and still correct under --nemesis partition.
You can read a Jepsen analysis or a Maelstrom results.edn, identify the consistency model being checked, and state whether the anomaly found would affect a named customer use case.

You can deliver the 20-minute explanation of replication, partitioning, consistency and consensus to a non-specialist architect without notes, recorded, with every claim tied to a user-visible anomaly.

You can spot the dual-write problem in a customer's architecture diagram and redraw it with an outbox plus CDC path, naming wal_level = logical, the replication slot, and the slot-lag disk risk that comes with it.
failureModes: An asynchronous Postgres replica was promoted after the primary died; the last thirty seconds of acknowledged writes were gone, and the old primary rebooted and kept accepting writes because nothing fenced it, leaving two divergent timelines that had to be merged by hand.
A Debezium connector was decommissioned but its logical replication slot was not dropped; the primary retained WAL for weeks until the disk filled at 03:00 and PostgreSQL stopped accepting writes.

A Cassandra cluster using last-writer-wins with client timestamps had one app server forty seconds behind on NTP; every update from that host was silently overwritten by older writes from the others and the team chased a 'random data loss' bug for three weeks.

A Kafka topic was bumped from 12 to 24 partitions to add throughput; the key-to-partition mapping changed under live consumers, per-key ordering broke, and the downstream aggregator emitted duplicate and out-of-order state that reached the customer's reports.

A 'distributed lock' built on Redis SET NX PX with a 30-second TTL and no fencing token; a JVM garbage-collection pause exceeded the TTL, two workers processed the same batch, and the storage layer happily accepted both.

A check-then-insert for booking a slot ran at Postgres's default READ COMMITTED; write skew let two customers book the same slot on a busy day, and the fix (a unique index plus a SERIALIZABLE retry loop) arrived only after the refund.

A three-node etcd cluster was split two-plus-one across two data centres; the two-node site lost power, the surviving node could not form a quorum, and the Kubernetes control plane was down even though every application node was healthy.
interviewQuestions: A customer runs Postgres with one asynchronous streaming replica and asks for 'zero data loss on failover'. Walk me through exactly what you would change - synchronous_commit, synchronous_standby_names, quorum shape, fencing - what it costs in write latency and availability, and what you tell them when the replica is in another region.

Explain linearizability as if I were a solutions architect with no distributed-systems background, then name three places in a typical SaaS application that genuinely need it and three that do not, with the cost of getting it in each case.

Design a globally unique, roughly time-ordered ID generator across three regions that stay available during partitions. What do you give up relative to a database sequence, and what happens when one node's clock jumps backwards?

An orders service writes to Postgres and then publishes to Kafka; users report missing events roughly once a day. Diagnose the mechanism, redesign it with an outbox or CDC, and state the new operational risks you have introduced and how you would monitor them.

A five-node Raft cluster: the leader in term 7 has committed through index 100; node B was partitioned and holds uncommitted entries 101-105 from term 6. The partition heals. Walk through what happens to B's log, step by step, and why those entries can or cannot be discarded safely.

Given this history - A writes x = 1 and gets an ack; B's read of x starts after A's ack and returns 0; C's read returns 1 - is it linearizable? Sequentially consistent? Which real databases produce it, under which configuration, and how would you stop it?

Your Gossip Glomers broadcast passes cleanly without a nemesis but under --nemesis partition some values never reach every node. Give me the three most likely bugs in order of probability and how you would prove each one from Maelstrom's logs and results.edn.
43.proofOfWork: A recorded 'consistency anomaly lab' checked into the portfolio repo next to the Glomers solutions: a docker-compose with a Postgres primary and one streaming replica plus a set of scripted demonstrations, each captured as a terminal recording with the exact commands and output. Demo one reproduces a stale read-after-write on the replica and then fixes it with the pg_current_wal_lsn / pg_last_wal_replay_lsn wait and separately with synchronous_commit = remote_apply, timing the latency cost of each. Demo two shows write skew on a slot-booking table at REPEATABLE READ in two psql sessions, then the SERIALIZABLE retry loop catching SQLSTATE 40001, and finally the unique-index alternative. Demo three kills the primary with synchronous_commit = off versus on, promotes the replica with pg_promote(), and counts the acknowledged rows that were lost in each case. Alongside it sits a Maelstrom results table for challenges 3d, 3e and 4 showing msgs-per-op and the stable-latency quantiles with and without --nemesis partition, and the recorded 20-minute architect explanation with its one-page decision table (use case, required guarantee, cost). A reviewer should be able to clone, run make lab, and reproduce every anomaly and every fix in under fifteen minutes.

44.topic: MIT 6.824 selected lectures: Raft, linearizability, transactions
44.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
44.why: Every customer environment you land in already runs consensus somewhere you did not choose: etcd under their Kubernetes control plane, ZooKeeper or KRaft under their Kafka, a MongoDB replica set, a Consul cluster, a CockroachDB or Spanner tier. When the platform team asks 'is it safe if we lose one node', 'why did the API server time out for 40 seconds', or 'why did two workers both think they held the lock', the FDE in the room has to answer from mechanism, not folklore, and then translate the answer into a flag change, a topology change, or a redesign of the customer's retry logic. The same vocabulary (quorum, commit, linearizable, stale read, blocking 2PC, idempotency across failover) is exactly what a Palantir, Databricks or Anthropic system-design loop probes, so the whiteboard fluency this topic builds is doing double duty.
prerequisites: Topic 39 (DDIA and Kleppmann lectures): chapters 5 (replication), 7 (transactions) and 9 (consistency and consensus) read, so terms like quorum, leader-based replication, snapshot isolation and total order broadcast are already familiar

Topic 2 (Networking): what a partition really looks like on the wire (dropped or delayed packets, asymmetric reachability, a slow link that is not down), TCP retransmit and connection timeouts, and why 'the node is unreachable' is indistinguishable from 'the node is slow'
Topic 29 (PostgreSQL at depth): MVCC, READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE, row locks, and what a transaction ID and xmin horizon are
Topic 1 (Linux internals): fsync/fdatasync semantics, why a write is not durable until the flush returns, and roughly what a flush costs on local NVMe vs a network block device
Topic 33 (Kafka): ISR, acks and min.insync.replicas, so the contrast between Kafka's data-plane replication and Raft-style consensus lands
Can read Go at the level of the Raft paper's pseudocode and the etcd/raft or hashicorp/raft README; the 6.824 lectures and the optional lab (Topic 41) assume it

subtopics.name: Replicated state machines, split brain and why majorities
subtopics.learn: State the problem Raft solves: N servers each applying the same deterministic log in the same order so that any one can take over, under a crash-stop plus network-partition failure model (no Byzantine nodes, unbounded message delay, clocks not trusted for safety). Be able to show on a whiteboard why a naive primary-backup with a single 'view server' can split-brain when the network partitions, and why requiring a majority of 2f+1 servers for every decision guarantees any two decisions share at least one server and hence carry the other's history. Know the practical consequences: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2, 4 tolerate the same as 3 but is slower, and an even-sized cluster is never a good trade. This is 6.824 lecture 'Fault Tolerance: Raft (1)' and section 5 of the paper.

resource.label: MIT 6.824 schedule (lecture videos and notes for Raft 1 and 2)

subtopics.name: Terms, elections and the election restriction
subtopics.learn: Walk the state machine follower -> candidate -> leader with the exact RequestVote fields (term, candidateId, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm) and reply (term, voteGranted), and be able to say what a server does on receiving any RPC with a higher term (adopt it, become follower, reset votedFor) or lower term (reject). Explain why election timeouts are randomised (paper uses 150-300 ms; etcd defaults heartbeat 100 ms / election 1000 ms), how a split vote resolves, and the requirement broadcastTime << electionTimeout << MTBF. Nail the election restriction: a voter grants only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date, comparing lastLogTerm first and lastLogIndex second, and be able to argue why this alone is what makes Leader Completeness hold. Step through the visualisation until you can predict every transition before clicking.

resource.label: The Secret Lives of Data - Raft interactive walkthrough

subtopics.name: AppendEntries, the consistency check and log repair
subtopics.learn: Know the AppendEntries fields (term, leaderId, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries[], leaderCommit) and the follower's algorithm: reject if the entry at prevLogIndex does not have prevLogTerm, otherwise delete any conflicting suffix and append. Explain the leader's per-follower nextIndex (initialised to lastLogIndex+1) and matchIndex (initialised to 0), how a rejection decrements nextIndex and retries, and the fast-backup optimisation from the 6.824 notes where the follower returns the conflicting term and the first index of that term (XTerm/XIndex/XLen) so the leader skips a whole term per round trip. Work every case of Figure 7 (a-f) by hand: for each follower, say what prevLogIndex the leader will settle on and which entries get truncated. Be able to state the Log Matching property and why a follower may never keep an entry the leader does not have.

resource.label: Raft extended paper (6.824 copy) - sections 5.3 and Figure 7

subtopics.name: Commitment, Figure 8 and the five safety properties
subtopics.learn: Define commit precisely: the leader advances commitIndex to N only when a majority have matchIndex >= N and log[N].term == currentTerm; followers learn it via leaderCommit and apply entries up to it. Reproduce Figure 8 on a whiteboard from memory: a leader in term 2 replicates index 2 to a majority, crashes, a term-3 leader with a different index-2 entry overwrites it later, so counting replicas of a prior-term entry would have 'committed' something that gets deleted; hence prior-term entries are only committed indirectly when a current-term entry above them commits, which is why real implementations append a no-op entry on election. Recite and justify Election Safety, Leader Append-Only, Log Matching, Leader Completeness and State Machine Safety, and be able to say which mechanism enforces each.

resource.label: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft paper, Figure 8 and section 5.4)

subtopics.name: Figure 2 as an executable spec: what is persistent and when to fsync
subtopics.learn: Classify every variable in Figure 2: persistent (currentTerm, votedFor, log[]) versus volatile (commitIndex, lastApplied, and on leaders nextIndex[], matchIndex[]) and be able to explain the bug that appears if each persistent one is lost (two votes in one term, forgetting a granted vote, resurrecting a deleted entry). Know that persistence means fsync before replying to the RPC, which is why every Raft deployment's latency floor is the WAL fsync and why etcd exposes etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds. Read the TLA+ spec alongside Figure 2 and map each action (Timeout, RequestVote, AppendEntries, BecomeLeader, ClientRequest, AdvanceCommitIndex) to the paper's rules; noticing that the spec has no clocks and no timeouts as safety inputs is the point.

resource.label: ongardie/raft.tla - formal TLA+ specification of Raft

subtopics.name: Snapshots and log compaction
subtopics.learn: Explain why an unbounded log is fatal (restart replays forever, disk fills) and how snapshotting works: the service serialises its state at some applied index, Raft discards the log prefix and remembers lastIncludedIndex and lastIncludedTerm so the consistency check still works for the next AppendEntries; lagging followers receive InstallSnapshot (lastIncludedIndex, lastIncludedTerm, offset, data, done). In etcd terms: --snapshot-count (default 100000 entries) triggers a Raft snapshot, --max-snapshots and --max-wals (default 5 each) bound retention, while the separate MVCC history is bounded by --auto-compaction-mode=periodic|revision and --auto-compaction-retention plus etcdctl defrag to reclaim file space. Know that hitting --quota-backend-bytes (default 2 GiB, hard cap 8 GiB) raises the NOSPACE alarm and makes the cluster read-only until you compact, defrag and etcdctl alarm disarm.

resource.label: etcd v3.5 operations guide - Maintenance (compaction, defragmentation, space quota, snapshots)

subtopics.name: Membership changes, learners and the quorum arithmetic trap
subtopics.learn: Explain why a naive switch from C_old to C_new can elect two leaders, and the two fixes: the paper's joint consensus (C_old,new) and the dissertation's simpler single-server-at-a-time change where any two adjacent configurations overlap in a majority. Know the operational hazards that follow: adding a fourth member to a 3-node cluster that already has one dead member drops you from quorum 2-of-3 with 2 healthy to quorum 3-of-4 with 2 healthy, an outage, which is why etcd enforces --strict-reconfig-check and why the rule is remove-then-add. Use etcdctl member add <name> --peer-urls=... --learner then etcdctl member promote so the new node catches up without counting toward quorum, and know that removing the current leader triggers a fresh election you should schedule for a quiet window.

resource.label: etcd v3.5 operations guide - Runtime reconfiguration

subtopics.name: Linearizability: definition and checking a history by hand
subtopics.learn: State the definition operationally: a history is linearizable if you can assign each operation a single point between its invocation and response such that the sequence of points is a legal sequential history of the object. Practise the 6.824 lecture method: draw the invocation/response intervals for concurrent reads and writes to one register, try to place the points, and either produce the order or exhibit the cycle that proves there is none (a read returning a value whose write started after the read completed, or two reads observing writes in opposite orders). Contrast with sequential consistency (no real-time constraint) and eventual consistency, and be able to say in one sentence why linearizability is the model that lets you ignore replication: it behaves like a single copy.

resource.label: Jepsen - Linearizability (consistency models reference)

subtopics.name: Linearizable vs stale reads: ReadIndex, leader leases and the deposed-leader problem
subtopics.learn: Explain why a Raft leader cannot simply answer reads from local state: it may have been deposed by a partition and be serving values a new leader has already overwritten. Know the two remedies: ReadIndex (record commitIndex, confirm leadership with a heartbeat round to a majority, wait until lastApplied >= that index, then serve) and lease-based reads (serve within a lease shorter than the election timeout, which trades a clock-drift assumption for a network round trip). Map this to etcd: etcdctl get --consistency=l (default, ReadIndex) vs --consistency=s (serializable, served locally by any member, may be stale), and know which one your customer's Kubernetes clients and any custom config loaders are actually using. Know what etcd guarantees for a linearizable read after a linearizable write from another client, and what 'serializable' means in etcd's vocabulary versus SQL's.

resource.label: etcd v3.5 - API guarantees (linearizability, serializable reads, revisions)

subtopics.name: Client sessions, duplicate detection and exactly-once semantics
subtopics.learn: Work through the failure: client sends Put, leader commits it, leader crashes before replying, client retries to the new leader, the Put executes twice. Know the standard fix from Raft dissertation chapter 6: each client registers a session ID, tags requests with a monotonically increasing sequence number, and the state machine (not the Raft layer) keeps a per-client table of last-applied sequence and cached reply so a duplicate returns the cached result without re-executing; the table must live in the replicated state so it survives failover, and it needs an expiry policy the cluster agrees on. Translate this to FDE work: an idempotency key column plus unique index in Postgres, or a Redis SETNX with TTL (Topic 31), is the same idea and has the same expiry problem.

resource.label: Diego Ongaro - Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice (Raft dissertation, ch. 6 client interaction)

subtopics.name: ZooKeeper's weaker model: linearizable writes, FIFO client order, watches
subtopics.learn: Understand why ZooKeeper deliberately serves reads from any replica (throughput scales with followers) and what it promises instead of full linearizability: writes are linearizable and totally ordered by zxid, each client's operations execute in the order it issued them, and a read after your own write sees that write; a client that needs a fresh read calls sync() first. Know the primitives that make it a coordination service rather than a database: ephemeral znodes tied to the session (so a crashed lock holder releases the lock), sequential znodes for fair locks, one-shot watches, and the herd-effect fix of watching only your predecessor. Be able to describe the 'ready znode' pattern for atomic multi-key config updates and why it depends on FIFO client order.

resource.label: ZooKeeper Programmer's Guide - consistency guarantees, watches, znodes

subtopics.name: Timeouts, disks and leader flapping in a real etcd cluster
subtopics.learn: Diagnose the most common customer-cluster pathology: leader elections every few minutes with kube-apiserver logging 'etcdserver: request timed out'. Know the causal chain (slow fsync or network delays heartbeats -> followers time out -> election -> writes stall) and the metrics that separate the causes: etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds p99 should be under 10 ms and etcd_disk_backend_commit_duration_seconds under 25 ms, etcd_network_peer_round_trip_time_seconds for network, etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total for the symptom, plus log lines 'failed to send out heartbeat on time' and 'apply request took too long'. Know the tuning levers and their limits: --heartbeat-interval should be near the peer RTT, --election-timeout about 10x heartbeat and never above 50000 ms, etcd on its own disk (never a shared network volume behind a busy database), and etcdctl check perf to baseline before and after.

resource.label: etcd v3.5 - Tuning (heartbeat, election timeout, disk and network)

subtopics.name: Quorum loss and disaster recovery
subtopics.learn: Enumerate etcd's failure classes (minority loss: fine, elect if needed; leader loss: election within one election timeout; majority loss: read-only at best and unrecoverable without operator action) and know which one the customer is in from etcdctl endpoint status -w table and etcdctl endpoint health. Practise the recovery path: regular etcdctl snapshot save, then etcdutl snapshot restore <file> --name <m> --initial-cluster ... --initial-cluster-token ... --initial-advertise-peer-urls ... --data-dir <new>, which rewrites member and cluster IDs so the old members cannot rejoin, and understand that everything after the snapshot is lost. Know --force-new-cluster as the single-surviving-member last resort and why it is dangerous if another old member later comes back. Tie this to Topic 24 (HA and DR): the RPO for a Kubernetes control plane is your etcd snapshot cadence.

resource.label: etcd v3.5 operations guide - Disaster recovery

subtopics.name: Testing consistency: Porcupine, Jepsen and fault injection
subtopics.learn: Learn how a linearizability checker works so you can use one on a customer system: record every operation's invocation time, response time, inputs and outputs, define a sequential model (a register or key-value map with a step function), and let the checker search for a valid ordering; Porcupine is the Go checker the 6.824 labs use, Knossos and Elle are Jepsen's. Read one Jepsen analysis end to end (jepsen.io/analyses) and identify the nemesis used (partition, clock skew, process kill, pause), the claimed model, and the minimal history that violated it. Know the fault-injection toolkit you can run on a customer's staging cluster: docker pause or kill -STOP for stop-the-world, iptables DROP or docker network disconnect for partitions, tc netem for latency, and why a paused process is worse than a dead one.

resource.label: anishathalye/porcupine - linearizability checker used by the 6.824 labs

subtopics.name: Two-phase commit and why it blocks
subtopics.learn: Draw 2PC precisely: coordinator sends PREPARE, each participant writes a prepare record (locks held, must survive crash) and votes, coordinator durably logs the decision then sends COMMIT/ABORT, participants ack. Identify the blocking window: participants that voted yes cannot unilaterally decide if the coordinator is unreachable, so they hold locks until it returns; contrast with Raft/Paxos where the decision is replicated and a new leader can finish it (Spanner's trick is to make the coordinator itself a Paxos group). Practise the Postgres mechanics: PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid', COMMIT PREPARED / ROLLBACK PREPARED, max_prepared_transactions (default 0, i.e. disabled), and the pg_prepared_xacts view, and know that an orphaned prepared transaction is invisible in pg_stat_activity yet holds its row locks and pins the xmin horizon so VACUUM cannot advance.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - PREPARE TRANSACTION

subtopics.name: Spanner: TrueTime, commit-wait and external consistency
subtopics.learn: Explain Spanner's architecture in FDE terms: data split into tablets, each replicated by its own Paxos group across zones, read-write transactions use 2PL for locks and 2PC across groups with a Paxos-replicated coordinator, and timestamps come from TrueTime, an API returning an interval [earliest, latest] bounded by GPS and atomic clocks. Nail commit-wait: a transaction is assigned timestamp s = TT.now().latest and the leader waits until TT.after(s) before releasing locks, so any transaction that starts after this one returns is guaranteed a larger timestamp, which yields external consistency (strict serializability); remove commit-wait and a later transaction could get an earlier timestamp and read-only transactions would observe an impossible order. Know why read-only transactions are lock-free (pick a timestamp, read the snapshot from any sufficiently up-to-date replica) and how Cloud Spanner exposes strong, bounded-staleness (max_staleness, min_read_timestamp) and exact-staleness (exact_staleness, read_timestamp) reads.

resource.label: Cloud Spanner docs - TrueTime and external consistency

subtopics.name: Isolation levels versus consistency models
subtopics.learn: Separate two axes that customers conflate: consistency models (linearizability) are about single operations on single objects across replicas and real time, while isolation levels (serializability) are about multi-object transactions on one logical database and say nothing about real time; strict serializability is both.
