Be able to give the classic anomaly per level with Postgres specifics: READ COMMITTED (default) allows non-repeatable reads, REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation and allows write skew (two doctors both going off-call), SERIALIZABLE uses SSI and aborts with SQLSTATE 40001 'could not serialize access', so every caller needs a retry loop. Then give the cross-system example: a Raft-backed key-value store is linearizable per key but not transactional across keys, and a single-node Postgres at SERIALIZABLE is serializable but its async read replica is neither.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Transaction Isolation

subtopics.name: Leases and fencing: leader election without owning a consensus library
subtopics.learn: Understand how Kubernetes components elect a leader without implementing Raft themselves: a coordination.k8s.io/v1 Lease object with holderIdentity, leaseDurationSeconds, acquireTime, renewTime and leaseTransitions, updated with optimistic concurrency against etcd (which is the actual consensus); client-go's defaults are LeaseDuration 15 s, RenewDeadline 10 s, RetryPeriod 2 s, and kube-controller-manager exposes them as --leader-elect-lease-duration and friends. Be able to explain why a lease is not a fence: a holder paused by GC or the hypervisor for longer than the lease can resume and act after a new holder exists, so any external side effect must carry a fencing token (etcd revision, ZooKeeper zxid, or a monotonically increasing epoch column) that the downstream store rejects if it is lower than the last one seen. Apply the same reasoning to any customer 'distributed lock' built on Redis SET NX PX.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs - Leases (coordination.k8s.io)

subtopics.name: Consensus in the systems you will inherit: KRaft, MongoDB, CockroachDB
subtopics.learn: Build the Rosetta stone you will use on site. Kafka: KRaft replaces ZooKeeper with a Raft-style controller quorum (process.roles, controller.quorum.voters or the dynamic controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers, the __cluster_metadata log) that is pull-based rather than push-based, while data partitions still use ISR replication where durability depends on acks=all, min.insync.replicas>=2 and unclean.leader.election.enable=false, not on Raft. MongoDB: replica-set elections with electionTimeoutMillis (default 10000 ms) and member priority, writeConcern w:majority to avoid rollback of acknowledged writes after failover, readConcern majority vs linearizable (primary only, re-confirms leadership). CockroachDB: each range (default 512 MiB) is its own Raft group, a leaseholder serves reads without a Raft round, and clock uncertainty (--max-offset, default 500 ms) is handled with hybrid logical clocks instead of TrueTime. For each, be able to state what 'lost one node' and 'lost a majority' mean operationally.

resource.label: Apache Kafka documentation - KRaft (section 6.9 and replication design)

subtopics.name: Whiteboard rehearsal: the 15-minute Raft explanation
subtopics.learn: Script and rehearse the deliverable: (1) the problem and the majority argument, (2) normal-case election with RPC fields and randomised timeouts, (3) normal-case replication with prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm and commit, (4) a leader failure with a Figure 7-style divergence and the repair, (5) the Figure 8 trap and the current-term commit rule, (6) a one-minute coda on persistence, snapshots and linearizable reads. Use RaftScope on raft.github.io to stage each scenario, pause it, and practise narrating the exact state on screen without reading it, then redo the same scenario on a blank whiteboard. Time yourself; if any segment exceeds its budget, cut detail rather than speed up, because the interviewer will interrupt at the point they care about.

resource.label: raft.github.io - Raft homepage with RaftScope interactive visualisation

outcomes: You can draw a 5-node Raft cluster on a whiteboard and narrate election, replication and commit with the correct RPC fields and persistence points, including the Figure 8 case, in under 15 minutes with no notes and survive interruptions at any step

You can take any Figure 7-style log configuration and state, per server, whether it can win an election, what prevLogIndex the leader will settle on for each follower, and which entries will be truncated
You can decide by hand whether a short history of concurrent reads and writes is linearizable, and confirm it by feeding the same history to Porcupine with a register model

You can look at etcd metrics and logs from a customer cluster and attribute leader flapping to fsync latency, network RTT or misconfigured timeouts, naming the exact flag or infrastructure change that fixes it
You can explain when two-phase commit blocks, list orphaned prepared transactions in Postgres from pg_prepared_xacts, and articulate why Spanner's Paxos-replicated coordinator does not block
You can explain commit-wait and external consistency to a non-Google engineer and translate it into what a customer should expect from Cloud Spanner's strong versus stale reads

You can map the words quorum, leader, commit, linearizable and stale to their concrete equivalents in Kafka KRaft, MongoDB replica sets, CockroachDB ranges and Kubernetes Leases in a live customer conversation
You can spot an unsafe distributed lock or leader lease in a customer's code and propose a fencing-token design with a specific token source and enforcement point
failureModes: etcd placed on a shared network volume alongside a busy database: WAL fsync p99 climbs past 10 ms, heartbeats are late, the cluster elects a new leader every few minutes and kube-apiserver returns 'etcdserver: request timed out' across the whole platform

Operator 'fixes' a 3-node cluster with one dead member by adding a replacement before removing the dead one: quorum goes from 2-of-3 to 3-of-4 with only 2 healthy, and the control plane goes read-only mid-incident

A config or leader-election loader reads etcd with --consistency=s (or ZooKeeper without sync()) and occasionally acts on a value the customer overwrote seconds earlier, producing two workers that both believe they own a shard

A JVM app using XA against Postgres crashes between PREPARE and COMMIT; the orphaned prepared transaction never shows up in pg_stat_activity but holds row locks for days and pins the xmin horizon until autovacuum warnings about wraparound appear
A client library retries a write after a leader change with no idempotency key, so the payment or Kafka publish executes twice; the team blames the database for 'duplicating data'

Kafka producers run with acks=1 or min.insync.replicas=1 plus unclean.leader.election.enable=true; a broker failover silently discards acknowledged messages and the customer's audit reconciliation fails weeks later

A worker holding a Redis or Lease-based lock is paused by a stop-the-world GC longer than the TTL, another worker acquires the lock, and both write to the downstream store because nothing checked a fencing token
interviewQuestions: Whiteboard this: a 5-node Raft cluster, the term-3 leader has replicated index 7 to two followers and then crashes. Walk through the possible elections that follow, state in each case what happens to index 7, and explain precisely why Raft refuses to count replicas of prior-term entries when advancing commitIndex.

A customer's 3-node etcd cluster under Kubernetes shows a leader change every few minutes and intermittent API server timeouts. What do you check, in what order, what metrics and log lines do you expect to see for each hypothesis, and what would you change first?

Explain the difference between linearizability, serializability and strict serializability with one concrete anomaly each. Name a production system that is serializable but not linearizable and describe the customer-visible symptom.

A service reads its shard assignment from etcd using serializable reads and a customer reports that after a rebalance two instances occasionally process the same shard for a few seconds. Explain the mechanism and propose three fixes with their latency and availability trade-offs.

Design exactly-once processing for inbound webhooks in a service that runs three replicas behind a load balancer and restarts during deploys. Where does the deduplication state live, how does it survive failover, and how do you expire it without reintroducing duplicates?
Why does Spanner make committing transactions wait, what would break if you removed commit-wait, and how does a system without TrueTime such as CockroachDB approximate the same guarantee?

A customer wants to coordinate two databases with two-phase commit from their application server. Walk through what happens if the application server dies after both participants voted yes, then tell me when you would push back and what you would build instead.
44.proofOfWork: A public 'stale read lab' repository: a docker-compose file that stands up a 3-member etcd 3.5 cluster plus Prometheus, a small Go or Python driver that runs N concurrent clients issuing put/get against a handful of keys while recording invocation and response timestamps and values, and a fault script that pauses the current leader (docker pause, simulating a stop-the-world) and partitions one member (docker network disconnect) during the run. The driver is run twice, once with reads at --consistency=s and once at --consistency=l, and both histories are fed to Porcupine with a register model; the repository commits the two checker outputs (the serializable run fails with the minimal violating sub-history highlighted, the linearizable run passes), Grafana screenshots of etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total and etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds across the fault window, and a one-page README that names the exact Raft mechanism (ReadIndex) responsible for the difference, what the same misconfiguration looks like in a customer's Kubernetes or ZooKeeper setup, and the flag or code change an operator should make. As a bonus, include annotated RaftScope screenshots reproducing the Figure 8 scenario step by step.

45.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
45.why: Reading the Raft paper makes you conversational; writing Raft and getting it past an adversarial tester makes you the person in the room who can say what a customer's etcd, Consul, CockroachDB or Kafka-KRaft cluster will actually do when a node's disk goes slow or a rack loses the network. FDEs get handed exactly these questions on-site — 'why did the API server freeze for 40 seconds', 'why did both workers hold the lock', 'is 4 nodes across 2 datacentres fine' — and the answers live in details you only internalise by hitting them: persist-before-reply, current-term-only commits, never truncating on a stale AppendEntries. It is also the strongest possible signal in a Palantir/Databricks/Anthropic loop that your distributed-systems knowledge is load-bearing rather than recited.
prerequisites: Topic 40 (6.824 selected lectures): the Raft paper's Figure 2 read at least twice, plus the lecture notes on elections, log matching and the Figure 8 commit rule — this lab is the implementation of exactly that material, not an introduction to it
Topic 39 (DDIA): chapters 5, 8 and 9 — leader-based replication, the unreliability of clocks and networks, and linearizability, so you know what property the tester's checker is actually enforcing

Go at Tour-of-Go level: goroutines, channels, sync.Mutex, sync.Cond, structs and interfaces, slices and their aliasing behaviour. There is no Go topic in this plan, so budget 2-3 hours on the Tour plus Effective Go before hour one of the lab; the lab itself will not teach you Go

Topic 2 (Networking): what a partition looks like on the wire — dropped, delayed, reordered and duplicated packets, asymmetric reachability — because labrpc simulates precisely these and your code must be correct under all of them

Topic 1 (Linux internals): fsync/fdatasync semantics and rough costs on local NVMe versus EBS/NFS, since 'persist before you reply' is the single most expensive rule in Raft and the reason customers' consensus clusters flap
Topic 4 (Git): the lab is distributed as a git repo you `git pull` repeatedly, and you will want branches per part and `git bisect` when a passing test starts failing

subtopics.name: Lab setup and a tour of the skeleton
subtopics.learn: Clone the 6.5840 repo, install a current Go toolchain, and run `make raft1` in `src` to watch every 3A test fail with 'expected one leader, got none' — that is your baseline. Read `src/raft1/raft.go` end to end before writing anything: `Make(peers, me, persister, applyCh)`, `Start(command) (index, term, isLeader)`, `GetState()`, the stub `ticker()` goroutine, and the example `sendRequestVote`/`RequestVote` pair. Then read `raftapi/raftapi.go` for the `ApplyMsg` fields and `tester1/persister.go` for `Save(raftstate, snapshot)`, `ReadRaftState()` and `ReadSnapshot()`. Know that peers may only communicate through labrpc — no shared variables, no files — and that the tester can delay, reorder, duplicate and drop every RPC.

resource.label: 6.5840 Lab 3: Raft — handout, Getting Started and 'The code'

subtopics.name: Figure 2 as an executable checklist
subtopics.learn: Transcribe Figure 2 of the extended paper into comments in raft.go and treat it as a spec you must satisfy line by line: persistent state (currentTerm, votedFor, log[]), volatile state (commitIndex, lastApplied), leader volatile state (nextIndex[] initialised to lastLogIndex+1, matchIndex[] to 0), the two RPC argument/reply structs, and the Rules for Servers. The rules that get skipped and cost days are: 'If RPC request or response contains term T > currentTerm: set currentTerm = T, convert to follower' (applies to replies too, and must clear votedFor), and 'If commitIndex > lastApplied: increment lastApplied, apply log[lastApplied]'. Write each rule as a named helper or an explicit branch so you can point at the line that implements it.

resource.label: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (extended) — Figure 2

subtopics.name: Go concurrency primitives and the race detector
subtopics.learn: Be fluent in `sync.Mutex` with `defer rf.mu.Unlock()`, `sync.Cond` for the applier, and why `time.Sleep` in a loop is what the handout wants instead of `time.Timer`/`time.Ticker`. Understand the Go memory model well enough to know that an unsynchronised read of `rf.currentTerm` is a data race even if it 'looks atomic', and run everything with `go test -race` (the Makefile already builds with -race; graders run without it, so both must pass). Know that Go 1.22+ scopes loop variables per iteration, which kills the classic `for i := range rf.peers { go func(){ use i }() }` bug — but that capturing `rf.currentTerm` inside a goroutine still snapshots a value that may be stale by the time the RPC returns.

resource.label: Go — Data Race Detector

subtopics.name: The locking protocol, applied to raft.go
subtopics.learn: Internalise the course's five locking rules and decide, before you write code, exactly where the mutex is held. The rules: hold the lock for every access to shared state; hold it across a whole multi-step invariant update (e.g. incrementing currentTerm, setting votedFor = me, and resetting the election timer must be atomic); never hold it while sending an RPC, sleeping, or sending on a channel; after re-acquiring, re-check every assumption — currentTerm may have advanced and you may no longer be leader; and prefer one coarse lock over clever fine-grained locking for this codebase. The concrete pattern: lock, copy the args you need into local variables, unlock, call `peer.Call(...)`, re-lock, then guard the reply with `if rf.currentTerm != argsTerm || rf.state != Leader { return }`.

resource.label: 6.5840 — Advice on locking in the labs

subtopics.name: Goroutine structure: ticker, heartbeater, applier
subtopics.learn: Settle on the canonical structure before coding: one long-lived `ticker()` goroutine that sleeps ~10ms and starts an election when now-lastHeard exceeds a randomised timeout; one goroutine per election that fans out RequestVote to every peer in its own goroutine and counts votes; a leader loop that fires AppendEntries to each peer every heartbeat interval; and a dedicated applier goroutine that is the only thing that ever writes to applyCh. Know why the applier must be separate: sending on applyCh can block on the service, and if you do it while holding rf.mu the whole peer deadlocks. Every goroutine must exit when `rf.killed()` is true, or the test binary accumulates leaked goroutines across the suite.

resource.label: 6.5840 — Advice on structuring your Raft lab

subtopics.name: Part 3A: leader election and heartbeats
subtopics.learn: Implement RequestVote and empty-entry AppendEntries until TestInitialElection3A, TestReElection3A and TestManyElections3A pass. The vote handler: reject if args.Term < currentTerm; step down if args.Term > currentTerm; grant only if (votedFor == nil || votedFor == candidateId) AND the candidate's log is at least as up to date (compare lastLogTerm first, then lastLogIndex). The discipline that decides whether 3A is one hour or six: reset your election timer on exactly three events — granting a vote, receiving a valid AppendEntries from the current leader, and starting your own election — and on nothing else. Resetting on a rejected vote or a stale-term heartbeat is the most common 3A bug and it hides until TestManyElections3A.

resource.label: 6.5840 lecture notes — Raft part 1 (elections)

subtopics.name: Timeout arithmetic, and the same arithmetic in etcd
subtopics.learn: Derive your constants rather than copying someone's: the tester caps heartbeats at 10 per second and demands a new leader within 5 seconds, so the paper's 150-300ms range is unusable — a heartbeat of ~100ms with an election timeout randomised over ~400-800ms (fresh random draw every time you reset) fits both constraints. Understand the invariant behind it, broadcastTime << electionTimeout << MTBF, and then map it to a real cluster: etcd defaults to --heartbeat-interval 100ms and --election-timeout 1000ms, recommends the 10x ratio, and recommends election-timeout be at least 5-10x the round-trip time between members — which is why a cross-region etcd with default flags flaps leaders under load.

resource.label: etcd — Tuning (heartbeat interval and election timeout)

subtopics.name: Part 3B: Start(), AppendEntries and the log-matching check
subtopics.learn: Implement `Start()` (append locally, return index/term immediately, never block) and full AppendEntries until all ten 3B tests pass, including TestBackup3B. Follow the handout's advice to make the log 0-indexed with a dummy entry at index 0, term 0, so the first RPC can legally carry PrevLogIndex 0. The follower's five steps in order: reject on stale term; reject if there is no entry at prevLogIndex with prevLogTerm; on a conflict at an existing index delete that entry and everything after it; append only entries not already present; and set commitIndex = min(leaderCommit, index of last new entry). Step 3 and step 4 must be a single careful loop — truncating unconditionally is the bug that eats committed entries.

resource.label: Ongaro, Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice — §3.5 Log replication and the Log Matching Property

subtopics.name: Commit rules: majority matchIndex plus the current-term restriction
subtopics.learn: Implement the leader's advance rule exactly: find N > commitIndex such that a majority of matchIndex[i] >= N AND log[N].Term == rf.currentTerm, then set commitIndex = N. Be able to explain, from Figure 8, why dropping the term check lets a replicated-on-a-majority entry from an old term be overwritten later, breaking State Machine Safety. Pair it with the election restriction (5.4.1) and show why the two together give Leader Completeness: the restriction guarantees a new leader holds every entry committed under the old rule, and the term check guarantees nothing is called committed before that guarantee applies. Know the consequence for entries from prior terms: they commit indirectly, once any current-term entry above them commits.

resource.label: 6.5840 lecture notes — Raft part 2 (commit, persistence, snapshots)

subtopics.name: The applier goroutine and applyCh ordering
subtopics.learn: Write one applier that waits on a `sync.Cond` signalled whenever commitIndex advances, then, in a loop, copies the entries between lastApplied and commitIndex out under the lock, releases the lock, and sends them on applyCh. Guarantee the two invariants the tester checks: every peer applies the same command at the same index (a mismatch prints 'apply error' and fails the run), and indices arrive strictly in order with no gaps or repeats. Understand why `for i := lastApplied+1; i <= commitIndex; i++ { applyCh <- ApplyMsg{...rf.log[i]...} }` while holding the lock deadlocks, and why re-reading rf.log after re-acquiring the lock can read a trimmed log once 3D lands.

resource.label: 6.5840 lecture notes — lab 3 A+B Q&A: applier thread, condvar signalling and locking

subtopics.name: The catalogue of Figure 2 misreadings
subtopics.learn: Read the Students' Guide once you have 3B passing and audit your code against every item: don't reset the election timer on a stale-term AppendEntries; don't truncate the log just because entries were sent; don't return early from RequestVote without persisting; do step down on a higher term seen in a *reply*, and then ignore the rest of that reply; don't set matchIndex = nextIndex-1 from stale state — derive it from the args you sent (prevLogIndex + len(entries)); don't let a stale AppendEntries reply lower nextIndex twice. Each one you find here is a day you don't spend on TestFigure8Unreliable3C.

resource.label: Students' Guide to Raft (Jon Gjengset)

subtopics.name: Part 3C: persistence and 'persist before you reply'
subtopics.learn: Implement `persist()` and `readPersist()` with labgob, encoding exactly currentTerm, votedFor and log[] (plus the snapshot bookkeeping in 3D) into `persister.Save(state, nil)`. Know that gob only serialises exported fields — lowercase fields in your log-entry struct silently vanish and labgob will warn you — and that decoding into a value that was never encoded leaves it zeroed. The rule that makes 3C pass and makes real systems safe: call persist() before you send any RPC reply that depends on the changed state, so a crash immediately after replying can never let the restarted node vote twice in one term or forget an entry it acknowledged. Insert persist() calls at every mutation of the three persistent fields, then grep to prove no mutation is missed.

resource.label: Go standard library — encoding/gob (exported fields, zero values)

subtopics.name: Fast log backup and the Figure 8 tests
subtopics.learn: Decrementing nextIndex one entry per RPC round trip is too slow for TestBackup3B and the 3C churn tests, so implement the handout's rejection payload: XTerm (term of the conflicting entry), XIndex (index of the first entry with that term) and XLen (log length). Leader logic: if the leader has no entry with XTerm, nextIndex = XIndex; if it has XTerm, nextIndex = (index of its last entry with XTerm) + 1; if the follower's log is simply too short, nextIndex = XLen. Then grind TestFigure83C and TestFigure8Unreliable3C — these take ~50s each and are where a wrong commit rule, a missing persist, or election timeouts that are too tight surface as intermittent failures. Run them with `-count 10` before believing they pass.

resource.label: etcd-io/raft — log.go, findConflictByTerm (production fast log backup)

subtopics.name: Part 3D: log compaction, Snapshot() and InstallSnapshot
subtopics.learn: Rewrite the log to store only the tail after lastIncludedIndex, with every array access going through explicit index-conversion helpers — this refactor, not the RPC, is where 3D is won or lost. Implement `Snapshot(index, snapshot []byte)` (called on every peer, not just the leader; discard entries before index; persist state and snapshot together via `persister.Save(state, snapshot)`) and the InstallSnapshot RPC sent whenever nextIndex[i] <= lastIncludedIndex, in one shot with no Figure 13 offset splitting. Deliver the snapshot to the service through applyCh, never move the service backwards, and after restart make sure the first applyCh message is either a higher snapshot or the command immediately after the restored index. Discard trimmed entries so the GC can free them: reslicing keeps the old backing array alive, so copy into a fresh slice.

resource.label: 6.5840 — diagram of Raft interactions: Start, applyCh, Snapshot and InstallSnapshot

subtopics.name: Debugging distributed Go: annotations, timelines, repetition
subtopics.learn: Build a debugging rig on day one rather than day five: a `DPrintf` gated by an env var, every line stamped with peer id, term, state, commitIndex and lastApplied, plus `tester.Annotate("Server 0", "short", "details")` calls so the tester's generated HTML timeline shows your events alongside its partitions, crashes and checks. Learn to read that timeline for the moment the invariant first breaks rather than the moment the test reports failure. Run failing tests in a loop — `go test -race -run 3C -count 20` piped to a file — because most Raft bugs appear in one run in twenty, and 'it passed once' is not evidence.

resource.label: 6.5840 — tester visualization of a failing run

subtopics.name: Performance budget: RPC counts, bytes, goroutines
subtopics.learn: Treat the tester's numbers as a performance spec, not decoration: each passing line reports elapsed time, peers, RPC count, RPC bytes and committed ops, and TestCount3B and TestRPCBytes3B fail outright on excess. The grader fails any submission where all of lab 3 exceeds 600 seconds or a single test exceeds 120; the reference solution is about 6 minutes without -race and 10 with. Hunt the usual causes of blowing the budget: loops that spin without sleeping or waiting on a cond, sending the entire log in every AppendEntries instead of the suffix from nextIndex, retrying an in-flight RPC before the previous one returns, and goroutines leaked per election. Use `go test -cpuprofile`/`-blockprofile` or a SIGQUIT goroutine dump when a run hangs.

resource.label: Go — Diagnostics (profiling, tracing, goroutine dumps)

subtopics.name: Linearizability and what Porcupine actually checks
subtopics.learn: Understand the layer above your Raft: the tester records a history of client operations with invocation and response intervals and asks whether some sequential ordering consistent with real time explains it — that is linearizability, and Porcupine is the checker that decides it (it writes an HTML visualisation on failure). Be able to say precisely what Raft gives you (a single totally ordered replicated log) and what it does not (linearizable *reads*, which need a log entry, a ReadIndex round trip, or a lease), and to read a Porcupine diagram to find the operation whose return value is impossible under every valid ordering.

resource.label: Porcupine — linearizability checker for Go

subtopics.name: Section 8 client interaction: exactly-once and read paths
subtopics.learn: Read section 8 of the paper and design what lab 4 will need: clients tag every command with a clientId and a monotonically increasing seqNo, the state machine keeps a last-applied-seq table per client so a retried command after a leader change is deduplicated rather than applied twice, and that table is part of the snapshot. Know why a new leader commits a no-op entry from its own term at election time (to learn its true commitIndex before serving reads) and the three read strategies with their costs: put the read in the log (safe, one round trip of consensus), ReadIndex (confirm leadership with a heartbeat quorum, then read locally), or a leader lease (fastest, but correctness depends on bounded clock drift).

resource.label: Raft extended paper — Section 8, Client interaction

subtopics.name: From lab Raft to the consensus in a customer's stack
subtopics.learn: Close the loop by reading etcd's raft library README and mapping every lab concept onto a production knob: the `Node` interface and `Ready` struct that make persistence and message sending the application's job; PreVote and CheckQuorum, which stop a partitioned node from bumping the term and disrupting a healthy leader (your lab Raft has this bug by design); learners (non-voting members) for safe node replacement; ReadIndex for linearizable reads; and the WAL plus snapshot-count settings that decide restart time. Then look at the operational failure surface you will actually be paged for: losing quorum in a 3-node cluster, `etcdctl snapshot save` / restore, `--force-new-cluster`, and why fsync latency on the etcd disk shows up as apiserver timeouts.

resource.label: etcd-io/raft — production Raft library README

subtopics.name: Quorum loss, recovery and cluster sizing for customers
subtopics.learn: Work the operational drill: for 2f+1 members you survive f failures, so 3 tolerates 1 and 5 tolerates 2, while 4 tolerates the same as 3 and is strictly slower — be able to shut down that 'let's add a fourth node for HA' request in one sentence. Walk etcd's documented failure modes: minority failure (self-heals when the member returns), majority failure (cluster is unavailable for writes and must be restored from a snapshot), and a partitioned member that returns with a higher term. Know the recovery sequence — stop members, `etcdutl snapshot restore` on each with a new cluster token, restart, verify with `etcdctl endpoint status --cluster` — and that a restore loses everything written after the snapshot, which is the number your customer actually needs to hear.

resource.label: etcd — Failure modes and disaster recovery

outcomes: You can run `make RUN="-run 3A" raft1` through `-run 3D` and pass all of 3A, 3B, 3C and 3D with `-race`, repeated with `-count 10`, with the whole suite under the 600-second grading limit and no individual test over 120 seconds

You can point at the specific line in your raft.go that implements each numbered rule in Figure 2, including the two easily-skipped ones (step down on a higher term seen in a reply; apply while commitIndex > lastApplied)
You can reproduce the Figure 8 scenario on a whiteboard in under five minutes and state exactly which line of your commit-advance code prevents it
You can explain, without notes, the three and only three events that reset your election timer, and demonstrate a test that fails when you add a fourth
You can take a failing run's tester timeline plus your own annotated logs and name the first violated invariant and the peer that violated it, rather than the test that reported it

You can translate any lab constant into its production equivalent — heartbeat interval, election timeout, snapshot trigger, quorum size — and defend those values for a customer's cluster given their RTT and disk fsync latency
You can describe three implementations of a linearizable read (log entry, ReadIndex, leader lease), rank them by latency, and name the assumption each one can violate
You can diagnose an etcd cluster that has lost quorum and give the exact recovery sequence plus the data-loss window it implies
failureModes: Replying to a RequestVote or AppendEntries before persisting currentTerm/votedFor/log, so a crash-restart in the same term votes twice or forgets an acknowledged entry — in the lab it is an intermittent 3C failure, in production it is two leaders writing divergent history

Truncating the follower's log on every AppendEntries instead of only at a genuine conflict, so a delayed or duplicated RPC deletes entries that were already committed and the peers diverge — the tester calls this 'apply error', a customer calls it lost writes

Advancing commitIndex by counting replicas without checking log[N].Term == currentTerm, which commits a previous-term entry that a later leader can legally overwrite (Figure 8) — silent, rare, and only reproducible under partitions

Holding rf.mu across a peer.Call or an applyCh send, which deadlocks the peer; the cluster keeps electing leaders that never make progress, and the production analogue is an etcd member that answers heartbeats but stalls every write

Election timeouts tuned too aggressively for the environment — a node whose fsync latency spikes (EBS burst credits exhausted, noisy-neighbour NVMe) misses heartbeats, terms climb, and the cluster flaps leaders every few seconds while the apiserver above it times out

Log compaction that reslices instead of copying, so trimmed entries stay reachable and never get freed; memory grows for days until the process is OOM-killed, mirroring an etcd cluster that hits its DB quota, raises a NOSPACE alarm and goes read-only

Retrying a client command against a new leader without a clientId/seqNo dedup table, so an operation that timed out is applied twice — harmless for an idempotent Put, corrupting for an increment, a debit, or an append
interviewQuestions: Walk me through why a Raft leader may not mark an entry from a previous term committed just because it is stored on a majority. Draw the Figure 8 sequence and tell me what your code does instead.

Exactly where in the protocol must state hit stable storage before you reply, and what concretely breaks if you reply first? Now estimate the write throughput ceiling that rule imposes given a 6ms fsync.

A customer's five-node etcd behind their Kubernetes control plane is electing a new leader every couple of minutes and apiserver p99 latency has gone from 20ms to 2s. What do you look at, in what order, and which of heartbeat-interval, election-timeout, snapshot-count, disk or network do you expect to be the cause?
Give me three ways to serve a linearizable read from a Raft cluster, in order of increasing latency, and tell me the specific failure each one can exhibit.

A client issues a write, gets no response, and retries against a different node that is now leader. How do you guarantee the command applies exactly once, and where does that dedup state have to live so it survives a snapshot and a restart?
The customer's platform team wants to go from three to four members 'for more redundancy' across two datacentres. What do you tell them, and what would you propose instead?
How do snapshots interact with AppendEntries and the applyCh contract? What invariants must hold about the order and indices of messages the service sees after a follower installs a snapshot?
45.proofOfWork: Beyond the passing test suite, build a fault-injection harness and a written failure atlas on top of your own implementation. Add a debug build flag that lets you deliberately break one invariant at a time — persist after reply instead of before, drop the current-term check in the commit rule, truncate the log unconditionally on AppendEntries, reset the election timer on stale-term RPCs, remove the election restriction from RequestVote — then, for each mutation, run the suite with `-count 20` and record which tests fail, at what rate, and what the first divergence looks like in the tester timeline. Write it up as a short document (kept private since it contains lab code, or published with the solution stripped to diagrams and log excerpts) where each entry has the broken invariant, the safety property it violates from the paper, the observed symptom, the failure rate across twenty runs, and the equivalent production symptom in etcd or Consul — leader flapping, apiserver timeouts, a stale read, a double-applied command. That document is both the artifact that proves you understand Raft as a set of enforced invariants rather than a pile of RPCs, and the thing you can hand an interviewer or a customer's platform team when they ask why a consensus tuning change is risky.

46.topic: System design playbook: load balancing, caching, sharding, queues, rate limits, IDs, search
46.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
46.why: An FDE is the person in the room when the customer's architect asks 'and what happens when we roll this to all 500 clients?' and you have to answer on a whiteboard with numbers, inside their constraints (their VPC, their Postgres, their Kafka, their security team) rather than in the abstract. Every deployment you scope is assembled from the same seven building blocks: something in front spreading traffic, something remembering answers, something splitting data, something absorbing bursts, something saying no, something naming things, and something finding them. The system design round is also where senior FDE loops at Palantir, Anthropic and Databricks separate 'can build a feature' from 'can own a customer's production system', and the interviewer is grading the same thing the customer is: can you run the conversation end to end, attach numbers, name trade-offs, and tell a credible story about what breaks first.
prerequisites: Networking from topic 2 (TCP/IP, DNS, TLS, HTTP/2, load balancers): handshake and TLS-termination cost, HTTP/1.1 keep-alive vs HTTP/2 multiplexing, DNS TTL behaviour, and exactly what an L4 proxy can and cannot see compared with an L7 proxy

PostgreSQL from topic 29: B-tree vs GIN indexes, `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, row locks and MVCC bloat, `max_connections` and pooling, and why random keys hurt insert locality; plus the RLS multi-tenant schema from topic 30
Redis from topic 31: TTL and expiry, `maxmemory` and eviction, `SET NX PX` locks, Lua/`MULTI` atomicity, and the token-bucket limiter and idempotency store you already built for DefenderMate

Kafka from topic 33: partitions as the ordering unit, consumer groups and rebalances, offset commits, `acks`, the idempotent producer, and the DefenderMate ingestion consumers with their duplicate/reorder drill results

DDIA vocabulary from topic 39 and Raft/linearizability from topic 40: single-leader replication and lag, read-your-writes, hash vs range partitioning and rebalancing, quorum, CAP/PACELC, and what 'exactly once' can and cannot mean
SLIs/SLOs and error budgets from topic 20, HA/DR (multi-AZ vs multi-region, RTO/RPO) from topic 24, and load testing with k6 from topic 22 so failure stories can be reproduced rather than imagined

A running DefenderMate stack (FastAPI, Postgres with RLS, Redis, Kafka/Redpanda, Next.js, SSE relay of Claude) and at least one week of real numbers: requests per endpoint, p50/p99, tokens per call, documents per tenant per day

subtopics.name: The 45-minute delivery frame: requirements, non-functionals as numbers, and the API you commit to
subtopics.learn: Run the clock deliberately: minutes 0-5 functional requirements (three core flows, an explicit out-of-scope list), 5-10 non-functionals written as numbers not adjectives (p99 per endpoint, availability target, consistency per operation, retention, tenancy isolation, cost ceiling), 10-15 core entities and the API (verbs, cursor pagination, `Idempotency-Key` on every write), 15-30 a high-level design that satisfies every functional requirement before any optimisation, 30-45 two or three deep dives chosen by the non-functionals, closing with the failure story. Write assumptions in a corner of the board and say them aloud so the interviewer or customer architect can correct them early; a wrong assumption stated is recoverable, a wrong assumption hidden is fatal. Adopt one trade-off vocabulary for the whole session (consistency vs availability per operation, latency vs cost, simplicity vs scale) and use it every time you pick between two options.

resource.label: Hello Interview - System Design Delivery Framework

subtopics.name: Back-of-envelope estimation: DefenderMate at 500 clients
subtopics.learn: Derive every number from a stated chain of assumptions and round aggressively: 500 tenants x 200 seats = 100k users; 10% daily active = 10k; 20 messages each = 200k messages/day = ~2.3/s average, x10 diurnal peak = ~25/s; each message is one Claude call at ~3k input and ~500 output tokens = 600M input tokens/day, so at roughly $3 per million input the bill is thousands of dollars a day and the largest lever is prompt caching (topic 59), not servers; 100 documents per tenant per day = 50k docs, 20 chunks each = 1M chunks/day, 1536 float32 dims = 6 KB each = ~6 GB of vectors per day = ~2 TB/year, which is what forces per-tenant partitioning and a real vector store rather than a single pgvector table; messages at 2 KB = 400 MB/day = 150 GB/year, so Postgres holds the transactional data for years without sharding. Memorise the latency table (L1 ~1 ns, RAM ~100 ns, SSD random read ~100 us, same-region RTT ~0.5 ms, cross-continent ~70-150 ms) and the powers of two (2^20 ~ 1M, 2^30 ~ 1G). Convert QPS to capacity: a FastAPI worker doing 50 ms of DB-bound work handles ~20 rps, a 4-worker pod ~80 rps, so 25 msg/s needs one pod plus headroom and the bottleneck is the queue and the upstream model, not the API tier. Always end the estimate with 'the thing that saturates first is X'.

resource.label: System Design Primer - Back-of-the-envelope calculations

subtopics.name: Traffic entry: DNS, anycast, CDN and where TLS terminates
subtopics.learn: Know the Route 53 routing policies (simple, weighted, latency, failover with health checks, geolocation, geoproximity, multivalue answer) and what each is actually for: weighted for canaries and migrations, latency for multi-region reads, failover for DR with a health-checked primary. Understand what a 60 s TTL buys and what it does not: recursive resolvers, JVM default caching, and mobile OS caches routinely ignore it, so DNS failover is minutes not seconds, which is why anycast or an ALB in front of both regions is the answer when RTO is tight. Draw the TLS termination point and defend it: terminate at the edge or ALB for cheap certificate management, re-encrypt to origin or run mTLS to pods when the customer's security team requires it, and price the handshake (1-RTT TLS 1.3, 2-RTT TLS 1.2, resumption avoids both). Put the customer's WAF on the diagram and state what it can inspect at each termination choice.

resource.label: Amazon Route 53 - Choosing a routing policy

subtopics.name: L4 vs L7 load balancing, algorithms and connection reuse
subtopics.learn: L4 (NLB, IPVS) balances TCP flows, preserves source IP and cannot see paths or headers; L7 (ALB, Nginx, Envoy) terminates HTTP and can route on path/host/header/cookie, retry idempotent requests, add `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Request-ID`, and terminate TLS. Know the Nginx upstream algorithms and when each wins: default weighted round-robin for uniform short requests, `least_conn` for long-lived SSE and LLM streams whose durations vary by 100x, `hash $key consistent` (ketama ring, minimal remapping when a server leaves) for cache locality per tenant, `ip_hash` only when you have no better affinity key. Configure connection reuse or pay a handshake per request: `keepalive 32;` in the upstream block plus `proxy_http_version 1.1;` and `proxy_set_header Connection "";` in the location. Use `max_fails` and `fail_timeout` for passive health detection and understand their default (1 failure, 10 s). Know two ways balancing silently goes wrong: HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests onto one client connection so an L4 balancer in front sees one flow and cannot spread them, and least-connections cannot tell a 30-second SSE stream from a 30 ms JSON call until the connection count already skewed.

resource.label: nginx - ngx_http_upstream_module (least_conn, hash consistent, keepalive, max_fails)

subtopics.name: Health checks, draining and zero-downtime rollouts behind the balancer
subtopics.learn: Separate liveness (the process is alive, restart me if not) from readiness (I can serve: pool warm, config loaded, not shutting down) and never make the balancer's check hit the database on every probe. Know the ALB target-group knobs and defaults: `HealthCheckIntervalSeconds` 30, `HealthyThresholdCount` 5, `UnhealthyThresholdCount` 2, `HealthCheckTimeoutSeconds` 5, and success matcher defaulting to `200` (a range such as `200-299` is opt-in), and that a target takes interval x threshold seconds to become healthy after a deploy, which sets your minimum rollout time. Reason about draining: the deregistration delay (default 300 s) must be longer than your longest in-flight request (an SSE stream can be 60 s) and shorter than or equal to the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, and the app must flip `/readyz` to 503 on SIGTERM and keep serving in-flight requests until the balancer stops sending new ones. Name the cascading risk of deep health checks: when a shared dependency blips, every target fails its check at once and the balancer takes the whole fleet out of rotation.

resource.label: AWS ALB - Health checks for target groups

subtopics.name: Cache placement and invalidation: cache-aside, write-through, TTLs, eviction and stampedes
subtopics.learn: Choose where the cache lives (in-process LRU, Redis, CDN) by hit ratio times cost-of-miss, and choose the write pattern: cache-aside (miss, load, `SET key val EX ttl`) is the default; write-through keeps the cache authoritative at the cost of write latency; write-behind buys write throughput at the cost of losing data on a crash. Design the key schema to include tenant and schema version (`t:{tenant}:conv:{id}:v3`) so a deploy can move to `v4` instead of flushing. Know the `maxmemory-policy` options (`allkeys-lru`, `allkeys-lfu`, `volatile-lru`, `volatile-ttl`, `noeviction`) and that `noeviction` at `maxmemory` makes writes fail with an OOM error rather than evicting, which turns a full cache into an outage. Prevent stampedes three ways and know when each applies: a single-flight lock (`SET lock:{key} 1 NX PX 5000`, others wait or serve stale), probabilistic early expiration (recompute before expiry with probability rising as TTL approaches zero), and jittered TTLs so a million keys written at deploy time do not expire in the same second. Cache 'not found' with a short TTL to stop lookups of nonexistent ids hammering the database. Compute what the database absorbs if the cache disappears: at 90% hit ratio, losing the cache is a 10x read spike.

resource.label: Redis docs - Key eviction (maxmemory-policy)

subtopics.name: HTTP and CDN caching semantics: Cache-Control, ETag, Vary and purge
subtopics.learn: Use the directives precisely: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=30, stale-if-error=600` for shared caches, `private` for per-user responses, `no-store` for anything with secrets; hashed static assets get `max-age=31536000, immutable`. Implement conditional requests: `ETag` plus `If-None-Match` returns 304 and saves bandwidth but not compute unless the ETag is cheap to derive. Understand `Vary`: omit `Vary: Accept-Encoding` and you serve gzip to a client that cannot decode it; omit `Vary: Authorization` (or fail to key on tenant) on a CDN-cached API response and one tenant sees another's data. Know the purge models: URL purge is exact and slow at scale, surrogate-key or tag purge invalidates every object tagged `tenant:42` in one call. Apply to DefenderMate: Next.js `_next/static` is immutable, the tenant branding/config endpoint gets a short `s-maxage` with an ETag, and nothing under `/api/conversations` is ever shared-cacheable.

resource.label: MDN - HTTP caching

subtopics.name: Read replicas, replication lag and read-your-writes
subtopics.learn: Streaming replication is the first scale-out step for reads and the first place users see 'my data disappeared'. Know the `synchronous_commit` levels (`off`, `local`, `remote_write`, `on`, `remote_apply`) and `synchronous_standby_names`: only `remote_apply` guarantees a replica read sees the committed write, and it charges every commit a network round trip. Measure lag with `pg_stat_replication` (`write_lag`, `flush_lag`, `replay_lag`) and on the standby `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()`; decide about `hot_standby_feedback` (prevents query cancellation on the replica, causes bloat on the primary). Route reads by consistency requirement: writes and anything read-after-write go to the primary; pin a session to the primary for N seconds after it writes, or record the commit LSN in the response and have the replica route compare it with `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` before serving; send list views, dashboards and analytics to replicas. Rehearse the failure: a user posts a message, the next GET hits a replica 300 ms behind, the message is missing, the UI retries the POST and creates a duplicate.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication

subtopics.name: Partitioning and sharding: key choice, hash vs range, rebalancing and scatter-gather
subtopics.learn: Partition inside one Postgres before sharding across many: `PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at)` for append-heavy time series such as `llm_calls` and `audit_log` (retention becomes `DETACH PARTITION` + `DROP` instead of a week-long DELETE), `PARTITION BY HASH (tenant_id)` to spread a hot table; partition pruning only happens when the partition key appears in the WHERE clause, so every query path must carry it. Shard across databases only when the single primary's write throughput, working set or blast radius forces it, and pick the key by three rules: high cardinality, present in every hot query, spreads writes. Hash keys spread evenly but kill range scans; range keys keep locality but make the newest range the hottest (a `created_at` shard key puts every write on one shard). Use consistent hashing with virtual nodes so rebalancing moves a fraction of keys, and study Redis Cluster's 16384 fixed hash slots and `{tenant}` hash tags as the concrete model for slot-based resharding without a stop-the-world. Anything not keyed by the shard key becomes scatter-gather: the slowest shard defines p99, and secondary indexes are either local (query every shard) or global (async, eventually consistent).

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Table Partitioning

subtopics.name: Hot keys, skew and the noisy-neighbour tenant
subtopics.learn: Detect skew before customers do: per-partition-key consumption in DynamoDB via CloudWatch Contributor Insights, per-partition end offsets in Kafka via `rpk topic describe -p`, hot Redis keys via `redis-cli --hotkeys` (requires an LFU policy) or `MONITOR` samples, per-tenant row counts and QPS in Postgres. Know the canonical hard ceiling, DynamoDB's 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU per physical partition, so 'one hot tenant' has a number attached. Mitigate in order of cost: cache the hot object; per-tenant rate limits so one bulk import cannot starve 499 tenants; write sharding (append `#0..N` to the key and fan in on read); move the whale tenant to its own shard or cell via a tenant-to-shard directory; split the partition key. State the price of each mitigation (write sharding makes reads N times more expensive; a directory becomes a critical dependency).

resource.label: DynamoDB - Best practices for designing and using partition keys

subtopics.name: Multi-tenant data layouts: pooled, siloed, bridge and cells
subtopics.learn: Compare the four layouts with numbers for 500 tenants: pooled (shared tables + `tenant_id` + RLS, one migration, largest blast radius, noisy neighbours), schema-per-tenant (500 schemas means 500x migration fan-out and catalog bloat), database-per-tenant (isolation and per-tenant restore, but 500 connection pools and 500 backups), and cell-based (a full stack per group of tenants, tenant-to-cell directory, a bad deploy or hot tenant hurts one cell). Recommend tiers: pooled for standard tenants, siloed for regulated or whale tenants, and make the tenant directory (`tenant_id -> cell, shard, region, tier, limits, keys`) an explicitly cached, versioned service because every request depends on it. Study Citus's distribute-by-tenant model as the middle path: tables co-located on the `tenant_id` distribution column so joins stay local, small reference tables replicated to every node. Know the tenant-move procedure (dual-write or CDC into the destination, backfill, verify counts, cut over behind the directory, keep the source read-only for rollback) because a customer will ask for it.

resource.label: Citus docs - Multi-tenant Applications

subtopics.name: Queues and async work: delivery semantics, visibility timeouts, ordering, DLQs
subtopics.learn: Put every LLM call and document ingest behind a queue for three reasons you can state: decouple request latency from processing, absorb bursts up to the queue's depth, retry without the user. Define the semantics precisely: at-most-once (ack before work), at-least-once (ack after work, duplicates on crash), and 'exactly once' meaning at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer with a dedup key, or Kafka transactions for Kafka-to-Kafka only. SQS mechanics: `VisibilityTimeout` must exceed worst-case processing or be extended with `ChangeMessageVisibility` on a heartbeat, `maxReceiveCount` in the redrive policy moves poison messages to the dead-letter queue, FIFO queues with `MessageGroupId` give per-tenant ordering at a 300 requests/s per-queue ceiling (3,000 batched) unless high-throughput mode is enabled. Kafka mechanics: the partition is the ordering unit, a rebalance pauses the group, commit the offset after the side effect, and `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 300 s) kicks slow consumers out. Design the DLQ path: who is paged, how a message is inspected and replayed, and how a poison message in a FIFO group is quarantined so it stops blocking the tenant behind it.

resource.label: Amazon SQS - Visibility timeout

subtopics.name: Backpressure, load shedding and queue sizing
subtopics.learn: Size with Little's Law (L = lambda x W): at 25 jobs/s and 8 s per Claude call you need ~200 concurrent workers or the queue grows without bound; an unbounded queue converts an overload into a latency disaster hours later when it finally drains and re-runs thousands of jobs nobody wants. Shed early and cheaply: bound concurrency at the balancer or gateway and return 503 with `Retry-After` when exceeded, keep separate queues and worker pools for interactive vs batch so a bulk import never queues in front of a chat message, and enforce per-tenant quotas so fairness is a property of the system rather than luck. Propagate deadlines (`X-Request-Deadline` or gRPC deadlines) and drop work whose caller has already timed out. Recognise the cascading pattern from the SRE book: one server dies, survivors take its load and slow down, clients retry, the retries kill the survivors.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Handling Overload

subtopics.name: Transactional outbox and CDC: publishing events without dual-write bugs
subtopics.learn: Dual-write (commit to Postgres, then publish to Kafka) loses events when the process dies between the two and publishes phantom events when the commit rolls back. Fix with an outbox table written in the same transaction as the business row and drained by a relay: either a poller (`SELECT ... FROM outbox ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`) or Debezium's outbox event router reading the WAL (`wal_level=logical`, columns `id`, `aggregatetype`, `aggregateid`, `type`, `payload`, routing to `outbox.event.<aggregatetype>` keyed by `aggregateid` so a tenant's or document's events stay ordered). The relay is at-least-once, so consumers still need idempotency (topic 33's dedup drill). Know the operational hazards: a stalled replication slot retains WAL until the primary's disk fills, and a poller with no index on the unsent flag becomes the slowest query in the database. Map it to DefenderMate: `document.uploaded` fans out to ingestion, `message.created` to the classifier and analytics.

resource.label: Debezium docs - Outbox Event Router

subtopics.name: Rate limiting: algorithms, placement and the 429 contract
subtopics.learn: Know the algorithms and their exact failure: fixed window (a 2x burst straddling the boundary), sliding window log (exact, O(n) memory per key), sliding window counter (O(1), approximate), token bucket (rate plus burst, the default for APIs), leaky bucket and GCRA (a single timestamp per key, no burst above rate). Place limits at three layers with different keys: edge via Nginx `limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s;` and `limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay;` (set `limit_req_status 429;` because the default is 503), gateway per API key, and application per tenant in Redis with an atomic Lua script or `MULTI`/`EXEC` on `rl:{tenant}:{window}`. Apportion inherited upstream limits: the Claude tokens-per-minute budget is shared by 500 tenants, so the per-tenant limiter must sum to less than the upstream ceiling and reserve headroom for retries. Honour the response contract: 429 with `Retry-After` and the IETF `RateLimit-Policy` / `RateLimit` headers (older drafts used `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, `RateLimit-Reset`) so client SDKs back off correctly, and distinguish 429 (you asked too often) from 503 (we are overloaded).

resource.label: nginx - ngx_http_limit_req_module (limit_req_zone, burst, nodelay, limit_req_status)

subtopics.name: Timeouts, retries, backoff with jitter and circuit breakers
subtopics.learn: Every hop gets a timeout shorter than its caller's, so a 60 s user budget becomes 55 s at the API, 50 s at the worker and 45 s at the model call, and nothing waits on a caller that has already gone. Retry only idempotent operations, only on retryable errors (connection reset, 429, 503, 529), and only within a retry budget (retries never exceed ~10% of first attempts) so a partial outage cannot triple load. Use full jitter (`sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))`) rather than plain exponential so retries do not arrive in synchronised waves. Add a circuit breaker per dependency (closed, open after N failures in a window, half-open with a single probe) to fail fast instead of consuming every worker's timeout on a dead dependency, and reserve hedged requests for read paths where duplicate work is safe. Multiply the layers to see a retry storm: client SDK 3x times API 3x times queue consumer 5x is 45 attempts per failed call.

resource.label: Amazon Builders' Library - Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

subtopics.name: Unique IDs at scale: UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7, Snowflake, ULID, sequences
subtopics.learn: Random UUIDv4 primary keys scatter inserts across the whole B-tree, causing page splits, WAL amplification and cache misses on a large `messages` table; UUIDv7 (RFC 9562: 48-bit Unix milliseconds, then version, then 74 bits of random or counter) and ULID are k-sortable so inserts append at the right-hand edge, and PostgreSQL 18 ships `uuidv7()` natively. Know the Snowflake layout and its arithmetic: 41-bit millisecond timestamp (about 69 years), 10-bit worker id (1,024 generators), 12-bit sequence (4,096 ids per ms per worker), and the two operational problems, assigning worker ids without collision (ZooKeeper, StatefulSet ordinal, database lease) and refusing to issue ids when the clock moves backwards. `bigserial` sequences are simplest on one primary but leak volume to customers and do not survive sharding; sharded systems either embed the shard id in the key or use a k-sortable id plus a directory. Decide per table: `bigint` sequence for internal joins, UUIDv7 for anything externally visible or destined for a shard.

resource.label: RFC 9562 - Universally Unique IDentifiers (UUIDv7)

subtopics.name: Idempotency keys and safe write APIs
subtopics.learn: Clients send an `Idempotency-Key` (a UUID they generate) on every POST that creates something; the server stores key, tenant/user scope, a fingerprint of the request body and the final response, with a TTL (Stripe keeps them 24 hours). A repeat with the same key and same body replays the stored status and body; the same key with a different body is rejected (Stripe returns 400, you may choose 422); a concurrent duplicate while the first is still running is fenced with `SET idem:{tenant}:{key} NX PX 30000` or a unique index on the key column and told 409 to retry later. Scope keys per tenant so two tenants using the same UUID cannot collide or leak. Chain it with consumer dedup so a retried webhook or a re-driven queue message cannot create a second document, and store the key with the row so support can answer 'why do I have two of these'.

resource.label: Stripe API reference - Idempotent requests

subtopics.name: Search: inverted indexes, analyzers, BM25, Postgres FTS and when to add a search engine
subtopics.learn: An inverted index maps term to posting list; the analyzer (tokenise, lowercase, stop words, stem) runs at index time and query time and must be identical or recall silently collapses. Understand BM25 versus TF-IDF in one sentence each (term-frequency saturation and document-length normalisation) so you can explain a ranking to a customer. Start in Postgres: a stored generated column `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED` with a GIN index, `@@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)`, `ts_rank_cd` for ordering, and `pg_trgm` with `gin_trgm_ops` for fuzzy and `ILIKE '%x%'`; always AND a `tenant_id` predicate and let RLS enforce it. Move to OpenSearch or Elasticsearch when you need facets, relevance tuning, highlighting, or search QPS that competes with OLTP, and know the costs: near-real-time visibility governed by `refresh_interval` (1 s default, so 'I just uploaded it and cannot find it'), mapping changes requiring a reindex behind an alias, tenant isolation via a mandatory `term` filter on `tenant_id` or an index per whale tenant. Hybrid retrieval that fuses BM25 with vector search via reciprocal rank fusion is topic 49.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Full Text Search

subtopics.name: Telling the failure story: trigger, propagation, detection, mitigation, design change
subtopics.learn: Close every design with a three-to-five-minute 'what breaks first' narrative built from the cascading-failure catalogue: a replica lags and users see vanished messages; Redis restarts and the database takes a 10x read spike; one tenant's bulk import fills the classifier queue for everyone; a deploy with a short grace period leaves the balancer sending to dead pods. Use a fixed structure so it lands under time pressure: trigger, propagation (why it spread instead of staying local), detection (which SLI moved, which alert fired, how long until a human knew), the 3 a.m. mitigation (shed, fail over, flip a flag, scale), and the design change that prevents recurrence, each with a number attached (lag in ms, queue depth, minutes to detect). Rehearse aloud until the story takes under five minutes and names at least one thing you would monitor from day one.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Addressing Cascading Failures

outcomes: You can run a 45-minute design of a stated system (DefenderMate at 500 tenants, or an unfamiliar prompt) against a visible clock and leave behind written requirements, a numbers table, a component diagram, two deep dives and a failure story without being prompted for any of them.

You can produce a capacity estimate in under five minutes from stated assumptions (average and peak QPS, storage per year, bandwidth, cache size for a target hit ratio, worker count from Little's Law) and name the component that saturates first with the number that proves it.

You can choose a load-balancing algorithm and connection-reuse configuration for a stated workload (short JSON calls vs long SSE streams) and write the Nginx upstream block or ALB target-group settings, including health-check thresholds and a deregistration delay that matches the pod's grace period.

You can specify a cache layer end to end (key schema with tenant and version, TTL with jitter, eviction policy, invalidation trigger, stampede protection) and state the database load if the cache is lost.
You can pick a partition or shard key for a given query mix, state the hot-spot risk and which queries become scatter-gather, and describe the rebalancing and tenant-move procedure step by step.

You can design a per-tenant rate limiter (algorithm, storage, key, 429 and header contract) and a retry policy (timeouts per hop, jitter, retry budget, circuit breaker) that together provably cannot amplify a partial outage, and show it with a k6 run.

You can design an async pipeline (outbox, queue with visibility timeout and DLQ, idempotent consumer) and say exactly what happens to a message on a crash at each of the five points between the user's POST and the stored result.

You can decide between Postgres full-text search and a dedicated search engine for a stated workload and write either the generated tsvector column with its GIN index or the index mapping and mandatory tenant filter.
failureModes: A Redis restart during a deploy expired every key at once; thousands of concurrent misses hit Postgres, connections pinned at `max_connections`, and the API served 500s for twenty minutes even though the database itself was healthy; jittered TTLs and a single-flight lock would have held.

The customer's Nginx ran round-robin with no upstream `keepalive` in front of SSE streams; every stream opened a fresh TCP connection and long conversations pinned one pod while others idled, tripling p99 time-to-first-token under mild load until `least_conn` and `keepalive 32` were added.

Reads were routed to a replica 400 ms behind the primary; a user posted a message, the conversation list did not show it, the frontend retried the POST without an idempotency key, and the tenant saw duplicates that support then had to delete by hand.

`created_at` was chosen as the shard key for `llm_calls`; every write landed on the newest shard, and one tenant's overnight bulk re-classification saturated that shard for all 500 tenants while the other shards sat idle.

Retries in the client SDK (3x), the API (3x) and the queue consumer (5x) compounded to 45 attempts per failed call during an upstream 529 event, exhausting the shared Claude rate limit for every tenant and leaving a backlog that took six hours to drain after the upstream recovered.

Deregistration delay was 300 s but `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` was 30 s, so on every rollout the ALB kept routing to pods that had already been SIGKILLed; the resulting five minutes of 502s per deploy were blamed on 'the network' for a month.

A CDN-cached per-tenant branding endpoint lacked `Vary` and a tenant-aware cache key; the first tenant to request after a purge had its logo and name served to every other tenant for the next five minutes.
interviewQuestions: Design DefenderMate for 500 tenants: 100k users, 200k messages a day, each message one Claude call with a 60-second user budget, plus 50k document uploads a day. Walk me through the queues, the shard or partition key, the per-hop latency budget, and the one component you expect to saturate first, with numbers.

A customer says 'just add read replicas' to fix a slow dashboard and a slow conversation view. When does that help, when does it not, and how do you handle the user who just posted a message and immediately reloads? Show me the routing rule and how you would measure lag.

You have a Redis-backed per-tenant limiter and an upstream Claude tokens-per-minute limit shared by all tenants. Design the fairness policy: how do you apportion the upstream budget, what does a tenant see when they hit their share, and how does a bursty tenant not starve a steady one? What headers do you return?

Debug: after every deploy, 502s spike for about four minutes then recover. The path is ALB to Kubernetes pods running FastAPI. Give me the three most likely causes, the exact ALB access-log fields and pod events you would check for each, and the fix.

Explain the transactional outbox pattern. Why is writing to Postgres and then publishing to Kafka broken, what does the outbox change, why do consumers still need idempotency, and what happens to the primary if the Debezium replication slot stalls for a day?

The `messages` table has reached 2 TB and the customer wants sub-100 ms conversation loads. Walk through partitioning versus sharding: how you choose the key, which queries break, how you migrate with zero downtime, and how you prove afterwards that it worked.

A tenant reports two search problems: newly uploaded documents are missing for up to a minute, and once a document from another tenant appeared in results. Diagnose both, name the exact settings or query clauses involved, and say what you would monitor to catch each before the customer does.
46.proofOfWork: A public 'design dossier' repository that goes beyond the six written designs: (1) a numbers workbook for DefenderMate at 500 tenants in which every capacity figure is derived from a named assumption cell, with a sensitivity column showing what changes at 5,000 tenants and which component saturates first at each scale; (2) an executable slice in docker-compose: Nginx with `least_conn`, upstream `keepalive` and a documented drain sequence, Redis running a Lua sliding-window per-tenant limiter that returns 429 with `Retry-After` and `RateLimit` headers, Postgres with a range-partitioned `llm_calls` table, a streaming replica, and a lag probe reading `pg_stat_replication`, plus an outbox table drained into Redpanda; (3) three k6 scripts that reproduce three failure stories (cache-flush stampede, replica-lag read-your-writes, layered retry storm) with before/after Grafana screenshots showing the mitigation working; and (4) a recorded 45-minute self-run of the DefenderMate design against a timer, scored on a written rubric (requirements, numbers, diagram, two deep dives, failure story) with timestamps for each section. A reviewer can clone the repo, run `make demo`, and watch each failure story happen and then not happen.

47.topic: LLM-era system design: serving, caching, batching, rate limits, retries, latency budgets
47.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
47.why: An LLM call breaks every assumption the classic system design playbook is built on: latency is a function of output length rather than of work done, the dependency is a metered third party that returns 429 and 529 under load you do not control, cost is per request and visible on the customer's invoice, and the response is non-deterministic so a naive retry can double-charge and double-write. As the FDE you are the one who has to tell the customer's architect, before go-live, what p95 will be at their peak, what a request costs, and what the system does when the model provider is degraded for forty minutes. Getting the answer wrong is not an SLO miss, it is a checkout page that hangs on Black Friday and a bill nobody approved.
prerequisites: The system design playbook from topic 42: back-of-envelope estimation, load balancing, cache key design and stampede protection, partitioning, queues, and the 45-minute delivery frame you will now run against an LLM-shaped prompt

FastAPI in production from topic 26 (async event loop, timeouts, graceful shutdown, worker sizing) and Redis from topic 31 (TTL, `maxmemory` eviction, Lua atomicity, token-bucket limiter, idempotency store)
Temporal from topic 34 and Kafka/queues from topic 33: retry policies, activity heartbeats and timeouts, visibility timeout, DLQ, and what an idempotent consumer actually requires

SLIs/SLOs and error budgets from topic 20, OpenTelemetry and Prometheus histograms from topic 21, and k6 load testing from topic 22 so latency claims are measured with `histogram_quantile()` rather than asserted

Working knowledge of the Anthropic Messages API: system vs user blocks, `stream: true` SSE events, `usage.input_tokens` / `output_tokens`, `stop_reason`, and the shape of a 429 vs a 529 (topic 60 goes deeper; the vocabulary is assumed now)

The Kaupex Task Compiler running locally under Docker Compose (FastAPI + Postgres + Temporal + httpx to Claude) with at least a few days of real per-request token counts and durations to anchor the numbers

subtopics.name: The LLM latency model: prefill vs decode, TTFT and TPOT, why p95 tracks output length
subtopics.learn: Internalise that an LLM request has two phases with completely different scaling behaviour: prefill is compute-bound and roughly linear in input tokens, producing time-to-first-token (TTFT); decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and produces one token per forward pass, so total latency is approximately TTFT + output_tokens x TPOT (time-per-output-token). The consequence is that trimming a 4k-token prompt to 2k saves tens of milliseconds while capping `max_tokens` from 1000 to 250 saves seconds; latency is governed by what the model writes, not what you send. Learn to read the four numbers that matter on any serving stack (TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end, queue wait) and to recognise from a latency histogram whether you are queueing (bimodal, flat right tail) or generating long outputs (smooth right tail correlated with `output_tokens`). Record `output_tokens` as an exemplar or label on every latency observation so you can prove which one you are looking at.

resource.label: vLLM docs - Production metrics (TTFT, TPOT, queue time histograms)

subtopics.name: Streaming as a latency product decision: SSE contract, cancellation, and what p95 you publish
subtopics.learn: Decide per endpoint whether the SLI is TTFT or full-completion latency, because streaming changes what the user experiences without changing total work. Know the Anthropic SSE event sequence (`message_start`, `content_block_start`, `content_block_delta`, `content_block_stop`, `message_delta` carrying `stop_reason` and final `usage`, `message_stop`, plus periodic `ping`) and that the token counts only settle on `message_delta`, so cost accounting must happen at the end of the stream, not the start. Handle the two failure cases customers actually hit: a client disconnect mid-stream, where you must propagate cancellation (in httpx, exit the `stream()` context; in FastAPI, detect `await request.is_disconnected()` or catch `asyncio.CancelledError`) or you keep paying for tokens nobody reads; and an error emitted mid-stream after a 200 status, which no HTTP status code will tell you about. Set the proxy correctly: `proxy_buffering off` in Nginx and an idle timeout longer than the longest generation, or the customer's load balancer will cut streams at 60 s.

resource.label: Anthropic docs - Streaming Messages

subtopics.name: Building a per-hop latency budget table and defending it
subtopics.learn: Write the budget as a table before you write code: ingress TLS + auth 15 ms, tenant lookup and RLS query 20 ms, retrieval (embed 40 ms + vector search 60 ms + rerank 120 ms), model call 1800 ms, post-processing and persistence 50 ms, egress 10 ms, leaving explicit slack. Then state the rule that a p95 end-to-end budget is not the sum of per-hop p95s: independent hops compose closer to the sum of means plus a tail allowance, and any hop you retry contributes its timeout, not its median. Set each hop's timeout from the budget (hop timeout = remaining budget, never a global 30 s default) and propagate a deadline down the call chain so a request that has already burned 4 s does not start a fresh 30 s model call. Publish the budget as two SLIs (TTFT and completion) with a stated `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(..._bucket[5m])))` expression so the customer's SRE can verify it on their own Grafana.

resource.label: Google SRE Workbook - Implementing SLOs

subtopics.name: Cost per request: token accounting, the unit-economics formula, and where it silently doubles
subtopics.learn: Write cost per request explicitly as (input_tokens x input_price + output_tokens x output_price + cache_write_tokens x write_price + cache_read_tokens x read_price) / 1e6, then multiply by the hidden multipliers nobody puts in the first draft: retries, an agent loop that makes N model calls per user action, tool-use round trips that resend the entire conversation each turn, and a reranker or judge model called per request. Learn to count tokens before you send with the count-tokens endpoint so you can enforce a per-request ceiling and reject oversized inputs at the edge with a 413-style error rather than discovering them on the invoice. Instrument `usage` from every response into a `llm_calls` table with tenant, feature, model, token counts and cache fields, because 'what does this feature cost per tenant per month' is a question the customer will ask in week two and you cannot answer retroactively.

resource.label: Anthropic docs - Token counting

subtopics.name: Prompt caching: cache_control breakpoints, prefix stability, TTL, and the economics of a hit
subtopics.learn: Understand that prompt caching is a prefix cache: everything before a `cache_control` breakpoint is cached, and a single changed byte anywhere in that prefix invalidates the whole thing. Structure the prompt so the stable material comes first (tool definitions, system instructions, the customer's schema or policy document, few-shot examples) and the volatile material last (retrieved chunks, user turn, timestamps); the classic bug is a rendered `datetime.now()` or a shuffled retrieval order at the top of the prompt driving a permanent 0% hit rate. Know the price asymmetry (a cache write costs more than an uncached token, a cache read costs a small fraction), which means caching is a loss on a one-shot request and a large win on a conversation or a fan-out where the same prefix is reused within the TTL. Verify with `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` in `usage` on every response and alert when the hit ratio drops, because a prompt-template PR is the usual cause of an overnight cost spike.

resource.label: Anthropic docs - Prompt caching

subtopics.name: Response caching: exact-match keys, semantic caching, and why tenant isolation is non-negotiable
subtopics.learn: Layer three caches with different keys and different risks. Exact-match: key = hash(model, prompt_version, normalised_input, temperature, tool_schema_hash) with the tenant id in the key prefix, TTL with jitter, and a stampede lock so a cold key does not fan out; this is safe and boring and should exist first. Semantic: embed the query, nearest-neighbour search, serve the cached answer above a cosine threshold; know that the threshold is a precision/recall dial where a wrong answer is served confidently, so it belongs on FAQ-shaped traffic and never on anything personalised. Understand the correctness trap in both: if the answer depends on retrieved documents, the cache key must include a version of the retrieval corpus or you will serve pre-update answers after the customer uploads a new policy. Never key on user text alone in a multi-tenant system: one tenant seeing another tenant's cached completion is a breach, not a bug.

resource.label: GPTCache - semantic cache for LLM queries (official repo)

subtopics.name: Async batch APIs: 50% cheaper, hours of latency, and the workloads that qualify
subtopics.learn: Learn the Message Batches shape: submit up to tens of thousands of requests with `custom_id` per item, poll `processing_status`, results return unordered as JSONL keyed by `custom_id`, with a completion window measured in hours and roughly half the per-token price. The design skill is classification: nightly re-scoring, backfills, bulk document extraction, eval runs and re-embedding jobs all qualify; anything a human is waiting on does not. Build the plumbing once (a submitter that chunks and records `custom_id` to row-id mapping, a poller with exponential backoff, a results reader that is idempotent because a re-read must not double-write) and reuse it.
