subtopics.learn: Render with Jinja2 using Environment(undefined=StrictUndefined) so a missing or misspelled variable raises at render time instead of silently producing an empty slot - that silent empty slot is the single most common cause of 'the model suddenly got confused'. Never use str.format or f-strings on text that contains JSON braces or the customer's own curly braces. Wrap every injected value in explicit delimiters (<document>...</document>, <tenant_taxonomy>...</tenant_taxonomy>) and strip or escape the closing delimiter out of the value so customer content cannot close your tag and start issuing instructions. Snapshot-test the rendered result: a golden file per (prompt version, fixture) so a one-line template change shows up in review as a rendered-text diff, which is what reviewers can actually reason about.

resource.label: Claude docs - Use XML tags to structure your prompts

subtopics.name: Messages API anatomy: system, turns, prefill, stop_reason
subtopics.learn: Know the request surface cold: POST /v1/messages with model, max_tokens (required, and a truncation risk not a safety net), system as a top-level parameter (string or list of content blocks - there is no role: system message), messages strictly alternating user and assistant, plus temperature, top_p, stop_sequences and metadata.user_id. Force output shape by prefilling: make the final message role assistant with partial content such as '{' or '<analysis>'; the prefill must not end in trailing whitespace or the API rejects it. Branch on stop_reason every single time - end_turn, max_tokens (truncated, never hand it to json.loads), stop_sequence, tool_use, refusal - and persist usage.input_tokens and usage.output_tokens with the trace, because cost regressions are as real as accuracy regressions.

resource.label: Claude API reference - Messages

subtopics.name: Structured output by forced tool use
subtopics.learn: Define exactly one tool whose input_schema is your output contract and set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_finding"} so the model must emit it; then read the tool_use content block's input dict rather than parsing prose or stripping markdown fences. Understand why this beats 'reply with JSON only': the schema travels in the request, decoding is steered toward it, and there is no preamble to strip. Understand the costs too - tool definitions are input tokens on every call, forcing a tool removes the model's ability to abstain, so add an explicit no_finding branch or nullable fields rather than letting it fabricate, and forced tool choice interacts badly with extended thinking. Generate input_schema from your Pydantic model so the schema and the parser can never drift apart. Agentic multi-tool orchestration and MCP are topic 47; here the tool is only a typing mechanism.

resource.label: GitHub - anthropics/anthropic-cookbook (tool use and structured extraction recipes)

subtopics.name: Strict JSON Schema modes and the subset they actually enforce
subtopics.learn: With OpenAI's response_format {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": ..., "schema": ..., "strict": true}}, constrained decoding guarantees the output parses and matches the shape - but only over a subset of JSON Schema: every object needs "additionalProperties": false, every property must appear in required (optionality is expressed as a ["string", "null"] type union, not by omission), and most value constraints (minimum, maxLength, pattern, format) are not enforced by the decoder. Anthropic's strict output-schema mode carries the same class of restriction. The operating rule: the schema guarantees shape, your validator guarantees meaning. Enum values outside a tenant's taxonomy, dates in the wrong century and confidence scores of 1.7 all still arrive as perfectly valid JSON.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform docs - Structured Outputs

subtopics.name: Writing schemas the model reliably obeys
subtopics.learn: Field order is causal: JSON is generated left to right, so {"reasoning": ..., "label": ...} gives you chain-of-thought before the decision while the reverse commits to a label and then rationalises it. Prefer enums over free strings, flat over deeply nested, and avoid anyOf/oneOf unions and recursive definitions, which degrade both adherence and decoder support. Use field descriptions as instructions (they are read by the model), ISO 8601 strings for dates rather than nested date objects, bounded arrays with maxItems, and only include a confidence field if you have written down what the number means and how you will calibrate it. Then test the schema itself: hand-write or generate 20 valid instances and assert your parser accepts every one before you ever call a model.

resource.label: Understanding JSON Schema (json-schema.org)

subtopics.name: Validate, repair once, then fail: the parse boundary
subtopics.learn: Every LLM call site returns a typed object or raises - nothing in between reaches the customer's system of record. Use Pydantic v2 model_validate_json for shape and field_validator / model_validator for semantics that no schema can express: end_date >= start_date, label in this tenant's taxonomy, entity IDs that exist in the customer's database. On ValidationError, feed error.errors() back as one repair turn and stop; an unbounded repair loop is a cost incident waiting to happen. Track repair_rate as a first-class metric next to accuracy - a rising repair rate is the earliest signal of prompt or model drift. The caller, not the parser, decides what a hard failure means: fallback model, queue for human review, or 422 to the customer's integration.

resource.label: Pydantic documentation (v2)

subtopics.name: Determinism controls and model snapshot pinning
subtopics.learn: temperature: 0 is greedy sampling, not determinism - batching, hardware and routing still produce run-to-run variation of roughly one to a few percent on borderline cases, so build for variance instead of pretending it is absent. Pin the dated snapshot string in prompt front-matter (for example claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929) rather than a moving alias, pin the anthropic-version header, set temperature explicitly and leave top_p unset (setting both is discouraged and interacts unpredictably). Make the eval runner record the resolved model id from the response body rather than the one you requested, so an aliased or silently upgraded model shows up in the results file. Treat a model alias in production exactly like :latest on a container image.

resource.label: Claude docs - Models overview (snapshot ids and deprecations)

subtopics.name: Building the regression set: case format, stratification, provenance
subtopics.learn: One JSONL file, one case per line: {id, inputs{}, expected{}, tags[], source, added_at, notes}. Populate from three streams and no others: every production failure the customer has ever reported, converted into a case on the day it is reported; a stratified sample across tenant, document type, language and length so no single slice dominates; and deliberately degenerate inputs (empty document, 200-page document, wrong language, PII-dense, an embedded instruction telling the model to ignore its instructions). A sharp 120-case set beats a vague 1,000-case one. Scrub before committing - real customer text in a fixtures directory is a data-handling problem, so redact, synthesise, or keep fixtures in a separate private store referenced by hash. The source field is what lets you answer 'which incident produced this test' a year later.

resource.label: GitHub - openai/evals (eval registry and JSONL case format)

subtopics.name: Deterministic graders before LLM judges
subtopics.learn: Climb the assertion ladder cheapest-first and stop as soon as it discriminates: schema validity, exact or normalised match on enums and IDs, set precision/recall/F1 for multi-label extraction, numeric tolerance, must-contain and must-not-contain regexes (banned phrases, no leaked system prompt, no 'XXXX' placeholder, no hallucinated URL), JSONPath field equality, and hard ceilings on latency and output tokens. Only genuinely open-ended outputs need a model-graded judge, and that machinery - judge prompts, rubrics, human agreement calibration - is topic 53; do not build it here. Aggregate per tag, never as one number, so the report says 'recall fell only on tenant=acme, doc_type=invoice'. With imbalanced classes report precision and recall per class; accuracy on a 5% positive rate is a number that cannot go down.

resource.label: promptfoo documentation - Introduction

subtopics.name: Baselines, thresholds and a flakiness budget
subtopics.learn: Commit baseline.json holding per-metric and per-tag scores plus the model snapshot, prompt hash and date that produced them. CI compares the current run to the baseline, fails on any regression beyond epsilon, and moving the baseline requires an explicit --accept-baseline commit that a human reviews. Derive epsilon empirically: run the suite three to five times against an unchanged prompt, compute the per-metric standard deviation, and gate at roughly two sigma. A gate tighter than measured noise produces false failures, and a team that sees four false failures marks the check non-required - at which point you have no gate at all. Track per-case flip history: a case that flips on 30% of runs is not a regression signal, it is a bad case, so sharpen it or move it to a flaky tag that reports without gating.

resource.label: pytest documentation

subtopics.name: Running the suite: pytest, concurrency, response caching, cost caps
subtopics.learn: Load cases in conftest.py and drive them with @pytest.mark.parametrize so each case is an individually named test that CI can report by id. Get concurrency from pytest-xdist -n 8 or an asyncio.Semaphore, and honour 429 with exponential backoff plus jitter and the retry-after header rather than hammering. Cache responses keyed on sha256(model + rendered_prompt + params + schema) into a local directory or bucket so re-running an unchanged prompt is free and a reviewer can reproduce the run offline; keep a --no-cache flag for the authoritative run. Emit results.jsonl plus a markdown summary table, and abort the whole run when accumulated usage crosses a configured USD ceiling so a retry loop cannot burn the customer's budget overnight. For large suites, the Message Batches API trades latency for roughly half the cost.

resource.label: pytest how-to - Parametrizing tests

subtopics.name: CI wiring: a gate that runs and does not get switched off
subtopics.learn: A GitHub Actions workflow on pull_request with paths filters ('prompts/**', 'src/llm/**', 'evals/**'), a concurrency group that cancels superseded runs, the API key from repository secrets, permissions scoped to contents: read and pull-requests: write, and never pull_request_target on a repo that takes fork PRs. Run two tiers: a smoke suite of ~20 stratified cases finishing in about a minute as a required check on every PR, and the full suite nightly on schedule plus on-demand via workflow_dispatch. Post the score table as a sticky PR comment showing the delta against baseline, upload results.jsonl as an artifact, and make the failure message name the three worst-regressed case IDs - a red X with no explanation gets overridden, a red X that says 'case inv-0142 flipped from correct to missing_total' gets fixed.

resource.label: GitHub Actions documentation

subtopics.name: The prompt pull request: changelog, review checklist, bisect
subtopics.learn: Keep a CHANGELOG.md per prompt in Keep a Changelog form: version, date, what changed, why (the customer ticket number), the metric delta from the eval run, and the model snapshot it was validated against. Give reviewers a fixed checklist: is the rendered-output diff attached, is the output schema unchanged or was MAJOR bumped, was a new regression case added for the bug being fixed, is the baseline delta explained, is the rollback version named. Because prompts are ordinary files, git log -p prompts/classify/ and git bisect actually work - practise bisecting a twelve-commit range to find which change moved recall on one tenant, because that drill is what converts 'prompts in Git' from a filing convention into a debugging capability.

resource.label: Keep a Changelog 1.1.0

subtopics.name: Runtime registry, rollback and trace linkage
subtopics.learn: At runtime, resolve prompts through a registry keyed by (prompt_id, version) with the active version per environment held in configuration, not in code. Log prompt_id, prompt_version, prompt_hash, model snapshot and schema_version on every call and persist them on the row your application writes - DefenderMate's llm_calls table - so 'which prompt produced this wrong answer in the customer's audit log' is one SQL query rather than an archaeology project. Rollback then means flipping a config value to v(N-1) and redeploying config, which is minutes, not reverting and rebuilding a service. If you adopt a hosted prompt registry such as Langfuse, keep Git as the single source of truth and sync one way into it; two writable sources of truth produce a production prompt that never appeared in any code review.

resource.label: Langfuse documentation (prompt management and tracing)

subtopics.name: Few-shot examples as versioned data, not prose
subtopics.learn: Store examples in examples/<prompt>/*.jsonl with an id per example and render them into <example> blocks at build time, instead of gluing them into the template body where they cannot be diffed, counted or attributed. Enforce four rules: examples must be drawn from the same distribution as production input; the set must include the negative or none-of-the-above case or the model will never emit it; formatting must be internally consistent, because models copy the format of examples far more strongly than they follow prose instructions; and any example used in the prompt is excluded from the regression set, otherwise you are grading on your own training data. Measure marginal value by running the suite at 0, 3 and 8 examples and keeping the smallest set that holds the score - every example is input tokens on every call forever.

resource.label: Claude docs - Use examples (multishot prompting)

subtopics.name: Prompt caching and prefix stability as a tested property
subtopics.learn: Mark cache breakpoints with cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"} on a content block. Caching is prefix-based: everything before the breakpoint must be byte-identical between calls, so a timestamp, a request id, a tenant name or a shuffled example order anywhere in the system prompt silently destroys every hit. Order the request static to dynamic - tools, then system instructions, then long shared documents with the breakpoint after them, then the per-request user content. Verify with usage.cache_creation_input_tokens and usage.cache_read_input_tokens rather than assuming; the minimum cacheable prefix is around 1024 tokens (2048 on the smallest models), the default TTL is five minutes with a one-hour option, and you get at most four breakpoints. Put cache hit rate in the eval report next to accuracy so a prompt edit that quadruples cost fails CI like any other regression.

resource.label: Claude docs - Prompt caching

subtopics.name: Multi-tenant variants without forking the prompt
subtopics.learn: Never create classify_v3_acme.md. Compose instead: one base prompt plus a per-tenant overlay containing only the delta - taxonomy enum values, domain glossary, tone, redaction rules - stored as tenant configuration data and injected into one fixed, clearly delimited slot. The regression set then carries a tenant tag and CI runs base plus every overlay, so a base change that breaks tenant seven fails before merge rather than during their pilot. Enforce overlay limits in code: an overlay may extend enums and glossaries, it may not alter the output schema (that is a base MAJOR bump) and it may not contain text that overrides safety or grounding instructions. Decide deliberately where the overlay sits relative to the cache breakpoint: before it means a per-tenant cache, after it means one shared prefix and cheaper cold starts.

resource.label: Claude docs - Giving Claude a role with a system prompt

subtopics.name: Model migration drill and per-version cost budgets
subtopics.learn: When a new snapshot ships or the customer asks for a cheaper model, you do not 'try it in prod'. Branch, change only the model field in front-matter, run the full suite with response caching disabled, and produce a three-column table - old, new, delta - per tag, plus p50/p95 latency and input/output tokens and USD per case computed from usage (or estimated up front with the count-tokens endpoint, which is free and lets you price a change before spending). Expect specific breakages: prompts that leaned on prefill or brittle formatting, few-shot sets over-fitted to the previous model's verbosity, and stricter refusal behaviour on customer documents that read as adversarial. Record a per-prompt token budget in front-matter and fail CI when a version exceeds it, keep the previous snapshot pinned and runnable for instant rollback, and diary the published deprecation date sixty days ahead.

resource.label: Claude docs - Token counting

outcomes: You can take any row in DefenderMate's llm_calls table and recover the exact prompt text, model snapshot and output schema that produced it, from Git, using only the logged prompt_id, prompt_version and prompt_hash.

You can run the smoke suite on a prompt change in under two minutes and get a per-tag score table with the delta against a committed baseline and the id of every case that flipped in either direction.

You can open a pull request that edits a prompt and have CI block the merge on a regression larger than two sigma, with the three worst-regressed case IDs named in the failure output and a sticky score comment on the PR.

You can return a validated typed object from every LLM call site, with schema violations counted as a repair_rate metric and semantic violations (bad enum, impossible date, unknown entity id) caught by validators rather than written into the customer's database.

You can convert a customer bug report into a labelled regression case, reproduce the failure locally, fix the prompt and show before/after scores on both that case and the full set within a single working session.
You can quantify a proposed model swap in one command: accuracy delta per tag, p50/p95 latency, tokens and USD per 1,000 documents, and the list of cases that only the old model gets right.
You can onboard a new tenant's taxonomy as an overlay without editing the base prompt, and prove from the CI run that every other tenant's scores were unchanged.
You can show a cache read/creation token ratio above 80% on the shared prefix and name three specific edits that would drop it to zero.
failureModes: A prompt is tweaked to satisfy one loud customer complaint and shipped without an eval run; recall on the other three document types drops five points and nobody notices until the customer's monthly summary shows findings that stopped appearing two weeks earlier.

The same system prompt exists as an f-string in three services and has drifted into three different versions, so the incident review cannot establish which text produced the output the customer is angry about.

Production pins a moving model alias rather than a dated snapshot; the alias advances, output formatting shifts slightly, the downstream parser starts writing nulls into the customer's CRM overnight, and there is no deploy in the timeline to correlate against.

The regression set was assembled from cases the current prompt already passes, so it reads 100% forever, provides zero signal on every PR, and the first genuine edge case is still discovered by the customer.

Someone prepends a timestamp or the tenant name to the system prompt for 'better context'; cache hit rate goes to zero, per-document cost quadruples, and it surfaces a month later as a billing question rather than as a failing test.

The eval gate is set at exactly the baseline with no noise allowance, produces four false failures in a fortnight, and is quietly removed from required checks - after which prompt changes merge unreviewed and the gate exists only in the runbook.

Real customer PDFs are committed as eval fixtures to make runs reproducible; the repo is later shared with a partner team or a contractor and a reproducibility decision has become a data-handling breach under the customer's DPA.
interviewQuestions: Three customers each need a slightly different classification taxonomy on the same extraction prompt. Walk me through your versioning design: what lives in Git, what lives in tenant config, what forces a major version bump, how CI proves a base-prompt change did not break tenant two, and how you stop this becoming three forked prompts in six months.

A customer says the extractor 'got worse this week' and you have no eval set. What do you do in the first hour, what do you do in the first day, and what do you put in place so that next time this question is answerable in five minutes with evidence?

Your structured output is a forced tool call with a JSON schema. The model returns valid JSON that is semantically wrong: a date in the wrong field and an enum value that does not exist in that tenant's taxonomy. Tell me exactly where each of those is caught, what the caller does in each case, and what you would have to change if the customer required zero human review.

Design the CI gate for prompt changes end to end. What is the pass threshold and how did you choose the number, what is fast enough to be a required check on every PR versus what runs nightly, what stops it burning money, and what specifically prevents the team from marking it non-required after the third false failure?

A new model snapshot is announced that is 40% cheaper and the customer wants it in production next week. Give me the migration plan, the evidence you would put in front of their engineering lead, and the two things you expect to break that will not show up as a schema error.

Explain prompt caching to a customer's architect who believes it is a semantic cache that will answer similar questions for free. What is actually cached, what invalidates it, how do you measure hit rate from the API response, and give me a one-line prompt change that quietly destroys it.

Your regression set has 200 cases and 12 of them flip between runs at temperature 0. Explain why that happens mechanically, and tell me what you do with each of those 12 - because 'set temperature lower' is not an answer.
50.proofOfWork: A public repository (`defendermate-prompts`, or the `prompts/` package extracted from DefenderMate) that a stranger can clone and exercise in under five minutes with a single `make eval`, including a fake-provider mode that needs no API key so a reviewer can run it for free. It contains: `prompts/<id>/vN.md` files with YAML front-matter (dated model snapshot, sampling params, declared variables, token budget, output schema reference) and a per-prompt `CHANGELOG.md`; `schemas/` with Pydantic v2 models that generate the JSON Schemas used as tool `input_schema`, so parser and schema cannot drift; `evals/cases/*.jsonl` with at least 120 labelled cases tagged by tenant, document type and difficulty, each carrying a `source` field so the handful that originated in real bug reports are traceable, all scrubbed or synthesised; a grader module implementing the deterministic assertion ladder with per-tag precision and recall; `baseline.json` plus a `bin/eval` runner with response caching, bounded concurrency, a USD cost ceiling and an explicit `--accept-baseline` path; and a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the smoke suite on `pull_request` behind path filters and posts a sticky score-delta comment. The README shows one real pull request where the gate failed, the failure message naming the regressed case IDs, and the follow-up commit that fixed it, alongside a short `MIGRATION.md` recording an actual model-snapshot swap with the old-versus-new table for accuracy per tag, p95 latency, tokens and USD per 1,000 documents. The thing that convinces an interviewer is not the harness - it is the CHANGELOG showing eight prompt versions, each with a metric delta and the customer ticket that motivated it.

51.topic: Tool use, structured outputs and MCP servers
51.why: Tool use is the seam where an FDE's work actually touches the customer: the model stops describing what it would do and starts writing into their HubSpot, their Snowflake, their ticketing system, inside their network, under their auth. An MCP server is the deliverable form of that seam - a small, reviewable process whose tool list is the exact set of capabilities you are asking the customer's security team to approve, and whose input schemas are the only thing standing between a hallucinated argument and a mutation of production data. Getting this right is the difference between a pilot that clears security review in a week and one that dies in it, so the FDE skill here is not 'can you call an API from an LLM' but 'can you draw the trust boundary, defend every arrow across it, and prove with tests that the server does nothing else'.
prerequisites: OAuth 2.x, OIDC and JWT validation from 'Auth: OAuth2, OIDC, JWT, RBAC, multi-tenant claims' (topic 27): authorization code flow with PKCE, what the aud, iss and exp claims mean, JWKS-based signature verification, and token introspection - the MCP authorization spec is a profile over these, not a new idea.

FastAPI/ASGI production shape from topic 26: lifespan startup and shutdown, dependency injection, settings via environment, and how you mount a sub-application - the Streamable HTTP MCP server is an ASGI app you will mount next to your existing routes.

pytest and contract testing from 'Testing and contracts' (topic 35): fixtures, parametrisation, async test support, and the idea that a schema is a contract you can assert on in CI rather than a comment.

Structured-output discipline from 'Prompt engineering as code' (topic 46): versioned prompts, regression sets and the habit of pinning a JSON Schema and diffing outputs against it - a tool description is a prompt and needs the same treatment.

HTTP and TLS mechanics from topic 2 plus SSE from 'Real-time transports' (topic 32): request framing, Content-Type and Accept negotiation, Origin and CORS, and what a text/event-stream response actually looks like on the wire.

The LLM-serving constraints from 'LLM-era system design' (topic 43): token and request rate limits, 429 with retry-after, retries with jitter, idempotency keys - your tools sit between a retrying agent loop and a customer API with a hard quota.
Python 3.10+ with async/await and Pydantic v2 model definitions, plus uv or pip, since the MCP Python SDK derives every input schema from type hints and Pydantic models.

subtopics.name: The trust boundary: name the five parties and the four attackers
subtopics.learn: Before writing code, draw the deployment: the human user, the host application (Claude Desktop, an IDE, your agent), the MCP client inside it, your MCP server, and the upstream system (the customer's CRM or database). Then name what crosses each arrow and who can lie on it. Four concrete attackers: a malicious or compromised server sending poisoned tool descriptions into the model's context; untrusted data returned by a tool that the model treats as instructions; a confused-deputy attack where your server holds a static upstream client_id and forwards consent it never obtained; and a stolen or misdirected token that your server accepts because it never validated the audience. Write the sentence you will say to a customer security reviewer: 'the server can do exactly these seven things, with these scopes, on behalf of this authenticated user, and every call is logged with the caller identity.' Everything later in this topic is a mechanism that makes one clause of that sentence true.

resource.label: MCP Specification - Authorization: Security Considerations (confused deputy, token passthrough, SSRF, session hijacking)

subtopics.name: JSON-RPC 2.0 framing and the MCP method surface
subtopics.learn: MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0 and nothing more exotic, so learn the envelope cold: a request has jsonrpc, id, method, params; a response has jsonrpc, id and exactly one of result or error; a notification has no id and gets no response. Memorise the reserved error codes you will actually see - -32700 parse error, -32600 invalid request, -32601 method not found, -32602 invalid params, -32603 internal error - and know that MCP partitions the server-error range: -32000 to -32019 stay implementation-defined while -32020 to -32099 are reserved for the spec (HeaderMismatch -32020, MissingRequiredClientCapability -32021, UnsupportedProtocolVersion -32022). Learn the method surface by heart: server/discover, tools/list, tools/call, resources/list, resources/read, resources/templates/list, prompts/list, prompts/get, subscriptions/listen, plus notifications/progress, notifications/cancelled and notifications/message. Be able to hand-write a tools/call request and read a raw frame from a log without an SDK.

resource.label: JSON-RPC 2.0 Specification

subtopics.name: Protocol eras: what 2026-07-28 removed, and why the customer's client is older
subtopics.learn: The protocol went stateless in the 2026-07-28 revision and you must be able to explain both sides of the change. Gone: the initialize / notifications/initialized handshake, the Mcp-Session-Id header, SSE resumability via Last-Event-ID, ping, logging/setLevel, and server-initiated JSON-RPC requests. In their place: every request carries _meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, clientInfo and clientCapabilities; server/discover advertises supported versions and capabilities up front; subscriptions/listen is the single opt-in stream for toolsListChanged, promptsListChanged, resourcesListChanged and resourceSubscriptions; results carry a required resultType of complete or input_required. Roots, Sampling and Logging are deprecated (SEP-2577). Now the FDE part: a customer running a client pinned to 2025-06-18 or 2025-11-25 still expects initialize and a session header, so read the versioning and backward-compatibility rules and decide explicitly whether your server serves legacy clients, and record that decision in the README.

resource.label: MCP Specification 2026-07-28 - Key Changes (changelog)

subtopics.name: Transports: stdio subprocess versus Streamable HTTP
subtopics.learn: Know the two bindings and when each is right. stdio: the client launches your server as a subprocess, messages are newline-delimited UTF-8 JSON on stdin/stdout, and the single rule that breaks more servers than anything else is that you MUST NOT write anything to stdout that is not an MCP message - a stray print() or a logging handler defaulting to stdout corrupts the stream, so send every log line to stderr. Credentials on stdio come from the environment, not OAuth. Streamable HTTP: one endpoint path serving POST, Accept must list both application/json and text/event-stream, a JSON-RPC request gets back either a single JSON object or a request-scoped SSE stream, and notifications/responses get 202 Accepted with no body. Two security musts before you expose it: validate the Origin header on every request to block DNS-rebinding from a web page, and bind to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0 when running locally. Learn the Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name request headers that mirror body fields for intermediaries, and that the body remains the source of truth.

resource.label: MCP Specification - Streamable HTTP transport binding

subtopics.name: Designing narrow tools: naming, descriptions, annotations, token budget
subtopics.learn: A tool list is a prompt, and a bad one costs tokens on every single turn. Design rules to apply and be able to defend: one verb-noun name per capability (hubspot_find_contact_by_email, not hubspot_query), names 1-128 characters and case-sensitive; a description that states what it does, what it will not do, and when the model should prefer a sibling tool; a title for human UI and description for the model. Use annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) to let hosts gate confirmation prompts - and know the spec's rule that clients MUST treat annotations as untrusted unless the server is trusted, so they are a hint to the host, never your authorisation mechanism. Prefer five narrow tools over one tool with a mode enum, because narrow tools are what a security reviewer can approve individually and what the model picks correctly. Serve tools/list in a deterministic order so clients can cache and prompt-cache hit rates hold. Count the tokens your tool list costs and treat 20+ tools as a design smell to be solved with scoping, not with a longer list.

resource.label: MCP Specification - Server Features: Tools

subtopics.name: inputSchema as the validation boundary, not documentation
subtopics.learn: The inputSchema is JSON Schema (2020-12 when no $schema is present) and it is the only thing between a model's guess and your upstream API. Write it so invalid calls fail before your function body runs: type: object with additionalProperties: false so a hallucinated extra field is rejected rather than silently dropped, explicit required, enum for closed sets, format: date / email / uri, minimum/maximum and minLength/maxLength on anything that becomes a query, and a description on every property because that string is what the model reads when choosing arguments. For a tool with no parameters, use {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": false} rather than an empty or null schema. In the Python SDK the type hints are the schema - a limit: int is rejected before your code sees "ten" - and Annotated[..., Field(description=..., ge=..., le=...)] is how you add constraints. Then internalise the limit: schema validation is a type check, not authorisation; tenant_id must never be a tool argument the model can set.

resource.label: JSON Schema - Understanding JSON Schema: object (properties, required, additionalProperties)

subtopics.name: outputSchema and structuredContent, and why it is not 'LLM structured output'
subtopics.learn: A tool result has two channels and they serve different consumers. content is the array the model reads (text, image, audio, resource_link, embedded resource); structuredContent is a JSON object the client application consumes programmatically. If you declare an outputSchema, the server MUST return structured results conforming to it and clients SHOULD validate - so the schema becomes a contract you can regression-test. For backwards compatibility, also serialise the same JSON into a TextContent block. Learn the distinction that trips people up in interviews: structuredContent is server-produced result data, unrelated to schema-constrained model generation; one is your API's response type, the other is a decoding constraint on the model. In the Python SDK, declaring a Pydantic model or a dataclass as the return annotation generates the outputSchema and fills structured_content for you, and a bare -> str is wrapped as {"result": ...}. Design the payload for the model, not for your database: return the three fields it needs and a resource_link for the rest, not a 40-key row.

resource.label: MCP Python SDK - Structured Output

subtopics.name: The client side: the tool_use loop end to end
subtopics.learn: Build the loop once by hand so you can debug it anywhere. Send a request with a tools array of {name, description, input_schema}; the response comes back with stop_reason: "tool_use" and a tool_use content block carrying id, name and input; you execute it and append a user message containing a tool_result block whose tool_use_id matches, with content and is_error where relevant; you resend the whole conversation. Know the controls: tool_choice of auto, any, tool or none; disabling parallel tool use when your upstream cannot handle concurrent writes; and that tool definitions sit at the front of the prompt so marking them with cache_control makes prompt caching pay for itself on multi-turn loops. Know the failure signatures: a missing tool_result for an emitted tool_use is a hard API error, not a warning; a tool result that is 50 KB of JSON blows the context window three turns later; and the model retrying the same failing call forever is what you get when is_error carries no actionable message.

resource.label: Claude Developer Platform - Handle tool calls

subtopics.name: Constrained decoding: when to force the shape of the model's output
subtopics.learn: Separate two mechanisms that both get called 'structured output'. Tool calling gets you a typed call to a function; constrained decoding gets you a response body that provably parses against a schema. Learn what each provider guarantees and what it costs: Claude's structured outputs and strict tool use both restrict which JSON Schema keywords are honoured, and unsupported keywords are ignored rather than enforced, so read the supported-subset list before you rely on a regex or a nested anyOf. The equivalent on OpenAI's API is response_format with type json_schema and strict: true, which requires additionalProperties: false and every key listed in required. Decide by consumer: if a human or a downstream service parses it, constrain it; if the model itself is going to read it back next turn, plain text is often cheaper and less brittle. Always keep a parse-failure path - schema-constrained does not mean semantically correct, and a refusal or a truncated max_tokens still yields unparseable output.

resource.label: Claude Developer Platform - Structured outputs

subtopics.name: Errors: three kinds, and which one the model is supposed to fix
subtopics.learn: There are exactly three failure classes and choosing wrong is a production bug. (1) A recoverable business error - record not found, bad argument value - is a successful JSON-RPC response with isError: true and a message the model can act on ('No contact with that email; try searching by domain'); in the Python SDK that is raise ToolError(...). Never return an error string, because is_error stays false and every client renders it as a successful answer. (2) A protocol error - unknown tool, invalid params, unsupported version - is a JSON-RPC error object with a code; the host sees it, the model does not; in the SDK that is raise MCPError(code=INVALID_PARAMS, ...). (3) An unexpected crash is neither: the SDK sanitises it into a generic internal error over the wire so you do not leak stack traces or connection strings to a remote caller, and the traceback goes to your log. Map upstream HTTP statuses deliberately: 404 to ToolError, 401/403 to a protocol error the host can act on by re-authorising, 429 to a ToolError that names the retry-after so the agent backs off instead of hammering the customer's quota.

resource.label: MCP Python SDK - Handling errors (ToolError vs MCPError)

subtopics.name: Resources, prompts, pagination and cacheable results
subtopics.learn: Know the three primitives and who controls each: tools are model-controlled, resources are application/user-controlled context addressed by URI (including URI templates like hubspot://contact/{id}), and prompts are user-invoked templates - which is why a slash-command workflow belongs in prompts/get, not in a tool. Implement cursor pagination on every list and read endpoint: return an opaque nextCursor, never an offset, and treat the cursor as an implementation detail clients must not parse. Learn the 2026-07-28 caching contract: tools/list, prompts/list, resources/list, resources/read and resources/templates/list results carry ttlMs (freshness hint in milliseconds) and cacheScope of public or private, and getting cacheScope wrong on a per-tenant result is how one customer's data ends up cached by a shared intermediary and served to another. Pair TTLs with the listChanged notification rather than choosing one.

resource.label: MCP Specification - Server Utilities: Caching (ttlMs and cacheScope)

subtopics.name: Long-running work: progress, cancellation, MRTR and the tasks extension
subtopics.learn: A tool that takes 90 seconds needs a plan, because the client will otherwise time out and the agent will retry into a duplicate write. Learn the four mechanisms. notifications/progress flows on the response stream of the request it relates to, so emit it with a monotonically increasing progress and a total when you know it. Cancellation is transport-specific: notifications/cancelled on stdio, closing the response stream on Streamable HTTP - so your handler must actually observe cancellation (asyncio.CancelledError) and roll back or mark the upstream write. Multi Round-Trip Requests replaced server-initiated requests: to ask the user something mid-tool you return resultType: "input_required" with inputRequests (for example an elicitation/create with a requestedSchema) plus an opaque requestState, and the client retries the original call with inputResponses and a new JSON-RPC id. For genuinely long jobs, use the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension with tasks/get polling and tasks/update, rather than holding a stream open. Make every mutating tool idempotent on a caller-supplied key so a retried call is a no-op.

resource.label: MCP Specification - Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR)

subtopics.name: Build it: MCPServer, typed handlers, lifespan and dependencies
subtopics.learn: Install with uv add "mcp[cli]", create an MCPServer, and register tools with @mcp.tool() on plain typed functions - the name comes from the function, the model-facing description from the docstring, the schema from the type hints. Run it two ways and know the difference: uv run mcp dev server.py to open the Inspector against a stdio subprocess, and uv run mcp run server.py --transport streamable-http to serve HTTP. Put every expensive or connection-owning object in the lifespan - an httpx.AsyncClient with explicit timeouts and connection limits, a database pool, a cached OAuth token - so it is created once at startup and closed on shutdown, and reach it from handlers via the Context / dependency mechanism rather than a module-level global. Use Context for progress and per-request logging. Structure the repo so business logic is a plain, importable Python package and the MCP layer is a thin adapter over it; that is what lets you unit-test the logic and contract-test the protocol separately, and what lets you expose the same logic as a REST endpoint when the customer asks.

resource.label: MCP Python SDK - Lifespan (startup, shutdown, shared state)

subtopics.name: Auth: your server is an OAuth 2.1 resource server, nothing more
subtopics.learn: For HTTP transports, MCP authorization is a profile over OAuth 2.1 and you must be able to walk it on a whiteboard. Your server is a resource server: it never signs anyone in and never mints a token. It MUST publish OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) containing authorization_servers, and MUST return 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header pointing at that metadata URL. The client discovers the authorization server, reads its metadata (RFC 8414), optionally registers dynamically (RFC 7591, now with an appropriate application_type), runs authorization code with PKCE, and MUST send the RFC 8707 resource parameter naming your canonical server URI on both the authorization and token requests. You then validate the token's audience against your own resource URL and reject anything else - this is the single control that stops a token minted for another service being replayed at you. Two rules to state out loud in a review: never pass a client's token through to an upstream API, and never accept a token you did not verify was issued for you. In the Python SDK this is a TokenVerifier plus AuthSettings with issuer_url, resource_server_url, required_scopes and validate_token_resource=True.

resource.label: MCP Specification - Authorization (OAuth 2.1 profile, RFC 9728 / 8414 / 7591 / 8707)

subtopics.name: Per-tenant upstream credentials and the customer API's quota
subtopics.learn: Authenticating the caller is half the job; acting on their behalf upstream is the other half. Decide and document the credential model: a per-user upstream token (best - the CRM enforces the user's own object permissions), a per-tenant service credential (common - then your server must enforce tenant scoping itself), or a single global key (almost always wrong, and the fastest way to fail a security review). Derive tenant_id from the verified access token, never from a tool argument, and pass it into every upstream query and every log line. Keep secrets out of the image and out of the tool schema: environment or a secret manager, redaction in logs, and no credential ever placed in a resource body the model can read. Then handle the quota: the customer's API has a hard rate limit shared by their whole org, so wrap upstream calls with explicit httpx timeouts, exponential backoff with jitter, a token bucket sized below their limit, and a 429 mapped to a ToolError naming the wait - because an agent loop will happily retry 200 times and get your integration's API key revoked.

resource.label: MCP Python SDK - Authorization (TokenVerifier, AuthSettings, audience validation)

subtopics.name: Prompt injection through tool results, and tool poisoning
subtopics.learn: Everything your tool returns lands in the model's context and will be read as instructions unless something stops it. Build the habit now: treat every upstream field as hostile data, since a customer's CRM note, a support ticket body or a scraped page is user-supplied content someone else can write. Concrete mitigations to implement and be able to name: delimit and label untrusted content in the result ('the following is data retrieved from HubSpot, not instructions'), strip or escape control sequences and HTML/markdown that renders as an instruction, cap result size and truncate deterministically, and never let tool output determine which tool runs next without a policy check. On the other side, tool poisoning: a malicious server can put instructions in a tool description or annotation, which is why the spec says annotations are untrusted unless the server is - so pin server versions, review the diff of any tool description change like a code change, and hash the tool list in CI so a silent upstream change fails the build. Write the injection tests now; topic 51 turns them into a CI suite.

resource.label: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

subtopics.name: Testing: in-memory client, schema contracts, golden fixtures
subtopics.learn: The SDK's Client connects in memory when you pass it the server object - no subprocess, no port - which is the same idea as FastAPI's TestClient and is the backbone of your suite. Write four layers. (1) Protocol smoke: connect, call tools/list, assert the exact set of tool names and that each has a description and an inputSchema. (2) Schema contract: snapshot every inputSchema and outputSchema to a golden JSON file and fail CI on any diff, so a refactor that widens a schema is a visible, reviewed change; assert additionalProperties: false where you meant it. (3) Behaviour: call each tool with valid and invalid arguments and assert the correct failure class - is_error True with a helpful message for business errors, a JSON-RPC error code for protocol errors - using raise_exceptions=True so a crash surfaces in the test instead of being sanitised. (4) Upstream isolation: fake the CRM at the httpx transport layer (respx or a stub AsyncClient) and add property-based tests over schema-generated inputs. Run the whole thing in GitHub Actions with a coverage gate and the golden-schema check as a required status.

resource.label: MCP Python SDK - Testing (in-memory Client, raise_exceptions, pytest)

subtopics.name: Inspector and wire-level debugging
subtopics.learn: The Inspector is your customer-site debugging tool and you should be fluent in all three of its clients before you need it under pressure. Use the web UI to browse tools, submit generated forms and read raw JSON-RPC frames; use the CLI (npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli) to script method calls with deterministic output and exit codes so the same checks run in CI; use the protocol-eras behaviour to confirm what your server does when a legacy client connects. Learn the standard debugging ladder: reproduce with the Inspector CLI first (it removes the host from the equation), then read stderr (on stdio, your only log channel), then capture the HTTP exchange. Know the top three silent failures and their signatures - a print() to stdout corrupting a stdio stream, a missing Origin check or CORS header making a browser-based client fail with no server-side error, and an OAuth 401 loop where the WWW-Authenticate header or the resource metadata URL is wrong. Keep a `make inspect` target in the repo so a customer engineer can reproduce your findings.

resource.label: MCP Inspector - CLI client (scripting, output formats, exit codes, CI recipes)

subtopics.name: Ship it: stateless deploy, tracing and publishing
subtopics.learn: Because the protocol is stateless, a Streamable HTTP server scales like any other web service - multiple replicas behind a normal load balancer with no sticky sessions - provided you kept no per-connection state; any cross-call state must be an explicit, server-minted handle passed back as an ordinary tool argument. Containerise with a multi-stage build, a non-root user and a pinned lockfile (topic 6), expose one port, add a plain HTTP health endpoint alongside the MCP endpoint, and set resource limits. Wire observability that answers customer questions: propagate OpenTelemetry trace context via the _meta keys traceparent, tracestate and baggage, emit a span per tools/call with tool name, tenant, duration, outcome and upstream status, and log an audit line per mutating call with caller identity. Then publish: a server.json for the MCP registry, semantic versioning, a README that states supported protocol revisions, required scopes and the exact tool list, and a SECURITY.md. Deployment and the README are what the customer's platform team reviews, not your handler code.

resource.label: MCP Python SDK - Deploy and scale

outcomes: You can draw the MCP trust boundary for a customer deployment on a whiteboard - user, host, client, server, upstream - and for each arrow name what crosses it, who authenticates it, and one concrete attack it enables if unprotected.

You can hand-write a valid tools/call JSON-RPC request and its two possible failure responses (a -32602 protocol error object versus a result with isError: true) without an SDK, and say which one the model is meant to recover from.

You can build a Streamable HTTP MCP server that validates Origin, publishes RFC 9728 protected resource metadata, returns 401 with a correct WWW-Authenticate header, and rejects a token whose audience is not your canonical server URI - demonstrated by a test that passes a valid token and one issued for another resource.
You can write a tool whose inputSchema rejects an unknown field, a wrong type and an out-of-range value before your handler body runs, and show the three rejections in test output.
You can declare an outputSchema, return conforming structuredContent plus a serialised TextContent fallback, and fail CI when a schema changes by diffing against a golden snapshot.

You can explain in one minute what the 2026-07-28 revision removed (initialize handshake, Mcp-Session-Id, SSE resumability, server-initiated requests) and state whether your server supports legacy clients and why.

You can debug a broken integration at a customer site using only the Inspector CLI and stderr, and identify a stdout-corrupted stdio stream, a missing Origin check, and an OAuth discovery misconfiguration from their distinct symptoms.
You can run a mutating tool twice with the same idempotency key against a stubbed upstream and show a single write, and show that a 429 becomes a backoff rather than a retry storm.
failureModes: A logging handler defaults to stdout in a stdio server, so one INFO line lands between two JSON-RPC frames, the client's parser dies mid-session, and the customer reports 'the integration randomly disconnects' with nothing in your logs because the log line was the bug.

The server accepts any signed JWT without checking the audience, so a token the customer's IdP minted for their internal analytics API is replayed at the MCP endpoint and grants full CRM tool access to a service that was never approved for it.

tenant_id is exposed as a tool argument because it made testing easier; the model, given a prompt containing another company's name, passes that tenant's id, and a multi-tenant data leak is discovered by the customer rather than by you.

A contact-search tool returns the full CRM record - 40 fields including notes - so three tool calls into an agent loop the context window is exhausted, the earliest turns are dropped, and the model starts re-calling tools it already called and duplicating writes.

A tool returns a business error as a plain string instead of raising, so isError stays false, the client UI shows 'Contact not found' as a successful result, and the agent proceeds to create a duplicate record on top of the one it failed to find.

A tool description is quietly changed upstream when a dependency is bumped, the model starts preferring a destructive tool over a read-only sibling, and nothing catches it because tool descriptions were never treated as reviewable, hash-pinned artifacts.

An agent retries a failing upstream call without jitter or a budget, burns the customer's shared API quota inside ten minutes, and their platform team disables the integration's key during business hours for every other consumer of that API.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through the trust boundary of an MCP server you would deploy inside a customer's VPC against their CRM. Who authenticates whom, where does the upstream credential live, and what exactly stops a prompt injection in a CRM note from causing a write to a different record?

Your MCP server is an OAuth 2.1 resource server. Trace the full flow from a client's first unauthenticated request to a successful tools/call: which metadata documents are fetched, what the resource parameter is for, what you validate on the token, and what you would deliberately not do with it.

A customer says the integration 'randomly drops' about once an hour. It is a stdio server behind Claude Desktop and there is nothing in your application log. How do you diagnose it, and what are the three most likely causes in order?

Design the tool surface for an agent that manages a customer's support tickets: create, update, escalate, close, search. How many tools, what are their schemas, which are annotated destructive, and how do you make the mutating ones safe to retry when the agent loop resends a call?

Explain the difference between a tool's outputSchema with structuredContent and schema-constrained model generation. When would you use each, and what does each actually guarantee about the bytes you receive?

The 2026-07-28 revision made MCP stateless and removed the initialize handshake and session header. What did that buy operationally, what did it cost, and how would you serve a customer whose client is pinned to an older revision without forking the server?

You inherit an internal MCP server with 34 tools that a customer's security team has rejected. How do you get it approved in two weeks - what do you cut, what do you instrument, and what document do you hand them?
51.proofOfWork: A written security and integration review of somebody else's MCP server - pick a non-trivial one from the modelcontextprotocol/servers repository or any public server your target companies would plausibly deploy - published as a repo or dashboard page, in the form a customer would receive from an FDE. It contains: (1) a one-page trust-boundary diagram with every arrow labelled by what crosses it, who authenticates it, and the concrete attack it enables if unprotected; (2) a tool-surface audit table listing every tool with its annotations, whether the inputSchema actually constrains (additionalProperties, enums, bounds) or merely documents, the token cost of the full tools/list payload, and a recommended cut list with reasoning; (3) reproducible findings driven by the Inspector CLI and a small pytest harness using the in-memory Client - each finding with the exact command, the raw JSON-RPC frames, and a pass/fail assertion, covering at minimum audience validation, Origin handling, error-class correctness (isError versus JSON-RPC error), result size, and behaviour on a malformed argument; (4) one deliberate injection test where a fixture puts instruction-shaped text in an upstream field and you show whether the result is delimited and labelled or passed through raw; (5) a protocol-era compatibility note stating which revisions the server serves and what breaks on the others; and (6) an upstream pull request or issue implementing or reporting the highest-severity finding, linked from the review. The review must be readable by a security engineer who has never used MCP, and it demonstrates the FDE skill the deliverable repo alone does not: evaluating and defending someone else's integration in front of a customer.

52.topic: Agents: workflows vs agents, planning, memory, multi-agent, human-in-the-loop
52.why: An FDE's first week at a customer is spent listening to a process described in human sentences ('then Maya checks the ticket against the SOP and pings legal if it is over 50k') and deciding which of those sentences becomes a switch statement, which becomes one templated LLM call with a strict schema, and which genuinely needs a model choosing its own next action. Getting that boundary wrong is the most expensive mistake in AI delivery: an agent where a workflow would do costs ten to twenty times the tokens, has no enumerable failure set, and cannot be signed off by a risk committee; a workflow where an agent was needed produces a brittle graph that snaps on the first input the customer's business did not describe to you. You will defend this line in a room with a customer architect who has read a vendor deck and wants 'agentic' on the roadmap, so the decision criteria, the cost arithmetic and the fallback design have to be in your head, not in a bookmark.
prerequisites: Tool-use mechanics from 'Tool use, structured outputs and MCP servers' (topic 47): you can already define a tool with a JSON Schema `input_schema`, parse a `tool_use` block, return a `tool_result` with the matching `tool_use_id`, and force a call with `tool_choice`. This topic is about the loop around those calls, not the calls themselves.

Prompt engineering as code from topic 46: prompts live in version control, have a regression set, and produce structured output. An agent's system prompt and each tool description are the same kind of artifact and get the same treatment.

LLM fundamentals from topic 45: tokenisation, the context window as a hard limit, cost per million input and output tokens, and the fact that latency scales with output tokens, not input. Every cost argument in this topic is arithmetic on those numbers.

Temporal at depth from topic 34: signals, queries, updates, `workflow.wait_condition`, retry policies, activity determinism constraints and saga compensations. Durable human-in-the-loop is a Temporal problem before it is an LLM problem.

Observability from topic 21: spans, attributes, context propagation across process boundaries, and how a trace gets from a worker into Grafana. An agent run is a trace with a span per step, and without it you cannot answer 'why did this run cost forty dollars'.
Multi-tenant data modelling from topic 30: row-level security, PII classification, audit trails. Agent memory is customer data in a new shape and inherits every one of those obligations.

subtopics.name: The workflow/agent boundary as a definition, not a vibe
subtopics.learn: Learn the operational split: a workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; an agent lets the model direct its own process, choosing how many steps to take and when to stop. Be able to state the two structural consequences out loud: in a workflow you can enumerate every path and write a test per path, so the failure set is finite; in an agent the path is runtime data, so your only real handles are the tool surface, the stopping condition and the trace. Internalise the default rule - find the simplest thing that works and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes - and be able to say what 'demonstrably' means, which is a held-out task set where the agent's success rate beats the workflow's by more than the cost multiple.

resource.label: Anthropic Engineering - Building effective agents

subtopics.name: The five workflow patterns and the signal that triggers each
subtopics.learn: Learn prompt chaining (task decomposes into fixed subtasks, gate between them), routing (inputs fall into distinct classes that want different prompts or models), parallelisation by sectioning (independent subtasks) and by voting (you want several attempts at the same judgement), orchestrator-workers (subtasks are not known until runtime), and evaluator-optimizer (you have a cheap external signal for 'better'). For each, be able to name the trigger condition in one sentence and the one thing it costs you. Then map them: DefenderMate's classify-then-route webhook path is routing plus a chain, not an agent; the weekly email is sectioned parallelisation; Kaupex's compile-and-publish is a chain with a saga behind it. Practise saying 'that is routing' out loud when a customer describes a fork.

resource.label: LangGraph Docs - Workflows and agents (all five patterns with runnable code)

subtopics.name: The agentic loop, mechanically
subtopics.learn: Write the loop yourself once, no framework: send `messages` plus `tools`; if `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, pull every `tool_use` block (each has `id`, `name`, `input`), execute them, append the assistant's `content` verbatim, then append a user message of `tool_result` blocks keyed by `tool_use_id`, setting `is_error: true` and a human-readable message when a tool fails; repeat while `stop_reason` stays `"tool_use"`. Know that parallel tool calls arrive in one response and that `tool_choice: {"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}` forces one at a time when your side effects are not safe to interleave. Know the server-side loop exists for server tools and hands back `pause_turn` when it hits its own iteration cap.

resource.label: Claude Docs - How tool use works (the agentic loop)

subtopics.name: Termination: stop reasons, iteration caps and token budgets
subtopics.learn: Handle every `stop_reason` explicitly rather than assuming `end_turn`: `max_tokens` (truncated mid-output, often mid-JSON), `stop_sequence`, `tool_use`, `pause_turn` (resend to continue), `refusal`, and `model_context_window_exceeded`. On top of the model's own exits, impose three of your own on every run: a hard iteration cap, a wall-clock deadline, and a cumulative token budget. Decide and implement what happens at each cap - the correct default is fail closed to a human with the partial trace attached, never a silent partial success. Add oscillation detection: if the same tool name and the same normalised arguments appear twice in a row, break and escalate rather than paying for a third identical call.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Stop reasons and fallback

subtopics.name: ReAct: interleaving reasoning and acting
subtopics.learn: Read the original framing: generating a reasoning trace and an action in the same interleaved stream beats acting alone (fewer hallucinated or irrelevant actions) and beats reasoning alone (the model gets grounded by observations). Understand why the trace is not decoration - it is the artifact you hand a customer when they ask why the agent did something, and it is what you grep when a run goes wrong. Know the characteristic failure: the model narrates a sensible plan in the thought and then emits an action that does not match it, which means your evaluation must check the actions taken, not the prose about them.

resource.label: arXiv - ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

subtopics.name: Planning: decomposition, plan artifacts and replanning triggers
subtopics.learn: Learn the difference between plan-then-execute (one planning call produces an ordered list, then execution is mechanical) and interleaved planning (the model replans every step). Make the plan a first-class typed object - a list of steps, each with tool name, arguments and an expected postcondition - because a typed plan can be shown to a human for approval before a single side effect fires, and a prose plan cannot. Define replanning triggers explicitly: a step fails twice, a postcondition check fails, or an observation contradicts an assumption the plan named. The failure to avoid is a plan generated once, displayed proudly, and never revised while execution drifts away from it.

resource.label: Lil'Log - LLM Powered Autonomous Agents (planning, task decomposition)

subtopics.name: Reflection and evaluator-optimizer: where self-critique earns its tokens
subtopics.learn: Learn the shape - a generator call and a separate evaluator call with its own prompt and criteria - and the precondition that makes it work: a cheap external signal for 'better'. A compiler, a test suite, a JSON Schema validator, `EXPLAIN` on generated SQL, or a 4xx from the CRM API all qualify. Self-critique with no external ground truth mostly yields confident rewrites that trade one error for another while doubling cost. Bound the loop at two or three iterations, log the delta on each iteration, and kill the pattern in review if the delta is not measurable on your held-out set.

resource.label: arXiv - Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning

subtopics.name: Tool surface design is the real lever on agent behaviour
subtopics.learn: Learn that you change agent behaviour far more by changing the tools than by adding sentences to the system prompt. Build tools around workflows rather than wrapping every REST endpoint; namespace them (`hubspot_search_contacts`, not `search`); return semantically meaningful values instead of raw UUIDs so the model does not have to join them itself; implement pagination, filtering and truncation with an explicit token budget and a visible `... N more results, refine your filter` marker; and write error strings that tell the model what to do next ('start_date must be ISO-8601, you sent 03/04/2025') rather than a stack trace. Evaluate tools with realistic multi-call tasks and read the transcripts - the rough edges show up as the model retrying the same call with cosmetic variations.

resource.label: Anthropic Engineering - Writing effective tools for AI agents

subtopics.name: Context as a finite resource
subtopics.learn: Treat the context window as a budget with diminishing returns rather than a bucket to fill. Learn the three practical levers: calibrate the system prompt to the altitude between hardcoded if-else logic and vague exhortation; prefer just-in-time retrieval, where the agent holds lightweight identifiers (file paths, record ids, queries) and loads content only when it needs it, over pre-loading everything; and isolate context in sub-agents so a noisy search does not pollute the main thread. Instrument tokens-in per step from the start - a run whose input tokens climb linearly with step count is the normal case, and it is what makes step twenty cost twenty times step one.

resource.label: Anthropic Engineering - Effective context engineering for AI agents

subtopics.name: Short-term memory: compaction, context editing and truncation policy
subtopics.learn: Know the two mechanisms and which side they run on: server-side compaction automatically summarises older conversation content as the run approaches the context limit, and client-side context editing clears specific tool results you nominate. Then do the hard part, which is deciding what must never be summarised away: the original task statement, any human approval already granted, the tenant identifier, the idempotency keys already issued, and the list of side effects already committed. Pin those outside the summarisable region (re-inject them, or keep them in a memory file). Learn to recognise `model_context_window_exceeded` and know it means your truncation policy failed, not that the model is too small.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Compaction

subtopics.name: Long-term memory: files over vectors, scoping and poisoning
subtopics.learn: Learn the file-based memory model: a `memory` tool whose `view`, `create`, `str_replace`, `insert`, `delete` and `rename` commands your application executes against storage you control, with `/memories` as a prefix you map onto a per-tenant directory or table. Implement the security requirements yourself - reject any path that does not resolve inside the memory root (`pathlib.Path.resolve()` then `relative_to()`), cap file size and total store size, and expire files that have not been read in N days. Understand why a readable file tree beats a vector store for agent memory in a customer deployment: deterministic reads, diffable in git, inspectable by the customer's DPO. Understand memory poisoning: one wrong fact written during a bad run is read back forever unless something validates or expires it.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Memory tool

subtopics.name: Prompt caching and the economics of an agent loop
subtopics.learn: Understand why agent loops are the single best case for prompt caching: every step resends the entire conversation, so uncached cost grows roughly quadratically in step count. Learn `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` breakpoints - at most four, with a twenty-block lookback, a five-minute default TTL and an optional `"ttl": "1h"`. Place the breakpoint after the stable prefix (system prompt plus tool definitions plus any fixed context) and never on the last, changing block, which is the classic mistake that produces a cache write on every single step. Verify by reading `cache_read_input_tokens` against `cache_creation_input_tokens` in the `usage` field of each response, not by assuming.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Prompt caching

subtopics.name: Orchestrator-workers: when parallel subagents actually pay
subtopics.learn: Learn the pattern that works in production: a lead agent decomposes the task and spawns subagents that each have their own context window, do read-heavy work in parallel, and return compressed results. Learn its precondition - the work must genuinely parallelise and the results must compress - and its economics: a multi-agent run burns on the order of fifteen times the tokens of a chat, so the task's value has to clear that bar. Learn the concrete prompting requirement: the lead must hand each subagent an explicit objective, output format, tool list and scope boundary, or subagents duplicate each other's searches and return overlapping prose. Learn where it fails: tasks with shared mutable state or tight sequential coupling.

resource.label: Anthropic Engineering - How we built our multi-agent research system

subtopics.name: Choosing a multi-agent topology
subtopics.learn: Learn the menu and the axis that separates the options: subagents (the parent calls a child as a tool and control returns), handoffs (control transfers and does not return), router (classify then dispatch to a fixed path, with no agency after the classification), and plain custom workflow code. The axis is who owns conversation state and whether control comes back. Be able to argue that most 'multi-agent' asks are actually a router plus better tools on one agent, and be able to name what you would need to observe before adding a second agent - typically a tool list that has grown past the point where the model reliably selects, or two genuinely independent context requirements.

resource.label: LangChain Docs - Multi-agent patterns

subtopics.name: Handoffs and shared-state hazards
subtopics.learn: Learn how a handoff is actually implemented - it is exposed to the model as a tool, conventionally named `transfer_to_<agent>`, so agent selection is just tool selection and inherits every tool-description problem. Learn input filters, which strip or trim the history passed to the receiving agent, and the recommended prompt prefix that tells an agent it is part of a handoff system. Then learn the three failure modes to design against: ping-pong, where two agents hand off to each other indefinitely (cap total handoffs per run); context loss, where an aggressive input filter removes the fact the user already approved something; and concurrent writes, where two agents update the same record and the last writer silently wins.

resource.label: OpenAI Agents SDK - Handoffs

subtopics.name: Human-in-the-loop gates: interrupt and resume
subtopics.learn: Learn the mechanics of a pause: `interrupt(payload)` persists graph state through a checkpointer and blocks indefinitely; you resume by re-invoking with `Command(resume=value)` and the same `thread_id`. Learn the rule that catches everyone: on resume the whole node re-executes from its start, so any side effect that ran before the `interrupt()` call happens twice unless it is idempotent - which is why the gate goes before the irreversible tool, not after it. Do not wrap `interrupt()` in try/except, and keep interrupt ordering stable within a node. Implement all four response shapes: approve, edit-then-approve, reject with feedback that goes back into the loop, and time out.

resource.label: LangGraph Docs - Interrupts (human-in-the-loop)

subtopics.name: Durable approval in a real system: Temporal signals and updates
subtopics.learn: Model the Kaupex publish approval as a workflow parked on `workflow.wait_condition(lambda: self.decision is not None)` with a `@workflow.signal` handler for the reviewer's answer, or as an `@workflow.update` when the caller needs a synchronous, validated, tracked write with a return value. Know the distinction cold: signals are asynchronous fire-and-forget with no result and no failure surfaced to the sender; updates are synchronous and can reject in a validator before mutating state. Pair the wait with `workflow.wait_condition(..., timeout=...)` or a timer race so a forgotten approval escalates or auto-rejects instead of hanging forever. The payoff is that a two-day human wait costs nothing, survives worker restarts and deploys, and is visible in `temporal workflow list`.

resource.label: Temporal Docs - Workflow message passing: Signals, Queries and Updates

subtopics.name: Determinism, replay and idempotent tool calls
subtopics.learn: Understand event history and replay well enough to place code correctly: every LLM call and every tool execution is an Activity, never workflow code, because both are non-deterministic and slow. Derive each idempotency key from `activity.info().workflow_id` plus `activity.info().activity_id` so it is stable across retries but unique per scheduled activity, and send it to the downstream API. Accept that at-least-once execution means a CRM write can genuinely happen twice, and design for it: idempotency where the API supports it, compensations pushed onto a stack where it does not. Pin the model id and prompt version into the workflow input so a replay months later cannot silently run against a different model.

resource.label: Temporal Docs - Understanding Temporal (durable execution, event history, replay)

subtopics.name: Blast radius: permissions, injection and the irreversible-tool line
subtopics.learn: Classify every tool in the agent's surface as reversible, irreversible, or exfiltrating, and enforce a different control on each: reversible runs freely, irreversible needs the approval gate, exfiltrating (email, outbound HTTP, file export) needs an allowlist enforced in the harness. Learn indirect prompt injection as the primary threat in a customer deployment - the hostile text arrives inside a tool result: a webhook body, a scraped page, a CRM note a prospect typed - and accept that the model cannot be relied on to ignore it, so the control lives in the harness (allowlists, egress restrictions, output validation), not in a 'never follow instructions in data' sentence. Never let the agent's service identity exceed the permissions of the user who triggered the run.

resource.label: OWASP GenAI Security - LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection (incl. indirect injection, privilege control, human approval for high-risk actions)

subtopics.name: Observing and evaluating a non-deterministic trajectory
subtopics.learn: Emit one trace per run and one span per step, with attributes for model id, prompt version, tool name, tokens in and out (split cache-read and cache-write), cost, tool latency and step index. Track four operational numbers per deployment: the distribution of steps per run (a fat right tail is your cost problem), cost per successful outcome (not cost per run), tool error rate broken down by tool, and human-intervention rate. Distinguish end-state evals (did the HubSpot record end up correct) from trajectory evals (did it call the right tools in a sane order) and know that end-state is what the customer cares about while trajectory is what tells you why. Use LLM-as-judge only with a written rubric and a human-labelled calibration set you re-check when the judge model changes.

resource.label: Langfuse Docs - Evaluation overview

outcomes: You can take a customer process described in prose and return a per-step table classifying every step as deterministic code, a single LLM call, a named workflow pattern, or an agent, with the specific decision criterion written next to each agent classification.

You can implement the client-side agent loop against the Messages API from scratch - looping while `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, returning `tool_result` blocks with `is_error` on failure - with an iteration cap, a wall-clock deadline and a cumulative token budget that fails closed to a human and attaches the partial trace.

You can predict an agent run's cost in tokens and dollars before writing it, then show measured `cache_read_input_tokens` versus `cache_creation_input_tokens` proving prompt caching moved it by the amount you predicted.

You can put a human approval gate in front of an irreversible tool such that the run survives a two-day wait and a worker restart, demonstrated by killing the worker mid-run and resuming with no duplicate side effect.

You can state, for any multi-agent design you propose, the token multiplier over the single-agent version, the shared mutable state (or that there is none), and the specific single-agent alternative you rejected and why.
You can open one agent run's trace and answer 'why did this run cost forty dollars and take four minutes' in under two minutes, naming the step, the tool and the token count responsible.

You can defend your workflow-versus-agent map to a customer architect who wants 'agentic' on the roadmap, including naming the measurable threshold that would make you convert a given workflow step into an agent.
failureModes: An agent loop with no token budget and a generous iteration cap burns several hundred dollars on one customer run because a tool kept returning 500s and the model kept retrying it with cosmetically different arguments, and nobody noticed until the monthly invoice.
