Instrument implicit feedback as well as explicit: whether the analyst edited the draft and by how much, dismissed the finding, or escalated it, because thumbs up/down has both terrible response rates and worse calibration. Drift detection and the rollout mechanics live in topics 57 and 58; here you are building the label supply that feeds them.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Annotation Queues (prioritised human review of production traces)

subtopics.name: The eval report the customer can forward to their exec
subtopics.learn: Write one page that an engineering lead and a non-technical sponsor can both read: what was measured, on how many examples, sampled how and from what window; a per-class table with precision, recall, support and 95% intervals; the confusion matrix; the top three failure categories with counts and one real example each; what changed since the last report; and an explicit section on what is not measured. State the chosen operating point and the human-agreement ceiling, so nobody expects 99% from a task where two experts agree 85% of the time. Frame the target as an SLO with an error budget rather than a promise of perfection - that framing is what converts an argument about a single bad output into a conversation about a budget - and never publish a number without n and an interval beside it.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives

outcomes: You can produce a 200-case labelled set for DefenderMate with a written sampling frame, at least 20% double-labelled, a reported Cohen's kappa, and every case carrying source, labeller and labelled_at provenance.

You can report per-class precision, recall and F1 with support and 95% Wilson intervals plus a confusion matrix, and can explain in one sentence why you refuse to answer 'what's the accuracy?' with a single number.

You can state whether the difference between two prompt or model versions is real: paired run over identical cases, McNemar or paired bootstrap, an interval on the delta, and the sample size that would be needed to detect the effect the customer cares about.

You can build an LLM judge for one named failure mode and show its TPR, TNR and kappa against human labels on a held-out set of judge decisions, then quote the bias-corrected estimate rather than the raw judge pass rate.

You can make CI fail a pull request on a per-class recall regression beyond two sigma, with the flipped case ids named in the failure output and a sticky per-class score comment, with the smoke tier finishing under two minutes.

You can run an error-analysis session over 50 real traces and finish with a counted, mutually exclusive failure taxonomy in which the top two categories account for the majority of errors, each with an assigned disposition.
You can choose and defend an operating point from a precision-recall curve in the customer's cost units, including an abstain path, and report coverage next to accuracy-on-covered.
You can hand the customer a one-page eval report they forward to their exec unedited, including the section listing what is explicitly not measured.
failureModes: The eval set was assembled from cases the current system already passes, so it reads 97% every run, provides zero signal on every pull request, and the first genuinely new failure is still discovered by the customer's analyst.

A single blended accuracy figure hides that the rarest and most contractually important class has recall of 0.3 on 11 examples, and it stays hidden until the quarterly review when someone asks for the breakdown.

The judge is written, eyeballed on five examples and shipped without ever being scored against human labels, so a 'faithfulness: 92%' number goes into a QBR deck while the judge is in fact passing every fluent answer regardless of evidence.

The judge model is silently upgraded or its prompt is tweaked mid-quarter, so every historical score shifts and the longitudinal improvement chart in the customer report is entirely an artefact of the measuring instrument.
Two annotators labelled without a written guideline, kappa comes out at 0.35, and three weeks of prompt iteration turns out to have been fitting noise in the labels rather than improving the system.

Test-set cases leak into the production prompt's few-shot block (or into the judge's few-shots), so the headline score is measured on the system's own worked examples and does not survive contact with the customer's next batch of documents.

The CI gate is set exactly at the baseline with no noise allowance, produces four false failures in a fortnight, gets quietly removed from required checks, and now the only thing standing between a prompt edit and the customer's production data is code review.
interviewQuestions: A customer asks 'how do you know your classifier works?' You have two weeks and one domain expert who can give you four hours total. Walk me through exactly what you build, in what order, what number you put in front of them at the end, and what you explicitly refuse to claim.

Your eval says 94% accuracy and the customer's analysts say it's wrong all the time. Both statements are true. Explain how that happens mechanically, and tell me how you find out which of the two matters for renewal.

Design an LLM-as-judge for 'is this finding summary faithful to the retrieved evidence'. Then convince a sceptical staff engineer that the judge itself is trustworthy - and tell me what you do if it agrees with your human labeller only 65% of the time.

You change a prompt and the score moves from 91.5% to 93.0% on 200 labelled cases. Is that an improvement? Show me the actual arithmetic that answers it, and tell me what would be different in your answer if the move had been 91.5% to 96.0%.

Design the eval CI gate for a customer-facing extraction pipeline end to end: what runs on every PR versus nightly, what the thresholds are and how you derived the numbers, what stops it costing four hundred dollars a day, and what specifically prevents the team from marking it non-required after the third false failure.

You inherit a system with no evals, no labels and 40,000 stored production traces. What do you do on day one? Be concrete about how you sample, what you write down, who you sit with, and what artefact you have at the end of the week.

The customer wants a single 'quality score' out of 10 on their dashboard, refreshed daily. Explain what you push back on, what you offer instead, and how you make whatever number you do publish stable enough to trend over six months without the instrument itself drifting.
58.proofOfWork: A public repository, `defendermate-evals`, that a stranger can clone and run end to end in five minutes with `make eval` against a recorded-response fixture mode requiring no API key, so a reviewer can reproduce every number in the README for free. It contains the frozen 200-case dataset as JSONL with the schema above (real cases scrubbed or synthesised, `source` distinguishing production, bug-report and adversarial origins), the versioned `LABELLING_GUIDE.md` with worked boundary examples, and an `agreement/` directory holding the double-labelled subset plus the script that computes Cohen's kappa and prints the adjudication log for every disagreement. It ships the failure taxonomy as `TAXONOMY.md` with counts from a real open-coding session over 50 traces and a disposition column mapping each category to a deterministic assertion, a judge, or a documented limitation; a `judges/` package with one binary judge per open-ended category, each pinned to a dated model snapshot and accompanied by its own validation set of human-labelled judge decisions and a reported TPR/TNR/kappa table plus the bias-corrected pass rate; and a `stats.py` implementing Wilson intervals, McNemar and the paired bootstrap, with a test that fails if any published number in the README lacks an interval. The GitHub Actions workflow runs the 30-case smoke tier on `pull_request` behind path filters and posts a sticky per-class delta comment, with the repository history showing at least one real PR where the gate failed on a single class's recall, the comment naming the flipped case ids, and the follow-up commit that fixed it. Finally, `REPORT.md` is the customer-facing one-pager - per-class table with support and intervals, confusion matrix, top three failure categories with examples, the human-agreement ceiling, the chosen operating point and coverage, and a 'what this does not measure' section - rendered from the results file by a script, so it can never drift from the run that produced it.

59.topic: LLM observability: traces, cost, latency, datasets
59.why: When a customer says 'the assistant gave a wrong answer at about 3pm yesterday' or 'finance says this thing cost eleven thousand dollars last month', an FDE either opens a trace and answers in ninety seconds or spends two days reconstructing the incident from application logs that never captured the prompt. LLM observability is the difference between debugging a non-deterministic system with evidence and debugging it with opinions, and it is the only mechanism that turns real production failures into a growing eval dataset instead of a growing list of complaints. It is also how you defend a deployment commercially: cost per tenant, p95 latency by prompt version, and refusal rate are the numbers that decide renewal, and nobody else on the account team can produce them.
prerequisites: Observability: OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana (topic 21) - spans, span context, the collector, OTLP exporters, and why a trace id is not a log line.

FastAPI in production (topic 26) - lifespan hooks, dependency injection, background tasks and worker processes, because that is where you install the tracer and where you must flush it before shutdown.
SRE fundamentals: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets (topic 20) - you will define availability, latency and cost SLIs for an LLM feature, not just stare at dashboards.
LLM fundamentals and prompt engineering as code (topics 45, 46) - tokenisation, context windows, streaming, prompt versioning; a trace without a prompt version attached is barely a trace.
Agents and RAG at depth (topics 48, 49) - the shape of the thing you are instrumenting is nested: retriever spans, tool calls, retries, sub-agents.
Docker Compose and enough Postgres/ClickHouse literacy (topics 5, 29) to stand up and reason about a self-hosted Langfuse deployment inside a customer VPC.

subtopics.name: The data model: trace, observation, and the ids you join on
subtopics.learn: Learn the object graph cold: a trace holds many observations; observations nest by parent id and carry a type - event, span, generation, agent, tool, chain, retriever, embedding, evaluator, guardrail. Only generation and embedding carry usage and cost. Trace ids are 32 hex chars, observation ids 16 hex, matching W3C trace-context, which is exactly why joining to your OTel backend is possible at all. Be able to draw, for one Kaupex request, which node is a span, which is a generation, and which fields (input, output, metadata, level, statusMessage) you would need to reproduce the bug without asking the customer anything.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Observability core concepts / data model

subtopics.name: Instrumenting the application: decorators, context managers, and flush
subtopics.learn: Instrument three ways and know when each is right: the `@observe()` decorator for whole functions, `start_as_current_observation(as_type=...)` for explicit blocks, and framework/provider auto-instrumentation for the model client. Set `as_type="tool"`, `"retriever"`, `"generation"` deliberately - the UI's agent graph and every later filter depend on it. The failure that bites everyone: the SDK batches and exports asynchronously, so short-lived processes (Lambda, Celery task, CLI, a `pytest` run) lose traces unless you call `langfuse.flush()` or shut the client down in a FastAPI lifespan handler. Verify with `auth_check()` at startup rather than discovering a bad `LANGFUSE_HOST` in production.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - SDK instrumentation

subtopics.name: Wiring LLM traces into the existing OTel pipeline
subtopics.learn: Langfuse receives OTLP on `/api/public/otel`; set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` to the region host (`cloud.langfuse.com`, `us.`, `jp.`, `hipaa.`, or your self-hosted origin) and pass basic-auth public/secret keys via `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`. Decide the topology up front: export from the app directly, or fan out from an OpenTelemetry Collector so the same spans reach both Tempo/Datadog and Langfuse. Know the collector-side pieces you will actually touch - `otlp` receiver, `batch` processor, multiple exporters in one pipeline - and that per-signal endpoint overrides exist because most enterprises already own the metrics path.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - OpenTelemetry (OTLP) integration

subtopics.name: Joining the LLM trace to the service trace
subtopics.learn: This is the depth target: one id from the customer's ingress to the model call. Propagate W3C `traceparent` (`00-<32 hex trace-id>-<16 hex span-id>-<flags>`) across service hops so the LLM spans land in the same trace, and use `get_current_trace_id()` / `get_current_observation_id()` to stamp the id into your own application logs and into the API response header you hand support. Use `create_trace_id(seed=...)` to derive a deterministic id from an external key (ticket id, DefenderMate scan id) so a customer's reference number resolves straight to a trace. Test the failure case: a queue hop or a `httpx` client without the propagator silently starts a fresh trace, and you get two orphan traces instead of one.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Trace IDs and distributed tracing

subtopics.name: OTel GenAI semantic conventions - naming attributes so they survive a vendor swap
subtopics.learn: Use the standard attribute names rather than inventing your own: `gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.operation.name`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.request.temperature`, `gen_ai.request.max_tokens`, `gen_ai.response.model`, `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`. Know that the conventions are still experimental and moved to their own repository, that prompt/completion content is captured under opt-in content-capture settings precisely because it is sensitive, and that span names follow `{operation} {model}`. The payoff is portability: when the customer's platform team standardises on Datadog LLM Observability or Grafana next year, conforming attributes migrate and bespoke `my_app.llm_tokens` does not.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry - GenAI semantic conventions repository

subtopics.name: Cost attribution: ingested vs inferred, usage types, custom models
subtopics.learn: Understand the precedence rule: values you ingest from the provider response win; otherwise Langfuse infers usage with a tokenizer and cost by matching the `model` string to a model definition with a price per usage type. Usage types are not just input/output - `cache_creation_input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `reasoning`, `audio` all price differently, and dropping them makes prompt-caching savings invisible. Register custom model definitions (regex match, unit prices, start date) for self-hosted, fine-tuned or Bedrock-renamed models, and know that a price change applies from its effective date rather than retroactively. Streaming responses are the classic silent failure: usage arrives in the terminal chunk, and if you close the span first, cost silently reads zero.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Token and cost tracking

subtopics.name: Latency decomposition: TTFT, self-time, retries, queueing
subtopics.learn: A generation span's wall time is not model latency. Decompose it into time-to-first-token (record it explicitly - it is the number that governs perceived speed for a streamed UI), inter-token latency, and total; then compute self-time (span duration minus children) to separate your orchestration overhead from provider time. Represent SDK retries as sibling spans with the HTTP status and `retry-after` in attributes, or you will see one 40-second call instead of three 429s and a success. Always report p50/p95/p99 rather than mean - LLM latency distributions are fat-tailed and the mean hides the tail the customer is complaining about.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry docs - Traces (spans, attributes, events)

subtopics.name: The dimensions that make traces queryable: sessions, users, tags, environments, release
subtopics.learn: Set `session_id` for a multi-turn conversation, `user_id` for the end user, `tags` for tenant/feature/model-tier, and `environment` to keep staging out of the production cost chart. Stamp `release` (git sha) and prompt `version` on every trace so a latency regression can be attributed to a deploy in one filter. Design this like a cardinality-conscious metrics label set: tenant slug yes, raw email no, request uuid never as a tag. The test of a good scheme is that you can answer 'cost per tenant per day for the last 30 days, excluding staging' without writing any code.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Sessions

subtopics.name: Linking prompt versions to traces
subtopics.learn: Attach the managed prompt object to the generation so every trace records which prompt version produced it, then compare cost, latency and scores across versions in one view. This is what makes 'we changed the system prompt on Tuesday' a testable claim rather than a hypothesis. Know the operational detail that the client caches prompts with a TTL and falls back to the last cached version when the control plane is unreachable, so a prompt-management outage degrades to stale-but-working rather than down.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Link prompts to traces

subtopics.name: Scores: attaching quality and feedback signals to traces
subtopics.learn: A score references exactly one of trace, observation, session or dataset run, and is numeric, categorical, boolean or text, optionally bound to a ScoreConfig that enforces range and allowed categories. Wire three sources: explicit user feedback (thumbs, correction), implicit signals (did the user re-ask, did they copy the answer, did the tool call succeed), and automated evaluators. Sending scores from the browser needs the trace id returned to the client, which is the practical reason you surfaced it in step four. Without a ScoreConfig you get 'helpfulness' scored 1-5 by one service and 0-1 by another, and every aggregate afterwards is garbage.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Scores data model

subtopics.name: Online evaluation and human review queues on sampled production traces
subtopics.learn: Configure an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator to run on a filtered slice of live traces (for example: only Kaupex traces tagged `tier=enterprise`, sampled at 10%) with variable mappings from trace input/output into the judge prompt, and know that the judge itself costs tokens and needs its own model connection and budget. Route low-scoring or flagged traces into an annotation queue so a human reviewer labels them and their verdict becomes the ground truth your automated judge is calibrated against. Track judge-versus-human agreement explicitly - an uncalibrated judge is a confident random number generator that will make you ship a regression.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - LLM-as-a-judge evaluation

subtopics.name: Datasets built from production traces, and runs linked back to them
subtopics.learn: Close the loop: when a trace is wrong, promote it to a dataset item in one action, capturing input, the expected output you wrote after diagnosis, and metadata (tenant, model, prompt version). Run experiments over the dataset so each item execution produces its own trace linked to the dataset run, letting you diff run A vs run B item by item rather than comparing two aggregate percentages. Keep dataset items versioned and immutable-by-convention, and split into a working set and a held-out set so you do not tune against the same fifty examples forever. The measure of a healthy deployment is that the dataset grows every week from real incidents.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Datasets

subtopics.name: Sampling, batching, and the overhead budget
subtopics.learn: Sampling is client-side and trace-level: set `LANGFUSE_SAMPLE_RATE` or the `sample_rate` constructor arg between 0 and 1, and if a trace is dropped every observation and score under it is dropped too - consistent, but it means you cannot sample at 0.1 and still expect complete cost totals, so keep usage aggregates on a separate always-on path. Know the export machinery you will have to debug: an in-process queue, a batch worker, `flush_at`/`flush_interval` style tuning, and what happens when the queue fills (drops, not blocks - which is the behaviour you want on the request path). Measure the added p95 on your own endpoint before and after instrumentation and state the number; 'observability is free' is not an answer a platform team accepts.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Sampling

subtopics.name: PII, masking and retention - the answer to the security review
subtopics.learn: Prompt and completion payloads are the most sensitive data in the system, so masking runs before export: the modern hook patches raw OpenTelemetry span attributes at export time (deleting or rewriting things like `gen_ai.prompt.*` content), while the legacy `mask` callback only covers data set through the SDK's own APIs - know which one covers third-party instrumentation, because that is where leaks happen. Combine regex/entity redaction with structural rules (never trace raw file bytes, hash identifiers, keep tenant id but drop names), and set project-level retention in days so trace payloads expire on a schedule you can point at in a DPA. Assume you will be asked 'where does this data live and for how long' in week one of an enterprise deployment.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Masking sensitive LLM data

subtopics.name: Dashboards, the Metrics API, and alerts that page someone
subtopics.learn: Build custom dashboards over the trace store, then learn the programmatic path: `GET /api/public/v2/metrics` takes a view, dimensions, metrics, filters and time granularity and returns aggregated cost, tokens, volume, latency and scores as JSON - that is how you produce a weekly cost-per-tenant report or feed a chargeback spreadsheet without exporting rows. Define real SLIs for the feature (availability = non-error traces, latency = p95 TTFT, quality = judge score above threshold, cost = USD per successful answer) and wire threshold alerts plus spend alerts to Slack or a webhook. An alert that nobody owns is a dashboard; make each one name the runbook step.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Custom dashboards

subtopics.name: Self-hosting inside the customer's boundary
subtopics.learn: Most regulated customers will not send prompts to a vendor cloud, so be able to stand the stack up yourself: the web/worker containers plus Postgres (transactional), ClickHouse (traces, observations, scores), Redis/Valkey (queue and cache) and S3-compatible blob storage for large payloads and events. Know the environment variables that matter (`DATABASE_URL`, `CLICKHOUSE_URL`, `REDIS_CONNECTION_STRING`, `LANGFUSE_S3_EVENT_UPLOAD_*`, `NEXTAUTH_URL`, the encryption and salt secrets), that the worker is what actually ingests, and the sizing consequence: ClickHouse is the component that grows, so retention and sampling are capacity decisions. Practise the ninety-second version of this for a customer architect: what runs where, what leaves the VPC (nothing), and how backups and upgrades work.

resource.label: Langfuse self-hosting guide

outcomes: You can take a single request id from a Kaupex API response and open one trace that shows the HTTP span, retrieval span, every model generation with its prompt version, token usage, USD cost and TTFT, and the tool calls in between - with no gap where the LLM call is an opaque 8-second block.
You can state cost per tenant per day and cost per successful answer for a deployment, pulled from the Metrics API rather than a provider invoice, and explain the difference between the two numbers.
You can show p50/p95/p99 latency broken down into time-to-first-token, provider time and your own orchestration self-time, and name which of the three you would attack first for a given complaint.
You can turn a customer-reported bad answer into a dataset item with an expected output in under five minutes, then re-run the dataset and show per-item pass/fail against the previous run.

You can demonstrate masking working end to end: a trace containing a synthetic national-ID string in the prompt arrives at the backend with that field redacted, including for spans produced by third-party auto-instrumentation.
You can quantify instrumentation overhead: measured p95 delta on your endpoint with tracing on versus off, plus the trace volume and storage growth per 1,000 requests at your chosen sample rate.
You can stand up a self-hosted Langfuse (web, worker, Postgres, ClickHouse, Redis, S3-compatible storage) from scratch and point your app at it by changing only environment variables.
You can define and defend four SLIs for one LLM feature with alert thresholds and, for each, the runbook step the alert triggers.
failureModes: Tracing is added to the request path but never flushed in the worker or Lambda, so the exact background jobs that fail at 3am are the ones with no traces, and the incident is reconstructed from nothing.

The customer's gateway strips or regenerates `traceparent` at the ingress, so every LLM trace is an orphan with no parent service span, and the join you promised in the design review quietly does not exist.

Streaming responses close the generation span before the final usage chunk arrives, so token counts and cost read zero for the entire streaming code path and the cost dashboard understates real spend by half.

A model is deployed under a custom or fine-tuned name that matches no price definition, so its cost silently records as zero, and the miss is discovered when finance compares the dashboard to the provider invoice.
Raw prompts containing customer PII are shipped to a vendor-hosted trace store before anyone reviews it, turning a debugging win into a data-processing incident and a contract escalation.
Sampling is set to 0.05 to control storage and then someone builds the monthly chargeback report off sampled traces, so one tenant is billed twenty times more or less than they used.

`user_id` is populated with a raw email address and `tags` with a per-request uuid, so the store's cardinality explodes, filters time out, and the dashboards become unusable exactly when traffic gets interesting.
interviewQuestions: A customer says one specific answer from your assistant was wrong yesterday afternoon. Walk me through, minute by minute, how you go from that sentence to a root cause, and tell me exactly which fields you need to have captured in advance for that path to work.

Design end-to-end tracing for an agent running in a customer VPC where the platform team already runs an OpenTelemetry Collector into Datadog, and legal will not allow prompt text to leave the VPC. What ships where, what is redacted, and where does the trace id come from?
Your LLM cost dashboard says $4,100 for the month and the provider invoice says $9,800. List the causes you would check, in the order you would check them, and how you would confirm each one.

You have a p95 latency SLO of 4 seconds and you are at 6.5. The generation span averages 5.2 seconds. How do you decide whether the fix is a smaller model, streaming, caching, retry tuning, or your own orchestration code - and what does the trace need to show for you to decide with evidence?

Explain how you would sample traces at high volume without breaking cost reporting, quality monitoring, or incident debugging. What do you sample, what do you never sample, and where do the aggregates come from?

Argue for or against using an LLM judge on live production traffic to a customer who is worried about both cost and correctness. What would you measure to prove the judge is trustworthy, and what would make you turn it off?

Two weeks after go-live, quality has visibly drifted but nothing was deployed. What in your observability setup lets you distinguish a provider-side model change, an input-distribution change, and a retrieval regression - and what would you have had to instrument on day one?
59.proofOfWork: Ship an 'LLM trace forensics kit' as a small repository plus a five-minute recorded walkthrough over Kaupex and DefenderMate. The repo contains a single instrumentation module both apps import (tracer setup, propagation, masking hook, sampling config, `as_type` conventions, prompt-version stamping) and a `tracectl` CLI with three commands: `tracectl explain <trace_id>` printing the span tree with per-span self-time, TTFT, tokens by usage type and USD cost; `tracectl cost --group-by tenant --since 30d` calling the Metrics API to produce the chargeback table; and `tracectl promote <trace_id>` turning a bad production trace into a dataset item with an expected output. Include a `load/` script that drives synthetic traffic with deliberate faults - a 429 storm, a streaming call that returns usage only in the final chunk, a request with an unpriced custom model name, and a prompt containing a synthetic national ID - and a `FINDINGS.md` recording, with screenshots, what each fault looked like in the trace before and after the fix, the measured p95 overhead of instrumentation on and off, and the storage growth per 1,000 traces. Finish with a one-page `SLO.md` defining availability, p95 TTFT, judge-score and cost-per-answer SLIs with thresholds, the alert wired to each, and the runbook step it triggers - so the artifact reads as an operable system a customer's platform team could adopt, not a screenshot of a demo dashboard.

60.why: The gateway is the one piece of an AI deployment an FDE can change on a Tuesday without asking the customer's platform team for anything: it is where you swap models, cap spend, survive a provider outage, and prove a new model is better before you make it everyone's problem. Enterprise customers do not accept 'we upgraded the model and it feels better' - they accept a 10% canary with a written comparison of quality, p95 latency, cost per request and error rate, and a rollback that took one config change. Without a gateway you are hard-coding a vendor SDK into the customer's application, which means every model decision becomes a code deploy, a change-advisory-board ticket, and a three-week delay you will personally own.
prerequisites: Evals as infrastructure (topic 53): a versioned eval set, a judge you have calibrated against human labels, and a CI gate - a canary without a quality metric is just a slower way to ship a regression.
LLM observability (topic 54): per-request traces carrying model, tokens, cost and latency, so 'the canary is worse' can be traced to specific requests rather than argued about.
Observability fundamentals (topic 21): Prometheus histograms, PromQL rate() and histogram_quantile(), Grafana dashboards, and OpenTelemetry span attributes.
SRE fundamentals (topic 20): SLIs, SLOs, error budgets - a canary is an error-budget spend decision and you need to be able to say how much budget it may consume.
LLM-era system design (topic 43): retries, rate limits, latency budgets, streaming and TTFT versus total latency, because a gateway multiplies every one of those concerns.
Kubernetes production ops (topic 8) and Redis (topic 31): the gateway runs as a horizontally scaled Deployment whose routing state (cooldowns, TPM/RPM counters) lives in Redis, not in process memory.

subtopics.name: What a gateway must own, and what it must not
subtopics.learn: A model gateway is a seam: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/responses`) in front of N providers, so the application never imports a vendor SDK and never learns a model id. Get clear on what belongs at the seam - credential custody, model aliasing, routing, retries, fallbacks, rate limits, budgets, cost attribution, logging and canary allocation - and what does not: prompt construction, retrieval, business retries, and anything requiring request-body semantics the gateway would have to parse and reinterpret. Know the cost you are accepting in exchange: one more network hop (measure it, LiteLLM exposes `x-litellm-overhead-duration-ms`), one more thing that can be down, and a shared blast radius across every team using it. Run `litellm --config config.yaml` locally and point an unmodified `openai` client at `base_url="http://0.0.0.0:4000"` to feel why the seam is the whole point.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Proxy quick start

subtopics.name: config.yaml anatomy and the alias indirection
subtopics.learn: Learn the four blocks and what each governs: `model_list` (deployments, each with `model_name` as the client-facing alias, `litellm_params` for the real upstream model/api_base/api_key, and `model_info` for `id`, `mode` and metadata), `router_settings` (routing strategy, fallbacks, cooldowns), `litellm_settings` (callbacks, caching, global defaults) and `general_settings` (master key, database, health-check behaviour). The single most important idea: many `model_list` entries can share one `model_name`, and that is simultaneously how you load-balance, how you fail over and how you canary - one alias, several deployments. Keep secrets out of YAML with `os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` references, pin a stable `model_info.id` per deployment so metrics and headers stay comparable across restarts, and treat config.yaml as code in the customer's repo with review and a diff, never as something edited in the admin UI.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Proxy config settings

subtopics.name: Routing strategies and where the state lives
subtopics.learn: Know the strategies by behaviour, not by name: `simple-shuffle` (the default and the production recommendation - weighted pick using per-deployment `weight`, or `rpm`/`tpm` as implicit weights, with effectively zero routing overhead), `usage-based-routing-v2` (async, picks the deployment with TPM/RPM headroom), `latency-based-routing`, `least-busy`, and `cost-based-routing`. The trap that catches everyone: routing state - cooldowns, in-flight counts, TPM/RPM windows - is per-process, so with `--num_workers 4` behind three pods you have twelve independent opinions unless you configure Redis, at which point a Redis stall becomes a routing stall. Understand that latency- and usage-based strategies add a read to the hot path and can oscillate (everyone stampedes the deployment that just looked fast), which is exactly why the docs recommend weighted shuffle in production. Set weights explicitly rather than relying on implicit rpm-derived weights, because that is the knob a canary turns.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Router: load balancing and routing strategies

subtopics.name: Timeouts, retries and cooldowns as one budget
subtopics.learn: Set `router_settings.timeout` globally and override per deployment with `litellm_params.timeout` (cap on the complete response) and `stream_timeout` (cap on time-to-first-chunk - the one that catches a provider that accepts your connection and then sits there). Understand the multiplication: `num_retries` x `timeout` x fallback chain length is your true worst-case latency, and if the caller's own client timeout is shorter than that product you will burn provider spend on responses nobody will ever read. Know `allowed_fails` and `cooldown_time` - after N failures a deployment is pulled from the pool for a cooldown window, which is why a single bad Azure region degrades gracefully instead of taking the alias down. Add `keepalive_seconds` on slow-first-token deployments so an intermediate load balancer does not kill an idle-looking SSE stream (it emits `: ping` comment frames), and remember it is operator-only unless `allow_client_keepalive_override: true` is set.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Timeouts (timeout, stream_timeout, keepalive_seconds)

subtopics.name: The three fallback types and their different meanings
subtopics.learn: LiteLLM splits failover into `fallbacks` (everything else - rate limits, 5xx, timeouts), `context_window_fallbacks` (for `ContextWindowExceededError`, i.e. route to a longer-context model) and `content_policy_fallbacks` (for `ContentPolicyViolationError`, i.e. route to a differently-filtered provider), plus `default_fallbacks` for a misconfigured group. They are applied in list order, so `["model-b", "model-c"]` means b then c, and each hop costs another full timeout. The design questions matter more than the syntax: is a cheaper/weaker fallback model actually acceptable for this workload, or is a 503 better than a quietly worse answer? Does the fallback support the same tool schema, JSON mode and system-prompt semantics, or will the retry fail differently? And is a content-policy fallback a compliance decision the customer's legal team must sign off on rather than an engineering default? Note that `mock_testing_fallbacks` is stripped on the proxy path from v1.85.0 - to test proxy fallbacks you point a deployment at a deliberately broken api_base and send a real request.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Fallbacks (provider failover)

subtopics.name: Exception mapping: normalising provider errors
subtopics.learn: The gateway's quiet superpower is turning every provider's idiosyncratic failure into one taxonomy - `RateLimitError`, `ContextWindowExceededError`, `ContentPolicyViolationError`, `AuthenticationError`, `ServiceUnavailableError`, `Timeout`, `APIConnectionError` - because fallback rules, retry policy and alerting all key off that classification. Learn which errors are retryable at all: a 429 with a `retry-after` is, a 400 for a malformed tool schema is not, and retrying it just multiplies the failure. Know that misclassification is a real production bug - a provider that returns a 500 for an over-length prompt will be retried three times and then failed over instead of being routed to a long-context model - so verify the mapping for the specific providers in the customer's stack rather than assuming. Wire the normalised class into your alerts (`exception_class` and `exception_status` are Prometheus labels) so 'the gateway is erroring' becomes 'Bedrock us-east-1 is throttling'.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Exception mapping

subtopics.name: Response headers as the attribution spine
subtopics.learn: You cannot analyse a canary you cannot attribute, and the headers are how attribution leaves the gateway. Learn them cold: `x-litellm-model-group` (the alias the client asked for), `x-litellm-model-id` (which deployment row actually answered - this is your canary arm label), `x-litellm-call-id` (join key into logs and traces), `x-litellm-attempted-retries` and `x-litellm-attempted-fallbacks` (a request that fell back is not a clean sample and must be excluded or bucketed separately), `x-litellm-response-cost` plus its input/output/cache-read/cache-creation components, and `x-litellm-response-duration-ms` versus `x-litellm-overhead-duration-ms` to separate your hop from the provider's. Note the sharp edge: the response body's `model` field is often restamped to the client-facing alias, so parsing the body to find out which model answered gives you the wrong answer - read the header. Provider headers are passed through prefixed `llm_provider-`, which is where you find real rate-limit remaining counts.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Response headers

subtopics.name: Tag-based routing as a canary allocator
subtopics.learn: Weights give you a random 10%; tags give you a chosen 10%, which is usually what a customer actually wants ('canary internal users first, never the regulated tenant'). Set `router_settings.enable_tag_filtering: true`, put `tags: ["canary"]` on the candidate deployment and `tags: ["default"]` on the incumbent so untagged traffic has a home, then send `metadata.tags` in the body or the `x-litellm-tags` header. Learn the full grammar because it is how you express real customer constraints: plain tags are OR, `&` prefix means required (AND), `!` prefix is a denylist that removes exactly-matching deployments (`!provider:anthropic` for a tenant with a vendor restriction), and matching is exact string comparison with no regex. Know the failure mode by name: if negation removes every candidate the request fails with `no_deployments_with_tag_routing`, and a banned primary group falls through to the configured `fallbacks` chain - which can silently send your 'never Anthropic' tenant to Anthropic if the fallback is untagged.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Tag-based routing

subtopics.name: Deterministic bucketing and sticky assignment
subtopics.learn: Per-request randomness is wrong for anything stateful: a conversation whose turn 1 came from model A and turn 3 from model B produces incoherent output and an uninterpretable comparison. Implement assignment as `bucket = crc32(salt + unit_id) % 1000`, where `unit_id` is the session, conversation or tenant - not the request - and `salt` is the experiment name so two concurrent canaries do not correlate their populations. Emit the arm as an explicit tag and as a span attribute so every downstream log, eval and trace carries it, and make the bucketing function a pure, unit-tested function with a test asserting the same unit_id always lands in the same arm and that allocation is within a point of the target across 100k synthetic ids. Decide the exclusion list up front - opt-out tenants, anything under a contractual model commitment, anything in a compliance scope - and enforce it as a denylist tag before bucketing rather than as a downstream filter.

resource.label: OpenFeature docs - flag evaluation and targeting concepts

subtopics.name: Canary design: population, dose, duration, blast radius
subtopics.learn: Write the canary plan before touching config: which population (internal, then low-risk tenants, then general), what percentage and for how long, which metrics decide, what the abort thresholds are, and who can press the button. Understand exposure as dose x duration - 10% for 24 hours and 100% for 2.4 hours expose comparable request counts but wildly different blast radius, and only one of them lets a slow-burning failure surface. Plan the ramp explicitly (1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with a bake time per step long enough to cover at least one full traffic cycle, because an AI canary started at 09:00 on Monday sees a completely different prompt mix than the same canary at 03:00. Know the two canary-specific traps: a canary that is too small never reaches statistical power on a quality metric with high variance, and a canary that runs too long normalises an unresolved decision into permanent dual-model production.

resource.label: Google SRE Workbook - Canarying Releases

subtopics.name: The Prometheus surface you actually need for a canary
subtopics.learn: Enable `litellm_settings.callbacks: ["prometheus"]` and scrape `/metrics`; with multiple workers you must set `PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR` or your counters are per-worker fiction, and `--prometheus_metrics_port 4001` moves scrape rendering off the inference path. Know the specific series a canary report is built from: `litellm_deployment_success_responses` and `litellm_deployment_failure_responses` (split by `model_id`, so per-arm error rate), `litellm_request_total_latency_metric` (end-to-end histogram in seconds), `litellm_llm_api_time_to_first_token_metric` (streaming only - the number users actually feel), `litellm_llm_api_latency_metric` versus `litellm_overhead_latency_metric` to prove the gateway is not the problem, `litellm_deployment_cooled_down`, `litellm_deployment_successful_fallbacks` / `litellm_deployment_failed_fallbacks`, and `litellm_spend_metric` for cost per arm. Watch label cardinality: `end_user`, `client_ip`, `hashed_api_key` and `user_agent` on high-traffic metrics will melt a small Prometheus, so use `prometheus_exclude_labels` deliberately.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Prometheus metrics

subtopics.name: Histograms and quantiles without lying to yourself
subtopics.learn: Compute quantiles the correct way - `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, model_id) (rate(litellm_request_total_latency_metric_bucket[5m])))` - and understand exactly why you can never average or take the max of two arms' p95s: quantiles are not linear and aggregating them is arithmetically meaningless. Know that a classic histogram quantile is an interpolation within a bucket, so its accuracy is capped by the bucket boundaries: if your buckets top out at 10s and the candidate model routinely takes 25s, its p99 will read as +Inf-adjacent garbage and you will conclude nothing. Always report p50, p95 and p99 together plus the request count per arm, because a p95 computed from 40 canary requests is noise wearing a decimal point. For LLM traffic specifically, separate TTFT from total latency and normalise by output tokens (`litellm_deployment_latency_per_output_token`), otherwise a more verbose model looks slower when it is merely wordier.

resource.label: Prometheus docs - Histograms and summaries

subtopics.name: Measuring quality on the canary slice, not in a notebook
subtopics.learn: Latency and error rate are the easy half; the reason model canaries are hard is that the regression is usually in output quality and it is invisible to the gateway. Build three layers: your offline eval set run against both arms as a gate before the canary starts, online proxy signals during it (refusal rate, JSON-parse failure rate, tool-call schema validity, empty-response rate, retry rate, output-token distribution shift - all cheap, all computable without a judge), and a sampled LLM-as-judge pass over paired production requests. Prefer paired comparison where possible: replay the same canary-arm prompts through the incumbent offline and judge A/B with position randomised, which removes population variance and needs far fewer samples than comparing two independent traffic slices. Route all of this through the tracing backend from topic 54 keyed on `x-litellm-call-id` and the arm tag, and capture explicit user feedback (thumbs, edits, regenerate clicks) as the one signal a customer executive will actually believe.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - tracing, scores and evaluation

subtopics.name: Enough statistics to defend the promote decision
subtopics.learn: Decide the minimum detectable effect and the sample size before you start, not after you look. For a rate metric (error rate, refusal rate, judge win rate) use a two-proportion test and know roughly what you can detect: distinguishing 2% from 3% at 80% power needs thousands of requests per arm, which tells you immediately whether a 10% canary for one day is even capable of answering the question. Understand the peeking problem - repeatedly checking a fixed-horizon p-value inflates the false-positive rate badly - so either fix the horizon in advance, or use a sequential/always-valid method, or state honestly that the canary is a guardrail rather than an experiment. Report effect sizes with confidence intervals, never bare p-values, and pre-register the decision rule ('promote if judge win rate CI lower bound > 0.45 and p95 regression < 15% and error rate not worse by >0.5pp') so the promote conversation is arithmetic rather than advocacy.

resource.label: SciPy documentation - statistical functions (scipy.stats)

subtopics.name: Automated analysis and one-action rollback
subtopics.learn: A canary a human has to watch is a canary that runs unattended at 3am. Study the Argo Rollouts model even if you implement it yourself: an `AnalysisTemplate` with metric providers (Prometheus queries), a `successCondition` expression, `interval`, `count`, `failureLimit` and `inconclusiveLimit`, attached to canary `steps` with `setWeight` and `pause` so a failing metric aborts and reverts the weight automatically. Map that onto the gateway: a controller that queries per-`model_id` error rate and p95 every 60s and rewrites `weight` in config, or the simpler and more honest version - a documented one-command rollback (`weight: 0` on the candidate, reload) with the exact command in the runbook, tested at least once before the canary goes live. Distinguish abort thresholds (hard, automatic, no discussion: error rate > 2x baseline, p95 > 2x, any content-policy or auth failure spike) from investigate thresholds, and make rollback strictly faster than diagnosis.

resource.label: Argo Rollouts docs - Analysis and progressive delivery

subtopics.name: Spend attribution and budget guardrails during the canary
subtopics.learn: A model canary is a spend experiment as much as a quality one, and 'the new model is 3x the price' is the finding that most often kills a promotion. Turn on cost tracking with a database configured, verify per-request cost lands in `x-litellm-response-cost` and `litellm_spend_metric` broken down by `model_id`, and set `custom_pricing` for any self-hosted or enterprise-contract model where LiteLLM's public price map would be wrong by an order of magnitude. Report cost per successful request rather than cost per token, because a model that is cheaper per token but retries more, thinks longer or produces more output tokens is not cheaper. Put a hard budget on the canary itself - a virtual key or team with `max_budget` and a reset interval scoped to the experiment - so a runaway loop against a premium model is capped by policy rather than discovered on the customer's monthly invoice.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Cost tracking

subtopics.name: Running the gateway as production infrastructure
subtopics.learn: The moment the gateway is in front of everything it is the highest-blast-radius component you introduced, so treat it accordingly. Wire `GET /health/liveliness` and `GET /health/readiness` as the Kubernetes probes (readiness returns 503 when the configured database is unreachable, which correctly pulls the pod), and keep `GET /health` - which issues real billed requests to every model - off the probe path; use `background_health_checks: true` with `health_check_interval` instead. Know the production checklist items that bite: run multiple workers and multiple replicas with Redis for shared routing state, do not put the spend database on the request critical path in a way that a slow write stalls inference, set `PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR`, disable verbose request logging (customer prompts are PII), and pin the LiteLLM image to a digest because routing behaviour changes between minor versions. Finally, write down what the application does when the gateway itself is down - a direct-to-provider break-glass path is a legitimate design, and 'we never thought about it' is not.

resource.label: LiteLLM docs - Production deployment checklist

outcomes: You can stand up a LiteLLM proxy in front of at least three providers where one `model_name` alias resolves to multiple deployments, and point an unmodified `openai` Python client at it with no application code change beyond `base_url`.

You can send 10% of traffic to a candidate model using a deterministic, session-sticky bucketing function plus tag routing, and prove from `x-litellm-model-id` on 10,000 requests that the realised split is within one percentage point of the target.

You can write the PromQL that produces a per-arm comparison table - request count, error rate, p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency, p95 TTFT, fallback count and cost per successful request - each series broken down by `model_id`, and explain why averaging two arms' p95 values is meaningless.

You can demonstrate three distinct failover behaviours on demand by breaking a deployment: `fallbacks` on a 429, `context_window_fallbacks` on an over-length prompt, and `content_policy_fallbacks` on a refusal, each visible as a `litellm_deployment_successful_fallbacks` increment.

You can state, before starting a canary, the minimum detectable effect your traffic volume supports for the chosen quality metric, and say honestly when the canary is a guardrail rather than an experiment.
You can roll back a canary to 0% in under two minutes with a single documented command, and show a rehearsal timestamp proving you have executed that command before the canary went live.

You can produce a written canary report that ends in an explicit PROMOTE / HOLD / ROLLBACK recommendation with pre-registered thresholds, and defend the cost-per-successful-request figure to a customer who only cares about the invoice.

You can explain and mitigate the gateway's own failure modes: shared routing state in Redis, health probes that do not bill you, PII-safe logging, image pinning, and a documented break-glass path when the gateway itself is unavailable.
failureModes: Routing state lives in per-process memory because Redis was never configured, so with four workers across three pods a deployment that should be in cooldown keeps receiving traffic from eleven other processes and the 'failover' never actually fails over.

The canary is assigned per request instead of per session, so a single conversation alternates between two models mid-thread, the output style flips between turns, and the customer reports the product as broken rather than as being tested.

A tenant with a contractual restriction is excluded from the candidate model with a `!provider:x` tag, but the fallback chain is untagged, so the first 429 on their primary silently routes their data to exactly the provider the contract forbids.

Latency histogram buckets were sized for the incumbent model and top out at 10 seconds; the reasoning-model candidate routinely takes 25 seconds, so its p95 reads as an artefact, the dashboard looks fine, and the regression is discovered by users.

The canary decision is made by watching the dashboard and calling it when the numbers look good, which is peeking at a fixed-horizon test - the team promotes on noise and the 'improvement' evaporates at 100%.

`num_retries: 3` with a 120-second timeout and a two-deep fallback chain produces a worst-case of over ten minutes, so during a provider brownout the gateway's connection pool fills with requests whose callers timed out minutes ago and the whole endpoint stops serving healthy traffic.

Cost is compared per token instead of per successful request, so the 'cheaper' candidate ships and the next invoice is 40% higher because it retries more, emits more output tokens, and gets no prompt-cache hits since its cached prefix differs.
interviewQuestions: A customer wants to move from GPT-class to Claude-class models across a live support product with 200k requests a day. Design the rollout end to end: allocation mechanism, what you measure, how long you run it, your abort criteria, and what you tell their VP of Engineering at each stage.

Your canary shows the candidate model is 4% better on judge win rate and 30% slower at p95. How do you decide? Walk me through what additional data you would pull and what you would need to know about the product before you had an opinion.

Explain the difference between load balancing, failover and canarying when all three are implemented by putting multiple deployments behind one model alias. Where do they conflict, and how do you keep a canary's traffic share from being distorted by cooldowns and retries?

Traffic to your gateway is 5% errors and the customer says 'the AI is down'. You have Prometheus and the gateway's response headers. Give me your first five minutes: what you query, what each result would rule in or out, and where you look for the difference between a provider outage, a gateway saturation problem and a bad config push.

Design a fallback policy for a healthcare intake workflow where a wrong answer is worse than no answer. Which of the three fallback classes do you enable, which do you deliberately leave off, and how do you make that decision auditable for their compliance team?

You have a 10% canary running for 24 hours on a metric that moves from 2% to 3%. Is that a real regression? Show me how you would reason about sample size and how your answer changes if the customer will only give you 1% of traffic.

The gateway is now a single point of failure for every AI feature in the customer's product and their platform team is nervous. Convince them it is the right architecture, then tell them honestly what you would build to survive the gateway itself being down.
60.proofOfWork: Ship a reusable `canary-kit` against the Kaupex stack: a LiteLLM proxy deployed on the cluster with a single `chat` alias fronting three deployments (incumbent, candidate, and a deliberately hostile fake provider you write as a small FastAPI service with configurable latency, 429 rate, content-policy refusals and over-length errors), a pure `assign_arm(unit_id, salt) -> str` bucketing module with tests asserting stickiness and allocation accuracy over 100k synthetic ids, and a `canary.py` CLI with three verbs - `start --pct 10`, `report`, `rollback` - where `rollback` is timed and its execution time recorded. The report verb queries Prometheus for per-`model_id` request count, error rate, p50/p95/p99 total latency, p95 TTFT, fallback and cooldown counts and cost per successful request, joins them to per-request quality signals (JSON validity, refusal rate, tool-schema validity, and a sampled paired LLM-as-judge run with randomised position) keyed on `x-litellm-call-id`, and emits a markdown report with a pre-registered decision rule at the top and a PROMOTE / HOLD / ROLLBACK verdict at the bottom. Include a Grafana dashboard JSON with the arm-split panels, a chaos script that drives the fake provider through each of the three fallback classes and captures the resulting `litellm_deployment_successful_fallbacks` deltas as evidence each path works, and a RUNBOOK.md giving the abort thresholds, the one-command rollback, the break-glass direct-to-provider path, and a short 'what I would tell the customer' section written for a non-engineer.

61.topic: Serving at scale: vLLM, quantisation, KV cache, batching, GPU maths
61.why: The moment a customer says 'we cannot send this data to an API' or 'the per-token bill does not survive procurement', the FDE becomes the person who has to say how many GPUs it takes, how fast it will feel, and what it costs per user per month - with numbers that hold up in front of their infrastructure lead and their CFO on the same call. Nobody else on the engagement can do that: the model vendor sells tokens, the platform team does not know transformer inference, and the customer's own estimate is a leaderboard screenshot. Being able to derive KV cache bytes per token on a whiteboard, tune vLLM until you find the knee of the load curve, and turn that into a one-page capacity plan is the difference between a deployment that ships and one that stalls in an architecture review for six weeks.
prerequisites: LLM fundamentals (topic 45): tokens, attention, what the KV cache actually stores, parameter counts, and the difference between prefill and decode as compute phases.
Serving models on Kubernetes and GPUs (topic 11): device plugin, GPU requests/limits, node pools with taints, image size and model-weight loading, and why a 40 GB weight pull dominates pod startup.
LLM-era system design (topic 43): latency budgets, streaming transports, retries and rate limits - serving tuning is meaningless unless you know the SLO the number has to satisfy.
Load testing and chaos (topic 22): open-loop vs closed-loop load generation, Poisson arrivals, percentile reporting, and warmup discipline; a benchmark run wrong is worse than no benchmark.
Observability (topic 21): Prometheus scraping, histogram quantiles, Grafana dashboards - you will be reading vLLM's /metrics and DCGM exporter for the whole engagement.

Cloud cost and FinOps (topic 19): on-demand vs reserved vs spot pricing, committed-use discounts, and unit-economics framing - the deliverable here is a cost model, not a benchmark table - plus enough comfort with bytes, GiB vs GB and FLOP/s to do 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 out loud in a meeting.

subtopics.name: The VRAM budget: what actually occupies a GPU
subtopics.learn: Decompose GPU memory into five buckets and be able to size each: model weights (params x bytes per param - 8B in bf16 is 16 GB, 70B is 140 GB and therefore does not fit one 80 GB card), the KV cache pool, peak activation and workspace memory during a forward pass, fixed overhead (CUDA context, NCCL communication buffers, CUDA graph pools - typically 1-3 GB), and fragmentation. Understand exactly what vLLM's --gpu-memory-utilization (default 0.90) means: a fraction of TOTAL card memory that vLLM may occupy, after which it runs a profiling forward pass, subtracts weights plus peak activations, and hands the entire remainder to the KV block pool. That is why the flag over-commits and OOMs at startup on any card that is shared with a monitoring agent, a second replica, or a leftover process - check nvidia-smi before you set it, and never assume 0.95 is free performance.

resource.label: vLLM docs - Optimization and Tuning (KV cache memory, gpu_memory_utilization, preemption)

subtopics.name: Roofline: why decode is bandwidth-bound and prefill is not
subtopics.learn: Derive it rather than memorising it. A decode step reads every weight from HBM to produce one token per sequence, so FLOPs are roughly 2N per token per sequence while bytes moved are roughly 2N once for the whole batch - arithmetic intensity is approximately the batch size. Compute the ridge point of your GPU: an H100 SXM at about 3.35 TB/s HBM and about 990 TFLOP/s dense bf16 turns over at roughly 300 FLOP/byte, an A100 80GB at 2.0 TB/s and 312 TFLOP/s at roughly 156, so decode stays memory-bound until batch sizes in the hundreds. That gives you a hard upper bound to sanity-check any vendor claim: 3.35e12 bytes/s divided by 16e9 bytes of bf16 8B weights is about 209 tokens/s for a single stream, and anyone quoting 800 is quoting aggregate throughput. The consequence drives every later decision: at batch 1 shrinking weights (quantisation) buys latency, at batch 256 only fewer FLOPs or faster tensor cores do.

resource.label: NVIDIA Deep Learning Performance Documentation (GPU performance background)

subtopics.name: The four numbers: TTFT, TPOT, throughput, goodput
subtopics.learn: Fix the vocabulary before you measure anything. Time to first token (TTFT) is dominated by prefill and queueing; time per output token (TPOT, also inter-token latency) is dominated by decode and by how many sequences share the batch; end-to-end latency is TTFT plus TPOT times output length; throughput is output tokens/s in aggregate and per GPU. Add goodput - requests per second that meet BOTH a p95 TTFT and a p95 TPOT target - because it is the only one of these that maps to 'the customer is happy', and it is the number your capacity plan must be denominated in. Internalise the tension: every knob that raises aggregate throughput (bigger batch, more concurrent sequences) raises per-user TPOT, so 'tokens per second' with no qualifier - input or output, per user or aggregate, at what concurrency, under what SLO - is not a number, it is a marketing artefact.

resource.label: Lilian Weng - Large Transformer Model Inference Optimization

subtopics.name: KV cache arithmetic and why GQA changed the economics
subtopics.learn: Memorise the formula: bytes per token = 2 (K and V) x num_layers x num_kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element. Work three examples until they are automatic - Llama-3-8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16) is 2x32x8x128x2 = 131,072 B = 128 KiB/token; Llama-2-7B with full multi-head attention (32 KV heads) is 512 KiB/token, four times worse, which is precisely why grouped-query attention made long context affordable; Llama-3-70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads) is 320 KiB/token. Then close the loop: an 8B on an 80 GB H100 at utilisation 0.90 leaves roughly 72 - 16 - 4 = 52 GiB of KV pool, which is about 426,000 tokens, which is about 52 concurrent sequences at 8k context or 6 at 64k. Know the variants you will meet - MQA (one KV head), GQA (grouped), MLA (DeepSeek's compressed latent KV) - and know that --max-model-len is the single largest lever on concurrency because it caps the per-sequence worst case the scheduler must respect.

resource.label: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models (arXiv 2305.13245)

subtopics.name: PagedAttention: blocks, block tables, preemption
subtopics.learn: Understand the actual mechanism, not the analogy. KV is stored in fixed-size non-contiguous blocks (block_size default 16 tokens) with a per-sequence block table, so the engine stops reserving max_model_len of contiguous memory per request - which in pre-paged servers wasted 60-80% of the pool to internal and external fragmentation. Copy-on-write block sharing means parallel samples, beam search and identical prefixes cost one copy of the shared blocks. Most importantly, know what happens when the pool fills mid-generation: the scheduler PREEMPTS a running sequence, either RECOMPUTE (discard its KV and re-run prefill when it is rescheduled) or SWAP (move blocks to pinned CPU memory, sized by --swap-space, default 4 GiB). Preemption surfaces to the user as a multi-second stall, never as an error, so vllm:num_preemptions_total is a first-class alert and not a curiosity.

resource.label: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (arXiv 2309.06180)

subtopics.name: Continuous batching and the two admission knobs
subtopics.learn: Static batching waits for the longest generation in the batch before anything is returned; continuous (iteration-level) batching evicts finished sequences and admits queued ones at every decode step, which is where most of vLLM's throughput advantage over a naive HuggingFace generate loop comes from. Learn the two knobs that control it and what each costs: --max-num-seqs caps concurrently running sequences (raises aggregate throughput, raises per-user TPOT, raises KV pressure and therefore preemption risk) and --max-num-batched-tokens caps tokens processed per scheduler step (raises prefill throughput and TTFT recovery, but a large value lets one big prefill dominate a step). Defaults have moved between the V0 and V1 engines, so read the values off the startup log for the version you are actually running rather than quoting a blog post, and always change one knob at a time against a fixed load profile.

resource.label: vLLM repository (engine arguments and scheduler source)

subtopics.name: Chunked prefill and prefill/decode disaggregation
subtopics.learn: This is the fix for the single most common complaint in a RAG deployment: 'the app freezes for everyone when one person pastes a document'. Without chunked prefill, a 32k-token prompt consumes an entire scheduler step and every streaming user's inter-token latency spikes by seconds. Chunked prefill splits that prefill into --max-num-batched-tokens-sized pieces and mixes them with decode tokens each step, trading a modest TTFT increase for the long request against a flat ITL for everyone else; it is on by default in the V1 engine, and you should be able to show the before/after ITL histogram. At larger scale, understand disaggregated serving - a prefill pool sized for compute and a decode pool sized for HBM bandwidth and KV capacity, with KV blocks shipped between them over NVLink or RDMA via a KV connector - and be equally able to say when that is over-engineering for a customer running four GPUs.

resource.label: LMCache (KV cache offloading and disaggregated prefill for vLLM)

subtopics.name: Automatic prefix caching and prefix-aware routing
subtopics.learn: Blocks are hashed by their content plus the hash of all preceding blocks, so any request sharing a prefix reuses those KV blocks instead of recomputing them. The wins are enormous and predictable: a 2,000-token system prompt plus few-shot examples on every request, a shared RAG document across a question set, and multi-turn chat where turn N re-sends turns 1..N-1. Watch the prefix cache hit-rate metrics (a gauge in V0, hits and queries counters in V1) as a primary KPI. Then learn the two production traps: the cache is per-replica and per-GPU, so a round-robin load balancer across eight replicas drives the hit rate towards zero and you need prefix-aware or session-affine routing to recover it; and cached blocks are evicted LRU from the same pool that serves running sequences, so hit rate collapses exactly when KV pressure is highest - which is exactly when you were counting on it.

resource.label: vLLM design docs - Automatic Prefix Caching (hash-based block reuse and eviction)

subtopics.name: Speculative decoding and when it backfires
subtopics.learn: A cheap drafter proposes k tokens, the target model verifies all k in a single forward pass, and the accepted prefix is kept - with rejection-sampling verification the output distribution is provably identical to the target model's, so this is a pure latency optimisation, not a quality trade. The governing quantity is the acceptance rate alpha; expected tokens per verification step is (1 - alpha^(k+1)) / (1 - alpha), so a drafter with alpha = 0.7 and k = 4 yields roughly 2.8 tokens per step before you subtract draft cost. Know the method families - n-gram / prompt-lookup drafting (free, and spectacular for code editing, diff generation and extractive RAG where output copies input), EAGLE-style and Medusa-style heads, and a genuinely smaller draft model - and configure them through vLLM's --speculative-config. The trap that catches people: speculation spends spare compute to save bandwidth, so it wins at batch 1 and can reduce total throughput at production concurrency; benchmark it at your real batch size or you will ship a regression.

resource.label: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding (arXiv 2211.17192)

subtopics.name: Quantisation: formats, granularity, and where the win is
subtopics.learn: Separate the axes. What is quantised: weight-only (W4A16, W8A16) versus weights and activations (W8A8). Format: INT4, INT8, FP8 e4m3 and e5m2, NVFP4. Granularity: per-tensor, per-channel, per-group of 128 - finer granularity costs a little memory and recovers most of the accuracy. Calibration method: GPTQ (second-order/Hessian error compensation), AWQ (activation-aware per-channel scaling to protect salient weights), SmoothQuant (migrating activation outliers into weights so INT8 activations behave). The operational rule that matters: weight-only INT4 shrinks weights 4x and therefore wins at LOW batch where you are bandwidth-bound, but the dequantisation costs compute, so without Marlin/Machete-class kernels it can be slower than bf16 at high batch; FP8 W8A8 on Hopper or Ada (SM 8.9/9.0) actually executes on FP8 tensor cores and so raises throughput at high batch too, at near-lossless quality. Always re-run the customer's own eval after quantising - the degradation lands on rare entities, non-English text and code, not on your three smoke-test prompts.

resource.label: llm-compressor (vLLM project) - quantisation recipes and formats

subtopics.name: KV cache quantisation for long-context workloads
subtopics.learn: Separate from weight quantisation and often more valuable: --kv-cache-dtype fp8 (choose e4m3 for range-limited precision or e5m2 for more exponent) halves KV bytes per token, which directly doubles either concurrency or maximum context at the same VRAM, and speeds decode because attention reads half the bytes. Understand that it needs scaling factors - either shipped in the checkpoint or derived at startup with --calculate-kv-scales - and that quality loss concentrates in exactly the place customers notice: very long contexts and needle-in-a-haystack retrieval from the middle of a document. Measure it with a long-context retrieval eval at the customer's real context length, never with perplexity on a generic corpus. Check kernel and backend support before you promise INT8 or INT4 KV to anyone; support varies by attention backend and GPU generation.

resource.label: vLLM docs - Quantized KV Cache (kv-cache-dtype fp8 e4m3/e5m2, calibrated scales)

subtopics.name: Attention kernels, CUDA graphs, and eager mode
subtopics.learn: FlashAttention tiles the attention computation so the N x N score matrix is never materialised in HBM, turning attention memory from quadratic to linear and making it IO-aware; FlashAttention-2/3 and FlashInfer add paged-KV decode kernels, and decode attention is a genuinely different kernel from prefill attention with different bottlenecks. CUDA graphs capture a whole decode iteration as one replayable graph, eliminating per-kernel launch overhead that dominates wall time at small batch sizes; vLLM captures graphs for a set of batch sizes at startup and pads to the nearest captured size, which is why startup takes a minute and why memory usage jumps at the end of initialisation. Know what --enforce-eager actually costs: it disables graph capture, saving a couple of GB and startup time, at a real decode throughput loss at low concurrency - it is a debugging flag, not a production setting, and shipping it because it silenced a startup error is a classic quiet regression.

resource.label: FlashAttention repository (Dao-AILab)

subtopics.name: Multi-GPU: tensor, pipeline, data and expert parallelism
subtopics.learn: Tensor parallelism shards every weight matrix across GPUs and requires an all-reduce roughly twice per transformer block, so it lives or dies on interconnect - excellent over NVLink/NVSwitch, potentially slower than a single GPU over PCIe. TP size must divide the attention head count, and with GQA at 8 KV heads a TP of 16 replicates KV rather than sharding it, which quietly costs you cache capacity. Pipeline parallelism shards layers with only point-to-point sends between stages, tolerates Ethernet or InfiniBand between nodes, and pays in bubbles unless enough requests are in flight - it is the cross-node tool. Data parallelism is N independent replicas, and it is the correct default answer whenever the model fits on one GPU: N replicas almost always beat TP=N on throughput per dollar and on blast radius. Add expert parallelism for MoE models. In vLLM these are -tp, -pp, --data-parallel-size and --enable-expert-parallel; be able to argue a topology from model size, interconnect and SLO rather than habit.

resource.label: NVIDIA NCCL User Guide (collectives and topology)

subtopics.name: Running a benchmark that is worth quoting
subtopics.learn: Drive a running server with vllm bench serve (previously benchmarks/benchmark_serving.py): --dataset-name sharegpt or random with --random-input-len / --random-output-len, --num-prompts, --request-rate for Poisson arrivals, --burstiness to control clumping, and --ignore-eos when you need output length pinned. Discard a warmup phase - CUDA graph capture, torch.compile and a cold prefix cache make the first requests unrepresentative. Never quote --request-rate inf: that measures saturation throughput, which is the one number you can never promise a customer. Match the customer's real length distribution, because a 200-in/200-out benchmark tells you nothing about a 20k-in RAG workload and the difference is an order of magnitude in prefill cost. Record, alongside every result row, the GPU SKU, driver, vLLM version, model revision, quantisation, and the complete server and client command lines - a benchmark you cannot re-run is a rumour.

resource.label: vLLM benchmarks directory (serving, throughput and latency harnesses)

subtopics.name: Finding the knee: queueing, Little's law, admission control
subtopics.learn: Sweep offered load and plot output tokens/s and p95 TTFT against request rate. Below the knee, latency is flat and set by service time; above it, the queue grows, TTFT rises without bound, and throughput merely plateaus - so the knee, not the peak, is the capacity number. Use Little's law (L = lambda x W) to convert '500 users' into concurrent in-flight requests: concurrency equals arrival rate times mean time in system, which is how a per-user behavioural estimate becomes a GPU count. Size to roughly 60-70% of the knee because arrivals are bursty and business-hour peaks are 3-5x the daily mean. Then close the failure mode: vLLM's queue is effectively unbounded, so an overload degrades into universal timeouts rather than partial service - add admission control (max queue depth, 429 with Retry-After, per-tenant concurrency caps) and decide deliberately who gets shed first.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Handling Overload

subtopics.name: Production observability for an inference server
subtopics.learn: Scrape vLLM's /metrics and build the dashboard before the first customer request: vllm:num_requests_running and vllm:num_requests_waiting, vllm:gpu_cache_usage_perc, prefix cache hits/queries, vllm:num_preemptions_total, and the histograms vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds, vllm:time_per_output_token_seconds and vllm:e2e_request_latency_seconds (use histogram_quantile, and alert on the quantile, never the mean). The critical insight for autoscaling: nvidia-smi GPU utilisation sits near 100% by design under continuous batching and is therefore useless as a scaling signal - scale on queue depth (num_requests_waiting) and KV cache utilisation instead. Add DCGM exporter for HBM used, SM occupancy, power draw against cap, clock throttle reasons and XID errors, because 'inference got slow this week' is sometimes a thermally throttled or power-capped card in the customer's under-provisioned rack, and you want that on a graph rather than in an argument.

resource.label: Prometheus documentation (querying, histograms, alerting)

subtopics.name: GPU economics and the self-host vs API break-even
subtopics.learn: Reduce serving to one unit: cost per million output tokens = (GPU price per hour) / (output tokens per second at SLO x 3600) x 1e6. Work it end to end - an H100 at roughly $3/hour sustaining 2,000 output tok/s at the SLO produces 7.2M tokens/hour, about $0.42 per million - and then price the same workload against list API pricing so the comparison is concrete. Model the costs people leave out of the spreadsheet: idle hours (a reserved GPU bills at 3am, a token API does not), N+1 redundancy, a staging replica, weight storage and egress, and the engineer-time to keep an inference stack patched. Understand the shape of the curve rather than a single answer: APIs win for spiky, low-volume and early-stage workloads; self-hosting wins on sustained high utilisation, data residency and air-gap requirements, custom or fine-tuned weights, and price predictability - and the crossover is a monthly token volume you can compute and defend.

resource.label: Google Cloud documentation - GPU platforms and machine types

subtopics.name: Writing the capacity plan a CFO will actually sign
subtopics.learn: One page, four blocks. Assumptions: users, sessions per user per day, requests per session, mean and p95 input and output tokens, peak-to-mean factor, business-hours concentration - every one of these a number the customer supplied or approved, not one you invented. Derivation: peak token rate, measured output tokens/s per GPU at the stated SLO with a link to the benchmark run id, GPU count with headroom and redundancy shown separately. Economics: monthly cost split into fixed and variable, cost per user per month, and the API alternative at the same volume so this is a comparison rather than a request. Sensitivity: what happens if output length doubles, if adoption is 2x plan, or if the SLO tightens by 200ms.
