64.proofOfWork: Build `llm-cost-lab`: a small repository that runs one fixed workload from the Kaupex Task Compiler under six named configurations - baseline, caching only, caching plus structured output, small model only, cascade with escalation, and batch for the offline half - through a single `make bench CONFIG=<name>` entrypoint that writes every call to a SQLite ledger and emits a generated markdown report. The report must contain one row per configuration with columns for cost per unit of work, total input/cache-write/cache-read/output tokens, cache hit rate, p50 and p95 TTFT, p95 end-to-end latency, eval score overall and by category, escalation rate where applicable, and n - every cell traceable to a stored run_id. Include three things that prove you measured rather than assumed: a plot of cost per request against cache hit rate as the inter-request gap sweeps past the 5-minute TTL boundary; a break-even chart for 5-minute versus 1-hour TTL as a function of reuse count for your actual prefix size; and a deliberate negative result documented in the README, such as a configuration where caching or cascading cost more, with the arithmetic explaining why. Add a CI job that fails the build if cost per unit rises more than 10% or any eval category drops more than 5 points, plus a two-page COST-REVIEW.md written for a non-engineer stakeholder that leads with cost per resolved unit and the quality delta, not with tokens.

65.topic: Platform fluency for take-homes: Anthropic and OpenAI APIs side by side
65.why: FDE take-homes and customer POCs are timeboxed, and the person grading you is watching whether your budget went into the problem or into plumbing you should already know. Customers almost never let you pick the vendor either — they are already on Bedrock, or Azure, or have a procurement contract with one provider — so 'can you do this on our stack?' has to be answerable with a running demo rather than a maybe. Being able to write the tool loop, the strict output schema, the streaming consumer and the batch job on either API from memory turns a two-day integration into an afternoon, and turns a vendor-migration question into a one-page diff instead of a project.
prerequisites: Topic 47 (tool use, structured outputs and MCP servers): the concepts of a tool schema, a tool-execution loop and a JSON output contract. This topic is those same ideas executed twice, fast, from memory, under a stopwatch.

Topic 46 (prompt engineering as code): a versioned prompt file, a golden set of inputs, and a one-command regression run — you need these to prove the two implementations actually produce equivalent output rather than merely both returning 200.

Fluent Python (and enough TypeScript to read SDK examples): `httpx`/`requests`, SSE parsing, `asyncio.gather`, Pydantic v2 models, `os.environ` secret handling, and comfort reading a raw `curl -i` response including headers.

JSON Schema literacy: `type`, `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `enum`, `const`, `anyOf`, `$ref`/`$defs`, and specifically the difference between a property that is not in `required` and one whose type is a union with `null`.

Topic 43 (LLM-era system design): retries with exponential backoff and jitter, timeouts, idempotency and latency budgets — without these your client is tutorial-shaped, not production-shaped, and graders notice.
Two funded API keys (Anthropic and OpenAI, roughly $20 each) and a stopwatch. This topic is a drill; without live keys against current models you are reading documentation, not building fluency.

subtopics.name: Auth, base URLs, and a scaffold you can type from memory
subtopics.learn: Both platforms are POST-JSON over HTTPS and the auth differs in exactly one header. Anthropic: `POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages` with `x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` (required — omitting it is a 400), and `content-type: application/json`. OpenAI: `POST https://api.openai.com/v1/responses` with `Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY`, plus optional `OpenAI-Organization` and `OpenAI-Project` headers. Both SDK clients read the key from the environment with zero arguments (`anthropic.Anthropic()`, `OpenAI()`). Build yourself a scaffold — pinned SDK versions, `.env.example`, a `smoke.py` that makes one call on each provider, and the equivalent `curl` in the README — and time it: keys to first 200 should be under ten minutes on both.

resource.label: Claude Docs — API getting started

subtopics.name: Request and response shapes, memorised in parallel
subtopics.learn: Anthropic minimal body: `{model, max_tokens (REQUIRED — omitting it 400s), messages: [{role, content}], system (top-level, there is no "system" role)}`, returning `{id, type: "message", role: "assistant", content: [blocks], stop_reason, usage: {input_tokens, output_tokens}}`. OpenAI Responses minimal body: `{model, input (string or item array), instructions, max_output_tokens (optional)}`, returning `{id: "resp_...", status, output: [items], usage: {input_tokens, output_tokens, total_tokens}}` with `output_text` as an SDK-only convenience. Anthropic `content` is always a list, so `response.content[0].text` breaks the moment a `thinking` or `tool_use` block precedes the text. Know the `stop_reason` enum — `end_turn`, `max_tokens`, `stop_sequence`, `tool_use`, `pause_turn`, `refusal`, `model_context_window_exceeded` — and its OpenAI counterpart `status: "incomplete"` plus `incomplete_details.reason`. Know too that `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k` are deprecated on Claude models released after Opus 4.6 (non-default values are rejected with a 400) and that OpenAI reasoning models reject `temperature` as well.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Messages API reference (body parameters and returns)

subtopics.name: System prompt placement and who owns conversation state
subtopics.learn: Anthropic has no system role: the system prompt is the top-level `system` parameter, either a string or an array of `TextBlockParam` (the array form exists so you can attach `cache_control` to it). OpenAI Responses uses top-level `instructions`, or a `developer`/`system` role item inside `input` — and `instructions` is not carried forward when you chain with `previous_response_id`, which surprises people mid-conversation. The larger difference is statefulness: Anthropic is always stateless, so you resend the full `messages` array every turn and you own truncation; OpenAI Responses can be stateful via `store: true` plus `previous_response_id`. Decide deliberately and be able to defend it: stateful means fewer tokens on the wire and less code, stateless is what most enterprise customers with data-retention rules will actually approve. Practise forcing stateless on OpenAI with `store: false` and resending the item list yourself.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform — Conversation state guide

subtopics.name: Content blocks and multimodal input on both
subtopics.learn: Anthropic message `content` is a string or a list of typed blocks: `{"type":"text"}`, `{"type":"image","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"image/png","data":...}}` or a `{"type":"url"}` source, `{"type":"document"}` for PDFs, plus `tool_use`, `tool_result` and `thinking`. OpenAI Responses uses input parts `{"type":"input_text"}`, `{"type":"input_image","image_url": <data URI or https URL>}` and `{"type":"input_file"}`, with model text returning as `output_text` parts carrying `annotations`. Drill both directions: base64 a PNG and a five-page PDF and get the same structured extraction out of each API. Respect the ceilings — an Anthropic Messages request caps at 32 MB and returns 413 `request_too_large` above it, so anything larger goes through the Files API rather than inline base64.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Vision (image and document inputs)

subtopics.name: Tool schemas: three envelopes around one JSON Schema
subtopics.learn: The parameter schema is identical JSON Schema on both platforms; only the wrapper differs, and this is the single most-fumbled thing under time pressure. Anthropic: `tools: [{name, description, input_schema: {type: "object", properties, required}}]` — note `input_schema`, not `parameters`. OpenAI Responses: `tools: [{type: "function", name, description, parameters, strict}]`, flat. OpenAI Chat Completions: `tools: [{type: "function", function: {name, description, parameters, strict}}]`, nested one level deeper. Build a `toolspec.py` that holds the raw JSON Schema once plus two adapter functions emitting the two envelopes, and unit-test the adapters. That file is the reusable asset a take-home actually rewards, and it is what you paste into a customer repo on day one.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform — Function calling guide

subtopics.name: The agent loop: tool_result vs function_call_output
subtopics.learn: Write both loops from memory. Anthropic: the response arrives with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and one or more `{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_...","name","input"}` blocks where `input` is already a parsed object; you append the assistant message verbatim with all blocks in original order, then append a **user** message whose content is `[{"type":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"toolu_...","content": <string or blocks>, "is_error": bool}]`, and every `tool_use` in a turn must get a matching `tool_result` in the immediately following message or the API 400s. OpenAI Responses: the model emits a `function_call` item with `call_id` and `arguments` as a **JSON string** you must `json.loads` (and defend against malformed JSON unless `strict: true`); you append that item plus `{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":...,"output":"<string>"}`. Chat Completions instead uses `tool_calls` on the assistant message answered by a `{"role":"tool","tool_call_id":...}` message. Always add a hard `max_iterations` guard.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Implementing tool use (the tool-result round trip)

subtopics.name: tool_choice, forcing, and parallel tool calls
subtopics.learn: Anthropic `tool_choice` takes `{"type":"auto"}`, `{"type":"any"}` (must call some tool), `{"type":"tool","name":"x"}` (must call that one) and `{"type":"none"}`, with `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` capping a turn at one call. OpenAI takes `tool_choice: "auto" | "none" | "required" | {"type":"function","name":"x"}` plus `parallel_tool_calls: false`. Understand what forcing costs before you reach for it: forced tool use is incompatible with some thinking configurations on Claude and returns a 'Forced tool use not supported' 400, and on both platforms forcing removes the model's ability to say 'I don't have enough information to call this' — exactly the behaviour a customer-facing agent needs. Handle the multi-call case properly: one assistant turn can contain N tool calls, you execute all N (concurrently is fine), and you return all N results together in the next turn.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Tool use overview (tool_choice and parallel use)

subtopics.name: Structured output on OpenAI: text.format and the strict subset
subtopics.learn: Responses API: `text: {format: {type: "json_schema", name: "...", schema: {...}, strict: true}}`. Chat Completions: `response_format: {type: "json_schema", json_schema: {name, schema, strict: true}}`. Under `strict: true` every object needs `"additionalProperties": false` and every declared property must appear in `required`; optionality is expressed as a union with null (`"type": ["string", "null"]`), and getting this wrong is the most common 400 in this whole topic. Prefer the SDK helpers over hand-rolled schemas: `client.responses.parse(..., text_format=MyPydanticModel)` then read `.output_parsed`, or `zodTextFormat()` in TypeScript. Handle the two escape hatches that both return HTTP 200 and neither matches your schema: a `refusal`, and `status: "incomplete"` with `incomplete_details.reason == "max_output_tokens"`.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform — Structured Outputs guide

subtopics.name: Structured output on Anthropic: output_config.format and strict tools
subtopics.learn: Anthropic gives two independent levers you can use together. JSON outputs: top-level `output_config: {format: {type: "json_schema", schema: {...}}}` constrains the assistant's text block to schema-valid JSON. Strict tool use: `strict: true` on an individual tool grammar-constrains that tool's name and inputs. Note the migration trap — the older beta field was `output_format` with header `structured-outputs-2025-11-13`, still accepted for a transition period, so old sample code compiles and modern SDKs may raise a `TypeError` on it. Use `client.messages.parse()` with a Pydantic model for the ergonomic path. Keep the portable fallback in muscle memory too: define one tool and force it with `tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":"emit"}`, then read `block.input` — it works on every model, every gateway, and older Bedrock deployments where constrained decoding is unavailable.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Structured outputs

subtopics.name: The schema subset both engines refuse, and grammar limits
subtopics.learn: Constrained decoding compiles your schema into a grammar, so both platforms support only a subset, and the subsets differ. On Anthropic, supported: `enum`, `const`, `anyOf`, `$ref`/`$defs`, `default`, string formats (`date-time`, `date`, `email`, `uri`, `uuid`, `ipv4`), and array `minItems` of 0 or 1 only. Not supported: recursive schemas, external `$ref`, numeric constraints (`minimum`, `maximum`, `multipleOf`), `minLength`/`maxLength`, and regex lookahead/lookbehind or backreferences — each returns a 400. Hard limits per request: 20 strict tools, 24 optional parameters across all strict schemas, 16 union-typed parameters, plus an internal compiled-grammar ceiling that surfaces as 'Schema is too complex for compilation' and a 180-second compile timeout. Compiled grammars cache for 24 hours from last use, so never benchmark latency on a cold schema. Finally: enum capitalisation is not guaranteed, so compare enum values case-insensitively.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Strict tool use

subtopics.name: Streaming Anthropic: the content-block state machine
subtopics.learn: With `stream: true` you get SSE with typed events: `message_start` (carries `usage.input_tokens`), then per block `content_block_start` → repeated `content_block_delta` → `content_block_stop`, then `message_delta` (carries the final `stop_reason` and cumulative `usage.output_tokens`), then `message_stop`, with `ping` and `error` interleaved. Learn the delta types: `text_delta`; `input_json_delta`, whose `partial_json` fragments you must concatenate before parsing (tool arguments stream as a fragmented JSON string even though the non-streaming field is an object); `thinking_delta`; and `signature_delta`. Use `with client.messages.stream(...) as stream:` and `stream.get_final_message()` (TypeScript `stream.finalMessage()`) rather than reassembling blocks by hand. Know the operational reason this matters: long non-streaming requests hit a server-side time limit, so high-`max_tokens` calls must stream.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Streaming Messages (event types and deltas)

subtopics.name: Streaming OpenAI: semantic events vs raw token deltas
subtopics.learn: The Responses API streams semantic events with a `type` and a monotonic `sequence_number`: `response.created`, `response.output_item.added`, `response.content_part.added`, `response.output_text.delta`, `response.function_call_arguments.delta`, `response.output_text.done`, then `response.completed` / `response.failed` / `response.incomplete`. Chat Completions instead streams raw `choices[0].delta` chunks terminated by `data: [DONE]`, and returns no usage numbers at all unless you pass `stream_options: {include_usage: true}` — forgetting that flag is why a cost dashboard goes blank the day someone enables streaming. Write one normaliser that reduces both providers' streams to the same `(event, text_chunk, tool_arg_fragment, usage)` tuple, and instrument it to report time-to-first-text-token separately from total wall-clock, because those two numbers move independently and customers feel the first one.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform — Streaming responses guide

subtopics.name: Anthropic thinking blocks inside a tool loop
subtopics.learn: Configure with `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` where N >= 1024 and N < `max_tokens`, or `{type: "adaptive"}`. Responses then carry `thinking` blocks before text, each with an encrypted `signature`. The rule that breaks people: in multi-turn and tool-use conversations you must pass thinking blocks back unchanged and in original order — you cannot edit, reorder or partially drop them (including `redacted_thinking` blocks) or you get a 400 saying the thinking block no longer matches the conversation, which typically fires on turn three of a live demo. Use `display: "omitted"` when you are not showing reasoning to users: the thinking text is empty but the signature is preserved for continuity, and time-to-first-text improves because the server skips streaming thinking tokens. Remember thinking tokens count against `max_tokens`, so a 10k budget under an 8k cap is a 400.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Thinking (signatures, preservation, tool use)

subtopics.name: OpenAI reasoning items, effort, and reasoning tokens
subtopics.learn: Set `reasoning: {effort: "low"|"medium"|"high", summary: "auto"}` on reasoning models. You pay for hidden reasoning tokens, reported at `usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`; they bill as output and they consume `max_output_tokens`, so a tight cap plus high effort yields `status: "incomplete"`, an empty message, and a full invoice. In a tool loop you must preserve reasoning context across turns: either chain with `previous_response_id`, or when running stateless (`store: false`) pass the reasoning items back in `input` and request `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]`. Build the same two-tool agent with reasoning enabled on both platforms and record tokens, latency and answer quality per effort level — that comparison table is precisely the kind of evidence a take-home write-up should lead with.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform — Reasoning models guide

subtopics.name: Prompt caching: explicit breakpoints vs automatic prefix caching
subtopics.learn: Anthropic is explicit: put `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` on a content block, or once at the top level of the request to let the breakpoint auto-advance as the conversation grows. The cached prefix spans `tools`, then `system`, then `messages`, in that order, up to and including the marked block; default TTL is 5 minutes, refreshed free on every hit, with a 1-hour option. Writes cost 1.25x base input and reads 0.1x, and you verify a hit by comparing `usage.cache_creation_input_tokens` against `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` — if reads stay zero your prefix is not byte-identical, and a timestamp in the system prompt, a reordered tool list, or a changed `output_config.format` will each do that silently. OpenAI caches automatically above roughly 1024 tokens with no breakpoints; you steer routing with `prompt_cache_key` and verify with `usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens`. Same discipline on both: static content first, volatile content last.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Prompt caching

subtopics.name: Batch: inline requests array vs JSONL file upload
subtopics.learn: Both are 50% cheaper with a 24-hour window; the mechanics are entirely different. Anthropic: `POST /v1/messages/batches` with `requests: [{custom_id, params: {<full Messages body>}}]` sent inline, up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, where `custom_id` must match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`; poll `processing_status` until it reads `"ended"` (not `"completed"`), read `request_counts.{processing,succeeded,errored,canceled,expired}`, then stream the `.jsonl` at `results_url` — results are unordered, so you join on `custom_id`. `max_tokens: 0` cache pre-warming is rejected inside a batch. OpenAI: first upload a JSONL of `{custom_id, method: "POST", url: "/v1/responses", body: {...}}` with `purpose: "batch"`, then `POST /v1/batches` with `input_file_id`, `endpoint` and `completion_window: "24h"`; poll `status` through `validating → in_progress → finalizing → completed`, then download `output_file_id` and, separately, `error_file_id`. Write one bulk-classification job both ways and record wall-clock and cost.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Batch processing (Message Batches API)

subtopics.name: Errors, retries, timeouts, rate-limit headers, request IDs
subtopics.learn: Memorise the Anthropic taxonomy: 400 `invalid_request_error`, 401 `authentication_error`, 403 `permission_error`, 404 `not_found_error`, 413 `request_too_large` (32 MB on Messages), 429 `rate_limit_error`, 500 `api_error`, 529 `overloaded_error`. Retry 429/500/529 with exponential backoff and jitter, honour `retry-after`, and never retry a 400. Read your remaining budget from `anthropic-ratelimit-{requests,input-tokens,output-tokens}-{limit,remaining,reset}` — `reset` is an RFC 3339 timestamp, not a seconds count — and from OpenAI's `x-ratelimit-remaining-{requests,tokens}` and `x-ratelimit-reset-*`. Both SDKs retry by default: set `max_retries` and a per-request `timeout` explicitly instead of inheriting defaults, and think hard about retrying a stream, since a mid-stream failure has already emitted partial output to the user. Log the `request-id` header (Anthropic) and `x-request-id` (OpenAI) on every call — without it you cannot file a useful support ticket, and filing one is a real FDE deliverable.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Rate limits (response headers and 429 handling)

subtopics.name: The portability layer and the 90-minute timed port
subtopics.learn: Build the thinnest abstraction that survives contact: one `generate(messages, tools, schema) -> Result` interface, two adapters, and a golden-file test asserting both providers parse to the same object across 20 fixed inputs. Resist the urge to add a config DSL — abstract the request envelope and the tool-result plumbing, and deliberately leave caching, thinking and batch leaky per-provider. Know the shortcut and its price: Anthropic exposes an OpenAI-SDK-compatible endpoint (point the OpenAI client at `base_url="https://api.anthropic.com/v1/"` with an Anthropic key), which is fine for a same-day bake-off but drops thinking, prompt caching, PDF support and citations, so it never ships to a customer. Then drill: set a 90-minute timer and rebuild the same feature — tool loop, strict schema, streaming, and a cost/latency report — on the other API without looking at the first repo. Log every stall and turn each one into a snippet in your scaffold.

resource.label: Claude Docs — OpenAI SDK compatibility (and its documented limitations)

outcomes: You can open a blank file with no documentation and write a working multi-turn tool-calling loop on the Anthropic Messages API and on the OpenAI Responses API in under twenty minutes each, including correct `tool_result` and `function_call_output` plumbing and a `max_iterations` guard.

You can recite the field-level diffs on demand — `input_schema` vs `parameters`, top-level `system` vs `instructions`, `max_tokens` required vs `max_output_tokens` optional, parsed `input` object vs `arguments` JSON string — and correct a colleague's code by reading it, without running it.

You can enforce a JSON contract three ways (OpenAI `text.format` with `strict: true`, Anthropic `output_config.format`, and the forced-tool fallback) and justify which one you would deploy on a customer's Bedrock estate and why.

You can consume both streaming protocols, reassemble a complete tool call from `input_json_delta` and `response.function_call_arguments.delta` fragments, and report time-to-first-token separately from total latency on the same prompt.
You can push the same 5,000-item job through both Batch APIs, join unordered results on `custom_id`, account for expired and errored requests, and produce a cost and wall-clock comparison table.

You can demonstrate a prompt-cache hit on both platforms by pointing at `cache_read_input_tokens` and `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, and diagnose in one sentence why a previously-hitting cache stopped hitting.
You can classify any API failure as retryable or not within seconds, name the header that tells you how long to wait, and produce the provider request ID needed to open a support ticket.
You can complete a 90-minute timed port of a feature from one API to the other and hand a grader a README they can run end to end with two commands.
failureModes: Returning only some of a turn's `tool_result` blocks — or dropping the assistant's `tool_use` blocks while trimming history for context — producing an opaque 400 that only appears on the third turn of a live customer demo.

Treating OpenAI's `arguments` as a dict because the Anthropic equivalent is one: the code passes on happy-path fixtures and throws the first time a real customer prompt yields a nested object under load.

Carrying `temperature=0` across from an older repo onto a current Claude or an OpenAI reasoning model, which hard-400s in the customer's environment while continuing to work locally against a pinned older model.

Setting `max_tokens` / `max_output_tokens` below the thinking or reasoning budget, so responses come back `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` or `status: "incomplete"` with empty content and a full bill, and the team spends a day blaming the prompt.
Enabling streaming on Chat Completions without `stream_options: {include_usage: true}`, silently zeroing the token counts that feed the customer's cost dashboard and internal chargeback report.
Putting a timestamp, session ID or reordered tool list at the front of the prompt, destroying every prompt-cache hit and roughly tripling input cost with no error surfacing anywhere.

Shipping the OpenAI-compatibility endpoint into a customer POC because it made the demo fast, then discovering during hardening that prompt caching, thinking and PDF support are unavailable on that path and the rewrite lands in the go-live week.
interviewQuestions: Whiteboard the tool-calling loop for the Anthropic Messages API and the OpenAI Responses API in parallel columns. Where does the tool result go in each, what is its identifier called, and what does the API do if you return two results for one call or none for one that was requested?

A customer must run on Bedrock and needs guaranteed schema-valid JSON on every request. Walk me through your options, what each costs in latency and flexibility, and what you do if their pinned model version does not support constrained decoding.

We swapped models and p95 latency doubled while input and output token counts stayed flat. Give me your debugging order across both APIs — what do you check first, and which specific usage field settles the argument?

Design a provider-agnostic LLM client for a team shipping to three customers on three different clouds. What do you abstract, what do you deliberately leave leaky, and how do you test that the abstraction has not started lying to you?

A bulk-extraction job over 200,000 documents must finish overnight at minimum cost. Compare the two Batch APIs concretely — submission, polling, result retrieval — and tell me exactly what you do about the requests that expire at the 24-hour boundary.

Explain prompt caching on both platforms to a customer's finance lead in plain language, then tell me three changes an engineer could ship tomorrow that would silently destroy the savings without raising a single error.
You have ninety minutes and a take-home that says 'build a research agent, any provider.' Which do you pick, what do you cut, what do you instrument, and what goes in the README?
65.proofOfWork: Beyond the two per-API repos, publish a third repo called `llm-api-parity` whose entire purpose is to prove the two are interchangeable and to document precisely where they are not. It contains one provider-neutral scenario file of roughly thirty cases — plain completion, single tool call, parallel tool calls, a tool that raises and must come back as `is_error` / an error string, strict-schema extraction, a deliberately unsupported schema feature, an oversized image, a forced stop at `max_tokens`, a cache-warm then cache-hit pair, and a ten-item batch — plus two thin adapters and a single `pytest` suite that runs every scenario against both providers and asserts the same parsed result object. `PARITY.md` is generated by the run, not hand-written: a table with one row per scenario and columns for both providers showing pass/fail, the exact request field names used, latency p50 and TTFT, input/output/cached/reasoning token counts, and cost, with a footnote for each behavioural divergence you found (for example which schema keywords 400 on which side, and what each returns when a tool result is missing). Add `CHEATSHEET.md`: a one-page side-by-side of endpoint, auth header, required fields, tool envelope, tool-result envelope, structured-output field, streaming event names, batch submission shape, and error taxonomy — short enough to read in ninety seconds before an interview. Add `PORT_LOG.md` recording the timed drill: start time, stop time, every point where you had to look something up, and the snippet you added to your scaffold so it never costs you a lookup again. Finally include `scripts/verify.sh` that runs the whole suite against live keys in under five minutes and prints a spend total, so anyone — a grader, a customer architect, a future you — can reproduce the parity claims rather than take your word for them.

66.why: An FDE is the person sitting in the room when the customer's security team returns a pentest report two weeks before go-live, and the deployment either survives that meeting or slips a quarter. You will be deploying your own code inside someone else's VPC, against their SSO, holding their regulated data, which means you personally own the authorization boundary, the secrets, and the answer to 'can tenant A see tenant B'. Reading the OWASP list is worthless here - you need to have actually exploited broken object-level authorization and a forged JWT with your own hands, because that is the only way you can look at a customer's API and see the bug before their auditor does.
prerequisites: Auth (topic 27): OAuth2 authorization-code flow, OIDC id_token vs access_token, JWT structure and claims (iss, aud, exp, sub), and how RBAC claims get into a request context - you cannot attack what you cannot draw.

Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems (topic 30): tenant_id propagation, Postgres row-level security, PII classification and audit trails, since most real findings in an FDE deployment are authorization findings, not memory-corruption findings.

FastAPI in production (topic 26) and PostgreSQL at depth (topic 29): dependency injection for auth, parameterised queries via bound parameters, and enough SQL to know why string interpolation into a WHERE clause is the whole bug.
Networking (topic 2): TLS handshake and certificate validation, HTTP request/response structure, headers, redirects, and proxies - you will spend ten hours reading raw HTTP in an intercepting proxy.
CI/CD and supply chain (topic 18): a pipeline you can add jobs to, plus SBOM/scanning concepts, because half of A06 is a CI problem rather than a code problem.

A local runnable copy of your own stack - Dokeo (Python/FastAPI/Postgres) and DefenderMate (TypeScript/Next.js) - with seeded data for at least two tenants and three roles, because the deliverable requires finding a real issue in your own code.

subtopics.name: Burp workbench: proxy, CA cert, scope, Repeater loop
subtopics.learn: Install Burp Suite Community, install its CA certificate into the browser trust store, and set target scope so Proxy history is not drowned in telemetry noise. Learn the loop you will run 200 times today: intercept a request, send it to Repeater with Ctrl+R, mutate one parameter, resend, diff status code / Content-Length / response time. Know Intruder's Sniper and Cluster bomb modes and that Community throttles Intruder hard, so scripted requests with Python plus `requests` are often faster for enumeration. Configure match-and-replace rules to swap the session cookie or Authorization header automatically - that is how you test cross-tenant access without re-logging in every request.

resource.label: PortSwigger: Burp Suite desktop documentation

subtopics.name: Map your own attack surface before touching a lab
subtopics.learn: Produce the artifact everything else hangs off: an endpoint inventory for Dokeo and DefenderMate with, per route, the HTTP method, whether authentication is required, which role/permission is checked, whether the object is tenant-scoped, what user input reaches a query/filesystem/HTTP client, and what it returns. Pull it from the OpenAPI schema plus route decorators rather than memory, and mark every route where the authorization check is 'the ORM filter happens to include tenant_id'. Also map trust boundaries: browser to edge, edge to API, API to Postgres, API to model provider, and any background worker that runs with elevated credentials. Every finding you produce later will be a cell in this table.

resource.label: OWASP WSTG: Identify Application Entry Points (WSTG-INFO-06)

subtopics.name: A01 Broken Access Control: IDOR and horizontal privilege escalation
subtopics.learn: Work the PortSwigger access-control labs end to end: unprotected admin functionality, admin functionality found via robots.txt or a JS bundle, user role controlled by a request parameter or a cookie, user ID controlled by a request parameter with and without an unpredictable GUID, and the 'user ID leaked in a redirect / in a different response' variants. The mechanism to internalise is that authentication answers 'who are you' and authorization answers 'may you touch this object', and almost every real breach is the second check missing on one route out of 200. Learn to test by identity swap: capture request R as user A, replay it verbatim with user B's session, and treat any 200 that should be 403 as a finding. Note that 404-instead-of-403 is a defensible design choice but only when it is deliberate and uniform.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Access control vulnerabilities

subtopics.name: API authorization: BOLA, BFLA, mass assignment, excessive data exposure
subtopics.learn: Learn the API-specific shape of A01 from the OWASP API Security Top 10: Broken Object Level Authorization (`GET /documents/{id}` with no tenant predicate), Broken Function Level Authorization (`POST /admin/users` reachable because the router guard was only applied to the GET), Broken Object Property Level Authorization / mass assignment (a Pydantic model or JS object spread that lets a client set `role`, `tenant_id`, `is_admin` or `credits`), and excessive data exposure where the API returns the whole ORM row and the frontend hides fields. Fix patterns matter more than exploits here: explicit response models with an allowlist of fields, separate input schemas that physically cannot carry privileged fields, and a single `authorize(actor, action, resource)` chokepoint rather than per-route ad hoc `if`. Then re-derive the same bugs against your own OpenAPI spec.

resource.label: OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks 2023 (BOLA, BOPLA, BFLA)

subtopics.name: A07 Authentication failures: brute force, enumeration, reset flows, MFA bypass
subtopics.learn: Run the authentication labs: username enumeration via subtly different responses and via response timing, password brute-force with IP-lockout bypasses (X-Forwarded-For, alternating valid logins), 2FA bypassed by skipping the second-step request, and password reset poisoning via a spoofed Host header used to build the reset link. The general lesson is that authentication is a state machine and attackers move between states out of order - test every step for 'what if I just call step 3 directly'. Know the correct defences concretely: constant-time comparisons, uniform error messages and timings, Argon2id or bcrypt with real cost parameters (never SHA-256 of a password), single-use time-bounded reset tokens generated by a CSPRNG and stored hashed, and rate limits keyed on account plus IP plus device rather than IP alone.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Authentication vulnerabilities

subtopics.name: JWT attacks: alg confusion, unverified signatures, jwk/jku/kid injection
subtopics.learn: Complete the JWT labs with Burp's JWT Editor: unverified signature, `alg: none`, brute-forced weak HMAC secret (hashcat mode 16500 against a short `secret`), signature bypass via an embedded `jwk` header, via `jku` pointing at an attacker-hosted JWKS, via `kid` path traversal to a known file such as `/dev/null`, and RS256-to-HS256 algorithm confusion where the public key is used as the HMAC key. In code, know the difference between `jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False})`, decoding without pinning `algorithms=['RS256']`, and decoding without checking `aud`, `iss` and `exp` - each is a separate real bug and the last one is why a staging token can work in production. Then grep your own codebase and your customer-facing SDK for every decode call and check all four properties.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: JWT attacks

subtopics.name: OAuth 2.0 and OIDC implementation flaws
subtopics.learn: Work the OAuth labs: authentication bypass via a flawed `state` parameter (CSRF on the callback, linking the victim's account to the attacker's identity), stealing an access token via an over-permissive `redirect_uri` (open redirect chained to the callback, path traversal in the redirect, or a naive `startswith` check), and unprotected dynamic client registration. Understand precisely why `redirect_uri` must be matched exactly against a registered allowlist, why implicit flow leaks tokens in the URL fragment and referer, why PKCE (`code_challenge` S256) exists for public clients, and why an access token is not proof of identity - only a validated `id_token` with checked `aud`, `iss`, `nonce` and signature is. This is the highest-frequency FDE integration and the place where a customer's IdP config will hand you a real finding.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: OAuth 2.0 authentication vulnerabilities

subtopics.name: Sessions, cookie attributes and CSRF
subtopics.learn: Do the CSRF labs: no token, token not tied to session, token validated only when present, token in a cookie (double-submit done wrong), and SameSite Lax bypass via a GET-based state change or a client-side redirect. Get the cookie flags exactly right rather than approximately: `HttpOnly` blocks JS theft, `Secure` blocks plaintext transmission, `SameSite=Lax` is the browser default and still allows top-level GET navigation, `SameSite=None` requires `Secure`, and the `__Host-` prefix pins a cookie to one origin with no `Domain` attribute. Know when CSRF is genuinely not exploitable (a pure `Authorization: Bearer` API with no ambient cookie) and when engineers wrongly assume it isn't, and know that a strict CORS policy is not a CSRF defence because the simple request still fires.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)

subtopics.name: A03 Injection: SQL injection by hand, then the correct fix
subtopics.learn: Run the SQLi track: UNION-based data extraction (determine column count with ORDER BY / NULL padding, find a text-compatible column, exfiltrate `information_schema.tables` on Postgres), blind boolean-based, blind time-based with `pg_sleep()`, and error-based via `CAST(... AS int)`. Then write the fix and prove it: bound parameters (`cursor.execute(sql, (value,))`, SQLAlchemy `text()` with `:param`), understanding that parameterisation binds values only - table names, column names and `ORDER BY` direction must be validated against an allowlist because they cannot be bound. Learn why ORMs are not automatically safe (`.filter(text(f"..."))`, `raw()`, string-built `IN` clauses) and why a WAF regex is a mitigation, not a fix. Finish by adding a least-privilege database role so even a successful injection cannot `DROP` or read another schema.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: SQL injection

subtopics.name: Injection beyond SQL: OS command, template, NoSQL, and LLM-adjacent sinks
subtopics.learn: Do the OS command injection labs (blind detection with `; sleep 10`, out-of-band via DNS) and the server-side template injection labs (identify the engine with `${7*7}` / `{{7*7}}`, then escalate through Python object attributes such as `__class__.__mro__` to reach `os.system` in Jinja2). The generalisation to carry: every injection is 'attacker data crossing into an interpreter', so enumerate your interpreters - shell, template engine, SQL, MongoDB query documents, YAML/pickle loaders, XPath, and now the model prompt itself. Fixes are structural: `subprocess.run([...], shell=False)` with an argument list, never `shell=True` with an f-string; sandboxed or logic-less templates; and `yaml.safe_load` over `yaml.load`. Cross-reference guardrails and prompt injection (topic 51) so you can explain to a customer why prompt injection is untrusted-input-into-an-interpreter with no parameterised query available.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: OS command injection

subtopics.name: XSS: reflected, stored, DOM-based, and a CSP that actually helps
subtopics.learn: Work reflected, stored and DOM XSS labs including a `document.write`/`innerHTML` sink reached from `location.hash`, and at least one context-escape lab (inside an attribute, inside a JS string, inside a template literal) so you internalise that escaping is context-dependent, not a single `escape()` call. Know the real fixes: contextual output encoding by the framework (React's JSX escaping, and precisely why `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` and Angular's bypass functions defeat it), DOMPurify for HTML you must render, and a Content-Security-Policy without `unsafe-inline` using nonces or hashes plus `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'none'`. Understand what XSS actually buys an attacker in your app: it runs in the victim's origin, so `HttpOnly` protects the cookie but not the session - the attacker just issues authenticated requests from the page.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Cross-site scripting

subtopics.name: SSRF and cloud metadata: the FDE's most dangerous feature request
subtopics.learn: Run the SSRF labs: basic SSRF to an internal admin interface, blacklist bypasses (alternate IP encodings, `127.1`, decimal integers, `localhost` variants, double URL-encoding), whitelist bypasses using the `@` userinfo trick, `#` fragments and DNS names that resolve to loopback, plus SSRF via the Referer header and via an open redirect chain. Then connect it to cloud reality: any 'give us a URL and we will import it' feature is one bad parse away from reading `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` and exfiltrating the instance role. The fix set is architectural - enforce IMDSv2 (token-required, hop limit 1), resolve the hostname yourself and validate the resulting IP against RFC1918/link-local/loopback ranges before connecting, re-validate after every redirect, and egress through a locked-down proxy with an allowlist rather than trusting a regex.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Server-side request forgery (SSRF)

subtopics.name: XXE, deserialization and file upload
subtopics.learn: Complete the XXE labs (file retrieval via an external entity, blind XXE via out-of-band DNS/HTTP and via error messages, XInclude when you cannot control the whole document) and know the one-line fix: disable DTD processing and external entity resolution in the parser - in Python use `defusedxml`, never bare `xml.etree` on untrusted input. Do at least one insecure deserialization lab and be able to state why `pickle.loads`, `yaml.load` and Java native deserialization on attacker data are remote code execution by design, not by bug. Then the file upload track: web-shell upload via a bypassed content-type check, extension blacklist bypass, and path traversal in the filename. Fixes to be able to write from memory: allowlist by sniffed content type, generate your own filename (never trust `filename`), store outside the web root or in object storage, and serve with `Content-Disposition: attachment` plus `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: XML external entity (XXE) injection

subtopics.name: A05 Security misconfiguration: CORS, headers, debug surface
subtopics.learn: Do the CORS labs and be able to explain the exact failure: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` reflected from the request `Origin` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is a cross-origin data read of every authenticated endpoint, and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null` is trivially forged from a sandboxed iframe. This is the single most common FDE-introduced bug because it is what you type at 11pm to unblock a customer's frontend. Then sweep the rest of A05 on your own deployment: `/docs` and `/openapi.json` exposed in production, DEBUG mode returning stack traces and settings, default credentials on a bundled Grafana or Redis, directory listing, missing `Strict-Transport-Security` / `X-Content-Type-Options` / `X-Frame-Options` or `frame-ancestors`, and verbose version banners. Use the OWASP Secure Headers project as the checklist and check the response headers of your own production URL right now.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS)

subtopics.name: Business logic flaws and abuse of legitimate functionality
subtopics.learn: Work the logic-flaw labs: excessive trust in client-side controls (a price or quantity in the request body), negative or overflowing quantities, inconsistent handling of the same value across two endpoints, flawed enforcement of workflow sequence, and authentication bypass via an email-domain check that trusts a user-supplied field. These are the findings a scanner will never produce and the ones customers care most about, because they map directly to money and to regulated actions. In an AI deployment the equivalents are concrete: an unmetered endpoint that lets one tenant burn the whole model budget, a job-submission API with no per-tenant concurrency cap, and a 'retry' button with no idempotency key that double-charges. Test by asking 'what does this endpoint assume, and can I violate that assumption while staying inside the API contract'.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Business logic vulnerabilities

subtopics.name: A02 Cryptographic failures and the secrets you actually hold
subtopics.learn: Audit data in transit and at rest rather than reading crypto theory: is TLS terminated at the edge and then plaintext HTTP inside the mesh, is `verify=False` set anywhere in an HTTP client, are database and Redis connections using TLS, is `sslmode=require` (which does not verify the certificate) mistaken for `verify-full`. On storage: passwords under Argon2id/bcrypt with per-user salts, tokens and API keys stored as hashes so a database dump is not a credential dump, envelope encryption with KMS for column-level PII, and a documented key rotation path. Know the anti-patterns by name - ECB mode, a static IV, `Math.random()` or `random` instead of `secrets.token_urlsafe`, home-rolled `==` comparison of MACs instead of `hmac.compare_digest`, and JWTs used as long-lived opaque session tokens with no revocation.

resource.label: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series: Cryptographic Storage

subtopics.name: A06 Vulnerable and outdated components in your own supply chain
subtopics.learn: Run real scanners against your real repos rather than reading about SCA: `pip-audit` against the resolved lockfile, `npm audit --omit=dev` against DefenderMate, and `trivy image` against both container images to catch OS-level CVEs the language tools never see. Learn to triage instead of panic - is the vulnerable function reachable from your code path, is it a dev-only dependency, is there a fixed version and does it break your API - and to record that reasoning, because a customer's security team will ask why a HIGH is still open. Wire Dependabot or Renovate with grouped update PRs so the fix path exists before the finding arrives, and pin by digest in Dockerfiles so a nightly rebuild cannot silently pull a new base layer. Keep an SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) as an artifact of every build so 'are we affected by CVE-X' takes minutes, not days.

resource.label: pip-audit (PyPA official repository)

subtopics.name: Security testing in CI: SAST, DAST and a gate policy people won't disable
subtopics.learn: Add three jobs and, crucially, decide what each one blocks. SAST with Semgrep or CodeQL on every PR, using a curated ruleset plus custom rules for your own footguns (any `jwt.decode` without `algorithms=`, any ORM query on a tenant-scoped table without a tenant filter, any `subprocess` with `shell=True`). Secret scanning with push protection so a key never reaches the remote in the first place. DAST with the OWASP ZAP baseline scan against an ephemeral environment for headers, cookie flags and low-hanging misconfiguration. The gate policy is the senior part: block the merge on new HIGH findings introduced by the diff, report-only on the pre-existing backlog, allow a documented, expiring, reviewer-approved suppression, and never a global `nosec` - a scanner everyone ignores is worse than no scanner because it manufactures false assurance.

resource.label: GitHub Docs: Code security (code scanning, secret scanning, Dependabot)

subtopics.name: A09 Logging and monitoring: making an attack visible
subtopics.learn: Decide what a security event is in your system and make it queryable: authentication success and failure with actor, source IP and user agent; authorization denials (a 403 spike from one principal across many object ids is IDOR probing in progress); privilege and role changes; token issuance and revocation; data export and bulk read; and admin actions. Emit structured JSON with a trace id so a security event joins the same trace as the request (build on OpenTelemetry from topic 21), keep an append-only audit trail with an integrity guarantee for regulated tenants, and set retention to survive the typical months-long dwell time. Equally important, log what you must never log: passwords, tokens, full card numbers, PII in URLs (which land in access logs and Referer headers), and raw prompts containing customer data. Then write two alerts and prove they fire against your own traffic.

resource.label: OWASP Top 10 2021: A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

subtopics.name: Find, score, fix and regression-test one real issue in your own stack
subtopics.learn: Turn the lab skills on Dokeo and DefenderMate and go until you have a genuine finding - most likely a missing tenant predicate, a mass-assignment field, a reflected CORS origin, or a JWT decode without audience validation. Write it up the way a customer's security team expects: title, affected endpoint and commit, severity with an explicit CVSS v3.1 vector string and a sentence on why environmental metrics adjust it for your deployment, minimal reproduction as a copy-pasteable `curl`, evidence, impact in business terms, remediation, and detection guidance. Then fix it, and write the test that would have caught it - a pytest case that authenticates as tenant B and asserts a 403/404 on tenant A's object - and confirm it fails on the vulnerable commit and passes on the fix. A finding without a regression test is a fix that will regress within two releases.

resource.label: FIRST: CVSS v3.1 Specification Document

You can take an unfamiliar API's OpenAPI spec and, within an hour, produce an authorization matrix of endpoint x role x tenant with the identity-swap test result in every cell, and name the highest-risk three routes.
You can exploit and then correctly fix a cross-tenant IDOR in your own code, and ship a pytest regression test that fails on the vulnerable commit and passes on the patched one.

You can forge a JWT four different ways (alg none, unverified signature, weak HMAC secret, jku/kid injection) and audit any codebase's decode calls for algorithm pinning, audience, issuer and expiry in a single grep-driven pass.

You can write a CVSS v3.1 vector for a finding, defend the base metrics you chose, and explain how the environmental score changes for a deployment inside a customer's private VPC versus a public SaaS.

You can explain to a customer's frontend engineer why reflecting the Origin header with credentials enabled is a full authenticated data read, and hand them the correct allowlist implementation in the same conversation.

You can add SAST, secret scanning and a ZAP baseline job to a pipeline with a written gate policy - blocking only diff-introduced HIGH findings, with expiring reviewed suppressions - and state the false-positive rate you measured before enabling the gate.
You can produce a security finding write-up that a customer's security team accepts without a follow-up call: reproduction, impact in business language, remediation, and detection guidance.
failureModes: A tenant-scoped endpoint filters by primary key only because 'the ORM session already has the tenant', row-level security was never enabled on that one table, and a customer analyst enumerating sequential document ids reads another business unit's contracts for six weeks before anyone notices.

The edge proxy and the application normalise paths differently, so an authorization middleware that protects `/admin/` never sees a request to `/admin%2fusers` or `/Admin/users`, and the whole admin surface is reachable unauthenticated behind a rule that looks correct in code review.

CORS was loosened to reflect any Origin with credentials during an on-site integration to unblock a customer's dev server, the change shipped in a hotfix branch with no ticket, and it stays in production until an external pentest finds it.

A JWT is validated for signature but not for `aud` and `iss`, so a token minted by the customer's staging IdP - or by a different application sharing the same identity provider - authenticates successfully against production.

A 'import from URL' document feature is deployed onto a node group where IMDSv1 was left enabled for a legacy agent, turning a low-severity SSRF into instance-role credential theft and an incident that involves the customer's cloud security team.

A dependency is pinned by floating tag in the Dockerfile, the nightly rebuild pulls a new transitive package with a known RCE, and because the SBOM is generated only on tagged releases nobody can answer 'which running images are affected' for two days.

Login rate limiting is enforced at the ALB per source IP, but the same authentication endpoint is reachable through an internal service-mesh route that bypasses the edge entirely, so credential stuffing from inside the cluster succeeds with no lockouts and no alert.
interviewQuestions: Two weeks before go-live, the customer's security team returns a pentest report with fourteen findings against your deployment. Walk me through how you triage it in the next twenty-four hours, which findings you push back on and how, and what you tell their CISO on the call.

Design authorization for a multi-tenant API where enterprise customers have nested org units, delegated admins and shared read-only collaborators. Where exactly is the check enforced, how do you make it impossible for a new endpoint to forget it, and how would you prove to an auditor that no IDOR exists?

Users occasionally see another tenant's data on the dashboard, but only under load and never reproducibly. Walk me through your investigation - what are the candidate mechanisms, and what would you instrument first?

Explain precisely what breaks in each of these three cases and how the exploit differs: a JWT library called with signature verification disabled, a service that accepts `alg: none`, and a service where the `kid` header is used to look up a key from disk without sanitisation.

Your product takes a customer-supplied URL and fetches the document. Enumerate every way that becomes SSRF, then tell me what a real fix looks like in an AWS deployment - not the regex, the architecture.
You find a stored XSS in a customer's production instance at 4pm on a Friday. What happens in the next hour, who do you tell, and what determines whether you hotfix or roll back?

How would you add security testing to a delivery pipeline for a team that will absolutely disable anything noisy? Be specific about what blocks a merge, what is report-only, how suppressions work, and how you would measure whether the gate is earning its keep.
66.proofOfWork: Publish an internal-pentest dossier repository for Dokeo and DefenderMate that reads like a professional engagement rather than a lab notebook. It contains: a scoped test plan mapped to OWASP ASVS Level 2 controls with each control marked pass, fail or not-applicable and a one-line justification; a generated authorization matrix of every endpoint crossed with every role and both seeded tenants, produced by a committed script that authenticates as each principal, replays each request and records the status code, so the matrix is regenerable on any commit rather than hand-typed; at least one genuine finding written up with a CVSS v3.1 vector string, a copy-pasteable `curl` reproduction, evidence, business impact and remediation; the patch itself as a linked pull request; and a pytest regression test proving the fix, demonstrated by a short recording or CI log showing the test red on the vulnerable commit and green on the patched one. Add the CI wiring that keeps it true - Semgrep with at least two custom rules written for your own footguns, secret scanning with push protection, a ZAP baseline scan against an ephemeral environment, and a documented gate policy explaining exactly what blocks a merge and how suppressions expire - plus a one-page `SECURITY.md` covering the disclosure contact, supported versions and expected response times, which is the document every enterprise procurement review asks for.

67.why: An FDE is the person sitting across from the customer's security architect in week two of a deployment, and the two artifacts that unblock or kill the project are a credible threat model and a credible answer to 'how do you rotate that credential without taking us down'. Nobody buys 'we take security seriously' - they buy a data-flow diagram with named trust boundaries, a STRIDE table where every threat has a mitigation and an owner, and a rotation runbook that has actually been rehearsed against a live system. Secrets are also the single most common way an on-site deployment breaks after handover: the credential expires, the rotation job flips the password at 03:00, and the service that cached it at import time goes down while you are on a plane.
prerequisites: Application security: OWASP Top 10 hands-on (topic 61) - you need to know what an IDOR, an SSRF and a broken-auth bug actually look like before you can predict them on a diagram.

Auth and identity (topic 27): OIDC authorization code + PKCE, JWT validation with issuer/audience/algorithms, JWKS, and what a refresh token rotation window is - half of secrets work is really identity work.

Data modelling for multi-tenant systems (topic 30): tenant_id propagation, Postgres row-level security, PII classification and audit tables, because tenant isolation is the threat every enterprise reviewer asks about first.

Linux and containers (Month 1-2): file permissions and umask, process environment via /proc/<pid>/environ, container image layers, and how a Kubernetes pod gets its filesystem and service account token.

Production Python and FastAPI (topics 25-26): dependency injection, connection pooling with SQLAlchemy (pool_recycle, pool_pre_ping), and retry with backoff - rotation correctness lives inside these mechanics.
Basic Terraform and CI (Month 3-4): remote state, plan output in pull requests, GitHub Actions job permissions - the two places secrets leak that nobody diagrams.

subtopics.name: Frame the system: DFD, assets, trust boundaries
subtopics.learn: Draw DefenderMate as a level-1 data flow diagram with exactly four element types - external entity, process, data store, data flow - and then draw the trust boundaries as lines that cross flows, not as boxes around components. A boundary is any place where the authority of the caller changes: browser to BFF, BFF to API, API to Postgres, API to model provider, Temporal worker to tenant object storage, operator laptop to production. Name the assets in the customer's language (tenant documents, classification decisions, audit log, model API key, signing key) and record who is allowed to see each. Finish by writing the three sentences a reviewer actually reads: what the system does, what it must never do, and what you are explicitly assuming about the environment it runs in.

resource.label: OWASP Community - Threat Modeling

subtopics.name: STRIDE per element and per interaction
subtopics.learn: Apply STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) mechanically: external entities get S and R; processes get all six; data stores get T, I, D and R; data flows get T, I and D. Do it per interaction - 'analyst browser -> BFF /api/classify' - not per box, because the interesting threats live on the arrows. Produce a table with columns id, element, STRIDE category, threat in one sentence, existing control, gap, severity, owner, status; a threat with no control and no owner is not a finding, it is a wish. Force yourself to write at least one threat per category per boundary crossing, then delete the ones that are genuinely not applicable and say why - the deletions are what proves you did the pass.

resource.label: Microsoft Learn - Threat Modeling Tool overview

subtopics.name: Threat modelling the AI surface
subtopics.learn: Add the threats classic STRIDE tables miss because the model is a confused deputy with a customer's credentials. Cover indirect prompt injection through retrieved documents and tool output (the attacker writes the payload into a PDF you ingest, not into the chat box), excessive agency (a tool that can DELETE when the task only needs SELECT), insecure output handling (model output rendered as HTML, or passed to a shell, a SQL string or an HTTP client, giving XSS and SSRF), system-prompt and tool-schema extraction, and cross-tenant leakage through a shared vector index or a shared prompt cache. For each, name the control layer: allow-listed tools with per-tool scopes, output treated as untrusted input, retrieval filtered by tenant_id before the model sees anything, egress allow-list on the agent's network namespace, and human confirmation gates on irreversible actions.

resource.label: OWASP Top 10 Risks and Mitigations for LLM and GenAI Apps (2025 list)

subtopics.name: Multi-tenant and authorization threats
subtopics.learn: Enumerate the isolation failures that actually happen: a query path that forgets SET LOCAL app.tenant_id so RLS silently passes, a table where RLS is enabled but not FORCED so the owner role bypasses it, an object storage prefix that is per-tenant by convention only, a background worker or admin endpoint running as a superuser role, and IDs that are sequential integers so enumeration is trivial. Write the negative tests as threats: 'analyst of tenant A can read /api/conversations/<uuid of tenant B>' with expected 404, not 403, because 403 confirms existence. Distinguish authentication (who), authorization (what), and tenancy (whose) - most real bugs are the third one, and they are invisible in a diagram unless you draw the data store per tenant.

resource.label: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series - Authorization

subtopics.name: Ranking risk without theatre
subtopics.learn: Score with CVSS v3.1 base metrics (AV, AC, PR, UI, S, C, I, A) when you need a number a customer's GRC team can reconcile with their vulnerability register, and understand why DREAD fell out of favour - two engineers score the same threat differently and the total is not comparable across systems. For threats with no CVE, use a two-axis likelihood x impact grid with written definitions of each level, and record the reasoning sentence, since the sentence is what survives the argument. Know that the scope metric (S:C) is what turns a container escape or an RLS bypass from High into Critical, and be able to defend a downgrade with a compensating control (network isolation, short credential TTL, monitored audit log).

resource.label: FIRST - CVSS v3.1 specification document

subtopics.name: From threats to controls, assumptions and accepted risk
subtopics.learn: Every row ends in one of four dispositions - mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept - and 'accept' requires a named human, a written justification and an expiry date, or it is just an open bug with better formatting. Map mitigations to real MITRE ATT&CK techniques where it helps a security team place your work in their language (T1552 credentials in files, T1078 valid accounts, T1195 supply chain). Write the assumptions section as testable claims: 'the cluster is not shared with untrusted tenants', 'egress is restricted to an allow-list', 'the customer's IdP enforces MFA for analysts'; when an assumption is later false, that is a change request, not a surprise. Keep an explicit out-of-scope list so the reviewer stops asking about the things you deliberately did not model.

resource.label: MITRE ATT&CK - Enterprise Mitigations (controls mapped to techniques)

subtopics.name: Keep the threat model alive in code review
subtopics.learn: A threat model written once for the security review is stale within a sprint. Store the model in the repo next to the code - a diagram source file plus the threat table as YAML or a pytm script that renders the DFD and the report from Python objects - so a pull request can change it and a reviewer can diff it. Add a CI check or a CODEOWNERS rule that fires when a new external dependency, network egress, data store or tool definition appears, and a review trigger list: new trust boundary, new PII field, new third-party API, new admin path. Track threats as issues with the same lifecycle as bugs, so 'we have a threat model' becomes a number: open threats by severity, mean age, count with no owner.

resource.label: OWASP pytm - Pythonic threat modelling framework (official repository)

subtopics.name: Inventory every secret and rank it by blast radius
subtopics.learn: You cannot rotate what you have not listed. Build a table of every credential in the system with: name, type (password, API key, signing key, encryption key, certificate, OAuth client secret, service account token), where it is stored, which workloads read it, what it can do if stolen, how long it lives, how it is rotated today, and how long a rotation takes. Include the ones people forget - the model provider API key, the webhook HMAC shared with the customer, the Postgres superuser used by migrations, the container registry pull secret, the TLS private key, the backup encryption key, and the SSH key on the bastion. Sort by blast radius times exposure, not by alphabetical order, and mark each as long-lived, short-lived, or dynamic; the goal state is that almost nothing in the top rows is long-lived.

resource.label: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series - Secrets Management

subtopics.name: Detect leaked secrets in code, history and logs
subtopics.learn: Run gitleaks (detect --redact over full history, protect --staged in a pre-commit hook) and trufflehog with verification enabled so you get 'this key is live' rather than 'this looks like entropy'; tune the allow-list so developers do not learn to ignore the tool. Understand what rewriting history does and does not achieve: git filter-repo or BFG removes the blob from your branch, but forks, clones, CI caches, and the provider's unreferenced-object storage may still serve it, so the only real remediation is revocation. Turn on provider-side push protection and secret scanning so the next one is blocked at push time. Extend the same thinking to runtime: scrub Authorization headers and api_key fields from structured logs, from error-reporting payloads, and from LLM traces, and add a test that asserts a known canary string never appears in log output.

resource.label: gitleaks (official repository)

subtopics.name: Storage: KV v2, versioning, and encryption at rest
subtopics.learn: Use a versioned KV store rather than a flat one: Vault kv-v2 gives you check-and-set writes (-cas=N) to prevent lost updates during concurrent rotation, version history for rollback, soft delete versus destroy, max_versions, and delete_version_after. Know the difference between deleting a version and destroying it, and why a rotation runbook must destroy the old value only after the overlap window closes. Understand the storage security model beneath it - Vault's barrier and seal/unseal, auto-unseal backed by a cloud KMS, and for Kubernetes Secrets the fact that base64 is encoding not encryption, so etcd needs an EncryptionConfiguration with a kms provider before you can claim encryption at rest. Read-path least privilege matters as much as encryption: a policy that grants read on secret/data/* is the same as no vault at all.

resource.label: HashiCorp Vault docs - KV secrets engine v2

subtopics.name: Getting a secret into the process without leaking it
subtopics.learn: Compare the three delivery shapes and their leak surfaces. Environment variables are readable at /proc/<pid>/environ by any process of the same uid, are inherited by every child process, show up in docker inspect, in crash dumps and core files, and are routinely captured wholesale by error-reporting SDKs. Files (tmpfs mount, mode 0400, owned by the app uid) are better, can be re-read on change, and are what most secret injectors use. A direct API fetch at startup with in-memory caching is best but demands you handle refresh. Whichever you pick, load secrets through one accessor function - never a module-level constant evaluated at import - so a rotation can invalidate the cache, and make __repr__ of any config object redact the value so a stack trace does not print it.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs - Secrets

subtopics.name: Workload identity: deleting the bootstrap secret
subtopics.learn: The recursive problem in secrets management is the credential that fetches credentials. Solve it with platform-issued identity: Vault's Kubernetes auth method validates a projected ServiceAccount token via the TokenReview API and binds a role to bound_service_account_names and bound_service_account_namespaces; JWT/OIDC auth trusts your CI provider's issuer with bound_claims on repository and ref. On clouds, the same pattern is an OIDC identity provider plus a role trust policy with a condition on sub and aud (IRSA on EKS, workload identity federation on GCP), which is how a GitHub Actions job deploys with zero stored access keys. Set automountServiceAccountToken: false where it is not needed, scope projected tokens with an explicit audience and short expirationSeconds, and be ready to explain to a customer why this is strictly better than a sealed long-lived key.

resource.label: HashiCorp Vault docs - Kubernetes auth method

subtopics.name: Dynamic secrets and lease mechanics
subtopics.learn: Configure the database secrets engine so the application never holds a static Postgres password: Vault holds a rotated root credential (vault write -f database/rotate-root/<config>), and each workload calls vault read database/creds/<role> to get a unique username and password with a lease. Learn the lease lifecycle properly - default_lease_ttl and max_lease_ttl, vault lease renew, vault lease revoke -prefix database/creds/<role> to kill every credential a compromised service ever received, and the revocation_statements that drop the role in Postgres (including REASSIGN OWNED / DROP OWNED, which is the usual reason revocation fails). Understand the operational cost you are trading for: credential churn shows up in pg_stat_activity and in connection-pool behaviour, so pool lifetime must be shorter than lease TTL or you will hold connections authenticated by a revoked user.

resource.label: HashiCorp Vault docs - Database secrets engine

subtopics.name: Zero-downtime rotation mechanics
subtopics.learn: Rotation is a two-valid-credentials problem, never a swap. Internalise the AWS Secrets Manager four-step model - createSecret, setSecret, testSecret, finishSecret - and the staging labels AWSCURRENT, AWSPENDING and AWSPREVIOUS, which exist precisely so a reader mid-rotation still resolves something valid. Prefer the alternating-users strategy (two database users, rotate the idle one, then flip the label) over single-user rotation, because a single user's password change breaks new connections while existing pooled ones keep working, producing a slow-burn partial outage. On the client side you need: a refresh path (file watch, TTL cache, or SIGHUP), a retry that re-reads the secret on an auth error instead of backing off blindly, connection pool settings (pool_recycle shorter than the overlap window, pool_pre_ping) and an overlap window longer than your longest connection lifetime plus deploy time. Rehearse the whole thing under load and measure error count, not vibes.

resource.label: AWS Secrets Manager User Guide - Rotate secrets

subtopics.name: Rotating verification keys: JWKS and webhook HMACs
subtopics.learn: Signing keys are the rotation case that breaks other people's systems, because verifiers cache. Publish a JWKS with a kid on every key, add the new key to the document and let it propagate for at least the Cache-Control max-age of the jwks_uri before you sign anything with it, then sign with the new kid, then keep the old public key until the longest-lived token issued under it has expired plus clock skew. Verifiers must select by kid, refresh the JWKS on an unknown kid with a rate limit, and never accept alg from the token. For shared HMAC webhook secrets the same overlap applies: accept a signature that matches either the current or previous secret during the window, compare with a constant-time function (hmac.compare_digest), and include a timestamp in the signed payload with a replay window. Announce the cutover dates to the customer in writing before you touch anything.

resource.label: RFC 7517 - JSON Web Key (JWK)

subtopics.name: Encryption keys, envelope encryption and re-wrapping
subtopics.learn: Distinguish rotating a key from re-encrypting data. With envelope encryption, a KMS-held key encryption key wraps per-object data keys, so rotating the KEK is cheap and instant while the ciphertext is untouched - you only re-wrap the data keys. Know what AWS KMS automatic key rotation actually does (new backing material, old material retained so old ciphertext still decrypts, key id unchanged) and why that is not the same as removing the compromised material. With Vault transit, rotate with vault write -f transit/keys/<name>/rotate, then re-encrypt existing ciphertext with transit/rewrap/<name> (which never exposes plaintext), and raise min_decryption_version only once the rewrap job has finished, or you will make old rows permanently unreadable. Estimate and schedule the rewrap cost before promising a date, and always test decrypt-after-rotate on a restored backup.

resource.label: AWS KMS Developer Guide - concepts (envelope encryption, key rotation)

subtopics.name: Secrets in CI, IaC and container builds
subtopics.learn: Three places secrets escape that never appear on a DFD. Terraform writes provider credentials, database passwords and generated keys into state in plaintext even when the variable is marked sensitive = true, so the backend must be encrypted, access-restricted and never committed - and plan output posted to a pull request comment is a public disclosure channel. CI runners need short-lived OIDC-federated identity rather than stored keys, job-level least-privilege permissions, and masked outputs, and you must assume any secret available to a workflow is available to a pull request from a fork unless the trigger says otherwise. Container builds must use build-time secret mounts (RUN --mount=type=secret) rather than ARG or ENV, since anything in a build argument or layer is visible via docker history and to anyone who pulls the image.

resource.label: Terraform docs - sensitive data in state

subtopics.name: Leak response, audit evidence, and the runbook
subtopics.learn: Write the runbook so a stressed engineer at 02:00 can execute it: revoke first, rotate second, investigate third - in that order, because a valid stolen credential is an ongoing incident and forensic curiosity is not. For each secret in the inventory, the runbook needs the exact commands, the expected duration, the blast radius of doing it, the rollback, and the verification step (a probe that proves the new credential works and the old one no longer does). Enable and read audit devices - Vault audit logs hash secret values with an HMAC so you can search for 'was this specific credential ever read, by whom, from which IP' without the log itself becoming the leak - and pair them with cloud trail events for GetSecretValue. Close the loop with a written timeline, the scope of what the credential could reach, and one systemic fix per incident.

resource.label: HashiCorp Vault docs - Audit devices

outcomes: You can produce a level-1 DFD of DefenderMate with numbered trust boundaries and a STRIDE-per-interaction table in under 90 minutes, where every row carries an existing control, a gap, a severity with a written justification, an owner and a status.

You can list every secret in a running system from a repo scan plus an infrastructure scan, and state for each one its blast radius, its current TTL, who reads it, and how many minutes a rotation takes.
You can rotate a live Postgres credential used by a running service under continuous load and show a request log with zero 5xx and zero authentication errors across the cutover.

You can stand up Vault Kubernetes auth so that no static credential exists in any manifest, image or file, and demonstrate that deleting the pod's projected token immediately stops it from fetching secrets.

You can revoke every dynamic credential ever issued to one compromised workload with a single command and then prove from the audit log which credentials existed, when they were read, and by which client IP.
You can rotate a JWT signing key without invalidating a single live session, and explain the ordering (publish, propagate, sign, retire) with the specific cache TTLs that make it safe.
You can defend a risk acceptance to a customer's security reviewer with a CVSS v3.1 vector, a compensating control, a named owner and an expiry date, rather than asking them to trust you.
You can find a secret committed to git history, and correctly explain why history rewriting is not remediation and revocation is.
failureModes: The application reads the database password once into a module-level constant at import time, so the 03:00 rotation job succeeds, the secrets manager shows the new value, and every pod keeps using the old credential until the next deploy - at which point everything fails at once, hours after the change that caused it.
