Ban every form of throat-clearing - no 'so basically', no team introduction, no tool tour, no apology for the environment - and rehearse the line until you can deliver it while your laptop is still waking the display.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing One - Short sentences (one idea per sentence, cut needless words)

subtopics.name: Demo environment as a shipped artifact
subtopics.learn: Treat the demo like production: a clean clone must reach a working system with one command in under three minutes, images pinned by digest rather than a floating :latest tag, and seed data restored from a checked-in dump or SQL fixture containing realistic but wholly synthetic names. Tag the exact state in git (demo-2026-03-12) so you can reproduce the run six weeks later when someone asks what they saw, and pre-pull every image the night before. Rehearse a cold boot on the machine, display resolution and network you will actually use - corporate guest wifi, the HDMI or Zoom share path, terminal at 16pt or larger, browser zoom at 125-150% - because half of all demo failures are environmental, not technical.

resource.label: Docker Compose Quickstart - one-command multi-service stack with volumes and healthchecks

subtopics.name: Determinism: making an LLM demo reproducible
subtopics.learn: Set temperature 0 with top_p 1, pin an exact model id rather than a floating alias, freeze the prompt version by hash, and put a request cache keyed on (model_id, prompt_hash, input_hash) in front of every call - and understand that temperature 0 is still not bit-identical across providers or batch conditions, so the cache is your only real guarantee. Build a replay mode (DEMO_REPLAY=1) that serves cached responses with a realistic simulated delay, so a provider incident or a 40-second tail latency degrades into a smooth demo instead of dead air. Set explicit client timeouts and max_tokens so a hang surfaces as a fast fallback, and fire one throwaway warm-up request before you present.

resource.label: Claude Developer Platform Docs (models, parameters, prompt caching)

subtopics.name: Capture rig and the tape-review loop
subtopics.learn: Record at 1080p30, capture a single window rather than the whole desktop, run a clean browser profile with no bookmarks or other customers' tabs, and put the OS into do-not-disturb before the first take. Get audio right once - a cheap cardioid at speaking distance, peaks around -12 to -6 dBFS - because bad audio makes a competent engineer sound uncertain. Then review the tape with a stopwatch and log four hard numbers per take: time-to-first-visible-value, seconds of dead air, filler words per minute, and the number of times you said 'I'll come back to that'. Do a second pass at 2x with the sound off to test whether the screen alone tells the story.

resource.label: OBS Studio Quick Start Guide - sources, window capture and audio mixer setup

subtopics.name: Failure drills: the demo breaks at minute four
subtopics.learn: Adopt a hard rule - 30 seconds of live debugging, then switch - and build the switch beforehand: a three-minute pre-recorded clip of the identical flow on the identical data sitting on local disk, a phone hotspot already paired, and a second machine booted with the demo warm. Rehearse the exact sentence you say when it breaks: name what failed, say what you are doing, keep moving, and do not apologise twice. Deliberately sabotage a rehearsal - kill the database container or drop the network at minute four - and time your recovery, because a clean recovery is itself the most persuasive reliability evidence in the room.

resource.label: Principles of Chaos Engineering - deliberate failure injection to build confidence

subtopics.name: Show the instrumentation, not the slide
subtopics.learn: During the demo, pull up one board or one trace covering the run the room just watched: p95 latency, cost per request, token counts, error rate, and the retrieval or tool calls that produced the answer. This converts 'it works on your laptop' into 'it is measured', and it pre-empts the cost question by putting the number on screen before anyone asks. Keep it to a single board with at most four panels and a time range that actually contains the demo - a wall of graphs reads as noise, and an empty panel reads as a lie.

resource.label: Grafana Docs - Dashboards

subtopics.name: Translating engineering into money, risk and time
subtopics.learn: Do the arithmetic out loud as a visible chain - cases per month x minutes saved x loaded hourly cost = dollars per year - and always separate the assumption row from the result row so the CFO argues with the assumption instead of with you. Learn the three currencies executives actually trade in: dollars (opex, avoided headcount), risk (audit findings, breach exposure, SLA credits, regulatory deadline), and time (weeks to launch, sooner revenue). Then state explicitly what you are not claiming; volunteering the boundary of your claim is what makes the rest of it credible.

resource.label: FinOps Framework - Quantify Business Value domain (mapping tech cost to business outcomes)

subtopics.name: The unit-economics sheet a CFO cannot dent
subtopics.learn: Build one page, denominated per 1,000 requests: input and output tokens at list price, retrieval and database, compute, egress, human review minutes, and amortised build cost. Add a sensitivity block - 10x volume, 50% model price cut, cache hit rates of 0/40/80%, batch versus interactive - plus payback period and break-even volume, and know the marginal-versus-fixed split cold because 'what happens when we go from 10,000 to 1,000,000 calls a month' needs a number and a slope, not an adjective. Keep the provider's own pricing page open in a background tab so any challenged figure is one click from its source.

resource.label: Amazon Bedrock Pricing - per-token list price, batch vs on-demand tiers

subtopics.name: Defending a trade-off: options table, rejected alternatives, one-way doors
subtopics.learn: For every decision likely to be attacked, arrive with a three-row options table scored on cost, latency, operational burden, time-to-first-value and blast radius, plus the specific reason each rejected option was rejected and the evidence that would change your mind. Separate reversible two-way doors (model choice, chunking strategy, dashboard layout - decide fast, say so) from one-way doors (tenancy boundary, data model, where customer data physically lands) and defend them at different intensities. Write it as an ADR before the demo with context, decision, consequences and alternatives, so under pressure you are retrieving a considered position rather than inventing one.

resource.label: Architecture Decision Records (adr.github.io)

subtopics.name: Committing to numbers: p95, availability, and what you will actually sign
subtopics.learn: Know your own p50/p95/p99 under realistic concurrency rather than from a single warm request, and say out loud which figures are demo observations and which you would sign as an SLO. Never commit an availability number without also stating the measurement window, the error budget it implies, and the exclusions (their IdP, their VPN, their upstream ERP), because 99.9% over 30 days and 99.9% over 12 months are different products. Practise the refusal: 'I will not commit to that in this room; I will send you a measured number with the methodology by Thursday' - since anything you say casually here is liable to be pasted verbatim into the SOW.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives

subtopics.name: Hostile question taxonomy and the answer-first pattern
subtopics.learn: Classify the question in the first three seconds - factual gap, scope probe, budget attack, credibility attack, 'we tried this before', or a trap built on a false premise - because each has a different response shape. Answer first in one sentence, give one sentence of reason, then stop talking; correct a false premise explicitly before answering it; and when you do not know, say so with a named method and a date rather than improvising. Never renegotiate scope live. Rehearse the fourth follow-up specifically, since hostility works by repetition and it is consistency across three restatements that earns trust; when the attack is about a past failure, describe it factually and blamelessly the way a good postmortem does.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

subtopics.name: The standing objection set: build-vs-buy, lock-in, data handling, model risk
subtopics.learn: Pre-write and rehearse a 60-second answer for the four objections that appear in every enterprise room. Build-vs-buy: answer in engineering-months plus ongoing maintenance and eval upkeep, not feature parity. Lock-in: name precisely what is portable (prompts, eval sets, retrieval corpus, your own data) versus what is not. Data handling: where data flows, retention, training opt-out, residency, subprocessors, and who can read it - have the one-page data-flow diagram ready as a leave-behind. Model risk: your measured error rate on their eval set, where the human approves, and what the audit trail records.

resource.label: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) - model risk, data handling, governance

subtopics.name: Q&A choreography and the close
subtopics.learn: Compress and restate each question before answering so the room hears the version you are answering, and park anything needing more than two minutes into a named follow-up with an owner and a date rather than derailing the session. Reserve the final 60 seconds for a concrete ask on screen - a pilot scope, a named dataset, a specific access request, a decision date - because ending on 'any questions?' hands the close to whoever in the room is least invested. Send the follow-up within 24 hours containing exactly the artifacts you promised and nothing extra.

resource.label: MIT OpenCourseWare - Patrick Winston, How to Speak (handling questions, how to stop)

subtopics.name: The four-take ladder and a scoring rubric that bites
subtopics.learn: Score every recorded take 0-2 on ten dimensions: claim clarity, time-to-first-visible-value, live-versus-slides ratio, telemetry shown, unit economics defended, trade-off defended with named alternatives, answer-first rate on hostile questions, seconds of dead air, filler words per minute, and specificity of the close. Structure the ladder deliberately - take 1 cold with notes, take 2 with no notes, take 3 with a recruited hostile questioner briefed to interrupt on cost and scope, take 4 with a failure injected at minute four. Diff the scores across takes and only re-record once you can name the exact line or segment you are changing, otherwise you are just accumulating footage.

resource.label: Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center - Creating and Using Rubrics (criteria, descriptors, performance levels)

subtopics.name: No-slides fallback: three boxes and an arrow
subtopics.learn: Be able to draw the entire system in three boxes and an arrow in 90 seconds on a whiteboard or tablet - the trust boundary and ingress, the thing that does the work, and where state lives - naming where their data resides, where the model call happens, and where a human approves. Keep three zoom levels ready: three boxes for the CFO, eight for the platform lead, and the real deployment diagram for the architect, and switch level based on the question rather than showing the biggest one you have. Rehearse this standing up with a marker, because it is what you do when the room has no screen or the projector dies.

resource.label: Azure Architecture Center (reference architectures and diagrams)

outcomes: You can deliver a ten-minute demo with no notes and hit measured targets on the tape: first visible value under 90 seconds, under 15 seconds of total dead air, and fewer than three filler words per minute.

You can stand the whole demo up from a clean clone on a machine you have never used in under five minutes, with digest-pinned images and seeded synthetic data, and reproduce the identical run six weeks later from a git tag.

You can answer 'what does this cost us at a million requests a month' with a number, the marginal-versus-fixed split, and a sensitivity row, straight off a one-page unit-economics sheet you built yourself.

You can defend any architectural choice in the demo with three considered options, the specific rejection reason for each, and the evidence that would change your mind - sourced from an ADR written before the meeting.
You can lose the network or the model provider at minute four and be back on a pre-recorded fallback within 30 seconds, narrating the failure once and continuing without apology.
You can distinguish out loud between a demo observation and a committable SLO, and decline to commit any availability or latency number without stating its measurement window and exclusions.
You can score your own four recordings against a ten-dimension rubric and show monotonic improvement, naming for each take the specific change that produced the delta.
You can answer the four standing objections - build-vs-buy, lock-in, data handling, model risk - in under 60 seconds each, with a leave-behind artifact for each.
failureModes: The demo runs against :latest images and a live provider endpoint, and a model deprecation or an unnoticed prompt-template change three days before the QBR turns a rehearsed flow into a wrong answer in front of the buyer.

The 'synthetic' seed data was quietly derived from a previous customer's export, a real company name appears on screen, and the meeting stops being a deal conversation and becomes a security incident.

Full-desktop screen sharing leaks a Slack notification, a calendar invite naming another prospect, or a terminal with a live credential in scrollback, and the customer's security lead notices before you do.
The CFO asks what it costs and the answer is 'it's pretty cheap', which converts a signable pilot into a three-week finance review and strands the champion with no numbers to defend internally.

A number said casually in the room - 'sub-200ms p95, 99.9% availability' - is copied verbatim into the SOW by the account team, and six weeks later it is a contractual obligation nobody sized or instrumented.
Everything is shown on a hand-picked happy path, the champion tries one genuinely messy record the next morning, it fails, and the internal narrative becomes 'it only works in their demo'.

Live debugging runs six minutes past the failure because the presenter cannot let go, consuming the entire defence segment so the trade-off and cost questions are never answered and the meeting ends unresolved.
interviewQuestions: You have ten minutes with a CFO who has already decided this project is over budget, and you are the engineer who built it. What is on screen in minute one, what do you deliberately not show at all, and what is your ask at minute ten?

Walk me through a technical decision you had to defend to someone who could cancel the project. What was the actual trade-off, what did they push hardest on, and what did you change afterwards as a result?

Your live demo hangs at minute four - the model call has not returned in 20 seconds and the room is silent. Tell me exactly what you do in the next 30 seconds, and what you had to prepare in advance for that answer to be possible.
A customer's VP asks in the demo whether you can hold 100ms p95 and 99.99% availability. You genuinely do not know. What do you say in the room, and what actually happens downstream if you say yes?

Design the demo environment for a system you will show to twenty different prospects over a quarter. What is pinned, what is seeded, what is faked or replayed, how do you keep it honest, and what breaks first as the product changes underneath it?

Compute cost per 1,000 requests for an LLM feature in front of me. Now the customer tells you their real volume is 20x your assumption and their documents are three times longer - which parts of your number move, and which do not?
The champion loved the demo, and two weeks later the platform team blocks the rollout. What did you fail to do during that demo, and what is your recovery plan for the next meeting?
74.proofOfWork: Ship a public 'demo kit' repository that makes the four recorded demos reproducible and defensible by someone who was not in the room. It contains a one-command cold-start environment (Compose file with digest-pinned images, a checked-in synthetic seed dump, a documented DEMO_REPLAY mode that serves cached model responses with realistic simulated latency) tagged per demo date so any recording can be re-run byte-for-byte; a defence pack holding the one-page unit-economics sheet with its sensitivity block, three ADRs covering the decisions most likely to be attacked, a one-page data-flow and retention diagram, and an objection matrix of twenty questions each with a written sub-60-second answer; a failure kit with the pre-recorded fallback clip, an asciinema capture of the terminal path, and a written 30-second recovery script; and a RUBRIC.md plus a scores table showing all four takes graded on the ten dimensions with the delta and the specific change that produced it. The README opens with the one-sentence claim and a 90-second architecture sketch in three boxes, so the repo itself demonstrates the skill it documents.

75.why: An FDE's output is mostly artifacts other people read without you in the room: the runbook the customer's on-call follows at 3am, the incident write-up their VP forwards to their CISO, the design doc that decides whether your integration ships. If the prose is vague, the deployment stalls in review; if it is precise, you buy trust you did not have to earn in a meeting. Public case studies do the same job pre-sales - a hiring loop or a prospect who has read three of your write-ups arrives already believing you can do the work, which is the single highest-leverage thing you can put on the internet in a job search.
prerequisites: At least three finished pieces of real work with a decision and a measurable outcome in them - ideally the Lumen FDE deployment, a migration or integration you owned, and a production incident you debugged end to end.
Working Git and Markdown: branches, PRs, fenced code blocks, and the docs-as-code idea from developer tooling and Git internals (topic 2).
Enough observability and SLO literacy (topics 27 and 29) to quote p50/p95/p99, error budgets and before/after numbers without hand-waving.
A publishing surface you control - rasul.in with a working build and deploy, plus the ability to add a route, an OG image and a feed.
Basic diagramming: you can draw a system as boxes with labelled arrows and know what a trust boundary is (threat modelling, topic 62).
Customer-facing judgement about what is confidential: contract terms, NDAs, and the difference between 'a fintech in Southeast Asia' and naming the account.

subtopics.name: Pick three stories that each contain a real decision
subtopics.learn: Before writing a word, list eight candidate stories from your own work and score each on: was there a decision with at least two defensible options, is there a number that moved, and can you publish it without leaking a customer. Keep the three that score highest and write one sentence per piece stating the reader ('a platform engineer evaluating whether to run this in their own VPC') and the one thing they should believe afterwards. Reject 'here is how I built a CRUD app' - a case study people share is one where the obvious answer was wrong and you show why. Write the three one-sentence promises down; every later cut is judged against them.

resource.label: Julia Evans - Some blogging myths (choosing what is worth publishing)

subtopics.name: The case-study spine: context, constraint, options, decision, mechanism, result
subtopics.learn: Adopt one skeleton and reuse it across all three pieces: (1) the situation and the hard constraint, (2) the two or three options actually on the table, (3) what you chose and the trade-off you accepted, (4) how the thing actually works, at the level of config keys and API calls, (5) what changed, with numbers, and (6) what you would do differently. This is the Architecture Decision Record shape (context / decision / consequences) stretched to narrative length. Draft all three spines as bullet outlines first and confirm each has a real 'consequences' section - the honest cost you paid is what makes readers trust the rest.

resource.label: Architecture Decision Records - adr.github.io

subtopics.name: Audience definition and the prerequisite contract
subtopics.learn: Work Google Technical Writing One's audience unit and apply it literally: write the reader's role, what they already know, and what they need to do after reading. Then compute the curse-of-knowledge delta - list every term you used that the reader does not have (IRSA, backpressure, idempotency key, ANN recall) and decide for each whether to define it inline, link it, or cut the sentence. State prerequisites explicitly at the top of a how-to ('assumes kubectl access and a namespace you can create Secrets in'). A reader who bounces at paragraph three because you assumed too much never tells you why.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing One

subtopics.name: Sentence-level surgery: active voice, one idea, no zombie nouns
subtopics.learn: Run a mechanical pass over your draft: find every passive construction (search for 'was', 'were', 'is being', 'by the') and name the actor or justify keeping it; split any sentence over roughly 25 words; convert nominalisations back into verbs ('performed an evaluation of' becomes 'evaluated'); delete 'in order to', 'it should be noted that', 'basically', 'simply', 'just', 'obviously'. Replace vague quantifiers with numbers: 'significantly faster' becomes 'p95 fell from 4.1s to 380ms'. Do this as a timed pass, not while drafting - drafting and editing in the same pass is how people produce 3000 words that say nothing.

resource.label: Federal Plain Language Guidelines

subtopics.name: Paragraphs, lists, tables, and summary-first structure
subtopics.learn: Apply Technical Writing Two's structural moves: one topic per paragraph with the point in the first sentence, three to five sentences max, and a hard rule that a reader skimming only your first sentences still gets the argument. Convert any sequence of 'and then' prose into a numbered list when order matters and a bulleted list when it does not; keep list items grammatically parallel. Convert any comparison of three or more things across two or more attributes into a table with the decision criterion as a column. Put the conclusion at the top of each section - technical readers scan, they do not read in order.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing Two

subtopics.name: Terminology discipline and a project word list
subtopics.learn: Pick one term per concept and never vary it for elegance - 'job' and 'task' and 'run' meaning the same thing across three sections is a bug, not style. Build a five-to-fifteen line word list at the top of your notes fixing your spellings and capitalisation (Kubernetes not k8s in prose, PostgreSQL not Postgres in headings, 'command-line' adjectival, 'sign in' verb vs 'sign-in' noun) and check it against Google's word list for the entries you are unsure about. Ban 'easy', 'simple', 'just' and 'obviously' outright: they tell a stuck reader the failure is theirs.

resource.label: Google developer documentation style guide - word list

subtopics.name: Diataxis: never blend tutorial, how-to, reference and explanation
subtopics.learn: Learn the four modes and their failure signature: a tutorial that stops to explain CAP theorem loses the beginner; a how-to that narrates your journey wastes an expert's time; reference that editorialises becomes untrustworthy; explanation with copy-paste commands gets pasted into production. Classify each of your three pieces (a case study is mostly explanation with a how-to appendix) and move any misplaced content out into a linked companion page. Apply the same test to the customer-facing docs you ship: if your runbook has a paragraph starting 'historically we...', it belongs somewhere else.

resource.label: Diataxis - the four kinds of documentation

subtopics.name: Blameless incident write-ups that survive a customer's exec reading them
subtopics.learn: Learn the postmortem template shape: impact stated in customer terms and duration, a timestamped timeline with timezone, root cause separated from triggering condition, what went well / what went badly / where we got lucky, and action items each with an owner, a due date and a type (prevent, detect, mitigate). Write in the passive-free but person-free register: 'the deploy script applied the migration before draining connections', never 'Priya forgot to drain connections'. Include the detection gap explicitly - how long between impact starting and anyone knowing - because that is the number that decides whether the customer trusts your monitoring.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

subtopics.name: Read five real published postmortems and steal their moves
subtopics.learn: Pick five write-ups from the post-mortems collection spanning different failure classes (cascading failure, config push, capacity exhaustion, data loss, dependency outage) and for each, annotate: how many sentences before you know the impact, where the timeline starts, how they describe the contributing cause without blame, and what they chose not to disclose. Notice that the widely-shared ones are specific and slightly uncomfortable - they name the wrong assumption. Extract three concrete devices (an impact box at the top, a 'why our monitoring missed it' section, a diagram of the request path at failure) and put them in your own template.

resource.label: danluu/post-mortems - collection of public postmortems

subtopics.name: Numbers that survive scrutiny: baselines, percentiles, and honest deltas
subtopics.learn: Every performance or cost claim needs four things stated: the baseline configuration, the measurement method and sample size, the percentile (never a bare average for latency), and the confounders you did not control. Write 'p99 ingest latency over 7 days of production traffic, ~2.1M requests/day, fell from 3.4s to 610ms after switching to batched upserts; hardware and traffic mix unchanged' rather than '5x faster'. Frame reliability numbers against an SLO and error budget rather than as raw uptime. If a number came from a synthetic benchmark, say so in the same sentence - a reader who catches you inflating one figure discounts the whole piece.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives

subtopics.name: One diagram per idea: C4 levels and drawing the trust boundary
subtopics.learn: Learn the C4 levels (system context, container, component, code) and pick exactly one level per diagram - the most common diagram failure is mixing a Kubernetes Pod, an AWS account boundary and a Python class in one picture. For a case study, a system-context diagram plus one container diagram is usually the whole visual budget. Label every arrow with protocol and direction of initiation ('HTTPS, service to API, mTLS'), draw the customer/vendor boundary explicitly, and give the diagram a caption that states its claim rather than its contents. Any diagram you cannot summarise in one sentence is two diagrams.

resource.label: The C4 model for visualising software architecture

subtopics.name: Diagrams as code, versioned next to the prose
subtopics.learn: Author diagrams in Mermaid (flowchart, sequenceDiagram, and the state and ER types) inside fenced ```mermaid blocks so they live in the same repo and PR as the text and never drift from it. Learn enough syntax to draw a request path with participants and activation bars, and a deployment topology with subgraphs for the VPC and cluster. Know the limits - once you need precise layout or annotation, export a hand-drawn SVG instead and commit the source file. Check that your site's renderer actually supports Mermaid before you commit to it; if not, render to SVG at build time.

resource.label: Mermaid docs - flowchart syntax (nodes, edges, subgraphs)

subtopics.name: Alt text, contrast, and images that survive dark mode
subtopics.learn: Write alt text that carries the informational content, not the filename: for a diagram, one sentence stating what it shows plus a pointer to the nearby prose that describes it fully; for decorative images, alt="" so screen readers skip them. Never put load-bearing information only in a screenshot - a terminal screenshot cannot be copied, searched, or read aloud, so paste the text too. Check contrast on diagram strokes and make sure exported PNGs with transparent backgrounds do not vanish on a dark-themed page; a flat background colour on the export is the cheap fix.

resource.label: W3C WAI - Images Tutorial (alt text decision tree)

subtopics.name: Code blocks and terminal transcripts that actually run
subtopics.learn: Every command you publish should be copy-pasteable: no leading '$' inside the copyable region, placeholders in an obvious form like <CLUSTER_NAME>, language tags on fences for highlighting, and long flags (--namespace not -n) so the reader can tell what they are running. Show the expected output right after the command so a reader can tell whether it worked. For multi-step flows, record an asciinema cast rather than a GIF - it is text, it is copyable, and it does not weigh 8MB. Before publishing, run every command in the piece on a clean machine or container; stale snippets are the number-one reason a technical post gets a scathing comment.

resource.label: asciinema - terminal session recorder

subtopics.name: Confidentiality: anonymise the customer, get approval, pick a licence
subtopics.learn: Establish a repeatable clearance loop: draft, strip identifying details (company name, headcount, exact ARR, cluster names, region if unusual, screenshots with hostnames and email addresses in them), replace with a category ('a Series-B logistics platform running ~200 services'), then send to your customer contact and get written approval before publishing - email is enough, verbal is not. Check the MSA/NDA for a publicity clause first. Redact credentials properly: rotate anything that appears in a screenshot rather than blurring it, and scrub .git history if a secret ever landed in the repo. Put an explicit licence on your own sample code so readers know they may use it.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Removing sensitive data from a repository

subtopics.name: Publishing mechanics on rasul.in: title, canonical URL, cards, dates
subtopics.learn: Ship each piece with: a title that states the specific claim ('Cutting p99 retrieval latency 5x by moving reranking off the request path' beats 'Lessons from an AI deployment'), a one-paragraph TL;DR above the fold, a stable slug you will never change, a canonical link tag, published and updated dates, and Open Graph plus Twitter card tags with a real og:image so the link renders as a card in Slack and LinkedIn instead of a bare URL. Test the card render with the platform's own debugger before you share. Confirm the page is server-rendered or statically generated so crawlers and link unfurlers see the text.

resource.label: Google Search Central - Canonical URLs and consolidating duplicate URLs

subtopics.name: Prose CI: Vale, markdownlint, and link checking in the build
subtopics.learn: Treat prose like code. Add markdownlint for structural rules (heading increments, fence languages, no trailing whitespace, line length) and Vale with a style based on the Google developer style guide plus a repo vocabulary file for your own terms and product names. Wire both into a GitHub Actions job on pull requests so a broken heading level or a banned word ('simply') fails the check before it ships. Add a link checker for internal and external links and run it on a schedule, not just on push, so rot in old posts surfaces. Set Vale's error/warning/suggestion levels deliberately - if everything is an error, you will disable it in a week.

resource.label: Vale - syntax-aware prose linter

subtopics.name: Ship, distribute, and handle the comment thread
subtopics.learn: Publishing is not distribution. For each piece: post to the two or three places your reader actually is, use the original title rather than editorialised bait, and be present for the first few hours to answer questions. Read the venue's rules before posting - most technical forums penalise self-promotional framing and reward a plain descriptive title and an author who replies substantively. When someone finds a genuine error, fix the post, add a dated correction note at the bottom, and thank them in the thread; when someone is just hostile, do not reply. Track which piece got forwarded internally by strangers - that, not raw traffic, is the signal the write-up worked.

resource.label: Hacker News guidelines

outcomes: You can take a 2000-word draft and cut it 30% in one editing pass without losing a claim, showing the before/after word count and a list of the passive constructions, nominalisations and vague quantifiers you replaced.
You can state, for any page you write, which Diataxis mode it is and what belongs on a different page - and you can point at content you actually moved out.

You can write an incident write-up with impact in customer terms, a timestamped timeline with timezone, root cause separated from trigger, a stated detection gap, and action items that each have an owner, a date and a prevent/detect/mitigate label.
You can defend every number in your write-up: baseline, measurement method, sample size, percentile, and the confounders you did not control.

You can produce a system-context and a container diagram at a single C4 level each, authored as Mermaid in the repo, with protocol-labelled arrows, an explicit trust boundary and alt text that carries the content.
You can run every command in a published post on a clean container and have them all work, with expected output shown inline.
You can run a customer-clearance pass that strips identifying details, rotates any exposed credential, and produces written approval before publish.
You have three case studies live on rasul.in with canonical URLs, OG cards that render in Slack, a feed, and a CI job that lints prose and checks links on every pull request.
failureModes: The write-up leads with the journey ('when we first kicked off the project...') and buries impact and outcome under 800 words, so the exec who was forwarded it closes the tab before learning what happened.

A runbook says 'simply restart the service' with no expected output and no failure branch, so the customer's on-call at 3am runs it, sees an unfamiliar error, and escalates to you anyway - the doc bought nothing.
A screenshot in a published post contains a hostname, an internal email address or a partially visible token, and the account's security team finds it before you do.
Commands in the post were written from memory or from a shell with unexported env vars already set, so they fail for every reader on a clean machine and the top comment is someone pasting the error.

An incident report names an individual or a team as the cause, the customer's manager reads it, and the next incident gets reported to you late or not at all because people learned that honesty is punished.

Performance claims quote an average instead of a percentile and omit the baseline, so a sceptical engineer in the customer's review reproduces a different result and the whole document loses credibility.

Diagrams live in a Figma or Lucidchart file outside the repo, drift from the deployed architecture within two sprints, and are then used by a new joiner to reason about a system that no longer exists.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through a write-up you published about your own work. What did you cut, and how did you decide what was safe to disclose about the customer?

You have 45 minutes to write the customer-facing incident summary for a 4-hour partial outage in the integration you deployed. What sections do you write, in what order, and what do you deliberately leave out of the first version?

A customer's on-call engineer has to run your failover procedure for the first time at 3am with no context. Write - out loud - the first five lines of that runbook, and tell me what makes them safe to follow.
Your post claims a 5x latency improvement. I'm the skeptical staff engineer in the room. Convince me the number is real.
How do you decide whether something belongs in a tutorial, a how-to, reference, or an explanation page - and give me an example of a doc you've seen that failed because it mixed two of them.
You wrote a design doc, three reviewers left conflicting comments, and one of them is the customer's architect who outranks the others. How do you converge the document without a meeting?

We want our FDEs publishing customer case studies. Design the process end to end: what gets written, who reviews it, what the legal and confidentiality gates are, and how you keep it from becoming marketing fluff.
75.proofOfWork: Beyond the three published case studies, build and open-source a 'write-up kit' repo that turns your process into something another engineer can adopt in an afternoon. It contains four Markdown templates (case study, incident postmortem, design doc / ADR, and customer runbook) with inline commentary explaining what each section is for and the failure it prevents; a Vale style package with a vocabulary file plus a rules set that flags banned hedges ('simply', 'just', 'obviously'), bare averages for latency, undefined acronyms and passive-voice hot spots; a markdownlint config and a GitHub Actions workflow that runs both plus a link checker on every pull request; a redaction and clearance checklist covering screenshot scrubbing, credential rotation, git-history scanning and the written-approval step; and a short README that links each of your three published pieces to the template it was built from. Prove it works, not just that it exists: include the CI run on your own posts, a before/after diff of one draft showing the word count drop and the specific lint findings you fixed, and one piece of evidence that a real reader acted on the writing - a forwarded thread, an issue someone opened against your snippets, or a customer sign-off email (redacted) approving publication.

76.why: An FDE negotiates for a living - what is in the pilot and what is not, whether the go-live slips, whether that 'small ask' becomes a change order - so the offer negotiation is the first time the people who will staff you on accounts watch you hold a position under pressure with a real relationship on the line. Folding in ten minutes because a recruiter said 'this is the band' is the same behaviour that later turns a fixed-scope deployment into six months of unpaid feature work. FDE compensation is also structurally messier than a straight software engineering offer - hybrid or field ladders with different equity bands, travel load, on-call for someone else's production, sometimes a variable component tied to deployment milestones - so the highest-leverage moves here are structural (which ladder, which level, what is written down) rather than an extra few percent on base.
prerequisites: A live pipeline from topics 82 and 83 - a target list of ~40 companies and loops running in waves - because leverage in this topic is almost entirely a function of having real alternatives at the same time, not of technique.

Your narrative from topic 72 (why FDE, why this company, travel, comp): the compensation-expectations question lands in the first ten minutes of the first recruiter call, before any of this material gets a chance to matter.
Public proof from topics 69 and 80 - published case studies, working repos, recorded demos - which is the evidence you point at when you ask for a level review rather than just asserting seniority.
Executive communication from topic 68: a counter is a ninety-second, bottom-line-up-front ask delivered on a call, not a four-paragraph email.

Basic financial modelling in a spreadsheet: annualising a four-year grant, discounting by probability, and comparing two offers on year-one cash versus four-year total versus risk-adjusted expected value.

Honest, written knowledge of your own constraints before anyone asks: monthly burn, months of runway, notice period, dependents, relocation or visa limits, and what you are contractually leaving behind (unvested equity, an unpaid bonus, a clawback).

subtopics.name: The full surface area of an FDE offer
subtopics.learn: Enumerate every component before valuing any of them: base, target bonus (percentage of base, discretionary or contractual, pro-rated in year one), equity (RSU or option, dollar-denominated or share-denominated, and its vesting shape), sign-on cash (often split across two years, always attached to a clawback), relocation, and the FDE-specific lines - travel load, per-diem and booking policy, on-call stipend for customer production, region and account assignment, and in field orgs a variable or MBO component tied to deployment milestones. Learn who can move what: a recruiter can usually move sign-on and start date alone, the hiring manager owns level and scope, and base above band or an out-of-band grant needs a compensation committee exception that takes days. Learn that a dollar-denominated grant converts to shares at a price fixed on a specific date - grant date, or a trailing 15/20/30-day average - so 'X dollars of equity' can shrink materially between handshake and grant notice unless the conversion date is stated in writing.

resource.label: GitLab Handbook - Compensation: pay bands, levels, variable pay and the parts of an offer

subtopics.name: Calibrating a market band before anyone asks you for a number
subtopics.learn: Build a band from at least three independent sources per target company and write it down before the first call: levels.fyi percentiles filtered by company, level and metro; the posted range (several US states and cities require the range in the posting or on request, so 'what is the band for this level?' is a legitimate, answerable question); and two humans who actually hold the role. Record P25/P50/P75 separately for base, annualised equity and total comp rather than one blended figure, because the shape differs enormously - AI labs load equity, consultancies and services orgs load base plus variable. Know the data hazards: self-reported data skews high and skews toward the roles people brag about, private-company numbers go stale the moment the 409A moves, and FDE-style titles are thin in every dataset, so map the role onto the nearest engineering level and search that instead of the literal title. The output is three numbers per company - floor, target, stretch - that you read off a page later instead of inventing under pressure.

resource.label: The Pragmatic Engineer - The Trimodal Nature of Software Engineering Salaries

subtopics.name: Level and ladder: the FDE slotting problem
subtopics.learn: The highest-value negotiation in an FDE offer is usually structural, not numeric. Ask directly and early: is this role on the software engineering job family or on a separate field/solutions/services ladder, what is the internal level code, what are the bands for the level above and below, and what is the written promotion rubric. Field ladders frequently carry lower equity bands, slower or absent refresh cycles, and a ceiling one or two rungs below the engineering ladder, and moving ladders after you join is far harder than being slotted correctly on day one. Read live FDE and deployment-strategist postings side by side (Anthropic, Palantir, Databricks, OpenAI, Scale) and learn to spot the tells - 'solutions', 'delivery', 'resident' versus a posting that sits in the engineering job family with a stated level. Then learn the counter that actually works: not 'pay me more' but 'given the scope you described - owning a deployment end to end with no engineering backstop - this looks like your L5; here is the evidence, can you take it to the leveling committee?'

resource.label: Engineering Ladders - the Developer track, level by level (jorgef/engineeringladders)

subtopics.name: Walk-away, BATNA and ZOPA: four numbers set in writing first
subtopics.learn: Pre-commit four numbers before any conversation, because you cannot compute them honestly while a recruiter is on the phone: the walk-away (below which you decline and mean it), the target (a good outcome), the stretch (your opening ask), and the indifference point between your top two live options. Get the vocabulary right - your BATNA is your best alternative if this negotiation fails (stay put, take the other offer, keep interviewing with N live loops) and its quality, not your desire for the job, is what creates leverage; your reservation price is the worst deal you will still accept. Derive the walk-away from real inputs - twelve-month burn, notice-period gap, dependents, relocation and visa costs, unvested equity you forfeit, opportunity cost of loops you abandon - never from current salary plus a percentage. Learn ZOPA, the overlap between their maximum and your minimum, and accept that when there is no overlap the right move is a fast, warm no rather than a slow grind that burns a relationship you will want in three years.

resource.label: Harvard PON - What is BATNA? How to Find Your Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement

subtopics.name: Never the first number: deflection that survives three asks
subtopics.learn: Drill the deflection until it is boring, because whoever names a number first defines the range and the recruiter will ask inside the first ten minutes. Sequence: (1) 'I would rather get fit and level right first - what range is budgeted for this role?'; (2) 'I am sure you will be competitive; what does the band look like at that level?'; (3) if pressed a third time, give a researched total-comp range with an explicit dependency - 'somewhere in the X to Y range depending on level and how the equity is structured' - never a single point. Know the legal backdrop: many US states and cities prohibit asking for salary history at all, and several require disclosure of the posted range on request, so declining to share history is normal rather than adversarial. Never misstate your current or competing compensation - it is sometimes verifiable, it destroys the offer when caught, and the FDE community at these companies is small enough that it follows you. Talk about the market rate for the work, not about your history.

resource.label: Patrick McKenzie - Salary Negotiation: Make More Money, Be More Valued

subtopics.name: Sequencing the pipeline so two offers land in the same fortnight
subtopics.learn: Leverage is mostly a scheduling problem, and it is solved weeks before the offer call. Start the slowest processes first, put your top-choice company second rather than first so you arrive practised and with a live alternative, and slow the fast ones deliberately ('I have two processes finishing in a fortnight - can we align final rounds?'). Learn the honest accelerants: telling a company truthfully that you are in final stages elsewhere, asking a recruiter to compress a loop into one week, asking for a decision date rather than a number. Learn the recovery when timing fails and you have one offer with the rest at round two: convert the offer into a disclosed deadline for the others, accept that some processes will not move, and decide in advance whether you would take the bird in hand. Keep one table with company, stage, recruiter name, next date and expected decision date, because every move in this topic depends on knowing at any moment what your real alternatives are.

resource.label: Haseeb Qureshi - How to Break Into the Tech Industry: Job Hunting and Interviews

subtopics.name: Exploding offers and buying time
subtopics.learn: A 24- or 72-hour fuse is a pressure tactic far more often than a real constraint, and asking for time almost never costs you an offer - a company that has spent six weeks and several engineers' days on your loop does not rescind over a one-week extension. Learn the specific asks: a written extension with a concrete reason ('I have a final round on the 14th and I will not commit to something I cannot honour'), time with two more people on the team, and the equity plan documents plus grant notice, which legitimately take days to read. Learn to name the tactic politely if it persists, and to treat a flat refusal as data - a company that manufactures urgency with a candidate will do it to you with a customer deadline. Learn the mirror-image obligation: once you have decided, move within a day, because slow-rolling a company you intend to decline costs you a relationship in a small market.

resource.label: NACE - Advisory Opinion: Setting Reasonable Deadlines for Job Offers

subtopics.name: The counter: a prioritised package, delivered live
subtopics.learn: Structure the counter as a package with an explicit priority order, deliver it on a call, and confirm in writing afterwards - long email threads strip the tone and leave only the number. The shape that works: genuine enthusiasm and a specific reason you want this role, the constraint or alternative that justifies the ask, two or three requests with the most important named first, and a clear close ('if you can do X, I will sign today' - and only say that if it is true). Mechanics that matter: ask for the level review before anything else because it lifts every other number; counter on total compensation when the base band is rigid; use sign-on to bridge a gap the band cannot close, including bridging unvested equity you are forfeiting, and bring the vest schedule as evidence; never state a number you would not accept, because your ask is a commitment. When they say no, ask the two follow-ups that keep the conversation alive: 'what would have to be true for that to be possible?' and 'if the cash is fixed, can we move start date, sign-on, or the equity refresh at the first review?'

resource.label: Haseeb Qureshi - How Not to Bomb Your Offer Negotiation

subtopics.name: Tactical empathy and calibrated questions on a recruiter call
subtopics.learn: Take the three moves from Never Split the Difference that survive contact with a professional recruiter and drill only those: labels ('it sounds like the band is a real constraint on your side'), mirrors (repeating their last three words so they keep talking and reveal what is flexible), and calibrated how/what questions ('how am I supposed to make this work against an offer that pays materially more?') that hand them the problem without an ultimatum. Use the accusation audit for the awkward opening - 'you are probably going to think I am being difficult here' - and use silence after you make the ask, because the pause is where a recruiter fills in a concession. Learn explicitly what not to import: hostage-negotiation aggression, invented deadlines and manufactured scarcity read as amateurish, and they are unnecessary when your alternative is real.

resource.label: FBI Law Enforcement Bulletin - active listening skills: an evaluation tool for crisis negotiators

subtopics.name: Equity mechanics: strike, 409A, vesting shapes, cliffs, refresh, dilution
subtopics.learn: Learn the vocabulary well enough to interrogate a grant rather than admire it: RSU versus ISO versus NSO; strike price versus 409A fair market value versus last preferred price; grant date versus vesting commencement date; the standard four-year vest with a one-year cliff and monthly or quarterly vesting after, and the variants (back-loaded shapes such as 5/15/40/40 propped up by year-one and year-two cash bonuses, front-loaded grants, and one-year grants that are really an annual re-negotiation). Then learn the details that decide whether the paper is money: the post-termination exercise window (commonly 90 days, sometimes extended to seven or ten years), double-trigger RSUs at private companies that need both time vesting and a liquidity event before a seven-year expiry, the refresh grant policy and whether field roles are on the same refresh cadence as engineering, and dilution from future rounds. Learn the preference stack - a 1x non-participating preferred over a large raised total means a mediocre exit pays common holders nothing - and always ask for fully diluted shares outstanding so a percentage means something.

resource.label: The Open Guide to Equity Compensation (jlevy/og-equity-compensation)

subtopics.name: Valuing the equity: turning a headline into a defensible range
subtopics.learn: Build the spreadsheet that converts each grant into annual expected value plus a range, never a point estimate. Public RSUs: shares times current price, split across the actual vest schedule, with year one written as zero until the cliff and an explicit share-price assumption you can defend. Private options: (exit price per common share minus strike) times shares, times probability of exit, minus the cash required to exercise and the tax required to hold - then run three scenarios (down-round or acqui-hire where common gets nothing, 2x, 10x) and show all three. Refuse the two standard sleights of hand: valuing common at the last preferred price, and quoting a four-year grant total as though it were an annual number. Compare offers on three normalised axes - year-one cash, four-year total, and risk-adjusted expected value - and keep the assumptions visible next to each cell so you can defend the comparison out loud when a recruiter challenges your maths.

resource.label: Cooley GO - Liquidation preference: why common stock can be paid last

subtopics.name: Tax and net: what you actually keep
subtopics.learn: Comparing gross numbers across offer structures is how people take the worse deal. For US-structured offers: RSUs are ordinary income at vest, and supplemental withholding at the flat statutory rate (22% federal up to the $1M threshold, 37% above) routinely under-withholds high earners into an April bill; sell-to-cover versus net-settle changes your cash position. ISOs create no ordinary income at exercise but the spread is an alternative minimum tax preference item that can generate a large cash tax on shares you cannot sell; NSOs are taxed as ordinary income on the spread at exercise. An 83(b) election on restricted stock or an early exercise must be filed within 30 days of transfer and the deadline is not recoverable. Know that the 90-day post-termination exercise window plus that tax bill is what silently converts a large option grant into zero. Do the arithmetic per offer, and route anything consequential through an actual tax professional - your job is to know which questions to ask, not to self-file.

resource.label: IRS Topic no. 427, Stock options

subtopics.name: Non-US and remote offer structures
subtopics.learn: If any target is an Indian entity, an international remote role or a contractor arrangement, learn the structure before you compare numbers. Indian offers are quoted as CTC, which bundles employer PF, gratuity accrual and a 'performance-linked' variable that is not guaranteed cash - strip it back to fixed monthly in-hand before you compare with a US total-comp figure. ESOPs from an Indian entity are typically taxed as a perquisite at exercise on the spread between fair market value and exercise price, then capital gains at sale, with a deferral regime for eligible startups; confirm the specifics with a chartered accountant rather than a blog. Notice period (30/60/90 days) is a negotiable start-date constraint and buyouts are a real ask. For remote or contractor roles, know the difference between employee and independent contractor treatment - who withholds, who pays employer-side taxes, what benefits and equity you do and do not get - because an eye-catching contractor day rate frequently nets less than a salaried offer.

resource.label: Income Tax Department, India - official portal

subtopics.name: Non-cash terms an FDE should negotiate harder than base
subtopics.learn: For a forward-deployed role, several non-cash terms are worth more over four years than the base delta you are arguing about. Negotiate and get in writing: expected travel percentage and cadence (three days a week on site is a different life from one week a month), who books and who approves, per-diem, whether loyalty points are yours, and the weekend-travel policy; region and account assignment, and what happens when your account is re-staffed; on-call expectations for customer production and whether there is a stipend or comp time; start date (a later start is often the cheapest concession they can give you); the date and criteria of your first performance and equity review, ideally at six months rather than the default annual cycle; and the internal mobility path to product engineering if the FDE org is a stepping stone for you. If a variable or MBO component exists, ask for the historical attainment distribution across the team and a guarantee or draw for the first two quarters while you ramp.

resource.label: Haseeb Qureshi - Ten Rules for Negotiating a Job Offer

subtopics.name: Reading the paperwork: clawbacks, IP assignment, notice and dispute clauses
subtopics.learn: Read the offer letter, the equity plan document and the grant notice as three separate contracts, because the offer letter is the least binding of them and the plan document is where the exercise window, the transfer restrictions, the company repurchase right and the change-of-control treatment actually live. Look specifically for: sign-on clawback terms (usually full or pro-rated repayment if you leave inside twelve months) and relocation repayment; the invention-assignment and outside-activities clauses, which matter a great deal to you because you have public repos and side projects - ask for a prior-inventions schedule listing them and a carve-out for work done on your own time and equipment; non-solicit and any non-compete (enforceability varies by jurisdiction and has been actively litigated); mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers; and the at-will language that makes every verbal promise revocable. The rule that saves you: anything a hiring manager promises - level, travel, region, a six-month review, a promotion timeline - is not real until it is in the letter, because managers change roles within a year.

resource.label: US FTC - Noncompete Rule and related materials

subtopics.name: The written negotiation plan and the decision matrix
subtopics.learn: Produce the deliverable: one document per top company with the researched band and its sources, your floor/target/stretch, the level you are asking for and the evidence for it, the exact opening sentence of your counter, your top three asks in priority order with a fallback for each, the concessions you will accept in return, and your walk-away with the arithmetic that produced it. Add a normalisation sheet that puts every live offer on the same axes - year-one cash, four-year total, risk-adjusted equity value, plus the non-cash terms - and a weighted decision matrix whose weights you set before any numbers arrive, so the choice is not made by whoever called last. Include the scripts for the four moments you will otherwise fumble: the expectations question, the 'what will it take to sign today' question, the extension request, and the decline. Pre-writing the plan is the entire point: everything in this topic is easy on paper and hard in a live twelve-minute call.

resource.label: Harvard PON - A Negotiation Preparation Worksheet: A Tool for Continuous Improvement

subtopics.name: Rehearsal and the close
subtopics.learn: Run at least six recorded role-plays with a friend playing a recruiter who has a written role card and instructions to push: the expectations question in the first five minutes, 'this is the top of the band', a 48-hour exploding deadline, 'we cannot move base but we can add equity', 'do you have a competing offer, and what are the numbers?', and 'what will it take for you to sign today?'. Score yourself on the recording for the things you cannot feel in the moment - did you name a number first, did you fill your own silence, did you apologise for asking, did you concede a dimension you had not planned to, how long between their objection and your capitulation. Then drill the close: accept verbally, ask for the full document set, re-read the grant notice for the share count and conversion date, sign, and only then decline the others personally and warmly, with a short reason and no auction-style gloating - those recruiters are the people who will source your next role.

resource.label: MIT OCW 15.665 Power and Negotiation - negotiation simulations and reflection assignments

outcomes: You can state, for each of your top ten target companies, a sourced band (P25/P50/P75 split into base, annualised equity and total), a target, a stretch and a walk-away number, with the arithmetic behind the walk-away written down.

You can deflect the compensation-expectations question three consecutive times on a recorded call without naming a number, without lying about current pay, and without sounding evasive - and then give a defended range if pressed a fourth time.

You can convert any option grant into a three-scenario expected-value range given strike, 409A FMV, last preferred price, fully diluted share count, preference stack and vesting shape, and name the inputs you would have to request to do it.
You can run a live counter that moves at least two dimensions beyond base - level review, sign-on, equity, start date, review timing - and closes with a commitment you are prepared to honour.
You can name the level and ladder a given FDE offer sits on, the bands for the adjacent levels, and the promotion rubric, and can make an evidence-backed case for a level review to a hiring manager.

You can explain the after-tax difference between an RSU offer and an ISO grant of nominally equal headline value, including flat supplemental withholding shortfall, AMT on the exercise spread, and the 30-day 83(b) window.

You can find, in an offer letter and equity plan document, the six clauses that materially change the deal - sign-on clawback, exercise window, invention assignment, non-solicit, arbitration, change-of-control treatment - and articulate what you would ask to change in each.

You can choose between two competing offers using a matrix whose weights you set before the numbers arrived, and decline the loser in a three-sentence call that keeps the recruiter relationship intact.
failureModes: You give a number in the first recruiter screen, the whole process gets calibrated to it, and you never learn that the band topped out 35% higher because nobody had a reason to tell you.

You hint at a competing offer you do not have, the recruiter asks a specific follow-up about the level and structure, and the resulting stumble costs you both the credibility and the offer in a field small enough that people compare notes.

You win a 6% base bump and accept the level as offered, so you sit two years under a lower ceiling with smaller refreshes, and the promotion you were verbally promised needs a committee packet nobody prepared.

You compare a Series B option grant against public RSUs by multiplying shares by the last preferred price, ignoring strike, the liquidation preference and future dilution, and discover at an acqui-hire three years later that common holders received nothing.

The hiring manager promises a specific region, a travel ceiling and a six-month equity review on a call, none of it enters the offer letter, and eleven months in you are on a different account, travelling four days a week, reporting to someone who never heard the promise.

You take a sign-on bonus with a full twelve-month clawback, the deployment turns out to be staff-augmentation work with no engineering ownership, and leaving in month eight now costs you cash you have already spent.

You negotiate entirely over email, your carefully framed package arrives at the compensation committee as a single bald number with no justification, and the answer comes back as a flat no you have no conversational room to reopen.
interviewQuestions: Recruiter screen, minute six: 'So that we do not waste each other's time - what are your compensation expectations for this role?' Answer it out loud, and then I am going to ask you the same thing twice more.
You have our offer and one from a competitor. Tell me what it would take for you to sign with us today - and be specific, because I have to take it to a committee and defend it.

Walk me through how you would compare two offers where one is a public company paying RSUs and the other is a Series C paying options. What do you need to know about the Series C before you can even put the two on the same page, and how would you present that comparison to your partner at home?
We cannot move base - it is the top of the band for this level. But I can add equity. Talk me through what you would want to know before you decide whether that is a good trade for you.

A customer's VP tells you two weeks before go-live that the deployment is unacceptable without a feature that is not in the SOW, and threatens to escalate to your VP. You cannot deliver it and hold the date. How do you run that conversation, and what do you actually say first?

You accepted our offer three weeks ago. During onboarding you discover you were slotted one level below what the hiring manager described in the loop, and the equity in the grant notice is 20% below what the letter implied because of the conversion date. What do you do, in what order, and with whom?

Tell me about a negotiation you lost - with an employer, a vendor or a customer. What did you concede too early, what would you set as your walk-away if you ran it again, and how would you know in the moment that you were about to fold?
76.proofOfWork: Build a negotiation dossier for your live pipeline and keep it as a private, versioned artifact you can walk an interviewer through. It has four parts. First, a comparison model - a spreadsheet with one row per live or target company and columns for sourced band and its three sources, level and ladder, year-one cash, four-year total, risk-adjusted equity expected value under three exit scenarios with the assumptions visible, and the non-cash terms priced explicitly (travel days per year, on-call weeks, notice-period gap, forfeited unvested equity); every private-company row must compute from strike, 409A FMV, fully diluted shares and the preference stack rather than a headline number. Second, a one-page plan per top-five company containing your floor, target and stretch, the level you will ask for with the two pieces of public evidence you will cite, the literal first three sentences of your counter, your three asks in priority order with a fallback for each, and the walk-away with its arithmetic. Third, six recorded role-play sessions - each under fifteen minutes, each with a written role card for the counterparty covering a different pressure move (expectations question, top-of-band refusal, exploding deadline, equity-for-base swap, competing-offer probe, sign-today close) - plus a self-scored rubric per recording tracking whether you named a number first, seconds of silence you filled, dimensions conceded that were not in the plan, and time from objection to capitulation, with a visible trend across the six. Fourth, a clause-by-clause annotation of one real offer letter and one real equity plan document (redact the employer) marking the sign-on clawback, exercise window, vesting shape and conversion date, invention-assignment and outside-activities language, non-solicit, arbitration and change-of-control treatment, with the specific redline you would request on each. Once the negotiation actually happens, add a two-page delta memo: what you asked for, what you got, what you left on the table, which sentence changed the outcome, and what you will do differently next time - that memo is the part that turns a lucky outcome into a repeatable skill.

77.topic: Domain fluency: fintech ops, healthcare intake, procurement, logistics
77.why: An FDE gets roughly fifteen minutes inside a customer's operation to prove they understand the business before the conversation collapses into a feature demo, and the proof is not enthusiasm - it is vocabulary, an accurate workflow map, and knowing which data you are not allowed to look at. These four domains cover the bulk of enterprise AI deployments, and each has a hard regulatory edge (PCI, HIPAA, SOX, ITAR) where a wrong default is not a bug but a reportable disclosure or an audit finding that kills the renewal. Knowing exactly who signs off is what converts a working prototype into a deployment, because in all four domains the approval, not the model, is the thing standing between you and production.
prerequisites: Discovery: finding the real problem (topic 66) - the question set and the listening discipline; this topic supplies the domain-specific ammunition that makes those questions land.

Compliance: SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, PCI (topic 64) - the control vocabulary, what a BAA and a DPA are, and the difference between a control and its evidence; here you apply it to four concrete operational domains.

Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems (topic 30): PII handling, row-level security, encryption boundaries and audit trails - the mechanics behind every 'this data may not move' rule you are about to write.

Agents: workflows vs agents and human-in-the-loop (topic 48) plus guardrails and prompt injection (topic 51) - you need a real model of what an agent can be allowed to propose versus execute before you can draw the autonomy line per domain.
Engagement documents (topic 67) - the one-pagers here are engagement artifacts, so you need the site-survey and design-doc muscle already built.
SQL and Postgres at depth (topic 29) plus Temporal (topic 34): idempotency, exactly-once illusions, sagas and compensating actions - money movement and claim submission are the canonical cases.

subtopics.name: The three-artifact method, fixed before you learn any domain
subtopics.learn: Lock the template first so all four domains produce comparable output. Per domain you will produce: three workflows drawn as swimlanes with one actor per lane, a named trigger, the systems of record touched at each step, and the two or three points where the process actually stalls; a data-never-move table listing each restricted data class with the specific rule that forbids it and the four boundaries it may not cross (leaving the customer network, entering a model prompt, landing in a log or trace attribute, entering an eval fixture); and a sign-off matrix of decision class, human role, threshold that triggers them, and the evidence their approval leaves behind. Learn just enough BPMN vocabulary - pool, lane, task, exclusive versus parallel gateway, message versus timer start event - that a customer's process owner can read your map and correct it, which is the entire point.

resource.label: OMG BPMN 2.0 specification

subtopics.name: Classifying the data before you touch any of it
subtopics.learn: Fix the legal spine that runs under all four domains: Article 4 personal data, Article 9 special categories (health, biometric, union membership) which captures most healthcare payloads, Article 6 lawful basis, Article 28 processor duties and the requirement to act only on documented instructions, Articles 44-49 on transfers, Article 30 records of processing, and Article 22 on solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects - the article that makes 'the agent decides and acts' a legal question rather than a product preference. Turn this into an engineering artifact: a column-level tag set (identifier, financial account, clinical, contractual price, export-controlled) with a per-class rule for network egress, embedding, prompt inclusion, trace attributes and retention. Write it before the first data-sharing call, not after.

resource.label: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), consolidated text

subtopics.name: Fintech: the rails, and what 'paid' actually means
subtopics.learn: For each rail know three things: who carries the risk, when finality occurs, and whether it is reversible. ACH moves in batches between an ODFI and an RDFI with SEC codes (PPD, CCD, WEB), same-day windows, and return codes that arrive after the fact - R01 insufficient funds within days, R10/R07 unauthorised within a sixty calendar-day consumer window, so an ACH 'success' is not final for two months. Fedwire is real-time gross settlement and effectively irrevocable; RTP and FedNow are instant, 24/7 and irrevocable, which flips every fraud control from detect-and-reverse to prevent-before-send. Cards run authorisation (hold, auth code, AVS and CVV results) then capture, clearing and settlement funding at T+1 or T+2 - an authorisation is not money. Learn the ISO 20022 families you will see in files: pain.001 initiation, pacs.008 interbank transfer, camt.053 end-of-day statement, camt.052 intraday, camt.054 notification, plus legacy MT940. Any workflow that says 'payment complete' must name which of these events it means.

resource.label: Federal Reserve: FedACH services — batch settlement, windows, and how ACH finality actually works

subtopics.name: Fintech: double-entry ledgers and the reconciliation break
subtopics.learn: Internalise the invariants: every movement is at least two entries, debits equal credits, the journal is append-only, and a correction is a reversing entry - never an UPDATE or a DELETE on a posted row. Know the account taxonomy you will meet (customer balance, clearing and settlement, fees, FX, suspense) and why a suspense account is where unexplained money lives until someone explains it. Learn the reconciliation loop concretely: ingest camt.053 or BAI2 or a processor payout report, match on amount plus value date plus reference, then classify every unmatched item as a timing break, fee break, FX break, duplicate, or genuinely missing; track break aging against the month-end close deadline because that deadline is the customer's real pain. Understand idempotency keys on every write path and that exactly-once is a lie without a dedupe table. The architectural line: an agent may propose a journal entry or explain a break, and must never post one or compute a balance - balances come from the ledger, the model narrates them.

resource.label: TigerBeetle docs: Financial Accounting (double-entry, debits and credits, account types)

subtopics.name: Fintech: disputes, chargebacks and the Regulation E clock
subtopics.learn: Dispute intake is the most heavily automated queue in fintech operations and it is entirely deadline-driven. Under 12 CFR 1005.11 a consumer has sixty days from the statement to assert an error; the institution has ten business days to investigate or must issue provisional credit and may then take up to forty-five days (ninety for new accounts, point-of-sale and foreign-initiated transactions), with notice of results within three business days of concluding. In parallel the card networks run their own machinery: reason codes, representment with compelling evidence, pre-arbitration and arbitration, each with deadlines counted in days. Know what goes in an evidence packet - AVS and CVV results, device and IP, delivery confirmation, terms acceptance, prior undisputed history - because assembling that packet is the automatable part while the disposition is regulated. The artifact you build here is a timer plus an immutable audit trail, not a chatbot.

resource.label: eCFR: 12 CFR Part 1005 (Regulation E, Electronic Fund Transfers)

subtopics.name: Fintech: KYC, CDD and sanctions screening as an ops queue
subtopics.learn: Know the onboarding chain: CIP collection (name, date of birth, address, identification number) under 31 CFR 1020.220, identity verification, customer due diligence including beneficial ownership at the 25 percent threshold plus one control person, risk rating, enhanced due diligence for politically exposed persons and high-risk profiles, then ongoing monitoring. Suspicious activity reporting runs on a thirty-day filing clock and carries an absolute prohibition on tipping off the customer - the existence of a SAR is itself protected. Sanctions screening against the OFAC SDN and consolidated lists is a strict-liability regime, matching is fuzzy across name variants, transliterations, dates of birth and addresses, and the false-positive rate dominates the operating cost, which is exactly why this queue attracts AI. The autonomy line: an agent may triage, enrich, deduplicate and draft an alert narrative; it may never dispose of an alert or file, and no SAR content may ever appear in a shared log, a prompt to an uncontracted vendor, or a customer-visible surface.

resource.label: eCFR: 31 CFR 1010.230 (FinCEN CDD rule - beneficial ownership for legal entity customers)

subtopics.name: Fintech: PCI scope and the fields a model must never see
subtopics.learn: Separate cardholder data (PAN, cardholder name, expiration date, service code) from sensitive authentication data (full track data, CAV2/CVC2/CVV2/CID, PIN and PIN block). SAD must never be stored after authorisation under any circumstance; PAN must be rendered unreadable in storage and masked on display to at most first six and last four. Learn what defines the cardholder data environment and how tokenization, hosted fields and iframes, and network tokens shrink it, along with what separates SAQ A from SAQ A-EP from SAQ D - because scope determines how expensive your integration is to the customer. Anything that can affect the security of the CDE is in scope, and that explicitly includes your log sink, your trace backend and your eval fixtures. The operating rule to write down: a PAN never enters a prompt, a span attribute, a screenshot in a demo deck, or a test dataset; if the model must reason about a card it gets last four plus BIN metadata plus a token.

resource.label: PCI SSC: PCI Data Security Standard (scope, cardholder data and sensitive authentication data)

subtopics.name: Fintech: who actually signs off
subtopics.learn: Learn the required program shape - internal controls, a designated BSA/AML compliance officer, training, independent testing, and customer due diligence - because those five pillars tell you which named human owns which decision. Then map real approvals: the BSA officer for alert and SAR dispositions, compliance for any customer-facing language and for adverse action notices, treasury or the controller for payment file release under dual control (maker-checker, two credentials, never one service account), the model risk function for anything that scores or ranks a customer, and - if your customer is a fintech riding a sponsor bank's charter - the partner bank, whose oversight team will read your agent's logs during their audit. Produce the matrix as change type to approver to evidence, and get it signed before you build, because retrofitting an approval step into a shipped agent is a rewrite.

resource.label: eCFR: 31 CFR Part 1020 (AML program requirements for banks)

subtopics.name: Healthcare: the intake workflow end to end
subtopics.learn: Walk the real sequence: referral or scheduling, pre-registration, insurance verification, prior authorisation, consent and intake forms, check-in and registration, patient matching and MRN assignment, triage, then the encounter.
