Patient identity is the load-bearing step and the one engineers underestimate: there is no national identifier, so matching is deterministic on MRN and probabilistic on name, date of birth, sex and address through an enterprise master patient index, duplicate rates of several percent are normal, and an incorrect merge is a clinical safety event rather than a data-quality ticket. Learn how FHIR models this - Patient.identifier as system plus value, the distinction between an MRN, a visit or account number and a payer member ID, and Patient.link for merges and replaces. Know where it stalls in practice: eligibility failures discovered at the desk, missing prior authorisation, and forms still arriving by fax.

resource.label: HL7 FHIR R4: Patient resource

subtopics.name: Healthcare: eligibility, prior authorisation and the claim lifecycle
subtopics.learn: Follow the money path: a 270 eligibility request returns a 271 with plan status, copay, deductible remaining and benefit detail (or an AAA rejection code that tells you why the payer refused to answer); a 278 services review carries prior authorisation, where the hard part is the payer-specific rule that determines whether an authorisation is even required; then an 837P or 837I claim, a 999 syntax acknowledgment and a 277CA claim acknowledgment, and finally an 835 remittance carrying CARC and RARC codes that explain each adjustment or denial, followed by appeal windows and the patient statement. Learn the code systems you will see in every payload: ICD-10-CM for diagnosis, CPT and HCPCS for procedures, NPI for providers, place-of-service and modifiers. The FDE-relevant conclusion: eligibility discovery, prior-auth packet assembly and denial triage are text-heavy, deadline-bound and non-clinical, which is where the value is; assigning or changing a diagnosis or procedure code is regulated billing work that a certified coder signs.

resource.label: HL7 FHIR R4: CoverageEligibilityRequest

subtopics.name: Healthcare: the three interchange formats you will actually integrate
subtopics.learn: HL7 v2 is pipe-delimited with MSH, PID, PV1 and OBX segments, event types like ADT^A01 admit, A04 register, A08 update and A31 update person, ORU^R01 for results, transported over MLLP on a raw TCP port through an interface engine (Mirth Connect, Rhapsody, Cloverleaf) with ACK and NACK semantics - and every site has Z-segments and local deviations, so v2 is a family of dialects rather than a standard. FHIR R4 is REST over JSON with typed resources, search parameters, Bundles, US Core profiles, SMART on FHIR OAuth2 scopes such as patient/*.read and system/*.read, and Bulk Data $export producing NDJSON for population-scale pulls. X12 carries the money: 270/271, 278, 837, 835, moved over SFTP or a clearinghouse. The practical asymmetry to internalise: reads are increasingly FHIR and comparatively fast to approve; writes usually still go through v2 interfaces or an EHR-vendor-specific programme with a months-long approval path, and that path length is your project timeline.

resource.label: HL7 FHIR R4 specification index

subtopics.name: Healthcare: PHI, minimum necessary, de-identification and BAAs
subtopics.learn: PHI is individually identifiable health information created, received or transmitted by a covered entity or business associate. There are exactly two lawful de-identification routes: Safe Harbor, which requires removing all eighteen identifier types - names, geography smaller than a state subject to the three-digit ZIP population rule, all date elements more specific than year, ages over 89, MRNs, account numbers, device identifiers, biometrics, full-face images and any other unique identifying number or code - plus no actual knowledge that re-identification is possible; or Expert Determination with documented statistical reasoning by a qualified person. Minimum necessary applies to everything except treatment. As a vendor you are a business associate: you need a signed BAA before touching PHI and a downstream BAA with every subprocessor, which includes your model provider - calling an inference endpoint with no BAA is the single most common violation in AI deployments. Assume free-text notes contain identifiers your scrubber missed, and contract accordingly rather than relying on regex.

resource.label: HHS: Guidance on De-identification of PHI (Safe Harbor and Expert Determination)

subtopics.name: Healthcare: who signs off, and the clinical autonomy line
subtopics.learn: Name the roles before the kickoff call: the designated Privacy Officer and Security Officer, compliance, health information management for record integrity, the CMIO or clinical informatics lead for anything that changes a clinician's screen or workflow, the revenue cycle director for billing-adjacent changes, legal for the BAA and its subprocessor list, and the IRB when data is used for research - and understand that secondary use of clinical data to train or tune a model reads as research to an IRB even when it feels like ordinary engineering. Write the autonomy line into the SOW in one sentence: the agent drafts, a licensed human signs; nothing autonomous writes to the chart; every suggestion carries its source so the clinician can inspect and override. Treat 'we would like to train on your data' as a separate approval requiring far more than a BAA - usually a data use agreement, an IRB determination and an executive sign-off.

resource.label: HHS HIPAA for Professionals (rules index)

subtopics.name: Procurement: requisition to pay and the three-way match
subtopics.learn: Trace the chain: requisition with cost centre and GL account, approval against a delegation-of-authority threshold, purchase order issued to the supplier, goods receipt when the item arrives, invoice receipt, then the three-way match comparing PO, GR and invoice on quantity and price within tolerance keys, posting through a GR/IR clearing account, then a payment run and remittance advice. Services differ: a service entry sheet replaces the goods receipt and many flows are two-way matched, while evaluated receipt settlement pays with no supplier invoice at all. The product surface is the exception queue - invoices blocked for price variance, quantity variance, missing goods receipt, duplicate invoice, wrong or missing PO (maverick spend), and mis-coded GL accounts - so learn what each block code actually means to an AP clerk. Pick up the buyer vocabulary too (spend under management, tail spend, catalogue versus punchout via cXML, contract price list, three-bid-and-a-buy), because misusing it in discovery costs credibility in the first ten minutes.

resource.label: SAP Help Portal: SAP S/4HANA Cloud documentation

subtopics.name: Procurement: supplier master data, onboarding and the fraud surface
subtopics.learn: The supplier master is the highest-value fraud target in the enterprise: legal name, tax identity (W-9 or W-8BEN-E, VAT number), remit-to address, bank account, payment terms, insurance and certifications, diversity flags, and identifiers such as DUNS, GLN and the internal vendor number. Onboarding runs tax validation, denied-party and sanctions screening, certificate checks and often a security review before a vendor can be transacted with. The control that matters most: any bank-detail change must be verified out of band against a number already on file, never against a number supplied in the requesting email, because supplier bank-change business email compromise is the most common seven-figure loss in this domain - which makes an agent with write access to vendor banking an attack surface rather than a feature. Duplicate and near-duplicate vendor records are also why every customer's spend analytics is wrong, and cleaning them is a legitimate, low-risk first deliverable.

resource.label: FBI: Business Email Compromise (supplier bank-detail change fraud and out-of-band verification)

subtopics.name: Procurement: segregation of duties, delegation of authority and SOX ITGC
subtopics.learn: Express separation of duties and least privilege in procurement terms: whoever creates a vendor cannot approve an invoice and cannot release a payment, and requester, approver and receiver must be different identities. Delegation of authority is a concrete table of spend thresholds by role and category, and splitting a purchase to stay under a threshold is a named audit finding, not a clever workaround. SOX IT general controls reduce to three things your deployment must produce evidence for: access provisioning and periodic review, change management, and job monitoring - who had access, what changed and who approved it, and proof that failed jobs were noticed and handled. The consequence that decides your architecture: a service account that can act as any user collapses SoD entirely, so the agent needs its own identity, its own narrow permission set, and an audit trail that distinguishes agent-proposed from human-approved on every record it touches.

resource.label: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 (AC-5 separation of duties, AC-6 least privilege)

subtopics.name: Logistics: order to delivery and the EDI backbone
subtopics.learn: Follow the physical and document chains together: order capture in the OMS, availability and allocation, warehouse work in the WMS (wave, pick, pack, SSCC-labelled cases), carrier selection and rating in the TMS, load tender, bill of lading, pickup, in-transit status, proof of delivery, then freight audit and pay. The message set you will integrate: 850 purchase order, 855 acknowledgment, 856 advance ship notice with its hierarchical shipment-order-pack-item loops, 810 invoice, 940 and 945 warehouse shipping order and advice, 204 motor carrier load tender, 990 tender response, 214 shipment status, 210 freight invoice, and the 997 functional acknowledgment that tells you whether anything was received at all. Transport is AS2 or SFTP through a VAN, and mapping errors surface as 997 or 824 rejects days after the fact. Understand that for a retail supplier the ASN is a financial document: a late or structurally invalid 856 triggers a vendor compliance chargeback regardless of whether the freight arrived.

resource.label: Stedi EDI Reference: X12 856 Ship Notice/Manifest (ASN loops and segments)

subtopics.name: Logistics: customs, classification and trade compliance
subtopics.learn: Every cross-border shipment carries a classification decision and a screening decision that attach personal liability to a named human. HS and HTS codes drive duty rates; country of origin drives eligibility and tariff treatment; incoterms (EXW, FOB, DAP, DDP) decide who owes duty and who bears risk at each point; ISF 10+2 must be filed before lading for ocean imports. Screening covers denied and restricted party lists, ECCN classification and licence exceptions under the EAR, ITAR for defence articles including technical data - which means a screen share or a shared drawing with a foreign national can itself be a deemed export - and embargoed destinations. Dangerous goods carry their own certification regime (IATA DGR, 49 CFR HMR) where only a trained, currently certified person may sign the declaration. The rule to state up front: classification and licence determination from an agent are advisory only, a licensed customs broker files the entry, and a certified human signs DG paperwork.

resource.label: CBP: Importer Security Filing '10+2' (pre-lading filing requirements for ocean imports)

subtopics.name: Logistics: the exception queue and who has authority over it
subtopics.learn: The exceptions are the domain: OS&D (over, short, damaged), refused delivery, misroute, missed appointment, dwell, detention and demurrage accessorials, reweigh and reclass, and lost freight. Freight claims run under the Carmack Amendment with carrier liability limits and filing windows - commonly nine months to file and two years to sue after declination - and a claim needs the bill of lading, a proof of delivery with the exception actually noted at delivery, invoice value and photographs; an exception not written on the POD is usually an unwinnable claim, which is why capture-at-the-dock is the automation with real ROI. Detention and demurrage accrue by the hour or day and are disputed entirely from timestamps, so clean event data converts directly into recovered money. Authority: the dispatcher or transportation manager approves re-routes and accessorials, the shipper of record owns the claim, and carrier scorecards including OTIF decide who gets the freight next quarter.

resource.label: eCFR: 49 CFR Part 370 (principles and practices for investigation of loss and damage claims)

subtopics.name: Writing the four one-pagers and passing the vocabulary test
subtopics.learn: Compress each domain onto one page a practitioner would not need to correct: three workflows with actors, systems of record and the two real bottlenecks; the data-never-move table with the rule cited by name (PCI SAD storage prohibition, HIPAA Safe Harbor identifiers, GDPR Article 9, ITAR technical data, supplier pricing under NDA); the sign-off matrix as decision to role to threshold to evidence; and a single agent-autonomy line stating what the agent may read, draft, propose and never do. Append a glossary of ten terms and five acronyms per domain and rehearse them aloud until they are unselfconscious, because fluency is judged in the first fifteen minutes by whether you say 'prior auth' and 'the 835' naturally or say 'the insurance thing'. Apply plain-language editing discipline - short sentences, active voice, one idea per line, define an acronym exactly once - then test each page by sending it to someone who works in that domain and counting their corrections; fewer than three is a pass, and every correction becomes a line in the glossary.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing One (plain-language editing: active voice, short sentences, defining terms)

outcomes: You can sketch from memory, for any of the four domains, three end-to-end workflows with actors, systems of record and the two points where the process actually stalls, and name the exception queue that is the real automation target.

You can state per domain which data must never enter a prompt, a log, a span attribute or an eval fixture, and cite the specific rule that forbids it - PCI's prohibition on storing sensitive authentication data, HIPAA's eighteen Safe Harbor identifiers, GDPR Article 9, ITAR technical data, contract pricing under NDA.

You can name the human who signs each decision class and the threshold that pulls them in - BSA officer, Privacy Officer, controller under dual control, category manager against a delegation-of-authority table, licensed customs broker, dispatcher - and say what evidence their approval must leave behind.

You can run a thirty-minute discovery conversation in any of the four domains using the domain's own vocabulary (SEC code, R10 return, camt.053, 271, 278, CARC, three-way match, GR/IR clearing, ASN, SSCC, detention) without stopping to ask what an acronym means.
You can classify any proposed agent capability into may decide, may draft for human approval, or may not touch this data at all, and defend the placement with a named rule rather than an opinion.

You can pick the right integration surface and estimate its approval path: FHIR R4 read versus HL7 v2 write versus X12 837/835 through a clearinghouse, ISO 20022 camt.053 versus a processor payout report, cXML punchout versus ERP API, EDI 856 over AS2.

You can inspect a customer's sample file before a demo, identify the fields that would make loading it an unlawful disclosure or a PCI scope expansion, and propose a masked or synthetic substitute the same day.
You can produce a one-page domain brief that a working practitioner in that domain corrects fewer than three times.
failureModes: Someone drops a 'quick sample' extract into Slack the night before a demo and it contains live PANs or unscrubbed clinical narratives, so the demo itself becomes a reportable disclosure and a PCI scope expansion before a single line of integration code exists.

The agent is given write access to the vendor master or the payment run so the workflow demos end to end, and the customer's SOX auditor records it as a segregation-of-duties failure that forces the integration out at renewal.

Payment success is modelled as the card authorisation or the ACH submission, so the product reports money that later returns under R10 up to sixty days afterwards, and the operations team stops trusting every number the system produces.

Free-text notes are sent to a model endpoint with no BAA because a data scientist removed the name column and called it de-identified, ignoring the seventeen other Safe Harbor identifiers embedded in the narrative text.

A prior-authorisation assistant optimised on approval rate quietly nudges toward diagnosis codes that get approved, which is billing fraud rather than a hallucination bug, and the eval set never catches it because it only scored approvals.

The generated 856 is syntactically valid but its shipment-order-pack hierarchy or SSCC labels are inconsistent, retailers reject it days later via 824 and levy vendor compliance chargebacks that exceed the value of the automation.

An export-controlled drawing is pasted into a shared workspace or shown on a troubleshooting screen share with a non-US engineer, which is a deemed export the customer's trade compliance officer is obliged to self-disclose.
interviewQuestions: A payments customer wants an agent that runs the dispute queue end to end. Which steps would you let it perform, which would you refuse, what regulatory clocks constrain the design, and what exactly must the system log so their examiner can reconstruct a decision two years later?

You have read access to a hospital's EHR and are building an intake assistant. Walk me from scheduling to a paid claim, name the interface you would use at each hop, and tell me the first three places the workflow actually breaks for the staff rather than for the software.

A prospect emails you a CSV of sample data the night before a demo. Talk me through your next ten minutes - once for a fintech customer, once for a hospital - and tell me precisely what differs between the two.

Design an invoice-exception agent for a procurement organisation that is audited under SOX. What identity does it run as, what records can it change, and how would you demonstrate to an auditor that no approval in the system was made by the agent?
Explain to me, as the customer's VP of Global Trade, why your system will not classify our goods or file our customs entries - and then tell me what it will do that is still worth paying for.

In healthcare, what is the difference between data that is de-identified and data you are permitted to send to a model vendor? Give me a concrete case where a team gets that distinction wrong and does not notice.

Pick a domain you have never worked in. How do you get to a credible discovery call in three days, and how would you tell the difference between genuine understanding and repeating jargon back at the customer?
77.proofOfWork: Ship a public 'demo-safe data kit and domain risk register' covering all four domains, built as working code rather than documents. The core is a machine-readable data-class policy per domain - YAML or JSON declaring restricted field patterns and the rule that forbids each one - enforced by a linter you wire into CI against one of your own agent projects: a PAN detector with a Luhn check plus BIN and last-four allowance, MRN and account-number patterns, a clinical free-text detector that flags dates finer than year and ages over 89, ECCN and ITAR keyword patterns, and supplier bank-detail fields. The linter runs in three places and must fail the build in each: on any prompt payload before it leaves the process, on OpenTelemetry span attributes and log records, and on every eval fixture in the repository, with a test suite proving each rule catches a crafted violation. Alongside it, ship a synthetic data generator per domain producing realistic but non-real records - test PANs that pass Luhn but are not issuable, HL7 v2 ADT^A04 and X12 271 and 835 fixtures with realistic CARC codes, PO/goods-receipt/invoice triples with deliberate price and quantity variances that exercise a tolerance check, and 856 ASNs including intentionally broken SSCC hierarchies - so that no customer data is ever needed to demo anything. Wrap it with the four one-pagers (three workflows, data-never-move table, sign-off matrix, autonomy line) and, for each domain, a recorded twenty-minute mock discovery call with someone who actually works in it, plus a short diff listing every correction they made and how you changed the one-pager in response. The corrections list is the part that proves fluency, because it shows where you were wrong and that you found out before a customer did.

78.topic: Releasing to a fleet of customer installs: support and skew policy, preflight gates, cohort rollout
78.why: An FDE does not ship to one production environment - they ship to twenty or forty customer-owned installs that are each pinned at a different version, on a different Kubernetes minor, behind a different change-approval board, and some of them are air-gapped so you cannot see them fail. Without a written support window, a skew policy and a preflight that hard-fails an unsupported jump, every upgrade is a bespoke rescue mission and the third-oldest install eventually becomes a version only you can operate, at 02:00, on a call with their CTO. The whole discipline reduces to two customer-facing promises you have to be able to keep: any install inside the support window can reach current on a documented path, and any upgrade can be rolled back with the customer's data intact.
prerequisites: GitOps: Helm charts and ArgoCD (Topic 9) - chart structure, values layering, `helm template`, Application/ApplicationSet objects and sync policies; this topic is about what you wrap around them.

Kubernetes production ops (Topic 8): Deployment rolling-update mechanics, readiness and startup probes, `progressDeadlineSeconds`, Jobs, PVCs and StatefulSet update strategy - a rollout gate is worthless if the workload never reports healthy correctly.
PostgreSQL at depth (Topic 31): transactions, lock modes, `pg_locks`, index builds and `EXPLAIN` - the expand-contract migration and its lock behaviour are the hard half of this topic.
CI/CD and supply chain (Topic 19): tagged, reproducible, signed artifacts and a release pipeline; a support policy assumes an immutable versioned artifact per release line.
SRE fundamentals (Topic 21): SLOs and error budgets, plus Incident response (Topic 24) - cohort rollout is an error-budget decision and a failed upgrade is an incident with a customer in the room.
Engagement documents (Topic 73): runbooks, ADRs and the habit of writing a policy the customer's change board can read and sign.

subtopics.name: The release contract: SemVer 2.0.0, chart version vs appVersion, and what 'breaking' means to a fleet
subtopics.learn: Know SemVer precisely: MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backwards-compatible additions, PATCH for backwards-compatible fixes; `1.4.0-rc.1` sorts *before* `1.4.0`; build metadata after `+` is ignored in precedence; `0.y.z` means you have promised nothing. In a Helm chart these are two different numbers - `version:` in Chart.yaml is the chart's own SemVer (required, and what `helm upgrade` resolves) while `appVersion:` is the application image tag (quoted, not required to be SemVer) - and conflating them is why a customer thinks a values-only chart fix is an application upgrade. Write down, for your product, the concrete list of what counts as breaking: a removed or renamed values key, a changed default that alters behaviour, a required new value with no default, a dropped API version, a migration that is not reverse-compatible, a raised minimum Kubernetes or Postgres version. Also set `kubeVersion:` in Chart.yaml (`>=1.28.0-0`) because Helm enforces it and it is the cheapest gate you own.

resource.label: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 specification

subtopics.name: Support window and EOL: how long a customer install stays supported
subtopics.learn: Steal a policy shape that has already survived a decade of enterprise argument. PostgreSQL: five years of support per major, minor releases on a fixed quarterly schedule, a published final-release date per major, and an explicit statement that running an EOL major is the user's risk. Translate that into your own RELEASES.md: how many minor lines you support at once (N-2 is the usual answer), how long each is supported in months and what date each currently-supported line goes EOL, what 'supported' actually buys (security fixes, data-corruption fixes, an upgrade path to current - not new features), and what happens when a customer goes out of window (best-effort, paid uplift, or upgrade-first-then-we-help). Publish the EOL table with dates, not relative language, because 'we support the last two versions' is unenforceable when a customer stops upgrading for a year.

resource.label: PostgreSQL - Versioning policy (support lifetime, minor release cadence, EOL dates)

subtopics.name: Patch and security backport policy: which lines get the fix
subtopics.learn: Kubernetes publishes exactly the artifact you need to copy: a monthly patch cadence, a cherry-pick deadline before each patch release, a support window per minor (roughly 12 months plus 2 months of maintenance mode), and a rule that security fixes land on the three most recent minors. Decide the same four things for your product and write them as a table: cadence (fixed date or on-demand), which severities are backported and how far (CVSS high and above to all supported lines, data corruption to all supported lines, everything else to current only), who approves an out-of-cadence emergency patch, and the maximum age of a supported line. Note the operational consequence: every extra supported line multiplies your build matrix, your preflight matrix and your migration test matrix - N-2 is a cost decision, not a technical one, and you should be able to state that cost.

resource.label: Kubernetes - Patch Releases (cadence, cherry-pick deadlines, support window)

subtopics.name: Component skew: which parts may differ, by how much, and the mandatory upgrade order
subtopics.learn: A customer install is never one version - it is a control plane, a set of agents or workers, a CLI the customer's operators run, a database schema, and possibly a browser extension or an on-prem connector, each upgraded at a different moment. Learn the kubeadm model as the reference implementation: upgrade one minor at a time, control plane first (api-server before controller-manager and scheduler), then node components, never the reverse, and never skip a minor; kubelet may lag the API server by a bounded number of minors, kubectl by one in either direction. Write the equivalent matrix for your components: which pairs are allowed to skew, in which direction, by how many versions, and what the required upgrade order is. The direction matters more than the number - if new server plus old agent is supported but old server plus new agent is not, then the rollout order is fixed and the rollback order is its exact reverse.

resource.label: Kubernetes - Upgrading kubeadm clusters (one-minor-at-a-time, component order)

subtopics.name: Deprecation policy: notice periods, warning headers, and proving nobody still calls it
subtopics.learn: Copy the Kubernetes deprecation contract because customers already recognise it: a GA API element is supported for at least 12 months or 3 releases after deprecation (whichever is longer), beta for 9 months or 3 releases, alpha for none; a deprecated element keeps working for its whole window and only the *announcement* is instant. Implement the two mechanics that make deprecation safe on a fleet you cannot see: emit an HTTP `Warning: 299 - "..."` header (and a structured log line) on every call to a deprecated endpoint or flag, and expose a counter metric per deprecated element so the deprecation decision is made from usage data rather than hope. State the rule you will not break: a removal only ships in a MAJOR (or an announced MINOR line for beta features), never in a patch, and never before the counter has read zero across every install in the support window for a full billing period.

resource.label: Kubernetes - Deprecation Policy (notice windows, warnings, removal rules)

subtopics.name: Supported upgrade paths: stopovers, no-skip rules, and the version matrix
subtopics.learn: The customer question is always 'we are on 1.2.7, can we go straight to 1.6.0?' and the answer must be a path, not a shrug. Study `pg_upgrade` as the model of an explicit path tool: it states the oldest source version it accepts, refuses mismatched binaries, requires a cleanly shut-down old cluster, and - critically - has a `--check` mode that validates the whole jump and changes nothing. Build your own matrix: rows are the source version, columns are the target, cells are `direct`, `via X.Y` (a required stopover, usually a release that carried a data migration you cannot skip), or `unsupported - reinstall`. Name the terminal versions (a release with a known-broken migration that must be stepped over) and pin the reason next to each cell, because unexplained cells get ignored by whoever is on-site next. Generate the matrix from a machine-readable file so the preflight, the docs and the CI test matrix all read the same source of truth.

resource.label: PostgreSQL - pg_upgrade (supported source versions, --check mode, path constraints)

subtopics.name: Preflight gates: collectors, analyzers, and pass/warn/fail outcomes
subtopics.learn: A preflight is a program that refuses to let an unsafe upgrade start, run from the customer's own terminal. With troubleshoot.sh you write a `Preflight` spec whose collectors gather cluster info, cluster resources, an HTTP egress probe, a `run` pod, or a live `postgres` connection, and whose analyzers turn that into outcomes: `clusterVersion` with `when: "< 1.28.0"` -> fail, `nodeResources` with a `filters` block on `cpuCapacity`/`memoryCapacity` -> fail below minimum and warn below recommended, `storageClass` present, `distribution` allowed, `secret`/`configMap` exists, `postgres` connected and above a minimum version. Every analyzer needs three outcomes - `fail`, `warn`, `pass` - each with a `message` a customer's platform engineer can act on and a `uri` to the exact runbook section. Run it as `kubectl preflight ./preflight.yaml --interactive=false --format=json` in their pipeline: a `fail` exits non-zero, and non-zero is what stops the upgrade.

resource.label: Troubleshoot.sh - Analyzing data (analyzer types and pass/warn/fail outcomes)

subtopics.name: Helm pre-upgrade hooks: hard-failing before a single manifest is applied
subtopics.learn: Annotate a Job with `helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade`, order it against siblings with `helm.sh/hook-weight: "-5"` (ascending), and control its lifecycle with `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded`. Understand the exact semantics you are buying: Helm always waits for a hook resource to reach its ready state, and if the pre-upgrade Job fails, the release is marked failed and the upgrade stops before any of your templates are applied - which is the entire point, because it means an unsupported version jump costs the customer nothing. Inside the Job, read the currently installed version out of the release (or a version ConfigMap you maintain), evaluate it against the upgrade-path matrix, and exit non-zero with a message naming the required stopover. Two traps: `hook-failed` in the delete policy destroys the pod and its logs, which is the difference between a five-minute diagnosis and an hour, and hooks are never rolled back, so a hook must be idempotent and must not mutate anything the rollback path depends on.

resource.label: Helm docs - Chart Hooks (hook types, weights, delete policies, failure behaviour)

subtopics.name: helm upgrade flags that decide the blast radius
subtopics.learn: Know exactly what each flag does before you type it on a customer's cluster: `--atomic` implies `--wait` and rolls the release back automatically if it does not become ready inside `--timeout` (default 5m0s); `--wait-for-jobs` additionally waits on Jobs, which matters when a post-upgrade migration is a Job; `--cleanup-on-fail` deletes resources created during a failed upgrade so the next attempt is not blocked; `--dry-run=server` renders and validates against the live API server (catching removed API versions and admission rejections) rather than just templating locally. Be very careful with `--force`, which deletes and recreates resources instead of patching - on a StatefulSet or a Service with a fixed IP that is an outage, not a fix. Understand Helm 3's three-way merge (old manifest, live state, new manifest), because it is why a customer's manual `kubectl edit` gets reverted on upgrade, and know that `--history-max` (default 10) silently prunes the revision you might have wanted to roll back to.

resource.label: Helm docs - helm upgrade (flag reference: --atomic, --wait, --timeout, --dry-run, --force)

subtopics.name: Rollback semantics: what `helm rollback` restores and what it can never restore
subtopics.learn: `helm rollback <release> [REVISION]` re-applies the manifest stored for that revision (Helm keeps each revision as a gzipped Secret named `sh.helm.release.v1.<release>.v<n>`), fires `pre-rollback`/`post-rollback` hooks, and accepts `--wait`, `--timeout` and `--cleanup-on-fail`. Enumerate what it does not do, because this is where FDEs lose data: it does not reverse a database migration, does not restore a dropped column or a rewritten row, does not recreate a PVC that a `--force` upgrade deleted, does not roll back CRDs installed from the chart's `crds/` directory, and does not un-run a Job that already completed. Establish the rule that makes rollback real: the schema at revision N must be readable and writable by the application at revision N-1, and any change that violates that (the contract phase, a destructive backfill) is a one-way door that is announced in the release notes and gated behind a verified backup. Practise reading `helm history` and identifying which revision is actually safe to return to.

resource.label: Helm docs - helm rollback

subtopics.name: Expand-contract migrations: the five phases that survive a rollback
subtopics.learn: The rule underneath every safe fleet release: during a rolling upgrade, and during any rollback, two application versions run against one schema, so the schema must be compatible with both. The phases are (1) expand - add the new nullable column, new table or new index concurrently, changing nothing existing; (2) dual-write - the new code writes both old and new representations, or a trigger keeps them in sync; (3) backfill in bounded batches with a throttle and a resumable checkpoint, never one giant `UPDATE`; (4) migrate reads and verify with a comparison query that both representations agree; (5) contract - only in a later release, after every install in the support window is past the expand release, drop the old column. Study pgroll for a working implementation of the idea: it exposes one database view per schema version so old and new application versions each see the schema they expect, uses triggers to keep columns in sync during the migration, and gives you `start` / `complete` / `rollback` as explicit steps rather than a single irreversible script.

resource.label: pgroll - zero-downtime, reversible Postgres schema migrations (expand/contract with versioned views)

subtopics.name: DDL lock behaviour: which ALTER quietly stops the customer's application
subtopics.learn: Know the lock levels before you write the migration. `ALTER TABLE` generally takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which conflicts with everything including plain SELECTs, and - the part that surprises people - a blocked ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request queues *ahead* of subsequent readers, so one long-running transaction turns a millisecond DDL into a full application stall. Adding a column with a non-volatile default is metadata-only on modern Postgres, but `SET NOT NULL` scans the whole table; get the same guarantee cheaply with `ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID` followed later by `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, which takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE. Build indexes with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (cannot run inside a transaction block, and leaves an INVALID index that must be dropped and rebuilt if it fails). Always set `lock_timeout` (a couple of seconds) plus a retry loop in the migration runner, so a migration that cannot get its lock fails fast instead of taking the customer's production down while it waits.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - ALTER TABLE (lock levels, rewrite vs metadata-only, NOT VALID constraints)

subtopics.name: Migration mechanics for installs you cannot reach: versioned revisions and offline SQL
subtopics.learn: Migrations must be linear, versioned, forward-only by default and recorded in the database itself (Alembic's `alembic_version` table is the canonical shape). Learn `alembic upgrade head --sql` and `alembic upgrade <from>:<to> --sql` - offline mode emits the SQL script without connecting, which is exactly what an air-gapped customer's DBA demands before they will let anything run, and it is also how you hand a change-approval board a reviewable artifact. Know its constraints: offline mode cannot branch on runtime inspection of the database, so migrations that depend on `inspect()` or on data must be written as explicit `op.execute` SQL or moved into the application. Learn `alembic stamp` for adopting an install whose schema was created by hand, `alembic history --verbose` to prove which revision an install is at, and branch labels plus merge revisions for the case you will actually hit: a hotfix migration on `release-1.4` that must later merge cleanly into main without producing two heads.

resource.label: Alembic - Generating SQL Scripts (offline mode)

subtopics.name: CRD and API-object versioning in the shipped chart
subtopics.learn: If your product ships CRDs, they are a second, slower-moving API with its own skew rules. A CRD's `spec.versions[]` entries each have `served` and `storage`, exactly one may be `storage: true`, and `status.storedVersions` records every version objects were ever written as; you cannot remove a version from the CRD until every stored object has been rewritten (read and write each object, then prune `storedVersions`). Multi-version CRDs need `spec.conversion.strategy: Webhook` unless the versions are structurally identical (`None` just relabels the apiVersion). The Helm-specific trap: files in a chart's `crds/` directory are installed once and are never upgraded or deleted by `helm upgrade`, so a fleet running your chart will silently keep an old CRD schema while the new controller expects new fields - handle it with an explicit pre-upgrade Job that applies CRDs and verifies stored versions, and assert the CRD version in the preflight.

resource.label: Kubernetes - CustomResourceDefinition versioning (served/storage versions, conversion, storedVersions)

subtopics.name: Feature flags: separating deploy from release across a fleet
subtopics.learn: The flag is what lets one artifact serve a fleet: you deploy the same version everywhere and turn behaviour on per install, per tenant or per cohort, which converts a risky release into a reversible config change that does not require a customer's change window. Distinguish the toggle categories - release toggles (short-lived, removed after rollout), ops toggles (kill switches for an expensive code path, long-lived and owned by on-call), permission toggles (per-customer entitlements, effectively permanent) - because they have different lifetimes and different removal rules. Enforce three practices: every flag defaults to the old behaviour so an install that never heard of it is unaffected, every release toggle ships with a removal ticket and a deadline, and flag state is visible in the support bundle, because 'it works on install A and not install B' is almost always a flag difference nobody recorded.

resource.label: Martin Fowler - Feature Toggles (types, lifetimes, and toggle debt)

subtopics.name: Cohort rollout: rings, ApplicationSets and per-install version pinning
subtopics.learn: Define rings before you need them: ring 0 is your own reference install, ring 1 is two or three design-partner customers who accepted early access in writing, ring 2 is the general fleet, ring 3 is the regulated or air-gapped installs that upgrade on their own change calendar. With Argo CD, an ApplicationSet generates one Application per install from a git file generator (one values file per customer, carrying its pinned `targetRevision` and its ring label), and `spec.strategy.type: RollingSync` with `steps` matched on those labels plus `maxUpdate` advances the fleet ring by ring rather than all at once. Set a soak time per ring with an explicit promotion criterion (no new error-budget burn, no new support tickets tagged to the release, migration completed on every install in the ring) and require a human to promote. The key property: pinning lives in git per install, so 'which version is customer X on' is answered by a file, not by asking someone.

resource.label: Argo CD - ApplicationSet (generators and progressive rolling sync strategy)

subtopics.name: In-cluster canary and automated abort, inside a single install
subtopics.learn: Cohorts stage the fleet; a canary stages one install. With Argo Rollouts you replace the Deployment strategy with `canary.steps` of `setWeight` and `pause`, attach an `analysis` block referencing an AnalysisTemplate that queries the customer's Prometheus for your SLI (error ratio, p95 latency), and set `failureLimit` so a failing measurement automatically aborts and shifts traffic back to the stable ReplicaSet without a human. Understand the honest limits in a customer environment: analysis needs a metrics source you may not own, canaries only protect stateless request paths (they do nothing for a migration that already ran), and a manual `pause` step with a human promote is often the right answer on an install where you cannot get a reliable SLI. Decide per install whether the abort is automated or a documented one-command manual rollback, and put that in the runbook.

resource.label: Argo Rollouts - Canary strategy (steps, analysis, automatic abort)

subtopics.name: Backporting a hotfix to the oldest supported line
subtopics.learn: Maintain a long-lived `release-X.Y` branch per supported minor and enforce the invariant that fixes land on main first, then travel backwards - a fix that exists only on an old branch is a fix that gets reverted by the customer's next upgrade. Use `git cherry-pick -x` so the commit message records the source SHA, expect and resolve the conflicts that come from refactors on main, and audit drift with `git log --left-right --cherry-pick --no-merges main...release-1.4`, which lists commits that are genuinely only on one side. Set an explicit backport bar (security, data corruption, and regressions introduced by us - nothing else) and require every backport to ship as its own patch release with its own changelog entry, its own preflight run and the full migration test against that line's oldest supported schema. The customer-facing habit: never hand-patch an install without opening the backport PR in the same hour, and record the patched version in the install's inventory.

resource.label: git-cherry-pick documentation (including -x for recording the source commit)

subtopics.name: Fleet inventory: knowing what is actually installed before you decide anything
subtopics.learn: Every policy in this topic is unenforceable without an inventory, and the inventory has to survive customers who will not phone home. Emit standard resource attributes on every telemetry signal - `service.name`, `service.version`, `service.instance.id`, `deployment.environment.name` - and expose a `build_info`-style gauge whose value is 1 and whose labels carry app version, chart version, git commit and schema revision, so a single Prometheus query answers 'who is on what'. For air-gapped installs, the same values go into the support bundle the customer sends you, and a version ConfigMap in the release namespace makes the answer available to anyone with `kubectl`. Turn the inventory into a weekly artifact: version per install, days since last upgrade, distance from current, EOL date for that line, and whether the install has any deprecated-API counters above zero - that table is what tells you when a deprecation is safe to execute and which customer needs the upgrade conversation this quarter.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry - Resource semantic conventions (service.version, service.instance.id, deployment.environment.name)

subtopics.name: Release notes and upgrade notes: the artifact the customer's change board reads
subtopics.learn: Write the changelog in the Keep a Changelog shape - an `Unreleased` section, one dated entry per version in ISO format, and the fixed categories Added / Changed / Deprecated / Removed / Fixed / Security - so nobody has to read commit logs. Then add the section that only fleet products need, `Upgrade notes`, containing: minimum source version and any required stopover, new minimum platform versions (Kubernetes, Postgres), new or renamed values keys with their defaults, whether a schema migration runs and roughly how long it takes on a large install, whether this release is rollback-safe and to which revision, any manual step, and the deprecation clock started or ended. Keep a short 'who is affected' line for each breaking item, because the customer's change board approves on risk, not on features. Mirror this exact structure in the release-policy repo so the notes, the upgrade-path matrix and the preflight cannot drift apart.

resource.label: Keep a Changelog 1.1.0

outcomes: You can take any install's current version and, from your own written policy, state in under a minute whether it is in the support window, what the supported upgrade path to current is (including required stopovers), and what the customer has to do if it is out of window.

You can write a RELEASES.md that a customer's change board accepts: SemVer definition of breaking for your product, dated EOL table, N-2 skew rules with the required component upgrade order, backport bar by severity, and a deprecation notice period.

You can write and run a preflight spec that hard-fails an unsupported version jump, a too-old Kubernetes or Postgres, and an under-resourced node pool, exits non-zero in the customer's pipeline, and prints a message plus runbook URI an engineer who has never met you can act on.

You can implement a Helm `pre-upgrade` hook Job that reads the installed version, evaluates it against a machine-readable upgrade-path matrix, and blocks the release before any manifest is applied - and you can show the failed-hook logs afterwards because you did not set `hook-failed` in the delete policy.

You can convert a rename-a-column change into a five-phase expand-contract migration, run it against a live table with `lock_timeout` set, and demonstrate the previous application version still reading and writing correctly at every phase.

You can roll a real upgrade back with `helm rollback` after a failed release and prove data integrity with a row-level comparison, and you can name in advance the exact point in the migration sequence after which rollback is no longer possible.
You can run a cohort rollout across installs pinned at different versions using per-install git pinning and ring-based promotion, and state the soak time and promotion criteria for each ring.

You can produce a fleet inventory table (version, chart, schema revision, days since upgrade, EOL date, deprecated-API usage) from telemetry or support bundles, and use it to decide whether a deprecated field can be removed this release.
failureModes: A customer three minors behind runs the upgrade straight to current; the intermediate release's backfill never executed because the jump skipped it, the new column stays NULL for their historic rows, and it surfaces six weeks later as blank fields in their month-end report rather than as an error.

The pre-upgrade hook Job carries `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: hook-failed`, so when the gate correctly blocks a bad upgrade the pod and its logs are deleted; the on-site engineer re-runs the upgrade three times looking for the reason and eventually disables the hook.

An upgrade is rolled back with `helm rollback` after a failed release, but the migration had already dropped the old column in its contract phase, so the previous application version crash-loops on `SELECT` and the only recovery is a point-in-time restore that loses two hours of the customer's writes.

Someone adds `--force` to `helm upgrade` to get past a stuck immutable field; Helm deletes and recreates the StatefulSet's resources, the PVCs are reprovisioned empty, and a database that was never in the backup rotation because 'it is just a cache' turns out to hold the customer's queue state.

`ALTER TABLE ... SET NOT NULL` runs during the customer's business hours behind a long-running analytics transaction; the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request queues and every subsequent read blocks behind it, so a metadata change reads to the customer as a twenty-minute total outage caused by your release.

The chart's CRDs live in `crds/` and Helm never upgrades them, so after three releases the new controller is silently ignoring fields the customer configured; nobody notices until a support case shows a policy that is present in the YAML and absent in behaviour.

An engineer hand-patches an urgent fix directly onto the customer's install during an incident and never opens the backport PR; the next scheduled upgrade cleanly reverts the fix and reproduces the original incident, this time with no goodwill left.

Argo CD auto-sync is enabled uniformly across the fleet with no rings, so a chart change with a bad default reaches all forty installs within a sync interval and the rollback has to be executed forty times, in forty change windows, by hand.
interviewQuestions: We have 40 customer-managed installs. Twelve are current, twenty are one minor behind, six are three minors behind and two are air-gapped and have not upgraded in a year. Design the support and skew policy you would publish, and tell me what you would do about the two air-gapped installs specifically.

Walk me through renaming a column that the application reads on every request, in a product shipped to customers who upgrade at different times and who may roll back. Give me the phases, which release each phase ships in, and the exact point after which rollback destroys data.

A customer runs your pre-upgrade preflight and it fails on a rule you added last month. They tell you it is a false positive and ask you to give them a flag to skip it. What do you do, and how do you decide whether they are right?

Design the gate that stops an unsupported version jump. Where does it run, what does it read to know the current version, what does it do when the customer's cluster has no network egress, and how do you make it impossible to bypass accidentally while still bypassable deliberately with an audit trail?

Debug: an upgrade reports success, all pods are Ready, and two hours later the customer reports that a feature configured in their values file has stopped taking effect. Where do you look, in what order, and what are the three most likely causes given what you know about Helm and CRDs?

You need to remove a deprecated API field. Tell me how you decide it is safe, what evidence you need from the fleet, how long the notice period is and why, and what you do about the one customer who is still calling it two weeks before removal.

A P1 security fix must reach every supported install this week, including two that are three minors behind and one that is air-gapped. Describe your release plan end to end: which branches get the fix, what you build, what you test, in what order the cohorts go, and what you tell each customer.
78.proofOfWork: Build a public `fleet-skew-harness` repo that proves the policy rather than asserting it: a CI matrix that, for every supported pair in your version matrix, boots the old application version against the new schema and the new application version against the old schema and runs the same contract test suite against both, so an incompatible migration fails a pull request instead of a customer. Around it, run a KinD-based simulation of three installs pinned at different versions with an Argo CD ApplicationSet doing ring-based rolling sync, and record a scripted drill with timings and terminal output: install A takes a direct upgrade, install B is blocked by the pre-upgrade hook and shown the required stopover, install C completes the expand phase, is deliberately failed mid-rollout and rolled back, after which a row-level checksum comparison proves the data is intact. Include the machine-readable `versions.yaml` that generates the upgrade-path matrix, the preflight spec, the RELEASES.md rendered from it, and a short `postmortem.md` for the one thing that broke during the drill that you had not predicted - that last file is the part an interviewer will read, because it is evidence you ran the drill rather than described it.

79.topic: Async engagement communication: weekly status update, escalation and slip notes, decision memo
79.why: An FDE is usually the only vendor-side person the customer's sponsor hears from, and that sponsor decides renewal, expansion or cancellation from a few hundred words a week read on a phone between meetings - not from your code, your dashboards or the two people on their side who actually know what you built. The engagements that die rarely die of engineering; they die because a slip was discovered by the customer rather than announced by you, because an ask sat unanswered in a Slack thread for three weeks with no owner, or because a decision taken verbally in month one was relitigated in month three with no written record. Async writing is also the only leverage you have across time zones and customer sites: a weekly update that is genuinely skimmable, an escalation that lands without humiliating your counterpart, and a decision memo that closes a question in one round are what let one FDE hold three engagements without a standing call on each.
prerequisites: A real multi-week engagement to report on with named milestones and dates - Dokeo, DefenderMate or Kaupex from the earlier tracks is enough, provided it has a plan someone could miss
A signed one-page problem statement and success metric from Topic 72 (Discovery), because a status update is progress against a stated outcome, not a list of activity
The engagement document pack from Topic 73 (site survey, PRD-lite, SOW, ADR log, runbooks) - the weekly update references those artifacts rather than restating them
Topic 24 (Incident response and postmortems): severity ladder, incident commander and communications-lead roles, and the blameless postmortem the exec incident note links to
Topic 21 (SRE fundamentals): SLIs, SLOs and error budgets, so the numbers you quote in an update mean something and match what the customer's dashboards say
Topic 74 (Demos and executive communication) as the synchronous counterpart - this topic is what you send when there is no meeting

subtopics.name: The channel charter and a response-time policy you will actually meet
subtopics.learn: Write the charter in week one and paste it into the kickoff note: which channel carries which traffic (shared Slack Connect channel for anything under a day, email for anything an exec must forward, the engagement doc repo for anything that must survive the engagement, phone plus PagerDuty for Sev1 only), who is named on each, and the response times you commit to - Slack within four business hours, email within one business day, Sev1 acknowledgement within fifteen minutes, weekly update every Friday 16:00 customer-local. State both sides' working hours and time zones, name a deputy for every channel you own, and say explicitly what happens out of hours, because an unanswered thread is the most common origin of 'the vendor went dark'. The rule that keeps the charter honest: any decision, number or commitment that appeared on a call or in chat is restated in the weekly update or a memo within 24 hours - chat is not a record, and neither counsel nor a CFO reads scrollback.

resource.label: GitLab Handbook - Communication (channels, response expectations, async norms)

subtopics.name: Reader model: five readers, five different first questions
subtopics.learn: Name your readers before you name your sections. The exec sponsor asks 'is this on track and what do you need from me' and can act only on a date, a risk or a decision; the customer's delivery or platform lead asks 'what lands on my team this week'; the operator asks 'what changes in my workflow'; security and procurement ask 'what did you change about data, access or scope'; your own account lead asks 'what should I be worried about before the customer tells me'. Write the primary update for the sponsor plus the delivery lead, and give the platform team its own 'asks this week' block they can act on without reading the rest. Anything that only interests you - refactors, tooling, effort spent - goes in an appendix or nowhere.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing One - Know your audience

subtopics.name: BLUF and the inverted pyramid: making the first 30 seconds sufficient
subtopics.learn: Put the verdict in the first 25 words and the ask in the first 60, then detail in decreasing importance, then an appendix nobody has to read - the exec sees the subject line and one phone screen, and everything after that is optional. Use a subject-line format that is itself the summary and is diffable week over week: '[Dokeo] Week 4 - AMBER, go-live 14 Nov at risk, need IAM role approved by Tue'. Kill the openings that destroy the top of the message: pleasantries, a chronology of your week, background the reader already has, and any sentence that begins 'As discussed'. Test it by deleting everything except the subject and the first three lines and asking whether the reader could still act correctly.

resource.label: Nielsen Norman Group - Inverted Pyramid: Writing for Comprehension

subtopics.name: Compression: fewer words, one ask per paragraph, easy to answer
subtopics.learn: Budget 200 words above the fold and enforce it. Delete effort narration ('spent significant time investigating'), adjectives, and every sentence whose deletion changes nothing; convert three or more parallel items into a table; replace 'we are continuing to work on the connector' with either a date or the blocker plus its owner. Make responding cheap: one question per message where possible, phrased as a binary or a numbered menu, with a deadline and a stated default, so the reader can reply with one word from a phone. Read the draft once purely as a cutting pass - a 320-word update that took you 25 minutes to compress beats a 900-word one that took ten.

resource.label: plainlanguage.gov Federal Plain Language Guidelines - Be concise

subtopics.name: Scannable structure and rendering: headings, tables, phones, forwarding
subtopics.learn: Headings state conclusions, not categories - 'Go-live slips to 14 Nov' beats 'Schedule'; bold carries only the decision and the date; never nest more than two levels. Never let a screenshot be the only carrier of a fact: images strip on forward, break in some clients and are unreadable on a phone, so the table goes in the body and the screenshot is supporting. Test the send every time - view it on a phone, forward it to yourself, confirm no link needs your VPN or a Google account the customer's SSO cannot open, and keep attachments small by linking the doc repo instead. Write for non-native readers by default: short sentences, no idioms ('circle back', 'long pole', 'punt'), acronyms expanded on first use, dates as '14 Nov 2026' rather than 11/14.

resource.label: Microsoft Writing Style Guide - Scannable content

subtopics.name: The kickoff note: the message that sets every expectation you will be held to
subtopics.learn: Send it within 48 hours of kickoff, to everyone who will ever receive a weekly update, containing: the problem and success metric restated in the customer's words from discovery, scope in and out with the SOW clause referenced, named roles (who decides, who contributes, who is informed), the milestone dates with your confidence in each, the channel charter and response times, the top three risks, and the three things you need from them in week one with owner and date. Close with an explicit correction window - 'if any of this is wrong, reply by Friday' - which converts silence into a shared record you can point at in week six. This note is also the template contract: every weekly update afterwards uses the same section names in the same order.

resource.label: Atlassian Team Playbook - Project Poster play

subtopics.name: The weekly update: seven fixed slots, same day, same shape
subtopics.learn: Lock the template and never reorder it: (1) headline - status colour, target date, one-sentence verdict; (2) what changed since last week, as deltas not activity; (3) next week, three bullets maximum; (4) decisions or actions needed from you, each with owner, deadline and default; (5) top three risks and issues with movement markers (new / worse / better / closed); (6) the success metric with last week's number beside this week's; (7) appendix and links. The stability is the product - a sponsor who can diff week 4 against week 3 in 30 seconds will read every one. Never skip a week: an absent update reads as bad news being concealed, so send the same template with 'no change' plus the reason, and number the updates so weeks 1 to 12 can be read as one chain in one thread or one doc.

resource.label: PagerDuty Stakeholder Communications - Templates

subtopics.name: Status colour and honest progress: thresholds, confidence, no percent-complete
subtopics.learn: Define the colour rules in writing in week one and apply them mechanically: GREEN means every committed date is unchanged and no blocker is unowned; AMBER means a date is at risk, or an ask has been open past its deadline, or a dependency has no owner; RED means a committed date will move or the outcome is unachievable as scoped. Colour describes the commitment, not your mood or effort, and a green that flips straight to red is the fastest way to lose a sponsor - amber exists precisely so the customer can spend a favour before it is too late. Report progress as scopes or milestones finished versus remaining and mark whether the remaining work is still uphill (unknowns to solve) or downhill (known execution); '70% complete' hides the fact that the missing 30% is the part nobody has figured out.

resource.label: Shape Up (Basecamp) - Show Progress (hill charts, uphill/downhill work)

subtopics.name: Asks: one human, one verb, one deadline, one default
subtopics.learn: Write every ask as 'Priya: approve the IAM role in ticket INF-4412 by Wed 12:00 CET; if not approved we deploy to staging with the read-only role and re-test Friday, moving the integration milestone by two days'. A team is not an owner, 'ASAP' is not a deadline, and an ask without a stated consequence is a request the reader can safely ignore. Keep a running asks table with the date first raised and days open, repeat it every week until closed, and treat an ask open past its second week as an escalation trigger rather than another bullet. When two people could plausibly own a decision, settle it with DACI (driver, approver, contributors, informed) in the kickoff note so 'who decides' is never the thing being negotiated inside the thread.

resource.label: Atlassian Team Playbook - DACI decision-making framework

subtopics.name: RAID in async: risk, issue, assumption, dependency - scored and moving
subtopics.learn: Keep the four categories distinct because they need different actions: a risk may happen and needs probability x impact plus a mitigation with an owner; an issue is already happening and needs a decision now; an assumption is something you will proceed on unless contradicted, so writing it down transfers the burden of correction; a dependency is someone else's deliverable with a date and a name. Score risks on a 1-5 probability by 1-5 impact grid so the register can be ordered and so 'high risk' means something, and surface only the top three in the message with the full register linked. Show movement every week - new, worse, better, closed - because the reader tracks the delta, not the list. The single most valuable line an FDE ever writes is a risk that later materialises and was already logged with a mitigation and an owner: that is what turns a slip into a managed event.

resource.label: HM Treasury Orange Book - Management of Risk: Principles and Concepts

subtopics.name: The slip note: send it the day you know, with a defensible new date
subtopics.learn: The trigger to write is evidence, not the missed milestone: an ask blows its deadline, a spike returns a bad number, a dependency owner goes quiet, measured throughput falls short of the plan for two weeks running. Structure: what changed, the new date and your confidence in it, why in one causal non-defensive paragraph, what it costs the customer, what you already did to absorb it, the options, and what you need. Anchor the date with a method rather than a feeling - remaining scopes, the last two weeks' actual completion rate, and an explicit uplift for optimism bias rather than a best case - because the second slip on the same milestone costs far more trust than the size of the first. Say the uncomfortable sentence plainly and early in the note; burying it in paragraph five is what readers remember.

resource.label: HM Treasury Green Book supplementary guidance - Optimism bias

subtopics.name: The replan menu: two or three costed options, one recommendation
subtopics.learn: Never send a new date alone; send the choice that produced it. Offer cut scope (name exactly which deliverables move to phase two and what the customer loses in the interim), move the date (with the downstream cost: their audit window, their launch, a payment milestone), lower the bar temporarily (a manual step for month one, backfilled later), or add people (state honestly what onboarding costs you in weeks before it helps). Give each option a cost, a risk and a reversibility, recommend one, and say why in a sentence. The framing to steal: the appetite is fixed and scope is the variable, so the conversation is about what to stop doing, not how to fit everything into a date that has already failed once.

resource.label: Shape Up (Basecamp) - Decide When to Stop (fixed appetite, variable scope)

subtopics.name: Escalation in writing without detonating the relationship
subtopics.learn: Agree the ladder at kickoff and then follow it visibly: day 3 nudge in channel, day 5 direct email to the owner copying your counterpart, day 8 email to the sponsor with the dated ask trail attached, Sev1 phone call plus a written summary within the hour. Always telegraph before you climb - 'if I do not have this by Thursday I will raise it with Dana on Friday' - and then do exactly what you said; a surprise escalation humiliates the person who was quietly unblocking it and buys you an information blackout for the rest of the engagement. Escalate the problem, not the person: fact, dated history, business consequence, the specific decision you need and by when, no adjectives, no 'as I have repeatedly said', and offer a way for the owner to close it before it lands on their boss's desk.

resource.label: Atlassian - On-call escalation policies

subtopics.name: Stakeholder cadence during an incident, while you are still fixing
subtopics.learn: Split the channels: the incident channel is for the people fixing, the stakeholder update is for the people deciding, and one named liaison (you or a deputy) carries traffic between them so responders never write to executives. Commit to a fixed interval up front and hold it even when nothing has changed - 'Sev1, update every 30 minutes; 14:00: no change, next update 14:30' - because silence between updates is read as loss of control. Each update states impact in the customer's terms, scope (which tenants, which function, since when), what you are doing now, and the time of the next update; it never speculates about root cause, never blames their network or their change, and never gives an ETA you cannot defend. Distinguish confirmed from suspected in every sentence.

resource.label: PagerDuty Stakeholder Communications - Communicating during investigation

subtopics.name: The exec incident note: one page the sponsor can forward unedited
subtopics.learn: Within 24 hours of resolution send a note written for people who were not on the bridge: one sentence of what happened in business language ('alert triage was unavailable for 47 minutes for EU-cluster tenants; no data was lost, 312 alerts queued and were fully processed by 15:10'), quantified impact, a five-line timeline, what you have already changed, what you will change with owners and dates, any action the customer must take, and a link to the blameless postmortem from Topic 24. Keep facts and open investigation visibly separate, and never characterise the event in legal or regulatory terms ('breach', 'violation') without their compliance function - Topic 70 covers why that sentence is not yours to write. Assume this note is the artifact their CTO forwards to a board, so it must survive being read with no context and no follow-up question.

resource.label: Atlassian - Incident communication templates

subtopics.name: The decision memo: options table, reversibility, deadline, default
subtopics.learn: One page: the decision stated as a question, the decider and the deadline, five lines of context, two to four options in a table with cost, time, risk and reversibility, your recommendation and its reason, what you need from the reader, and what happens automatically if nobody answers by the deadline. Classify reversibility explicitly - two-way doors (a retry policy, a queue depth, a dashboard layout) get decided fast and delegated, one-way doors (tenancy model, data residency, PII flows, a vendor you cannot exit) get the memo and the meeting. File the outcome as an ADR in the doc repo (Topic 73) and restate it in the next weekly update, because a decision that lives only in a call gets relitigated in month three by a platform lead who was not there. When you lose the decision, record your objection once, in writing, then commit and stop re-fighting it in every subsequent thread.

resource.label: Amazon 2016 Letter to Shareholders - one-way vs two-way doors, disagree and commit

subtopics.name: Commitment language and calibrated confidence
subtopics.learn: Retire the words that carry no information: 'shortly', 'should be fine', 'mostly done', 'we are aligned', 'as soon as possible', 'minor issue'. Bind your probability words to numbers once, in the charter, and use them consistently thereafter - the estimative-probability convention (likely = roughly 70-85%, roughly even chance = 45-55%, unlikely = 15-30%) exists precisely because readers otherwise substitute their own scale, and a sponsor's 'likely' may be your 'almost certain'. Write '80% confident on 14 Nov; the 20% is their IAM approval' rather than 'we should be OK'. Separate three registers explicitly: commitments (will - you would sign it into the SOW), plans (intend to, subject to a named dependency) and hopes (do not send these), and only ever commit to something you control or that has a named owner with a date.

resource.label: CIA Studies in Intelligence - Sherman Kent, Words of Estimative Probability

subtopics.name: Everything you write is forwarded, screenshotted and discoverable
subtopics.learn: Write every message as if it will be pasted into a board deck, shown to a competitor, and produced in litigation as electronically stored information - which under discovery rules it can be. That means no blame of named individuals, no speculation about cause while an incident is open, no legal or regulatory characterisations, no jokes about their team, and no promises you have not costed. Keep customer PII, tokens, credentials, hostnames and raw log excerpts out of email and chat entirely: link to the ticket or document inside their tenant instead, and know the retention and membership of the shared channel you are typing into. The corollary works in your favour: a dated written trail of asks, risks and decisions is exactly what protects both you and your counterpart when the schedule is reviewed six months later.

resource.label: Cornell LII - Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Rule 34 (discovery of electronically stored information)

subtopics.name: Sanitise, templatise and test the pack on real readers
subtopics.learn: Turn the four weeks into a reusable kit: Markdown templates with placeholders, a redaction pass that replaces customer names, hostnames, tenant ids and dollar figures with stable pseudonyms, and a pre-send checklist (one ask per paragraph, every ask has owner plus date plus default, colour matches the declared thresholds, under 200 words above the fold, zero hedge words, every number traceable to a dashboard or query). Then test comprehension rather than trusting your own taste: hand the update to three people who know nothing about the project, give them 30 seconds, and ask what the status is, what is needed from them, and by when. Any miss means you rewrite the first screen, not the appendix, and you re-run the test.

resource.label: plainlanguage.gov Federal Plain Language Guidelines - Test your assumptions

outcomes: You can write a weekly engagement update in under 20 minutes that three readers who have never seen the project can each answer 'what is the status, what is needed from me, by when' from in 30 seconds, verified by a timed blind-read test with the results recorded.
You can state your GREEN/AMBER/RED threshold rules in one sentence each, apply them to four consecutive weeks of a real project, and defend an amber that your own manager wanted reported as green.

You can send a slip note the day the evidence appears rather than the day the milestone is missed, with a new date justified by remaining scopes plus measured completion rate plus an explicit optimism-bias uplift, and two or three costed replan options with a recommendation.

You can escalate a three-week-old unanswered ask through an agreed ladder in writing - telegraphed first, dated ask trail attached, business consequence stated, no adjectives - and explain why your counterpart is not damaged by it.

You can produce a one-page decision memo with the question, decider, deadline, an options table including reversibility, a recommendation and a stated default if nobody answers, and file the outcome as an ADR that the next weekly update references.

You can run stakeholder communications during a Sev1 on a committed 30-minute cadence that separates confirmed from suspected, and send an exec incident note within 24 hours that the sponsor forwards without editing.
You can audit any piece of your own writing for buried leads, ownerless asks, dateless commitments, hedge words and untraceable numbers, and state the specific rewrite for each finding.
You can publish a channel charter with response-time commitments and show four weeks of evidence that you met them, including what you did on the week there was nothing to report.
failureModes: Five weekly updates say green because the team is working hard, then the go-live date moves in week six; the sponsor hears it first from their own platform lead, and the renewal conversation becomes about whether you can be trusted rather than about a two-week slip.

The ask is buried in paragraph four as 'we'll need someone to approve the IAM role'; nobody owns it, three weeks pass, and when the slip is challenged the trail cannot be reconstructed because it lived in a Slack channel with 90-day retention.

The update goes out Friday 18:00 customer-local before a public holiday, as a Google Doc link their SSO cannot open and an inline screenshot that strips on forward; the 'you never told us' conversation then happens in the steering committee.

An escalation email goes to the sponsor's boss with no warning, over a ticket the counterpart was already unblocking; that person is embarrassed in front of their VP and stops volunteering information for the remaining ten weeks.

During a Sev1 the FDE speculates in the exec-visible channel that 'it looks like their firewall change caused this'; root cause turns out to be the vendor's own migration, and the retraction damages the account more than the 47-minute outage did.

The weekly update quotes a p95 latency from a Grafana panel whose filter excludes one tenant, so the number disagrees with the customer's own dashboard by 40%; after that single mismatch every figure in every future update is treated as marketing.

A decision taken verbally on a call - 'we'll use your existing Postgres rather than RDS' - is never written up or filed as an ADR; a new platform lead reverses it in month three, three weeks of integration work is rebuilt, and there is nothing to point at.

An incident note is sent with a screenshot containing a tenant id and an alert payload holding customer PII, and the sponsor forwards it to a partner organisation; a communications artifact becomes a reportable data incident of its own.
interviewQuestions: Show me the weekly update you would send in week three of an engagement where the customer still has not granted the data access you asked for on day one. Read me the first two lines, and tell me what you deliberately left out.

You learn on Tuesday that a milestone three weeks out will slip by two weeks. Who do you tell, in what order, in what medium, and by when? Draft the first 60 words of the note and tell me how you arrived at the new date.

Design the communications plan for a twelve-week deployment into a regulated customer with an exec sponsor, a platform team that did not ask for you, and a security reviewer who has already vetoed two vendors: channels, cadence, artifacts, response-time commitments, escalation ladder, and what you do in week one.

You have asked the same person for the same firewall change four times over three weeks. Write the escalation. Who is on it, what does it say, what do you do the day before you send it, and how do you keep working with that person afterwards?

Define what your amber means precisely enough that someone else could apply it to your project without asking you. Then tell me about a time you reported amber when your own leadership wanted green, and what happened.
Here is a real status update [handed a bad one]. Tell me everything wrong with it, rank the problems by cost to the engagement, and rewrite the first 40 words.

It is 02:00 during a Sev1 and the customer's CTO joins the bridge asking for a root cause and an ETA. What do you say, what do you refuse to say and why, and what exactly is in the written update you send 30 minutes later?
