79.proofOfWork: A public repo `engagement-comms-kit` that turns the sanitised four-week pack into something another FDE can pick up on day one: Markdown templates for the kickoff note, weekly update, slip-and-replan note, escalation email, exec incident note and decision memo, each with the section order fixed and placeholders for the customer-specific parts; a declared threshold card defining GREEN/AMBER/RED, the escalation ladder with day counts, and the estimative-probability table mapping words to percentage ranges. The gate is a `lint_update.py` run in GitHub Actions over every template and every sanitised example: it fails the build on more than 200 words above the first heading, on any line under 'Decisions needed' that does not match owner plus ISO date plus a stated default, on any hedge word from a maintained list ('shortly', 'ASAP', 'should be fine', 'mostly', 'aligned'), on any number without a linked source, and on any status colour that contradicts the threshold rules given the open-asks table. Include the evidence that it works: a results table from timed blind reads - three readers, 30 seconds each, three questions, scored per week for four weeks, with the week-1 misses and the exact first-screen rewrite that fixed them - plus an anonymised before/after pair of a real update showing 780 words cut to 240 with the ask moved from paragraph four to line two, and a one-page retro naming which of the four weeks' asks were closed on time and what the ask-age curve looked like.

80.topic: Narrative: why FDE, why this company, travel, comp
80.why: An FDE loop is the only engineering loop that screens for staffing risk as hard as it screens for skill, because the hire gets put in front of a paying customer within weeks and every hour is either billable or burning a deployment budget. 'Why FDE', 'how much can you travel' and 'what number are you looking for' are not warm-up questions - they are the hiring manager deciding whether you will still be willing to fly to a customer site in month seven and whether your comp expectation fits the band they already have signed off. The same muscle is the job itself: compressing a complex situation into sixty seconds for a specific audience, and stating a constraint as a number you can actually hold, is what you do in every kickoff, every steering meeting and every scope conversation with a customer.
prerequisites: Executive communication and trade-off defence from 'Demos, executive communication, defending trade-offs' (topic 68) - specifically the discipline of leading with the outcome and holding a hard time box.

The negotiation mechanics from 'Negotiation and offers' (topic 70): BATNA, reservation value, anchoring, and the difference between a range and a number. This topic supplies the number; that topic supplies the conversation.

At least three shipped pieces of customer-facing work you can describe with a metric - the Lumen FDE deployment, one integration or migration you owned, and one production incident you debugged - written up per 'Technical writing and public write-ups' (topic 69).
A resume you have stopped restructuring, since every claim in the narrative has to survive 'Resume defence: every line' (topic 73) two weeks later.

A working shortlist of 8-12 target companies with real job postings saved as text (the precursor to the 40-company list in topic 82), including at least one enterprise-deployment shop, one frontier-lab, and one Series A/B startup - the three answers differ.
Your own financial floor computed before you start: current total comp, monthly burn, months of runway, and the number below which you would say no. Do this in a spreadsheet, not in your head.

subtopics.name: Decode what 'FDE' means at each target company
subtopics.learn: The title is not one job. Read three saved job descriptions side by side and classify each on four axes: how much time is on customer premises versus remote, whether you own production for the customer or hand off to their team, whether you write product code that ships back into core or only deployment-specific code, and whether the role is quota-adjacent (pre-sales POCs) or delivery-only (post-signature). Palantir-lineage FDE means embedded, on-site, owns the customer's outcome; a frontier-lab 'applied AI engineer' usually means prototypes and integration patterns that feed back into product; a startup FDE means you are also support, solutions architect and sometimes AE. Write the classification down per company - your 'why FDE' answer must match the axis they actually staff for, or it reads as a canned answer.

resource.label: Palantir Blog - A Day in the Life of a Palantir Forward Deployed Software Engineer

subtopics.name: The positioning spine: one paragraph you can say in your sleep
subtopics.learn: Write a single 70-90 word paragraph with four slots: what you are now (role plus the domain you actually operate in), the two or three capability proofs that are unusual together (e.g. production Kubernetes plus LLM eval infrastructure plus direct customer delivery), the arc that explains why those combined (not a chronology - a reason), and the one sentence about what you want next. Constraint: no adjectives about yourself ('passionate', 'driven', 'strong communicator') - only nouns and verbs that a listener could verify. Test it by reading it aloud with a stopwatch: 70-90 words lands at 30-38 seconds at interview pace, which is half of a 'tell me about yourself' answer and the entire spine of everything else in this topic.

resource.label: Exponent - Forward Deployed Engineer interview guide

subtopics.name: Build the 60-second 'why FDE' answer
subtopics.learn: Structure: (1) the moment you discovered the thing FDE work does that pure product work does not - a specific incident, named and dated, not a preference; (2) the evidence that you already do this and like it (a customer meeting you ran, a scope you renegotiated, a deployment you did inside someone else's VPC); (3) the explicit acknowledgement of the cost - travel, ambiguity, being the only engineer in the room, other people's legacy systems - because an answer that does not name the cost signals you have not done the job; (4) the forward statement tying it to their axis from subtopic 1. Hard limits: 150-170 spoken words, no more than two proper nouns the interviewer will not recognise, and no sentence longer than 25 words. Write it, cut 20%, then never read it aloud from the page again.

resource.label: MIT CAPD - Using the STAR method to structure a behavioral interview answer (worksheet included)

subtopics.name: Evidence pack: three receipts that make the answer non-hypothetical
subtopics.learn: For each of the three claims in your 'why FDE' answer, attach one receipt you can produce in five seconds if asked: a link, a number, or a named artifact. Example receipts - 'the runbook their on-call still uses' (link), 'cut p95 from 4.1s to 900ms by moving reranking off the request path' (number plus method), 'ran the Thursday steering call for eleven weeks' (cadence plus duration). Rehearse the follow-up form of each: interviewers do not challenge the story, they challenge the number, so know the baseline, the measurement window and the confounder for every metric you cite. Any claim with no receipt gets deleted from the answer - it is a liability in the resume-defence round.

resource.label: Yale Office of Career Strategy - Writing impactful, quantified accomplishment bullets

subtopics.name: The 30-minute company dossier
subtopics.learn: Standardise a one-page dossier you can fill for any target in half an hour: who pays them and for what (segment, ACV shape, self-serve versus enterprise), the delivery motion (do they have an FDE/solutions org, is it pre- or post-sales, who does the customer's integration today), the current strategic bet stated in their own words from the last 90 days, one named competitor and the honest reason a buyer picks them instead, and the constraint you would hit in week one of a deployment there (data residency, air-gapped environments, on-prem, FedRAMP, a customer base of hospitals). For public companies, pull the risk factors and segment revenue from the latest 10-K rather than trusting the marketing site.

resource.label: SEC EDGAR full-text search

subtopics.name: 'Why this company' as a deployment-shaped hypothesis
subtopics.learn: The answer that works is not admiration, it is a hypothesis about their delivery problem plus your fit to it, in three beats: 'here is the specific hard part of shipping your product into a customer's environment as I understand it', 'here is why I believe that (evidence from the dossier, not the homepage)', 'here is the thing I have done that maps to it'. Say one falsifiable thing - a claim they can correct - because being corrected turns a monologue into a conversation and proves you did work. Explicitly ban three phrasings: mission worship with no mechanism, 'I love your product' with no usage evidence, and any sentence that would be equally true of two competitors. Produce one version per target company; the spine is shared, beat one is bespoke.

resource.label: Palantir Apollo docs - Introduction: delivering software into customer-owned, on-prem and air-gapped environments

subtopics.name: Second-sourcing the company from primary material
subtopics.learn: Build the dossier from sources the marketing site does not control: the company's own engineering and research posts from the last two quarters, their public docs and changelog (what shipped, how fast, what is still beta), their open GitHub repos and issue tracker (response latency, who answers, what customers are actually blocked on), their status page history, their pricing page and enterprise tier gates, and their job postings across the whole org (what they are hiring for tells you the roadmap better than the roadmap does). Note one thing you learned that a casual candidate would not know, and place it in beat two of the 'why this company' answer. Never cite a number from a source you cannot name in the room.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Searching issues and pull requests (mining a company's public tracker)

subtopics.name: Travel: convert vibes into a number and a schedule shape
subtopics.learn: Answer with a unit and a shape, not an adjective: '25-40% travel, comfortable with Monday-to-Thursday on-site during a deployment ramp, up to two consecutive weeks abroad, one international trip a quarter' beats 'I'm flexible' every time, because the second answer is heard as either 'unlimited' or 'unknown', and both are staffing risk. Compute the number from real constraints - dependants, visa processing times, a partner's schedule, health, cost of living in the customer's city - and write the arithmetic down so you can defend it. State one thing you will not do (e.g. permanent relocation, or four-week continuous rotations) rather than discovering it in month two, and learn the standard distributed-delivery vocabulary - core hours, timezone overlap, async-by-default, on-site cadence - so you can describe how you cover a customer you are not physically with.

resource.label: GitLab Handbook - All-Remote

subtopics.name: Work authorisation, borders, and the logistics that kill offers
subtopics.learn: Know your own status cold and be able to state it in one sentence without hedging - what you hold, what it permits, what would need sponsoring, and the realistic lead time. Learn the categories that matter for a travelling FDE: business-visitor entry for meetings and training versus authorisation to perform productive work, employer-sponsored work status, the difference between the petition and the visa stamp, and the practical timelines including any lottery or consular appointment queue. Know the second-order items interviewers and recruiters will ask about: passport validity window, prior refusals, whether a customer's site requires citizenship or a clearance you cannot obtain, and whether the role is billable to a government customer. Raise sponsorship early with the recruiter, not after the offer - it is a budget and timeline question, and late disclosure reads as concealment.

resource.label: USCIS - H-1B Specialty Occupations: LCA, I-129 petition, cap and validity periods

subtopics.name: Customer-site reality: access, security and the trips you cannot take
subtopics.learn: Rehearse the operational answers a delivery lead actually needs: can you work in a facility with no personal devices and no internet egress, can you clear a background check, can you badge into a bank or hospital, are you comfortable in a country your government advises against, do you have any travel restriction by nationality. Learn what an air-gapped or SCIF-style engagement does to your workflow - no cloud IDE, no pasting logs into a chat window, code moved by review and transfer, debugging from screenshots - and say plainly whether you have done it or not. Honest 'I have not, here is the closest thing I have done' beats bravado; the failure mode is an FDE who says yes and then cannot be staffed on the only account that needed them.

resource.label: DCSA - Background investigations and the security clearance process for applicants

subtopics.name: Comp: derive the band before anyone asks
subtopics.learn: Produce one spreadsheet with a row per target company and columns for base, bonus target, equity value per year with the assumed price, sign-on, and a total-comp figure with the assumptions written next to it. Pull level-and-location bands from aggregated data, and calibrate the level first - senior FDE at a frontier lab, a public data company and a Series B are three different bands and often three different level ladders. Compute three numbers you will carry into every call: your walk-away (below this you decline), your target (defensible from data, top of band for the level), and your ask (target plus the negotiation margin). Never state a number you cannot source in one sentence.

resource.label: Levels.fyi - Software Engineer compensation data

subtopics.name: Cross-check the band with independent sources
subtopics.learn: Aggregated self-reported data skews high and is thin at senior levels for niche titles, so triangulate with at least two more sources before you commit to a number: statutory salary disclosures filed for work-visa petitions (real base salaries, by employer, job title and year, though base only - no equity), pay-transparency ranges published in the job posting itself where jurisdictions require them, and published company compensation frameworks where a company documents its own formula. Reconcile the spread rather than averaging it: understand why the filed base is lower than the aggregate total (equity and bonus), and never quote a total-comp figure back to a recruiter as if it were base.

resource.label: US DOL Office of Foreign Labor Certification - Performance and public disclosure data (filed LCA wages by employer)

subtopics.name: Equity literacy: what the number is actually made of
subtopics.learn: Be able to hold your own on the mechanics without a calculator: RSUs versus ISOs versus NSOs and who owes tax when, the standard four-year vest with a one-year cliff versus front-loaded or backloaded schedules, single- versus double-trigger acceleration, refresh grants and the cliff-year total-comp dip, strike price versus 409A versus preferred price, the post-termination exercise window and why 90 days is a trap, and dilution and liquidation preference in a private company. Then apply it: recompute each offer's annual equity value under a flat-price assumption and again at zero, and note which offers survive both. Ask for the grant document terms, share count and current preferred price - a total-comp number quoted without them is marketing.

resource.label: The Holloway Guide to Equity Compensation

subtopics.name: The comp script: deflect early, anchor once, hold the number
subtopics.learn: Rehearse three scripts verbatim. Early screen: deflect without stonewalling - 'I want to understand the level and scope first; what band is this role approved at?' - and never volunteer current salary. If pressed to a number, give one figure with a one-line justification plus 'and I'm flexible on the mix between base and equity' - a single number anchors better than a range whose bottom becomes the offer. After an offer: acknowledge, thank, ask for it in writing with the full breakdown, take 24 hours, and come back with one prioritised ask supported by a competing data point, not three vague ones. Practise saying the number out loud until your voice does not rise at the end of it - the recording is where you find out that it does.

resource.label: Haseeb Qureshi - How Not to Bomb Your Offer Negotiation (the deflect, anchor and counter scripts)

subtopics.name: Recording rig and the 60-second discipline
subtopics.learn: Set up a repeatable capture: webcam scene plus a visible countdown timer source, external mic set so peaks sit around -12 to -6 dB with no clipping, camera at eye level, key light in front rather than a window behind you, and a fixed file-naming convention (topic_company_takeN_date). Record every take unedited including the bad ones. Discipline rules while recording: start on the answer, not on 'so, um, basically'; hit the point by second ten; stop talking when the answer is done even if the timer has time left. If a take runs over sixty seconds, do not fix it by talking faster - cut a clause and re-take.

resource.label: OBS Studio - Quick Start Guide

subtopics.name: Transcript-based self-review and the rehearsal loop
subtopics.learn: Do not review by feel. Transcribe each take with a local speech-to-text model and score the transcript on five countable things: filler count per minute (target under three), time to first substantive claim (target under ten seconds), hedges ('kind of', 'I guess', 'sort of' - target zero), longest sentence in words (target under 25), and total word count against the time box. Diff take N against take N-1 and keep only the changes that moved a metric. Run the loop until three consecutive takes land in range, then run two adversarial drills: the cold open (hit record and answer with no warm-up) and the interrupt (have someone cut you off at second twenty with 'sorry - can you make that concrete?' and recover without restarting).

resource.label: openai/whisper - speech recognition model and CLI

outcomes: You can deliver a 'why FDE' answer in 55-65 seconds, on the first take, that contains a dated specific moment, one verifiable metric, and an explicit acknowledgement of the cost of the role.

You can deliver a company-specific 'why this company' answer that states one falsifiable claim about their delivery problem, sourced from a primary document you can name, and that would be false if said about their nearest competitor.
You can state your travel availability as a percentage, a trip shape and a hard limit, and defend the arithmetic behind it when asked 'what if we needed more?'.
You can state your work-authorisation status, what would need sponsoring, and the realistic lead time in one sentence with no hedging.
You can name your target total-comp number, cite the two independent sources it came from, and split it into base, bonus, equity and sign-on without a calculator.
You can explain double-trigger acceleration, the 90-day post-termination exercise window, and why a private-company equity figure is an assumption, in plain language, to a non-technical recruiter.
You have transcript metrics showing three consecutive takes under three fillers per minute, under ten seconds to first substantive claim, and zero hedge phrases.
You can survive the interrupt drill: cut off at second twenty with 'make that concrete', you produce a specific example within five seconds and still finish inside the time box.
failureModes: You say 'I'm totally flexible on travel' in the loop, get staffed on a rotation you cannot sustain, and the account team loses a quarter re-staffing the engagement - the reputational damage lands on you, not on the recruiter who wrote it down.

You give the first number in the screening call without having calibrated the level, anchor 25% under band, and the offer comes in exactly where you anchored, permanently resetting every future refresh and promotion off that base.

The 'why this company' answer is assembled from the homepage and the About page, the interviewer is the person who wrote neither, and the answer reads as interchangeable across their three closest competitors.

You quote a metric in the narrative round that you cannot reconstruct in the resume-defence round two weeks later, and the loop's feedback becomes 'inflates impact' - the single hardest tag to recover from in a debrief.

Sponsorship or a border constraint surfaces after the offer rather than in the recruiter screen, the role turns out to be budgeted without it, and the offer is withdrawn for a reason that had nothing to do with your engineering.

You accept a private-company offer on a headline total-comp figure without the share count, preferred price or exercise window, and discover at exit that the equity was worth a fraction of the number you traded base salary for.

You claim comfort with air-gapped or clearance-gated customer sites you have never worked in, get assigned to exactly that account because it is the one that needed the answer, and cannot do the work.
interviewQuestions: Why forward-deployed rather than a product engineering role at the same company? Be specific about what you get from it and what you give up.
This role is roughly 40% travel, mostly to customer sites in other timezones, sometimes at short notice. Walk me through what that actually looks like in your life, and tell me where your limit is.
What do you think is the hardest part of getting our product into a customer's production environment? You have not worked here - I want your hypothesis and what it is based on.

You are three weeks into a deployment and it is clear the thing in the SOW will not solve the customer's actual problem. Your champion has already told their VP it will. What do you do, and in what order do you talk to whom?
What are you looking for in compensation, and how did you arrive at that number?
You have another offer. Tell me honestly how you are comparing them - what would make you pick us, and what is the thing about us that worries you?
Six months in, what would make you conclude this was the wrong job? Give me the concrete signal you would be watching for.
80.proofOfWork: Beyond the three recordings, build a private 'narrative kit' repo that turns the answers into a system you can run against any company in thirty minutes. It contains: a filled one-page dossier for each of your top ten targets, each with the delivery motion, the strategic bet in their own words with the primary source cited, the named competitor and the honest reason a buyer picks them, and the week-one deployment constraint you would hit; a comp model spreadsheet with a row per target showing level assumption, base, bonus, equity with the price assumption made explicit, an equity-at-zero column, and your walk-away, target and ask, with every cell traceable to at least two independent sources; a one-page travel and authorisation constraint sheet with the arithmetic behind the percentage, the hard limits, and your work-authorisation status in one sentence; and a rehearsal log recording every take with its transcript, filler count per minute, time to first substantive claim, longest sentence, and total word count, plus a short note on the single edit that moved a metric between takes. Prove the loop closed rather than that the folder exists: include the take-1 and take-final transcripts side by side with the metric deltas, the recording of the interrupt drill where you were cut off and recovered without restarting, and a dated log of every real recruiter or interview conversation where you used a number from the kit, what you said, and what came back - including the ones where the band came in lower than your model, and what you changed in the model afterwards.

81.why: An FDE loop is a credibility audit disguised as a conversation: the interviewer picks one line off your resume, asks 'how did you measure that', and keeps pulling until either a real system appears or the claim collapses - because that is exactly what a customer's staff engineer will do to you in week two of a deployment. Every unfalsifiable number on your resume ('45% improvement in targeting accuracy') is a trap you set for yourself, and one collapsed claim contaminates every other number in the document. This session converts a marketing artifact into a defensible technical record: for each bullet, the mechanism, the measurement, the thing that broke, and the design you would not repeat.
prerequisites: A current resume you actually send out, with every metric bullet in it - the Omnibound, RemoteState and FalconWise lines, verbatim.

Access to whatever produced your numbers: HubSpot/Smartlead/Instantly exports, Supabase or Postgres tables, n8n and Clay run histories, Slack threads, GA4 or Mixpanel views. If an account is gone, the screenshots and CSVs you kept.
Enough SQL and percentile literacy from the observability and SLO topics to state a metric as good events over valid events, over a named window, rather than as a bare percentage.
The STAR / narrative structure work from topic 72 (why FDE, why this company) so a defence answer has a shape and an ending, not just facts.
The technical-writing pass from topic 69 - specifically the numbers-that-survive-scrutiny discipline: baseline, method, sample size, percentile, confounders.
A peer or mock partner willing to be genuinely adversarial for 45 minutes, plus a recorder (audio is enough) and a transcription tool.

subtopics.name: Explode the resume into atomic, falsifiable claims
subtopics.learn: Put every bullet in a table with one row per distinct claim, not per bullet - 'cut deploy time 2 weeks to under 3 days and sustained 1.5%+ positive reply rates across 300+ mailboxes' is four claims (a before, an after, a rate, a fleet size). Tag each row with claim type: metric, mechanism, scope, or scale. Mark which ones you can produce evidence for in under five minutes, which need reconstruction, and which are vibes. Expect 20-40 rows off a two-page resume; the count itself tells you how much surface area you are defending.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing One - audience and clear claims

subtopics.name: Number provenance: baseline, window, instrument, sample
subtopics.learn: For each metric row, write down five things or delete the number: the baseline value and how it was measured, the measurement window and whether before and after used the same length, the instrument (a HubSpot report, a Smartlead campaign export, a SQL query, a stopwatch, or your memory), the sample size, and who else could reproduce it. '48h to under 4 hours' must resolve to something like 'median time from signal event timestamp to first-touch send timestamp, over 412 accounts in Feb-Mar 2026, from a Supabase query joining signal_events to outreach_sends'. If it resolves to 'it felt faster', that is a mechanism claim wearing a metric costume - rewrite it as one.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives

subtopics.name: Attribution isolation: what else changed at the same time
subtopics.learn: For every improvement claim, list everything else that moved during the same window - new domains warmed, a different ICP, a seasonality effect, a pricing change, a headcount change, a list source swap. The killer follow-up is 'reply rate went up, but you also changed the list and the copy in the same sprint - how do you know which one did it?' Have an answer that is either a real control (a holdout segment, a staggered rollout, an A/B with the same list), or an honest 'I could not isolate it; here is the directional evidence and here is what I would have held constant'. Never claim causation from a single before/after with three simultaneous changes.

resource.label: Confounding - definition and control strategies

subtopics.name: Denominators, cohorts, and the metric that games itself
subtopics.learn: Write every rate as an explicit fraction with a named numerator and denominator, the way an SLI is defined as good events over valid events. '1.5%+ positive reply rate' is meaningless until you say positive replies over delivered (not sent), where positive means a human-labelled interested/meeting-booked and not an out-of-office, deduped by contact and not by email. Do the same for '18-39% SQL conversion' (of what population, qualified by whom, over what lag window) and '95%+ deliverability' (inbox placement from a seed test, or simply not-bounced). Then ask what the metric incentivises: a reply rate you can raise by shrinking the denominator is a number a senior interviewer will immediately probe.

resource.label: Google SRE Workbook - Implementing SLOs

subtopics.name: Mechanism ladder for the enrichment agent bullet
subtopics.learn: Take '6+ hrs/batch manual research to sub-30-min automated pass, Python Playwright + asyncio over 100+ domains' and rehearse three depths. Level one: the pipeline stages. Level two: the concurrency model - asyncio.Semaphore bound, asyncio.gather vs as_completed, why you chose N workers, browser context reuse versus a fresh context per domain, per-request timeouts, retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and where the 30 minutes actually goes. Level three: what breaks - a hung page with no navigation timeout pinning an event-loop slot, memory growth from unclosed contexts, a blocking requests call inside a coroutine serialising the whole run, robots and rate-limit handling, and how you would prove the run was actually 30 minutes rather than 30 minutes for the domains that did not fail.

resource.label: Python docs - asyncio tasks and coroutines

subtopics.name: Mechanism ladder for the LLM pipeline and scoring rubric
subtopics.learn: For '7-stage LLM pipeline' and 'composite 0-100 score from firmographic + technographic + behavioral', be ready to state: the exact stage boundaries and why they are separate calls rather than one prompt, the model and why, how each stage's output is constrained (JSON schema, tool use, or free text plus a parser) and what happens when parsing fails, the token and cost per account, the latency budget, and the retry and idempotency behaviour on partial failure. For the score, give the actual weights, how they were chosen, whether they were ever validated against closed-won outcomes, what a 71 versus a 68 means operationally, and how you detected drift when the model version changed. 'The AI scores it' is a failing answer; the follow-up is always 'scores it how, and how do you know it is right?'

resource.label: Claude platform documentation

subtopics.name: Infrastructure-scale claims: 300+ mailboxes, 150+ domains
subtopics.learn: Scale numbers invite 'walk me through how you operate that'. Be able to describe per-domain SPF, DKIM selector rotation and DMARC policy (p=none to quarantine, aggregate report handling), warmup ramp schedules and daily send caps per mailbox, how you detected a domain going bad (bounce class breakdown, spam-placement seed tests, reputation signals) and what your pull-the-domain threshold was. Know the difference between hard bounces, soft bounces, and blocks, and what your actual bounce rate was. Also be ready for the uncomfortable version of this question about deliverability practice and consent - answer it directly rather than dodging, because an FDE who cannot discuss the compliance edge of their own system is a liability in a customer's security review.

resource.label: RFC 7489 - DMARC

subtopics.name: Integration claims: webhooks, idempotency, and the CRM schema
subtopics.learn: 'Webhook schema designed with Product and Engineering for clean CRM ingestion' and 'real-time CRM sync eliminated 15h/week' both cash out as an integration design question. Be able to name: the event payload shape and its version field, how you guaranteed at-least-once delivery did not create duplicate contacts (idempotency key, upsert on a natural key, dedupe window), retry and backoff on 429 and 5xx, how you handled HubSpot rate limits and partial batch failures, signature verification on the receiving endpoint, and what your dead-letter path was. Then state the failure you actually hit - a replayed webhook, a race between two sources writing the same contact, a schema change that silently dropped a field - and what the alert was.

resource.label: Stripe docs - webhooks, retries and idempotency

subtopics.name: The 'what broke' file: one real failure per bullet
subtopics.learn: Every bullet needs an attached incident, written in postmortem shape: impact in business terms and duration, how it was detected and the detection gap (how long between breakage and anyone noticing), the triggering condition separated from the root cause, the fix, and the guardrail added afterwards. A bullet with no failure attached reads as either trivial or unowned. Aim for variety across the set: a data-quality failure, a rate-limit or quota failure, a silent-wrong-output failure (the pipeline ran clean and produced garbage), and a human-process failure. Keep each to eight sentences you can say out loud in 90 seconds.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture

subtopics.name: Narrating the debug, not just the fix
subtopics.learn: Interviewers score how you found the problem far more than what the problem was. For each incident, reconstruct the actual sequence: the first symptom and where you saw it, your first two hypotheses and how you cheaply falsified them, the specific tool that gave you the decisive signal (a log line, a diff of two runs, bisecting a batch, printing the payload that failed schema validation, timing each stage), and the moment you realised your model of the system was wrong. Practise saying 'my first hypothesis was wrong, and here is what the evidence was that killed it' - that sentence is worth more than a clean story where you guessed right immediately.

resource.label: MIT Missing Semester - Debugging and Profiling

subtopics.name: 'What I'd do differently' as a decision record, not a humblebrag
subtopics.learn: For each bullet, write a three-line ADR-shaped regret: the decision you made, the constraint that made it reasonable at the time, and the specific alternative you would now choose plus the cost you would accept for it. Good examples: 'I put scoring weights in the prompt instead of a config table, so every reweighting was an untracked prompt edit - I would move weights into version-controlled config and log the score components per account'. Bad examples: 'I would have documented more' or 'I would have moved faster'. The tell for a senior candidate is that the regret is architectural and has a named tradeoff; the tell for a junior one is that the regret is about effort.

resource.label: Architecture Decision Records

subtopics.name: Scope honesty: I versus we, and what you did not build
subtopics.learn: For each bullet, write the honest ownership split: what you designed, what you implemented, what existed before you, who else touched it, and what you would not be able to rebuild alone. Then rehearse volunteering it - 'I owned the enrichment and scoring path end to end; the HubSpot object model was already there and our RevOps lead owned the routing rules'. Interviewers at Palantir-style loops probe scope deliberately and reward the candidate who draws the line themselves, because overstated ownership in a resume predicts overstated commitments to a customer. Also prepare the deflation answer for anything a small team did: naming your collaborators makes the claim more credible, not less.

resource.label: Amazon Leadership Principles - Ownership and Dive Deep

subtopics.name: Three depths per bullet: 45 seconds, 3 minutes, whiteboard
subtopics.learn: Write and time three versions of each story. The 45-second version is claim plus mechanism plus outcome, no names, no chronology - this is the answer to 'tell me about this line'. The 3-minute version adds the constraint, the option you rejected, the failure and the fix. The whiteboard version is the architecture you would draw if asked to go deep: boxes, data flow direction, where state lives, where the failure was. Practise stopping cleanly at the end of the short version and letting the interviewer pull - candidates who dump the 10-minute version on a 45-second question read as unable to calibrate to a customer's exec.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing Two - structure and summarising

subtopics.name: Rewrite pass: cut or repair every undefendable line
subtopics.learn: Go back through the claim table and act on it. Delete any number you could not source - a resume with six defensible numbers beats one with fourteen where two collapse. Repair the rest into claim + mechanism + measurement form: '45% improvement in targeting accuracy' becomes something like 'raised ICP match rate from 52% to 75% on manual review of 200 sampled accounts by adding technographic filters from BuiltWith and a title-mapping stage'. Replace unqualified superlatives and ranges you cannot explain ('18-39%' invites 'why the spread?' - either explain the segments or state one number). Keep a diff of the old and new resume; the deletions are the most useful output of this session.

resource.label: Federal Plain Language Guidelines

subtopics.name: Evidence pack, redaction, and what you may legally show
subtopics.learn: Assemble a folder mapping each surviving claim to an artifact you could actually screen-share: a public repo commit, a redacted dashboard screenshot, a query with the output row count, an anonymised architecture diagram. Then run the confidentiality pass - strip customer names, ARR figures, prospect PII, hostnames, API keys, and any inbox or domain list; replace with categories ('a $12M-ARR IT services firm selling into US/EU enterprise'). Check your employment agreement before showing anything derived from internal data. Rotate, do not blur, any credential that appears. An FDE who leaks a former employer's data in an interview has answered a question nobody asked.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - repositories and visibility

subtopics.name: Cross-artifact consistency audit
subtopics.learn: Line up resume, LinkedIn, portfolio site, GitHub README and any recorded talk side by side and diff them for: employment dates and month boundaries, job titles, metric values, the name of each system, and headcount or scope claims. Fix the numbers that disagree - a recruiter who sees 40% on LinkedIn and 45% on the resume will not ask, they will just discount. Standardise terminology the way a style guide does: pick one name per system and use it everywhere ('signal layer', not 'signal layer' here and 'scoring engine' there), and define each coined term in one sentence you can deliver on demand, because 'what do you mean by agent?' is a real question and a vague answer is expensive.

resource.label: Google developer documentation style guide - word list

subtopics.name: Adversarial drill, recording, and grading
subtopics.learn: Run the whole set under pressure. Solo pass first: shuffle the bullets, hit record, give the 45-second version cold, then have your partner or a script fire the three hardest follow-ups per bullet ('how did you measure that', 'what else changed', 'what broke', 'what would you do differently', 'what part did you not build'). Transcribe and grade each answer on four axes: was there a number with a denominator, was there a mechanism at config-key level, was there a named failure, did you stop on time. Log every question you could not answer as a gap ticket and close it by finding the evidence or cutting the claim. Finish with a live peer mock so a human sees the flinch you cannot hear in your own recording.

resource.label: Exponent - practice interviews

outcomes: You can state, for any metric on your resume, the numerator, the denominator, the measurement window, the instrument that produced it and the sample size, without hedging and without looking anything up.
You can name what else changed during each improvement window and say explicitly whether you isolated the cause, including saying 'I could not isolate it' when that is the truth.

You can go three levels deep on every technical bullet - stages, then concurrency/retry/schema mechanics with real config values, then the failure conditions - and stop where your knowledge actually ends.
You can attach one real production failure to every bullet, told in postmortem shape with impact, detection gap, trigger versus root cause, fix and guardrail, in under 90 seconds.
You can give a 'what I'd do differently' for each bullet that names an architectural alternative and the tradeoff you would accept, not an effort or documentation regret.
You can draw the ownership boundary on each project unprompted, naming what you did not build and who owned it, without shrinking the claim.
You have a rewritten resume with every unsourceable number deleted or repaired into claim + mechanism + measurement form, and a diff showing exactly what you cut.
You can survive a 45-minute adversarial teardown with a recorded transcript in which every follow-up you failed has a corresponding closed gap ticket.
failureModes: A rate is quoted with a silently favourable denominator - positive replies over delivered rather than over sent - and when the interviewer recomputes it over sent, the number drops by a third and every other figure on the page becomes suspect.

The before-number was never measured; it was estimated after the fact to make the after-number look good, and the candidate cannot say who timed the 'two weeks' or where the '6+ hours per batch' came from.

An improvement is claimed from a window in which the list source, the copy and the sending infrastructure all changed together, so the causal story collapses on the first 'how do you know it was the pipeline?'

The candidate describes an LLM scoring system entirely at the level of 'the model evaluates fit' and cannot state a weight, a schema, a parse-failure path or a single validation against closed-won outcomes - which reads as having operated a tool rather than built a system.

A throughput claim covers only the successful subset: the automated pass finished in 30 minutes for the 60 domains that did not time out, and the failures were silently dropped rather than retried or reported, so the real end-to-end coverage was never measured.

Ownership is stated in the first person for work a four-person team did, the interviewer asks one implementation detail that only the actual builder would know, and the ambiguity retroactively taints the honest bullets too.

Confidential material leaks in the enthusiasm to prove a claim - a screenshot with customer names, a prospect list, or a live API key visible in a terminal recording - which ends the loop regardless of how good the answer was.
interviewQuestions: You say you cut lead qualification from 48 hours to under 4. Define both numbers precisely for me: what event starts the clock, what event stops it, is that a median or a mean, and over how many accounts?

Walk me through the enrichment agent. Now go one level down: how many concurrent workers, what bounded them, what happened when a page hung, and how did you verify the run actually completed for every domain rather than just the ones that succeeded?
Your scoring model outputs a composite 0-100. How were the weights chosen, and how would you know today whether the score has any relationship to accounts that actually closed?

During the window where reply rate improved, you also changed the target list and the copy. Design me the experiment you would run now to separate those effects, given you only get one production sending fleet.

Tell me about a time this system produced confidently wrong output that nobody noticed for a while. How was it eventually detected, and what did you add so it would be caught in an hour instead of a week?
Pick the bullet on your resume you are least proud of technically and tell me why - then tell me what you would build instead today and what that would cost you.

A customer's data engineer reviews your integration and says the webhook consumer can double-write contacts on retry. Is he right? Walk me through your idempotency story and what you would change if he is.
81.proofOfWork: Beyond the per-bullet defence notes, publish a redacted 'metrics provenance' repository that reconstructs two of your headline numbers from raw evidence to claim. For each one, include the actual query or script that computes it against a synthetic or anonymised dataset with the same schema as production (signal_events, accounts, outreach_sends, replies), a README stating the numerator, denominator, window, sample size and instrument, a section listing every confounder present in the original window and what you would have held constant, and a sensitivity table showing how the number moves under three defensible alternative definitions - for example reply rate over sent versus delivered versus deduped-by-contact, so a reader sees the honest range rather than the flattering endpoint. Commit alongside it a diff of your resume before and after this session, with a short note per deleted line explaining what evidence was missing, and a 20-minute recording of a peer grilling you on the surviving bullets, with a timestamped list of every question you could not answer and a follow-up commit that closes each gap by either producing the evidence or cutting the claim. The artifact people will remember is the sensitivity table: it demonstrates that you understand your own numbers well enough to attack them before anyone else does.

82.topic: Take-home rehearsals (four, five hours each, recorded walkthrough)
82.why: The FDE take-home is the closest proxy any loop has to the actual job: an underspecified prompt, a dirty dataset, a hard clock, and a reviewer who behaves like a customer's staff engineer - skimming your README, running one command, and deciding in eight minutes whether you are safe to put in front of an account. What gets scored is almost never the model call; it is whether you scoped a defensible slice, wrote down what you cut and why, made it reproducible on a stranger's machine, and could narrate the trade-offs without hedging. Four timed builds with recorded walkthroughs turn that from a hope into a rehearsed motion, and they double as portfolio artifacts you can send before anyone asks.
prerequisites: The AI engineering block as working knowledge, not reading: RAG at depth (topic 49), tool use and structured outputs (47), agents and human-in-the-loop (48), and evals as infrastructure (53) - you should be able to write a retriever and a judge from scratch without a tutorial open.
Production Python you can type fast: packaging and layout (topic 25), FastAPI with lifespan and dependency injection (26), and pytest with fixtures, parametrize and markers (35).
PostgreSQL fluency from topic 29 - EXPLAIN ANALYZE, indexes, transactions, ON CONFLICT - plus enough Docker (topics 5 and 6) to write a two-service compose file from memory.
CI from topic 18: a GitHub Actions workflow with a matrix, caching, secrets and a required check, written without copying an existing repo.
Provider fluency from topic 60: Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs side by side, streaming, tool schemas, token counting, and cost per 1k tokens for the models you would actually pick.
Writing and demo craft from topics 68 and 69 - you can write a README that leads with the outcome and talk over a screen share for ten minutes without saying 'as you can see here'.

subtopics.name: Build the prompt corpus and reverse-engineer the rubric
subtopics.learn: Collect 8-12 real FDE and AI-engineer take-home prompts (company careers pages, public GitHub repos named *-takehome, the Anthropic and OpenAI cookbooks' example tasks) and tabulate them: input format, stated deliverable, stated time budget, and what the prompt is silently testing. Then write the rubric you believe the reviewer uses - typically five axes: correctness on the happy path, handling of dirty or adversarial input, evidence the thing works (tests and evals), reproducibility on a clean machine, and communication (README plus the walkthrough). Score two public take-home repos against your own rubric before you build anything; if you cannot separate a good one from a mediocre one on paper, you cannot self-grade your own runs.

resource.label: OpenAI Cookbook (official examples repository)

subtopics.name: The five-hour clock: a phase protocol with hard checkpoints
subtopics.learn: Commit to a fixed budget and set real timers: 0:00-0:20 read the prompt twice and write the scope contract (three in-scope capabilities, an explicit out-of-scope list, and the one assumption that would invalidate the design if wrong); 0:20-0:35 scaffold from your template; 0:35-2:30 thinnest end-to-end path that produces real output on real data; 2:30-4:00 the one hard thing the prompt is actually testing; 4:00-4:30 tests, eval or data-quality gate, and CI green; 4:30-5:00 README, LIMITATIONS, and record. The two ways every run dies are (a) polishing ingestion for ninety minutes and never reaching an answer, and (b) starting the README at 4:55. Enforce a hard rule: at 2:30 there must be a committed path from raw input to final output, however ugly, or you cut scope on the spot and write the cut into LIMITATIONS.

resource.label: MIT Missing Semester - Command-line Environment (job control, timers, tmux)

subtopics.name: Clone-and-go scaffold: git init to first passing test in under ten minutes
subtopics.learn: Build one template repo you reuse for all four runs: uv-managed pyproject with pinned deps, src/ layout, a settings module reading a typed pydantic-settings config from .env with a checked-in .env.example, structured JSON logging, a typer CLI entrypoint, pytest with a conftest fixture that loads a tiny fixture dataset, ruff and mypy wired into pre-commit, and a GitHub Actions workflow that runs lint plus tests on push. Include a Makefile with setup, test, lint, run and eval targets so the reviewer never has to guess a command. Time yourself cloning it and getting a green test run; if it is over ten minutes, the template is too clever - delete the parts you did not use in your last dry run.

resource.label: uv - Working on projects (uv init, lockfile, uv run)

subtopics.name: Reviewer-runnable in five minutes on a clean machine
subtopics.learn: Assume the reviewer has Docker and nothing else, no API key of yours, and twenty minutes of patience. Ship a docker-compose.yml with your app plus Postgres, a seed script that loads a committed sample of the data (small enough for git, real enough to be interesting), a documented offline or fake-provider mode so the whole pipeline runs with no network and no key, and exact expected output in the README. Verify it the only honest way: `docker system prune -af`, clone into a fresh directory, follow your own README literally without touching your shell history, and fix everything that breaks. Unexported env vars and a globally installed CLI you forgot about are what silently kill otherwise-good submissions.

resource.label: Docker Compose Quickstart (multi-service app from a clean checkout)

subtopics.name: Scope to a documented 70% and make the cut list a feature
subtopics.learn: Decide in advance that you will ship roughly 70% of the imagined ideal and that the missing 30% will be written down with more precision than most people write their code. Maintain a LIMITATIONS.md with three sections: Not implemented (what, why it was the right cut given five hours, and roughly what it would cost to add), Known broken (concrete failure input and observed behaviour), and Assumptions (each with the evidence that would falsify it). Use lightweight ADRs for the two or three real forks - pgvector versus a local index, LLM judge versus string match, batch versus streaming - with context, decision and consequences. A reviewer reads an honest cut list as senior judgement; they read silence as you not knowing the gap existed.

resource.label: Architecture Decision Records (adr.github.io)

subtopics.name: README as the primary deliverable
subtopics.learn: Write to a fixed skeleton so you can produce it in twenty minutes at hour 4:30: one-line what-it-does; the problem framing in the customer's terms; Quickstart with copy-pasteable commands and expected output; an architecture section with a Mermaid diagram of the data path; Design decisions with the trade-off you accepted for each; How I verified it (tests, evals, numbers with percentiles not averages); Limitations linked out; and What I would do with another day, ranked. Keep it in explanation-plus-how-to mode - no build journal, no 'first I tried'. The first screen must let a reviewer decide to keep reading; anything they have to scroll to find does not exist.

resource.label: Diataxis - the four kinds of documentation

subtopics.name: Recording rig and the ten-minute walkthrough spine
subtopics.learn: Set up OBS (or QuickTime screen recording) at 1080p with a scaled terminal font, external mic, notifications silenced, and a browser profile with no personal tabs. Rehearse one spine and reuse it for all four: 0:00-1:00 the problem and what you chose to build; 1:00-2:00 live demo of the happy path, real output on screen; 2:00-5:00 architecture walk following one request end to end through the code; 5:00-7:30 the hard part and the trade-off, including one thing you got wrong and fixed; 7:30-9:00 how you know it works - run the tests or evals live; 9:00-10:00 limitations and next steps. Record in one take, do not edit beyond trimming the ends, and hard-stop at ten minutes; a fourteen-minute video signals you cannot prioritise.

resource.label: OBS Studio - Quick Start Guide (sources, audio, recording settings)

subtopics.name: Run 1 (timed, 4h20): RAG over a messy heterogeneous corpus with citations
subtopics.learn: Prompt yourself with a realistic corpus - a few hundred documents mixing PDF, HTML, Markdown and CSV with duplicates, boilerplate headers and near-identical revisions - and build retrieval that a customer could trust. Do structure-aware chunking with overlap and preserved section headers in metadata, embed into Postgres with pgvector and an HNSW index (vector_cosine_ops, m=16, ef_construction=64), add lexical search over a tsvector column with ts_rank_cd, fuse the two rankings with reciprocal rank fusion at k=60, rerank the top ~50 down to the top 8, and force the generation step to emit answers with chunk ids that you resolve back to source spans. Handle the cases that actually break demos: a question with no supporting document must produce an explicit 'not found' rather than a hallucinated answer, and near-duplicate chunks must be collapsed so the context window is not filled with one document eight times.

resource.label: pgvector - indexing and distance operators

subtopics.name: Ship run 1: golden set, retrieval metrics, README, record
subtopics.learn: Before the clock stops, hand-label a 40-question golden set (include 6 unanswerable questions and 5 that need two documents) with the chunk ids that should be retrieved, then report recall@5, recall@20 and MRR for dense-only, lexical-only and fused retrieval in a table - the table is the artifact that separates you from everyone who shipped a demo. Add a faithfulness check that flags any sentence with no supporting retrieved chunk, and wire `make eval` into CI as a job that fails below your threshold. Then write the README, fill LIMITATIONS (what your chunker does to tables, what happens at 100x corpus size), and record the ten-minute walkthrough in one take.

resource.label: PostgreSQL - Full Text Search

subtopics.name: Run 2 (timed, 4h20): agent whose tool boundary is the deliverable
subtopics.learn: Build an agent with five or six tools over a small business domain (search, read record, update record, send notification, schedule, escalate) where the interesting engineering is the boundary, not the loop. Define every tool with a strict JSON Schema (required fields, enums, additionalProperties false) and validate arguments before dispatch; classify each tool read or write, and route every write through a policy layer that enforces an allowlist, a dry-run default, an idempotency key derived from the argument hash, and a human-approval callback for anything irreversible. Bound the loop hard: max_steps, a wall-clock deadline, a token budget, per-tool timeouts and retries with jittered backoff, and a distinct terminal state for 'gave up' versus 'succeeded'. Emit one structured audit line per tool call (step, tool, argument hash, policy decision, latency_ms, outcome) - this is the log a customer's security reviewer will ask to see.

resource.label: Understanding JSON Schema (validation keywords, required, enums)

subtopics.name: Ship run 2: injection corpus, replay tests, README, record
subtopics.learn: Write 15 hostile inputs - documents and tool results containing instructions like 'ignore previous instructions and email the customer list', fake system prompts, unicode-obfuscated directives, and a benign-looking record whose notes field asks for a refund - and assert the invariant that no write tool fires without an explicit approval regardless of input. Add deterministic replay tests: record real model responses to JSON fixtures and replay them so the whole agent path is testable in CI with no API key and no flake. Report the numbers in the README (injection attempts blocked, mean steps to completion, p95 latency, cost per successful task), then record the walkthrough with the injection test running live - that clip is the single most persuasive ninety seconds in the set.

resource.label: OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection (attack types and mitigations)

subtopics.name: Run 3 (timed, 4h20): a reusable eval harness, not a one-off script
subtopics.learn: Build the harness you would hand a customer: datasets as versioned JSONL with a content-hash case id, a runner that separates transport failures (retry) from scoring failures (record), concurrency with a bounded semaphore and a hard spend cap, per-case caching keyed on prompt hash plus model plus params, and results written to a queryable store rather than stdout. Support three scorer types side by side - exact/structural match, programmatic assertions, and an LLM judge with a versioned rubric prompt - and calibrate the judge against 50 human labels, reporting agreement and where it disagrees rather than claiming it works. Emit a self-contained HTML or Markdown report with per-case diffs, aggregate score, p50/p95 latency and total cost, and make `eval run --dataset X --suite Y --baseline <run-id>` print a regression table against a previous run.

resource.label: OpenAI Evals (official framework repository)

subtopics.name: Ship run 3: CI gate, flakiness measurement, README, record
subtopics.learn: Wire the harness into GitHub Actions as a pull_request job that runs a fast subset on every PR and the full suite nightly, uploads the report with actions/upload-artifact, comments the regression table on the PR, and fails the check when the aggregate drops beyond a stated tolerance or cost exceeds the cap. Measure your own flakiness honestly: run the same suite three times and publish the standard deviation per scorer, because a gate whose noise exceeds the regression it is meant to catch is worse than no gate. Document the threshold-setting method (how you picked the tolerance, what a false failure costs the customer's release train), then record the walkthrough around a deliberately broken prompt change that the CI check catches.

resource.label: GitHub Actions documentation

subtopics.name: Run 4 (timed, 4h20): idempotent data pipeline over deliberately dirty input
subtopics.learn: Ingest a genuinely nasty dataset - CSV with a UTF-8 BOM and mixed encodings, embedded newlines in quoted fields, four spellings of null ('', 'NULL', 'N/A', '-'), ambiguous DD/MM vs MM/DD dates, duplicate natural keys with conflicting values, and rows arriving out of order. Land raw rows immutably with a load_id and ingested_at, then normalise into typed tables via idempotent upserts (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (natural_key) DO UPDATE ... WHERE excluded.source_updated_at > target.source_updated_at) so re-running the same file changes nothing. Make it incremental with a watermark table plus a deliberate overlap window for late arrivals, route unparseable rows to a dead-letter table carrying the raw payload and the error, and provide a backfill command that is safe to run twice. Finish with a mart of three or four business metrics and a one-page readout of what the data actually says.

resource.label: PostgreSQL - INSERT ... ON CONFLICT

subtopics.name: Ship run 4: data quality assertions, reconciliation, README, record
subtopics.learn: Add executable data tests rather than prose promises: uniqueness on the natural key, not-null on required columns, accepted-value sets on enums, referential integrity across the mart, freshness on the watermark, and row-count reconciliation from source file to raw to normalised to mart printed as a funnel with the drop reason at each stage. Make the failure behaviour explicit - which assertions block the load and which only warn - because a pipeline that silently publishes a mart built from 40% of the rows is how a customer's dashboard lies for a quarter. Record the walkthrough showing a re-run of the same file producing zero row changes and a corrupted file landing cleanly in the dead-letter table.

resource.label: dbt - data tests

subtopics.name: Cross-run scorecard: find the phase that keeps costing you
subtopics.learn: For each run log the actual phase timings against the planned budget, the moment you first had end-to-end output, what you cut and when, and a self-grade on the five rubric axes; then look for the repeating pattern rather than the individual mistake. The usual culprits are scaffolding drift (you 'improved' the template mid-run), premature abstraction before the happy path existed, and a README written in the last four minutes. Watch each of your own videos at 1.5x with a notepad and count filler phrases, moments you narrate code instead of intent, and questions you invited but could not answer. Turn the top two findings into changes to the template or the clock protocol before the next run - the point of four runs is the delta between run one and run four.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

subtopics.name: Publish and pass the code-defence pass
subtopics.learn: Before anything goes public, run a secrets sweep over the whole history (gitleaks or GitHub secret scanning, not just a glance at the current tree), rotate any key that ever touched a commit, scrub customer-shaped data from fixtures, add a licence, and squash the embarrassing commit messages only if it does not destroy the honest timeline you want to show. Then sit with each repo and defend it out loud as a reviewer would: why this chunk size, why HNSW over IVFFlat, why an LLM judge here and a string match there, what happens at 100x data, where is the race condition, what breaks if the model provider returns 429 for ten minutes. Publish each repo with the video linked at the top of the README and a one-paragraph summary, and keep the four links in one place so you can send them within an hour of a recruiter conversation.

resource.label: GitHub - code security and secret scanning

outcomes: You can take an ambiguous take-home prompt and produce, within twenty minutes, a written scope contract naming three in-scope capabilities, an explicit out-of-scope list, and the assumption whose falsity would change the design.
You can go from empty directory to a green CI run on your own scaffold in under ten minutes, timed and repeatable, without copying from a previous project.
You can ship four public repos that each run end to end on a clean machine from a single documented command, verified by cloning into a fresh directory and following your own README literally.

You can quantify your own work instead of asserting it: recall@k and MRR for the RAG build, injection-blocked rate and cost per successful task for the agent, judge-versus-human agreement and suite variance for the eval harness, and a source-to-mart row reconciliation funnel for the pipeline.
You can deliver a ten-minute unedited walkthrough that demos, explains one request end to end, names a trade-off you accepted, runs the tests live, and finishes inside the time limit.
You can write a LIMITATIONS document a reviewer reads as judgement rather than as an excuse - each gap paired with why it was the right cut at five hours and what adding it would cost.
You can defend every design fork in your own code out loud - index type, chunk size, scorer choice, upsert strategy - including the failure mode of the option you rejected.
You can show measurable improvement from run one to run four in phase-timing adherence, time-to-first-end-to-end-output, and self-graded rubric score, with the log to prove it.
failureModes: Four and a half hours go into ingestion, parsing and a beautiful abstraction layer, and the submission never produces an answer to the actual question the prompt asked.

The repo runs perfectly on your laptop and fails on the reviewer's machine because an env var was already exported in your shell, a CLI was installed globally months ago, or the seed data was gitignored.
The RAG demo answers confidently on a question with no supporting document, and the reviewer's first test - an off-corpus question - produces a fluent hallucination with fabricated citations.
The agent's write tools have no approval gate or idempotency key, so a retried step double-sends a notification or double-updates a record, and the audit log has no way to prove which call did it.
The eval harness reports a single aggregate number with no variance, so a re-run swings by more than the regression it is supposed to gate and the customer stops trusting the check within two weeks.
The pipeline silently drops malformed rows instead of dead-lettering them, so the mart is built from a subset nobody counted and the dashboard understates volume for a quarter before anyone notices.
The walkthrough runs seventeen minutes, narrates code line by line instead of intent, and buries the demo at minute nine - so the reviewer stops at minute three having seen nothing work.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through the take-home you were least happy with. What did you cut, what did the cut cost, and what would you have done differently with the same five hours?

You have five hours and a customer corpus of 200,000 heterogeneous documents. Describe exactly what you build, what you deliberately do not build, and how you would prove to the customer that retrieval is good enough to deploy.

Your agent has a tool that issues refunds. Design the boundary around it: schema, authorisation, idempotency, approval, audit, and the tests that prove a malicious document in the context window cannot trigger it.

An eval you built as a CI gate starts failing intermittently on unchanged code. Debug it out loud - what do you check first, and how do you decide between fixing the harness, the judge, or the threshold?

A customer reruns your nightly ingest for the same day after a partial failure and their revenue metric doubles. What is the most likely cause, how do you confirm it, and what do you change so it cannot happen again?
How would you set the pass threshold on an LLM-as-judge gate when you have 50 human labels and no baseline? Tell me what agreement number would make you refuse to ship the gate at all.
We give candidates a take-home and half the submissions look identical. If you were designing our rubric, what would you score that actually separates a senior FDE from a strong generalist?
82.proofOfWork: Beyond the four repos and videos, publish a fifth repo - fde-takehome-kit - that turns your process into something another engineer can run tomorrow, and prove it was used rather than merely written. It contains the clone-and-go scaffold (uv pyproject, src layout, typed settings with .env.example, typer CLI, structured logging, pytest with fixture data, ruff/mypy pre-commit, a Makefile with setup/test/lint/run/eval, a docker-compose with Postgres, and a GitHub Actions workflow), the five-axis rubric you reverse-engineered from real prompts, the five-hour clock protocol as a printable checklist with the hard 2:30 end-to-end checkpoint, the README and LIMITATIONS templates, and the ten-minute walkthrough script. The evidence section is what makes it credible: a RUNS.md logging all four timed runs with planned-versus-actual phase timings, the timestamp at which each run first had end-to-end output, the cut list made in the moment, the self-graded rubric score, and a short retro naming the one change to the template or protocol that the run caused - so the file reads as a visible improvement curve from run one to run four. Add a fresh-machine verification record for each repo (the commands run in a clean container and their output), the secret-scan and key-rotation confirmation, and a single index page linking the four repos, their videos, and their headline numbers, so the whole set can be sent as one link within an hour of a recruiter asking what you have built.

83.why: The decomposition round maps one-to-one onto day one of a real deployment: a customer says a single sentence like 'we want AI to reduce claim denials' and you have to return a plan someone can staff, budget, sequence and kill. FDE loops use this round specifically to catch the engineer who starts drawing architecture ninety seconds in, because that engineer builds the wrong thing confidently and burns a quarter of a customer's patience doing it. Ten timed reps is what converts the framework from something you can describe into something you can execute while a stranger interrupts you, halves your timeline, and takes away production data access.
prerequisites: Discovery technique from topic 66 - separating the stated ask from the real problem, and knowing who the decision owner is.
The engagement document set from topic 67: site survey, PRD-lite, SOW and ADR shapes, so the drill write-up has somewhere real to land.
System design vocabulary from topics 42 and 43 - queues, caching, retrieval, batching - so decomposition can name components without hand-waving.
Evals-as-infrastructure from topic 53: what an eval set costs to build, who labels it, and what an acceptance threshold looks like.
SLO and error-budget literacy from topic 20, so 'production ready' means numbers rather than vibes.
Compliance ground truth from topic 64 (SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA) and domain context from topic 71 (fintech ops, healthcare intake, procurement, logistics).
At least one delivered engagement of your own - the Lumen FDE deployment - to mine for reference-class durations.

subtopics.name: Read the round: what the 30 minutes actually scores
subtopics.learn: Treat this as a rubric, not a conversation. Interviewers mark five things roughly independently: did you constrain the problem before proposing anything, is the breakdown collectively exhaustive with no orphaned work, does every piece carry a number and a confidence, is the order risk-first, and did you re-plan correctly when they injected a constraint. Write those five lines on a card and keep it visible for all ten drills - you are graded against the same card every time. Learn the dominant anti-signal explicitly: boxes and arrows inside the first two minutes reads as 'will build the wrong thing fast', and nothing in the remaining 28 minutes fully recovers it.

resource.label: Exponent - Forward Deployed Engineer interview guide

subtopics.name: The five-minute clarification protocol
subtopics.learn: Build a fixed question set you can run cold and finish inside five of the thirty minutes, grouped so you never wander: (a) who is the user and what do they do today, step by step, without your system; (b) what decision or action changes if this works, and who makes it; (c) what does success look like numerically, by when; (d) what data exists, where does it live, who approves access; (e) what is out of scope, what is politically untouchable, what has already been tried and failed; (f) hard constraints - on-prem vs cloud, PII, latency, budget, how many people you get. Practise a three-question compression for terse interviewers: current manual process, the decision it feeds, the metric that must move. Every question must be one whose answer changes your plan; if you cannot name the branch it opens, cut it.

resource.label: system-design-primer - outline use cases, constraints and assumptions

subtopics.name: From 'we want AI' to a falsifiable outcome metric with a baseline
subtopics.learn: Convert the ask into one sentence shaped as: move <metric> from <baseline> to <target> for <population> by <date>, measured by <instrument>. Force a baseline out of the interviewer even as a rough estimate - a plan with no baseline cannot be judged, and 'we don't measure that today' is itself workstream one. Separate the model metric (extraction F1, precision@k, recall at a fixed alert volume) from the business metric (analyst minutes per case, denial rate, on-time delivery) and state the transfer function you are assuming between them, because that unstated assumption is where these engagements actually die. Always name the non-ML baseline you would ship first - a SQL rule, a sorted work queue, a regex - and what it would plausibly score.

resource.label: Google - Introduction to Machine Learning Problem Framing

subtopics.name: Data reality check before any architecture
subtopics.learn: Interrogate the data on six axes and say them as a table: system of record, grain (one row equals what, exactly), volume and growth, freshness and arrival latency, quality (null rates, duplicates, late-arriving corrections, free text vs coded fields), and access path (CDC, nightly extract, read replica, vendor API with a rate limit - and who signs off). Ask for one real example row and the row count; those two answers move a plan more than any architecture choice. Name the classic traps out loud so the interviewer knows you have hit them: no join key between the two systems, no history because the source table is mutated in place, labels that only exist post-hoc, and a 'warehouse' that turns out to be a folder of CSV drops.

resource.label: Microsoft Learn - Team Data Science Process overview

subtopics.name: MECE workstreams and the 100% rule
subtopics.learn: Decompose into five to seven workstreams that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, and enforce the work-breakdown 100% rule: children sum to the parent, no more and no less. The default deployment spine is access and environment, data ingestion and contracts, core logic or model, workflow and interface integration, evaluation and monitoring, rollout and handoff - plus one explicitly named customer-side stream holding everything you cannot do yourself. Test each node twice: can it be assigned to a single owner, and does it produce something a human can look at? A node with no demoable output is a task, not a workstream. Then state the excluded set out loud - what you are deliberately not doing is scored as hard as what you are.

resource.label: Work breakdown structure - the 100% rule

subtopics.name: Environment and access: the customer-side critical path
subtopics.learn: The estimate that kills FDE plans is not model quality, it is getting a network route and a credential. Enumerate it every drill: VPC peering or PrivateLink or VPN, SSO/OIDC integration, an identity with the right role (IRSA, workload identity, a service account someone must approve), egress rules and proxy allow-lists, whether outbound calls to a hosted model API are permitted at all, security review and vendor onboarding, and a DPA or BAA. Size these in calendar weeks, not engineering days, and attach a named customer-side owner to each. State the parallel mitigation: synthetic or sampled data in your own environment so code gets written while approvals are pending.

resource.label: AWS Well-Architected Framework

subtopics.name: Thin vertical slice first: the walking skeleton
subtopics.learn: Sequence so the first deliverable crosses every layer end to end for one narrow case - one source, one entity type, one user, one endpoint or screen, deployed where it will actually live - instead of completing any layer. The slice's job is to falsify integration assumptions, not to be accurate: can you read the source at the required grain, run inside their network, write back into the system of record, and get a human to look at the output. Say what it proves and what it deliberately does not. The anti-pattern to name: three weeks of pipeline work before anyone sees a result, discovered in week four to have been joined on a key that is not unique.

resource.label: Google Cloud - MLOps: continuous delivery and automation pipelines

subtopics.name: Sizing: appetite, reference classes, three-point estimates
subtopics.learn: Every workstream gets a number with its method attached. Prefer fixed-time-variable-scope appetite ('two weeks, and here is what fits in it') over open-ended estimates; use reference-class forecasting where you have history ('the last three ingestion integrations took 6, 9 and 4 days'); use three-point estimates (expected roughly (O + 4M + P) / 6) only where you can actually defend the pessimistic case. Quote ranges with a confidence level, never bare single numbers, and state the multiplier you apply for a first-time customer environment and say why. Keep a rabbit-hole list and a circuit breaker: work that blows past its appetite gets cut, not extended.

resource.label: Shape Up, Chapter 3: Set Boundaries - appetite as fixed time, variable scope

subtopics.name: Dependency graph, critical path, and parallelism you can actually buy
subtopics.learn: Draw the workstreams as a DAG with every edge labelled by what actually blocks - data access, a schema decision, a customer sign-off - then trace the longest path and say it out loud, because that path, not the sum of the work, is the delivery date. Separate hard technical dependencies from convenient ordering; most edges in a first-draft plan are the latter and can be cut with a mock, a stub, or a contract agreed up front. Then answer the question the interviewer is about to ask: what does a second engineer buy you? If the critical path is a three-week security review, the honest answer is 'nothing', and saying so is a strong senior signal.

resource.label: Critical path method

subtopics.name: Risk-first ordering: spikes, kill criteria, pre-mortem
subtopics.learn: List the assumptions the plan rests on, tag each with impact-if-wrong and cost-to-check, and schedule the cheapest checks on the highest-impact assumptions into week one as timeboxed spikes with a written exit question. Attach kill criteria to the engagement itself - 'if extraction F1 on 200 held-out documents is under 0.85 by week four, we stop and recommend the rules-based path' - because volunteering the conditions under which you would tell a customer to stop is the most senior move available in this round. Run a two-minute pre-mortem before presenting: assume it is six months later and this failed, name the three likeliest causes, and fold one mitigation for each into the sequence.

resource.label: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
