subtopics.name: Success criteria, acceptance tests, and the pilot-to-production exit
subtopics.learn: Define done at three levels and never conflate them. Demo: a scripted path that works on chosen data. Pilot: a numeric threshold on a held-out set plus an operational bar - p95 latency, uptime, human-review rate, cost per case. Production handoff: runbook, an on-call owner, alerts on the SLIs, a defined process for prompt or model updates, and a named person at the customer who owns it after you leave. Write acceptance criteria as testable statements naming the population and the measurement window, and say who does the measuring and where the number is visible. A pilot whose numbers only you can produce gets re-litigated in every steering meeting.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - The Evolving SRE Engagement Model (PRR)

subtopics.name: Delivery mechanics: the 30-minute clock and the artifacts you leave on the board
subtopics.learn: Fix a time budget and rehearse against a visible timer: 5 minutes clarify, 3 restate and get explicit agreement, 8 decompose, 5 size and sequence, 5 risks and cut list, 4 held back for their curveball. Produce exactly three artifacts - a one-line problem statement, a workstream table with owner, size and confidence, and a phase timeline with a named milestone per phase - plus at most one system-context sketch at a single level of abstraction. Narrate your reasoning continuously and check in twice ('does that split match how your team is organised?'). Announce the restate step explicitly; getting agreement on the problem before proposing a solution is the exact behaviour being tested.

resource.label: C4 model - one level of abstraction per diagram

subtopics.name: The write-up template and a 10-point self-scoring rubric
subtopics.learn: Standardise a two-page template you fill in within ten minutes of every drill: prompt verbatim, questions asked with the answers you were given or invented, restated problem, assumption register, workstream table (name, owner, size range, confidence), dependency DAG, phase plan with milestones, risks with mitigations and kill criteria, what you would cut at half the time, and what you got wrong. Append a 10-point rubric - clarified before proposing, baseline stated, MECE with an exclusion list, access path sized in weeks, thin slice first, critical path named, ranges with confidence, kill criteria present, cut list present, time budget held - and score yourself out of 10 in the same file. The score trend across ten drills is the deliverable; no single write-up is.

resource.label: Architecture Decision Records - context / decision / consequences

subtopics.name: Drills 1-3: regulated data, where compliance is on the critical path
subtopics.learn: Three timed drills, each written up immediately: (1) a health payer wants to cut avoidable 30-day readmissions using claims plus an EHR feed; (2) a bank wants to cut false positives in AML transaction-monitoring alerts without missing true hits; (3) a state agency wants faster benefits eligibility decisions from scanned documents. For each, force the specific gates into the plan as sized calendar dependencies: BAA and minimum-necessary access, de-identified vs identified data, explainability for an adverse decision, immutable audit logging, data residency, and whether regulation requires a human decision-maker in the loop regardless of model quality. Notice where phase one is correctly not a model at all, but a labelled dataset plus a measurement of the current human baseline.

resource.label: HHS - HIPAA for Professionals

subtopics.name: Drills 4-6: physical operations and telemetry
subtopics.learn: Three drills where the constraint is the physical world: (4) predictive maintenance across a fleet of industrial machines with intermittent sensor uplink; (5) daily route planning for 200 vehicles with delivery time windows and driver-hours rules; (6) a manufacturer wants one inventory view across three ERPs after an acquisition. Practise identifying when the problem is optimisation or entity resolution rather than ML - for (5), say 'capacitated VRP with time windows, a solver not a model' - and decompose around edge and offline constraints, clock skew, duplicate and missing telemetry, backfill of late data, and the fact that a dispatcher will override any answer that cannot explain itself. Size the change-management workstream; in ops deployments it is usually larger than the engineering one.

resource.label: Google OR-Tools - Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows

subtopics.name: Drills 7-8: LLM-shaped scopes where the customer has picked the technology
subtopics.learn: Two drills: (7) 'deflect 40% of support tickets with an AI assistant' over a stale help centre plus a five-year Zendesk archive; (8) extract 30 fields from 12 contract templates into their CLM. Decompose to the eval set first - how many labelled examples, sampled from where, labelled by whom, at what per-field acceptance threshold - then corpus and retrieval quality, then the human-in-the-loop and escalation path, then a stated cost and p95 latency budget per request, then the ticket-taxonomy work nobody volunteers for. Name the metric trap out loud: deflection measured as 'no follow-up ticket' scores abandoned, angry users as successes, so define the counter-metric (CSAT on deflected sessions, escalation rate) in the same breath.

resource.label: Hamel Husain - Your AI Product Needs Evals

subtopics.name: Drills 9-10: adversarial and under-specified scopes, plus the mid-drill curveball
subtopics.learn: Two drills that are wrong as asked: (9) 'migrate this 12-year-old undocumented Java monolith off the mainframe in six months' - practise strangler-fig decomposition, seam identification, and proposing a read-only shadow phase that runs both systems and diffs outputs before any cutover; (10) an executive asks for a real-time dashboard when the actual problem is that two departments disagree on the definition of an active customer - practise redirecting to the definition and the decision owner without telling the sponsor they were wrong. In both, have someone inject a curveball at minute 18 (timeline halved, production data access revoked, a competitor already failed at this) and re-sequence out loud, naming what you drop and which risk you are now knowingly accepting.

resource.label: Martin Fowler - Strangler Fig Application

subtopics.name: Regrade, calibrate, and extract your three repeated failures
subtopics.learn: After all ten, re-score drills 1-5 against the rubric as it stood at the end rather than the one you started with, and diff each early plan against how you would write it now. Build a personal reference-class table from the set - the sizes you assigned to ingestion, environment access, eval-set creation - and check those against real durations from your own delivered work; most people under-size access approvals and labelled-data creation by two to four times. Write the three patterns that recur (jumped to architecture, no baseline, no kill criteria) as three sentences on a card and re-read it in the sixty seconds before every real interview.

resource.label: Reference class forecasting

outcomes: You can run a 30-minute decomposition cold on an unseen prompt: five minutes of clarifying questions, a restated problem you get explicit agreement on, five to seven MECE workstreams with owners, sized ranges, a sequenced phase plan and stated risks - holding the time budget to within two minutes, on video.
You can turn any vague ask into one sentence containing a metric, a baseline, a target, a population, a date and the instrument that measures it, and name the non-ML baseline you would ship first.

You can enumerate the customer-side access path (network route, identity and role, egress policy, security review, DPA or BAA) unprompted, size it in calendar weeks, and attach a named owner to each item.
You can draw the workstream DAG, state the critical path, and correctly answer whether adding a second engineer moves the delivery date.
You can attach kill criteria to your own plan - the threshold, the dataset it is measured on, and the week it is evaluated - and say the sentence in which you would recommend stopping.
You can absorb a mid-drill constraint change (timeline halved, production data revoked) and re-sequence out loud, naming what you cut and which risk you now accept.
You can quote every size as a range with a stated method (appetite, reference class, or three-point) and defend the pessimistic end when challenged.
You have ten written drill records self-scored against a fixed 10-point rubric with a visible upward trend, plus a first-versus-last diff on one repeated prompt.
failureModes: You start drawing architecture in the first two minutes, the interviewer writes 'proposed before understanding', and the remaining 28 minutes of good work do not overturn it.
The plan carries no baseline, so 'reduce denials by 20%' is unfalsifiable and the pilot ends in a meeting where the customer and you quote different numbers from different queries.
Access and security review are a footnote rather than a workstream, so the model sits finished on your laptop for six weeks waiting on a VPC peering approval nobody was chasing.
The decomposition is layer-by-layer - all ingestion, then all modelling, then all UI - so the first end-to-end result lands in week six and reveals the join key is not unique.
Every workstream is a single-point estimate with no range or confidence, so the first slipped date reads as incompetence instead of the uncertainty you had already priced in.

You accept the customer's stated solution ('we need a dashboard', 'we need a fine-tuned model') as the problem, deliver it exactly to spec, and it goes unused because the real blocker was a disputed definition or an absent decision owner.
The plan has no cut list, so when the timeline is halved mid-engagement the customer chooses what to drop and drops the evaluation, leaving you unable to prove the thing worked.
interviewQuestions: A hospital network's COO tells you: 'we want to use AI to reduce patient no-shows.' You have thirty minutes. Go.

You are four weeks into a ten-week deployment and the customer's security team just confirmed that no hosted model API is reachable from their network. Re-plan out loud: what changes, what gets cut, and what do you tell the sponsor tomorrow morning?
Size the data-ingestion workstream for a customer you have never worked with before. Give me a number, tell me how you got it, and defend the pessimistic end.
You have two engineers and eight weeks. Show me the phase plan, then tell me which phases a second engineer actually shortens and which ones they do not.
How do you decide the very first thing you build in an engagement? Give me an example where the obvious first thing turned out to be wrong.
What would make you recommend that a customer stop this project? Be specific: which metric, measured on which dataset, in which week.
The customer's data science team already has a model they say is 92% accurate and they want you to 'just productionise it'. Decompose that.
83.proofOfWork: Beyond the ten drill write-ups, publish a decomposition kit as a public repo that another engineer could pick up and run in an afternoon: the two-page drill template, the 10-point rubric, a clarification question bank grouped by the six axes with a note on which branch each question opens, and a calibrated reference-class table listing the durations you assigned to environment access, ingestion, eval-set creation, integration and handoff, with the real durations from your own delivered engagements next to them and the multiplier between the two. Include all ten completed drills as filled-in instances of the template with the honest self-scores visible, plus a regrade pass in which drills one through five are re-scored against the final rubric and the diff is written up in a short 'what I was systematically wrong about' note. Anchor it with one unedited 30-minute video of a drill run against a live opponent who injects a curveball at minute 18 - timeline halved or production data revoked - showing the timer, the board artifacts and you changing the plan out loud, plus the write-up produced within ten minutes of the recording ending. The kit proves the process is repeatable and calibrated, not that a single plan happened to be good.

84.why: The LLM design round is the one place in an FDE loop where the interviewer is explicitly checking whether you can be trusted to put a non-deterministic system in front of a paying customer: not whether you know what RAG is, but whether you can put a number on p99 latency, cost per request, and what happens when the model is wrong. In the field this exact conversation happens in the customer's architecture review, where their security lead asks where the tokens go, their finance lead asks what it costs at 10x volume, and their staff engineer asks how you know it is working - and you get one whiteboard and 45 minutes to answer all three. Topics 43 and 45-60 gave you the material; this topic trains delivering it under a clock, with four recordings so you can see the gap between what you know and what you can actually say in the room.
prerequisites: The classic design motion from 'System design mocks' (topic 44): the 45-minute phase budget, back-of-envelope estimation, C4 container diagrams with numbered flows, and deep-dive-with-two-options is assumed muscle memory here - this topic only adds the LLM layer on top.
LLM-era serving constraints from topic 43 and 'Serving at scale' (topic 56): prefill versus decode, KV cache sizing, continuous batching, and why p99 is in seconds and depends on output length.
RAG at depth (topic 49): chunking strategies, hybrid BM25-plus-dense retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoder reranking, contextual retrieval, and metadata pre-filtering for tenant isolation.

Evals as infrastructure (topic 53) and LLM observability (topic 54): golden sets, LLM-as-judge with agreement measured against human labels, online scoring, and OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* spans - you must be able to draw these as boxes, not mention them as intentions.

Gateway, routing, fallbacks and canaries (topic 55), cost and latency engineering (topic 59), and guardrails and prompt injection (topic 51): prompt caching economics, batch APIs, model tiering, token-bucket admission control on RPM and TPM, and the OWASP LLM Top 10 - so 'a malicious document in the corpus' is a constraint you draw rather than a question that stalls you.

A working rig: OBS or QuickTime capturing screen plus mic, Excalidraw with a saved LLM-architecture stencil, a visible countdown timer, and a private repo to hold four 45-minute recordings, four diagrams and four scorecards.

subtopics.name: What the LLM round scores that the classic round does not
subtopics.learn: Tabulate the five extra dimensions an LLM design round grades and that a pure distributed-systems answer misses: (1) quality is a design output, not a given - you must name the metric and how it is measured; (2) latency is dominated by generation, so TTFT and output-token count are design variables, not implementation details; (3) unit cost is a first-class NFR with a dollar figure; (4) the failure mode is a confident wrong answer, not a 500, so monitoring and rollback look different; (5) data movement is a compliance question because the tokens leave the customer's perimeter. Write these five on a card and force yourself to hit each one in every mock. The single most common senior-level miss is a beautiful architecture with no answer to 'how do you know it is good enough to ship?'

resource.label: Hello Interview - System Design in a Hurry: Introduction (how you are evaluated)

subtopics.name: The 45-minute phase budget for an LLM problem
subtopics.learn: Adapt the classic budget so the AI-specific content is not stranded at the end: 0-6 requirements including a quality bar and a cost ceiling; 6-11 estimation (QPS, tokens in and out per request, cost per request, GPU or TPM capacity); 11-16 API surface plus the data and index model; 16-24 high-level diagram with the sync path and the async path drawn separately; 24-38 two deep dives, one of which must be retrieval-or-agent-loop and the other evals-or-serving; 38-45 failure modes, rollout and the operability close. Enforce a hard rule that the evaluation story is on the board before minute 40 - if you leave it to the close it always gets cut and the interviewer reads that as you not having shipped one. Practise saying the transition sentences out loud ('that is the happy path - let me now show how we detect it degrading').

resource.label: Hello Interview - System Design in a Hurry: Delivery Framework

subtopics.name: Writing the rubric: what 4/5 means on each LLM dimension
subtopics.learn: Write your own 1-5 rubric as observable behaviours across six dimensions: requirements and quality bar, estimation with token and dollar math, architecture and data flow, LLM-specific depth (retrieval or agent loop or serving), evaluation and observability, and communication under pushback. A 4 on 'quality bar' means you defined success as a measurable criterion with a target and a measurement method before drawing any box - for example 'answer is grounded in a retrieved chunk, judged by an LLM judge with kappa above 0.6 against 150 human labels, target 95 percent on the golden set, gate at 92'. A 3 is 'we would evaluate it'. Score two of your own topic-44 recordings on this rubric first so you know your own baseline before mock 1.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Define your success criteria (test and evaluate)

subtopics.name: Four archetypes, interviewer cards and the recording rig
subtopics.learn: Pick four problems that cover disjoint ground rather than four flavours of RAG: (1) grounded question answering over a customer corpus, (2) an agent that takes write actions in the customer's systems, (3) an eval and observability platform for a fleet of LLM features, (4) high-volume batch extraction under a fixed cost ceiling in an air-gapped environment. For each, write an interviewer card with the deliberately vague opening prompt, three clarifying answers you will only give if asked, two curveballs to fire at minute 30, and one hard pushback on your primary choice. Configure the rig once: 1080p capture, mic tested, Excalidraw stencil containing gateway, queue, worker, vector index, object store, judge, trace store and a legend for sync versus async, plus a visible timer.

resource.label: Exponent - Forward Deployed Engineer interview guide

subtopics.name: Token and throughput math in three minutes
subtopics.learn: Rehearse until it is automatic: state tokens-in and tokens-out per request (chunks retrieved x chunk size + system prompt + history for input; a sentence is roughly 20 tokens, a page roughly 500), multiply by QPS to get input and output tokens per minute, and compare against the provider's ITPM and OTPM limits rather than only RPM. For self-hosted, size the KV cache as 2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element x sequence_length per sequence, subtract weights from device memory, and show how many concurrent sequences fit - that number, not the GPU count, is your concurrency. Every figure you write must be followed by the decision it changes: 'that is 4M output tokens per minute, which is over the tier limit, so we shard across two keys or move the bulk path to the batch API'.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Token counting API

subtopics.name: Latency budget: TTFT, TPOT, and every hop around the model
subtopics.learn: Draw the budget as a stacked bar before you optimise anything: auth and gateway, embedding of the query, vector search, cross-encoder rerank, prompt assembly, TTFT, then output_tokens x TPOT, then post-processing and guardrail checks. Know the shape of the two model phases - prefill is compute-bound and scales with input length, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and scales with output length - so 'shorten the prompt' fixes TTFT while 'cap max_tokens' or 'stream' fixes perceived total. Name the three levers you will actually use: stream tokens via SSE so perceived latency equals TTFT, run reranking and guardrails concurrently rather than serially, and cache the static prefix. State a target as a pair, e.g. p50 TTFT under 800 ms and p95 full answer under 6 s, and say which component you would cut first to hold it.

resource.label: vLLM docs - Optimization and tuning (TTFT, ITL, chunked prefill, batching)

subtopics.name: Cost model on the whiteboard and the three levers
subtopics.learn: Compute cost per request live: (input_tokens/1M x input_price) + (output_tokens/1M x output_price), multiply by monthly volume, and compare it to whatever the customer pays for the process today - that ratio is the only cost argument that lands. Then show the three levers with their real multipliers: prompt caching (cache writes cost more than base input, cache reads a small fraction, so it only pays when the shared prefix is large and reused within the cache TTL), the batch API (roughly half price with a 24-hour completion window, therefore only for the async path), and model tiering (a small model handles the 80 percent of requests a router classifies as easy, with escalation on low confidence). Say explicitly what each lever costs you in quality or freshness; a lever with no downside signals you have not run it.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Pricing (input, output, cache read/write, batch)

subtopics.name: Retrieval architecture that survives questioning
subtopics.learn: Be able to defend, in 90 seconds each: chunking (fixed 300-600 tokens with overlap versus structure-aware splitting, and why chunk boundaries destroy tables), hybrid retrieval (BM25 for identifiers and rare tokens, dense for paraphrase, fused with RRF), reranking (retrieve top 50-100, cross-encode down to top 10-20, and its latency cost), and contextual retrieval (prepend a short generated summary of the parent document to each chunk before embedding). Draw the index refresh path as a real pipeline with a document version, a delete tombstone and a reindex job, because deletion and staleness are where customers get burned. For multi-tenant, insist on pre-filtering by tenant_id in the vector query rather than filtering after top-k, and explain the recall collapse that post-filtering causes on small tenants.

resource.label: Anthropic Engineering - Introducing Contextual Retrieval

subtopics.name: The agent loop: step budget, durability, human-in-the-loop
subtopics.learn: When the problem involves actions, draw the loop explicitly: planner or model call, tool selection, tool execution, observation, termination check. Then draw the four controls a customer will demand: a hard step and token budget with a defined behaviour at exhaustion (escalate to human, never silently truncate), idempotency keys on every write tool so a retry cannot double-charge, an approval gate on the subset of tools with irreversible effects, and durable execution so a worker crash resumes rather than replays side effects. State the workflow-versus-agent decision out loud: if the steps are known, a deterministic workflow with LLM steps inside is cheaper, more testable and easier to sell than a free-running agent, and saying so is a seniority signal.

resource.label: Anthropic Engineering - Building effective agents

subtopics.name: Evals drawn as infrastructure, not promised as a slide
subtopics.learn: Put four concrete boxes on the diagram: an offline golden set (100-300 labelled cases, versioned in git, built from real customer traffic plus adversarial cases) run in CI as a required check with a regression threshold; an online scorer sampling a percentage of production traces and writing scores back to the trace; a human review queue fed by low-confidence and low-score traces, whose labels flow back into the golden set; and a dataset builder that promotes interesting production traces into fixtures. Name the judge design - pointwise with a rubric versus pairwise against a reference, why you randomise position to fight position bias, and that you report agreement with human labels before trusting the judge as a gate. Give the metric a target and a gate value, and say what you do when the gate fails on a release you must ship.

resource.label: Langfuse Docs - Evaluation overview (datasets, experiments, scores)

subtopics.name: Guardrails, injection and tenant isolation as design elements
subtopics.learn: Treat every retrieved chunk and every tool output as untrusted input in the design, not as an afterthought: the classic break is a document in the customer's own corpus containing instructions that the model follows. Draw the mitigations as boxes - structural separation of instructions from data, a tool allowlist scoped to the caller's permissions rather than the agent's, output handling that never renders model output as HTML or executes it, and an egress check on anything the model emits toward an external system. Add the tenancy layer: per-tenant index namespace or mandatory metadata filter, per-tenant keys and rate limits, PII redaction before the payload leaves the perimeter, and prompt-and-completion logging with masking so the trace store does not become the biggest PII repository the customer owns.

resource.label: OWASP GenAI - LLM01: Prompt Injection

subtopics.name: Serving choice: hosted API versus self-hosted vLLM
subtopics.learn: Be ready to justify either direction with numbers rather than preference. Hosted wins on time to value, model quality, elasticity and no GPU ops; self-hosted wins when data cannot leave, when volume is high and steady enough to beat per-token pricing, or when the customer needs a fine-tuned or open-weight model. If self-hosted, name the knobs: tensor parallel size, gpu_memory_utilization, max_model_len, max_num_seqs and max_num_batched_tokens, prefix caching for the shared system prompt, and quantisation to fit a larger model on the same card. Say what continuous batching does to the latency-versus-throughput trade-off, and give a rough utilisation break-even so the customer's finance team sees the reasoning rather than an assertion.

resource.label: vLLM documentation (serving, engine args, deployment)

subtopics.name: Gateway layer: routing, fallback ladders, rate limits, canary
subtopics.learn: Draw one gateway in front of every model call and load it with the things a customer actually needs: per-tenant token buckets on both requests and tokens, a queue with admission control that sheds with a clear 429 and Retry-After rather than queueing forever, retries with exponential backoff and jitter that respect 429 and 529 differently from 500, a per-request timeout larger than p99 TTFT plus expected generation, and a fallback ladder (primary model, then a smaller or alternate-provider model, then a cached or templated response, then an honest failure). Say the dangerous part out loud: a fallback that silently degrades quality without emitting a metric is worse than an error, so every fallback fires a counter and is visible on the eval dashboard. Add canaries by tenant percentage gated on eval scores, not just error rate and latency.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Rate limits (RPM, ITPM, OTPM, 429 and 529 handling)

subtopics.name: Failure modes, curveballs and the operability close
subtopics.learn: Rehearse a fixed close: the four golden signals plus four LLM-specific ones (grounding or judge score, refusal and fallback rate, tokens and dollars per request, p95 TTFT), the three alerts you would actually page on, and the rollback unit - which for an LLM system is usually a prompt version or a model pin, not a deployment. Pre-drill eight curveballs and answer each by pointing at the diagram, quantifying and choosing within three minutes: provider outage, 10x volume, one tenant is 70 percent of traffic, the customer forbids data egress, quality drops after a model version change, a document must be deleted for GDPR within 24 hours, the customer wants citations for every sentence, and the cost ceiling is halved. Understand cascading failure specifically for LLM stacks: retries on a saturated model endpoint amplify load exactly when TTFT is already degraded.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Addressing Cascading Failures

subtopics.name: The FDE twist: designing inside the customer's constraints
subtopics.learn: Practise the swap table until the redesign takes 60 seconds on the board: hosted model to self-hosted open-weight in the customer's VPC; managed vector database to pgvector in their existing Postgres; SaaS trace store to self-hosted; provider batch API to your own queue and worker pool. Know the data-control vocabulary customers use - zero data retention, no training on inputs, regional processing, BYO key encryption, audit log of every prompt and completion - and where each is a provider setting versus your own responsibility. In the mock, ask the constraint question in the requirements phase rather than discovering it at minute 35: 'can prompts containing customer content leave your network, and does the answer differ for the pilot and for production?'

resource.label: OpenAI Platform - Your data (retention, training, controls)

subtopics.name: Mock 1 - grounded QA over a customer's document corpus
subtopics.learn: Prompt: 'Design an assistant that answers questions over 2 million internal documents for 40 enterprise tenants, with citations.' Solo, timed, recorded. Non-negotiables for a pass: a stated grounding metric with target and gate; ingestion drawn as a versioned pipeline with deletes and reindex; hybrid retrieval plus rerank with the latency cost accounted; tenant isolation by pre-filter; a latency budget with streaming; cost per question and the caching lever; and the answer to 'what happens when the corpus does not contain the answer' being an explicit abstain path, not a hope. Immediately after the timer, write three bullets of raw impression before watching anything.

resource.label: Anthropic Cookbook (RAG, citations, evaluation notebooks)

subtopics.name: Mock 2 - agent platform with write access to customer systems
subtopics.learn: Prompt: 'Design a system where an agent resolves support tickets by reading a knowledge base and taking actions in Zendesk and the customer's billing system.' Non-negotiables: workflow-versus-agent decision stated with a reason; tool schemas and an authorisation model tied to the requesting user, not a service account with god rights; idempotency on every write; step and token budget with a defined exhaustion behaviour; durable execution for crash recovery; an approval gate on irreversible tools; a full audit trail linking trace id to the action taken; and a prompt-injection story for the knowledge base. Expect the curveball 'a malicious ticket instructs the agent to refund itself' and answer it on the diagram.

resource.label: Anthropic Engineering - How we built our multi-agent research system

subtopics.name: Mock 3 - eval and observability platform for a fleet of LLM features
subtopics.learn: Prompt: 'A customer has 12 teams shipping LLM features and no idea which ones are getting worse. Design the platform that tells them.' This is the archetype most candidates fumble because it has no model in the hot path. Non-negotiables: a trace data model (trace, span, generation, score, session, user) with cost and token attributes; ingestion sized for high-cardinality writes with sampling and an async collector; prompt versioning linked to traces so a regression is attributable to a change; datasets built from production traces; scheduled and CI-triggered experiments; judge calibration against human labels; masking and retention for PII; and per-team dashboards with an alert on score drift rather than only error rate.

resource.label: Langfuse Docs (tracing data model, prompt management, experiments)

subtopics.name: Mock 4 - high-volume extraction under a hard cost ceiling, air-gapped
subtopics.learn: Prompt: 'Extract 30 structured fields from 40 million scanned documents per year. It must run inside the customer's data centre and the unit cost must be under a stated ceiling.' Non-negotiables: throughput and GPU maths done live (tokens per document, batch size, tokens per second per GPU, GPUs needed for the SLA window); a self-hosted serving design with the vLLM knobs named; a cheap-model-first cascade with escalation on schema-validation failure or low confidence; structured output enforcement and what you do with a malformed response; a dead-letter path with human review; checkpointing and resumability for a multi-day job; and a sampling-based quality measurement because you cannot label 40 million documents. Then defend the ceiling with arithmetic when the interviewer halves it.

resource.label: Exponent - free peer mock interview practice

subtopics.name: Self-review protocol, score table and the pattern ledger
subtopics.learn: For each recording, watch at 1.5x with the rubric open and log phase-transition timestamps against the planned budget, every filler stall longer than five seconds, every question you answered with an adjective instead of a number, and every moment you drew a box you could not defend. Maintain three columns per mock: 'said', 'should have said', 'did not know' - the third column is the only one that generates study, and if it is empty you chose problems that were too easy. Keep a running pattern ledger of reusable answers (latency budget template, cost formula, judge calibration script, fallback ladder, tenancy filter) so mock 4 costs less preparation than mock 1. Ship only when three consecutive mocks score 4 or better on all six dimensions, including LLM-specific depth and evaluation.

resource.label: Hello Interview - System Design in a Hurry: Core Concepts

outcomes: You can take an underspecified LLM prompt to a written set of requirements in six minutes that includes a measurable quality bar with a target and a measurement method, a latency target expressed as TTFT and total, a cost ceiling per request, and an explicit statement of where customer data is allowed to go.

You can compute, in under four minutes and out loud, tokens in and out per request, tokens per minute against provider ITPM and OTPM limits, cost per request and per month, and - for self-hosted - concurrent sequences from KV cache maths, naming for each number the design decision it changes.

You can draw an evaluation and observability subsystem as boxes on the diagram before minute 40 in every mock, including golden set in CI with a gate value, online sampling and scoring, a human review queue feeding labels back, and judge agreement against human labels.

You can deep dive retrieval or the agent loop for at least seven minutes with two named options, a quantified reason for your choice, its dominant failure mode, and the metric you would watch to catch it.

You can answer any of eight rehearsed curveballs (provider outage, 10x volume, hot tenant, no data egress, model version regression, GDPR delete, per-sentence citations, halved cost ceiling) in three minutes by locating it on the diagram, quantifying it and committing to a choice.

You can perform the constraint swap - hosted model to in-VPC open weights, managed vector store to pgvector, SaaS tracing to self-hosted, batch API to your own queue - in under 90 seconds and state precisely what is lost in each swap.
You can score your own recording against your six-dimension rubric with timestamped evidence and land within half a point of a peer's independent score on at least four dimensions.
You can show three consecutive mocks at 4/5 or better on every dimension, evidenced by the recordings, the exported diagrams and the score table with the 'did not know' column emptying over time.
failureModes: The design assumes a hosted provider throughout; the customer's security review then forbids prompts leaving their network, and the whole retrieval, serving and tracing stack has to be re-chosen on site because the in-VPC swap was never rehearsed.

Multi-tenant retrieval filters by tenant_id after the top-k vector search, so small tenants get near-empty result sets and their users are told the answer is not in the corpus while the documents sit in the index.

A document deleted for a GDPR request is removed from the source of truth but never tombstoned in the vector index, so the assistant keeps citing it for weeks and the customer discovers it before your monitoring does.

The fallback ladder silently drops to a smaller model during a provider incident with no counter and no eval score attached, so quality degrades for two days and the customer's first signal is an angry end user rather than a dashboard.
The agent's write tools run under a service account with broad permissions and no idempotency key, so a retried step double-refunds a customer and the audit log cannot prove which invocation did it.

Cost was estimated on average prompt length; production prompts carry conversation history and ten retrieved chunks, input tokens triple, prompt caching never hits because the prefix changes per request, and the bill lands at four times the number given to the customer's finance team.

The LLM-as-judge gate was never calibrated against human labels, so it passes a release that humans consider clearly worse, the team stops trusting the gate within a month, and it is disabled in CI without being replaced.
interviewQuestions: Design a grounded question-answering system over two million documents for forty enterprise tenants, one of which will not allow any data to leave their network. Give me the shared architecture, then tell me exactly which components change for that tenant and what capability they lose.

You are told the assistant is 'not accurate enough'. Before touching the prompt, how do you determine whether the problem is retrieval, the generation step, the chunking, or the question distribution - and what measurement distinguishes each?

Walk me through your latency budget for a streamed answer with a p95 target of six seconds. Where does the time actually go, which component would you cut first, and how does the answer change if the customer requires reranking and a guardrail check on the output?

Your agent takes write actions in the customer's billing system. Design the boundary: authorisation model, idempotency, approval gates, step budget, audit trail, and the test that proves a malicious document in the knowledge base cannot trigger a refund.
The customer wants unit cost cut by half without a quality drop they can notice. Give me the levers in order, quantify each one, and tell me which of them you would refuse to pull and why.

I want to push back: you chose a self-hosted open-weight model on four GPUs instead of a hosted API. Defend it with arithmetic, tell me the volume at which the decision flips, and describe the migration for a live customer if it flips.

How would you gate a deployment on an LLM-as-judge score when you have 150 human labels and no baseline? Tell me the agreement number below which you would refuse to ship the gate, and what you would do instead in the meantime.
84.proofOfWork: A public `llm-design-mocks` repository (or a section of the FDE dashboard) that a hiring manager can skim in ten minutes and a peer can reuse in one, built around a reusable LLM Design Kit rather than four one-off recordings. It contains `rubric.md` with the six dimensions defined as observable behaviours at each of 1-5, plus a score table for all four mocks showing self-score, peer score and the per-dimension gap, with the three consecutive 4/5 sessions highlighted; four exported Excalidraw diagrams, each with the requirements, token maths and cost-per-request written on the canvas as they were during the session, alongside a `scorecard-NN.md` listing phase-transition timestamps against the planned budget and the 'said / should have said / did not know' table; and the kit itself - a one-page latency budget template with the TTFT and TPOT decomposition, a cost-per-request spreadsheet with cache-hit, batch and model-tier levers wired as formulas, a curveball card deck with the eight scenarios and your three-minute answers, and a constraint swap table mapping each hosted component to its in-VPC equivalent with the capability lost. The differentiator is a short `calibration.md` showing one small runnable artifact: a judge prompt scored against 50 hand-labelled examples with the agreement number reported, which turns the eval section of every mock from an assertion into something you have actually measured.

85.topic: Coding drills: data manipulation and AI-assisted production builds
85.why: The FDE coding round is not a LeetCode round - it is a simulation of the thing you do on day three of an engagement: a customer hands you a CSV export or read access to a schema nobody documented, and you have to produce a defensible number while someone watches. Databricks, Palantir and Anthropic-style loops score two axes at once - can you actually manipulate data under time pressure, and can you keep a human in the loop while you do it - which means silence is scored as failure even when the code is right. The AI-assisted half is now standard because the job is now standard: you will build customer code with an assistant in the room, and the interviewer is watching whether you review what it wrote or paste it and hope.
prerequisites: Python you can type without a tutorial open: comprehensions, dict/set idioms, collections.Counter and defaultdict, itertools.groupby, dataclasses, and the csv/json/datetime standard-library modules - the working level assumed by topic 25 (Production Python architecture).
PostgreSQL at the depth of topic 29: window functions, CTEs, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, join algorithms, and NULL semantics. You should already know why NOT IN with a nullable subquery returns nothing.
pytest fluency from topic 35 - fixtures, parametrize, tmp_path - because in the AI-assisted drills the test is the thing you write first and the thing the interviewer will ask you to run.

The AI engineering working set: structured outputs and tool schemas (topic 47), evals as infrastructure (topic 53), and provider fluency across the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs (topic 60) - the 45-minute builds assume you can call a model with a strict schema without reading docs.
The take-home scaffolding and recording rig from topic 74: a clone-and-go repo template, OBS or QuickTime configured, and a habit of one-take recordings.
Demo and narration craft from topic 68 - talking over a screen share for ten minutes without filler, and stating a trade-off in one sentence.

subtopics.name: Reverse-engineer the actual coding bar and write the self-grade rubric
subtopics.learn: Before drilling, decide what you are drilling for. Read the published FDE loop structures and note the pattern: a 45-60 minute data-manipulation round (pandas or SQL on a provided dataset, easy-to-medium difficulty, hard time limit) plus an increasingly common AI-assisted build round where an assistant is allowed and reviewing its output is part of the test. Write a five-axis rubric you will score every recording against: correctness of the final number, correctness of the method (did you validate the join, or just merge and move on), time discipline (first correct partial answer before minute 15), narration continuity (longest silence in seconds), and recovery (what you did when you were wrong). Grade two of your own past sessions against it first; if you cannot make the rubric discriminate, it is too vague to improve against.

resource.label: Exponent - Databricks Forward Deployed Engineer interview guide

subtopics.name: Continuous narration protocol: never go silent for more than fifteen seconds
subtopics.learn: Narration is a mechanical skill and it degrades exactly when you need it - the moment you hit a bug. Drill four fixed phrases until they are automatic: (1) restate the ask and the output shape - 'you want one row per customer per month with revenue and refund rate, I will produce a DataFrame with those four columns'; (2) announce before you type - 'I'm going to check dtypes and null counts before I aggregate, because if amount came in as object the sum will silently concatenate'; (3) name the assumption out loud with its falsifier - 'I'm assuming order_id is unique; if the merge inflates row count I'm wrong and I'll dedupe on the max updated_at'; (4) narrate the failure without apologising - 'that returned 1.2 million rows, more than either input, so this is a fan-out on a non-unique key; I'll check value_counts on the join key'. Practise the hardest case explicitly: keep talking while reading a traceback. Set a rule that any silence over fifteen seconds must be filled with 'let me say what I'm looking at' and then read the error aloud.

resource.label: Exercism - Python track (timed practice exercises)

subtopics.name: Build the drill rig: fixture datasets, timer, one-take recording, grade sheet
subtopics.learn: Assemble the harness once so no drill costs setup time. Curate three real, messy CSV corpora from your own exports (bank or payments transactions, a CRM or email-tool export, and a log or event stream) at 50k-2M rows, each with genuine defects: mixed date formats, thousands separators in numeric columns, trailing whitespace in keys, duplicated rows with different updated_at, and a column that is 40% null. Load the same data into a local Postgres via docker compose so every question can be asked in both pandas and SQL. Set up a visible countdown timer in the recorded frame, a scratch notebook template with the first cell already doing df.info(), df.isna().sum() and df.head(), and a GRADES.md table with one row per drill and columns for the five rubric axes plus longest-silence seconds. Record at 1080p with a large terminal font - unreadable text makes the tape useless for review.

resource.label: OBS Studio (open-source screen recording)

subtopics.name: pandas operation vocabulary you must type cold, no lookup
subtopics.learn: Rehearse the ~15 operations that cover the overwhelming majority of interview data manipulation until muscle memory: groupby().agg() with named aggregations (df.groupby(['a','b']).agg(rev=('amount','sum'), n=('id','nunique')).reset_index()), transform for group-broadcast columns, merge with explicit how and validate='one_to_many', concat with ignore_index, pivot_table with aggfunc and fill_value versus melt for long form, sort_values with ascending as a list, drop_duplicates(subset=..., keep='last') after a sort, assign for chained derivation, query and boolean masks with parentheses around each condition, loc-based assignment to avoid SettingWithCopyWarning, nlargest/rank(method='dense'), cut and qcut for bucketing, and value_counts(dropna=False). Know the two idioms for 'top N per group' - sort_values then groupby().head(n), and rank over a transform - and which one is faster. Drill by writing each from a blank cell against your fixture data and checking the shape of the result before looking at the values.

resource.label: pandas User Guide - Group by: split-apply-combine

subtopics.name: Dirty-data reflexes: dtypes, missing-value semantics, and parsing
subtopics.learn: The interview dataset is dirty on purpose, and the score is decided in the first three minutes. Build a fixed opening move: df.info(), df.isna().sum(), df.nunique(), df.describe(include='all'), and df.duplicated().sum(). Then know the specific traps and their fixes - an object-dtype numeric column from thousands separators or currency symbols (pd.to_numeric(s.str.replace(r'[^0-9.\-]','',regex=True), errors='coerce') and count the coerced NaNs, do not hide them); mixed date formats (pd.to_datetime(..., format='mixed', errors='coerce') or explicit format plus a fallback pass, and never trust dayfirst inference); float NaN versus pd.NA versus None and why NaN != NaN breaks equality filters; integer columns that become float64 the moment a null appears, and Int64 nullable dtype as the fix; whitespace and case in join keys (str.strip().str.lower()) which is the single most common silent zero-match cause; and category dtype for memory when a key column has 20 distinct values over 2M rows. Say the null count out loud every time you coerce - interviewers are listening for whether you noticed you destroyed data.

resource.label: pandas User Guide - Working with missing data

subtopics.name: SQL window functions under time pressure
subtopics.learn: Window functions are the single highest-yield SQL topic in FDE loops because they are how every 'compare each row to its group' question is answered. Get fluent enough to write without hesitation: ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK with PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY and know exactly how they differ on ties; LAG/LEAD with the offset and default arguments for period-over-period deltas; SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) for rolling windows, and the critical distinction between ROWS and RANGE frames when the order key has duplicates; FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE and why LAST_VALUE needs an explicit frame to do what you meant; NTILE for bucketing; and named windows via the WINDOW clause when three expressions share a frame. Know the ordering rule that WHERE cannot reference a window result, so top-N-per-group needs a CTE or subquery in Postgres - and that Snowflake and Databricks give you QUALIFY instead. Drill by writing the same 'second-highest order per customer' query three ways.

resource.label: PostgreSQL - Window Functions (function reference)

subtopics.name: Join semantics, NULL traps, and aggregation correctness in SQL
subtopics.learn: Most wrong answers in a SQL round are join or NULL bugs, not syntax. Internalise: LEFT JOIN plus a filter on the right table's column in WHERE silently becomes an INNER JOIN (the predicate must move into the ON clause); a join on a non-unique key fans out rows and inflates every downstream SUM, so the reflex is to check counts before and after and use COUNT(DISTINCT id) or pre-aggregate the many-side in a CTE; NOT IN with a subquery containing a single NULL returns zero rows while NOT EXISTS does the right thing; COUNT(col) skips NULLs but COUNT(*) does not; AVG ignores NULLs so a mean over a partially-null column is over a different denominator than you think; and integer division truncates unless you cast. Know COALESCE versus NULLIF, FILTER (WHERE ...) on aggregates as the clean alternative to CASE-inside-SUM, and DISTINCT ON as the Postgres shortcut for per-group latest. Practise stating the invariant before running: 'this should return exactly one row per customer per month; I will assert that with a GROUP BY HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 check.'

resource.label: PostgreSQL - Table Expressions (joins, ON vs WHERE, lateral)

subtopics.name: AI-assisted build: rules of engagement and review discipline
subtopics.learn: In the assistant-allowed round the assistant is not the subject - your control loop is. Fix a protocol before the drills: state the plan and the file layout out loud before prompting; prompt in units small enough to review in under a minute (one function, one endpoint, one test file) rather than 'build the whole thing'; read every generated diff line by line out loud, naming what you accept and what you reject and why; write or at least specify the tests yourself so the assistant cannot grade its own homework; and never paste code you cannot explain. Know the specific things assistants get wrong that you must catch on sight: invented library functions and kwargs, silent except: pass, off-by-one in slicing and date ranges, timezone-naive datetimes mixed with aware ones, no pagination on a list endpoint, secrets or absolute paths hardcoded, and tests that assert the implementation rather than the behaviour. Practise saying 'I'm rejecting this because...' - the sentence the interviewer is waiting for.

resource.label: Claude Developer Platform documentation

subtopics.name: Drill 1 (25 min, recorded): messy transaction CSV to a reconciled monthly metric
subtopics.learn: Timed pandas drill on the payments corpus. Task: produce monthly net revenue per customer segment from a raw export where amount has currency symbols, dates come in two formats, refunds appear as separate negative rows with a matching original_transaction_id, and roughly 3% of rows are exact duplicates from a re-export. Requirements you must hit inside 25 minutes: profile first and say the row count and null counts aloud; dedupe explicitly with a stated key; coerce numerics and report how many values failed to parse; produce one row per (segment, month) with revenue, refund_amount, refund_rate and transaction count; and finish with a reconciliation - the sum of your output must equal the sum of the cleaned input, asserted in code, not eyeballed. Score yourself on whether you had a defensible partial answer by minute 15.

resource.label: pandas User Guide - IO tools (read_csv parsing options, dtypes, parse_dates)

subtopics.name: Drill 2 (25 min, recorded): multi-table join with fan-out you must catch
subtopics.learn: Timed pandas drill designed so the naive answer is wrong. Given orders, order_items, customers and a customers_history table with one row per attribute change, compute revenue per customer tier as of the order date. The traps: joining customers_history without an as-of condition multiplies every order by the number of history rows; order_items has a many relationship to orders so a naive merge inflates order-level totals; and a few customer_ids exist in orders but not customers. Do it correctly with merge(..., validate='m:1') to make the fan-out raise instead of silently corrupting, an explicit pre-aggregation of order_items before joining up, and pd.merge_asof for the point-in-time tier lookup with by= and direction='backward'. Narrate the row-count check after every merge - 'orders was 84,102 rows, after the merge it is 84,102, good' - because that sentence is what a senior reviewer is listening for.

resource.label: pandas User Guide - Merge, join, concatenate and compare

subtopics.name: Drill 3 (25 min, recorded): event stream sessionisation and rolling windows
subtopics.learn: Timed pandas drill on the event corpus. Task: from raw timestamped events, define sessions with a 30-minute inactivity gap per user, then report median session length, events per session, and a 7-day rolling count of active users. The mechanics you must execute cleanly: sort by user and timestamp, compute the gap with groupby('user_id')['ts'].diff(), build session ids with (gap > pd.Timedelta('30min')).groupby(level).cumsum(), aggregate per session, then resample('D') and rolling('7D') on a DatetimeIndex. Handle the real complications out loud: timestamps arriving as UTC strings that must be tz-localised before comparison (mixing naive and aware raises), days with zero events that must appear as zeros rather than be dropped by groupby, and a user whose clock is skewed producing a negative diff. Report medians and p95, not means.

resource.label: pandas User Guide - Time series and date functionality

subtopics.name: Drill 4 (30 min, recorded): SQL window analytics on an undocumented schema
subtopics.learn: Timed SQL drill against your local Postgres with the schema shown but not explained - the realistic customer situation. Answer four escalating questions in one session: monthly revenue with month-over-month percent change using LAG; each customer's second-largest order using ROW_NUMBER in a CTE; a 28-day trailing average of daily orders with an explicit ROWS frame; and each customer's rank within their segment by lifetime value with ties handled by DENSE_RANK. Constraints that make it real: you must first orient yourself out loud by querying the catalog (information_schema.columns, plus a quick COUNT(*) and a five-row sample per table) rather than assuming, and every query must be preceded by a one-sentence statement of the expected grain of the result. Verify each result with an independent check - a spot-check on one customer computed a different way.

resource.label: PostgreSQL Tutorial - Window Functions

subtopics.name: Drill 5 (30 min, recorded): dedupe, point-in-time correctness, gaps and islands
subtopics.learn: Timed SQL drill on the three patterns that separate people who have shipped customer pipelines from people who have not. One: deduplicate a change-data-capture table to the latest row per business key using ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC) = 1, and explain why the tiebreak column matters when updated_at is not unique. Two: an as-of join - attach the price that was in effect when each order was placed, using a LATERAL subquery or a range-bounded join, and demonstrate the wrong answer you get without it. Three: gaps and islands - find each customer's longest run of consecutive active months using the difference-of-row-numbers trick, and separately find the missing months with generate_series and a LEFT JOIN. Say the grain and the expected row count before executing every one.

resource.label: PostgreSQL - WITH Queries (Common Table Expressions)

subtopics.name: Drill 6 (45 min, recorded, AI-assisted): CSV to a tested, runnable service
subtopics.learn: Timed build with an assistant in the loop. Deliverable: a small FastAPI service that ingests one of your messy CSVs, normalises it, and exposes GET /metrics with query params for date range and segment, plus a health endpoint, with pytest tests that pass and a one-command run. Sequence it deliberately - contract first (write the response Pydantic model and one failing test before any implementation), then the loader, then the endpoint, then pagination and input validation. Non-negotiables that the interviewer will look for: typed request/response models with explicit field constraints, 422 on bad input rather than a 500, a test that exercises the empty-result case and a test on the parsing of one deliberately dirty row, and no unbounded response. Narrate every accept/reject decision on generated code, and at minute 40 stop building and spend five minutes running the tests and stating what is not done.

resource.label: FastAPI - Tutorial: User Guide

subtopics.name: Drill 7 (45 min, recorded, AI-assisted): LLM extraction with strict schema and a mini eval
subtopics.learn: Timed build: turn 200 unstructured records (support tickets, invoices or emails from your own corpus) into validated structured rows. Required shape: a Pydantic model with enums and constrained types as the extraction schema, a provider call using structured output or a tool schema so the model cannot return free text, validation on the way out with a rejected-rows path rather than a silent drop, bounded concurrency with a semaphore, retries with jittered backoff on transient errors only, and a per-record cache keyed on content hash so re-runs are free. Then the part most candidates skip and the one that wins the round: hand-label 20 records, score the extractor field-by-field, and report precision on the two fields that matter plus a count of records that failed validation. Say the cost and the p95 latency out loud at the end.

resource.label: Pydantic documentation (models, validation, constrained types)

subtopics.name: Drill 8 (45 min, recorded, AI-assisted): mid-build requirement change
subtopics.learn: The realistic FDE variant: build for 25 minutes, then have a pre-written envelope change the requirement, exactly as a customer does on a Thursday. Sample changes to draw from - the metric must now be computed per timezone-local day instead of UTC; the input arrives as a stream of JSON lines instead of one CSV; the customer needs the last 12 months backfilled and the job must be idempotent on re-run; a second file format must be supported with the same output contract. What is scored is the first ninety seconds after the change: do you restate the new requirement, name what breaks, propose the smallest change that satisfies it, and say explicitly what you are dropping to fit the time - or do you silently start refactoring. Keep the existing tests green through the change, add one test that would have failed before it, and finish with a spoken summary of what shipped, what regressed, and what you would do next.

resource.label: pytest documentation (fixtures, parametrize, tmp_path)

subtopics.name: Watch the tapes: error taxonomy and the second pass
subtopics.learn: The recordings are worthless unless you mine them. For each of the eight, log in GRADES.md: minutes to first correct partial answer, longest silence in seconds, the number of times you ran code before saying what you expected it to return, every correctness bug and its class (dtype, join fan-out, NULL, timezone, off-by-one, assistant-generated), and the one sentence you wish you had said. Build a running error taxonomy and note that the same two classes will account for most of your failures - drill those specifically rather than doing more random exercises. Then do a second pass on the two worst drills under the same clock and confirm the delta with numbers, not feeling. Add assert-based self-checks to your fixture repo (pandas.testing.assert_frame_equal against a saved expected output) so future re-runs are graded automatically instead of by memory.

resource.label: pandas - Testing utilities (assert_frame_equal)

outcomes: You can profile an unfamiliar dirty dataset and state its row count, null profile, duplicate count and the two dtype problems that will bite you, out loud, within the first three minutes of a timed drill.
You can produce a correct grouped, joined and time-bucketed answer in pandas within 25 minutes on a dataset you have never seen, and reconcile the output total against the cleaned input in code.
You can write ROW_NUMBER, LAG, a ROWS-framed rolling aggregate, an as-of join and a gaps-and-islands query in SQL without a reference open, and explain the ROWS-versus-RANGE difference on demand.
You can catch a join fan-out at the moment it happens because you state the expected row count before every merge and check it after - visible on every one of your eight tapes.

You can complete a 45-minute AI-assisted build that ends with passing tests, a typed contract, and a spoken list of what is not done, having narrated an accept/reject decision on every block of generated code.
You can absorb a mid-build requirement change and, within ninety seconds, restate it, name what breaks, propose the minimal change, and say what you are cutting to fit the clock.
You keep your longest silence under fifteen seconds across all eight recordings, including while reading a traceback, measured from the tape rather than estimated.
You can show an error taxonomy across eight drills with your two dominant bug classes named, and a second-pass recording that demonstrates a measured improvement on both.
failureModes: You merge two customer tables without checking cardinality, the many-side fans out, and every revenue number you present to the customer is inflated by a factor nobody notices until finance reconciles the quarter.
A numeric column arrives as object because of thousands separators, the sum silently concatenates strings or coerces to NaN, and the dashboard ships with a metric that is off by orders of magnitude.
A LEFT JOIN with the right table's column filtered in WHERE quietly becomes an INNER JOIN, so customers with no matching rows vanish from the report and the customer's own count never matches yours.
Timestamps are compared across a mix of tz-aware and naive datetimes, so daily aggregates are shifted by hours and month boundaries land in the wrong bucket for every customer outside UTC.
You accept assistant-generated code with a bare except that swallows parse errors, and the pipeline reports success while silently discarding every malformed record for weeks.

You go quiet for four minutes debugging, the interviewer loses the thread, and the write-up says 'strong coder, unclear how they would work with a customer in the room' - which is a no for an FDE role.
You spend twenty of your twenty-five minutes perfecting ingestion and never produce a number, so there is nothing to grade on the axis that actually matters.
interviewQuestions: Here is a 900k-row export and a question about monthly revenue. Talk me through your first three minutes before you write any aggregation - what do you check and what would make you stop and ask me something?
You join orders to a customer attributes table and the row count goes from 84,000 to 310,000. Walk me through how you diagnose it and what the correct query looks like if attributes change over time.
Write, out loud, the query for each customer's second-largest order. Now do it in a dialect without QUALIFY, and tell me what changes if two orders tie exactly.
You used an assistant to generate this loader. Show me a line you rejected and tell me why - and tell me what class of bug you have learned to look for first in generated code.
Your extraction pipeline reports 98% success but the customer says records are missing. The code has no errors in the logs. How do you find out what happened?

Halfway through a build the customer says the metric must be per local business day, not UTC, and they need twelve months backfilled idempotently. What do you change, what do you drop, and what do you tell them by end of day?
You are on a screen share with a customer's data engineer and your first answer turns out to be wrong. What do you actually say, and what do you do next?
85.proofOfWork: Beyond the eight recorded drills, publish a repository called fde-drill-kit that turns your practice into a reusable, evidence-backed system another engineer could run tomorrow. It ships three synthetic-but-realistic corpora (payments, CRM and event-stream) generated by a seeded script so the defects are reproducible and documented - a defects.md naming each planted trap (mixed date formats, currency-symbol numerics, CDC duplicates with non-unique updated_at, whitespace in join keys, a tz-skewed clock, orphan foreign keys) and the query or cell that exposes it. It ships a docker compose that loads the same data into Postgres so every prompt exists in both pandas and SQL form, a prompts/ directory with all eight drill prompts written the way an interviewer would write them (underspecified, with the ambiguity deliberate), and a solutions/ directory with a reference answer plus an assert-based grader using pandas.testing.assert_frame_equal and SQL count assertions, so anyone can self-score without your judgement. The credibility comes from the evidence section: a GRADES.md with one row per drill recording minutes-to-first-partial-answer, longest silence in seconds, bug classes hit, and rubric score across all five axes, plus the second-pass rows for the two worst drills showing the measured delta; an ERRORS.md distilling the taxonomy down to your two dominant failure classes with the specific drill timestamps where each occurred; and an index page linking the eight unedited recordings. Send that one link when a recruiter asks how you prepare, and it answers the coding question and the self-improvement question at once.

86.why: The two rounds that actually decide an FDE loop are the ones with no whiteboard: a role-play where an interviewer plays a customer stakeholder who does not want you there, and a learning round where they hand you an unfamiliar API or internal DSL and expect working output in twenty minutes. Both are direct simulations of the job - week two on site you are in a room with an architect whose system you are replacing, and week three you are reading someone's undocumented internal service at 9pm because the demo is Thursday. What gets you rejected is almost never ignorance; it is talking past a hostile question, and saying 'yes, we can do that by Friday' about something that needs their security team, which is the same behaviour that kills real deployments.
prerequisites: Your narrative and motivation work from topic 72, so the sim does not stall on 'why are you here' and you can spend the whole clock on the customer's problem.

The resume-defence discipline from topic 73: numerator, denominator, window, instrument - because in a client sim you will be asked to back a claim you make about your own past work while the clock runs.
Decomposition drills (topic 75) and LLM system design mocks (topic 76): the sim collapses if you cannot cut a vague ask into a demoable slice in under five minutes.

SLO literacy from the observability/SLO topic - good events over valid events over a window - so 'we need it to be 100% accurate' becomes a negotiable threshold conversation rather than a promise or a fight.

Enough hands-on fluency from topics 25-30 and 45-49 (Python services, Postgres, RAG, evals) that the technical objections in the sim - schema, latency, PII, retrieval quality - land on real knowledge rather than talking points.
Two or three practice partners willing to play adversarial for 45 minutes without rescuing you, plus a recording setup (screen + audio) and a transcription tool you have already tested end to end.

subtopics.name: Reverse-engineer what each round actually scores
subtopics.learn: Write the two rubrics before you practise anything, because you cannot improve against a vibe. Client sim scores roughly: discovery quality (did you find the real constraint, or the one they volunteered), structure (did the conversation have a shape and an ending), pushback handling (did you stay in the room), commitment hygiene (did you promise things you do not control), and closing (is there a dated next step with named owners). Learning interview scores: how fast you get to a first working call, whether your questions are falsifying rather than clarifying, whether you narrate a mental model out loud, and how quickly you notice and correct a wrong assumption. Convert each dimension into a behavioural anchor you can count on tape - 'asked 9 questions before naming a solution' - not a 1-5 gut score.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Structured interview (behavioural anchors and scoring)

subtopics.name: Build four scenario packs from real deployment shapes
subtopics.learn: Write four packs your partner reads and you do not: (1) a mid-size insurer wants LLM triage on claims notes and the ops director thinks it is a headcount cut; (2) a stalled deployment where your champion left and the new VP wants to cancel in 30 days; (3) integration blocked by a security architect who will not allow data to leave the VPC; (4) a customer who was burned by the previous vendor's pilot that never reached production. Each pack gives the persona a goal, a fear, one hidden constraint that only surfaces if you ask the right question (e.g. the 'API' is a nightly SFTP drop of fixed-width files), and three landmines to detonate at minute 10, 25 and 35. Add a success bar per pack: exactly what you must have extracted and committed to for it to count as a pass.

resource.label: CISA Tabletop Exercise Packages - scenario design with objectives, injects and discussion questions

subtopics.name: The ten-minute pre-brief you run before any customer call
subtopics.learn: Standardise a pre-call kit and run it before every sim so it is muscle memory on site: how the company makes money and which line item your work touches; the org around your champion (who signs, who blocks, who gets blamed); the systems of record they already run (Salesforce? SAP? a Snowflake they just migrated to?); public signals - 10-K risk factors, earnings call language, job postings that reveal their stack, status page incident history, engineering blog. Turn it into three written hypotheses about where the pain is, each phrased so a single question in the meeting can kill it. Walking in with hypotheses is what separates discovery from an interrogation.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Form 10-K (risk factors, MD&A, segment reporting)

subtopics.name: The discovery ladder: symptom to workflow to system to metric
subtopics.learn: Drill a fixed four-rung sequence. Symptom: 'what happens today, walk me through the last time it went wrong.' Workflow: who touches it, in what order, in which tool, and what do they do when the tool is wrong. System: what is the system of record, what writes to it, how does data arrive and at what cadence, what is the actual schema. Metric: volume per day, minutes per unit, error rate, cost of a false positive versus a false negative, and who currently owns that number. Ban solution-shaped questions ('would you want a dashboard?') until you are on the fourth rung - the customer will happily design the wrong thing with you. Practise until you can run all four rungs in eight minutes without a script.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Five whys (root-cause questioning and its limits)

subtopics.name: Constraint and authority elicitation in the room
subtopics.learn: Get the boring blockers on the table in the first meeting, because they are what actually slip deployments: where the data physically lives and whether you can get a sample this week, who provisions credentials and how long that has historically taken, whether there is a VPC/air-gap/on-prem requirement, whether a DPA or vendor security review is needed and who runs it, what date is genuinely fixed (board demo, audit, contract renewal) and what happens if it slips. Then map authority explicitly - who is responsible, who approves, who must merely be consulted or informed - and ask out loud 'who else has to say yes after this meeting?' Anyone you fail to name will surface in week four as a surprise veto.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Responsibility assignment matrix (RACI)

subtopics.name: Hostile stakeholder taxonomy and what each one actually wants
subtopics.learn: Learn the five archetypes and the tell for each. The threatened incumbent built the pipeline you are replacing and attacks your design because attacking his own record is unthinkable - he wants credit and continuity, so make him the owner of the interface. The burned buyer opens with 'the last vendor promised this too' and wants a checkable near-term proof, not a roadmap. The gatekeeper architect asks latency and encryption questions as a proxy for control - answer precisely, then ask him to define the acceptance bar. The proxy attends for an absent decision-maker and cannot say yes, only no - your goal is a meeting with the principal. The budget skeptic wants a number tied to their own P&L line. Misreading which one you are facing produces technically correct answers that lose the room.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Chesterton's fence (why the existing system exists)

subtopics.name: De-escalation mechanics: acknowledge, specify, bound
subtopics.learn: Under attack, run a three-beat pattern instead of defending. Acknowledge by restating the objection more precisely than they stated it ('you are saying that if the classifier is wrong on a high-value claim, your adjuster carries the liability, not us'). Specify by separating the factual claim from the fear - which part is measurable, which part is trust. Bound by giving an answer with a number and a condition ('on the 200 notes you gave us, precision at the threshold we would ship is X; below that we route to a human'). Never counter-assert, never 'actually', never speed up. On tape, watch for the physical tells - words per minute jumping, filler stacking, the pronoun switching from 'we' to 'I' - because interviewers score composure from exactly those signals.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Active listening (reflection, paraphrase, clarification)

subtopics.name: Disagreeing on technical substance without losing the room
subtopics.learn: Rehearse the three standard wrong asks and hold the line on each. 'Just fine-tune it on our data' - agree with the goal, name why retrieval and evals come first, offer a cheap test that settles it. 'Put everything in the vector database' - ask what queries must be answered and show which ones need filters, joins or recency that similarity search will not give. 'It has to be 100% accurate' - reframe as an error budget: what is the cost of each error class, what threshold routes to a human, what is the review loop. The move is always: accept the objective, name the constraint that breaks their approach, propose a decisive experiment with a date. Practise saying 'I think that will not work, and here is the test that would prove me wrong' out loud until it sounds calm.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives (error budgets)

subtopics.name: Security, PII and data-residency objections
subtopics.learn: The single most common blocker in an AI deployment conversation is 'our data cannot go to a model provider', and vague answers here read as unserious. Be able to state, without notes: enterprise zero-retention and no-training-by-default terms, in-VPC or cloud-marketplace model hosting as an alternative, what redaction at the boundary can and cannot remove, why prompt injection makes tool permissions the real attack surface rather than the prompt, and what you log for audit (inputs, outputs, retrieved doc ids, user, timestamp). Then invert the question: ask what their existing approved path for a SaaS vendor looks like, and which control they need evidence for. You are trying to convert a blanket objection into a named control with an owner.

resource.label: OWASP LLM02:2025 - Sensitive Information Disclosure (PII exposure, sanitisation limits, controls)

subtopics.name: Commitment hygiene: the four verbs you are allowed to use
subtopics.learn: Every future-tense sentence in a customer meeting is a contract. Restrict yourself to four forms: 'I will X by DATE' only when every dependency is inside your control; 'I will find out and come back to you by DATE' for anything that needs someone else; 'we could X, which would cost roughly Y' for an option that is explicitly not yet a commitment; and 'we will not do X' as a stated boundary. Ban the killers outright - 'that should be easy', 'we can definitely', 'by end of week' about anything crossing a team boundary, 'no problem'. Practise catching yourself mid-sentence and converting: 'we can have that by Friday' becomes 'I can have the pipeline running Friday if I have read access by Tuesday; the SSO piece depends on your identity team, so I will get you a date from them by Wednesday.'

resource.label: Wikipedia - Statement of work (deliverables, acceptance, dependencies)

subtopics.name: Estimating live without lying
subtopics.learn: When asked 'how long', never emit a single number. Decompose out loud into 3-5 chunks (access and data landing, ingest and normalisation, the model/logic slice, evaluation, the integration to their system of record), give a range on each, and name the top two uncertainty drivers plus the assumption that would blow the estimate up ('this assumes the notes are text, not scanned PDFs'). Anchor on a reference class - 'the last three deployments of this shape took 4-7 weeks to first production traffic' - rather than on optimism. The strongest available answer is often a timeboxed spike: 'give me three days and the sample file and I will replace this range with a real number.' Note explicitly that your estimate is conditional on a dated input from them, which makes slippage a shared fact rather than your failure.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Reference class forecasting

subtopics.name: Scope the thin slice and land the close
