You can cost a recursive solution correctly as nodes times work-per-node, and separately account for recursion depth and output size in the space answer.
failureModes: You write list.pop(0) inside a loop because it read fine on the 200-row sample; the customer's 2 million-row nightly export turns a four-minute job into six hours and misses the delivery SLA that your team wrote into the statement of work.

You go quiet for four minutes debugging an index error, the interviewer loses the thread entirely, and the write-up reads 'competent coder, unclear how they would work in front of a customer' - which is a no for an FDE role regardless of whether the code compiled.
You reach straight for the clever O(n) solution, tangle the hash-map bookkeeping, and hand in nothing at minute 45 when the brute force you skipped would have passed and left ten minutes to optimise.

You claim O(n) for a loop that contains `if x in some_list`, the interviewer asks you to walk the complexity again, and you cannot see it - the scorecard records that you do not reason about cost, which is the exact signal the round exists to test.
A recursive DFS you shipped over a customer's dependency graph works on the 300-node test fixture and dies with RecursionError on their 50,000-node production graph, at 02:00, in a job with no retry.

You mark BFS nodes visited at dequeue rather than enqueue; the queue fills with duplicates, memory blows up on a 2000x2000 grid, and the same bug in a customer's crawler quietly multiplies API calls until they hit a rate limit.

You group customer records with a hash map keyed on a raw string that was never normalised for case and trailing whitespace, so 'Acme Corp ' and 'acme corp' become two accounts and the dedupe report you presented is wrong in the meeting.

You memorised specific solutions rather than patterns, so a one-clause variation - duplicates now allowed, k may exceed n, the array is rotated - leaves you with nothing to say and no way to rederive it.
interviewQuestions: Explain why appending to a Python list is O(1) but inserting at index 0 is O(n), what structure you use when you need both ends, and what amortized complexity means. When does the amortization argument stop being a fair thing to tell a customer?

Given an array of up to 10^5 integers and a target, decide whether two of them sum to it. Give me the brute force and its cost, then the optimisation, and tell me precisely what you traded to get it and when that trade would be the wrong one.

Write a topological sort. Now: the input is a customer's pipeline config and it contains a cycle. How does your code detect it, and what exactly does the error message say so their engineer can fix it without calling you?
Debug: this solution passes the provided samples and times out on the hidden tests. Walk me through how you find the accidental quadratic with no profiler, and what you would change first.
Your BFS over a 2000 x 2000 grid runs out of memory. Where is the memory going, what are three ways to cut it, and which one would you pick if this were running on a customer's 2 GB container?

When is a heap the right answer instead of just sorting, and vice versa? Give me the concrete n and k where you would switch, and tell me how you would get a max-heap and a stable tiebreak out of Python's heapq.
You are 25 minutes into a 45-minute screen. You have a working O(n^2) and you can see an O(n log n) but you are not sure you can land it. What do you do, and what exactly do you say to me?
92.proofOfWork: Beyond the tagged 60-problem log and the three recorded mocks, publish `patterns-from-memory` - a single reference module plus test suite that proves recall rather than recognition. It contains one file per pattern (two_pointers.py, sliding_window.py, binary_search.py, heap_topk.py, monotonic_stack.py, linked_list.py, tree_traversals.py, graph_bfs_dfs.py, toposort.py, union_find.py, backtracking.py, dp.py), each written from a blank file in a single timed sitting with the stopwatch time recorded in the module docstring alongside the invariant, the time and space complexity, and the one failure mode that template exists to prevent. Every file has a pytest suite with parametrized samples plus a brute-force reference and a Hypothesis-style random fuzz loop that shrinks to the smallest failing input, and the whole thing runs in GitHub Actions so a reviewer can see it green. Add a BENCHMARKS.md that reproduces two of the failure modes with real numbers on your own machine - list.pop(0) versus deque.popleft at n = 200k, and `in list` versus `in set` at n = 100k - because the point of the artifact is not that you can solve puzzles but that you can predict cost before a customer discovers it. Finish with a one-page COMPLEXITY-CARD.md, the sheet you would hand a customer's junior engineer during an engagement: the container cost table, the operations-per-second rule of thumb, and the six questions to ask before writing a loop over their data.

93.topic: Linear algebra for ML: vectors, matrices, eigendecomposition, SVD
93.why: Every model an FDE deploys is a matrix problem in disguise: a regression whose coefficients flip sign, a PCA that keeps the wrong components, an embedding index that returns the same five documents for every query, and a fine-tune that refuses to learn are all diagnosable from a singular-value spectrum in under five minutes. Without that you are reduced to swapping hyperparameters in front of the customer and hoping; with it you can point at a condition number of 1e12 or a rank-3 embedding table, name the cause and name the fix. It is also the layer at which you defend a model in a technical review - why the coefficients are unstable, why you kept 40 components, why rank-8 LoRA is enough - to people who will check the arithmetic on the whiteboard behind you.
prerequisites: Python 3.11 with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, Matplotlib and pytest installed - every claim in this topic is checkable in ten lines and the deliverable is a tested NumPy-only library
School algebra fluency: solving 2x2 systems by hand, the quadratic formula (you will apply it to characteristic polynomials), summation notation, and sin/cos for rotation matrices

Enough calculus to differentiate a quadratic form, since the normal equations come from setting the gradient of ||Xb - y||^2 to zero - Topic 94 (Calculus and optimisation) picks this up immediately after
Jupyter plus Matplotlib for the diagnostic plots this topic is really about: log-scale singular-value spectrum, scree, reconstruction error versus k, coefficient paths versus lambda
git and a CI runner (Topic 0, Topic 35) so the from-scratch implementations ship with tests asserting agreement with numpy.linalg to 1e-8 rather than a notebook that ran once
No prior linear algebra course is assumed; if 'the columns of A span a subspace' currently means nothing, run MIT 18.06 lectures 1-10 alongside the first two subtopics

subtopics.name: Vectors, norms, inner products and projections
subtopics.learn: Get fluent with the objects a model actually stores: a feature row, a gradient and an embedding are all vectors in R^n. Be able to compute and hand-derive the L1, L2 and L-infinity norms (np.linalg.norm(x, ord=1|2|np.inf)), the inner product identity <x,y> = ||x|| ||y|| cos(theta), the orthogonal projection of b onto span(a) as (a^T b / a^T a) a, and the residual b - proj which is orthogonal to a - that single fact is the whole of least squares. Know why cosine similarity is just the inner product of L2-normalised vectors, why it is scale-invariant while Euclidean distance is not, and why an unnormalised vector index ranks by magnitude rather than direction. Derive Cauchy-Schwarz and the triangle inequality once by hand so the bounds are yours rather than memorised.

resource.label: Maths, CS & AI Compendium - Ch. 01 Vectors

subtopics.name: Matrices as linear maps: the four fundamental subspaces and rank-nullity
subtopics.learn: Read A as the function x -> Ax and be able to state, for a concrete 4x3 matrix, its column space (which outputs are reachable), null space (which inputs are annihilated), row space and left null space, plus rank(A) + dim(null(A)) = n. Find a basis for each by hand via row reduction and in code with scipy.linalg.null_space and scipy.linalg.orth, then connect them to modelling facts: a design matrix with a redundant one-hot column plus an intercept has a non-trivial null space, so beta is not unique and any solver's coefficients are arbitrary along that direction. Know rank(AB) <= min(rank A, rank B) - the reason a width-r bottleneck layer caps the rank of everything downstream. Be able to say in one sentence what 'A is singular' means to a customer: some direction in their feature space carries no information, so its effect cannot be separated.

resource.label: MIT OCW 18.06 Linear Algebra (Strang) - lecture notes and problem sets

subtopics.name: Matrix multiplication: the four views, shapes, batching and einsum
subtopics.learn: Be able to compute AB four ways - entrywise dot products, A times each column of B, each row of A times B, and the sum of outer products sum_k a_k b_k^T - and say which view explains a given piece of code; the outer-product view is what makes low-rank updates and rank-1 gradient steps obvious. Enforce shape discipline: (n,d) @ (d,k) -> (n,k), X @ W + b for a dense layer, O(n*d*k) flops so you can predict cost before you run anything. Use np.einsum('bij,bjk->bik', A, B) and torch.matmul broadcasting for attention-shaped batched products (B, H, T, d), and know einsum is not automatically fast - pass optimize=True or inspect np.einsum_path for the contraction order. Practise reading a shape error as a modelling error, since transposed samples-versus-features is the single most common cause.

resource.label: NumPy docs - numpy.einsum (and einsum_path)

subtopics.name: Vectorisation, broadcasting, strides and what BLAS is doing underneath
subtopics.learn: Internalise the broadcasting rule - align trailing dimensions, each must be equal or 1 - and use it deliberately: X - X.mean(axis=0) centres columns, (X - mu) / sigma standardises, x[:, None] - y[None, :] builds a pairwise difference tensor, and that last one silently allocates n*m*d floats, which is how a 10k-row distance computation becomes an OOM. Know that a NumPy array is a pointer plus shape plus strides, that .T is a free view with swapped strides, that np.ascontiguousarray copies, and that A @ B dispatches to a BLAS gemm whose speed depends on that layout and on the thread count. Benchmark a Python triple loop against @ on 1000x1000 matrices and be able to quote the ratio - two to three orders of magnitude - to the customer engineer who wants to 'just loop over the rows'.

resource.label: NumPy docs - Broadcasting

subtopics.name: Orthogonality, Gram-Schmidt and the QR factorisation
subtopics.learn: Prove that for orthonormal Q you get Q^T Q = I, ||Qx|| = ||x|| and Q^-1 = Q^T, then derive classical Gram-Schmidt and demonstrate numerically why it loses orthogonality (||Q^T Q - I|| grows with the condition number on a Hilbert matrix) while modified Gram-Schmidt and Householder reflections do not. Implement Householder QR: each reflector H = I - 2 v v^T / (v^T v) zeroes everything below the diagonal of one column, giving A = QR with R upper triangular in roughly 2mn^2 - 2n^3/3 flops. Check against np.linalg.qr(A, mode='reduced') to 1e-8 and plot orthogonality loss for both Gram-Schmidt variants versus Householder. Know rank-revealing QR with column pivoting, scipy.linalg.qr(A, pivoting=True), as the cheap way to name which columns are the redundant ones.

resource.label: NumPy docs - numpy.linalg.qr (modes and LAPACK backing)

subtopics.name: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors: diagonalisation, similarity, and where it fails
subtopics.learn: State Av = lambda v, form the characteristic polynomial det(A - lambda I) = 0, and solve 2x2 cases by hand including one rotation matrix with complex eigenvalues. Understand A = P D P^-1 as a change of basis, why A^k = P D^k P^-1 makes power-iteration and Markov-chain behaviour obvious, and the two failure cases: defective matrices where algebraic multiplicity exceeds geometric multiplicity (the classic [[1,1],[0,1]]) have no eigenbasis at all, and non-symmetric matrices can have ill-conditioned eigenvectors so np.linalg.eig returns numbers that move a lot under a 1e-10 perturbation. Keep the invariants at hand - trace equals the sum of eigenvalues, determinant equals their product - and be clear that eigenvalues are not singular values unless the matrix is symmetric PSD.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Eigendecompositions

subtopics.name: Symmetric and positive semi-definite matrices: spectral theorem, Cholesky, quadratic forms
subtopics.learn: State and use the spectral theorem: every real symmetric A factors as Q Lambda Q^T with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors, so np.linalg.eigh - not eig - is the correct call for covariance, Gram and Hessian matrices; it is faster, returns sorted real eigenvalues, and never hands you an imaginary part to discard. Define PSD as x^T A x >= 0 for all x, prove any Gram matrix X^T X is PSD, and connect it to practice: a covariance estimate with a -1e-17 eigenvalue from round-off makes np.linalg.cholesky raise LinAlgError, and the fix is diagonal jitter of about 1e-6 or eigenvalue clipping, not switching library. Read a quadratic form geometrically - the Hessian's eigenvalues are curvature along its eigenvectors and their ratio is the condition number that sets how badly gradient descent zig-zags, which is where Topic 94 begins.

resource.label: NumPy docs - numpy.linalg.eigh (symmetric/Hermitian eigendecomposition)

subtopics.name: Power iteration, the Rayleigh quotient and the QR algorithm
subtopics.learn: Implement power iteration - x <- Ax / ||Ax||, with the eigenvalue estimated by the Rayleigh quotient x^T A x / x^T x - and derive its convergence rate |lambda_2 / lambda_1|^k, so you can predict that a spectral ratio of 0.99 needs hundreds of iterations and explain why PageRank's damping factor of 0.85 is precisely a spectral-gap fix. Extend to deflation, A - lambda_1 v_1 v_1^T, for the next eigenpair, then to the unshifted QR algorithm: repeat A_k = Q_k R_k, A_k+1 = R_k Q_k and watch it converge to a quasi-triangular Schur form; note that production LAPACK adds Hessenberg reduction and Wilkinson shifts to get cubic convergence. Test on a column-stochastic matrix where the answer is known (the stationary distribution) and assert agreement with np.linalg.eig to 1e-8.

resource.label: NetworkX docs - pagerank (power iteration, damping, tolerance, max_iter)

subtopics.name: SVD: what it says, why it always exists, and deriving a 2x2 by hand
subtopics.learn: Write A = U Sigma V^T for any real m x n matrix, with U and V orthonormal and sigma_1 >= ... >= sigma_r > 0, and derive it: V and the sigma_i^2 are the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of A^T A, and u_i = A v_i / sigma_i. Do one 2x2 fully by hand - take [[3,0],[4,5]], form A^T A, get the eigenvalues, normalise V, produce Sigma and U, multiply back out and check. Read the geometry as rotate, scale along axes, rotate again, and use it to explain rank (count of non-zero sigma), the four subspaces (the first r columns of U span the column space, the last n-r columns of V span the null space), ||A||_2 = sigma_1 and ||A||_F^2 = sum sigma_i^2. Note the ambiguity: columns of U and V are determined only up to a shared sign flip (and up to rotation within a repeated-sigma block), which is why 'my PCA components flipped between runs' is not a bug.

resource.label: MIT OCW 18.065 Matrix Methods in Data Analysis, Signal Processing, and Machine Learning

subtopics.name: Computing the SVD in practice: full_matrices, drivers, cost and verification
subtopics.learn: Call np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False) by default so you get thin (m,k), (k,) and (k,n) factors rather than an m x m U that is a memory bomb on a 1e6 x 300 matrix, and remember the third return value is already transposed (Vt, not V). Know the cost is O(min(m,n)^2 * max(m,n)), so a dense SVD of 200k x 50k is not happening on a laptop, and that LAPACK's gesdd (divide and conquer) is NumPy's default while gesvd is the slower, more robust fallback for hard inputs. Compare torch.linalg.svd and torch.svd_lowrank for GPU and autograd contexts, and know gradients through an SVD are undefined when singular values are degenerate. Verify every factorisation by relative reconstruction error ||A - U S Vt||_F / ||A||_F against a stated tolerance rather than by eyeballing the factors.

resource.label: NumPy docs - numpy.linalg.svd (full_matrices, shapes, notes)

subtopics.name: Eckart-Young-Mirsky: low-rank approximation and what truncation costs
subtopics.learn: State the theorem: the best rank-k approximation of A in both spectral and Frobenius norm is A_k = sum over i <= k of sigma_i u_i v_i^T, with ||A - A_k||_2 = sigma_k+1 and ||A - A_k||_F^2 = sum over i > k of sigma_i^2 - so the spectrum tells you the error you will incur before you truncate anything. Implement image compression with your own SVD, compute the storage ratio k(m + n + 1) / (mn), and plot reconstruction error against k; then do the same on a TF-IDF matrix with sklearn's TruncatedSVD (LSA) and note that TruncatedSVD deliberately does not centre, which is exactly why it works on sparse data where PCA would densify it. Be able to answer 'how many components?' with a number and a reason - cumulative explained variance, the sigma_k+1 error bound, or a downstream CV metric - never a squint at a scree plot.

resource.label: scikit-learn docs - TruncatedSVD (LSA on sparse data)

subtopics.name: Numerical rank, condition number and error amplification
subtopics.learn: Define kappa_2(A) = sigma_1 / sigma_n and read it as an error amplification factor: a relative perturbation eps in b produces up to kappa * eps relative error in the solution of Ax = b, so kappa = 1e10 in float64 (machine epsilon about 2.2e-16) leaves roughly six correct digits. Compute numerical rank as the count of sigma_i > tol with tol = max(m,n) * eps * sigma_1, which is what np.linalg.matrix_rank does, and show a matrix that is mathematically rank-deficient coming back numerically full rank with sigma values around 1e-16. Practise the whole diagnostic loop on a real design matrix: plot log sigma_i, find the cliff, name the offending columns with pivoted QR or the correlation matrix, then drop, combine or regularise - and be able to tell a customer in plain words why their 'stable' regression's coefficients swing 300 percent when one row changes.

resource.label: NumPy docs - numpy.linalg.cond (condition number in several norms)

subtopics.name: Least squares three ways: normal equations, QR and SVD/pinv
subtopics.learn: Derive the normal equations by setting the gradient of ||Xb - y||^2 to zero, giving X^T X b = X^T y, and note that kappa(X^T X) = kappa(X)^2 - forming the Gram matrix squares your conditioning and can turn a solvable problem into a singular one. Solve the same system three ways on a deliberately ill-conditioned X and compare coefficients and residuals: scipy.linalg.solve on the normal equations, QR (solve R b = Q^T y by back substitution), and np.linalg.lstsq or pinv via the SVD, b = V Sigma^+ U^T y, which returns the minimum-norm solution when X is rank-deficient instead of raising. Know that lstsq's rcond decides which singular values are treated as zero, that sklearn's LinearRegression is a thin wrapper over lstsq (so it silently returns an arbitrary minimum-norm fit under exact collinearity), and derive the hat matrix H = X(X^T X)^-1 X^T as the orthogonal projection onto the column space.

resource.label: NumPy docs - numpy.linalg.lstsq (rcond, rank, singular values)

subtopics.name: Ridge as spectral filtering, and diagnosing multicollinearity
subtopics.learn: Derive b_ridge = (X^T X + lambda I)^-1 X^T y and rewrite it in the SVD basis: each direction's contribution is shrunk by sigma_i^2 / (sigma_i^2 + lambda), so ridge leaves large-sigma directions almost untouched and crushes the small-sigma directions that were amplifying noise - that one expression is the entire explanation of why regularisation fixes instability. Show that adding lambda lifts every eigenvalue of X^T X, so kappa falls from sigma_1^2/sigma_n^2 to (sigma_1^2 + lambda)/(sigma_n^2 + lambda), and compute effective degrees of freedom as sum sigma_i^2/(sigma_i^2 + lambda). Diagnose collinearity with concrete numbers - VIF_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2), the correlation matrix, and condition indices sigma_1/sigma_i - and remember ridge is not scale-invariant, so standardisation is part of the model rather than optional hygiene (this feeds Topic 100).

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Linear Models (Ridge, coefficient paths, collinearity)

subtopics.name: PCA done properly: centring, scaling, explained variance and choosing k
subtopics.learn: Derive PCA twice - as the eigendecomposition of the sample covariance (1/(n-1)) Xc^T Xc, and as the SVD of the centred matrix Xc = U Sigma V^T with components V and explained variance sigma_i^2/(n-1) - and know sklearn's PCA takes the SVD route, centres for you, and does not scale. Be able to say precisely what changes under standardisation: PCA on raw columns with mixed units is PCA of whichever column has the largest variance, so a dollar-denominated feature will swamp a probability. Use explained_variance_ratio_ and its cumulative sum, components_ (rows are components, columns are features) and the loadings V * sigma to interpret a component to a customer, and know whiten=True divides scores by sigma so downstream distances become isotropic. Fit PCA inside a Pipeline on training folds only; fitting on the full dataset before cross-validation is textbook leakage (Topic 103).

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Decomposing signals in components (PCA, whitening, variants)

subtopics.name: Randomised and incremental factorisation when the matrix does not fit
subtopics.learn: Understand the randomised range finder: draw a Gaussian test matrix Omega with k + p columns (oversampling p around 10), form Y = A Omega, orthonormalise Q from a QR of Y, SVD the small matrix B = Q^T A, then lift back with U = Q U_B - cost around O(mnk) with expected error close to the Eckart-Young optimum, plus q power iterations using (A A^T)^q A when the spectrum decays slowly. Call it as sklearn.utils.extmath.randomized_svd or PCA(svd_solver='randomized'), and know the result is seed-dependent so random_state must be pinned before you show a customer two runs. Add the streaming option, IncrementalPCA with partial_fit over batches for data that will not fit in memory, and scipy.sparse.linalg.svds (ARPACK/LOBPCG) when you want a handful of components of a large sparse matrix.

resource.label: arXiv - Halko, Martinsson, Tropp, Finding Structure with Randomness (randomised SVD)

subtopics.name: Sparse matrices: CSR, the memory arithmetic, and sparse linear algebra
subtopics.learn: Know the layouts and when each is right - COO to build, CSR for row slicing and matrix-vector products, CSC for column operations - and be able to do the memory arithmetic in front of a customer: a 1e6 x 5e4 TF-IDF matrix at 0.1 percent density holds about 5e7 non-zeros, roughly 600 MB in CSR against roughly 400 GB dense. Recognise the operations that densify and explode - X.toarray(), mean-centring a sparse matrix (exactly why sklearn's PCA rejects sparse input while TruncatedSVD accepts it), appending a dense intercept column - and prefer scipy.sparse.linalg.svds, a LinearOperator, or estimators that accept sparse input natively. Check density with X.nnz / (X.shape[0] * X.shape[1]) before choosing any algorithm, and know that a matvec on CSR costs O(nnz), not O(mn).

resource.label: SciPy docs - Sparse arrays (formats, construction, sparse linear algebra)

subtopics.name: Embedding matrices: cosine, normalisation, anisotropy and collapse
subtopics.learn: Treat an embedding table or a batch of encoder outputs as a matrix E of shape (n, d) and diagnose it with linear algebra rather than vibes: compute the singular-value spectrum of the centred E, an effective rank such as exp(entropy of the normalised sigma_i) or the participation ratio (sum sigma_i^2)^2 / sum sigma_i^4, and the mean cosine between random pairs. Healthy embeddings show a slowly decaying spectrum and near-zero mean pairwise cosine; a degenerate or collapsed table shows sigma_1 dominating by an order of magnitude and mean cosine of 0.7 or higher, all vectors sitting in a narrow cone. Know that this anisotropy is a documented property of trained language models, not something you invented, and that the standard remedies are subtracting the mean vector, whitening, or removing the top one or two principal directions before similarity search. Always L2-normalise before cosine or inner-product retrieval, and be able to demonstrate with numbers why an unnormalised index returns the same high-norm items for every query.

resource.label: arXiv - Representation Degeneration Problem in Training Natural Language Generation Models

subtopics.name: Low-rank structure in deep learning: LoRA, bottlenecks and attention shapes
subtopics.learn: Read LoRA as arithmetic you can do on a napkin: freeze W of shape (d, k) and learn W + BA with B of shape (d, r) and A of shape (r, k), so trainable parameters fall from d*k to r(d + k) - for d = k = 4096 and r = 8 that is 16.8M down to about 65k, a 256x reduction - and understand that the update is constrained to rank r, a modelling assumption you may have to defend when a customer's fine-tune underfits. Trace shapes through scaled dot-product attention: Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V, then softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V, where QK^T is (T, T), which is the whole reason memory grows quadratically in sequence length. Be able to run np.linalg.svd on a trained weight matrix, plot its spectrum on a log axis, and say whether a rank-r approximation would preserve behaviour - the honest, checkable version of 'can we compress this model?'.

resource.label: arXiv - LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

subtopics.name: Floating point and numerical stability in linear algebra
subtopics.learn: Know the numbers cold: float64 has a 53-bit mantissa (eps about 2.22e-16, roughly 16 decimal digits), float32 has 24 (eps about 1.19e-7, roughly 7 digits), and float16/bfloat16 have 11 and 8 - which is why a Gram matrix accumulated in fp32 on a GPU can come back with negative eigenvalues and fail a Cholesky. Understand catastrophic cancellation through the canonical case, the naive variance formula E[x^2] - E[x]^2, and use a two-pass or Welford update instead; the same cancellation is why X^T X is worse than QR for least squares. Never compare floats with ==: use np.allclose(a, b, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8), and write your from-scratch tests as reconstruction-error assertions with a stated tolerance. Use np.finfo(dtype).eps in rank tolerances, and know matrix multiplication is not associative in floating point, so A@(B@C) and (A@B)@C differ in the last digits - which is why a 'deterministic' pipeline gives different numbers under a different BLAS or thread count.

resource.label: Goldberg - What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic

outcomes: You can hand-derive the SVD of an arbitrary 2x2 matrix at a whiteboard in under ten minutes - A^T A, eigenvalues, V, Sigma, U - and multiply back to verify, with no notes.

You can implement power iteration, Householder QR plus the QR algorithm, and one-sided Jacobi SVD in NumPy only, each with a test asserting agreement with numpy.linalg to 1e-8 on well-conditioned, rank-deficient, defective and Hilbert fixtures.

You can take any real design matrix and produce a one-page diagnostic - log-scale singular-value spectrum, numerical rank at a stated tolerance, kappa_2, the offending columns from pivoted QR and VIF - and say whether an OLS fit is trustworthy and what to do if it is not.

You can explain in two sentences, using sigma_i^2 / (sigma_i^2 + lambda), why ridge stabilises a collinear regression, and back it with measured coefficient paths and the drop in condition number as lambda increases.

You can choose a number of PCA components with a defensible justification (cumulative explained variance, the sigma_k+1 error bound, or a downstream CV metric) and demonstrate that fitting PCA outside the CV fold inflates the reported score.

You can take an embedding table or encoder output, compute its effective rank and mean pairwise cosine, state whether it has collapsed, and show the measured recall@10 change from mean-centring plus L2 normalisation.
You can size a factorisation before running it: predict flops and peak memory for a dense SVD versus randomized_svd versus svds at a given (m, n, k), and pick the one that fits the customer's box.
You can state the numerical case for QR or SVD over the normal equations, quote kappa(X^T X) = kappa(X)^2, and show the measured digit loss on an ill-conditioned example in float64 and float32.
failureModes: A one-hot encoder without drop='first' plus an intercept makes the design matrix exactly rank-deficient; LinearRegression calls lstsq and silently returns one arbitrary minimum-norm solution, so the coefficients shown to the customer as feature importance are one of infinitely many and shift with row order or library version.

PCA is fitted on the whole dataset before the train/test split, so the components encode test-set variance; cross-validation comes back several points high, the deck quotes that number, and the model degrades exactly when it reaches the customer's production data.

PCA is run on unstandardised columns where one feature is in dollars and another is a probability; component 1 is essentially that one column, the 'explains 92 percent of variance' line is meaningless, and truncating to two components discards every real signal.

np.linalg.eig is used on a covariance matrix instead of eigh; round-off yields complex eigenvalues with 1e-18 imaginary parts, someone takes .real, the eigenvectors come back unsorted, and the 'top two components' actually plotted are components five and one.

np.linalg.svd is called with the default full_matrices=True on a 2e6 x 300 matrix; the job requests a 2e6 x 2e6 U, the pod is OOM-killed, and the incident is investigated for a day as a Kubernetes memory-limit problem rather than a one-word API fix.

A vector index is built without L2 normalisation and scored by inner product; a handful of high-norm vectors win almost every query, offline recall looks acceptable because those items happen to be popular in the eval sample, and users see the same five results for unrelated searches.

Two runs of PCA produce sign-flipped components and the dashboard's axes invert; a day is spent hunting a data-pipeline bug that is only the SVD's sign ambiguity, which nobody pinned with a deterministic convention such as forcing the largest-magnitude loading positive.

A model is 'compressed' by truncating weight matrices to rank 16 from a spectrum that was never plotted on a log axis; sigma_17 onward still carry 30 percent of the Frobenius mass, accuracy drops eight points, and the regression is blamed on quantisation instead of the truncation.
interviewQuestions: Derive the SVD of this 2x2 matrix at the whiteboard, then tell me what happens to U, Sigma and V if I multiply one column of A by 1000, and what that implies for PCA on unstandardised features.

A customer's linear regression reports R^2 = 0.94, but the coefficient on their most important feature flips sign when a week of new data arrives. Diagnose it in linear-algebra terms, name the first two numbers you would compute, and give two different fixes with their trade-offs.

Explain why solving least squares through the normal equations is numerically worse than QR or SVD. Quantify it: what happens to the condition number, and roughly how many correct digits remain in float64 when kappa(X) = 1e8?
Write the ridge solution in the SVD basis and use that expression to explain to a non-mathematical stakeholder what regularisation is actually doing to their model.

Design: a customer has a 3-million-document TF-IDF matrix over a 200k-term vocabulary and wants topic clusters on a 32 GB box. Walk me through the factorisation you would use, the memory arithmetic, how many components you would keep, and how you would defend that number.

Debug: after a fine-tune, a retrieval system's recall@10 collapses and every query returns near-identical results. What do you compute on the embedding matrix, in what order, and what does each result rule in or out?

What is the difference between an eigendecomposition and an SVD, when does the eigendecomposition fail to exist, and for which matrices do the two coincide? Then tell me what np.linalg.eigh assumes and why calling eig on a covariance matrix is a bug rather than a style choice.
93.proofOfWork: A public `spectrum-doctor` CLI and report generator that ingests any matrix - a pandas design matrix, a scipy sparse TF-IDF matrix, or a .npy embedding table - and emits a one-page diagnostic: the singular-value spectrum on a log axis, numerical rank at three tolerances with the tolerance formula printed alongside, kappa_2, effective rank and participation ratio, cumulative explained variance with the k that first reaches 90/95/99 percent, the Eckart-Young error bound sigma_k+1 at each k, the most collinear column groups found by pivoted QR and VIF, and for embedding inputs the mean pairwise cosine before and after mean-centring plus top-direction removal. Ship it with a `pathologies/` directory that reproduces four failures end to end, each with a before/after number: a duplicated one-hot column that makes OLS coefficients arbitrary and a ridge fit that fixes them, an unstandardised PCA where a dollar-denominated column eats component one, a rank-collapsed embedding table where centring plus L2 normalisation restores recall@10, and a full_matrices=True SVD that OOMs on a tall matrix while the thin call finishes in seconds. Back the whole thing with a pytest suite asserting that your from-scratch power iteration, Householder QR and one-sided Jacobi SVD reproduce numpy.linalg to 1e-8 on Hilbert, rank-deficient, defective and complex-eigenvalue fixtures, and finish with a two-page memo written for a customer's data lead that uses their own numbers to explain why their regression was unstable and exactly what you changed.

94.topic: Calculus and optimisation: gradients, chain rule, convexity, gradient descent variants
94.why: Every model an FDE ships - a logistic regression scoring the customer's leads, an XGBoost ranker, a LoRA fine-tune - is a loss function being walked downhill, and when the walk goes wrong the customer sees 'the AI does not work' while you have to say in the room whether it is the learning rate, the feature scaling, a leaking label, or a backward pass that has been silently zero since Tuesday. Optimisation is the only part of ML where the failure is usually a mechanical fact you can prove in ten minutes with a finite-difference check and a log-scale loss plot, rather than a matter of opinion. It is also the layer where you either can or cannot answer 'why is Adam better here than SGD, and what would you have to change about the data to make SGD fine?' - which is exactly the question that separates someone who runs training scripts from someone a customer trusts with their model.
prerequisites: Linear algebra at the level of Topic 93: quadratic forms x^T A x, symmetric positive-definite matrices, eigendecomposition, spectral norm and why lambda_max/lambda_min is a meaningful ratio
Single-variable derivative rules from memory: product, quotient, chain, and the derivatives of exp, log, x^n, sigmoid and tanh
NumPy fluency: broadcasting, axis semantics, dtype (float32 vs float64) and machine epsilon (Topic 99 goes deeper on floating point; you need enough here to choose a finite-difference step)
Python packaging and pytest from Topic 39, plus matplotlib, because the deliverable is a tested module with convergence plots, not a notebook
Enough ML framing to know what a loss is a function of: a parameter vector theta, a dataset, and a scalar output (Topic 100, supervised learning, builds directly on this)
Comfort reading summation notation and index notation for matrix products, since every backward-pass derivation is an index-bookkeeping exercise

subtopics.name: The derivative as local linearisation: Taylor, and the descent lemma
subtopics.learn: Stop thinking of f'(x) as 'the slope' and start thinking of it as the coefficient of the best local linear model: f(x + d) = f(x) + f'(x)d + O(d^2). Write the first-order multivariate Taylor expansion f(x + d) ~= f(x) + grad f(x)^T d + (1/2) d^T H d and derive the descent lemma for an L-smooth f: f(x - eta * grad f) <= f(x) - eta(1 - L*eta/2)||grad f||^2, so any eta in (0, 2/L) strictly decreases f and eta = 1/L gives the guaranteed decrease ||grad f||^2 / (2L). You should be able to say, from that one inequality, why 'the loss went up' is either eta > 2/L or a bug, with nothing in between.

resource.label: Maths, CS & AI Compendium - Chapter 03.01 Differential calculus

subtopics.name: Gradient, directional derivative, Jacobian, Hessian - and their shapes
subtopics.learn: Fix the shape algebra once so you never lose an hour to a transpose: for f: R^n -> R the gradient is n x 1 and points in the direction of steepest ascent (prove it from the directional derivative D_u f = grad f^T u maximised at u = grad f / ||grad f||); for g: R^n -> R^m the Jacobian J is m x n; the Hessian H is n x n and symmetric for C^2 functions (Schwarz/Clairaut). Know that grad(a^T x) = a, grad(x^T A x) = (A + A^T)x = 2Ax for symmetric A, and that the Hessian of (1/2)||Xw - y||^2 is X^T X - which is where the condition number of your data walks straight into the optimiser. Be able to compute grad and H by hand for least squares and for logistic regression's negative log-likelihood.

resource.label: Maths, CS & AI Compendium - Chapter 03.03 Multivariate calculus

subtopics.name: The chain rule on a real network: softmax + cross-entropy end to end
subtopics.learn: Derive, on paper, the gradient of L = -sum_k y_k log p_k with p = softmax(z), z = W2 * relu(W1 x + b1) + b2. Get to the two results you should never look up again: dL/dz = p - y (the softmax Jacobian diag(p) - p p^T collapses against the cross-entropy gradient, which is why frameworks fuse them into one kernel and why torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss takes logits, not probabilities), and dL/dW = delta * a^T with delta backpropagated as delta_1 = (W2^T delta_2) * 1[pre-activation > 0]. Write out every shape at every step. This derivation, closed-book, is a standard whiteboard ask and is also the exact code you will debug in Topic 110.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Calculus (gradients, chain rule, shapes)

subtopics.name: Reverse-mode autodiff: VJPs, the cost asymmetry, and when forward mode wins
subtopics.learn: Understand autodiff as an ordering choice on a chain of Jacobian products J_n ... J_2 J_1. Forward mode computes J v (a JVP) in one sweep per input direction, costing n sweeps for n parameters; reverse mode computes v^T J (a VJP) in one sweep per output, so a scalar loss over 10^9 parameters costs one forward plus one backward - roughly 2-3x the forward pass in FLOPs, at the price of storing every activation. That asymmetry is the entire reason deep learning is trainable, and the reason memory, not compute, is what OOMs your customer's fine-tune. Know that jacrev/jacfwd (or torch.func.jacrev/jacfwd) let you pick, and that Hessian-vector products are cheap as forward-over-reverse without ever materialising H.

resource.label: JAX - The Autodiff Cookbook (JVPs, VJPs, forward vs reverse)

subtopics.name: Building the tape: a scalar reverse-mode engine
subtopics.learn: Implement a Value class holding data, grad, _prev (parents) and a _backward closure; overload __add__, __mul__, __pow__, exp, log, tanh and relu so each records its local derivative; then backward() does a topological sort of the DAG and walks it in reverse, accumulating with += rather than = so a value used twice (weight sharing, residual connections) gets both contributions. Know why accumulation is the default in PyTorch too, hence why the loop needs optimizer.zero_grad(). Understand what detach() and torch.no_grad() do to the tape, and be able to explain why calling .item() or converting to NumPy mid-graph silently severs gradient flow.

resource.label: karpathy/micrograd - a 100-line scalar autograd engine

subtopics.name: Gradient checking: central differences, step size, and relative error
subtopics.learn: The check is (f(x + h e_i) - f(x - h e_i)) / (2h) versus your analytic partial, compared as relative error |a - b| / max(|a|, |b|, 1e-8). Central differences have O(h^2) truncation error against O(eps/h) roundoff, so the optimum is h ~ eps^(1/3) ~ 6e-6 in float64 (forward differences are O(h) and want h ~ sqrt(eps) ~ 1e-8) - and in float32 the whole exercise is worthless because eps = 1.19e-7 swamps the signal, so cast the model to float64 first. Accept < 1e-7 in float64, treat 1e-4 as a bug not noise, and never check at a kink: relu, abs, max-pool and hinge loss have no derivative at 0, so perturb away from the kink or the check will flag a correct gradient. Use scipy.optimize.check_grad and torch.autograd.gradcheck rather than hand-rolling once you know what they do.

resource.label: SciPy - scipy.optimize.check_grad

subtopics.name: Convexity: definitions, certificates, and which ML losses are actually convex
subtopics.learn: State all three characterisations and know which one you would use in an argument: the chord definition f(theta x + (1-theta) y) <= theta f(x) + (1-theta) f(y); the first-order condition f(y) >= f(x) + grad f(x)^T (y - x), i.e. every tangent plane is a global underestimator, which is why grad f = 0 implies a global minimum; and the second-order condition H psd. Build the certificate toolkit - nonneg combination, composition with an affine map, pointwise max, and the fact that a convex function of an affine function of w stays convex in w. Then classify honestly: least squares, ridge, logistic NLL, hinge/SVM and Lasso are convex in the parameters; a neural network with one hidden layer, k-means, matrix factorisation and anything with a learned nonlinearity inside are not. Know Jensen's inequality E[f(X)] >= f(E[X]) because it reappears in Topic 98 as the ELBO.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Convexity (Jensen, local minima, constraints)

subtopics.name: Smoothness, strong convexity, the condition number, and convergence rates
subtopics.learn: Learn the two constants that govern everything: L-smoothness (grad is L-Lipschitz, i.e. H <= L I) upper-bounds curvature and caps the step at 2/L; mu-strong convexity (H >= mu I) lower-bounds it and buys a linear rate. Their ratio kappa = L/mu is the condition number, equal to lambda_max/lambda_min of the Hessian for a quadratic. Memorise the rate table: convex + smooth GD gives O(1/t); strongly convex + smooth GD gives (1 - 1/kappa)^t, so ~kappa*log(1/eps) iterations; Nesterov's accelerated method gives (1 - 1/sqrt(kappa))^t, so ~sqrt(kappa)*log(1/eps); plain SGD gives O(1/sqrt(t)) with a fixed noise floor. The practical upshot you will say out loud to a customer: kappa = 10^6 in your features means a million-fold more iterations, and rescaling the columns is a cheaper fix than a bigger GPU.

resource.label: Boyd & Vandenberghe - Convex Optimization (free full text; ch.9 unconstrained minimisation, condition number and convergence)

subtopics.name: Gradient descent on a quadratic: deriving the zigzag
subtopics.learn: Take f(x) = (1/2) x^T A x with A symmetric positive-definite. In the eigenbasis the update x <- x - eta*A*x decouples into x_i <- (1 - eta*lambda_i) x_i, so convergence requires |1 - eta*lambda_i| < 1 for every i, i.e. eta < 2/lambda_max; the best fixed step is eta = 2/(lambda_min + lambda_max) with contraction (kappa - 1)/(kappa + 1). Derive that and you have derived the zigzag: the step is set by the steepest direction while progress is limited by the flattest, so the iterate oscillates across the narrow valley and creeps along it. Implement it in NumPy for kappa = 1, 10, 1000 and plot the iterate trajectory over contours - this plot is the single best asset for explaining 'why is training slow' to a non-specialist.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Gradient Descent (learning rate, local minima, ill-conditioning)

subtopics.name: SGD: the gradient as an estimator, its variance, and step-size conditions
subtopics.learn: The minibatch gradient is an unbiased estimator of the full gradient when the batch is sampled i.i.d. - E[g_B] = grad f - with covariance scaling as 1/B, so halving the batch doubles the gradient variance and roughly doubles the noise floor SGD settles at. That is why a constant step size does not converge to the optimum but to a ball around it of radius proportional to eta*sigma^2, and why the Robbins-Monro conditions sum(eta_t) = infinity and sum(eta_t^2) < infinity (satisfied by eta_t = eta_0 / t^a with a in (0.5, 1]) are what buy asymptotic convergence. Know the two ways the i.i.d. assumption breaks in customer data - a sorted-by-class or sorted-by-time file with shuffle=False, and duplicated rows from a bad join - and that both make the estimator biased within an epoch while every metric still looks plausible.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Stochastic Gradient Descent (noise, dynamic learning rates)

subtopics.name: Momentum and Nesterov acceleration
subtopics.learn: Heavy ball: v <- beta*v + g; x <- x - eta*v, which in steady state takes an effective step of eta/(1 - beta), so beta = 0.9 is a hidden 10x on the learning rate - changing beta without changing eta is changing two things at once. Understand it as an exponentially weighted average that cancels the oscillating component across the valley and reinforces the consistent component along it, i.e. it partly buys back the kappa penalty. Nesterov evaluates the gradient at the look-ahead point x - eta*beta*v, which acts as a correction term and is what gets the provable (1 - 1/sqrt(kappa)) rate on smooth strongly convex problems. Know that PyTorch's SGD uses the 'v <- beta*v + g, x <- x - eta*v' convention (not the 'v <- beta*v + (1-beta)*g' one), so the same beta means different things across frameworks and blog posts.

resource.label: Distill - Why Momentum Really Works

subtopics.name: AdaGrad and RMSProp: diagonal preconditioning
subtopics.learn: AdaGrad accumulates s <- s + g*g and steps x <- x - eta * g / (sqrt(s) + epsilon), which is a diagonal approximation to a preconditioner: coordinates with historically large gradients get small steps. Its guarantee is for convex problems and its defect is mechanical - s is monotonically nondecreasing, so the effective step decays like 1/sqrt(t) forever and a long deep-learning run stalls before it converges. RMSProp fixes exactly that by making it a leaky average s <- gamma*s + (1 - gamma)*g*g with gamma ~ 0.9, giving a stationary scale. Be able to say why AdaGrad is still the right answer for sparse features (a rare one-hot column gets a large step precisely when it finally fires) and why epsilon lives outside the sqrt in the reference implementations.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - AdaGrad (preconditioning, sparse features)

subtopics.name: Adam: derive the bias correction and know what the first step does
subtopics.learn: Adam is RMSProp plus momentum plus a correction: m <- b1*m + (1-b1)*g; v <- b2*v + (1-b2)*g*g; mhat = m/(1 - b1^t); vhat = v/(1 - b2^t); x <- x - eta * mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + eps). Derive the correction: with m_0 = 0, E[m_t] = (1 - b1^t) E[g], so early estimates are shrunk toward zero and the divisor undoes it exactly - without it, with b2 = 0.999, the second-moment estimate is ~1000x too small at t = 1 and the first step explodes. Then compute the first step by hand: at t = 1, mhat = g and sqrt(vhat) = |g|, so the update is exactly -eta * sign(g) per coordinate, independent of gradient magnitude. That single fact explains both Adam's robustness to bad loss scaling and why it happily takes a full-size step on pure noise, which is the argument for warmup. Read the paper for the bounds and know AMSGrad exists because the original convergence proof was wrong.

resource.label: arXiv 1412.6980 - Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization (Kingma & Ba)

subtopics.name: Weight decay vs L2, and why AdamW is not a cosmetic change
subtopics.learn: For plain SGD, adding (lambda/2)||w||^2 to the loss and adding lambda*w to the gradient are the same thing. For Adam they are not: the L2 term enters g, so it is divided by sqrt(vhat) along with everything else, and coordinates with large gradient history get *less* decay - the opposite of the intended regularisation, and the reason 'Adam generalises worse' was folklore for years. AdamW decouples it: x <- x - eta * (mhat/(sqrt(vhat)+eps) + lambda*x). Know that torch.optim.Adam(weight_decay=) is the coupled L2 form while torch.optim.AdamW is the decoupled one, that decoupled lambda does not transfer numerically from a tuned coupled one, and that you should exclude biases and LayerNorm/BatchNorm gain-and-bias parameters from decay via parameter groups.

resource.label: arXiv 1711.05101 - Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (Loshchilov & Hutter)

subtopics.name: Learning-rate schedules, warmup, and the LR range test
subtopics.learn: Know the shapes and what each is for: step/multistep decay, exponential, polynomial, cosine annealing (with and without warm restarts), one-cycle, and inverse-sqrt for transformers. Understand linear warmup as a variance argument - adaptive second moments are unreliable for the first few hundred steps, so you ramp eta from ~0 rather than let Adam take sign-sized steps on noise - and the linear scaling rule (multiply eta by k when you multiply the batch by k, with a few epochs of warmup) that makes large-batch training match small-batch. Run an LR range test: sweep eta geometrically over one epoch, plot loss against eta on a log x-axis, and take roughly an order of magnitude below the minimum as the max LR. In PyTorch know the trap that scheduler.step() belongs per-epoch for most schedulers but per-batch for OneCycleLR and warmup schedules.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Learning Rate Scheduling (warmup, cosine, factor schedulers)

subtopics.name: Conditioning as a modelling choice: scaling, normalisation, and what BatchNorm buys
subtopics.learn: The condition number of X^T X, not the optimiser, is usually what makes a customer's tabular model slow to train: one column in dollars (1e6) next to one in [0,1] gives kappa around 1e12 and a plain SGD run that looks broken. Standardising columns (sklearn StandardScaler inside a Pipeline so the statistics are fit on train folds only - this is a leakage vector, see Topic 103) is a preconditioner that costs nothing. Understand normalisation layers as the same idea applied to activations mid-network, and know the honest state of the argument: the BatchNorm paper attributes the gain to reduced 'internal covariate shift', while later work argues the real mechanism is a smoother loss surface (smaller effective L). Be able to state the deployment consequences an FDE owns: BatchNorm's train/eval behaviour differs, it breaks with batch size 1 and with non-i.i.d. batches, and LayerNorm or GroupNorm is what you use when the customer's serving path is one row at a time.

resource.label: arXiv 1502.03167 - Batch Normalization (Ioffe & Szegedy)

subtopics.name: Reading a bad loss curve: an ordered diagnostic
subtopics.learn: Build the decision tree and rehearse it until it is reflex. Check the initial loss first: multiclass cross-entropy must start at ln(C) (2.3026 for 10 classes) and binary at ln(2) = 0.693 - a different starting value means the head is initialised wrong or the labels are misaligned. Loss exactly flat from step 0: no gradient reaching the parameters (requires_grad False, a detach, an optimizer constructed over the wrong parameter list, eta ~ 0). Loss to NaN/inf within tens of steps: eta above 2/L, a log(0) or division in the loss, or fp16 overflow. Smooth decrease then a sudden jump: one pathological batch or an exploding step - check grad-norm history, not just loss. Sawtooth that never descends: eta too high by ~10x. Slow monotone crawl with a huge grad-norm ratio between layers: ill-conditioning, fix by scaling/normalisation before touching the optimiser. And the master test that separates bug from hyperparameter: overfit a single batch of 8 examples to near-zero loss - if that fails, no learning rate will save you.

resource.label: CS231n - Neural Networks Part 3: Learning and Evaluation (gradient checks, sanity checks, babysitting the learning process)

subtopics.name: Beyond first order: Newton, Gauss-Newton, and L-BFGS
subtopics.learn: Newton's step is d = -H^{-1} grad f, which is affine-invariant (immune to kappa) and quadratically convergent near the optimum, but costs O(n^3) and is undefined when H is indefinite - hence damping/trust regions. For least squares, Gauss-Newton approximates H by J^T J (dropping the residual-curvature term) and Levenberg-Marquardt adds lambda*I to interpolate toward gradient descent. L-BFGS builds an implicit inverse-Hessian from the last m ~ 10-20 (s, y) pairs via the two-loop recursion, needs no matrix, and is the right default for smooth deterministic problems with up to ~10^5 parameters - which is why scipy.optimize.minimize(method='L-BFGS-B') and sklearn's LogisticRegression(solver='lbfgs') use it. Know precisely why it fails on deep learning: the curvature pairs assume a consistent objective, and minibatch noise makes s^T y unreliable, so the line search and the Hessian estimate both degrade.

resource.label: SciPy - scipy.optimize.minimize (BFGS, L-BFGS-B, Newton-CG, trust-region methods)

subtopics.name: Non-smooth and constrained: subgradients, proximal steps, projection, and clipping
subtopics.learn: |w| has no derivative at 0; its subdifferential is [-1, 1], and the optimality condition 0 in subdiff f(x*) is what makes Lasso produce exact zeros. Plain subgradient descent is slow (O(1/sqrt(t))) and never produces exact sparsity in floating point, so use the proximal step: prox for eta*lambda*||w||_1 is soft-thresholding, sign(w)*max(|w| - eta*lambda, 0) - that one line is ISTA and explains sklearn's coordinate-descent Lasso output. For constraints, projected gradient descent is x <- Proj_C(x - eta*grad f), and the KKT conditions (stationarity, primal/dual feasibility, complementary slackness) are the constrained analogue of grad f = 0. Recognise that torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, c) is literally a projection of the gradient onto the L2 ball of radius c - g <- g * min(1, c/||g||) - which is why it changes the descent direction not at all but the step length a lot, and why you log ||g|| before clipping to know whether it is firing.

resource.label: CMU 10-725 Convex Optimization - lecture notes (subgradients, proximal gradient, KKT)

subtopics.name: Benchmarking optimisers honestly: Rosenbrock, ill-conditioned quadratics, and log-scale plots
subtopics.learn: Build the two-function test bench you will use for the deliverable: a quadratic (1/2)x^T A x with A = diag(1, kappa) so you can dial conditioning and know f* = 0 exactly, and Rosenbrock f(x,y) = (1 - x)^2 + 100(y - x^2)^2, whose minimum is (1,1) with a curved narrow valley that defeats fixed-step first-order methods (scipy.optimize.rosen, rosen_der and rosen_hess give you reference implementations to check against). Plot suboptimality f(x_t) - f* on a log y-axis against iterations - a linear axis makes every optimiser look identical once they are all 'near zero' while one is 100x closer - and separately plot against wall-clock and against gradient evaluations, because Adam's per-step cost is not L-BFGS's. Fix the seed, the init and the budget across methods, sweep eta per method rather than sharing one, and report the best-tuned curve for each: a benchmark that compares a tuned Adam with an untuned SGD is worse than no benchmark.

resource.label: SciPy - scipy.optimize.rosen (with rosen_der and rosen_hess)

outcomes: You can derive, closed-book on a whiteboard in under 15 minutes, dL/dz = p - y for softmax + cross-entropy and then backpropagate through a two-layer MLP with every tensor shape stated, explaining why frameworks fuse the softmax into the loss.

You can implement a scalar reverse-mode autodiff engine (Value, topological sort, accumulate with +=) from an empty file and gradient-check it against central differences in float64 to relative error below 1e-7.
You can write down, from memory, the update rules for SGD, momentum, Nesterov, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam and AdamW, derive Adam's bias correction, and state what Adam's very first step equals and why.

You can compute the condition number of a quadratic's Hessian, predict the number of GD iterations to a target accuracy from kappa, and demonstrate empirically that momentum and Nesterov recover roughly the sqrt(kappa) improvement on a diag(1, 1000) problem.

You can look at a loss curve and a grad-norm log and say, with a named next experiment for each, whether the cause is learning rate, momentum, conditioning, a data-ordering violation of i.i.d., or a backward-pass bug - and you use the overfit-one-batch test to separate the last from the rest.

You can explain to a customer's engineer, without jargon, why standardising their two features changed training from 40,000 iterations to 200, and show the contour-plus-trajectory plot that proves it.

You can state which of a given list of losses (MSE, ridge, logistic NLL, hinge, Lasso, k-means objective, a one-hidden-layer MLP) are convex, give the certificate for each convex one, and say what that changes about how you would tune it.
You can choose between L-BFGS and a first-order method for a stated problem, justify it by problem size, smoothness and gradient noise, and name the specific failure of L-BFGS under minibatching.
failureModes: The gradient check is run on a float32 model with h = 1e-8, so roundoff dominates and every partial disagrees by ~1e-2; the engineer concludes 'finite differences are just noisy', ships a sign error in one backward path, and the model trains to a worse-but-plausible loss that nobody questions.

The gradient check is done at a point where a relu or an abs is exactly at its kink, the central difference straddles two different linear pieces and reports a huge mismatch, and a correct backward implementation gets 'fixed' into a wrong one.

optimizer.zero_grad() is missing inside the training loop, so PyTorch's accumulate-by-default behaviour makes the effective step grow with every iteration; the loss looks fine for 200 steps then diverges, and a day is spent hunting for a bad batch in the customer's data.

L2 regularisation is added into the loss while training with Adam and called 'weight decay'; the adaptive denominator scales it per coordinate so the highest-gradient weights receive the least decay, the model overfits anyway, and the diagnosis lands on 'we need more data' instead of switching to AdamW.

Features arrive on wildly different scales (revenue in dollars beside a 0-1 flag), kappa is around 1e12, plain SGD zigzags and plateaus, and the team reports back that 'a linear model does not work on this data' - a conclusion about optimisation dressed up as a conclusion about the domain.

scheduler.step() is called once per epoch while using OneCycleLR (or a per-batch warmup), so the learning rate completes its whole schedule in the first few hundred steps, training silently stalls at a mediocre plateau, and the run is reported as converged.

The training file is sorted by label or by date and the DataLoader is built with shuffle=False, so each minibatch gradient is a biased estimate of the full gradient; loss still decreases, validation on an equally sorted split still looks fine, and the model is systematically worse on the customer's live traffic.

Optimiser comparison plots use a linear y-axis on raw loss over 50 epochs, so three methods look indistinguishable at 'about zero' while one is two orders of magnitude closer to the optimum; the slowest method is adopted because its curve happened to look smoothest.
interviewQuestions: Derive the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the logits when the model ends in a softmax. Show the softmax Jacobian explicitly, show what cancels, and explain why PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss takes logits rather than probabilities.

Write down Adam's update and derive the bias-correction terms from first principles. What exactly is the magnitude of Adam's first step for a single coordinate, and what does that imply about warmup and about Adam's tolerance for badly scaled losses?

Define the condition number of a smooth strongly convex problem and state gradient descent's convergence rate in terms of it. Why does momentum help, what rate does Nesterov achieve, and what would you change about the data instead of the optimiser to get the same win?

Debug: a customer's training run produces NaN loss at step 40. Give me your ordered checklist, what you would log, and how you would distinguish a learning rate that is too large from a numerically unstable loss from an fp16 problem.

A customer says 'your model does not learn'. Design the experiment sequence that determines whether the problem is a bug in the gradients, an optimisation problem, or a data problem - and tell me which single experiment you run first and why it is the most informative.

When would you reach for L-BFGS instead of Adam, and what specifically breaks about L-BFGS under stochastic minibatch gradients? What problem sizes and smoothness assumptions make it the right default?

Explain what makes a loss convex, give me the certificate for logistic regression's negative log-likelihood, and then explain why non-convexity in a neural network is not the practical obstacle people assume it is.
94.proofOfWork: A public write-up and companion repo, `optimiser-forensics`, that turns the deliverable's optimiser module into a diagnostic instrument rather than a study exercise. Take one small real model - logistic regression plus a two-layer MLP on a tabular dataset - and inject, one at a time, seven reproducible pathologies: a sign flip in one layer's backward pass, a missing zero_grad, unscaled features giving kappa around 1e10, a label-sorted loader with shuffle=False, coupled L2 under Adam instead of AdamW, a per-epoch scheduler.step() with OneCycleLR, and a learning rate 20x above 2/L. For each, commit the loss curve, the per-layer gradient-norm trace, the parameter-update-to-weight ratio, and the result of the overfit-one-batch test, then write the two-sentence diagnosis and the one-line fix. Include a `python -m forensics diagnose run.jsonl` CLI that reads a training log and emits the ranked hypothesis list from the ordered diagnostic in this topic, plus a notebook that reproduces the contour-and-trajectory figures for GD, momentum, Nesterov and Adam on diag(1, kappa) for kappa in {1, 10, 1000} and on Rosenbrock, all on log-suboptimality axes with per-method tuned learning rates. Finish with a one-page 'why your training is slow' explainer written for a customer's non-ML engineer, using only those figures.

95.topic: Probability: distributions, Bayes, conditional independence, the CLT
95.why: Every model an FDE deploys is a probability statement, and the questions that end a deployment are probabilistic ones: is this 3.2 percent lift real, why does the classifier say 0.91 when it is right 60 percent of the time, why did the pilot metric not survive rollout. Being able to name the generative story behind a customer's column (counts that are over-dispersed rather than Poisson, latencies that are log-normal rather than normal), derive a Beta-Binomial posterior on a whiteboard, and say out loud which variables are conditionally independent given what is what lets you defend a model in a room where the customer's data scientist is hostile and n is 400. Without it you will ship a metric that flatters a useless model and find out from the customer rather than from your own diagnostics.
prerequisites: Topic 93 (linear algebra for ML): vectors, matrices, positive semi-definiteness - a covariance matrix is the object, and the multivariate normal density needs a determinant and an inverse
Topic 94 (calculus and optimisation): definite integrals, differentiation, the chain rule - normalising constants, change-of-variables Jacobians and log-likelihood maximisation are all calculus
NumPy fluency: ndarray semantics, broadcasting, boolean masking, cumsum/searchsorted, and the modern RNG entry point rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) rather than the legacy np.random.* global state
Enough matplotlib to produce a histogram on a log axis, an ECDF, a QQ-plot and a reliability diagram from scratch without copying a template
Comfort translating summation and integral notation into vectorised code: you must be able to move between E[X] = sum x p(x) and (x * p).sum() without thinking about it
Jupyter plus git, so the notebook deliverable is reproducible from a clean kernel with a pinned requirements.txt and a fixed seed

subtopics.name: Axioms, sample spaces, and the three ways to describe a random variable
subtopics.learn: Write down Kolmogorov's three axioms (non-negativity, P(Omega) = 1, countable additivity) and derive the complement, union and inclusion-exclusion rules from them instead of memorising them. Define a random variable as a function from the sample space to the reals, and keep the three descriptions straight: the pmf p(x) = P(X = x) for discrete, the pdf f(x) where P(a < X < b) is the integral of f, and the CDF F(x) = P(X <= x), which is the only one that exists for both. Be able to say why P(X = x) = 0 for a continuous X, and why a density may exceed 1 (Beta(5,1) near x = 1) without breaking anything - the constraint is that the integral is 1, not the height. Know the quantile function F^-1 as the inverse of the CDF, because that is precisely the object inverse-transform sampling consumes.

resource.label: Maths, CS & AI Compendium - Ch.05.02 Probability concepts

subtopics.name: Conditional probability, the chain rule, total probability, and Bayes derived by hand
subtopics.learn: Derive Bayes in one line from the definition: P(A|B) = P(A,B)/P(B) and P(A,B) = P(B|A)P(A), so P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B), with the denominator expanded by the law of total probability P(B) = sum over a of P(B|a)P(a). Work the base-rate problem numerically until it is reflex: 1 percent prevalence, 99 percent sensitivity, 95 percent specificity gives a positive predictive value near 17 percent, not 99. Prefer the odds form when arguing with a customer - posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio - because it makes it obvious that a test with LR 20 moves 1:99 to 20:99 and no further. Treat the chain rule P(x1..xn) = prod P(xi | x1..xi-1) as the factorisation that every graphical model and every autoregressive language model is a special case of.

resource.label: Maths, CS & AI Compendium - Ch.05.04 Bayesian

subtopics.name: Expectation, variance, LOTUS and the law of total variance
subtopics.learn: Compute E[g(X)] without deriving the distribution of g(X) via LOTUS (sum g(x)p(x), or the integral of g(x)f(x)dx), and know that E is linear regardless of dependence while Var(X+Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2Cov(X,Y) is not. State and use the law of total expectation E[X] = E[E[X|Y]] and Eve's law Var(X) = E[Var(X|Y)] + Var(E[X|Y]); the second term is exactly the between-segment variance you point at when a customer asks why the pooled conversion rate is noisier than any individual segment. Know that zero covariance does not imply independence (X ~ N(0,1) with Y = X^2 is the standard counterexample) and that correlation only measures the linear part. Derive Var(mean of n iid) = sigma^2/n yourself - that one line is where every 1/sqrt(n) error bar in the rest of the plan comes from.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Random Variables (appendix: maths for deep learning)

subtopics.name: The discrete zoo and how to pick one for a real count column
subtopics.learn: Build the family tree by generative story, not formula sheet: Bernoulli(p) is one trial; Binomial(n,p) is n independent trials with fixed n; Geometric and Negative Binomial count trials to the k-th success; Poisson(lambda) is the limit of Binomial(n, lambda/n) and is the default for events in a fixed exposure window; Categorical and Multinomial generalise to k outcomes. Learn the diagnostic that matters in production: Poisson forces Var = E, so compute the sample variance-to-mean ratio on the customer's count column, and when it comes back 4 or 11 (as it does for API calls per account or tickets per customer) reach for Negative Binomial - which is a Gamma-mixed Poisson - or a zero-inflated model. In code this is scipy.stats.binom / nbinom / poisson with .pmf, .cdf and .rvs, and in a GLM it is the choice between family=Poisson() and NegativeBinomial(); getting it wrong leaves the point estimates roughly right while the standard errors come out two to three times too small.

resource.label: Maths, CS & AI Compendium - Ch.05.03 Distributions

subtopics.name: The continuous zoo, parameterisation traps and heavy tails
subtopics.learn: Know the shapes and their parameterisation traps: Normal(mu, sigma) where scipy takes scale=sigma not sigma^2; Exponential and Gamma as waiting times where scipy uses scale = 1/rate; Beta(a,b) on [0,1] as the natural object for a rate; LogNormal as what you get when the log is normal; Weibull for hazards; Student-t and Pareto as the heavy-tailed cases. Internalise that request latency is approximately log-normal, so the mean is not the typical value and mean +/- 2sd puts the lower bound below zero - report p50/p95/p99 and model log(latency). Recognise failure of the second moment: for Pareto with alpha <= 2 the variance is infinite, the sample variance grows with n instead of converging, and every CLT-based interval built on it is fiction. Fit with scipy.stats.<dist>.fit and confirm with a QQ-plot rather than eyeballing a histogram, and always use a log axis when the range spans decades.

resource.label: SciPy user guide - Continuous distributions in scipy.stats

subtopics.name: Exponential families, sufficiency and conjugacy: deriving Beta-Binomial
subtopics.learn: Write a density in exponential-family form h(x)exp(eta.T(x) - A(eta)) for Bernoulli, Poisson and Normal, and see that T(x) is the sufficient statistic - for n Bernoulli trials the entire dataset compresses to (successes, n). Derive the Beta-Binomial update by hand and completely: prior Beta(a,b) proportional to p^(a-1)(1-p)^(b-1), likelihood p^s(1-p)^(n-s), therefore posterior Beta(a+s, b+n-s); read off the posterior mean (a+s)/(a+b+n) and recognise it as the raw rate s/n shrunk toward the prior mean with weight (a+b)/(a+b+n). Do the same derivation for Gamma-Poisson on a rate and Normal-Normal with known variance, where the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of prior mean and sample mean. This is the machinery behind smoothed conversion rates, empirical-Bayes ranking of accounts, and the reason a variant with 2 conversions out of 3 must not sit at the top of the customer's leaderboard.

resource.label: Conjugate prior - table of conjugate distributions and posterior updates

subtopics.name: Pseudo-random number generation and reproducibility across workers
subtopics.learn: Use rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) (PCG64) rather than np.random.seed plus the global Mersenne Twister legacy API, and know why: the Generator stream is explicitly not guaranteed identical across NumPy versions while the legacy RandomState is, so pinning numpy is part of your reproducibility contract. Understand SeedSequence spawning - rng.spawn(k), or SeedSequence(entropy).spawn(k) - as the correct way to give each worker, fold or bootstrap replicate an independent stream, because seeding workers with seed + i can draw overlapping or correlated streams. Know that a uniform draw is the raw material for everything in the deliverable: it all starts from rng.random(). Use the secrets module for anything security-adjacent, never a statistical PRNG, and never re-seed inside a loop.

resource.label: NumPy docs - Random Generator (default_rng, spawn, PCG64)

subtopics.name: Inverse-transform sampling and the probability integral transform
subtopics.learn: Prove the probability integral transform: if U ~ Uniform(0,1) then X = F^-1(U) has CDF F, because P(F^-1(U) <= x) = P(U <= F(x)) = F(x). Implement it in closed form for Exponential (X = -ln(1-U)/lambda), Bernoulli (U < p) and Geometric (ceil of ln(U)/ln(1-p)), and for any discrete distribution by np.cumsum on the pmf plus np.searchsorted, which is O(log k) per draw. Know the converse, F(X) ~ Uniform(0,1), which is the basis of PIT residual checks: push held-out observations through the model's predicted CDF and the histogram must be flat, otherwise the model is miscalibrated. When F has no closed-form inverse, numerical inversion is a legitimate method rather than a hack - scipy.stats.sampling.NumericalInversePolynomial builds the inverse from a pdf and then samples at constant cost.

resource.label: SciPy docs - Random number generation (scipy.stats.sampling, numerical inversion)

subtopics.name: Rejection sampling, Box-Muller, and why neither scales
subtopics.learn: Implement rejection sampling: pick a proposal g and a constant M with f(x) <= M g(x) everywhere, draw x ~ g and u ~ U(0,1), accept if u <= f(x)/(M g(x)); prove that accepted draws have density f, and note that the acceptance rate is exactly 1/M, so a lazily chosen M turns a 10k-sample cell into a coffee break. Implement Box-Muller (Z1 = sqrt(-2 ln U1) cos(2 pi U2), Z2 = sqrt(-2 ln U1) sin(2 pi U2)) and understand why the polar/Marsaglia variant is what libraries actually ship. Understand that acceptance decays exponentially with dimension, which is why nobody rejection-samples a 50-dimensional posterior and why MCMC exists at all. Be able to say where a library method like scipy.stats.sampling.TransformedDensityRejection applies - log-concave densities, with a precomputed hat function - versus where you must roll your own.

resource.label: SciPy docs - TransformedDensityRejection (rejection sampling with a hat function)

subtopics.name: Joint, marginal, conditional, and independence versus conditional independence
subtopics.learn: Move fluently between a joint table, its marginals (sum out the other variable) and its conditionals (divide by the marginal), and state independence as the factorisation p(x,y) = p(x)p(y), not as 'unrelated'. State conditional independence precisely - X is conditionally independent of Y given Z iff p(x,y|z) = p(x|z)p(y|z) for every z with p(z) > 0 - and demonstrate both directions of the trap: two variables dependent marginally but independent given a common cause, and two independent variables made dependent by conditioning on a common effect. Do the Simpson's-paradox arithmetic once with plausible numbers (a treatment that helps in both severity strata yet hurts in the pooled table) so you recognise it in a customer's dashboard. Write the check in code: a chi-square or G-test on the contingency table, stratified by Z and then pooled, and compare.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Probability and Statistics (joint, conditional, Bayes)

subtopics.name: DAGs, colliders and d-separation: reading independence off a graph
subtopics.learn: Read conditional independence off a graph rather than out of algebra: in a chain A -> B -> C and a fork A <- B -> C, conditioning on B blocks the path; in a collider A -> B <- C the path is blocked by default and conditioning on B, or on any descendant of B, opens it. Learn 'explaining away' as the concrete consequence - among admitted students, test score and essay quality become negatively correlated even when independent in the applicant pool - and recognise it as the mechanism behind most selection-bias artefacts in customer data. Know the Markov blanket (parents, children, children's other parents) as the set that renders a node independent of everything else, which is exactly the feature set that can matter. For any proposed feature be able to say whether conditioning on it blocks a confounding path (include it) or opens a collider path (exclude it) - that decision is the difference between a model that transfers to next quarter and one that does not.

resource.label: pgmpy guide - Causal identification (d-separation, backdoor criterion, adjustment sets)

subtopics.name: Naive Bayes: the conditional-independence assumption, stated and priced
subtopics.learn: Write the classifier out as argmax over c of log P(c) + sum over j of log P(xj | c), and be explicit that the sum is only valid under the naive assumption p(x|c) = prod p(xj|c). Fit GaussianNB, MultinomialNB and BernoulliNB from sklearn.naive_bayes and know why Laplace/Lidstone smoothing (the alpha parameter) is not optional - one unseen token otherwise drives the whole product to zero. Then observe empirically what the violated assumption costs: with correlated features the argmax, and therefore accuracy and AUC, often survives, while predict_proba is pushed hard toward 0 and 1 and is worthless as a probability. That is the canonical model that ranks acceptably and calibrates terribly, and it is exactly why the calibration subtopic exists.

resource.label: scikit-learn user guide - Naive Bayes

subtopics.name: LLN versus CLT: two different theorems, and where the CLT fails
subtopics.learn: State both precisely and keep them apart. WLLN/SLLN: for iid Xi with finite mean, the sample mean converges to mu in probability / almost surely - a statement about the limit with no rate attached. CLT: with finite variance sigma^2, sqrt(n)(Xbar - mu) converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2), so error shrinks like 1/sqrt(n) and the standardised mean becomes normal even when X is nothing like normal. Know the assumptions that actually break in customer data: infinite variance (Cauchy, where the mean of n draws is again Cauchy so averaging never helps, and Pareto with alpha <= 2), dependence (autocorrelated series, repeated events from the same user, so effective n is far below the row count), and non-identical distributions where you need Lyapunov or Lindeberg conditions. Be able to say it out loud without hedging: the CLT is about the sampling distribution of the mean, never about the data being normal, and no n makes a skewed population normal.

resource.label: Introduction to Probability, Statistics and Random Processes - Central Limit Theorem

subtopics.name: How many samples is enough: skewness rules, Berry-Esseen, and QQ diagnostics
subtopics.learn: Replace 'n > 30' with something defensible. Berry-Esseen bounds the CDF error by C rho / (sigma^3 sqrt(n)) with C below 0.5, so the required n scales with the cubed third moment; Cochran's practical rule n > 25 x skewness^2 means a revenue column with skew 6 needs n > 900, not 30. For a proportion the np > 10 and n(1-p) > 10 rule is why a 0.2 percent conversion rate needs thousands of observations before a normal-approximation interval is honest, and why you should use Wilson or Clopper-Pearson instead.
