Diagnose rather than assume: build the sampling distribution empirically by resampling means at n = 5, 30, 100, 1000 and QQ-plot each with scipy.stats.probplot, reading the S-curve as skew and fat ends as kurtosis - do not run a normality test, which rejects everything once n is large and accepts everything when n is small.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.probplot (QQ / probability plots)

subtopics.name: Transformations of random variables: Jacobians, the delta method, Jensen
subtopics.learn: Derive the change-of-variables rule f_Y(y) = f_X(g^-1(y)) |d g^-1/dy| and use it to get the log-normal density from a normal. Learn the delta method: for smooth h, Var(h(Xbar)) is approximately h'(mu)^2 Var(Xbar), which is how you attach a standard error to a ratio, a log-odds or a lift; build the interval on the transformed scale (log or logit) and map the endpoints back, so the interval cannot cross zero or exceed 1. Recognise the same Jacobian term in code: torch.distributions TransformedDistribution with log_abs_det_jacobian, and rsample's reparameterisation trick, which is exactly why a VAE can backpropagate through a sample. Remember Jensen: E[log X] is not log E[X], so a mean of per-row log costs is not the log of the mean cost, and reporting the wrong one is a live way to misstate a customer's spend.

resource.label: PyTorch docs - torch.distributions (TransformedDistribution, log_abs_det_jacobian, rsample)

subtopics.name: Concentration inequalities: guarantees without assuming normality
subtopics.learn: Learn the three bounds that give a guarantee with no distributional assumption: Markov P(X >= a) <= E[X]/a for non-negative X, Chebyshev P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for anything with finite variance, and Hoeffding P(|Xbar - mu| >= t) <= 2 exp(-2 n t^2 / (b-a)^2) for bounded variables. Use Hoeffding to answer 'how many users do we need' for a bounded metric before any data exists: a 1 percentage-point margin at 95 percent confidence on a 0/1 metric needs about n = ln(40)/(2 x 0.01^2), roughly 18,400. Understand that these are distribution-free and therefore loose - Chebyshev gives 25 percent at two sigma where the normal gives 5 percent - and that the loose-but-valid bound is the right thing to quote when the CLT assumptions are shaky. These are also the backbone of generalisation bounds and of the confidence width in UCB bandits.

resource.label: Hoeffding's inequality - statement, proof sketch and bounded-variable conditions

subtopics.name: Monte Carlo estimation: error bars on the simulation itself
subtopics.learn: Treat every simulation as an estimator with its own error: the MC estimate of E[h(X)] has standard error s/sqrt(N), so report it, and note that going from two to three significant digits costs 100x the draws. Know the variance-reduction tools by name and effect - common random numbers when comparing two configurations, antithetic variates, control variates, and importance sampling with the diagnostic that matters, effective sample size ESS = (sum w)^2 / sum w^2, which tells you when a handful of weights carry the whole estimate. Understand that dependent draws (MCMC) inflate the error by the integrated autocorrelation time, which is exactly why Stan and ArviZ report ESS and MCSE next to every posterior summary. In the deliverable this is the checking machinery: the Monte Carlo answer must agree with the analytic Beta-Binomial posterior to within a few MC standard errors, and if it does not, one of the two is wrong and the MCSE tells you which claim you are allowed to make.

resource.label: Stan Reference Manual - Posterior analysis (effective sample size, MCSE)

subtopics.name: Bootstrap, and interval construction for a rate
subtopics.learn: Implement the nonparametric bootstrap in six lines (resample n rows with replacement B times, recompute the statistic, take percentiles), then use scipy.stats.bootstrap with method='BCa' to correct for bias and skew. Know where it fails: extreme order statistics (max, min, p99.9 with few tail points), heavy tails with no finite variance, small n, and dependent data - for the last, resample users or clusters, or use a block bootstrap, never individual rows of a session log. For a single proportion, do not bootstrap and do not use Wald: statsmodels proportion_confint with method='wilson' or 'beta' (Clopper-Pearson) stays correct near 0 and 1 where Wald yields intervals containing negative numbers. Be able to state the difference cleanly: a 95 percent confidence interval is a property of the procedure over repeated samples, a 95 percent credible interval is a probability statement about the parameter given this data and this prior.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.bootstrap (percentile, basic, BCa)

subtopics.name: Priors, credible intervals, posterior summaries and posterior predictive checks
subtopics.learn: Choose a prior and defend it: Beta(1,1) uniform, Jeffreys Beta(0.5,0.5), or a weakly-informative Beta fitted to the customer's own history - Beta(20, 1980) encodes 'about 1 percent, with the weight of 2000 observations'. Make prior-sensitivity a routine step: rerun with three priors and either show the customer the conclusion is unchanged or admit that it is not. Summarise deliberately - the posterior mean minimises squared loss, the median minimises absolute loss, the MAP minimises neither - and report an equal-tailed or HDI credible interval alongside the decision-relevant quantity P(p_B > p_A) or P(lift > 2 percent) computed from posterior draws, because that is the number a business stakeholder can act on. Run posterior predictive checks (arviz plot_ppc style): simulate replicated datasets from the posterior and compare a test statistic - the max, the zero count, the variance - against the observed value, which is how you discover that a Poisson model cannot reproduce the customer's excess zeros.

resource.label: PyMC - General overview (priors, posteriors, posterior predictive sampling)

subtopics.name: Calibration: turning model scores into probabilities you can multiply by money
subtopics.learn: Separate discrimination (AUC, ranking) from calibration (does 0.7 actually mean 70 percent). Build a reliability diagram by binning predicted probabilities and plotting observed frequency per bin, and score it with the Brier score - which decomposes into reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty - and with log loss. Fix miscalibration with sklearn.calibration.CalibratedClassifierCV using Platt scaling (sigmoid, parametric, fine on small data) or isotonic (nonparametric, needs roughly a thousand or more calibration points and cannot extrapolate), and fit the calibrator on data the model has never seen, because calibrating on training predictions is leakage that produces a beautiful curve and useless probabilities. Know that resampling for class imbalance (SMOTE, class_weight) shifts the base rate and therefore decalibrates the model, so a prior-correction term of log(pi_train/pi_test) on the logit, or recalibration at the original prevalence, is mandatory before anyone multiplies a score by a dollar amount.

resource.label: scikit-learn user guide - Probability calibration

outcomes: You can derive Bayes' theorem from the definition of conditional probability, expand the denominator with the law of total probability, and compute a positive predictive value for a 1-percent-prevalence screening problem in your head to the nearest five points.

You can generate exact samples from five named distributions using nothing but rng.random() - at least two by closed-form inverse transform and one by rejection sampling - and verify each against scipy's CDF with a KS test and a QQ-plot.

You can derive the Beta-Binomial posterior by hand, state the posterior mean as a shrinkage of the raw rate toward the prior, and reproduce it in NumPy so the analytic and Monte Carlo quantiles agree to within a few MC standard errors.

You can look at a customer's column and justify a distribution out loud: variance-to-mean ratio for counts, log-axis histogram plus QQ-plot for latency and revenue, and name exactly what breaks downstream if you assume normal instead.

You can say how many observations a mean needs before the normal approximation is safe using the skewness rule and Berry-Esseen rather than 'n > 30', and demonstrate it empirically with QQ-plots as n grows for a deliberately skewed source.

You can draw the DAG for a customer's data-generating process, mark chains, forks and colliders, state which variables are conditionally independent given what, and decide feature by feature whether conditioning blocks a confounder or opens a collider.

You can distinguish a confidence interval from a credible interval in one sentence a non-statistician follows, produce both for the same conversion-rate question, and say which one goes in the customer deck and why.

You can take a classifier with AUC 0.85 and useless probabilities, show the reliability diagram and Brier decomposition, fix it on held-out data, and explain why the class-imbalance resampling step caused the problem.
failureModes: Per-account API calls were modelled as Poisson because the mean matched, but the variance-to-mean ratio was 11; every standard error in the capacity forecast came out roughly three times too narrow and an ordinary busy week was reported to the customer as a five-sigma anomaly.

A latency dashboard reported mean +/- 2sd on a log-normal distribution, giving a lower bound of -40 ms and a 'p95' that 12 percent of requests exceeded; nobody caught it until the customer's SRE replotted the histogram on a log axis.

The isotonic calibrator was fitted on the same rows used to train the model, so the reliability diagram was a perfect diagonal in the notebook and badly S-shaped in production - a leakage bug that presents as a calibration success.

An A/B readout applied a normal-approximation interval to a 0.15 percent conversion rate with 800 users per arm; np was 1.2, the interval ran below zero, and the 'significant' 40 percent lift was a single extra conversion.

Eight parallel bootstrap workers were each seeded with seed + worker_id, the streams overlapped, replicates were correlated, and the resulting confidence interval came out about 30 percent too narrow with no visible symptom anywhere in the output.

A churn model conditioned on 'opened a support ticket', a collider between product dissatisfaction and account size; the coefficient flipped sign relative to the population, the model validated beautifully on the historical split, and it inverted on the next cohort.

A Monte Carlo check of a posterior used 2,000 draws and matched the analytic answer to two decimals by luck; when the prior changed the two diverged, and because no MC standard error was ever reported, three days went into debugging an analytic derivation that was correct.

Per-row log costs were averaged and exponentiated to produce a 'mean cost per call' 18 percent below the invoice - Jensen's inequality, escalated to the customer as a billing discrepancy before anyone checked the arithmetic.
interviewQuestions: Derive Bayes' theorem from the definition of conditional probability, then use it: a test with 99 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity on a disease with 1 percent prevalence comes back positive. Give me the posterior, and then tell me in odds form how many independent positive tests it takes to get past 95 percent.

You are handed a column of per-account monthly API-call counts. Walk me through choosing a distribution: what do you compute first, what would make you reject Poisson, what would you fit instead, and what specifically goes wrong downstream if you choose wrong?

State the central limit theorem precisely, including its assumptions. Then give me three concrete situations in real product data where it does not apply, and how you would build an interval in each case.

Design: a customer wants to know whether variant B's 3.4 percent conversion beats variant A's 3.1 percent with 900 users per arm. Do it as a Bayesian - pick the prior and defend it, write down the posterior, say which quantity you report to the business, and tell me what you would do if the prior-sensitivity check changed the answer.
Explain conditional independence using a collider example, then tell me how you would decide whether a given feature belongs in a model that has to keep working on next quarter's data.

Debug: a fraud classifier has AUC 0.88 in validation, but the ops team says its 0.9-probability alerts are right about a third of the time. Nothing in the training loop errored. Where do you look, in what order, and what is your leading hypothesis?

You need samples from a distribution with no closed-form inverse CDF. Walk me through inverse-transform versus rejection sampling: what each requires, how you would choose the proposal, what the acceptance rate is, and why neither is what you would use in fifty dimensions.
95.proofOfWork: A public repo `distribution-triage` that turns the notebook's machinery into a tool you can run on a customer's table in the first week of a deployment. One command takes a CSV or a SQL query and, per column, classifies it (bounded rate, count, duration, monetary, categorical), computes the variance-to-mean ratio, skewness, excess kurtosis and a tail-index estimate, fits two or three candidate distributions with scipy's .fit, ranks them by AIC and a KS statistic, and emits a one-page HTML report containing a log-axis histogram, an ECDF and a QQ-plot per column plus a plain-English recommendation ('over-dispersed, variance/mean = 11.4 - model as Negative Binomial; a Poisson GLM will understate standard errors by roughly 3x'). The same report answers the sample-size question for every numeric column: the Cochran n > 25 x skew^2 threshold, the empirical n at which the resampled-mean QQ-plot straightens, and a Hoeffding bound for the bounded columns. It ends with a conditional-independence section: a hand-drawn DAG of the customer's data-generating process checked in as a Graphviz file, every claimed independence tested on the data with a stratified chi-square, and every collider named explicitly as a feature to exclude. Check in the seeded-worker bug and the calibrate-on-training-data bug as failing tests with fixes so both are demonstrable, and close with a two-page memo written for a non-statistician stakeholder explaining the single conclusion the tool produced on a real public dataset.

96.topic: Statistical inference: estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, ANOVA
96.why: Every claim an FDE makes about a model - 'the new retriever is 4 points better', 'this drift is real', 'the pilot beat the baseline' - is an inference from a finite sample, and the customer's data scientist will ask which test you used and which assumption it rests on. Without this you will ship a model whose 4-point lift is inside the noise of a 900-row eval set, or kill a working model because a Shapiro test on 50k rows told you the data was 'not normal'. This is also the layer where silent modelling errors live: a p-value from correlated cross-validation folds, a Wald interval on a 2-out-of-40 conversion rate, an omnibus F that is significant only because one group has three rows and enormous variance.
prerequisites: Random variables, expectation, variance, independence, and the normal / t / chi-square / F families, plus the CLT and its finite-sample caveats (Topic 95, Probability)
Differentiation and the chain rule well enough to take d/dtheta of a log-likelihood and set it to zero, and to recognise a Hessian (Topic 94, Calculus and optimisation)
Vector projection and orthogonal decomposition - the ANOVA sum-of-squares identity is Pythagoras on the column space of the group-indicator matrix (Topic 93, Linear algebra for ML)
NumPy at working level: broadcasting, axis=, dtype and ddof=, np.random.default_rng - the deliverable is pure NumPy and the bootstrap must be vectorised, not a Python loop
pytest with parametrize and pytest.approx, since the deliverable's contract is 'matches scipy.stats to 1e-6 on three real datasets' (Topic 39, Testing and contracts)
pandas basics for loading and grouping the three datasets (read_csv, groupby, dropna) so time goes into the statistics, not the ETL

subtopics.name: The inference frame: estimand, estimator, estimate, sampling distribution
subtopics.learn: Separate the four objects and use the words correctly in front of a customer: the estimand is the population quantity you care about (mu_A - mu_B, the true AUC, the conversion rate), the estimator is a function of the sample (a random variable, e.g. Xbar), the estimate is the one number you computed, and the sampling distribution is the distribution of the estimator over hypothetical repeat samples. Everything in this topic - standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values - is a statement about that sampling distribution, which you never observe and must either derive analytically, approximate asymptotically, or simulate by bootstrap/permutation. Practise writing the estimand as a sentence before any code: 'the difference in mean handle time between the agent-assisted and control cohorts, over the population of tickets this deployment will see'; if you cannot write it, no test is the right test.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Statistics (estimators, evaluating estimators, hypothesis tests)

subtopics.name: Properties of estimators: bias, variance, MSE, consistency, the plug-in principle
subtopics.learn: Be able to derive, on paper, that E[Xbar] = mu, Var(Xbar) = sigma^2/n, and that the plug-in variance (1/n)sum(x_i - xbar)^2 has expectation ((n-1)/n)sigma^2, which is exactly why the unbiased estimator divides by n-1 and why NumPy's default ddof=0 quietly biases every variance you compute (np.var(x, ddof=1) is the one you want for inference). Decompose MSE(thetahat) = Bias^2 + Variance and say why a biased-but-low-variance estimator (ridge, shrunk covariance) can beat the unbiased one - the same trade-off you will meet again as bias-variance in Topic 100. Define consistency (thetahat ->p theta) and know it is a large-n promise that says nothing about your n=40 pilot, and know the plug-in principle: estimate a functional T(F) by T(Fhat_n), which is the entire justification for the bootstrap later in this topic.

resource.label: Maths, CS & AI Compendium - Chapter 04.05 Inference

subtopics.name: Maximum likelihood: score, Fisher information, and where every asymptotic SE comes from
subtopics.learn: Derive an MLE end to end: write the log-likelihood l(theta) = sum log f(x_i; theta), take the score U(theta) = dl/dtheta, solve U = 0, and check the second derivative is negative - do this for the Bernoulli (thetahat = xbar), the normal (muhat = xbar, sigmahat^2 = (1/n)sum(x_i-xbar)^2, biased), and the exponential. Then get the standard error from the information: I(theta) = -E[d^2 l/dtheta^2], sqrt(n)(thetahat - theta) -> N(0, I(theta)^-1), so SE(thetahat) = 1/sqrt(n*I(thetahat)) or, in practice, sqrt of the diagonal of the inverse observed-information (negative Hessian) matrix - which is precisely where statsmodels' `bse` column and every logistic-regression coefficient p-value come from. Know the invariance property (the MLE of g(theta) is g(thetahat)) and that this asymptotic normality is exactly what fails at small n or on a boundary (a fitted probability of 0 or 1 gives an infinite SE, which is separation, not a bug).

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Maximum Likelihood

subtopics.name: Confidence intervals: coverage, t vs z, and the sentence you are allowed to say
subtopics.learn: A 95% CI is a procedure-level guarantee: P(L(X) <= theta <= U(X)) = 0.95 over repeated sampling; the realised interval [1.2, 4.8] either contains theta or does not, so 'there is a 95% probability the true lift is between 1.2 and 4.8' is a Bayesian credible-interval statement, not this. Build the one-sample interval xbar +/- t_{1-alpha/2, n-1} * s/sqrt(n) using scipy.stats.t.ppf, and be able to say why the t rather than the z: s is itself estimated, (n-1)s^2/sigma^2 ~ chi2_{n-1}, and the ratio of a standard normal to sqrt(chi2/df) is Student's t - which is why the interval is wider at small n and converges to +/-1.96 as df grows. Report a CI next to every point estimate in customer-facing work, and check coverage empirically once by simulation (draw 10,000 samples from a known distribution, count how often the interval covers) - that simulation is the only honest test of a CI you wrote yourself.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.t (ppf, sf, interval)

subtopics.name: Proportions: why the Wald interval is broken and what to use instead
subtopics.learn: The textbook interval phat +/- z*sqrt(phat(1-phat)/n) has actual coverage far below its nominal 95% for small n or p near 0 or 1, and degenerates to zero width at phat = 0 - so '0 failures in 40 calls' becomes the interval [0, 0], which is the single most common way an FDE overclaims reliability in a pilot readout. Use statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportion_confint(count, nobs, method='wilson') by default, 'beta' (Clopper-Pearson) when you must be conservative for a compliance claim, and know the rule of three: with 0 events in n trials the upper 95% bound is about 3/n. Wilson centres the interval at (phat + z^2/2n)/(1 + z^2/n), which is why it never leaves [0,1] and behaves at the edges; use proportion_confint on the difference of two proportions (or a bootstrap) rather than eyeballing two overlapping single-arm intervals, because non-overlapping intervals are a sufficient but not necessary condition for a significant difference.

resource.label: statsmodels - proportion_confint (normal, wilson, beta, jeffreys, agresti_coull)

subtopics.name: The nonparametric bootstrap: percentile, basic, BCa, and where it fails
subtopics.learn: Implement the algorithm you will be asked to defend: resample n points with replacement B times, recompute the statistic each time to get thetahat*_1..B, then form the percentile interval [q_{alpha/2}(thetahat*), q_{1-alpha/2}(thetahat*)], the basic/reverse-percentile interval [2thetahat - q_{1-alpha/2}, 2thetahat - q_{alpha/2}], and understand BCa's two corrections - the bias correction z0 = Phi^-1(#{thetahat* < thetahat}/B) and the acceleration a computed from jackknife leave-one-out values - which is what scipy.stats.bootstrap does by default (method='BCa'). Know the failure list cold, because 'we bootstrapped it' is not a defence: the bootstrap is inconsistent for extremes (max/min), for non-smooth functionals, at tiny n where the resample space is degenerate, for dependent data (use a moving-block bootstrap on time series), and it does not fix a biased estimator or a leaky evaluation - it only estimates the sampling variability of whatever you handed it. For paired or clustered data, resample the cluster (the user, the ticket, the tenant), never the row.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.bootstrap (percentile, basic, BCa; paired and n_resamples)

subtopics.name: Bootstrapping in NumPy: vectorised resampling, B, seeds and Monte-Carlo error
subtopics.learn: Write it once as a vectorised draw - rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=(B, n)); stats = statistic(x[idx], axis=1) - instead of a Python loop, so B=10,000 on 50k rows runs in seconds; use rng.choice only when you need weights or replace=False. Choose B by the precision you need on the interval endpoint, not by habit: the Monte-Carlo standard error of a bootstrap quantile falls as 1/sqrt(B), so B=1,000 is fine for a standard error and too coarse for a 2.5% percentile - rerun with two different seeds and if the CI endpoints move in the third significant figure, raise B. Seed with a SeedSequence and record it in the artifact so the customer's data scientist reproduces your interval exactly; never reuse a global np.random seed across parallel workers, spawn child streams. Memory is the real limit: an (B, n) index matrix at B=10,000 and n=1e6 is 80 GB, so chunk over B and accumulate.

resource.label: NumPy docs - Generator.choice (resampling with/without replacement)

subtopics.name: The Neyman-Pearson frame: null, test statistic, alpha, beta, power
subtopics.learn: State any test as five objects: H0, the test statistic T(X), the distribution of T under H0, the rejection region for a chosen alpha, and the power 1-beta at the effect size you care about. Understand the asymmetry - alpha is the Type I error rate you fix in advance, beta is the Type II error you only control by design (sample size and effect size), and 'fail to reject' is not evidence for H0 unless you can also state the power (an underpowered test fails to reject almost everything, which is why 'no significant difference' from a 60-row eval means nothing). Know that a one-sided test has more power but must be declared before seeing the data, and that the whole frame is a decision rule for repeated use, not a measure of belief in this particular result.

resource.label: Maths, CS & AI Compendium - Chapter 04.04 Hypothesis testing

subtopics.name: What a p-value licenses, and the misinterpretations that end credibility
subtopics.learn: Define it precisely: p = P(T >= t_obs | H0 and the entire model - iid sampling, the assumed variance structure, the pre-specified analysis), so a small p indicts the whole package, not just the null mean. Be able to recite the four denials on demand: it is not P(H0 | data), not the probability the result is a fluke, not 1 minus the replication probability, and its magnitude is not an effect size (p=0.001 on n=2,000,000 can be a 0.01% lift no customer would pay for). Know that p is uniform on [0,1] under H0, which is why peeking and re-testing inflate the false-positive rate, and adopt the habit of leading every readout with the estimate and CI and putting the p-value in parentheses afterwards - reversing that order is how a 0.3-point 'significant' improvement gets into a customer deck.

resource.label: Greenland et al. 2016 - Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals and power: a guide to misinterpretations (open access)

subtopics.name: Two-sample means: Student vs Welch, Behrens-Fisher, Satterthwaite df
subtopics.learn: Derive both statistics. Student pools: s_p^2 = ((n1-1)s1^2 + (n2-1)s2^2)/(n1+n2-2), t = (xbar1-xbar2)/(s_p*sqrt(1/n1+1/n2)) on n1+n2-2 df, and it assumes equal population variances. Welch does not pool: t = (xbar1-xbar2)/sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2) with the Satterthwaite approximation df = (s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2)^2 / [ (s1^2/n1)^2/(n1-1) + (s2^2/n2)^2/(n2-1) ], a non-integer df you must pass to scipy.stats.t.sf. Make Welch (scipy.stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)) your default for unequal or unknown variances and unequal group sizes, because the pooled test's Type I error can be badly wrong when the larger variance sits in the smaller group; invert the same statistic to get the CI on the difference, xbar1-xbar2 +/- t_{1-alpha/2, df_welch} * sqrt(s1^2/n1+s2^2/n2), and confirm it agrees with your bootstrap interval to two significant figures.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.ttest_ind (equal_var=False is Welch)

subtopics.name: Paired and blocked designs: the cheapest variance reduction you will ever get
subtopics.learn: When the same unit is measured twice (same prompt under model A and B, same ticket before and after), analyse the differences d_i = x_i - y_i with a one-sample t on d (scipy.stats.ttest_rel), because Var(Xbar - Ybar) = (sigma_x^2 + sigma_y^2 - 2*cov)/n collapses when the pairing is strongly correlated - the same 200 examples can go from inconclusive to decisive with no extra data. Recognise the FDE version of this: evaluating two prompts or two retrievers on the same eval set is inherently paired, and running an unpaired ttest_ind on it throws away the correlation and understates your own improvement. Know the failure: paired analysis on data that is not actually paired (unequal lengths, misaligned order after a groupby, a dropped row shifting the alignment) silently computes differences between unrelated units.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.ttest_rel (paired two-sample t-test)

subtopics.name: Assumption diagnostics: QQ plots, Levene, Shapiro, and what actually has to be normal
subtopics.learn: The t-test does not require normal data - it requires the sampling distribution of the mean to be approximately normal, which the CLT supplies at moderate n unless the data are heavily skewed, heavy-tailed, or contaminated by outliers (latency distributions are all three). Diagnose by eye first: scipy.stats.probplot(x, dist='norm', plot=ax) for a QQ plot (an S-curve is skew, fat ends are heavy tails), a histogram, and a plot of the bootstrap distribution of the statistic itself, which directly shows whether the normal approximation is safe. Use scipy.stats.levene(*groups, center='median') - Brown-Forsythe, robust to non-normality - rather than bartlett for equal variances, and treat scipy.stats.shapiro as diagnostic only: its power grows with n, so it rejects irrelevant deviations at n=10,000 and misses real ones at n=20, making 'Shapiro said p<0.05 so we used a nonparametric test' an anti-pattern. Prefer choosing the test from the design and the plot, not from a chain of pre-tests, which itself inflates Type I error.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.probplot (QQ plot against a reference distribution)

subtopics.name: Permutation and rank alternatives: exchangeability instead of normality
subtopics.learn: When the null is 'the labels carry no information', build the null distribution by shuffling: recompute the statistic on B random relabelings and report p = (1 + #{|T*| >= |T_obs|})/(B+1) - the +1 in numerator and denominator is not cosmetic, it keeps the test valid and prevents a p of exactly 0. scipy.stats.permutation_test handles the three flavours: permutation_type='independent' (two independent samples), 'samples' (paired, flips signs within pairs), 'pairings' (correlation/association), and it works for any statistic including median difference, p95 difference or AUC, where no closed form exists. The assumption is exchangeability under H0, which clustered or time-ordered data violates - permute clusters, not rows. Know the rank options and what they actually test: scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu tests P(X > Y) != 1/2 (stochastic dominance), and it is only a test of medians under an additional identical-shape assumption people routinely forget to state.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.permutation_test

subtopics.name: One-way ANOVA: the sum-of-squares identity and the F statistic
subtopics.learn: Derive SST = SSB + SSW: with group means xbar_j and grand mean xbar, SSB = sum_j n_j (xbar_j - xbar)^2 on k-1 df and SSW = sum_j sum_i (x_ij - xbar_j)^2 on N-k df; then MSB = SSB/(k-1), MSW = SSW/(N-k), and F = MSB/MSW which under H0 (all mu_j equal, normal errors, equal variance, independence) follows F(k-1, N-k) - get the p-value from scipy.stats.f.sf(F, k-1, N-k), never 1-cdf, which loses precision in the tail. Understand what the ratio means: MSW always estimates sigma^2, MSB estimates sigma^2 plus a term proportional to the spread of the true group means, so F is 'between-group signal per unit of within-group noise'. Verify two identities in your implementation - for k=2 the F equals the square of the pooled two-sample t, and SSB/SST is eta^2, the effect size you should report because a significant F on 400k rows says nothing about magnitude.

resource.label: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook 7.4.3.3 - The ANOVA table and tests of hypotheses about means

subtopics.name: ANOVA as a linear model: OLS, dummy coding, and Type I/II/III sums of squares
subtopics.learn: See that one-way ANOVA is just OLS on group indicators - fit smf.ols('y ~ C(group)', data=df).fit() and sm.stats.anova_lm(model, typ=2) returns the same F and p as scipy.stats.f_oneway on balanced data - which is why the reference-level coefficient is a contrast against the baseline group and why the residual df is N-k. Once there are two or more factors, know that Type I SS is sequential and therefore order-dependent, Type II tests each main effect after the other main effects but ignores interactions, and Type III tests each term with all others in the model (and needs sum-to-zero contrasts to be meaningful); on balanced designs all three agree, on unbalanced designs they do not and quoting the default without saying which one is how two analysts get two answers from the same data. This framing is also the bridge to Topic 100: an ANOVA is a regression, a t-test is a regression with one dummy, and both are special cases of the linear model you will regularise later.

resource.label: statsmodels - anova_lm (typ=1/2/3 sums of squares)

subtopics.name: Heteroscedastic and unbalanced ANOVA: Welch's F and Alexander-Govern
subtopics.learn: Classical F assumes equal variances, and it is not robust to violation when group sizes are unequal - the error rate inflates when the small group has the large variance and deflates in the reverse case, so an unbalanced design plus heteroscedasticity is the standard way an ANOVA lies. Use statsmodels.stats.oneway.anova_oneway(data, groups, use_var='unequal') for Welch's F (a weighted between-group statistic with a Brown-Forsythe/Welch adjusted denominator df), or scipy.stats.alexandergovern, and report which you used. Check the design first: print n_j, mean_j and s_j per group before the test, because a group with n_j=3 dominates the df arithmetic and is usually a data-quality problem (a mislabelled cohort, an unfilled category) rather than a real stratum.

resource.label: statsmodels - anova_oneway (use_var='equal' | 'unequal' | 'bf')

subtopics.name: Post-hoc comparisons: Tukey HSD, Dunnett, and why you cannot just run k(k-1)/2 t-tests
subtopics.learn: A significant omnibus F says 'not all means are equal' and nothing about which pair differs, so you need a post-hoc procedure that controls the family-wise error rate across all k(k-1)/2 comparisons - scipy.stats.tukey_hsd (or statsmodels pairwise_tukeyhsd) uses the studentized range distribution and returns simultaneous confidence intervals, which are what you show a customer. When every group is compared to a single control (baseline model vs four candidates) use scipy.stats.dunnett, which is more powerful because it makes k-1 comparisons rather than k(k-1)/2. Know why raw pairwise t-tests are wrong: with k=5 groups and alpha=0.05 the chance of at least one false positive is about 1-(0.95)^10 = 40%, and know the honest alternative when you have one pre-registered comparison of interest - state it in advance and skip the omnibus.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.tukey_hsd (simultaneous CIs via the studentized range)

subtopics.name: Multiplicity beyond post-hoc: FWER vs FDR, Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg
subtopics.learn: Distinguish the two error rates and pick deliberately: FWER = P(at least one false rejection), controlled by Bonferroni (alpha/m, valid always, very conservative) or Holm's step-down (uniformly more powerful, same guarantee); FDR = E[V/max(R,1)], the expected fraction of your rejections that are false, controlled by Benjamini-Hochberg at level q (scipy.stats.false_discovery_control, or statsmodels multipletests with method='fdr_bh'). Use FWER when a single false positive is expensive (a regulatory claim, a go/no-go on a deployment) and FDR when you are screening many features or many segments and can tolerate a known false-discovery fraction. The real-world version of this is subgroup analysis: slicing a flat A/B result by 30 segments until one is 'significant' is a 30-test family whether or not you admit it, and the fix is to pre-register the segments or to report BH-adjusted q-values for all of them.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.false_discovery_control (Benjamini-Hochberg / Benjamini-Yekutieli)

subtopics.name: Effect size and power: sizing the eval set before you run it
subtopics.learn: Convert an effect into standardised units - Cohen's d = (mu1-mu2)/s_pooled for means, eta^2 = SSB/SST for ANOVA - and invert the two-sample formula n_per_arm approx 2(z_{1-alpha/2} + z_{1-beta})^2 * sigma^2 / delta^2 to see the brutal quadratic: halving the detectable effect quadruples the sample. Use statsmodels TTestIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=d, nobs1=None, alpha=0.05, power=0.8, ratio=1) for means and FTestAnovaPower for k groups, and turn the answer around into the number that actually matters to a customer: the minimum detectable effect at the eval-set size they are willing to label. Do this before the experiment - a post-hoc 'observed power' computed from the observed effect is a deterministic function of the p-value and carries no information, and refusing to run an underpowered eval is a more valuable thing to say in a customer meeting than a non-significant result.

resource.label: statsmodels - TTestIndPower (solve_power for effect size, n, alpha or power)

subtopics.name: Inference on model metrics: comparing two models without fooling yourself
subtopics.learn: The classic mistake is running a paired t-test across k cross-validation folds as if the folds were independent: they share training data, so the variance is underestimated, the t is inflated and 'model B is significantly better' is manufactured - use a corrected resampled t-test (Nadeau-Bengio) or repeated 5x2cv, and read scikit-learn's worked comparison of grid-search candidates that shows the correction term explicitly. For a single held-out test set, get a CI on accuracy/F1/AUC by bootstrapping the test set (resampling the evaluation unit - the user or document, not the row, when rows are clustered), and use McNemar's test on the discordant-pairs table when two classifiers are scored on the same examples. Always report the metric difference with its interval, and remember that a metric computed on a leaky split has a beautifully tight CI around the wrong number - the interval measures sampling noise, never leakage (Topic 103 goes at this in depth).

resource.label: scikit-learn - Statistical comparison of models using grid search (corrected paired t-test)

outcomes: You can implement, in pure NumPy and from the formulas, Welch's t (with Satterthwaite df), the one-way ANOVA F from the SS decomposition, and percentile/basic/BCa bootstrap intervals, and show a pytest suite asserting agreement with scipy.stats.ttest_ind, f_oneway and bootstrap to 1e-6 on three real datasets.

You can produce a confidence interval for a difference in means two ways - analytically by inverting the Welch statistic and empirically by bootstrap - and explain in one sentence why they agree here and where they would diverge (skew, small n, a non-smooth statistic).

You can state, for any test you run, the exact null hypothesis, the reference distribution, and the specific assumption you are leaning on, and name the diagnostic (QQ plot, Levene, group-wise n and s table) you used to decide it was tenable.
You can say precisely what a given p-value licenses and refuse the four standard misreadings out loud, including the case where p<0.001 accompanies an effect too small to be worth deploying.

You can size an evaluation before it runs: given a minimum effect worth caring about, alpha and power, produce the required n per arm, and given a fixed labelling budget produce the minimum detectable effect instead.

You can take a multi-group result, decide between classical F, Welch's F and a permutation test, run the correct post-hoc procedure (Tukey HSD or Dunnett), and report simultaneous intervals plus eta^2 rather than a bare p-value.
You can identify when a comparison is a multiple-testing family, choose FWER or FDR control with a stated reason, and adjust with Holm or Benjamini-Hochberg.

You can explain why a paired t-test across cross-validation folds is invalid, implement a corrected resampled t-test or bootstrap-over-test-set alternative, and put an honest interval on a reported model-metric difference.
failureModes: The pilot readout says '0 failures in 40 calls, so reliability is 100%'; the Wald interval collapsed to zero width at phat=0 and the Wilson bound (or the rule of three, ~7.5%) would have shown the honest upper limit before it reached the customer's slide.

Two models are compared with a paired t-test over 10 cross-validation folds; the folds share training data so the variance is understated, the p-value is manufactured, and the 'significantly better' model loses in production.

A significant ANOVA F is driven entirely by one cohort with n=3 and huge variance created by a mislabelled category in the source table - a data-quality bug read as a scientific finding because nobody printed n_j, mean_j and s_j before testing.

A flat A/B result is sliced by 30 customer segments until one comes back at p=0.03; nobody adjusted for the family, and the resulting 'the product works for mid-market healthcare' claim does not replicate in the next quarter.

The team runs Shapiro-Wilk on 50,000 latency measurements, gets p<1e-20, abandons the t-test for a rank test that answers a different question (stochastic dominance, not means), and then reports the result as a difference in means anyway.

The bootstrap resamples rows when the data is clustered by user - one heavy user contributes 400 rows - so the interval is several times too narrow and the model's apparent lift survives a resampling check it should have failed.

The evaluation harness computes p = 1 - f.cdf(F, dfn, dfd) instead of f.sf(F, dfn, dfd); for large F the subtraction cancels to exactly 0.0 in float64, the test suite's 1e-6 comparison against scipy passes on the easy datasets and hides the bug until an extreme statistic appears.

A pooled Student t-test is used on cohorts of size 900 and 60 where the small cohort has three times the variance; the equal-variance assumption inflates the Type I error, and the resulting 'significant' improvement is an artefact of the imbalance rather than of the model.
interviewQuestions: Derive Welch's t-statistic and its Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, then tell me exactly when you would use it instead of the pooled Student version and what happens to the false-positive rate if you get that choice wrong.

Write out the sum-of-squares decomposition for one-way ANOVA and show that F = MSB/MSW. For k=2, what is the relationship between this F and the two-sample t? What does a significant F entitle you to say, and what does it not?

A customer's data scientist says 'the 95% CI is [1.2, 4.8], so there's a 95% chance the true lift is in that range'. Is that correct? Give the correct interpretation, and describe how you would empirically verify that an interval you wrote actually has 95% coverage.

Design: we have budget to human-label 2,000 evaluation examples once, and we want to know whether a new retriever beats the incumbent. Specify the design, the estimand, the test, the interval, how many examples you actually need, and how you would present a null result to the customer.

Debug: an offline eval reports the new model is 4 points better with p=0.004, but the online A/B shows no difference. Walk me through the candidate explanations in the order you would check them, and say which of them a confidence interval would and would not have caught.
When does the bootstrap fail? Give me at least three concrete cases, and for each one tell me what you would do instead.

You have 6 model variants and want to know which beat the baseline. Lay out the testing strategy: omnibus or not, which post-hoc procedure, FWER or FDR, and how you would explain the multiplicity correction to a product manager who thinks you are hiding a win.
96.proofOfWork: A public repo `inference-from-scratch` that goes one step past the deliverable by turning `inference.py` into a falsifiable claim about correctness. Alongside the NumPy implementations of Welch's t, the one-way ANOVA F and percentile/basic/BCa bootstrap intervals, add a simulation harness that empirically measures the two things the formulas promise: a coverage study that draws 20,000 samples from normal, lognormal, t(3) and a 5%-contaminated mixture at n = 10, 30, 200 and reports actual coverage of each interval type (analytic t, percentile, basic, BCa) as a table plus a coverage-vs-n plot, and a Type-I-error study that runs Student, Welch, Mann-Whitney and a permutation test under H0 across equal and unequal variance and unequal group sizes, reporting the realised rejection rate against the nominal 0.05. The README states, in numbers, where each method breaks - the n and the skew at which percentile coverage drops below 90%, the variance ratio and imbalance at which pooled Student's error rate exceeds 8% while Welch holds at 5% - with a short 'which test do I use' decision note written for a customer's analyst. CI runs the pytest suite (matching scipy to 1e-6 on three real datasets) plus a fast, fixed-seed version of both simulations as regression tests, and every figure is regenerated from a recorded seed so the numbers are reproducible.

97.topic: Experimentation and causality: A/B design, power, sequential testing, confounding
97.why: Every model an FDE ships eventually has to survive the question 'did it actually do anything?', and the answer is an experiment, not an offline AUC. You will be the person sizing the rollout before it launches, defending a readout to a customer's analytics team who peeked at it daily, and explaining why the 30% lift in the pilot region is a marketplace cannibalisation artefact rather than value you can invoice for. Causal literacy is also what stops you shipping a model trained on a target that a confounder generated - the difference between 'our churn model has 0.89 AUC' and 'intervening on the thing it scores changes churn' is the entire commercial argument.
prerequisites: Probability at the level of Topic 95: random variables, expectation and variance algebra, Bernoulli/binomial/normal, the CLT and why sample means are asymptotically normal
Statistical inference at the level of Topic 96: estimators and their sampling distributions, standard errors, confidence intervals, Type I/II error, the t-distribution
NumPy vectorisation and a reproducible RNG (Topic 99): you will run 10,000-replicate Monte Carlo simulations, so np.random.default_rng(seed) and array-level thinking, not Python loops
pandas group-by and joins plus enough SQL (Topic 29/40) to pull an assignment log, an exposure log and a metric table and reconcile their row counts
Linear regression as an estimator, not a black box (Topic 93/94): the OLS normal equations, what a coefficient means, and why heteroskedasticity changes the standard error but not the point estimate
matplotlib for the three diagnostic plots this topic lives on: MDE-vs-N curve, p-value histogram from an A/A suite, and a propensity-overlap histogram

subtopics.name: Potential outcomes, estimands and SUTVA
subtopics.learn: Write the Rubin model down: each unit has Y_i(1) and Y_i(0), the individual effect Y_i(1)-Y_i(0) is never observed (the fundamental problem of causal inference), and consistency links them to data as Y_i = T_i·Y_i(1) + (1-T_i)·Y_i(0). Be able to derive in three lines that the naive contrast decomposes as E[Y|T=1] - E[Y|T=0] = ATE + (E[Y(0)|T=1] - E[Y(0)|T=0]) + (1-p)(ATT - ATC), so the bias term is a statement about counterfactuals, not about sample size. State the identification assumptions by name - ignorability (Y(1),Y(0)) ⟂ T | X, positivity 0 < P(T=1|X) < 1, SUTVA (no interference between units, no hidden versions of treatment) - and get in the habit of writing the estimand as one English sentence ('the ATE of showing the recommendation panel on 7-day retained revenue per assigned user') before touching any data.

resource.label: Hernán & Robins - Causal Inference: What If (free full text)

subtopics.name: Randomisation as identification, A/A tests and balance checks
subtopics.learn: Understand precisely what randomisation buys: it forces T ⟂ (Y(1),Y(0)) by construction, which zeroes the selection-bias term above without you having to know, measure or model a single confounder. Check balance with standardised mean differences (|mean_T - mean_C| / pooled SD, flag above 0.1), not with a p-value per covariate - testing 30 covariates at α=0.05 and finding one 'imbalanced' is testing your RNG, not your design. Build the A/A harness you will reuse all topic: replay the assignment hash on historical data 1,000-10,000 times with no treatment applied, collect p-values, and assert they are Uniform(0,1) (KS test does not reject) and that the empirical rejection rate sits at α within Monte Carlo error. An A/A that fails means your variance estimator, your randomisation unit or your bucketing hash is broken - fix that before you evaluate any feature.

resource.label: Causal Inference for The Brave and True - Ch. 02 Randomised Experiments

subtopics.name: Metric design: OEC, guardrails, ratio metrics and capping
subtopics.learn: Pick exactly one OEC (overall evaluation criterion) before launch and write it into the pre-registration; everything else is a guardrail or a debug metric with a different decision rule. Classify each metric by shape because the shape determines the variance formula: per-user sums (additive, plain t-test), ratio-of-sums like CTR = Σclicks/Σimpressions (analysis unit is not the randomisation unit - needs the delta method), and quantiles like p95 latency (no closed-form variance; bootstrap or a Cochran-style order-statistic interval). Guardrails are one-sided non-inferiority tests against a pre-agreed margin - 'p > 0.05 so no harm' is not a guardrail, it is an underpowered test dressed up as a pass. Pre-register a winsorisation percentile for heavy-tailed revenue metrics and report capped and uncapped side by side, so the customer sees that one whale did not decide the launch.

resource.label: Dmitriev et al., KDD 2017 - A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls in Online Controlled Experiments (PDF)

subtopics.name: The difference-in-means estimator, Welch's t-test and the two-proportion z
subtopics.learn: The estimator is τ̂ = Ȳ_T - Ȳ_C and its Neyman variance is σ²_T/n_T + σ²_C/n_C - note it never assumes equal variances, so use scipy.stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False) (Welch, with the Welch-Satterthwaite df) as the default, because a treatment that changes the mean usually changes the spread too. Report τ̂ ± z_{1-α/2}·SE in both absolute and relative terms; a p-value alone is not a readout. For a binary metric, know that the correct test statistic pools p̂ under H0 (SE = √(p̂(1-p̂)(1/n_T+1/n_C))) while the confidence interval must use the unpooled SE - using the pooled SE for the interval is a very common inconsistency that makes the CI and the p-value disagree at the boundary. At n in the hundreds of thousands the CLT makes normality a non-issue for Bernoulli and mildly skewed metrics; what actually breaks the t-test is an extreme tail (revenue, session length), not the shape near the middle.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.ttest_ind (Welch's t-test, equal_var=False)

subtopics.name: Deriving power, MDE and sample size from first principles
subtopics.learn: Derive it, do not look it up: you reject when |τ̂|/SE > z_{1-α/2}; power 1-β against a true effect Δ requires Δ/SE ≥ z_{1-α/2} + z_{1-β}; with equal arms SE = σ√(2/n), so n per arm = 2σ²(z_{1-α/2}+z_{1-β})²/Δ². For α=0.05 two-sided and 80% power, (1.96+0.8416)² ≈ 7.849, giving the number you should be able to quote in a meeting: n ≈ 15.7σ²/Δ², and for a proportion n ≈ 15.7·p(1-p)/Δ². Internalise the quadratic: halving the MDE quadruples N, so a customer asking to detect 1% instead of 2% is asking for four times the traffic, not twice. Understand Type M (exaggeration) and Type S (sign) error - conditional on significance, a 20%-powered test overstates the true effect by roughly 2-3x and has a non-trivial chance of the wrong sign, which is exactly why an underpowered 'win' is the most expensive result in the readout.

resource.label: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook 7.2.2.2 - Sample sizes required

subtopics.name: The MDE-vs-N curve, allocation ratio, triggering and runtime
subtopics.learn: Use statsmodels TTestIndPower().solve_power(effect_size, nobs1, alpha, power, ratio) to solve for whichever of the five quantities is unknown, and plot MDE against N on a log-x axis - this single curve is what you show a customer who wants a two-day test. Handle unequal allocation properly: with fraction k in treatment the variance scales as 1/(k(1-k)n), so a 90/10 split costs 2.78x the users of 50/50 for the same MDE (sometimes still correct, when the point is risk containment on a risky change). Convert N into runtime through daily eligible units and always round up to whole weeks, because day-of-week seasonality otherwise leaks into the contrast. Handle triggering explicitly: if only 20% of assigned users ever reach the surface, the effect measured on all assigned users is diluted to 0.2·τ_exposed, so you either analyse the triggered population (with symmetric counterfactual logging in control) or size for the diluted effect - and say which one the number in the deck is.

resource.label: statsmodels docs - TTestIndPower (solve_power for power / nobs / effect size)

subtopics.name: Variance is the enemy: De Moivre's equation and heavy tails
subtopics.learn: The most dangerous equation is SE = σ/√n: small groups produce both the highest and the lowest observed rates, so any 'top 5 segments by lift' table is largely a ranking by inverse sample size, and any per-tenant leaderboard on a small customer's data is noise with a story attached. Since N is usually fixed by the customer's traffic, the lever you actually control is σ - capping, trigger-only analysis, choosing a less variable OEC (bounded engagement rather than raw revenue), and the variance-reduction techniques later in this topic. Estimate σ from the customer's own historical data, never from an assumption; for a long-tailed metric get σ and the sampling distribution from a bootstrap over historical users rather than trusting the normal approximation, and check the resulting MDE against what the business calls a meaningful change before agreeing to run anything.

resource.label: Causal Inference for The Brave and True - Ch. 03 Stats Review: The Most Dangerous Equation

subtopics.name: Ratio metrics: the delta method and the user-level bootstrap
subtopics.learn: When the metric is R = X̄/Ȳ (clicks per impression, revenue per session) but randomisation is per user, derive the variance from the first-order Taylor expansion of f(x,y) = x/y around (E[X], E[Y]): Var(R) ≈ (1/n)·[ Var(X)/E[Y]² - 2·E[X]·Cov(X,Y)/E[Y]³ + E[X]²·Var(Y)/E[Y]⁴ ], where n is the number of users and X_i, Y_i are per-user sums. Implement it in NumPy from the per-user aggregates and confirm against a bootstrap that resamples users (not impressions) and recomputes the ratio - the two should agree within a few percent. Then reproduce the bug it exists to fix: compute the naive impression-level SE on the same data and observe it is typically 2-5x too small, which is how an A/A test on CTR 'detects' a lift. Extend the same expansion to a difference of two ratios and to CUPED-adjusted ratio metrics.

resource.label: Deng, Knoblich & Lu - Applying the Delta Method in Metric Analytics (arXiv:1803.06336)

subtopics.name: Randomisation unit vs analysis unit: ICC, design effect and clustered SEs
subtopics.learn: When you randomise accounts but analyse seats, the observations inside a cluster are correlated and the variance inflates by the design effect DEFF = 1 + (m̄ - 1)·ρ, where ρ is the intra-cluster correlation and m̄ the mean cluster size; effective sample size is n_eff = n/DEFF. Be able to compute it: ρ = 0.3 with 20 seats per account gives DEFF ≈ 6.7, so an interval computed as if seats were independent is √6.7 ≈ 2.6x too narrow - which is exactly the readout that gets torn apart in front of the customer's data scientist. Three fixes, in order of preference: aggregate to the randomisation unit and run the plain t-test, use cluster-robust standard errors (OLS with cov_type='cluster', groups=account_id), or fit a GEE with an exchangeable working correlation. Know the small-cluster caveat: cluster-robust asymptotics need roughly 40+ clusters, so a pilot across 12 enterprise accounts must use randomisation inference (permute the account-level assignment and read the exact p-value off the null distribution) instead.

resource.label: statsmodels docs - Generalized Estimating Equations (clustered/correlated data)

subtopics.name: Sample ratio mismatch: the check that invalidates a readout
subtopics.learn: Before reading any lift, test the assignment counts against the intended split with a chi-square goodness-of-fit on 1 df: scipy.stats.chisquare([n_T, n_C], f_exp=[N/2, N/2]); at N=1,000,000 a 50.2/49.8 split gives p ≈ 6e-5. Use a strict threshold (p < 0.001) and treat a hit as a hard stop - an SRM means the two groups are no longer exchangeable, so every downstream number is uninterpretable and 'the lift is still probably real' is the wrong sentence. Learn the standard root causes so you can triage in minutes: bot/fraud filtering applied after assignment, differential redirect latency or crash rate dropping treatment users out of the log, a triggering condition evaluated after the treatment already changed behaviour, deduplication on a key that behaves differently per arm, and delayed telemetry flush for one variant. Run SRM per day and per reported segment too, since an overall-balanced experiment can be badly skewed inside the exact slice you are about to present.

resource.label: SciPy docs - scipy.stats.chisquare (goodness-of-fit test)

subtopics.name: Peeking: why fixed-horizon p-values collapse under optional stopping
subtopics.learn: A fixed-horizon p-value is only calibrated at the single pre-declared N; the distribution of the p-value at a data-dependent stopping time is not uniform. Simulate it rather than believing it: 10,000 A/A replications of a Bernoulli metric, evaluate the two-sample test after every 100 users, stop and declare a winner the first time p < 0.05, and watch the empirical false-positive rate climb to roughly 0.2-0.3 for a handful of looks and past 0.5 for continuous monitoring. The law of the iterated logarithm makes the limiting case exact: monitor forever and you reject at α = 0.05 with probability 1, so 'we watched the dashboard until it went green' is a procedure with 100% Type I error. Understand that the fix is not a longer run or a Bonferroni over looks (which is both wrong and needlessly conservative for dependent partial sums) but a procedure whose error is controlled uniformly over the whole monitoring path.

resource.label: Johari, Pekelis & Walsh - Always Valid Inference: Bringing Sequential Analysis to A/B Testing (arXiv:1512.04922)

subtopics.name: Always-valid inference: confidence sequences, mSPRT and alpha spending
subtopics.learn: A confidence sequence is a family (L_t, U_t) satisfying P(∀t ≥ 1 : τ ∈ (L_t, U_t)) ≥ 1 - α - the quantifier is inside the probability, which is exactly what licenses stopping whenever you like. Understand the machinery well enough to implement one: a mixture likelihood ratio Λ_t = ∫ (L_θ(data_t)/L_0(data_t)) dH(θ) is a nonnegative martingale under H0, so Ville's inequality gives P(∃t : Λ_t ≥ 1/α) ≤ α, and inverting Λ_t ≤ 1/α yields the interval; the mSPRT of the previous reference is this with a normal mixing distribution, and sub-Gaussian / empirical-Bernstein constructions give the characteristic √(log log t) boundary. Know the discrete alternative: pre-declare K interim analyses and spend α with an O'Brien-Fleming (very strict early, near-α at the final look) or Pocock (constant boundary) spending function. Quantify the price honestly - at the planned N an always-valid interval is typically 1.3-2x wider than the fixed-horizon one - and say that out loud when you propose it, because the trade is 'the right to stop early' against 'a bigger sample if you do not'.

resource.label: Howard, Ramdas, McAuliffe & Sekhon - Time-uniform, nonparametric, nonasymptotic confidence sequences (arXiv:1810.08240)

subtopics.name: CUPED: variance reduction from pre-experiment data
subtopics.learn: Define Y_cuped = Y - θ(X - E[X]) where X is a strictly pre-treatment covariate; because X is unaffected by treatment, E[Y_cuped] is unchanged and the estimator stays unbiased, while Var(Y_cuped) = Var(Y)(1 - ρ²_{X,Y}) at the optimal θ* = Cov(Y,X)/Var(X). Do the arithmetic that sells it: ρ = 0.7 removes 51% of the variance, which halves the required runtime for the same MDE - the single highest-leverage thing you can offer a customer with thin traffic. The best X is almost always the same metric measured over the 14-28 days before assignment; estimate θ pooled across both arms, and give users with no pre-period the pooled mean of X (they simply get no variance reduction). The failure that matters: any covariate measured during the experiment is post-treatment, so adjusting on it reintroduces bias - verify your implementation by rerunning the A/A suite with CUPED enabled and confirming the false-positive rate is still α and the p-values still uniform.

resource.label: Deng, Xu, Kohavi & Walker, WSDM 2013 - Improving the Sensitivity of Online Controlled Experiments by Utilizing Pre-Experiment Data (CUPED, PDF)

subtopics.name: Regression adjustment done right: Lin's estimator and stratification
subtopics.learn: Regressing Y on T alone reproduces the difference in means exactly, so covariates in a randomised experiment are about precision, not bias. Know Freedman's critique - naive additive adjustment Y ~ T + X can be less efficient than the unadjusted estimator and its usual OLS standard errors are wrong under treatment-effect heterogeneity - and know Lin's fix: centre the covariates and interact them all with treatment, Y ~ T + X_c + T:X_c, which is asymptotically never worse than the unadjusted difference in means, paired with HC2 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Recognise CUPED as the one-covariate special case of exactly this, and post-stratification as the categorical version. If randomisation was blocked or stratified, the strata must appear in the analysis - analysing a blocked design as simple randomisation is conservative, which sounds safe until you tell a customer they need 40% more traffic than they actually do.

resource.label: Winston Lin - Agnostic notes on regression adjustments to experimental data: Reexamining Freedman's critique (arXiv:1208.2301)

subtopics.name: Multiple comparisons: FWER, FDR and pre-registered segments
subtopics.learn: With m independent tests at level α the family-wise error is 1-(1-α)^m: 20 secondary metrics gives a 64% chance of at least one false positive, which is why every experiment dashboard has something green on it. Know the three procedures and when each is right - Bonferroni (α/m, controls FWER, needlessly harsh), Holm-Bonferroni (step-down, uniformly more powerful, still exact FWER control), and Benjamini-Hochberg (reject the k largest p-values with p_(k) ≤ k·q/m, controls the false discovery rate) - and run them with statsmodels multipletests(pvals, method='holm'|'fdr_bh'). Apply a tiered policy rather than one blanket correction: the single OEC at full α, guardrails as one-sided non-inferiority tests where you want power against harm, and the long tail of secondary metrics under BH at q = 0.1. Post-hoc segment slicing is the worst offender in practice - pre-register the segments, or estimate a CATE function (causal forest, X-learner) and treat any segment story as a hypothesis for the next experiment rather than a finding in this one.

resource.label: statsmodels docs - multipletests (Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg)

subtopics.name: Interference: network effects, marketplaces, cluster randomisation and switchbacks
subtopics.learn: SUTVA fails whenever a control unit's outcome depends on who else was treated: social graphs and shared feeds, two-sided marketplaces where treatment consumes finite supply so control is actively depressed (the measured lift then overstates the global effect, sometimes by more than the whole effect), shared caches and rate limits, and any ML system retrained on traffic the experiment generated. Learn the designs that restore identification - graph cluster randomisation (partition into communities, randomise clusters, and define an exposure model so partially-exposed units are handled explicitly), market/region-level randomisation with randomisation inference because you have tens of clusters not millions, and switchbacks that randomise time buckets with a burn-in after each switch and a bucket length chosen to trade carryover bias against variance. The FDE skill is naming the bias direction out loud: 'in a marketplace this is an upper bound on the global effect' is a defensible sentence and buys you far more credibility than a confident point estimate.

resource.label: Ugander, Karrer, Backstrom & Kleinberg - Graph cluster randomization: network exposure to multiple universes (arXiv:1305.6979)

subtopics.name: Non-compliance and dilution: ITT vs LATE, and why 'as-treated' is a trap
subtopics.learn: Intention-to-treat compares assigned groups and is always unbiased for the question 'what happens if we ship this', but it is diluted whenever some assigned users never receive treatment. The complier average causal effect recovers the effect on the exposed: LATE = ITT / P(comply), which is 2SLS with assignment as an instrument for exposure, valid under relevance, the exclusion restriction (assignment affects Y only through exposure) and monotonicity (no defiers). The trap to be able to name instantly is 'as-treated' analysis - comparing users who actually engaged with the feature against all of control conditions on a post-treatment variable and reintroduces precisely the selection bias randomisation removed, and it is the single most common way an internal dashboard reports a 40% lift that evaporates on rollout. Triggered analysis is the disciplined version: log the counterfactual trigger in control symmetrically, verify the trigger rates match between arms, and report both the triggered effect and the diluted all-users effect.

resource.label: Causal Inference for The Brave and True - Ch. 08 Instrumental Variables

subtopics.name: DAGs: d-separation, the backdoor criterion, colliders and bad controls
subtopics.learn: Draw the graph before you choose controls. Master the three building blocks - chain T → M → Y, fork T ← C → Y, collider T → K ← Y - and d-separation: a path is blocked if a non-collider on it is conditioned on, or if a collider (and every descendant of it) is not conditioned on. State the backdoor criterion exactly: a set Z identifies the effect of T on Y if it blocks every path into T that starts with an arrow into T, and contains no descendant of T. Then learn the three ways adjustment actively makes things worse, because 'control for more variables' is the customer's instinct: conditioning on a mediator removes the very effect you are estimating, conditioning on a collider (or a selected sample, which is the same thing) opens a spurious path and produces M-bias, and conditioning on an instrument amplifies whatever residual confounding is left. Build the graph in DAGitty, read off the minimal sufficient adjustment set, and then test the graph's implied conditional independences against the data - a DAG that fails its own testable implications is a hypothesis you just refuted.

resource.label: DAGitty - Learn (d-separation, adjustment sets, testable implications)

subtopics.name: Adjusting for confounding without randomisation: propensity scores, IPW, DML and refutations
subtopics.learn: Define the propensity score e(X) = P(T=1|X) and write the IPW estimator τ̂ = (1/n)Σ [ T_i·Y_i/ê(X_i) - (1-T_i)·Y_i/(1-ê(X_i)) ], unbiased under ignorability and positivity. The diagnostic that decides whether the analysis is possible at all is the overlap plot: histogram ê(X) by arm, and if treated units pile up near 1 with no control mass there, no weighting scheme creates comparable units - trim to the common support and say the estimand narrowed, rather than shipping weights of 400. Know that AIPW/doubly-robust is consistent if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correct, and that double/debiased ML adds cross-fitting plus a Neyman-orthogonal score so that slow-converging ML nuisance estimates do not contaminate the rate on τ̂. Finish every observational estimate with the refutation battery: placebo treatment (estimate must go to zero), random common cause (estimate must not move), data-subset and bootstrap stability, and a sensitivity analysis - the E-value or Rosenbaum Γ answering 'how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be to erase this?'

resource.label: Causal Inference for The Brave and True - Ch. 11 Propensity Score

subtopics.name: Quasi-experiments and writing the readout
subtopics.learn: For the very common 'we already rolled it out to Region A' situation, know difference-in-differences: τ̂ = (Ȳ_post,treat - Ȳ_pre,treat) - (Ȳ_post,ctrl - Ȳ_pre,ctrl), identified by parallel counterfactual trends, not by matching pre-period levels - so always plot the event study of pre-period leads and require them to be flat and insignificant. Know that two-way fixed effects with staggered adoption is biased under time-varying heterogeneous effects (it puts negative weights on already-treated comparisons) and that Callaway-Sant'Anna or Sun-Abraham estimators fix it; keep synthetic control for a single treated unit with a long clean pre-period, and regression discontinuity when eligibility follows a threshold rule. Then write the artefact that actually gets read: estimand in one sentence, design and randomisation unit, pre-registered α / power / MDE / runtime, SRM and A/A checks passed, τ̂ with a CI in absolute and relative terms, guardrail results, variance-reduction method and its A/A validation, the interference or confounding caveat with its bias direction, and a ship / no-ship recommendation that states what evidence would change your mind.

resource.label: Roth, Sant'Anna, Bilinski & Poe - What's Trending in Difference-in-Differences? (arXiv:2201.01194)

outcomes: You can derive n = 2σ²(z_{1-α/2}+z_{1-β})²/Δ² on a whiteboard from the rejection rule, apply it to a 3% baseline conversion with a 5% relative MDE, and match statsmodels TTestIndPower to within 1%, then produce the MDE-vs-N curve and translate it into whole-week runtime for a stated daily traffic.

You can run a 10,000-replicate Monte Carlo A/A study showing the false-positive rate of a daily-peeked fixed-horizon t-test rising well past 5%, and show an always-valid confidence sequence on the same simulated streams holding at 5% while quantifying how much wider its interval is at the planned N.

You can implement CUPED from the pre-period covariate up (θ* = Cov(Y,X)/Var(X)), report the realised variance reduction against the predicted 1-ρ², and prove correctness by rerunning the A/A suite with adjustment on and showing uniform p-values.

You can compute a ratio-metric standard error with the delta method from per-user aggregates, match it against a user-level bootstrap, and demonstrate on real data how much the naive impression-level SE understates it.

You can look at an assignment log and decide in under five minutes whether the experiment is readable: chi-square SRM test overall and per segment, trigger-rate symmetry between arms, allocation ratio versus intent, and pre-period balance by standardised mean difference.

You can compute the design effect for a cluster-randomised rollout (DEFF = 1 + (m̄-1)ρ), restate the effective sample size and corrected CI, and choose between aggregation, cluster-robust SEs, GEE and randomisation inference based on cluster count.

You can draw a DAG for a customer's observational question, name the minimal sufficient adjustment set from the backdoor criterion, identify at least one variable they wanted to control for that is a mediator or collider, and state why adding it would bias the estimate.

You can read a finished readout and deliver a verdict that names the specific defect and the specific fix - sequential bound, CUPED, delta-method SE, cluster-robust SE, backdoor adjustment, ITT instead of as-treated - rather than 'run it longer'.
failureModes: The team watched the dashboard daily and shipped the first day p dipped below 0.05; the fixed-horizon test had no sequential bound, the true false-positive rate for that procedure was above 25%, and the effect vanished on full rollout while the customer had already told their board about it.

CTR was computed as total clicks over total impressions with an impression-level standard error while randomisation was by user; the SE came out roughly four times too small, an A/A test would have flagged it, and a 0.4% 'significant' lift was pure noise.

A 50.4/49.6 split with a p-value of 1e-6 on the SRM chi-square was waved through as 'basically balanced'; the imbalance came from treatment users crashing before their telemetry flushed, so the surviving treatment users were systematically healthier and every metric looked better.

The guardrail was a two-sided test on p95 latency that came back p = 0.3, reported as 'no regression'; it was powered to detect only a 40 ms change, the true regression was 18 ms across every request, and support tickets started three weeks after launch.

In a two-sided marketplace, treatment buyers absorbed inventory that control buyers would otherwise have bought; the measured 12% conversion lift was mostly redistribution, and the global rollout produced a fraction of it because the control group had been the source of the gain.

Analysts compared users who actually opened the new panel against the entire control group; conditioning on a post-treatment engagement variable reintroduced selection bias, turning a roughly flat effect into a reported 35% lift that no rollout ever reproduced.

CUPED was applied with a covariate computed over the experiment window rather than the pre-period; the adjustment absorbed part of the treatment effect itself, shrinking the estimate toward zero, and the A/A validation that would have exposed it was never rerun after the covariate changed.

Forty segments were sliced post-hoc with no correction, one came back at p = 0.03, and 'the feature works for enterprise users on Android' became a roadmap commitment built on an expected-by-chance result in a segment of 900 users.
interviewQuestions: Derive the per-arm sample size for a two-sample test of proportions from the rejection rule and the power requirement. Baseline conversion is 4%, the product team wants to detect a 5% relative lift at 80% power and α = 0.05 two-sided, and you get 40,000 eligible users per day. How long does the test run, and what are three legitimate ways to shorten it without changing α or power?

Explain to a customer's VP of Product, who has been checking the dashboard every morning, exactly why that invalidates the p-value. Then explain what a confidence sequence guarantees that a fixed-horizon confidence interval does not, and what it costs them at the planned sample size.

Debug: an A/A test on your platform returns significant results about 15% of the time on the click-through-rate metric but exactly 5% of the time on revenue per user. What are the two most likely causes, how do you distinguish them from the assignment and exposure logs, and what is the fix for each?

Design: a customer wants to know whether their new AI-assisted support triage reduces time-to-resolution. Agents work in teams, they talk to each other, and only 6 of their 30 teams handle the relevant ticket volume. Give me the design - randomisation unit, estimand, how you get a standard error you would defend, and what you would tell them you cannot measure.

Write down the CUPED estimator, prove it is unbiased, and derive the variance reduction factor. What exactly goes wrong if the covariate is measured during the experiment instead of before it, and what test would catch that mistake before the readout ships?

A customer has no experiment - they rolled the feature out to their EU region in March and want the impact. Draw the DAG you would sketch with them, state the identifying assumption for difference-in-differences in one sentence, name the plot that would falsify it, and say what you would do differently if six regions adopted it at six different times.

You are handed a readout showing a 22% lift on the primary metric with p = 0.001, computed on the users who were exposed to treatment versus everyone in control, with a 60/40 assignment split. List everything you would check before letting that number leave the building, in the order you would check it.
97.proofOfWork: A public `experiment-review-board` repo that turns the ab-toolkit into something a customer's analytics team can actually adopt. It contains (1) a `preregister` CLI that takes baseline mean and variance from the customer's own historical data, an MDE, α, power and daily traffic, and emits a signed pre-registration YAML - estimand sentence, randomisation unit, OEC, guardrails with non-inferiority margins, pre-declared segments, analysis method, planned N and runtime in whole weeks - plus the MDE-vs-N plot; (2) an `audit` command that consumes an assignment log, an exposure log and a metric table and returns a pass/fail card covering SRM (chi-square, overall and per segment and per day), trigger-rate symmetry, pre-period standardised mean differences, allocation ratio versus intent, and whether the analysis unit matches the randomisation unit, refusing to print a lift when any hard check fails; (3) a `variance` module implementing delta-method SEs for ratio metrics, cluster-robust and GEE options with the DEFF computed and printed, CUPED with the realised-versus-predicted variance reduction, and Lin's interacted regression adjustment, each shipped with an A/A calibration test in CI that fails the build if the false-positive rate drifts outside [0.04, 0.06] over 10,000 replications; and (4) six deliberately broken readouts in `cases/` - peeked, SRM, impression-level ratio SE, as-treated, marketplace interference, post-hoc segment - each with a one-page written verdict naming the defect, the corrected number where one can be recovered, and the single design change that would have prevented it. The README opens with the pre-registration template as a fill-in-the-blanks page a customer can use without reading any of the code.

98.topic: Information theory and loss functions: entropy, KL, cross-entropy, maximum likelihood
98.why: Every loss you will ever ship to a customer - logistic regression's log loss, a transformer's next-token cross-entropy, a gradient-boosted Poisson deviance on their count data - is a negative log-likelihood, and the number it prints has a unit, a floor and a direction that their data scientist will ask you about in the room. Without this topic you cannot say whether a validation loss of 1.9 nats is good, whether the loss that stopped falling is irreducible label noise H(P) or model error KL(P||Q), or why a model that looks fine on AUC is quietly overconfident on the minority class the customer actually cares about. With it you can derive the objective on their whiteboard in five minutes, name which divergence and which direction it minimises, and tell the difference between a data ceiling, a leakage artefact and a training bug - which is most of what defending a model in front of a customer consists of.
