prerequisites: Probability at Topic 95 level: discrete and continuous distributions, joint/conditional/marginal factorisation, Bayes' rule, and independence vs conditional independence
Calculus and optimisation from Topic 94: partial derivatives, the chain rule, what convexity buys you, and what one gradient-descent step does to a parameter vector
Statistical inference from Topic 96: estimators and their bias, and the habit of reading the likelihood as a function of parameters with the data held fixed
Logs and exponentials at speed: log(ab), log(a/b), change of base log2(x) = ln(x)/ln(2), Jensen's inequality for a convex function, and the fact that log is monotone so argmax is preserved
NumPy fluency: broadcasting, axis= reductions, float32 vs float64 accumulation, and np.testing.assert_allclose (Topic 99 goes deeper on the stability side)
Enough PyTorch to run a forward and backward pass and read a loss tensor: shapes, .backward(), an optimiser step (Topic 112 goes deeper)

subtopics.name: Self-information, units, and the code-length reading of a log
subtopics.learn: Define surprisal I(x) = -log p(x) and know why the log is forced rather than chosen: additivity over independent events, continuity in p, and monotonicity in 1/p pin it down up to the base. Fix your units and say them out loud every single time - log base 2 gives bits, natural log gives nats, 1 nat = 1/ln(2) = 1.4427 bits - because every library hides a different default (scipy.stats.entropy is base e unless you pass base=2; torch cross_entropy is always nats) and a large fraction of 'our loss is 2.1' arguments are pure unit confusion. Connect it to Kraft's inequality and Shannon's source coding theorem: an optimal prefix code spends about -log2 p(x) bits on symbol x, so entropy is not a metaphor for compressed size, it is the achievable average code length in the limit. Be able to state that a fair 8-sided die costs exactly 3 bits per roll and that no code beats it.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - Chapter 05 Probability, 05. Information Theory

subtopics.name: Shannon entropy: the formula, its bounds, and hand computation
subtopics.learn: Compute H(P) = -sum_x p(x) log p(x) by hand for at least three distributions before you touch a library: uniform over 4 outcomes (2 bits, the maximum for a 4-symbol alphabet), a point mass (0 bits), and the skewed [0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125] (1.75 bits, and note the code lengths 1, 2, 3, 3 that make it exact). Know the properties you will use as sanity checks forever: 0 <= H(P) <= log|X| with equality on the right iff P is uniform, H is concave in P, and the 0 log 0 = 0 convention - which is precisely why your implementation must use np.where or scipy.special.xlogy rather than adding a global epsilon to every probability. Reproduce all three by hand and with scipy.stats.entropy(pk, base=2), then be able to tell a customer that 'the model cannot get below 1.31 bits here' is a statement about their labels, not about your architecture.

resource.label: SciPy - scipy.stats.entropy (Shannon entropy and the two-argument KL form)

subtopics.name: Joint and conditional entropy, the chain rule, and mutual information
subtopics.learn: Derive H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) from the definitions in three lines, and note that H(Y|X) = sum_x p(x) H(Y|X=x) is an average over x, not the entropy of one conditional slice you happened to pick. Define mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) = KL(P(x,y) || P(x)P(y)) >= 0, with equality iff X and Y are independent, and read it as 'bits of X you learn by observing Y'. Know that MI sees arbitrary nonlinear dependence where Pearson correlation reports zero (y = x squared on a symmetric x), which is exactly why sklearn.metrics.mutual_info_score and mutual_info_classif are the right first screen when a customer says a feature 'has no correlation with the target'. Compute I on a 2x2 contingency table by hand and confirm it against sklearn.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.metrics.mutual_info_score

subtopics.name: KL divergence: Gibbs' inequality, asymmetry, and where it becomes infinite
subtopics.learn: Define KL(P||Q) = sum_x p(x) log(p(x)/q(x)) and prove KL >= 0 in four lines from Jensen applied to the convex function -log: -sum p log(q/p) >= -log sum p (q/p) = -log 1 = 0, with equality iff P = Q wherever P has mass. Internalise that KL is not a metric - KL(P||Q) is not KL(Q||P) and the triangle inequality fails - so 'the distance between the two distributions' is the wrong sentence in a customer meeting and you should say 'divergence' and name the direction. Know the support condition cold: KL(P||Q) = +infinity whenever q(x) = 0 while p(x) > 0, which is the same mathematics behind a saturated softmax returning inf loss on the true class and behind a binned drift monitor exploding the first time a reference bin is empty. Implement it with scipy.special.rel_entr and summing, and know why that is the numerically sane route rather than hand-writing p*log(p/q).

resource.label: SciPy - scipy.special.rel_entr (elementwise relative entropy)

subtopics.name: The identity CE(P,Q) = H(P) + KL(P||Q) and the irreducible floor
subtopics.learn: Derive the decomposition in two lines: CE(P,Q) = -sum p log q = -sum p log p + sum p log(p/q) = H(P) + KL(P||Q). Read the consequence straight off the page: for a fixed data distribution P, minimising cross-entropy over Q minimises KL exactly, because H(P) contains no parameters - it is the irreducible loss floor set by label noise and by any two identical feature rows carrying different labels. Verify it numerically on two 4-outcome distributions and check the three numbers agree to 1e-12 in float64, in both bits and nats. This identity is the single sentence you will repeat most often on site: 'your loss cannot go below about 0.42 nats because 12 percent of your rows are labelled inconsistently, and everything above that line is our model'.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Softmax Regression (cross-entropy loss and its information-theory basics)

subtopics.name: From maximum likelihood to cross-entropy in a few lines
subtopics.learn: Start with i.i.d. rows and write the log-likelihood l(theta) = sum_i log q_theta(y_i | x_i); divide by N and it becomes an expectation under the empirical distribution P_hat, so -l/N = CE(P_hat, Q_theta) = H(P_hat) + KL(P_hat || Q_theta). Conclude the two things that matter: maximum likelihood is minimising the forward KL from the empirical distribution to the model, and 'cross-entropy loss' is nothing but NLL written as an expectation over one-hot targets, where the one-hot collapses -sum_c p_c log q_c into the single term -log q_{y_i}. Be able to reproduce this whole derivation on a whiteboard, closed book, in under five minutes. Then be precise about what it does not assume: no Gaussianity, no linearity, only that your model emits a normalised distribution over the label space and that rows are independent given x - which is exactly the assumption that fails on the customer's clustered, repeated-measures or time-ordered data.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Maximum Likelihood (appendix)

subtopics.name: Softmax, logits, and the log-sum-exp trick
subtopics.learn: Write softmax(z)_c = exp(z_c) / sum_j exp(z_j), show it is shift-invariant so softmax(z + a) = softmax(z), and use that to derive the stable form log_softmax(z)_c = z_c - logsumexp(z) where logsumexp(z) = m + log sum_j exp(z_j - m) with m = max(z). Derive the gradient of NLL with respect to the logits and commit the result to memory: dL/dz = softmax(z) - y_onehot, which is why the backward pass of a classifier is a subtraction and why fusing log_softmax with NLL is a correctness fix, not just a speed-up. Know exactly what you are avoiding: exp(800) overflows to inf and exp(-800) underflows to 0 in float32, so computing log(softmax(z)) in two steps returns -inf and then nan gradients, while log_softmax returns a finite number. Implement logsumexp yourself and check it against scipy.special.logsumexp on inputs of magnitude 1e3.

resource.label: SciPy - scipy.special.logsumexp (numerically stable log-sum-exp)

subtopics.name: Bernoulli likelihood, binary cross-entropy, and the logistic gradient
subtopics.learn: Write the one-row Bernoulli log-likelihood log p(y|x) = y log sigma(z) + (1-y) log(1 - sigma(z)) with sigma(z) = 1/(1 + exp(-z)), then derive dL/dz = sigma(z) - y and dL/dw = (sigma(z) - y) x - the same shape as the linear-regression gradient, which is not a coincidence but the canonical link of the exponential family. Show the loss is convex in w by rewriting it as log(1 + exp(-(2y-1) z)), so logistic regression has a unique optimum and any 'it did not converge' is a scaling or solver bug rather than a landscape problem. In code, always reach for torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss rather than sigmoid followed by BCELoss: it folds in the log-sum-exp stabilisation and carries pos_weight for imbalance. Confirm for yourself that BCE on one logit and CrossEntropyLoss on two logits give the same number for the same problem.

resource.label: PyTorch - torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss

subtopics.name: Regression losses are likelihoods too: Gaussian to MSE, Laplace to MAE, Poisson and Tweedie
subtopics.learn: Plug the Gaussian density into the negative log-likelihood and watch the constants fall out: -log N(y; f(x), s^2) = (y - f(x))^2 / (2 s^2) + log s + 0.5 log(2 pi), so minimising MSE is exactly maximum likelihood under homoscedastic Gaussian noise and under nothing else. Do the same algebra for the Laplace density and get MAE (which fits the conditional median, hence its outlier robustness), for the Poisson and get the deviance term y_hat - y log y_hat used on count targets, and for the Tweedie family which covers the zero-inflated positive targets that dominate insurance, usage and revenue data. The rule you will apply on customer data: pick the loss from the conditional distribution of the target and use the matching link - sklearn's PoissonRegressor and TweedieRegressor and XGBoost's count:poisson objective exist precisely because squared error on right-skewed counts fits the mean of the wrong noise model and happily predicts negative demand.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Generalized Linear Models (Poisson, Gamma, Tweedie deviances and links)

subtopics.name: torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss in practice: the arguments that silently change your objective
subtopics.learn: Know the contract exactly: it consumes raw logits of shape (N, C) - never softmax outputs - plus either integer class indices or a full probability target, and applies log_softmax followed by NLL internally. Read every argument as an edit to the objective rather than a convenience: weight= rescales per-class terms and therefore changes the implied class prior, ignore_index= removes padding from both the numerator and the denominator, label_smoothing= replaces the one-hot target entirely, and reduction='mean' averages over non-ignored elements - so a mean loss over a batch with 40 percent padding is not comparable with one over a batch with 10 percent. For sequence models the tensor must be (N, C, L) or flattened to (N*L, C), and the perennial bug is forgetting to shift logits and labels by one position, which produces a loss that trains down beautifully while the model learns to copy. Prove you understand it by reproducing F.cross_entropy's exact value with your own NumPy implementation on the same batch to 1e-6.

resource.label: PyTorch - torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss (weight, ignore_index, label_smoothing, reduction)

subtopics.name: Forward vs reverse KL: mode-covering, mode-seeking, and the ELBO
subtopics.learn: Contrast the two directions on a bimodal target P fitted by a single Gaussian Q. Forward KL(P||Q) is mode-covering and zero-avoiding, because any x where p > 0 and q is near 0 costs an unbounded penalty, so Q smears across both modes and puts mass in the empty valley between them. Reverse KL(Q||P) is mode-seeking and zero-forcing, because the expectation is taken under Q, so Q collapses onto one mode and pays nothing for ignoring the other. Map that onto objectives you will actually meet: supervised training and MLE minimise forward KL; variational inference and the ELBO (E_q[log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x) || p(z))) minimise reverse KL, which is why an under-powered VAE produces blurry averages and why posterior collapse is a thing; RLHF and DPO-style penalties hold a policy near a reference in reverse KL. For any objective a customer shows you, state the direction and predict the bias: over-smoothing or collapse.

resource.label: arXiv - Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (Kingma and Welling, the ELBO and its KL term)

subtopics.name: JS divergence, f-divergences, and what a GAN is actually minimising
subtopics.learn: Define JSD(P||Q) = 0.5 KL(P||M) + 0.5 KL(Q||M) with M = (P + Q)/2, and note the three properties that make it useful in production: it is symmetric, it is bounded by log 2 (one bit), and it stays finite even on disjoint supports where KL is infinite; its square root is a genuine metric. Know the original GAN result that against an optimal discriminator the generator is minimising 2 JSD(P_data || P_g) - log 4, and the consequence that when the supports barely overlap JSD sits pinned at log 2 with a vanishing gradient - the motivation for the Wasserstein alternatives. Place both inside the f-divergence family D_f(P||Q) = sum q f(p/q), where KL, reverse KL, JS, total variation and chi-squared are just choices of f. In practice you will use JSD as your bounded, symmetric drift statistic between last month's feature histogram and this month's, exactly where KL would return inf on one newly empty bin.

resource.label: arXiv - Generative Adversarial Networks (Goodfellow et al., the JSD result in Section 4)

subtopics.name: Perplexity and bits-per-character: reporting a loss that means something
subtopics.learn: Perplexity is exp(mean NLL in nats) = 2^(mean NLL in bits), and it reads as an effective branching factor: a character model at 2.45 nats/char has perplexity 11.6, meaning it is as uncertain as a uniform choice among 11.6 characters out of the 27 available. Convert in both directions at speed, and always state the unit and the tokenisation, because perplexity is only comparable across models that share a vocabulary - a byte-level and a BPE model on the same corpus give different numbers for identical underlying quality, which is why bits-per-byte or bits-per-character is the honest cross-tokeniser metric. Learn the sliding-window evaluation protocol for long contexts and why naive non-overlapping chunking inflates the score by scoring the first tokens of each chunk with almost no context. For the bigram deliverable, report the same model in nats, in bits/char and as perplexity, and show the counting table and the gradient-trained softmax landing on all three identically.

resource.label: HuggingFace Transformers - Perplexity of fixed-length models (sliding-window evaluation)

subtopics.name: Proper scoring rules, calibration, and temperature scaling
subtopics.learn: A scoring rule is proper when its expectation is minimised by reporting the true probability; log loss and the Brier score are proper, accuracy and F1 are not, which is how a model improves on accuracy while getting worse at every decision you would actually make with a probability. Decompose log loss and Brier into calibration plus refinement, and understand why two models with identical AUC can have wildly different log loss: AUC only sees ranking and is invariant to any monotone transform of the scores. Build a reliability diagram with sklearn's calibration_curve, summarise it as expected calibration error, and know the two fixes and their trade-offs - post-hoc temperature scaling (one scalar T fitted on held-out logits, cannot change the argmax so accuracy is untouched) versus isotonic or Platt scaling through CalibratedClassifierCV, which can. Be able to state the Guo et al. finding that modern deep networks are systematically overconfident and that the remedy is a single parameter, because 'the model says 0.99' is a claim you will be asked to defend.

resource.label: arXiv - On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks (Guo et al., reliability diagrams, ECE, temperature scaling)

subtopics.name: Label smoothing: editing the target distribution on purpose
subtopics.learn: Label smoothing replaces the one-hot target with (1 - eps) * onehot + eps/K * uniform, so the minimiser is no longer an infinite logit gap but a finite one - that is the entire mechanism, and it is why it caps confidence and acts as a regulariser. Derive what it does to the objective: cross-entropy against a smoothed target equals (1 - eps) CE(onehot, Q) + eps CE(uniform, Q), which is the original loss plus a term pulling Q toward uniform, equivalently a KL-to-uniform penalty up to an additive constant. Know the trade-off Mueller et al. document: it usually improves accuracy and calibration but it erases the class-similarity geometry in the penultimate layer, which measurably degrades any teacher you then distil from. Never compare a smoothed training loss against an unsmoothed validation loss - the floor has moved, and this is a recurring cause of 'why is my validation loss below my training loss' panics.

resource.label: arXiv - When Does Label Smoothing Help? (Mueller, Kornblith, Hinton)

subtopics.name: Class weights, focal loss, and prior shift
subtopics.learn: Reweighting class c by w_c is mathematically a change of the assumed label prior: you have fitted the model to a reweighted P, so its outputs are calibrated for that reweighted world and not for the customer's one-in-five-hundred base rate. Know the correction and apply it before quoting a probability to anyone - for a binary model the logit shift back to the true prior is log(pi_train/(1 - pi_train)) - log(pi_true/(1 - pi_true)), added to the logit. Contrast with focal loss FL(p_t) = -(1 - p_t)^gamma log(p_t), which leaves the prior alone and instead down-weights already-easy examples so gradient mass moves to the hard ones; know gamma around 2 with alpha-balancing as the Lin et al. defaults, and that it is not a proper scoring rule, so you must calibrate afterwards. Have a defensible answer ready for 'should we just SMOTE it?': resampling changes the prior and usually the calibration for no ranking gain, and the way to settle it is a PR-AUC plus a reliability plot before and after.

resource.label: arXiv - Focal Loss for Dense Object Detection (Lin et al.)

subtopics.name: Knowledge distillation: cross-entropy against a soft teacher
subtopics.learn: Distillation minimises the KL (equivalently the cross-entropy up to the teacher's fixed entropy) between the student and a temperature-softened teacher: L = alpha * T^2 * KL(softmax(z_t/T) || softmax(z_s/T)) + (1 - alpha) * CE(onehot, softmax(z_s)), where the T^2 factor restores the gradient magnitude that dividing logits by T removes. Understand why it works in information terms: the teacher's soft distribution carries the relative probabilities of the wrong classes, so each example delivers many more bits than a one-hot label does. In PyTorch, torch.nn.KLDivLoss expects log-probabilities as the input and probabilities as the target with reduction='batchmean'; the two most common bugs in a distillation script are passing raw logits and leaving reduction='mean', which divides by N*C and shrinks the term by a factor of the vocabulary size. This is the standard lever when a customer wants the accuracy of a large model at the latency budget of a small one.

resource.label: PyTorch - torch.nn.KLDivLoss (log-probability input, batchmean reduction)

subtopics.name: Estimating entropy and MI from finite samples: bias, binning, and high-cardinality traps
subtopics.learn: The plug-in estimator from empirical counts is biased downward - roughly (K-1)/(2N) nats for K bins - so entropy comes out too small and mutual information too large on small samples, and the bias grows with cardinality. That single fact is the mechanism behind the classic leak: a near-unique identifier column scores enormous mutual_info_classif because every level 'predicts' its own single row perfectly. For continuous features scikit-learn's mutual_info_classif and mutual_info_regression use the Kraskov k-nearest-neighbour estimator (n_neighbors=3 by default, with jitter added, so results are not reproducible without random_state) rather than histogram binning, and the choice of k or bin width is a real hyperparameter of the answer you report. The discipline: compute MI on the training split only, permute the target to build a null distribution, and treat any feature whose MI clears that null by an implausible margin as a leakage suspect rather than a discovery.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Feature selection (univariate selection and mutual-information estimators)

subtopics.name: Building infotheory/ in NumPy and proving it correct to 1e-6
subtopics.learn: Implement entropy, cross_entropy, kl_divergence and js_divergence reducing over the last axis, with an explicit base= argument, correct broadcasting, and a normalisation check that raises on a vector summing to 0.97 rather than silently renormalising it. Handle the edge cases deliberately: 0 log 0 = 0 via np.where or scipy.special.xlogy (never a global epsilon added to every probability, which perturbs every value including the good ones), q = 0 with p > 0 returning inf rather than a clipped lie, and float64 accumulation for the reduction. Test with np.testing.assert_allclose(rtol=1e-6) against scipy.stats.entropy in both its one-argument and two-argument forms, against scipy.spatial.distance.jensenshannon (note it returns the square root of JS and defaults to base e despite what people assume - a classic factor-of-confusion), and against torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy on random logits. Add property tests: H <= log K, KL >= 0, KL(P||P) == 0, JS <= log 2, and CE(P,Q) == H(P) + KL(P||Q).

resource.label: SciPy - scipy.spatial.distance.jensenshannon (returns the JS distance, i.e. the square root)

subtopics.name: Bigram character LM: counting MLE, gradient descent, and smoothing as a Dirichlet prior
subtopics.learn: Build the 27x27 bigram count matrix N, normalise each row to get the closed-form MLE q(next|prev) = N[i,j] / sum_j N[i,j], and score the corpus with the mean NLL. Then fit the same model as a one-hot input times a weight matrix through a softmax, trained by gradient descent, and watch the loss descend to the same number - because the counting solution is the unique minimiser of the identical cross-entropy objective, which is the cleanest demonstration you will ever get that for this family 'training' and 'counting' are the same estimator. Add-k smoothing is not a hack: N + k is the posterior mean under a Dirichlet(k+1) prior, and in the gradient version it is equivalent to an L2 penalty pulling the logits toward uniform - verify that claim numerically by matching a k against a weight-decay value. Report the final figure in nats and bits/char, and show that the unsmoothed model assigns probability 0, hence infinite loss, to any bigram unseen in training.

resource.label: Dive into Deep Learning - Language Models (n-gram counting, Laplace smoothing, perplexity)

outcomes: You can derive cross-entropy loss from maximum likelihood on a whiteboard, closed book, in under five minutes - i.i.d. log-likelihood, division by N, empirical distribution, CE(P_hat, Q_theta) = H(P_hat) + KL(P_hat || Q_theta) - and state which assumptions you used and which you did not.

You can hand-compute H, KL and CE for two small discrete distributions in both bits and nats, confirm CE(P,Q) = H(P) + KL(P||Q) to 1e-12 in NumPy, and convert any of those numbers to perplexity and back.

You can look at any objective put in front of you - MLE, an ELBO, a GAN loss, a distillation term, an RLHF KL penalty - and name the divergence, the direction, and the bias it will produce (mode-covering over-smoothing or mode-seeking collapse).

You can choose a loss from the conditional distribution of a customer's target - Bernoulli, categorical, Gaussian, Laplace, Poisson, Tweedie - and justify it as a likelihood with the matching link rather than as a preference.

You can ship an infotheory/ module whose entropy, cross-entropy, KL and JS agree with scipy.stats.entropy, scipy.spatial.distance.jensenshannon and torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy to 1e-6, with 0 log 0, zero-support and unnormalised-input cases tested explicitly.

You can derive dNLL/dlogits = softmax(z) - y, implement a stable log_softmax with the max-subtraction trick, and explain why fusing log_softmax with NLL is a correctness requirement and not merely an optimisation.

You can decide whether a plateaued training loss is an irreducible H(P) floor from inconsistent labels or a model and optimisation gap, and put a number on the label-noise floor from a duplicate-feature-row audit.

You can produce a reliability diagram and an ECE for a model, fit a temperature on held-out logits, and show log loss improving while accuracy and AUC are unchanged - and explain to a customer exactly why those two did not move.
failureModes: A team reports 'loss 2.1' with no unit; the model was training in nats while the published baseline was in bits/char, so a real gap of nothing at all was chased for a month across a factor of 1.4427.

The training script does softmax, then log, then NLL instead of log_softmax plus NLL; one logit reaches 90 on a hard example, the softmax underflows to exactly 0 on the true class, the loss becomes inf and the gradients nan - and because the nan appears mid-epoch it gets filed as a corrupt data batch.

Class weights were added for imbalance and never undone; the model is calibrated for a 50/50 world, the customer's ops team sets a 0.5 threshold on the raw output, and a review queue sized for 20 cases a day receives 900.

Mutual-information feature screening put a near-unique transaction identifier at the top of the list because the plug-in estimator's finite-sample bias rewards high cardinality; the column survived into training, cross-validation looked superb, and the model was worthless in production.

label_smoothing=0.1 was set on the training criterion but not on the evaluation criterion, so validation loss came out below training loss, the team concluded the model was underfitting and burned three more days of GPU on a larger one.

A drift monitor computed KL(current || reference) over binned features; one reference bin was empty, KL returned inf, the dashboard clamped it to its axis maximum, and a genuine distribution shift a fortnight later was invisible because it produced the identical clamped value.

A distillation script passed raw student logits into torch.nn.KLDivLoss with reduction='mean'; the loss was divided by N*C so the distillation term shrank by a factor of the vocabulary size, contributed nothing to the gradient, and the student quietly trained on hard labels only while the config claimed otherwise.

Model selection was done on AUC because 'the customer only cares about ranking', but the customer's actual decision multiplies the predicted probability by transaction value; the winning model was badly overconfident, and every expected-cost figure they acted on was wrong by roughly a factor of three until log loss and a reliability plot were finally checked.
interviewQuestions: Derive cross-entropy loss from maximum likelihood. Then, using CE(P,Q) = H(P) + KL(P||Q), tell me which term your optimiser can reduce and which it cannot, and what that means for a model whose validation loss has been stuck at 0.42 nats for twenty epochs.

KL is not symmetric. Sketch the result of fitting a single Gaussian to a bimodal target by minimising KL(P||Q) and then by minimising KL(Q||P), and tell me which direction a VAE's ELBO uses and which one ordinary supervised training uses.

Debug: your language model's loss goes 3.1, 3.0, 2.9, then nan at step 4000. Walk me through what you check and in what order, and say which candidate causes would show up in the logits, which in the data loader, and which only in the loss implementation itself.

Design: a customer has a fraud label with a 0.2 percent base rate and wants a number they can multiply by transaction value to set a review threshold. What loss do you train, what do you do about the imbalance, and how do you guarantee that what you hand them is a probability rather than a score?

Explain why perplexity is not comparable between two models with different tokenisers and what you would report instead. Then tell me what a perplexity of 11.6 on a 27-symbol character model actually says about that model.

A stakeholder says 'the model is 99 percent confident'. What do you check before letting that sentence leave the room, what plot do you produce, and what is the cheapest correct fix if the number is wrong?

Someone rebalanced the classes by reweighting and reports better recall. Explain what the reweighting did to the implied prior, write down the logit correction that returns the outputs to the true base rate, and tell me when you would reach for focal loss instead.
98.proofOfWork: A public repo `loss-function-forensics` that takes the infotheory/ module past unit tests and into a customer-facing diagnostic kit. It ships `label_noise_floor.py`, which estimates the irreducible H(P) on any tabular dataset by grouping exact-duplicate feature rows (plus near-duplicates via a hashed or k-NN key), computing the empirical label entropy within each group, and reporting the count-weighted average as the loss floor - then plots a trained model's validation cross-entropy against that floor so 'we are 0.11 nats above the ceiling of this dataset' becomes a number rather than an opinion. It adds `divergence_zoo.ipynb`, which fits a single Gaussian to one fixed bimodal mixture three times - minimising forward KL, reverse KL and JS with the same optimiser - and overlays the three fits on one figure with the numeric divergences in the legend, which is the mode-covering versus mode-seeking picture you will draw on a customer's whiteboard. `calibration_report.py` takes any scikit-learn or PyTorch classifier plus a held-out set and emits log loss, Brier, ECE, a reliability diagram and the fitted temperature, with a before/after table showing accuracy and AUC unchanged while log loss improves. Finally `units.md` is a one-page conversion table for nats, bits, perplexity and bits-per-character alongside the exact library defaults (scipy.stats.entropy is base e, scipy.spatial.distance.jensenshannon returns the square root, torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy is nats and mean-reduced over non-ignored elements), written so a customer's data scientist can settle a units argument in thirty seconds. CI runs the property tests (H <= log K, KL >= 0, JS <= log 2, CE = H + KL, KL(P||P) = 0) plus the 1e-6 agreement tests against SciPy and PyTorch on every push.

99.topic: Numerical computing: NumPy vectorisation, floating point, numerical stability
99.why: Every model you defend in front of a customer is a pile of floating-point arithmetic, and the failure that gets you paged is almost never a stack trace - it is a variance that came out negative, a loss that went nan at step 4000, a distance matrix that ranked the wrong neighbours, a column of gradients that a test declared 'close enough' at atol=1e-8. This topic is what lets you say in the room whether the wrong number is their data, the conditioning of the problem itself, or a bug in your algorithm - three different conversations with three different owners, and the senior move is knowing which one you are in before you promise a fix. It is also the difference between a demo notebook and a pipeline that survives their 200 million rows: vectorised NumPy is the only Python fast enough to preprocess at that scale, and being able to state the peak memory of a broadcast before you press enter is what keeps you from OOM-ing the customer's box live on a screenshare.
prerequisites: Working NumPy, not read-about NumPy: array creation, slicing, axis= reductions, dtype and astype, and having already written something non-trivial with it
Linear algebra from Topic 93: singular values and the SVD, because the condition number is sigma_max/sigma_min and np.linalg.lstsq is an SVD solve
Calculus from Topic 94: gradients and the chain rule, so that 'the backward pass, not the forward pass, produced the nan' is a statement you can reason about
Softmax, cross-entropy and log-likelihood from Topic 98, which is where the stable log-sum-exp is used in anger rather than as an exercise
pytest and np.testing from Topic 39, because every claim in the deliverable is a test that must fail on the naive implementation and pass on yours
Enough PyTorch to run a training loop, register a forward hook and read a loss tensor (Topic 112 goes deeper on the framework itself)

subtopics.name: What a float actually is: IEEE 754 binary64, binary32, and np.finfo
subtopics.learn: Decompose a float into sign, exponent and significand, and be able to say from first principles why 0.1 has no exact binary representation and why 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004. Memorise the four numbers per dtype and read them off np.finfo rather than from memory when it matters: float64 carries a 53-bit significand, eps = 2^-52 = 2.22e-16, max about 1.8e308, smallest normal about 2.2e-308; float32 carries 24 bits, eps = 2^-23 = 1.19e-7, max 3.4e38, smallest normal 1.18e-38; float16 tops out at 65504 with eps about 9.8e-4; bfloat16 keeps float32's exponent range but only 8 significand bits. Derive the integer ceiling that follows - consecutive integers are exact only up to 2^53 in float64 and 2^24 = 16777216 in float32 - so a Unix-epoch timestamp held as float32 is quantised to 128-second steps and an ID column cast to float32 silently collides. Print np.spacing(x) at 1e0, 1e6 and 1e9 so you can quote the absolute resolution at the magnitude the customer's data actually lives at.

resource.label: NumPy - numpy.finfo (eps, max, tiny, resolution per dtype)

subtopics.name: Machine epsilon, ulps, and comparing floats without lying
subtopics.learn: Distinguish absolute error |a-b|, relative error |a-b|/|b| and distance in units in the last place, and default to relative error for everything except quantities that legitimately pass through zero. Know the two different default tolerances you will meet in the same afternoon: np.isclose and np.allclose test |a-b| <= atol + rtol*|b| with rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8 - asymmetric in b, and that atol declares every gradient of magnitude 1e-9 equal to zero - while np.testing.assert_allclose uses rtol=1e-7, atol=0 and reports the maximum relative mismatch and its index. Set tolerances from the computation rather than from taste: a float32 reduction over n terms accumulates on the order of n*1.2e-7 relative error naively, so 1e-6 is a defensible rtol for a float32 layer and 1e-12 is a test that will flake on someone else's BLAS. Write assertions whose failure message names the element and the size of the miss, and never write `assert a == b` on floats outside exact integer arithmetic.

resource.label: NumPy - numpy.testing.assert_allclose (rtol/atol semantics and mismatch reporting)

subtopics.name: The three archetypes: overflow, underflow and subnormals, catastrophic cancellation
subtopics.learn: Learn the three failure shapes and their exact thresholds so you can name one from the wrong answer alone. Overflow: np.exp returns inf above 709.78 in float64 and above 88.7 in float32, which is why a logit of 100 kills a naive softmax only after someone enables mixed precision. Underflow: results below the smallest normal degrade into subnormals, losing significand bits gradually and running an order of magnitude slower on some CPUs before flushing to zero, so a product of 500 probabilities is exactly 0.0 long before it stops being meaningful. Catastrophic cancellation: subtracting two nearly equal numbers annihilates the leading digits and promotes rounding noise into the result - the mechanism behind mean(x^2) - mean(x)^2 returning a negative variance on data centred at 1e9, behind the naive quadratic formula, and behind sklearn's known float32 euclidean-distance error when it expands ||x-y||^2 as ||x||^2 - 2xy + ||y||^2. Reproduce all three in five lines each before you go further.

resource.label: Fundamentals of Numerical Computation - Floating-point numbers

subtopics.name: Conditioning: when the problem, not your code, is the problem
subtopics.learn: Define the condition number as the factor by which relative input error is amplified into relative output error: kappa = |x f'(x)/f(x)| for a scalar function, kappa(A) = sigma_max/sigma_min for a linear system, which is Topic 93's SVD read as an error-amplification statement. Learn the digit-counting rule and use it out loud: float64 buys about 16 decimal digits, so kappa = 1e8 leaves you 8 and kappa = 1e16 leaves you none no matter how careful your algorithm is. Separate conditioning - a property of the problem, fixable only by reformulating, rescaling or regularising - from stability, a property of your algorithm, which you can fix by rewriting; being able to say which one you are facing is the difference between 'we will ship a patch' and 'your matrix is singular and we need to talk about the features'. Compute np.linalg.cond on the customer's design matrix and quote the number instead of saying the data is 'a bit collinear'.

resource.label: Fundamentals of Numerical Computation - Problems and conditioning

subtopics.name: Stability in the wild: normal equations vs QR/SVD, and why scaling is numerical
subtopics.learn: Reproduce the canonical instability yourself: forming X^T X squares the condition number, so kappa(X) = 1e8 becomes 1e16 and solving the normal equations in float64 returns coefficients that are noise, while np.linalg.lstsq (an SVD/gelsd solve, with rcond truncating singular values below a threshold) on the same X returns the right answer. Generalise it into the rule you will apply weekly: never form a Gram matrix, an explicit inverse or a squared quantity when a factorisation will do - use lstsq or np.linalg.solve, never inv(A) @ b, and prefer scipy.linalg.cho_solve or solve_triangular over an inverse you built yourself. Connect it to modelling decisions: unscaled features (dollars beside fractions) inflate kappa, which is why gradient descent zigzags and why a hand-rolled least squares disagrees with sklearn's LinearRegression on the same data; ridge with penalty alpha adds alpha to every eigenvalue of X^T X and therefore caps the condition number, making regularisation a numerical statement as well as a statistical one.

resource.label: NumPy - numpy.linalg.lstsq (SVD least squares, rcond, singular-value truncation)

subtopics.name: NaN and inf semantics, and turning silence into an exception
subtopics.learn: Know the arithmetic cold: nan != nan (so equality-based dedup, sorts and np.unique all misbehave), every comparison with nan is False, 0/0 and inf-inf and 0*inf produce nan while 1/0 produces inf, and one nan poisons every reduction downstream - np.mean returns nan, np.nanmean does not and quietly changes the denominator you are dividing by. NumPy's defaults are divide='warn', over='warn', under='ignore', invalid='warn', and a RuntimeWarning is printed once per location and then never again, which is exactly how a nan factory runs unnoticed for two hours in a notebook. In anything you own, wrap the numeric core in `with np.errstate(divide='raise', over='raise', invalid='raise')` or call np.seterr in conftest.py so the first bad operation raises FloatingPointError with a traceback rather than a warning that scrolls away. Add `assert np.isfinite(x).all()` at every module boundary: one pass over the array converts a three-day bisect into a stack trace.

resource.label: NumPy - numpy.errstate (raise on divide, overflow, invalid)

subtopics.name: The ndarray memory model: dtype, strides, C vs F order, contiguity
subtopics.learn: An ndarray is a data pointer, a dtype, a shape and a strides tuple, and every performance and aliasing question you will be asked is answered from those four. Predict strides without running anything: a C-order (1000, 100) float64 array has strides (800, 8); .T is a view with the strides swapped and is therefore F-contiguous, not C-contiguous; a reshape that cannot be expressed as a stride change copies silently. Know the consequences you pay for: walking the slow axis fetches a 64-byte cache line (8 float64) per element used, np.ascontiguousarray before a BLAS call is occasionally the entire optimisation, and dtype promotion decides your memory bill - under NEP 50 a float32 array plus a Python float stays float32, but float32 plus a float64 array upcasts everything and doubles the footprint. Inspect with arr.strides, arr.flags, arr.nbytes and arr.dtype rather than guessing, and put arr.nbytes in your log lines so an OOM has a paper trail.

resource.label: NumPy - The N-dimensional array (memory layout, strides, flags)

subtopics.name: Views vs copies: the aliasing bugs that give a wrong number, not a crash
subtopics.learn: Internalise the one rule that generates most of them: basic slicing returns a view that shares memory, while fancy (integer or boolean) indexing returns a copy. From it fall the two classics - `b = a[mask]; b += 1` leaves a untouched while `a[mask] += 1` does not, and `a[idx] += 1` with a repeated index increments that element exactly once, because a read-modify-write is not an accumulate; when you mean scatter-add use np.add.at (the ufunc .at method) or np.bincount and accept that .at is slow by design. Diagnose with np.shares_memory(a, b), arr.base and arr.flags['OWNDATA'] rather than id(). The related trap that reaches production: `X -= X.mean(0)` inside a 'preprocess' helper mutates the caller's array in place, so you have standardised the customer's backing store and the second call in the notebook produces different numbers - take a copy at the boundary or document the mutation in the signature.

resource.label: NumPy - Copies and views

subtopics.name: Broadcasting, and predicting the temporaries before you press enter
subtopics.learn: Apply the rule mechanically: right-align the shapes, each dimension must be equal or 1, missing leading dimensions are treated as 1, and the output takes the maximum in each position. Then do the arithmetic that prevents the OOM: the pairwise-difference idiom (X[:, None, :] - Y[None, :, :]) with X and Y of shape (50000, 100) materialises 50000*50000*100 float64 = 2 TB, and the same line at (5000, 100) is 20 GB - say the number out loud before running it, then reach for the gemm-based expansion (with the float64 upcast that keeps it stable) or scipy.spatial.distance.cdist. Learn the diagnostics: np.broadcast_shapes(...) checks compatibility without allocating, and the mismatch that does not raise is the dangerous one - adding a (n,) array to an (n, 1) array yields (n, n) rather than (n,), which is how a residual vector silently becomes a matrix and a loss becomes the mean of n^2 terms while still decreasing smoothly. Annotate every shape in expressions with more than three operands.

resource.label: NumPy - Broadcasting (rules and examples)

subtopics.name: Killing the loop: ufuncs, axis reductions, masks and where
subtopics.learn: Build the rewriting vocabulary until the broadcast form is what you type first: elementwise ufuncs, reductions along an explicit axis with keepdims=True, np.where for branchless conditionals, boolean masks for filtering, np.clip, np.cumsum and prefix-sum tricks, np.diff, and the ufunc methods .reduce, .accumulate, .outer and .at. Never write a Python-level loop over rows to build a feature. Know the two cases where vectorising is not automatically right: arrays below roughly a thousand elements are dominated by microsecond-scale ufunc dispatch overhead so the loop can genuinely win, and an algorithm with a real sequential dependency (an EWMA, a Kalman filter, a bisection) needs scipy.signal.lfilter, a restructured recurrence or numba rather than a fake vectorisation that hides an O(n^2) materialisation. For the deliverable, time each rewrite against the loop it replaces and record both the speedup and the peak memory, because the honest answer is sometimes 'the loop was fine'.

resource.label: NumPy - Universal functions (ufunc): broadcasting, out=, casting, reduce/accumulate/at

subtopics.name: Index-driven algorithms: argsort, searchsorted, bincount, unique
subtopics.learn: Learn the vectorised replacements for the loops that actually appear in customer data work: np.argsort plus np.take for a permutation, np.searchsorted for as-of joins and bucketing (side='left' versus 'right' is exactly the include-the-boundary decision), np.bincount(labels, weights=w) for a group-by sum, np.unique(..., return_inverse=True, return_counts=True) to factorise a categorical column, np.digitize for histogram bins, and a matmul against a one-hot matrix when the aggregation is really a linear map. Know the complexity and the memory you are buying: searchsorted is O(log n) per query on a pre-sorted array, while bincount is O(n) but allocates max(label)+1 slots, so passing a raw customer ID as the label allocates gigabytes and looks like a memory leak. Remember that all of these return copies, so the aliasing rules from the previous subtopic apply to every result.

resource.label: NumPy - Indexing on ndarrays (basic slicing vs advanced indexing)

subtopics.name: Why vectorised code is fast: SIMD, cache lines, bandwidth, the interpreter tax
subtopics.learn: Be able to explain a speedup, not merely observe it. A Python-level loop pays roughly 50-100 ns per element in interpreter dispatch and scalar boxing; a ufunc pays about one cache-line fetch and one SIMD instruction per 8 float32 lanes on AVX2, so 10-100x is the expected order of magnitude and a claimed 10000x means you accidentally changed the algorithm or timed a lazily-allocated array. Know which regime you are in: large elementwise work is memory-bandwidth bound, so `a*b + c` costs four passes over memory (three reads, one write) and the fix is fusing with out= or tiling to L2-resident chunks, not a faster CPU; matmul is compute bound at O(n^3) work over O(n^2) data, which is why BLAS wins there and nowhere else. Measure with timeit.repeat and take the minimum of several runs rather than the mean (the mean measures your laptop's other processes), warm up once first, and never benchmark inside a notebook cell that also allocates.

resource.label: Maths/CS/AI Compendium - Chapter 16 SIMD and GPU programming, 01. hardware fundamentals

subtopics.name: Memory discipline: out=, temporaries, sliding windows, chunking
subtopics.learn: Count the allocations in an expression before you run it: `x = (a - b) ** 2 / c` allocates three full-size temporaries, so peak memory is several times the size of the result, and the fix in a hot path is np.subtract(a, b, out=buf); buf **= 2; buf /= c with buf reused across iterations. Use np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view for rolling windows: it is a zero-copy strided view, so a 1e7-point series with a 100-step window costs nothing until a reduction materialises it, and it is returned read-only precisely because overlapping writes would be nonsense. When the natural expression does not fit in memory, chunk it and carry an accumulator - which is what sklearn does inside pairwise_distances_chunked and StandardScaler.partial_fit, and what the Welford update below makes exact. Instrument with tracemalloc.get_traced_memory() or resource.getrusage so the benchmark table in the deliverable reports a measured peak rather than an estimate.

resource.label: NumPy - sliding_window_view (zero-copy strided rolling windows)

subtopics.name: matmul, einsum and BLAS: where the FLOPs and the nondeterminism live
subtopics.learn: Know that @ and np.dot dispatch 2-D float32/float64 arrays to BLAS sgemm/dgemm and send everything else - integer dtypes, object dtype, awkward strides - to a much slower NumPy fallback, so a matmul that suddenly takes 40x longer is nearly always an accidental dtype or a non-contiguous input. Use np.einsum whenever there are more than two operands or the axes deserve names, but pass optimize=True: without it einsum contracts in the order you wrote and can be asymptotically worse, and np.einsum_path prints the chosen order with its FLOP count. Control threads explicitly with threadpoolctl or OMP_NUM_THREADS, because the BLAS thread count changes the reduction order and therefore the last bits of the result - which is why 'it gives different numbers on the customer's 64-core box' is a real and explainable phenomenon rather than a bug. When the inner dimension runs to millions in float32, accumulate in float64 or chunk the contraction, since sgemm accumulates in float32.

resource.label: NumPy - numpy.einsum (subscripts, optimize=, einsum_path)

subtopics.name: Summation error: naive, pairwise, Kahan and fsum
subtopics.learn: Naive left-to-right summation has error bounded by roughly n * eps * sum|x_i|, which is why summing 1e8 float32 ones in a Python loop stops dead at exactly 16777216: once the running total exceeds 2^24, adding 1 lands below half an ulp and rounds to nothing. NumPy's reductions use pairwise summation over contiguous fast axes, dropping the bound to about log2(n) * eps - so np.sum beats the loop on accuracy as well as speed - but that guarantee weakens along a strided axis or in a hand-rolled .accumulate. Implement Kahan (or Neumaier) compensated summation yourself and know the four lines by heart: y = x[i] - c; t = s + y; c = (t - s) - y; s = t, recovering near-full precision for about 4x the arithmetic. Use math.fsum when you want the exactly rounded result and speed is irrelevant, and remember the cheapest production fix of all: np.sum(a32, dtype=np.float64) accumulates a float32 array in a float64 accumulator for almost nothing and deletes the entire bug class.

resource.label: Python docs - math.fsum (exactly rounded floating-point summation)

subtopics.name: Welford: streaming mean, variance and covariance that do not blow up
subtopics.learn: Derive and implement the online update until you can write it from memory: for each new x, n += 1; delta = x - mean; mean += delta / n; M2 += delta * (x - mean) - the second delta uses the already-updated mean, which is the whole trick - then var = M2 / n for the population and M2 / (n - 1) for the sample. Be able to explain precisely why the textbook shortcut E[x^2] - E[x]^2 fails: on data centred at 1e9 the two terms agree to about 18 significant digits, float64 carries 16, so the difference is rounding noise, is often negative, and np.sqrt of it is nan - and that nan then propagates through your standardiser into every feature. Learn Chan's parallel merge formula for combining per-chunk (n, mean, M2) triples so the same estimator works over a chunked or distributed pass, which is how you compute normalisation statistics for a dataset that does not fit in memory. While you are here, note the ddof trap: np.std defaults to ddof=0 and pandas .std() to ddof=1, so the same column standardised in two places differs by sqrt(n/(n-1)) - small, systematic, and enough to move a decision threshold.

resource.label: Algorithms for calculating variance (naive, two-pass, Welford, Chan parallel merge)

subtopics.name: log-sum-exp, softmax and cross-entropy: the max-subtraction trick
subtopics.learn: Derive log sum_j exp(z_j) = m + log sum_j exp(z_j - m) with m = max(z) and note that it is an exact identity, not an approximation - the shift cancels algebraically, but numerically every exponent is now <= 0 so nothing overflows and the largest term is exactly 1. Use it to write softmax as exp(z - logsumexp(z)) and cross-entropy as -(z_y - logsumexp(z)), which is why F.log_softmax followed by nll_loss, or F.cross_entropy directly, is a correctness fix rather than an optimisation (Topic 98 derives the loss itself). Handle the all -inf row explicitly: for a fully masked attention row m is -inf, m - m is nan, and that is the actual mechanism behind nan losses in padded transformer batches - the standard fixes are masking with a large finite negative in float32 rather than -inf, or scipy.special.logsumexp with its b= weights and return_sign. Implement your own logsumexp and check it against SciPy on inputs of magnitude 1e3 where the naive expression returns inf and then nan gradients.

resource.label: SciPy - scipy.special.logsumexp (stable log-sum-exp with weights)

subtopics.name: log1p, expm1, log-space arithmetic and stable sigmoids
subtopics.learn: When x is small, forming 1 + x rounds away x's low bits, so log(1+x) loses relative precision while np.log1p(x) keeps it - and symmetrically np.expm1(x) versus exp(x) - 1. This is not academic: it is the difference between a correct and a worthless log-return, compound-growth or small-probability calculation on a customer's financial data. Multiply probabilities in log space with np.logaddexp / logsumexp instead of clipping products at 1e-300. Write the branch-free stable sigmoid (1/(1+exp(-z)) for z >= 0, exp(z)/(1+exp(z)) for z < 0, which is scipy.special.expit) and the stable softplus max(z, 0) + log1p(exp(-|z|)), and be able to explain why. Know that np.clip(p, 1e-15, 1 - 1e-15) before a log is a blunt instrument that biases every value rather than only the bad ones - acceptable inside a reported metric such as sklearn's log_loss, not acceptable inside a training objective where the gradient is what you are corrupting.

resource.label: NumPy - numpy.log1p (accurate log(1+x) for small x; see expm1, logaddexp)

subtopics.name: Precision in training: float64, float32, TF32, bf16, fp16 and loss scaling
subtopics.learn: Choose precision from the range and resolution you need, not from habit. float32 is the training default because float64 doubles memory and is anywhere from 2x to 64x slower on consumer and datacentre GPUs; fp16 has max 65504 and smallest normal 6.1e-5, so activations overflow and small gradients underflow to exactly zero - which is the entire reason torch.amp.GradScaler exists: it multiplies the loss by a scale factor, unscales before clipping, and skips the step and halves the scale when it observes inf or nan. bf16 keeps float32's exponent range with only 8 significand bits, so no scaler is needed but every accumulation must remain in float32. TF32 on Ampere and later silently truncates matmul inputs to 10 mantissa bits under torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32, a 1e-3-level perturbation and a legitimate suspect when a ported model's numbers move in the third decimal. The sentence to give a customer: compute in reduced precision, accumulate and keep master weights in float32, and never compute an evaluation metric in fp16.

resource.label: PyTorch - torch.amp: Automatic Mixed Precision (autocast, GradScaler, dtype coverage)

subtopics.name: Debugging a nan in a live training loop
subtopics.learn: Run a fixed triage instead of guessing. First establish direction: log the step and determine whether the loss went inf before the gradients went nan (a forward problem - overflow, log(0), a division by a zero denominator) or the gradients went nan with a finite loss (a backward problem). Bisect the forward pass by registering a hook on every module that asserts torch.isfinite(out).all(), which hands you the first offending layer and batch index; dump that batch, because roughly half the time the input already carried a nan produced upstream by a division by a zero count. Then run one iteration under torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) to get the backward operation that produced the nan with the forward traceback attached, accepting the large slowdown for a single run. Memorise the operators with a finite forward and an infinite backward: sqrt at exactly 0 (hence the norm of a zero vector, and the eps inside every LayerNorm and Adam denominator), x**p for 0 < p < 1, and any division by a mask sum that can be zero. Finally rule out the non-numerical causes with the same evidence - a learning-rate spike, an unclipped gradient, a fully masked row, a corrupt shard.

resource.label: PyTorch - Autograd anomaly detection (set_detect_anomaly, nan-producing backward ops)

outcomes: You can look at a nan, an inf or a silently-wrong number in a training loop and name the cause and the fix on the spot - subtract-the-max in logsumexp, log_softmax instead of log(softmax(z)), log1p instead of log(1+x), Welford instead of E[x^2]-E[x]^2, a float64 accumulator instead of float32 - and say whether the evidence points at the forward pass, the backward pass or the data loader.

You can rewrite any Python loop over an array as a broadcast NumPy expression, and before running it state the expected speedup to an order of magnitude and the peak memory of the temporaries to within a factor of two, then confirm both with timeit.repeat and tracemalloc.

You can implement stable logsumexp, softmax and cross-entropy in NumPy, prove they agree with scipy.special.logsumexp and torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy to 1e-6, and produce a test where the naive version returns inf or nan in float32 while yours does not.

You can implement Welford streaming variance and Kahan summation from memory, and demonstrate the naive alternatives failing concretely: a negative variance on data centred at 1e9, and a float32 loop sum that stalls at exactly 16777216.

You can compute np.linalg.cond on a customer's design matrix, predict how many decimal digits survive, show the normal equations and np.linalg.lstsq disagreeing on an ill-conditioned X, and explain in two sentences which part is the problem's conditioning and which part is your algorithm's stability.

You can locate the first non-finite tensor in an unfamiliar PyTorch model using forward hooks plus torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly, name the offending operator, and distinguish a genuine numerical failure from a bad batch.

You can set defensible tolerances in a numerical test - relative rather than absolute, sized from the dtype and the length of the reduction - and explain why np.allclose's default atol=1e-8 would have passed a gradient check on a gradient that was silently zero.

You can explain to a customer's engineer why the same script produces different last bits on their 64-core machine, name the three usual sources (BLAS thread count and reduction order, TF32 or mixed precision, non-deterministic GPU kernels), and say which are acceptable and which must be pinned.
failureModes: A standardiser computes variance as mean(x^2) - mean(x)^2 on a Unix-timestamp column near 1.7e9; catastrophic cancellation makes the result slightly negative, np.sqrt returns nan, the whole feature becomes nan, the imputer replaces it with the column mean of 0, and the model trains happily on a constant column while the feature-importance chart still lists it.

An ID column is cast to float32 somewhere in a Spark-to-pandas hop; above 2^24 consecutive integers are no longer representable, distinct customer IDs collide onto the same value, the train/test split leaks, and offline AUC beats production by fifteen points.

A residual is computed as y - yhat where y has shape (n,) and yhat has shape (n, 1); broadcasting yields an (n, n) matrix, the loss becomes the mean of n^2 terms, it still decreases smoothly during training, and nobody notices until the deployed model's predictions are off by a constant factor.

Feature counts are accumulated with `counts[idx] += 1` where idx contains repeats; the read-modify-write applies once per unique index, so every count above one is wrong, the pipeline runs clean, and the downstream frequency-encoded feature is quietly garbage until np.add.at is used instead.

A metric helper clips probabilities to [1e-15, 1-1e-15] before taking a log, so a model that outputs hard 0 and 1 predictions scores a finite, respectable log loss instead of infinity; the clip flatters the very overconfidence the metric was supposed to expose.

An attention mask fills padded positions with -inf; a row that is entirely padding makes max(z) = -inf, so z - max is nan inside softmax, the loss becomes nan at a random step deep into training, and the incident is filed for two days as a corrupt data shard.

A nearest-neighbour or RAG retrieval computes squared distances in float32 via the ||x||^2 - 2xy + ||y||^2 expansion on high-magnitude embeddings; cancellation leaves the small true distances as rounding noise, the returned neighbours are wrong but plausible, and the retrieval quality drop is blamed on the embedding model.

A gradient check passes because np.allclose's default atol=1e-8 declares an analytic gradient of 1e-9 equal to a numeric gradient of 3e-9; a whole branch of the backward pass is effectively dead, training converges to a worse optimum, and it is never revisited because there is a green test.
interviewQuestions: Derive the log-sum-exp trick and show it is an exact identity, not an approximation. Then tell me what happens when an entire row of logits is -inf, why that occurs in a padded transformer batch, and what you would change in the masking to fix it.

Your training loss goes 3.1, 3.0, 2.9 and then nan at step 4000. Walk me through your triage in order, and say which candidate causes would show up in the forward activations, which only in the backward pass, and which in the data loader - and how you would tell them apart with evidence rather than intuition.

Why can var = mean(x^2) - mean(x)^2 return a negative number in float64? Write the Welford update on the whiteboard, tell me what M2 is, and extend it to a merge formula so I can compute the variance of a 400 GB dataset in parallel chunks.

A customer's linear model gives different coefficients from ours on the same data. Their code solves the normal equations, ours calls np.linalg.lstsq. Explain what the condition number of X has to do with it, how many digits each approach retains, and what you would tell them to change in their feature preparation.

Here is a Python loop that computes pairwise distances over 50000 rows of 100 features. Rewrite it as a broadcast NumPy expression, tell me the peak memory before you run it, then tell me why the fast gemm-based version is numerically dangerous in float32 and what you would do instead.

The same script on my laptop and on the customer's 64-core server agrees to only seven decimal places. Give me every mechanism that could explain that, say which ones are acceptable to ship, and describe how you would pin the ones that are not.
When is vectorising a loop the wrong move? Give me two concrete situations, and tell me how you would benchmark to make that case to a teammate who believes all loops are bugs.
99.proofOfWork: A public `numerics-triage-kit` repo that turns the from-scratch library into something you can run on a customer's box during an incident. It ships `nan_hunt.py`, a drop-in that registers forward hooks asserting torch.isfinite on every module output, records the first offending (step, module, batch_index), dumps that batch to disk, and then re-runs exactly that batch under torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly to print the backward operator responsible - demonstrated on three deliberately planted bugs (a sqrt-at-zero norm, an all -inf masked attention row, and an fp16 activation overflow that only appears under autocast). It adds `precision_audit.py`, which takes any NumPy or pandas table and reports per-column the magnitude, the resolution at that magnitude, whether the column survives a float32 round-trip (integer collisions above 2^24, timestamps quantised to 128-second steps), and the condition number of the resulting design matrix with the digit-loss estimate spelled out in plain English for the customer's data engineer. `vectorisation_ladder.ipynb` takes one real preprocessing task up five rungs - Python loop, list comprehension, naive broadcast, out=/in-place fused, chunked with a Welford accumulator - with a predicted-versus-measured table of wall time (minimum of timeit.repeat) and peak memory (tracemalloc), including at least one rung where the prediction was wrong and a written explanation of why. Finally `STABILITY-CHECKLIST.md` is a one-page review sheet a customer's team can apply to their own code: no log without a stable form, no exp without a max subtraction, no variance without Welford, no float32 reduction without a float64 accumulator, no inverse where a factorisation exists, no float equality assertion, and np.errstate set to raise in every test suite. CI runs the whole thing on every push and fails if any naive-versus-stable regression test stops failing on the naive path.
